“Edith,” said Margaret again, softly, as if a quieter syllable might coax wakefulness without breaking it. “Edith!”

But Edith had slipped away from speech as easily as a ribbon slides from a careless knot. Curled upon the crimson damask sofa in the back drawing-room of Harley Street, she lay in white muslin and blue bows, the very picture of a delicate creature who belonged more to a painted tale than to a London house that smelt, faintly and continually, of lamps and polished wood and the last course of dinner. If Titania had ever been fashioned for a Season—white muslin instead of gossamer, blue ribbons instead of dew—she might have looked as Edith looked now, asleep with her lips slightly parted, her silken curls loosened by the warmth of the room.

Margaret watched her cousin’s face as if she had only lately learned how to see it. They had grown up side by side; Edith’s prettiness had been remarked on by everyone except Margaret, who had taken it for granted like daylight. But in these last days—these days measured out by fittings and visits and lists—beauty had acquired an edge, as things do when one is about to lose them. Edith was to be married; the word had been spoken so often that it had begun to sound less like a promise and more like a summons, calling them all to hurry.

Before Edith’s drowsiness had deepened, they had been whispering of wedding dresses and the arrangement of lace, of what Captain Lennox had told her about Corfu—its sea-wind and white glare, its quarters that were to be home—and, with equal seriousness, of the difficulty of keeping a piano in tune in such a place, as if the strings’ obedience were the chief safeguard of married happiness. They had planned Scotland after the wedding: what gowns would do, what cloaks, what colours Edith could bear. Then the talk had softened, thinned, and fallen away; and now Margaret, with no listener, found herself turning inward to her own change.

She had been on the verge of speaking of Helstone—the country parsonage where her father and mother lived, where her happiest holidays had always been passed, though for ten years Harley Street had been called her home. In place of speech she had silence; in place of Edith’s answers she had the hum of another room.

From the front drawing-room drifted the sound of women’s voices: a cultivated ripple, now rising, now sinking, threaded through with the occasional sharp bark of laughter. Mrs. Shaw was entertaining the five or six ladies who had dined there, their husbands still lingering below among the deeper sounds of male conversation and wine. These were the familiar neighbours of the house; friends, in Mrs. Shaw’s sense—people with whom one exchanged dinners and favours, and for whom one did not scruple to call before luncheon if there was anything to ask or anything to offer.

They had been invited in honour of Edith’s approaching marriage, to eat a farewell dinner. Edith had objected, for Captain Lennox was expected by a late train; but objection was not Edith’s talent for long. She yielded, as she always did, the more readily because her mother had ordered “those extra delicacies of the season” which London women believed capable of soothing any grief, provided it was properly fed. Edith had sat at dinner leaning back, playing with her food as if it were a set of toys, her mind absent and her face grave, while those around her enjoyed Mr. Grey’s pointed little sayings. Mr. Grey, who always took the bottom of Mrs. Shaw’s table, had been particularly agreeable; the gentlemen had stayed downstairs longer than usual—a mercy, judging by what Margaret caught through the doorway now.

“I suffered too much myself,” Mrs. Shaw’s voice said, soft and plaintive as a flute heard through a wall. “Not that I was not extremely happy with the poor dear General; but still, disparity of age is a drawback—one that I was resolved Edith should not have to encounter. Of course, without any maternal partiality, I foresaw that the dear child was likely to marry early. Indeed I had often said I was sure she would be married before she was nineteen. I had quite a prophetic feeling when Captain Lennox—” Her voice dropped to a whisper; Margaret could fill the rest as well as any of them.

The course of true love, in Edith’s case, had run smooth enough to look almost planned. Mrs. Shaw had “given way to the presentiment,” and had urged on the marriage though it was below the expectations others had formed for a young, pretty heiress. She declared her only child should marry for love, and sighed as if love had not figured in her own marriage to General Shaw. Mrs. Shaw enjoyed the romance far more than Edith did.

Not that Edith was not properly in love; she was. Still, she would have preferred a good house in Belgravia to all the picturesque makeshift Captain Lennox described in his soldier’s future. The very bits that made Margaret’s heart warm—camp talk, sudden moves, foreign rooms with bare floors and thin curtains—made Edith pretend to shiver, partly for the pleasure of being coaxed out of her dislikes, partly because she truly hated discomfort. And yet, had some splendid man come with title and estate and wide staircases and servants in livery, Edith would still have held to her Captain while the temptation lasted. Afterwards—when the glitter had passed—it was possible she might have felt a little prick of regret that her love could not have been attached to a person who united everything that was desirable. In this she was her mother’s child. Mrs. Shaw, who had married the General with respect rather than affection, had spent years quietly lamenting, with the air of one enduring a martyrdom, that she was bound to a man she could not love.

“I have spared no expense in her trousseau,” came Mrs. Shaw again. “She has all the beautiful Indian shawls and scarfs the General gave to me, but which I shall never wear again.”

“She is a lucky girl,” replied Mrs. Gibson, whose voice Margaret knew—quick, practical, with an edge of self-satisfaction. One of Mrs. Gibson’s daughters had been married within the last few weeks; she listened with a double ear, measuring Edith’s good fortune against her own. “Helen had set her heart upon an Indian shawl, but really when I found what an extravagant price was asked, I was obliged to refuse her. She will be quite envious when she hears of Edith having Indian shawls. What kind are they? Delhi? with the lovely little borders?”

Margaret heard her aunt’s tone change, as if Mrs. Shaw had turned her head toward the dimmer back room. “Edith! Edith!” she called; and then her voice sank again with a little sigh of fatigue, as though even raising it were an exertion that cost her.

Margaret stepped forward at once. “Edith is asleep, Aunt Shaw. Is it anything I can do?”

Every woman in the other room chimed in with “poor child!” at the news, as if sleep were a calamity and not a refuge. In Mrs. Shaw’s lap a minute dog—Tiny—began to bark, stirred up by the burst of pity as by a gust of wind.

“Hush, Tiny! you naughty little girl! You will waken your mistress.” Mrs. Shaw’s hand smoothed the dog’s glossy head. “It was only to ask Edith if she would tell Newton to bring down her shawls. Perhaps you would go, Margaret dear?”

Margaret went.

Up, up, to the old nursery at the very top of the house, where the air always felt thinner and the sounds from below grew faint—London’s endless clatter reduced to a distant breathing. Newton was there among boxes and tissue-paper, busy with the lace required for the wedding. The room held the smell of stored things: starch and old linen, and the faint metallic tang of pins. Margaret paused at the threshold, looking in.

This had been her first familiar room in Harley Street nine years ago, when she had been brought, untamed and bewildered, from the forest-like freedom of Helstone to share her cousin’s home, play, and lessons. She remembered the London nursery’s dimness—coal-darkened light at the window, and the rule of an austere, ceremonious nurse with hands as clean as her conscience, who was terrible about torn frocks. Margaret remembered that first tea up here, separate from her father and aunt, who were dining somewhere down below at what seemed, to her childish mind, an immeasurable depth of stairs—as if, unless she were up in the sky, they must be far down in the bowels of the earth.

At home, in the country parsonage, her mother’s dressing-room had been her nursery. They kept early hours there; Margaret had always eaten with her father and mother. The contrast had wounded like a sudden cold. Even now, tall and stately at eighteen, she could recall the wild tears of nine-year-old grief, smothered under bedclothes that first night; could hear the nurse bidding her not to cry because it would disturb Miss Edith; could feel the child forcing her sobs into silence until her newly-seen grand aunt had come softly upstairs with Mr. Hale to show him his little sleeping daughter.

She had hushed herself then, lying as if asleep, for fear of making her father unhappy. She had not dared to show grief before her aunt; she had even half believed it wrong to feel sorrow after all the long hoping and planning and contriving at Helstone—after the careful arranging of her wardrobe to suit grander circumstances, after papa’s leaving his parish to come up to London even for a few days.

Now she had come to love this old nursery, dismantled as it was. The idea of leaving it for ever in three days touched her with a kind of cat-like regret, an instinctive clutching at what had sheltered her.

“Ah, Newton,” she said, “I think we shall all be sorry to leave this dear old room.”

“Indeed, miss, I shan’t for one,” Newton replied, tugging at a length of lace with practised fingers. “My eyes are not so good as they were, and the light here is so bad I can’t see to mend laces except just at the window, where there’s always a shocking draught—enough to give one one’s death of cold.”

“Well, I dare say you will have both good light and plenty of warmth at Naples,” Margaret said. “You must keep as much of your darning as you can till then. Thank you, Newton; I can take them down—you’re busy.”

Newton went, not without a muttered grumble, to undo the shawls which had already been produced and admired four or five times that day. When she returned, she handed Margaret a pile of soft, heavy folds.

Margaret carried them down carefully, the weight warm against her arms. As she descended, she drew in their scent: not London’s soot and beeswax polish, but something spiced and dry and far-travelled—like cedar chests and sun-baked markets, like pepper and sandalwood crushed together in memory. The smell rose each time the fabric shifted, as if the shawls themselves breathed out a foreign heat.

In the drawing-room her aunt asked her to stand as a lay figure on which to display them, since Edith still slept.

No one remarked on it, but Margaret’s tall, finely made figure in her plain black silk—mourning for some distant relative of her father’s—set off the gorgeous folds far better than Edith’s slight form would have done. The shawls would have half-smothered Edith; on Margaret they hung in long, splendid lines, colour deepening under the chandelier’s light—ruby and ochre and indigo, patterned with minute borders that seemed like writing in a language the eye could almost, but not quite, read.

Margaret stood silent and passive while her aunt adjusted the draperies. Occasionally, as she was turned, she caught her own reflection in the mirror over the chimney-piece: the familiar face framed by foreign splendour, a princess costume laid over a parson’s daughter. She smiled at the sight—quietly, as a child smiles when allowed to dress up—then touched the fabric with her fingertips, enjoying its softness, its coolness where it lay in shade, the slight roughness where the weave grew denser. She liked, without vanity, the sensation of beauty laid upon her.

At that moment the door opened, and Mr. Henry Lennox was announced.

Some of the ladies started back as if caught in a guilty pleasure, half ashamed of their absorbed interest in dress. Mrs. Shaw held out her hand to the new-comer. Margaret remained very still, thinking she might still be wanted as a block for the shawls, but she looked at Mr. Lennox with a bright, amused face, sure of his sympathy in the ridiculousness of being surprised in such an occupation.

Her aunt was absorbed at once in questions—about his brother the bridegroom, his sister Janet coming from Scotland to be bridesmaid, and various other members of the Lennox family. Margaret saw she was no longer required as shawl-bearer and began to attend, instead, to the other visitors her aunt had forgotten.

Almost immediately Edith came in from the back room, winking and blinking at the stronger light. She shook back her slightly ruffled curls and looked, all at once, like the Sleeping Beauty startled from dreams into ceremony. Even asleep, it seemed, she had instinctively understood that a Lennox was worth waking for.

She began at once with a multitude of questions about dear Janet—the future unseen sister-in-law for whom Edith professed such eager affection that, had Margaret been less proud, she might have felt a flicker of jealousy at the speed with which a stranger could be welcomed. As Margaret sank a little into the background, she saw Henry Lennox’s eyes go toward the vacant chair near her; and she knew, as certainly as if he had spoken, that he meant to sit there as soon as Edith loosed him from questioning.

She had not been sure he would come that night. It was a pleasant surprise; and with it came the sense of a pleasant evening. He liked and disliked nearly what she did. Her face brightened into honest openness.

By-and-by he came to her.

She received him with a smile that held no shyness, no self-consciousness. It was the smile of someone who was glad of an equal mind near at hand.

“Well,” he said, settling himself, “I suppose you are all in the depth of business—ladies’ business, I mean. Very different to my business, which is the real true law business. Playing with shawls is very different work to drawing up settlements.”

“Ah, I knew how you would be amused to find us so occupied in admiring finery,” Margaret answered. “But really Indian shawls are very perfect things of their kind.”

“I have no doubt they are,” he said. “Their prices are very perfect too. Nothing wanting.”

The gentlemen began to drop in one by one; the room’s sound thickened, voices overlapping like the layers of a city street. Even here, behind curtains and polish, the world had its own noise—London’s perpetual buzz finding its way into every pause.

“This is your last dinner-party, is it not?” Mr. Lennox asked. “There are no more before Thursday?”

“No. I think after this evening we shall feel at rest—at least, that kind of rest when the hands have nothing more to do, and all the arrangements are complete for an event which must occupy one’s head and heart. I shall be glad to have time to think, and I am sure Edith will.”

“I am not so sure about her,” he said, “but I can fancy that you will. Whenever I have seen you lately, you have been carried away by a whirlwind of some other person’s making.”

“Yes,” Margaret replied, and sadness shaded her voice. The month’s commotion about trifles—visits, lists, tries-on, consultations over effect—pressed upon her suddenly with a tired weight. “I wonder if a marriage must always be preceded by what you call a whirlwind, or whether in some cases there might not rather be a calm and peaceful time just before it.”

“Cinderella’s godmother ordering the trousseau, the wedding-breakfast, writing the notes of invitation, for instance,” he said, laughing.

“But are all these quite necessary troubles?” Margaret asked, looking straight up at him. She wanted, truly, some quiet idea of marriage—something that belonged to real life and not to show.

“Oh, of course,” he replied, and his tone sobered. “There are forms and ceremonies to be gone through, not so much to satisfy oneself, as to stop the world’s mouth—without which stoppage there would be very little satisfaction in life. But how would you have a wedding arranged?”

“Oh, I have never thought much about it,” she said, “only I should like it to be a very fine summer morning; and I should like to walk to church through the shade of trees; and not to have so many bridesmaids, and to have no wedding-breakfast. I dare say I am resolving against the very things that have given me the most trouble just now.”

“No, I don’t think you are,” he said. “The idea of stately simplicity accords well with your character.”

Margaret did not like that; it pricked her, not because it was unkind, but because it slid too easily into that familiar way of his—trying to draw her into talk about herself, with himself as the interpreter. She cut it short.

“It is natural for me to think of Helstone church, and the walk to it, rather than of driving up to a London church in the middle of a paved street.”

“Tell me about Helstone,” he said. “You have never described it to me. I should like to have some idea of the place you will be living in, when ninety-six Harley Street will be looking dingy and dirty, and dull, and shut up. Is Helstone a village, or a town, in the first place?”

“Oh, only a hamlet; I don’t think I could call it a village at all. There is the church and a few houses near it on the green—cottages, rather—with roses growing all over them.”

“And flowering all the year round, especially at Christmas—make your picture complete,” he said.

“No,” Margaret replied, annoyance sharpening her words. “I am not making a picture. I am trying to describe Helstone as it really is. You should not have said that.”

“I am penitent,” he answered. “Only it really sounded like a village in a tale rather than in real life.”

“And so it is,” Margaret said eagerly, her eyes lighting. “All the other places in England that I have seen seem so hard and prosaic-looking after the New Forest. Helstone is like a village in a poem—in one of Tennyson’s poems. But I won’t try and describe it any more. You would only laugh at me if I told you what I think of it—what it really is.”

“Indeed, I would not. But I see you are going to be very resolved.” He paused, then added, “Well, then, tell me that which I should like still better to know: what the parsonage is like.”

“Oh, I can’t describe my home,” she said. “It is home, and I can’t put its charm into words.”

“I submit. You are rather severe to-night, Margaret.”

“How?” She turned those large soft eyes full upon him, surprised into openness. “I did not know I was.”

“Why, because I made an unlucky remark, you will neither tell me what Helstone is like, nor will you say anything about your home, though I have told you how much I want to hear about both—the latter especially.”

“But indeed I cannot tell you about my own home,” she said. “I don’t quite think it is a thing to be talked about, unless you knew it.”

“Well, then,” he said, after a moment, “tell me what you do there. Here you read, or have lessons, or otherwise improve your mind, till the middle of the day; take a walk before lunch, go a drive with your aunt after, and have some kind of engagement in the evening. There, now fill up your day at Helstone. Shall you ride, drive, or walk?”

“Walk, decidedly. We have no horse—not even for papa. He walks to the very extremity of his parish. The walks are so beautiful, it would be a shame to drive—almost a shame to ride.”

“Shall you garden much? That, I believe, is a proper employment for young ladies in the country.”

“I don’t know. I am afraid I shan’t like such hard work.”

“Archery parties—picnics—race balls—hunt balls?”

“Oh no!” She laughed. “Papa’s living is very small; and even if we were near such things, I doubt if I should go to them.”

“I see,” he said. “You won’t tell me anything. You will only tell me that you are not going to do this and that. Before the vacation ends, I think I shall pay you a call, and see what you really do employ yourself in.”

“I hope you will,” Margaret answered. “Then you will see for yourself how beautiful Helstone is. Now I must go. Edith is sitting down to play, and I just know enough of music to turn over the leaves for her; and, besides, Aunt Shaw won’t like us to talk.”

Edith did sit down to play, and played brilliantly—her fingers swift and sure, her face turned a little upward as if to catch applause in advance. Margaret stood by to turn the leaves, listening not so much to the melody as to the way the room changed under it: the talk subdued, the feet stilled, the very air seeming to arrange itself around sound. For a moment the house held a kind of order that London noise seldom allowed—music making a clearing, as a wind makes a clearing in smoke.

In the middle of the piece the door half-opened. Edith’s eyes flew there; she saw Captain Lennox hesitating on the threshold. The music stopped at once. She flung down the sheets and rushed out, leaving Margaret with her hands still lifted, caught mid-duty, blushing and confused. The guests stared; Margaret had to explain, stumbling a little, what vision had appeared to cause Edith’s sudden flight.

Captain Lennox had come earlier than expected—or was it really so late? Watches were drawn out; exclamations followed; people were properly shocked at the hour and took their leave with hurried politeness.

Then Edith came back, glowing, half shy and half proud, leading in her tall handsome Captain as if she were bringing a prize into a room that had been waiting for it. His brother shook hands with him. Mrs. Shaw welcomed him in her gentle, kindly way that always carried something plaintive in it—an echo of long habit, of years spent considering herself a victim to an uncongenial marriage. Now the General was dead, she had ease and money and freedom with very few drawbacks; yet she had been perplexed to find herself anxious all the same. Of late she had settled on her own health as a suitable source of apprehension, and produced a nervous little cough whenever she thought of it. A complaisant doctor had ordered precisely what she desired: a winter in Italy.

Mrs. Shaw had wishes as strong as most people’s, but she disliked doing anything from the open motive of her own pleasure. She preferred to be compelled into gratification by another person’s command or necessity; it enabled her to moan in her soft manner while taking what she wanted. In this way she began to speak of her journey to Captain Lennox, who assented, as duty required, though his eyes were always seeking Edith.

Edith, meanwhile, was at the tea-table, rearranging it with bright importance, ordering up all sorts of good things in spite of her lover’s assurances that he had dined within the last two hours. She was determined to show how well she could behave as a soldier’s wife—competent, bustling, cheerful in a way that looked, to her, like courage.

Mr. Henry Lennox stood leaning against the chimney-piece, amused by the family scene. Close beside his handsome brother, he seemed the plain one in a singularly good-looking family; but his face was intelligent, keen, and mobile. Margaret wondered, now and then, what thoughts moved behind his silence. He observed everything with an interest that had a faintly sarcastic edge—called out, perhaps, by Mrs. Shaw’s plaintive self-portrayal—separate from the warmer interest awakened by what he saw.

He thought it pretty, the sight of the two cousins busying themselves about cups and plates, sugar and cream, napkins folded just so. Domestic ritual had its own gravity. It was all very well to speak of Corfu and Scotland and Naples; it was here, in the small acts of serving and arranging, that women were trained into the shape of their futures.

Edith chose to do most herself. She discovered the water in the urn was cold and ordered up the great kitchen tea-kettle. The consequence was that, meeting it at the door and insisting on carrying it, she found it too heavy. She came in pouting, with a black mark on her muslin gown and a little round white hand indented by the handle. She held it up to Captain Lennox like a hurt child; and the remedy was as inevitable as in childhood—his quick taking of her hand, his murmured concern, her pleasure in being fussed over.

Margaret, more practical, set up a spirit-lamp with swift quiet skill. The flame steadied under the kettle, heat gathering without commotion—an effective contrivance, though not at all like the gypsy encampment Edith sometimes declared to be the nearest resemblance to barrack life. Still, the water warmed; tea was made; the room filled with the scent of it—dark, comforting, familiar—rising into the overlay of Eastern spice from the shawls and the faint lemony bite of wax and polish.

After that evening, all was bustle until the wedding was over.

Margaret sat again in the plain morning gown that belonged to Helstone rather than to Harley Street, the cloth softened by many washings, the seams mended with a thrift that tried to look like choice. The train carried her south, and with it the last confused taste of London—hot rooms, trampled carpets, the sharp scent of crushed flowers from bridal nosegays, and that sickly sweetness of sugared almonds that lingers on the tongue long after one has ceased to be hungry.

Her father was with her. He had come up to London for the wedding, and now returned as quietly as he had gone, as if he would rather slip back into parish lanes and familiar hedges than be seen in any public triumph. Her mother had stayed behind at home, kept there by a tangle of little reasons that did not quite make a cord strong enough to bind her, and yet somehow did. Margaret only knew that “it was not convenient.” Mr. Hale knew more: he had pleaded, with the tender logic he used when he wished not to wound, for a grey satin gown—neither new enough to pretend, nor old enough to confess poverty—and his pleading had fallen harmlessly to the floor. There was not money to clothe Mrs. Hale afresh from head to foot; so she would not go, not even to see her only sister’s only child married.

If Mrs. Shaw had guessed the true cause, she would have tossed gowns at Maria as easily as she tossed bonbons to children, for she had long since forgotten what it was to want. Nearly twenty years had smoothed away every grievance except the one she cherished as a kind of elegant sorrow—how unhappy a woman must be when her husband is much older than herself. She could speak of that disparity for half an hour without drawing breath, because it did not touch her own life. Dearest Maria, in Mrs. Shaw’s memory, had married for love, and what else could such a woman desire? Blue-black hair that one seldom saw, a sweet temper, a delightful preacher of a husband; from these she made her usual, careless conclusion: “Married for love, what can dearest Maria have to wish for in this world?” Mrs. Hale, had she spoken truth, might have answered with a housewifely, humiliating exactness—silk of such a shade, a bonnet of such a make, the small decent things that make a woman fit to show herself among others; and then the hundreds of small decent things that make a house feel like more than a shelter.

Margaret, for her part, was not sorry that the first meeting should be in the quiet of the parsonage rather than in the fever of Harley Street. In London she had been wanted everywhere at once—hands for tying ribbons, eyes for missing parcels, ears for last-minute messages; she had been like a servant and a manager and a daughter all together. Now, with the carriage rocking and the rail rhythm drumming beneath, her mind and body ached in the after-sense of those forty-eight hours. The good-byes, hurriedly pressed in between other good-byes, came back upon her with a slow weight. It scarcely mattered whether the past had been happy; it had been hers, and it was gone. And oddly—almost shamefully—her heart felt heaviest at the thought of going home, to the place she had longed for through London summers and London winters. Homesickness is sometimes sharpest at the moment of return, like hunger when the bread is already in the hand.

She wrenched herself away from memory and forced her eyes upon what was before her. Her father slept in the corner of the carriage, his head a little fallen back. The blue-black hair of which Mrs. Shaw was still fond of speaking had gone thin and grey across his brows. The bones of his face showed too plainly, but the fineness of the lines saved him from harshness. In sleep there should have been peace; yet his repose looked like rest after weariness, not the calm of an untroubled spirit. Margaret, watching, was struck with a kind of pain at the anxious grooves about the mouth and the brow.

“Poor Frederick,” she thought, and the thought came as naturally as the sigh that followed it. If only Frederick had been a clergyman, safe at home and vexing no law but a bishop’s preference! If only he had never gone to sea; never been swallowed, as it were, by that “terrible affair” of which she had heard in fragments and never understood. Aunt Shaw’s explanations had been all vapour—much display, little substance—until the whole story had sunk under a soft blanket of silence. Frederick could not come back to England; that was all. “Poor dear papa,” she thought, glancing again at the worn face. “I am so glad I am going home—to be near him and mamma.”

When he woke she was ready with a smile bright enough to cheat him into believing she had no fatigue. He returned it, faintly, as if smiling were now an effort that cost him, and almost immediately the habitual lines drew back into place. He had a trick of half-opening his mouth as if he meant to speak, and then not speaking; it gave him an air of indecision that did not belong to his real gentleness of purpose. His eyes were like Margaret’s—large, soft, slowly moving, as if they looked not only at objects but through them; the transparent white lids made them seem more tender still.

Margaret resembled him more than her mother. People sometimes wondered that two such handsome parents had a daughter who was not regularly beautiful—“not beautiful at all,” some would say when they wished to be decisive. Her mouth was wide, not a rosebud mouth trained for “yes” and “no” and “an’t please you, sir”; but the wideness was a softness, a curve of rich red lips that could kindle into laughter or set itself in resolve. Her skin was not the pale fairness that passes for delicacy, yet it had an ivory smoothness and fineness. Often her face looked too grave for youth; but now, talking to her father, it brightened into dimples and eager glances, like morning breaking through cloud.

It was late July when she returned to Helstone. The forest stood in one deep, full, dusky green; the ferns beneath caught slanting shafts of sun and held them like gilt upon their fronds. The air was sultry, broodingly still, as if the whole place listened. The soundscape of Helstone wrapped itself about Margaret with the first step out of the station and into the lane: bees worrying the foxglove bells, a pigeon’s slow complaint from somewhere high in the beech, the thin hiss of wind in grass, and—most dear of all—the quietness between sounds, the spaces of country silence that London never allows. Even the vicarage kitchen, with its clink of china and the low murmur of Dixon’s instructions, seemed to speak a language of home.

Margaret tramped by her father’s side along the forest paths, crushing the ferns with a child’s cruel glee as they yielded under her light foot and sent up their peculiar fragrance—green, resinous, and damp as if the earth itself had been bruised to show its juice. Out on the broad commons the warm light smelled of sun on heather, of dry dust and distant hay. Creatures—wild, free, living—revelled in it all: a lark flung itself into the sky on a thread of song; rabbits flashed white tails into the gorse; an unseen stream talked steadily over stones.

These walks were everything she had anticipated. She took a pride in her forest as in a possession, not in the sense of owning it, but of belonging to it. Its people were her people. She made hearty friends with them; learned their peculiar words and delighted in trying them upon her tongue, feeling how a dialect is not merely different sounds but a different way of tasting experience. In Harley Street one ate what one was served and spoke as one was expected; in Helstone she could carry bread and broth to a sick cottager, and the very names of herbs and household things—given in the old local speech—seemed to keep some half-vanishing history alive.

She took up her freedom amongst them: nursed their babies with steady arms, read aloud slowly and distinctly to the old people who could not see well, and carried “dainty messes” to the sick—simple dishes made with care, as if tenderness were an ingredient. A pot of broth rich with a marrow-bone and garden onions; a rice pudding baked until the top browned and crackled like thin toffee; a little currant tea when fever made water taste metallic. Dixon would scold about the waste of eggs, but Margaret knew how food could comfort in the way words failed. She resolved that before long she would teach at the school where her father went every day as if it were an appointed duty; but she was continually tempted away by news of some individual friend—man, woman, or child—in some cottage deep in the green shade.

Her out-of-doors life was perfect. Her in-doors life had thorns.

With the healthy shame of youth, she blamed herself for seeing that all was not as it should be within the vicarage walls. Her mother—her mother who was always kind and tender to her—seemed now and then restless, dissatisfied, as if every chair pinched and every view from a window reminded her of something she did not possess. Mrs. Hale thought the bishop strangely neglected his episcopal duties in not giving Mr. Hale a better living. She almost reproached her husband because he could not bring himself to say that he wished to leave Helstone for a larger parish.

Mr. Hale would sigh aloud and answer, gently, that if he could do what he ought in little Helstone he should be thankful; but every day he felt more overpowered, the world more bewildering. At each repeated urgency from his wife, Margaret saw her father shrink a little further inward, as if preferment were not simply ambition but a test he feared he might fail. When the tension rose, Margaret tried to reconcile her mother to Helstone—praising the air, the trees, the sense of sheltered peace.

But Mrs. Hale complained that the near neighbourhood of so many trees affected her health. Margaret, sure that her mother had grown too much into an indoor creature, tried to tempt her out on the broad upland common, where sun-streaks and cloud-shadows chased one another over the grass. For a time it did good; the fresh wind carried away the scent of closed rooms and the small irritations that grow in them. Yet as autumn approached and weather turned uncertain, her mother’s idea of Helstone’s unhealthiness increased. She repined more frequently that her husband—more learned than Mr. Hume, a better parish priest than Mr. Houldsworth—had met with no preferment as those former neighbours had done.

This constant discontent was what Margaret had not prepared herself for. She had expected to give up luxuries and thought she could do it proudly; indeed, she had sometimes revelled in the notion that she would be free of the trammels of Harley Street. Her senses were keenly alive to pleasure—the scent of wet earth, the taste of warm bread with fresh-churned butter—but her pride balanced it: she could do without, if need were. Yet the cloud came from a quarter she had not watched: not from want of things, but from the unquiet of hearts.

In September the rains and storms came. Margaret was forced to remain more within doors. Helstone lay far from neighbours of their own education and habits. “It is undoubtedly one of the most out-of-the-way places in England,” Mrs. Hale said one day in her plaintive tone, as if the remoteness were a personal injury.

“I can’t help regretting constantly that papa has really no one to associate with here; he is so thrown away—seeing no one but farmers and labourers from week’s end to week’s end. If we lived at the other side of the parish it would be something; we should be almost within walking distance of the Stansfields; certainly the Gormons would be within a walk.”

“Gormons,” Margaret repeated, tasting the name as if it were something bought and sold. “Are those the Gormons who made their fortunes in trade at Southampton? Oh, I’m glad we don’t visit them. I don’t like shoppy people. I think we are far better off knowing only cottagers and labourers, and people without pretence.”

“You must not be so fastidious, Margaret, dear,” said her mother—who, in spite of her reproving voice, remembered a young and handsome Mr. Gormon she had once seen.

“No! I call mine a very comprehensive taste,” Margaret returned, with the quick certainty of youth. “I like all people whose occupations have to do with land. I like soldiers and sailors, and the three learned professions. I’m sure you don’t want me to admire butchers and bakers and candlestick-makers, do you, mamma?”

“But the Gormons were neither butchers nor bakers, but very respectable coach-builders.”

“Very well. Coach-building is a trade all the same—and I think a much more useless one than that of butchers or bakers. Oh, how tired I used to be of the drives every day in Aunt Shaw’s carriage, and how I longed to walk!”

And walk Margaret did, in spite of weather. When she got out, with her father beside her, the wind and the wet seemed only part of the country’s speech. With the soft violence of the west wind behind her as she crossed a heath, she felt borne onward like a fallen leaf, light and willing. She listened, too, with a kind of fierce gratitude, to the clean sounds of Helstone even in storm: rain knitting itself into the thatch, gusts combing the bare branches, the far-off answering call of rooks. London’s noise had been an unceasing battering—wheels on stone, shouted names, music hired for show. Here every sound belonged, and because it belonged it soothed. Margaret could not help thinking, when her mother complained of the place’s “unhealthiness,” that it was not the trees but the inner fretting that made breathing difficult.

Yet evenings were hard. Immediately after tea—tea that Dixon made strong and fragrant, as if it could warm the spirit as well as the hands—Mr. Hale withdrew to his small library, and mother and daughter were left alone in the drawing-room. Mrs. Hale had never cared much for books; early in their married life she had discouraged her husband’s wish to read aloud while she worked, preferring talk that turned, inevitably, upon people and prospects. Once they had tried backgammon, but as Mr. Hale grew more involved with school and parishioners, interruptions came; and Mrs. Hale regarded these calls as hardships, not as the natural conditions of his office. So, while the children were still young, he had retreated into his library to spend his evenings—if he were at home—among speculative and metaphysical books that fed some hunger of his mind.

When Margaret had been at Helstone in earlier days, she had brought down a great box of books recommended by masters or governess, and found summer days too short for all she meant to read. Now there were only the well-bound, little-read English classics weeded from her father’s shelves to fill the small bookcase in the drawing-room. Thomson’s Seasons, Hayley’s Cowper, Middleton’s Cicero—these were by far the lightest and newest and most amusing. The shelves offered scant resource.

So Margaret told her mother the particulars of her London life. Mrs. Hale listened with interest, sometimes amused and questioning, sometimes sliding into comparisons—how easily her sister lived, how narrowly they managed at Helstone. At such moments Margaret would stop rather abruptly and listen to the drip-drip of rain upon the leads of the little bow window. The sound was so steady it seemed to count out time. Once or twice she found herself mechanically counting it, as if numbers could give her courage to venture a question that lay near her heart: Where was Frederick now? What was he doing? How long since they had heard?

But each time she approached the subject, she turned away. A consciousness haunted her that her mother’s delicate health and her positive dislike to Helstone dated from the time of the mutiny in which Frederick had been engaged—a story Margaret had never heard whole, and which seemed doomed to be buried in a sad oblivion. When she was with her mother she thought her father the best one to ask; when with her father she felt she might speak more easily to her mother. So the question remained always one room away, one moment too late.

Perhaps there was nothing new to know. Before leaving Harley Street, Margaret had received a letter from her father: they had heard from Frederick; he was still at Rio, well in health, and sent his best love. Dry bones of information, not the living intelligence she yearned for. Frederick’s name, when spoken at all, was accompanied by the same phrase, like a refrain: “Poor Frederick.”

His room was kept exactly as he had left it. Dixon—Mrs. Hale’s maid, who touched no other part of household work—went in regularly to dust and order it. Dixon always remembered, with the stiff pride of long service, the day when she had been engaged by Lady Beresford as ladies’ maid to Sir John’s wards, the pretty Miss Beresfords, the belles of Rutlandshire. She had never forgiven Mr. Hale for being, in her view, the blight upon her young lady’s prospects. If Miss Beresford had not been in such a hurry to marry a poor country clergyman, there was no knowing what she might have become. Yet Dixon was too loyal to desert her in what she considered affliction and downfall—alas, her married life. She remained, devoted to her mistress’s interests, considering herself the good protecting fairy whose business it was to baffle the malignant giant, Mr. Hale.

Master Frederick had been Dixon’s favourite and pride. When she entered his room with cloth and brush, her dignified look softened; she arranged everything weekly as carefully as if he might come home that very evening. The room smelled faintly of lavender and aired linen, of closed drawers and old paper—like stored time.

Margaret could not help believing there had been some late intelligence of Frederick, unknown to her mother, which made her father anxious and uneasy. Mrs. Hale did not seem to notice any alteration in her husband’s looks or ways. Mr. Hale had always been tender in spirits, easily depressed by what he saw or heard of others’ suffering—he would be cast down for days after a death-bed, or after hearing of any crime. But now Margaret noticed in him an absence of mind, as if his thoughts were held fast by some subject that could not be relieved by the daily actions of a clergyman: comforting survivors, teaching children, hoping to lessen evils in the next generation. He went out among his parishioners less than usual. He shut himself in his study more. He grew anxious for the village postman.

The postman’s summons was a rap on the back-kitchen window shutter. Once it had often to be repeated before anyone in the house roused themselves to attend. Now Mr. Hale would loiter in the garden if the morning was fine, and if not he would stand dreamily by the study window until the rap came—or until the postman had already gone down the lane. Margaret would sometimes hear the retreating footsteps in the wet gravel, the little click of the gate, and then, a moment later, her father’s hurried movement, too late. If he did catch sight of the man going past the sweet-briar hedge and the great arbutus, he would give a half-respectful, half-confidential shake of the head, as if they shared some knowledge that could not be spoken. Then he would turn back into his room with all the signs of a heavy heart and an occupied mind.

Margaret was at an age when apprehensions not grounded in facts can be blown away for a time by a bright day. When, after the storms, fourteen brilliant fine days of October came, her cares lifted like thistledown. She thought of nothing but the glories of the forest. The fern-harvest was over, and now that rain had withdrawn, many a deep glade became accessible into which she had only peeped during July and August. She had learnt drawing with Edith, and during the long wet weeks had regretted her idle revelling in beauty while the weather was fine; so she determined to sketch what she could before winter set in.

One morning she was busy preparing her board—paper smoothed and fixed, pencils sorted, a little cake of colour ready to be wetted—when Sarah, the housemaid, threw wide the drawing-room door and announced, with a formality that made the moment ring as distinct as a spoon against a cup,

“Mr. Henry Lennox.”

“The More Haste the Worse Speed.”

Margaret had been thinking of Henry Lennox only an instant before—of his quick, half-amused questions in Harley Street, and the way he had asked what she did with her hours now that London was laid aside. It was as if speaking of sun had brought its warmth at once: when Sarah announced him, a brightness ran over Margaret’s face; she set down her work and went forward with both hands held out.

“Tell mamma, Sarah,” she said. “Mamma and I want to ask you so many questions about Edith; I am so much obliged to you for coming.”

“Did not I say that I should?” he answered; and though his words were simple enough, his voice dropped into a lower key, as if they were suddenly alone in the room.

“But we heard of you so far away in the Highlands that I never thought Hampshire could come in.”

“Oh,” he replied lightly, “our young couple were playing such foolish pranks—running all sorts of risks, climbing this mountain, sailing on that lake—that I really thought they needed a Mentor. Indeed they did. They were quite beyond my uncle’s management, and kept the old gentleman in a panic for sixteen hours out of the twenty-four. When I once saw how unfit they were to be trusted alone, I thought it my duty not to leave them till I had seen them safely embarked at Plymouth.”

“Have you been at Plymouth? Oh! Edith never named that. To be sure, she has written in such a hurry lately. Did they really sail on Tuesday?”

“Really sailed, and relieved me from many responsibilities. Edith gave me all sorts of messages for you. I believe I have a little diminutive note somewhere—yes, here it is.”

Margaret’s fingers closed over the scrap as if it were something alive.

“Oh! thank you,” she exclaimed; and then, half wishing to read it unwatched, she made her excuse of going—again—to tell her mother (for Sarah must surely have mistaken) that Mr. Lennox was there.

When she left him, Henry Lennox did what was habitual with him: he took the measure of his surroundings as swiftly as he took the measure of men. The little drawing-room was at its best under the morning sun that streamed through the bow-window. One casement stood open; roses and scarlet honeysuckle leaned in as if they belonged indoors, and the small lawn beyond burned with bright geraniums and verbenas. Yet the very glory without made the colours within seem gentler, older—faded chintz that had been washed often, a carpet that had lived long past its first youth. It was a poorer frame than he had expected for Margaret—Margaret, with her queenly carriage and clear, steadfast eyes.

He picked up a book from the table. Dante—Paradiso—in old Italian vellum and gold; beside it a dictionary, and a list of words in Margaret’s handwriting. Dull words in themselves; and yet he lingered over them, liking the look of her careful strokes, the patient, almost reverent way she had netted meaning. He set them down with a sigh.

“The living is evidently as small as she said,” he thought. “Strange, for the Beresfords belong to a good family.”

Margaret had found her mother in one of Mrs. Hale’s fitful moods, when every common arrangement turned into an oppression. The very fact of a visitor—Edith’s brother-in-law, almost a relation—took the shape of a hardship, though under it a shy gratification trembled.

“It is most unfortunate!” Mrs. Hale said. “We are dining early, and having nothing but cold meat, in order that the servants may get on with their ironing; and yet, of course, we must ask him to dinner. And your papa is in such low spirits this morning about something—I don’t know what. I went into the study just now, and he had his face on the table, covering it with his hands. I told him I was sure Helstone air did not agree with him any more than with me, and he suddenly lifted up his head and begged me not to speak a word more against Helstone—he could not bear it; if there was one place he loved on earth it was Helstone. But I am sure, for all that, it is the damp and relaxing air.”

Margaret listened with the patience she always kept ready for her mother’s complaints; but as she heard of her father’s bowed head, it was as if a thin cold cloud had slid between her and the sun. Still she drew her mother gently back to what was needful.

“Papa likes Mr. Lennox; they got on together famously at the wedding breakfast. I daresay his coming will do papa good. And never mind the dinner, dear mamma. Cold meat will do capitally for a lunch—which is the light in which Mr. Lennox will most likely look upon a two o’clock dinner.”

“But what are we to do with him till then? It is only half-past ten now.”

“I’ll ask him to go out sketching with me. I know he draws, and that will take him out of your way, mamma. Only do come in now; he will think it so strange if you don’t.”

Mrs. Hale took off her black silk apron and smoothed her face into the pretty, lady-like composure that sat on her as naturally as a well-folded shawl. She greeted Mr. Lennox with cordiality due to one who was almost family. He evidently expected to be asked to spend the day, and accepted with a readiness so frank that it made Mrs. Hale wish—absurdly, remorsefully—that she could add something to the cold beef.

He was pleased with everything; delighted with Margaret’s idea of going out sketching; would not have Mr. Hale disturbed for the world, with the prospect of meeting him at dinner. Margaret brought out her drawing materials for him to choose from—paper, brushes, a little box of colours, the clean sharp scent of pencil-wood when she opened the case. After due selection, they set out with the merriest spirits in the world.

“Now, please, just stop here for a minute or two,” said Margaret. “These are the cottages that haunted me so during the rainy fortnight, reproaching me for not having sketched them.”

“Before they tumbled down and were no more seen,” he said. “Truly, if they are to be sketched—and they are very picturesque—we had better not put it off till next year. But where shall we sit?”

“Oh! you might have come straight from chambers in the Temple, instead of having been two months in the Highlands! Look at this beautiful trunk of a tree which the woodcutters have left just in the right place for the light. I will put my plaid over it, and it will be a regular forest throne.”

“With your feet in that puddle for a regal footstool! Stay—I will move, and then you can come nearer this way. Who lives in these cottages?”

“They were built by squatters fifty or sixty years ago. One is uninhabited; the foresters are going to take it down, as soon as the other is dead—poor old fellow! Look—there he is—I must go and speak to him. He is so deaf you will hear all our secrets.”

The old man stood bareheaded in the sun, leaning on his stick at the front of his cottage. His stiff features softened into a slow smile as Margaret went up and spoke to him—her voice pitched a little higher, not from condescension but from the instinct to send kindness across a failing sense. Even her steps altered; she moved as if she belonged to the place, as if these cottages and this old Isaac were part of her own history and would be part of it still when roofs had sunk and names been forgotten.

Henry Lennox, with the quick economy of a practised draughtsman, set the two figures into his sketch—lightly at first, as a subordinate incident—then with a subtle emphasis that betrayed itself only when they compared their work.

When at last Margaret came back—putting away the little slips of wet paper, tipping out the grey water from her brush-cup—she saw what he had done. She laughed, and blushed in the same breath.

“Now, I call that treacherous. I little thought you were making old Isaac and me into subjects when you told me to ask him the history of these cottages.”

“It was irresistible,” he answered. “You can’t know how strong a temptation it was. I hardly dare tell you how much I shall like this sketch.”

He was not quite sure whether she heard that last sentence before she went down to the brook to wash her palette; the water took the faint stains from her fingers, and the air smelt of wet earth and crushed fern. She came back rather flushed, but with a look perfectly innocent, unconscious—unaware of what her presence could do to another person’s mind. He was glad of that; the words had slipped from him unawares, a rare thing for one who so often premeditated his actions.

When they reached home, the aspect of it was all right and bright. The clouds on Mrs. Hale’s brow had cleared under the propitious influence of a brace of carp, most opportunely presented by a neighbour. The fish lay on a dish like two silvered torpedoes, their clean river-smell rising sharp and fresh; already Dixon’s footsteps sounded in brisk purpose, as if the kitchen had awakened into ceremony. Even the house seemed to breathe more freely for the promise of something hot, something properly cooked, instead of cold slices eaten in apology.

Mr. Hale had returned from his morning’s round and was awaiting his visitor just outside the wicket-gate. He looked a complete gentleman in his rather threadbare coat and well-worn hat. Margaret’s pride in him sprang up, fresh and tender as always; yet her quick eye travelled over his face and found traces of unusual disturbance—put aside, not cleared away.

Mr. Hale asked to look at their sketches.

“I think you have made the tints on the thatch too dark, have you not?” he said, returning Margaret’s and holding out his hand for Mr. Lennox’s, which was withheld from him one moment—no more.

“No, papa! I don’t think I have. The house-leek and stone-crop have grown so much darker in the rain. Is it not like, papa?” She peeped over his shoulder as he looked at the figures in Mr. Lennox’s drawing.

“Yes, very like. Your figure and way of holding yourself is capital. And it is just poor old Isaac’s stiff way of stooping his long rheumatic back. What is this hanging from the branch of the tree? Not a bird’s nest, surely.”

“Oh no! that is my bonnet. I never can draw with my bonnet on; it makes my head so hot. I wonder if I could manage figures. There are so many people about here whom I should like to sketch.”

“I should say that a likeness you very much wish to take you would always succeed in,” said Mr. Lennox. “I have great faith in the power of will. I think myself I have succeeded pretty well in yours.”

Mr. Hale had preceded them into the house while Margaret lingered to pluck some roses, meaning to fasten them at her throat and waist for dinner. The flowers were warm from the sun; their scent rose thick and sweet when her fingers bruised a leaf.

“A regular London girl would understand the implied meaning of that speech,” thought Henry Lennox. “She would be up to looking through every sentence a young man made her for the arrière-pensée of a compliment. But I don’t believe Margaret—Stay!” he exclaimed, suddenly. “Let me help you.”

He gathered for her some velvety cramoisy roses above her reach; then dividing the spoil, he placed two in his own button-hole, and sent her in pleased and happy to arrange her flowers.

At dinner, talk flowed quietly and agreeably. There were plenty of questions—news of Mrs. Shaw’s movements in Italy to exchange, scraps of travel, hints of Edith’s letters. In the interest of what was said, in the unpretending simplicity of the parsonage ways, and above all in the neighbourhood of Margaret, Mr. Lennox forgot the little disappointment of that morning—forgot the shabbiness he had noted, the smallness of the income she had spoken of so simply, as if money were merely another kind of weather.

“Margaret, my child,” said Mr. Hale, as a freshly-decanted bottle of wine was placed on the table with something of hospitable pride, “you might have gathered us some pears for our dessert.”

Mrs. Hale started, hurried. Desserts had the air of being impromptu and unusual things at the parsonage, though if Mr. Hale had only looked behind him he would have seen biscuits and marmalade and other little stored comforts arranged with formal care upon the sideboard. But the idea of pears had seized him and would not be dislodged.

“There are a few brown beurrés against the south wall,” he said, with the pleased insistence of a man clinging to the zest and perfection of an hour stolen from anxiety. “They are worth all foreign fruits and preserves. Run, Margaret, and gather some.”

“I propose that we adjourn into the garden, and eat them there,” said Mr. Lennox. “Nothing is so delicious as to set one’s teeth into the crisp, juicy fruit, warm and scented by the sun. The worst is, the wasps are impudent enough to dispute it with one, even at the very crisis and summit of enjoyment.”

He rose as if to follow Margaret, awaiting Mrs. Hale’s permission. She would rather have wound up the meal properly, with all the little ceremonies that had gone on so smoothly hitherto—especially as she and Dixon had fetched the finger-glasses from the store-room on purpose, to be as correct as became General Shaw’s widow’s sister. But Mr. Hale got up directly, prepared to accompany his guest, and she could only submit.

“I shall arm myself with a knife,” said Mr. Hale. “The days of eating fruit so primitively as you describe are over with me. I must pare it and quarter it before I can enjoy it.”

The garden received them with a softness of sound as palpable as scent. Bees hummed busily in the hives along the south wall; their small, steady labour made a kind of domestic music, a kindly underpinning to the hush. The leaves overhead held still; now and then a bird gave one clear call that seemed less a note than a mark of place. It was not silence, but a living quiet—each sound in proportion, no harsh clangour to startle the mind.

Margaret brought back the pears in her apron, and made a plate of a broad beet-root leaf, which threw up the brown-gold colour admirably. Their skins looked russeted with sun; their fragrance, when she lifted one, was honeyed and faintly spicy.

Mr. Lennox looked more at her than at the fruit. Mr. Hale, absorbed, chose fastidiously the ripest, sat down on the garden bench, and began to enjoy it at leisure, peeling it in one long strip of silver-paper thinness.

Margaret and Mr. Lennox strolled along the little terrace-walk under the south wall, where the bees still worked, and where heat lay stored in the bricks like a gentle secret.

“What a perfect life you seem to live here!” he said. “I have always felt rather contemptuously towards the poets before, with their wishes—‘Mine be a cot beside a hill’—and that sort of thing; but now I am afraid the truth is I have been nothing better than a Cockney. Just now I feel as if twenty years’ hard study of law would be amply rewarded by one year of such an exquisite serene life as this—such skies!” He looked up. “Such crimson and amber foliage, so perfectly motionless as that!”

“You must please to remember that our skies are not always as deep a blue as they are now,” Margaret replied. “We have rain, and our leaves do fall, and get sodden. Though I think Helstone is about as perfect a place as any in the world. Recollect how you rather scorned my description one evening in Harley Street—‘a village in a tale.’”

“Scorned, Margaret! That is rather a hard word.”

“Perhaps it is. Only I know I should have liked to have talked to you of what I was very full at the time, and you—what must I call it then?—spoke disrespectfully of Helstone as a mere village in a tale.”

“I will never do so again,” he said warmly.

They turned the corner of the walk. He hesitated—so unusual a pause in the fluent lawyer that Margaret looked up in questioning wonder. In that instant, from something about him she could not name—his altered breathing, the way his voice was about to change—she wished herself back with her mother, with her father, anywhere away from him; for she knew he was going to say something to which she would not know how to reply.

Then her pride rose to meet her fear. She would not shrink. She could answer—and answer rightly. It was poor and despicable to tremble before words, as if she had not the power to end them with her high maidenly dignity.

“Margaret,” he said, taking her by surprise, getting sudden possession of her hand so that she was forced to stand still and listen—despising herself for the fluttering at her heart all the time—“Margaret, I wish you did not like Helstone so much—did not seem so perfectly calm and happy here. I have been hoping for these three months past to find you regretting London—and London friends—a little—enough to make you listen more kindly” (for she was quietly, firmly striving to extricate her hand from his grasp) “to one who has not much to offer, it is true—nothing but prospects in the future—but who does love you, Margaret, almost in spite of himself. Margaret, have I startled you too much? Speak!”

He saw her lips quiver as if she were going to cry. The steady garden sounds—the bees’ hum, the soft scrape of his boot on gravel—seemed suddenly too loud, too near, as if the world had narrowed to this one stretch of walk and the pressure of his hand.

She made a strong effort to be calm. She would not speak till she mastered her voice; and then she said:

“I was startled. I did not know that you cared for me in that way. I have always thought of you as a friend; and, please, I would rather go on thinking of you so. I don’t like to be spoken to as you have been doing. I cannot answer you as you want me to do, and yet I should feel so sorry if I vexed you.”

“Margaret,” he said, looking into her eyes—eyes so open and straight, so full of good faith and reluctance to wound—that what he was going to ask died on his lips. “Forgive me! I have been too abrupt. I am punished. Only let me hope. Give me the poor comfort of telling me you have never seen any one whom you could—” Again he paused; he could not end the sentence.

Margaret reproached herself acutely as the cause of his distress.

“Ah! if you had but never got this fancy into your head! It was such a pleasure to think of you as a friend.”

“But I may hope—may I not, Margaret—that some time you will think of me as a lover? Not yet, I see—there is no hurry—but some time—”

She was silent for a minute or two, trying to discover the truth as it was in her own heart before replying; and then she said slowly:

“I have never thought of—you—but as a friend. I like to think of you so; but I am sure I could never think of you as anything else. Pray let us both forget that all this—” She had been going to say “disagreeable,” but stopped short—“conversation has taken place.”

He paused before replying. Then, in his habitual coldness of tone, he answered:

“Of course, as your feelings are so decided, and as this conversation has been so evidently unpleasant to you, it had better not be remembered. That is all very fine in theory, that plan of forgetting whatever is painful; but it will be somewhat difficult for me, at least, to carry it into execution.”

“You are vexed,” she said sadly. “Yet how can I help it?”

She looked so truly grieved that he struggled a moment with his real disappointment, and then answered more cheerfully—yet with a little hardness that cut even through his attempt at ease.

“You should make allowances for the mortification—not only of a lover, Margaret, but of a man not given to romance in general—prudent, worldly, as some people call me—who has been carried out of his usual habits by the force of a passion. Well—we will say no more of that. But in the one outlet which he has formed for the deeper and better feelings of his nature, he meets with rejection and repulse. I shall have to console myself with scorning my own folly. A struggling barrister to think of matrimony!”

Margaret could not answer. The whole tone annoyed her. It called out, as if with a needle’s point, the very differences that had often repelled her in him; and yet he was the pleasantest man, the most sympathising friend, the person who in Harley Street had seemed to understand her better than any other. Pain was there—true pain at having refused him—yet a tinge of contempt mixed with it. Her beautiful lip curled in slight disdain.

It was well that, having made the round of the garden, they came suddenly upon Mr. Hale. His whereabouts had been forgotten by them both. He had not yet finished the pear he had peeled so delicately; he still ate it with deliberate enjoyment, as if time were his obedient servant. It was like the tale of the eastern king who dipped his head into a basin at the magician’s command, and in the instant it took to lift it out had gone through the experience of a lifetime.

Margaret felt stunned, unable to recover her self-possession enough to join in the trivial talk that followed between her father and Mr. Lennox. She was grave and little disposed to speak, full of wonder when Mr. Lennox would go and allow her to relax into thought on the events of the last quarter of an hour.

He was almost as anxious to depart as she was for him to leave; but a few minutes of light, careless talking—carried on at whatever effort—was a sacrifice he owed to his mortified vanity or his self-respect. He glanced from time to time at her sad, pensive face.

“I am not so indifferent to her as she believes,” he thought. “I do not give up hope.”

Before a quarter of an hour was over, he had fallen into a way of conversing with quiet sarcasm—speaking of life in London and life in the country as if he were conscious of his own second, mocking self, and afraid of his satire. Mr. Hale was puzzled. His visitor was different from the man he had seen at the wedding breakfast, and at dinner to-day—a lighter, cleverer, more worldly man; and, as such, dissonant to Mr. Hale, as a sudden harsh note jars in the midst of a gentle piece.

It was a relief to all three when Mr. Lennox said he must go directly if he meant to catch the five o’clock train. They proceeded to the house to find Mrs. Hale and wish her good-bye.

At the last moment Henry Lennox’s real self broke through the crust.

“Margaret, don’t despise me. I have a heart, notwithstanding all this good-for-nothing way of talking. As a proof of it, I believe I love you more than ever—if I do not hate you—for the disdain with which you have listened to me during this last half-hour. Good-bye, Margaret—Margaret!”

He was gone; the click of the garden-gate had died away into the thickening evening, and the house gathered itself up, shutters and curtains and all, as if to keep the day’s sweetness from escaping. The last of the deep blue and the crimson edge of the sunset were smothered by the familiar indoor dimness. Margaret went up to dress for early tea, and found Dixon in one of those tempers that made every pin seem an insult, and every passing footstep an interruption contrived on purpose.

Dixon’s brush tugged through Margaret’s hair with a business-like cruelty, as if haste were a virtue that would excuse impatience. All the while she talked—half to herself, half to the absent mistress—of the day’s disturbances: of the ironing-blanket, burnt again, as if fire were forever lying in wait for household linen; and of how a certain Susan Lightfoot had been seen with artificial flowers in her bonnet, those stiff, everlasting blossoms that smelt of nothing and yet proclaimed vanity louder than any scent. In Dixon’s mouth even a bonnet became a moral history.

Yet, for all Dixon’s hurry, Margaret had to wait a long while alone in the drawing-room before her mother came down. The fire had been newly fed; the unlighted candles stood in readiness behind her like pale sentinels. She sat close to the hearth, letting its heat creep into her chilled hands, and tried to put the day into order within her mind—as one might lay out a supper-table, each dish in its place, so the meal will not reproach you with confusion.

There had been the happy walk, the pleasant sketching, the cheerful dinner—how the roast had smelt when it was set down, how the gravy had shone, how the bread had been torn with that quiet domestic sound that always seemed to make a home—and then the uncomfortable, miserable walk in the garden, where every leaf had looked the same and yet everything had altered. How different men were to women. She was shaken and unhappy because her very instinct had made anything but a refusal impossible; while he—scarcely minutes after meeting what should have been the deepest, holiest rejection of his life—could speak as if briefs and success, and the superficial conveniences of a good house and clever society, were the only avowed objects of desire.

If he had but been different—different in something that went low, deep down—how she could have loved him. And then, as if her heart were determined to try every argument against itself, she wondered whether his lightness had been assumed, a bright crust over bitterness, such as might have stamped itself on her own heart had she loved and been rejected. The thought was like tasting an unknown herb—sharp, unsettling, and yet compelling you to taste again.

Her mother came in before Margaret could settle the whirl into any shape that resembled peace. Margaret had to shake off the day as one shakes flour from one’s hands before touching clean linen, and become the sympathising listener to Dixon’s reports: the burnt blanket, the vain bonnet, the little village judgments that were, for Mrs. Hale, as necessary as tea itself.

Tea was brought in—always at Helstone with a quiet certainty, as if the very kettle knew its hour. Mr. Hale sipped in abstracted silence. Margaret, answering her mother, found herself making all the responses as if her father were absent, though he sat there; and she could not understand how both her parents could be so forgetful, so regardless of the companion through the day, as never once to speak his name. She forgot—how could she not?—that he had not made them an offer.

After tea Mr. Hale rose and stood with his elbow on the chimney-piece, leaning his head on his hand. From time to time he sighed—deeply, as if each breath were a burden lifted and set down again. Mrs. Hale went out to consult with Dixon about winter clothing for the poor—flannel, shawls, the small provisions by which comfort is doled out in parcels. Margaret drew her mother’s worsted work towards her, arranging the skeins and needles with hands that wanted employment, and shrank from the thought of the long evening. She wished for bed-time, that she might go over the events of the day again in solitude, as one returns to taste in private what one could not swallow in company.

“Margaret!” said Mr. Hale at last, in a sudden, desperate way that made her start.

“Yes, papa?”

“Is that tapestry thing of immediate consequence? I mean—can you leave it and come into my study? I want to speak to you about something very serious—to us all.”

The words struck her like a cold draught through a warm room: very serious to us all. For one instant her mind flew, with shame and guilt, to what had happened—whether Mr. Lennox had contrived to speak to her father privately at last, and whether her refusal had been—was it for her to decide? But almost as soon as she entered the study and saw her father’s face, she knew it was not that. This sorrow was older; it had been feeding in him like a hidden fire.

He made her take a chair near him. He stirred the fire, though it did not need stirring; he snuffed the candles with needless care, as if light could be regulated into courage. He sighed once or twice before he could make up his mind. When the words came, they came with a jerk, as if torn free.

“Margaret! I am going to leave Helstone.”

“Leave Helstone, papa! But—why?” The very name tasted in her mouth like bread she had eaten all her life; to be told it would be taken away was to feel hunger at once.

Mr. Hale did not answer immediately. He played with some papers on the table, opening his lips to speak and closing them again, as though the truth had edges that cut. Margaret could not bear his suspense; it seemed to hurt him even more than her.

“But why, dear papa? Do tell me.”

He looked up suddenly, and then said with a slow, enforced calmness, “Because I must no longer be a minister in the Church of England.”

For a moment her mind refused to take it in. She had imagined anything else—some preferment at last, some change imposed by fortune that would still leave him what he had always been. Even the thought of leaving Helstone for some cathedral close, grand and silent, would have been pain enough. But this—this struck at the root of her idea of him. The study wavered before her eyes.

What could he mean? The mystery made it worse. On his face there was such piteous distress—almost an imploring of mercy from his own child—that a sudden sickening seized her. Could it be Frederick? Frederick, the outlaw—had her father connived at something, out of love? Her thoughts ran desperately, as if searching cupboards in the dark for some lost necessity.

“Oh! what is it? do speak, papa! tell me all! Why can you no longer be a clergyman? Surely, if the bishop were told all we know about Frederick, and the hard unjust—”

“It is nothing about Frederick,” he said, quickly. “The bishop would have nothing to do with that. It is all myself. Margaret, I will tell you about it. I will answer any questions this once; but after to-night let us never speak of it again. I can meet the consequences of my painful, miserable doubts; but it is an effort beyond me to speak of what has caused me so much suffering.”

“Doubts, papa! Doubts as to religion?” The words came from her with a kind of frightened reverence, like touching something sacred and fearing you have soiled it.

“No! not doubts as to religion; not the slightest injury to that.” He paused; Margaret felt as if she stood on the verge of some new horror. He began again, speaking rapidly, as if speed could carry him over anguish.

“You could not understand it all, if I told you—my anxiety, for years past, to know whether I had any right to hold my living—my efforts to quench my smouldering doubts by the authority of the Church. Oh! Margaret, how I love the holy Church from which I am to be shut out!”

He could not go on for a moment. The silence in the room thickened, and outside, far off, the evening birds were calling in their accustomed order. Margaret heard them with a strange clearness, as if the world’s sounds were taking note of their grief. She could not tell what to say; it seemed to her as terrible and inexplicable as if her father were about to turn to an alien faith.

“I have been reading to-day of the two thousand who were ejected from their churches,” he continued, with a faint, painful smile, “trying to steal some of their bravery; but it is of no use—no use—I cannot help feeling it acutely.”

“But, papa, have you well considered? Oh! it seems so terrible—so shocking.” The tears broke loose at last, hot and uncontrollable. The one staid foundation of home—the idea of her beloved father—seemed rocking under her.

The sight of her distress nerved him into trying to comfort her. He swallowed down the sobs that had been rising, and went to the bookcase. Taking down a volume he had often read of late, he came back and put one arm round her waist.

“Listen, dear Margaret.” She took his hand and grasped it hard, but she could not lift her head; she could hardly attend, for agitation thundered within her like a storm heard from inside a house.

“This is the soliloquy of one who was once a clergyman in a country parish, like me,” he said. “It was written by Mr. Oldfield, minister of Carsington, in Derbyshire, a hundred and sixty years ago, or more. His trials are over. He fought the good fight.” The last words fell low, as if he spoke to himself.

Then he read aloud, the old sentences shaped by a conscience that had lived and suffered before his. As he read, he gained resolution—felt, for a few moments, as if he too could be brave and firm in doing what he believed to be right. But when he ceased, Margaret’s low, convulsive sob came like an answer, and his courage sank under the keen sense of what he was bringing upon those he loved.

“Margaret, dear!” he said, drawing her closer. “Think of the early martyrs; think of the thousands who have suffered.”

“But, father,” she cried, lifting her flushed, tear-wet face, “the early martyrs suffered for the truth, while you—oh! dear, dear papa!”

“I suffer for conscience’ sake, my child,” he replied, with a dignity trembling only from the very sensitiveness of his nature. “I must do what my conscience bids. I have borne long with self-reproach that would have roused any mind less torpid and cowardly than mine.”

He shook his head as he went on, and his words came out as if they had been stored up painfully, like winter provisions hoarded against famine.

“Your poor mother’s fond wish—gratified at last in the mocking way in which over-fond wishes are too often fulfilled—Sodom apples as they are—has brought on this crisis, for which I ought to be, and I hope I am thankful. It is not a month since the bishop offered me another living; if I had accepted it, I should have had to make a fresh declaration of conformity to the Liturgy at my institution. Margaret, I tried to do it; I tried to content myself with simply refusing the additional preferment, and stopping quietly here,—strangling my conscience now, as I had strained it before. God forgive me!”

He rose and walked up and down, speaking low words of humiliation that Margaret was thankful to hear but brokenly. The very floor seemed to take the weight of his steps unwillingly. At last he stopped.

“Margaret, I return to the old sad burden: we must leave Helstone.”

“Yes—I see. But when?” The question felt like asking the date of an execution.

“I have written to the bishop—I dare say I have told you so, but I forget things just now—informing him of my intention to resign this vicarage. He has been most kind; he has used arguments and expostulations, all in vain—in vain. They are but what I have tried upon myself, without avail. I shall have to take my deed of resignation and wait upon the bishop myself, to bid him farewell. That will be a trial. But worse—far worse—will be the parting from my dear people. There is a curate appointed to read prayers—a Mr. Brown. He will come to stay with us to-morrow. Next Sunday I preach my farewell sermon.”
