The arrangements were so far advanced—so near completion—before she had even been told, that Margaret felt stunned, as if she had been struck and could not yet feel pain. Perhaps it was better to be stunned than to have the wound pricked day after day. Yet one thought rose, heavy as lead.

“What does mamma say?” she asked.

Her father began to pace again before he answered, as if the room could not hold that truth still. At length he stopped.

“Margaret, I am a poor coward after all. I cannot bear to give pain. I know so well your mother’s married life has not been all she hoped—all she had a right to expect—and this will be such a blow to her, that I have never had the heart—the power—to tell her.” He looked at Margaret with a wistful helplessness. “She must be told though, now.”

The idea that her mother knew nothing, while the deed was written and the curate coming, almost overpowered Margaret.

“Yes—indeed she must,” she said, and heard in her own voice the breaking and the effort. “Perhaps, after all, she may not—Oh yes! she will—she must be shocked.”

“Where are we to go to?” she asked at last, as if naming a place might make the change more bearable, as if one could swallow a bitter draught better for knowing what cup it was in.

“To Milton-Northern,” he answered, in a dull indifference that frightened her; as if his feelings had burnt down to ash.

“Milton-Northern! The manufacturing town in Darkshire?”

“Yes.”

“Why there, papa?”

“Because there I can earn bread for my family. Because I know no one there, and no one knows Helstone, or can ever talk to me about it.”

Bread. The word, in his mouth, sounded stripped of all comfort—mere necessity, not the warm loaf cut at a home table. She began, “Bread for your family! I thought you and mamma had—” and stopped, checked by the gloom gathering on his brow.

But he, with quick intuitive sympathy, read her thought and turned it aside with an effort.

“You shall be told all, Margaret. Only help me to tell your mother. I think I could do anything but that. The idea of her distress turns me sick with dread. If I tell you all, perhaps you could break it to her to-morrow. I am going out for the day, to bid farmer Dobson and the poor people on Bracy Common good-bye. Would you dislike breaking it to her very much, Margaret?”

She did. She shrank from it more than from anything she had ever had to do. For a moment she could not speak. He said, gently, as if he already knew the answer, “You dislike it very much, don’t you, Margaret?”

Then she conquered herself. She lifted her head and looked bright and strong, not because she felt so, but because he needed it of her.

“It is a painful thing,” she said, “but it must be done, and I will do it as well as ever I can. You must have many painful things to do.”

He shook his head, despondent, and pressed her hand in gratitude. The gesture nearly undid her; she felt tears rise again, but forced her thoughts to the practical, as one forces a frightened mind to count spoons and plates in the midst of disaster.

“Now tell me, papa—what are our plans? You and mamma have some money, independent of the income from the living, have you not? Aunt Shaw has, I know.”

“Yes. I suppose we have about a hundred and twenty pounds a year of our own. Seventy of that has always gone to Frederick, since he has been abroad. I don’t know if he wants it all,” he added, hesitating. “He must have some pay for serving with the Spanish army.”

“Frederick must not suffer,” said Margaret, decidedly. “In a foreign country; so unjustly treated by his own. A hundred is left. Could not you, and I, and mamma live on a hundred a year in some very cheap—very quiet part of England? Oh! I think we could.” In her mind she saw small rooms, plain food, careful fires—yet still England, still familiar lanes, still the old soft speech round them.

“No!” he said. “That would not answer. I must do something! I must make myself busy, to keep off morbid thoughts. Besides, in a country parish I should be so painfully reminded of Helstone, and my duties here. I could not bear it, Margaret. And a hundred a year would go a very little way, after the necessary wants of housekeeping are met, towards providing your mother with all the comforts she has been accustomed to, and ought to have. No: we must go to Milton. That is settled.”

Then, as if he felt the need to excuse the many decisions already made in secret, he added, “I can always decide better by myself, and not influenced by those whom I love. I cannot stand objections. They make me so undecided.”

Margaret resolved to keep silence. After all, what did place signify compared to this terrible change? Yet even while she tried to submit, she felt already the ache of leaving—not only walls and trees, but the sounds that had made Helstone what it was: the lowing of cattle at dusk, the distant clink of a pail, the church-bell’s familiar voice over the fields. She did not know Milton, but the name itself sounded hard—like a hammer on iron.

Mr. Hale went on, speaking now more steadily, as if narrative helped him bear his own choice.

“A few months ago, when my misery of doubt became more than I could bear without speaking, I wrote to Mr. Bell—you remember Mr. Bell, Margaret?”

“No; I never saw him, I think. But I know who he is. Frederick’s godfather—your old tutor at Oxford, don’t you mean?”

“Yes. He is a Fellow of Plymouth College there. He is a native of Milton-Northern, I believe. At any rate he has property there, which has very much increased in value since Milton has become such a large manufacturing town. Well; I had reason to suspect—to imagine—I had better say nothing about it, however. But I felt sure of sympathy from Mr. Bell. I don’t know that he gave me much strength. He has lived an easy life in his college all his days. But he has been as kind as can be. And it is owing to him we are going to Milton.”

“How?” Margaret asked.

“Why, he has tenants, and houses, and mills there; so, though he dislikes the place—too bustling for one of his habits—he is obliged to keep up some sort of connection; and he tells me that he hears there is a good opening for a private tutor there.”

“A private tutor!” Margaret could not keep the scorn from her voice. “What in the world do manufacturers want with the classics, or literature, or the accomplishments of a gentleman?” Her mind filled with a vague image of men all noise and money, eating quickly and speaking roughly, as if meals were only fuel for work.

“Oh,” said her father, “some of them really seem to be fine fellows, conscious of their own deficiencies, which is more than many a man at Oxford is. Some want resolutely to learn, though they have come to man’s estate. Some want their children to be better instructed than they themselves have been. At any rate, there is an opening, as I have said, for a private tutor. Mr. Bell has recommended me to a Mr. Thornton, a tenant of his, and a very intelligent man, as far as I can judge from his letters. And in Milton, Margaret, I shall find a busy life, if not a happy one, and people and scenes so different that I shall never be reminded of Helstone.”

There was the secret motive, naked and human, and Margaret understood it, for it was in herself too. Different. However discordant—however bleak and hateful all she had ever heard of the North, the manufacturers, the people—there was this one dreadful comfort: it would not be Helstone. It would not whisper Helstone at every corner.

“When do we go?” she asked, after a short silence that seemed filled with the crackle of the fire and the measured ticking of the clock, each sound marking time as if time were an enemy.

“I do not know exactly. I wanted to talk it over with you. You see, your mother knows nothing about it yet: but I think, in a fortnight—after my deed of resignation is sent in, I shall have no right to remain.”

“In a fortnight!” The words left her mouth like breath knocked out by a blow.

“No—no, not exactly to a day. Nothing is fixed,” he said anxiously, noticing the sudden film of sorrow that came over her eyes, the change in her colour.

But she recovered herself at once. “Yes, papa, it had better be fixed soon and decidedly, as you say. Only mamma to know nothing about it! It is that that is the great perplexity.”

“Poor Maria!” he answered tenderly. “Poor, poor Maria! Oh, if I were not married—if I were but myself in the world, how easy it would be! As it is—Margaret, I dare not tell her!”

“No,” said Margaret, sadly. “I will do it. Give me till to-morrow evening to choose my time.” Then, as if her heart would not let her rest with mere resolve, she broke out with sudden passionate entreaty: “Oh, papa—say—tell me it is a nightmare—a horrid dream—not the real waking truth! You cannot mean that you are really going to leave the Church—to give up Helstone—to be for ever separate from me, from mamma—led away by some delusion—some temptation! You do not really mean it!”

Mr. Hale sat rigidly still while she spoke, as if motion would betray him. Then he looked her full in the face and answered slowly, hoarsely, with measured force, each word laid down like a stone.

“I do mean it, Margaret. You must not deceive yourself in doubting the reality of my words—my fixed intention and resolve.”

He held her with that steady, stony look for some moments after he had finished. Margaret gazed back with pleading eyes, as if her will could bend his. When she could not, she rose and went towards the door without another word.

Her fingers were on the handle when he called her back. He was standing by the fireplace, shrunk and stooping; but as she came near he drew himself up to his full height. Placing his hands on her head, he spoke with solemn gravity.

“The blessing of God be upon thee, my child!”

“And may He restore you to His Church,” she answered, straight from the fulness of her heart.

The next moment she feared the response might be irreverent—might wound him coming from his daughter—and she threw her arms round his neck. He held her to him for a minute or two. She heard him murmur, as if to keep himself from failing, “The martyrs and confessors had even more pain to bear—I will not shrink.”

They were startled by hearing Mrs. Hale inquiring for her daughter. The sound—a simple domestic call—fell into the study like a spoon dropped on a flagstone: ordinary, innocent, and suddenly ominous. They started apart in full consciousness of all that lay before them.

Mr. Hale spoke hurriedly. “Go, Margaret, go. I shall be out all to-morrow. Before night you will have told your mother.”

“Yes,” Margaret replied. And she returned to the drawing-room in a stunned and dizzy state, as if she had walked out of one world and into another without crossing any visible boundary.

Margaret could sit for hours while her mother arranged small mercies for the parish poor—each plan spoken in that gentle household voice that meant comfort, and yet struck Margaret like a knife.

Before the first hard frost, they were to be gone from Helstone. She saw it already: old Simon, knotted with rheumatism, blinking at the fire with his book unopened because no one read aloud anymore; the little porringer she had always brought him—broth kept rich with marrow-bone and barley—gone cold in memory. She pictured Mary Domville’s crippled boy dragging himself to the threshold, listening for the familiar step on the path and hearing only the wood’s indifferent hush. They would not understand. They would only know she had vanished, and the village would give her absence some blunt name—pride, caprice, London ways—anything but the truth.

Mrs. Hale spoke on, warming to her own purpose. “Your papa has always spent what he had from the living among the parish. Perhaps I am encroaching upon next dues, but the winter is like to be severe. Our poor people must be helped.”

“Oh, mamma—let us do all we can.” Margaret’s eagerness had no prudence in it; it was the clutch of someone trying to leave gifts behind, as if gifts could stand in for a farewell. “We may not be here long.”

Mrs. Hale’s face altered instantly. “Do you feel ill, my darling? You look pale—tired. It is this soft, damp, unhealthy air.”

“No—no, mamma. It is delicious air.” Margaret tried to steady her voice by fastening it to sensation: the scent of wet earth, crushed evergreen, the faint sharpness of wood-smoke that belonged to cottage hearths and not to London chimneys. “It smells of the freshest, purest fragrance after Harley Street. But I am tired. It must be near bedtime.”

“Not far. Half-past nine. Go to bed at once. Ask Dixon for some gruel. I will come when you are in bed. I am afraid you have taken cold—or the bad air from some stagnant ponds—”

“Oh, mamma,” Margaret smiled faintly and kissed her, “I am quite well. Don’t alarm yourself. I am only tired.”

Upstairs, to soothe that anxious love, she let Dixon bring a basin of gruel—oats simmered till they surrendered into softness, a pinch of salt, a little milk stirred in at the last so it did not scorch. The steam smelled faintly of comfort and nursery hours, and yet it sat in her throat like something she must swallow for someone else’s sake. She lay back, languid, while her mother came in with the last questions and the last kiss; and when she heard, after a little interval, the click of Mrs. Hale’s lock, Margaret sprang from bed as if released.

She threw on her dressing-gown and began to pace; then the creak of a board admonished her. The house had its own acoustics—old wood complaining softly, the roof timbers holding night-sounds the way an empty church holds a whisper. She moved more carefully, and curled herself into the window-seat in the deep recess.

That morning her heart had danced at the bright clear light on the church tower—sun promising a day that would be simple and known. Now, scarcely sixteen hours later, she sat too full for tears, pressed by a cold dull pain that seemed to have squeezed the youth out of her. Mr. Henry Lennox’s visit, his offer—those words that ought to have shaken the whole world—had taken on the unreality of a dream. The hard fact stood like stone: her father had let doubt enter him until he would become a schismatic—an outcast. All the coming changes gathered round that one blighting centre.

She looked out at the church tower’s dark-grey lines, square and upright against the transparent blue depths beyond. Space opened and opened, as if her gaze could travel for ever and find nothing—no sign, no answering face. The silence out there felt less like peace than mockery, as if the cries of earth could rise and rise and be lost in that vastness before they ever reached a throne. Even Helstone’s night was full of small sounds—an owl’s call, the river’s far rush, the faint stir of a branch—but beyond them was an immeasurable quiet that made her feel more alone than any roof of iron could have done.

In that mood her father entered without her hearing him. Moonlight was strong enough to show her crouched in the recess, her hair loosened, her posture strange with misery. He came close and touched her shoulder before she knew he was there.

“Margaret. I heard you were up. I could not help coming in—to ask you to pray with me. To say the Lord’s Prayer. That will do good to both of us.”

He did not argue; he did not explain. He asked only that ancient sequence of words, spoken by countless mouths in countless dialects, held in the memory of the world even when meanings blur and hearts wander. They knelt by the window-seat—he looking up, she bowed down, ashamed. God was there close around them, hearing her father’s whispered voice. Her father might be, in the world’s phrase, a heretic; but she had been, five minutes before, a more utter sceptic in her despair.

She did not speak after. She crept back into bed when he had left her, like a child ashamed of her fault. If the world was full of perplexity, she would trust. She would ask only to see the step needed for the hour.

That night Mr. Lennox haunted her dreams. He climbed a tree of fabulous height to reach a branch where her bonnet hung; he fell; she struggled to save him, and was held back by some invisible force. He lay dead. Then the scene shifted, and she was again in the Harley Street drawing-room, speaking to him as she had done a hundred times, while a cold knowledge persisted behind every word: she had seen him killed.

She woke with a start, unrefreshed, her mouth dry, her body heavy as if she had carried weights in sleep. Reality came back sharper than any dream—not merely sorrow, but discord in sorrow. Where had her father wandered in mind? How far from the faith she had grown up breathing as naturally as air? She longed to ask; she would rather have bitten her tongue than hear the answer.

Downstairs the fine crisp morning put colour into Mrs. Hale. At breakfast she seemed almost happy, talking of village kindness, of who must have what when the cold set in—unheeding her husband’s silence and Margaret’s monosyllables. There was tea poured, bread cut, butter spread; the homely sounds—cup on saucer, knife on plate—went on with their accustomed small music, as if the house meant to drown whatever was coming.

Before the table was cleared, Mr. Hale rose. He leaned one hand on the wood as if it steadied him.

“I shall not be home till evening. I am going to Bracy Common, and will ask Farmer Dobson to give me something for dinner. I shall be back to tea at seven.”

He did not look at either of them. But Margaret understood. By seven, the words must be said to her mother.

Mr. Hale would have delayed, if delay could soften what had to be borne. Margaret could not. She could not carry the weight all day, watching her mother’s cheerful plans bloom and knowing she was about to trample them down. Better do it now, and leave the day—short as winter days were—for comfort.

Yet as she stood by the window, waiting for the servant to leave the room so she might begin, her mother went upstairs to dress for the school. She came down quickly, brisker than usual, bonnet tied, cloak arranged, full of purpose.

“Mother—come round the garden with me this morning. Only one turn,” Margaret said, slipping her arm round her waist, as if she could hold her up through whatever might happen.

They passed out through the open window. The air bit pleasantly; the gravel gave its crisp sound underfoot; a robin scolded from the hedge. Mrs. Hale spoke—some light remark, perhaps—but Margaret did not catch it. Her mind seized on a bee pushing into a deep-belled flower, its body almost swallowed by the purple throat. When the bee came out again, dusted with gold, she would speak. That would be the sign, like a childish charm.

Out it came.

“Mamma! Papa is going to leave Helstone!” Margaret blurted, the words hard as stones. “He’s going to leave the Church, and live in Milton-Northern.”

Mrs. Hale stopped as if struck. “What makes you say so? Who has been telling you such nonsense?”

“Papa himself.” Margaret longed for some gentle wrapping to put round the blow, but there was none; only the blow.

They had reached a garden-bench. Mrs. Hale sank onto it and began to cry—not loud, but with that helpless, wounded sound of someone whose world has been quietly stolen.

“I don’t understand you,” she said. “Either you have made some great mistake—or I don’t quite understand you.”

“No, mother. I have made no mistake.” Margaret forced herself into plainness, because anything softer would seem like deceit. “Papa has written to the bishop, saying he has such doubts that he cannot conscientiously remain a priest of the Church of England, and that he must give up Helstone. He has consulted Mr. Bell—Frederick’s godfather, you know—and it is arranged that we go to live at Milton-Northern.”

Mrs. Hale looked up at Margaret’s face while she spoke, reading truth there against her will. Her own features darkened under the shadow of belief.

“I don’t think it can be true,” she said at last, as if by refusing she could reverse it. “He would surely have told me before it came to this.”

The thought struck Margaret with pain: her mother ought to have been told. However much Mrs. Hale repined, however much she narrowed her world to her own ailments and disappointments, this was her husband’s heart being torn, and he had left her to learn it from their child. Margaret sat down beside her and drew her mother’s head to her breast, bending her cheek against that soft hair, stroking as if touch could translate what words could not.

“Dear, darling mamma. We were so afraid of giving you pain. Papa has felt it so acutely. You know you are not strong. There must have been such suspense.”

“When did he tell you, Margaret?” Her tone had a sharp edge of jealousy, though tears still ran.

“Yesterday—only yesterday.” Margaret answered quickly, and then, to turn her mother outward toward pity instead of inward toward grievance, she added, “Poor papa.”

Mrs. Hale lifted her head. “What does he mean by having doubts? Surely he does not mean he thinks differently—knows better than the Church.”

Margaret could only shake her head. Tears came into her eyes; the question touched her own bare nerve. She had not asked her father what those doubts were; she had not dared. It was like standing on the edge of a deep well and fearing to look down, not because of the darkness but because of what her own voice might echo back.

“Can’t the bishop set him right?” Mrs. Hale asked, half impatiently, as if authority were a poultice.

“I’m afraid not. But I did not ask. I could not bear to hear what he might answer. It is settled, at any rate. He is going to leave Helstone in a fortnight. I am not sure—he may have sent in his deed of resignation.”

“In a fortnight!” Mrs. Hale cried. “I do think this is very strange—not at all right. Very unfeeling.” And, as if tears could wash away the humiliation, she took relief in weeping. “He has doubts and gives up his living and all without consulting me. If he had told me his doubts at first, I could have nipped them in the bud.”

Margaret, who had reproached her father in her heart, could not bear to hear him blamed aloud. She knew his reserve had begun in tenderness—cowardly perhaps, but not unfeeling.

“I almost hoped you might be glad to leave Helstone, mamma,” she said after a pause, groping for any thread that could pull her mother toward acceptance. “You have never been well in this air.”

“You can’t think the smoky air of a manufacturing town—chimneys and dirt like Milton-Northern—would be better than this. This air is pure and sweet, if it is too soft and relaxing.” Her voice gathered speed as pride and fear took the rein. “Fancy living in the middle of factories—and factory people! And, of course, if your father leaves the Church, we shall not be admitted into society anywhere. It will be such a disgrace. Poor dear Sir John! It is well he is not alive to see what your father has come to. Every day after dinner, when I was a girl at Beresford Court, Sir John used to give for the first toast—‘Church and King, and down with the Rump.’”

Margaret was almost glad her mother ran to old phrases, those inherited watchwords that sounded sturdy and certain even when their meanings were more posture than prayer. They were a kind of dialect, a badge—belonging, and also power. The pain was not only what her father believed now; it was what language would be used against him once he stepped outside the approved vocabulary. One word—Dissenter—could do the work of a hundred condemnations.

“You know we have very little society here, mamma. The Gormans—our nearest neighbours, to call society—have been in trade just as much as these Milton people.”

“Yes,” said Mrs. Hale, almost indignant, “but at any rate the Gormans made carriages for half the gentlemen of the county. They were brought into some kind of intercourse with them. But these factory people—who on earth wears cotton that can afford linen?”

“Well, mamma, I give up the cotton-spinners. I am not standing up for them. Only—we shall have little enough to do with them.”

“Why on earth has your father fixed on Milton-Northern?”

“Partly,” Margaret said, and sighed as she spoke, “because it is so very different from Helstone. Partly because Mr. Bell says there is an opening there for a private tutor.”

“Private tutor in Milton! Why can’t he go to Oxford and be a tutor to gentlemen?”

“You forget, mamma. He is leaving the Church because of his opinions. His doubts would do him no good at Oxford.”

Mrs. Hale fell silent, crying quietly as if her tears were a private argument she could not yet put into words. Then, abruptly, she clutched at something she could grasp.

“And the furniture—how in the world are we to manage the removal? I never removed in my life. And only a fortnight to think about it!”

Margaret felt a strange relief. Furniture—tables and beds and linens—were at least things that could be counted, wrapped, lifted, labelled. One could not pack doubt into a chest, but one could pack sheets. She began at once to plan and promise, drawing her mother into arrangements: what could be sold, what must go, what might be stored, what must be kept close because it held the smell of home—her mother’s shawls, the tea-service, the very saucepan whose bottom bore the marks of years of careful simmering. She spoke briskly, and for a while Mrs. Hale listened as if practical decisions were a sedative.

Throughout the day Margaret scarcely left her mother, bending her whole soul toward sympathy as feelings veered—anger, grief, shame, fear. Toward evening, her anxiety shifted to her father: she wanted him to find a gentleness waiting at home, a welcome that did not ask him to defend himself. She spoke of what he must have borne in secret for long; Mrs. Hale answered coldly that he ought to have told her, and would then have had an adviser.

At last Margaret heard his step in the hall. Her heart turned faint. She dared not go to meet him and tell him what she had done, for fear her mother’s jealousy would flare. He lingered, as if awaiting Margaret—or some sign. She dared not stir. Mrs. Hale’s lips twitched; her colour changed; she too heard him.

He opened the door and stood uncertain on the threshold, not sure if he had a right to enter. His face was grey and pale; his eyes had a timid, fearful look—something almost pitiful in a man, that despondent uncertainty, that fatigue of mind and body. It touched Mrs. Hale’s heart at last. She rose, crossed to him, and threw herself against his breast.

“Oh, Richard—Richard—you should have told me sooner!”

Margaret could not bear the intimacy of their grief. She slipped away as soon as she could, fled upstairs, and threw herself upon her bed, pressing her face into the pillows to stifle the sobs that broke through at last after the rigid self-control of the day.

How long she lay there she could not tell. The house had gone quiet, but not truly silent; there were always tiny sounds—boards settling, a far door-latch, the muted tick of a clock. Yet no one came until the housemaid entered to arrange the room. The girl, startled by Margaret’s crying, stole out again on tiptoe and told Dixon that Miss Hale sobbed as if her heart would break, and would make herself ill if she went on.

So Dixon came, candle held a little behind her so the light should not strike harshly on swollen eyes. Margaret started up, trying to gather herself, smoothing her wet hair back with trembling fingers, trying to look as if she had only woken.

“Oh, Dixon—I did not hear you come. Is it very late?” She let her feet touch the floor but did not quite stand, as if the act of standing meant facing everything.

“I can hardly tell what time it is,” Dixon replied, aggrieved as if the world’s clock had offended her. “Since your mamma told me this terrible news, when I dressed her for tea, I’ve lost all count. I’m sure I don’t know what is to become of us all. When Charlotte told me you were sobbing, Miss Hale, I thought—no wonder, poor thing! And master thinking of turning Dissenter at his time of life—when, if it’s not to be said he’s done well in the Church, he’s not done badly after all.” Her tongue ran on in the familiar groove of servant commentary. “I had a cousin turned Methodist preacher after he was fifty, and a tailor all his life; but then he’d never been able to make a pair of trousers to fit, so it was no wonder. But for master! As I said to missus—what would poor Sir John have said? He never liked your marrying Mr. Hale, and if he could have known it would come to this, he’d have sworn worse oaths than ever—if that was possible.”

Dixon had been long used to venting such opinions to Mrs. Hale, who received them or not according to mood. She did not notice Margaret’s sudden stillness—the flashing eye, the nostril dilating with indignation. To hear her father spoken of so to her face was intolerable.

“Dixon,” Margaret said in the low tone she used when strongly moved—quiet, but with a distant threatening sound in it, like storm far off. “Dixon. You forget to whom you are speaking.” She rose fully now, upright and firm, and fixed Dixon with steady, discerning eyes. “I am Mr. Hale’s daughter. Go. You have made a strange mistake—one I am sure your own good feeling will make you sorry for when you think of it.”

Dixon hovered, uncertain whether to resent or to cry. Either would have suited Mrs. Hale; neither suited Margaret. Margaret repeated, evenly, “You may leave me, Dixon. I wish you to go.”

Dixon, who would have flared at anyone less decided, was subdued by Margaret’s haughtiness and control. She muttered to herself that Miss Margaret had a touch of “the old gentleman” about her, as well as poor Master Frederick, and at last ventured in a half-humble, half-injured voice, “Mayn’t I unfasten your gown, miss, and do your hair?”

“No. Not to-night, thank you.”

Margaret gravely lighted her out, bolted the door, and leaned her forehead against the wood for a moment, breathing through the tremor. From that hour Dixon both obeyed and admired her. She would say it was because Margaret was like Master Frederick; the truth was simpler: Dixon liked being ruled by a nature that did not waver.

Margaret soon needed Dixon’s help in action and her silence in words—for a time Dixon thought it proper to show offence by speaking little, so her energy came out in doing rather than talking. A fortnight was a short time for so serious a removal. Dixon would begin, “Anyone but a gentleman—indeed almost any other gentleman—” and then, catching a look at Margaret’s straight, stern brow, cough the rest away and meekly take the horehound drop Margaret offered to stop the “little tickling at my chest, miss.”

But it was true: almost anyone but Mr. Hale would have had enough practical knowledge to see how hard it would be, in so short a time, to fix on a house in Milton-Northern—or anywhere—to receive the furniture that must be carried from Helstone Vicarage.

Mrs. Hale, overpowered by grief and by the necessity of immediate household decisions, became truly ill. Margaret almost felt it as relief when her mother took to her bed and left management to her. Dixon attended as a body-guard to her mistress, emerging only to shake her head and murmur to herself in a way Margaret chose not to hear. For Margaret had one thing straight before her: they must leave Helstone. Mr. Hale’s successor was appointed; there must be no lingering now, for her father’s sake as much as for any other.

Each evening he came home more depressed, worn out by the leave-takings he had resolved to make with every parishioner. Farewell after farewell—each one a small tearing—must have filled his ears all day: the sound of voices that had once answered to him as pastor now answering to him as a man who was going away under a cloud. Margaret could imagine how the same words—“God bless you, sir”—changed their tone when spoken to a clergyman who was no longer a clergyman.

She, inexperienced in matter-of-fact business, did not know to whom to turn for advice. The cook and Charlotte worked willingly at the packing—strong arms, stout hearts, cupboards emptied, linens folded, crockery wrapped in old paper that crackled like dry leaves. Margaret’s sense served her there: she could see what should be kept together, what must be marked “fragile,” what should be left accessible for the last days—kettle, tea-canister, a pan for broth, a jar of jam for her mother’s tray upstairs. Yet beneath every practical decision lay the question that made everything else uncertain.

Where were they to go? In a week they must be gone. Straight to Milton—or somewhere on the way? So many arrangements depended on it that one evening Margaret resolved to ask her father, though he looked as if thought itself hurt him.

“My dear,” he said, passing a hand over his brow, “I have really had too much to think about to settle this. What does your mother say? What does she wish? Poor Maria!”

His sigh was answered by another from the doorway. Dixon had come in for another cup of tea for Mrs. Hale, and catching his last words, protected by his presence from Margaret’s rebuking glance, dared to say, “My poor mistress!”

“You don’t think her worse to-day?” Mr. Hale turned hastily, alarm sharpening him.

“I am sure I can’t say, sir. It’s not for me to judge. The illness seems so much more on the mind than on the body.”

Mr. Hale’s face grew more distressed, as if every word were another weight on him.

“You had better take mamma her tea while it is hot, Dixon,” Margaret said, with quiet authority.

“Oh! I beg your pardon, Miss. My thoughts was otherwise occupied—in thinking of my poor—of Mrs. Hale.”

When Dixon had gone, Margaret turned to her father. “Papa—it is this suspense that is bad for you both. Of course mamma must feel your change of opinions—we can’t help that.” Her voice softened. “But now the course is clear, at least to a certain point. I think I could get mamma to help me plan, if you would tell me what to plan for. She has never expressed any wish; she only thinks of what cannot be helped. Are we to go straight to Milton? Have you taken a house there?”

“No,” he replied. “I suppose we must go into lodgings, and look about for a house.”

“And pack the furniture so it can be left at the railway station until we have found one?”

“I suppose so. Do what you think best. Only remember—we shall have much less money to spend.”

They had never had much superfluity; Margaret knew that. Yet hearing it said so plainly made the future narrow at once, like a road that leaves open country and enters between high walls. She felt a great weight drop onto her shoulders.

Four months ago, the only decisions required of her had been what dress to wear for dinner, or helping Edith with lists—who should take down whom, who must be invited lest they feel slighted, who could be omitted without offence. In that house life had run with the regularity of clockwork; even the annual debate about where to spend summer—Isle of Wight, Scotland, abroad—ended with Margaret safely drifting into whatever harbour her aunt chose.

Now, since the day Mr. Lennox came and startled her into a decision of her own, each day brought another question—momentous, sharp-edged—demanding that she choose, act, speak. And in the midst of packing-paper and tea-trays and gruel for her mother, while the familiar sounds of Helstone still soothed the ear—birds, wind, the church-bell marking hours—another sound waited in her mind: the imagined, unceasing roar of Milton-Northern, where even air and speech would be altered, and where the very words people used might make strangers of them before they had even set down their trunks.

The last day came round upon Helstone as if it had been folded, long ago, into the year’s turning like a pressed leaf—foreseen, yet shocking when at last it lay in the hand.

The parsonage was choked with packing-cases. Men’s boots thudded in and out; straw, shaken loose from hampers, drifted and lodged upon the little lawn as if the house were already shedding itself. Doors were left gaping; windows stood bare of curtains; and the rooms, emptied of their familiar weight, gave back every sound with a hollow reply—boards answering heels, walls answering voices—so that even a spoken word seemed to come from a farther place than the mouth that uttered it. There was the rasp of cord drawn tight round wood, the dull knock of a lid being nailed down, the cart’s rumble at the front, and beyond all that, a country quiet so deep it made those few noises feel intrusive.

Mrs. Hale’s dressing-room was saved for the end, as if delay could keep one chamber faithful. There, she and Dixon moved more like mourners than like women at work. A drawer slid out; linen, sweet with long-locked lavender, breathed up its old, domestic comfort. Each time a small relic rose from the folds—a child’s ribbon, a tiny shoe, some broken toy put away because it could not bear to be thrown—hands paused, and the past came back with such tenderness that the present job of tying parcels became impossible for minutes at a time.

Downstairs Margaret stood where she could see and be seen, calm in her very stillness, receiving questions, directing, judging what must go first and what might stay. She watched the men as she watched everything—exactly, gravely, as if her eyes could keep order in a world that was breaking into pieces. The cook and Charlotte cried as they went about their tasks, and between tears wondered at her. They had settled, with the quick decision of those who feel themselves lesser in such matters, that the young lady must not care as they did; London had blunted her, they thought, or else she was proud.

They did not know that her heart was aching under a pressure that made breathing feel like work; that she had learned, in one long day, to keep pain from mastering her by mastering the smallest necessities of the hour. If she yielded, who would act? Her father had his papers, his registers, his books—things no one else could pack without offending his habits of mind. Strange men were in the house; even friends of the kitchen were witnesses; and Margaret was not one to break down where she must also command.

At last the four hired helpers disappeared to the kitchen for tea, their voices muffled at once by distance and walls. Margaret, stiff from standing, moved away through the dismantled drawing-room, where the light, unsoftened by curtain, lay raw upon stripped spaces. She went out into the garden.

An early November dusk had come, with a soft dull mist that did not hide the world so much as change it, washing every hedge and trunk with a lilac-grey and making the last golds of the leaves glow like embers. A robin sang—thin, distinct, as if the little throat were offering its own brave defiance to departure. Margaret thought, with a pang, that it might be the very robin her father had spoken of as his winter favourite, for which he had made, with his own hands, a small shelter by the study-window. The orchard wall, trained with pear-trees, held a faint scent—damp bark, bruised leaf, earth turned cold—while overhead the branches still wore their splendid dying. The first hard frost would take it all down. Even now, one or two leaves came loosening with a slow, unhurried fall, amber and gold in the last slant of sun.

She went along the walk under the pear-tree wall, a path she had not trodden since she paced it with Henry Lennox. Here, near a bed of thyme—still pungent if you brushed it with your shoe—he had begun to speak of what she must not think of now. She remembered how, as she tried to answer, her eyes had caught at a late rose, and at the delicate, feathery carrot-leaves in the kitchen-bed as if they were brighter truths than speech. Only a fortnight. Yet the days in between had stretched like years.

Where was he now? In London—moving through his circles, dining with his Harley Street acquaintance or laughing with younger friends. She could picture him shutting away his law-books after a day’s satisfied toil, then running out to the Temple Gardens, as he had told her he did, letting the city’s great inarticulate roar beat upon him like surf—thousands of men unseen, near at hand, all intent on appointments and arrivals—while at a turn he might catch a glimpse of lamps rising out of the river’s dark.

Here there was no such roar. The robin’s song ceased, as if it had flown into the great stillness. Now and then, very far off, a cottage door opened and shut with a wooden clap to admit a labourer; the sound travelled thinly, diminished by distance, like a memory half-swallowed. Beyond the garden, from the forest floor, came a stealthy creeping crunch among crisp fallen leaves—so close it seemed within the hedgerow itself.

Margaret knew that sound. More than once in the autumn, sitting up in her room with the candle put out, she had watched the poachers’ noiseless leap over the garden fence, their quick tread across the lawn silvered by dew and moon, and their vanish into black shadow under the trees. Their life—wild, risky, unowned—had had a strange charm for her then; she had wished them success, and felt no fear. But to-night something in her blood changed the rustle into menace. The house, with its open doors and stripped windows, felt less like a home than like a shell.

She heard Charlotte inside, shutting up for the night, fastening latches, drawing bolts—unaware anyone had gone out. Then, in the nearest part of the wood, a small branch fell with a heavy crack—rotten perhaps, or forced. Margaret ran, swift as sudden terror makes a body swift, to the drawing-room window and rapped with trembling haste.

“Let me in! Let me in! It is only me, Charlotte!”

Charlotte started, and in a moment Margaret was inside again, the window secured, the familiar walls closing round her, shutting out the dark and the sound, shutting in her shaken breathing. She sat down upon a packing-case. The room was cheerless and chill; there was no fire, no friendly lamp—only Charlotte’s long candle, unsnuffed, making a wavering, greasy light.

Charlotte looked at her in surprise. Margaret, feeling the look more than meeting it, rose and tried to smile.

“I was afraid you were shutting me out altogether, Charlotte,” she said, half-playfully. “And then you would never have heard me in the kitchen, and the doors into the lane and churchyard are locked long ago.”

“Oh, miss, I should have been sure to have missed you soon. The men would have wanted you to tell them how to go on. And I have put tea in master’s study, as being the most comfortable room, so to speak.”

“Thank you, Charlotte. You are a kind girl. I shall be sorry to leave you. You must try and write to me, if I can ever give you any little help or good advice. I shall always be glad to get a letter from Helstone, you know. I shall be sure and send you my address when I know it.”

The study was ready. A good blaze leaped and settled on the hearth, and the fire’s sound—little snaps and sighs—was as comforting as warmth itself after the garden’s muffled hush. Candles stood unlighted on the table. Tea waited, breathing up that homely smell of comfort—hot leaf, milk, a faint sweetness—one of those domestic scents that seem to promise continuity even when everything else is being taken away.

Margaret sat on the rug close to the grate, partly to warm herself, for damp clung to her dress and over-fatigue had turned her cold to the bone. She clasped her hands about her knees to steady herself. Her head drooped; the posture spoke despondency even while her will kept watch.

When she heard her father’s step on the gravel outside, she sprang up. She pushed her heavy black hair back with hurried fingers, wiped away tears that had come unbidden, and went to open the door before he could touch the latch.

He came in looking older than the morning had left him. His face had the strained gentleness of one who has been doing violence to himself. He scarcely answered her efforts at cheerful talk, and when tea was poured he did not touch it.

“Have you been a very long walk to-day?” she asked at last, watching his refusal with quiet concern.

“As far as Fordham Beeches. I went to see Widow Maltby; she is sadly grieved at not having wished you good-bye. She says little Susan has kept watch down the lane for days past.—Nay, Margaret, what is the matter, dear?”

Little Susan—standing, day after day, in childish faithfulness, looking down the lane for a face that did not come—was the last drop. It was not forgetfulness, not coldness, but sheer imprisonment in duties that had kept Margaret from going; yet the thought of the child’s repeated disappointment struck her with a sharpness she could not bear. Tears broke through at once. She sobbed as if something in her chest had cracked.

Mr. Hale was helpless before it. He rose and walked to and fro, his hands moving nervously, his distress making him restless like a man hunted. Margaret tried to stop, ashamed to add to his pain, but her body would not obey her pride. She heard him speak as if to himself, his voice low and broken.

“I cannot bear it. I cannot bear to see the sufferings of others. I think I could go through my own with patience. Oh, is there no going back?”

“No, father,” said Margaret at last, forcing steadiness into her voice, looking straight at him. “It is bad to believe you in error. It would be infinitely worse to have known you a hypocrite.”

She lowered her tone on the last words, as if even imagining hypocrisy beside his name were irreverent. Then, as tears threatened again, she added more gently, as if she could lay a cloth over the rawest part of the wound.

“Besides, it is only that I am tired to-night; don’t think that I am suffering from what you have done, dear papa. We can’t either of us talk about it to-night, I believe. I had better go and take mamma up this cup of tea. She had hers very early, when I was too busy to go to her, and I am sure she will be glad of another now.”

The morning that followed did not belong to Helstone. It belonged to time-tables.

Railroad time—inexorable, indifferent—wrenched them away. They saw the last of the long, low parsonage, half-covered with China-roses and pyracanthus, homelike beyond endurance in the clear morning sun that glittered upon its windows—each window a remembered room, each pane a witness. Almost before they had settled into the car sent from Southampton to fetch them, they were moving, and Helstone slid backwards into the past.

Margaret’s heart stung to look out for one last glimpse of the old church tower, that at one turn showed itself above a wave of forest trees. She strained for it—then saw her father’s face, and remembered it was his tower more than hers. She silently yielded him the window. She leaned back, shut her eyes, and tears welled and hung for an instant on her lashes, glittering, before they rolled down and dropped upon her dress unnoticed.

They were to stop in London for the night, at a quiet hotel. Mrs. Hale cried in her languid, persistent way nearly all day, as if tears were the only action left to her. Dixon showed sorrow by sharpness: a continual irritable guarding of her mistress’s petticoats from even brushing against Mr. Hale, whom she held, in her mind, to be the cause and author of all this breaking-up.

London received them with its own music—wheels on stone, calls and footsteps, the dense overlapping of voices, a ceaseless clatter that pressed upon the ears and nerves. To those who had come out of Helstone’s great spaces of hush, the sound felt like a storm made of iron and breath. They drove through streets Margaret knew by heart, past houses once familiar, past shops where she had stood impatient by her aunt’s side while some purchase was debated into eternity. They passed acquaintances in the street; for though the morning had been so long to them that it seemed it ought to have ended in darkness and rest, it was the busiest time of a London November afternoon when they arrived.

Mrs. Hale, long absent, roused herself almost like a child at a fair, looking out with startled eagerness.

“Oh, there’s Harrison’s, where I bought so many of my wedding things. Dear! how altered! They’ve got immense plate-glass windows, larger than Crawford’s in Southampton. Oh, and there, I declare—no, it is not—yes, it is—Margaret, we have just passed Mr. Henry Lennox. Where can he be going, among all these shops?”

Margaret started forward, and as quickly fell back, half-smiling at her own involuntary movement. They were a hundred yards away by then, and he was gone among the crowd; but the mere sight—or thought—of him came like a fragment of Helstone transported into the London din, associated with a bright morning and an eventful day. She would have liked to see him without his seeing her; to keep the past intact, not forced into speech under the eyes of strangers.

The evening, with nothing to do, dragged heavily in a high hotel room. Mr. Hale went out to his bookseller’s and to call upon one or two friends; the women remained with their weariness and the muffled city-noise below. Everyone they saw in passages and stairways, in street and doorway, hurried as if drawn by an appointment—expected, or expecting. They alone seemed without place, without claim, without the thread that binds a life into other lives.

And yet Margaret knew—within a mile of where they sat—house after house where she, for her own sake, and her mother, for Aunt Shaw’s, would be welcomed if they came in gladness, or even in peace. But to come sorrowing, asking sympathy for trouble that could not be neatly named or easily shared—this would make them a shadow at the threshold. In London there is too much motion, too much noise, too much perpetual exchange, to admit readily even one hour of that deep, reverent silence with which the friends of Job sat down beside grief too great for speech.

The next afternoon, with the day already paling towards an early winter dusk, they left the main line some twenty miles from Milton-Northern, and were carried on a little branch railway that slipped away toward Heston. The carriage shook and sang on the rails with a thinner, more domestic sound than the great line—less roar, more rhythm—as if even the iron had manners here. Margaret, who had been holding herself stiff through so many changes, found that measured clatter loosening something within her, like a lid lifted from a pot to let the first steam escape.

Heston proved a single, straggling street set along the seashore, and it wore its difference openly. There was none of the painted gaiety Margaret remembered in southern bathing-places—no bright parasols, no languid lounging at shop-doors as if air itself were entertainment. Everything here had a use. The carts seemed shod and braced with more iron than wood; the harness was contrived for endurance rather than show. Even in the faces of people who had come, nominally, to take their pleasure, there was that look of minds still ticking over accounts and errands. The very colours of the town felt sober—greys that would not rub off.

She noticed, too, what was absent: the old country smock-frocks she had seen in other places, those roomy garments that carried a whole rural history in their folds. Here they had vanished, as if some word in an ancient dialect had dropped out of use; they hindered movement, they caught on machinery, they were not “fit” any longer, and so they were gone. It struck Margaret, with a little pang she could not have translated for her mother, that fashions could die the way languages did—by being made inconvenient under a louder, more dominant tongue.

The next morning she and Mrs. Hale went out to look for lodgings. Two nights at hotels had cost more than Mr. Hale had reckoned, and they were glad—almost too glad—to take the first clean, cheerful rooms that were willing to receive them. When they were fairly within them, with the door shut upon the public passages, Margaret felt, for the first time in many days, something like rest.

It came with a curious dreaminess, as if her mind, having been whipped onward too long, would now float. The sea lay at a little distance, and its sound—lap, withdraw, lap—was as steady as a clock that did not nag. Nearer, the donkey-boys cried and bickered, their voices carrying on the salt air; and even that rough piping felt harmless beside the hard metallic clamour she feared in the North. The scenes that passed before her—odd faces, purpose-driven steps, carts going by—seemed to move like pictures hung for an instant and then taken down again. She went down to the beach, breathing in air that tasted faintly of kelp and wet sand, soft and warm even at the end of November. A long misty sea-line touched a tender-coloured sky; a distant sail caught a pale sunbeam and turned briefly to silver. It all tempted her to believe she might dream her life away in that luxurious pensiveness, making the present enough because she dared not unpack the past, nor look too long at the future.

But the future, however stern and iron, had its summons. One evening it was settled that on the morrow Margaret and her father should go to Milton-Northern and seek a house. Mr. Hale had received several letters from Mr. Bell, and one or two from Mr. Thornton, and he was anxious to learn plainly what might be learned only by an interview—his position in Milton, his chances, the shape of life they were stepping into. Margaret knew removal could not be postponed. Yet her whole being shrank from a manufacturing town; and she clung to the belief—perhaps too eagerly—that the Heston air was doing her mother good, and that anything that hurried them away from this sea-breath would be a kind of cruelty.

They went.

For several miles before Milton they could see it: a deep, lead-coloured cloud hanging over the horizon in the direction where the town lay. It looked the darker because Heston had already shown the earliest signs of frost; the sky above them was a pale grey-blue, thin and cold, and the cloud ahead seemed like a bruise upon it. As they drew nearer, the air took on a faint taste and smell of smoke—perhaps less a positive odour than a stealing-away of all green fragrance, as if grass and herbage had been cooked out of the very wind. It sat on the tongue with a dry bitterness, as tea does when it has stood too long and lost its fine scent.

Then they were whirled into long, straight streets that seemed to have been ruled off by some severe hand—hopeless in their regularity, built all of small brick houses, each one like the next. Here and there a great oblong factory rose up, many-windowed, dominating its little domestic neighbours; and from it poured out black smoke—unapologetic, insolent, “unparliamentary”—which sufficiently explained the cloud Margaret had mistaken for weather. The sound changed too. In Heston the sea had given a measured music; here the air was full of harsh, hurried noise: wheels grinding, hooves striking stone, men calling sharp directions, and, beneath all, a continual throb, as if some giant heart beat in the walls. It was not merely loud; it was restless, the kind of sound that does not allow thought to settle. Margaret felt, without having words for it, that such noise could shape the mind as surely as diet does—that a town might feed its people on clangour until they knew no other flavour of peace.

From the station to the hotel they had to stop constantly; great loaded lurries blocked the not over-wide streets. In London, when Margaret had driven with her aunt, the heavy vehicles seemed varied in purpose—wood here, stone there, provisions somewhere else. Here every van, waggon, and truck bore cotton: in raw bags that had a dull, greasy look, or in bales of calico packed tight as if the cloth inside were a secret to be guarded. People thronged the footpaths. They were well-dressed as to material, but there was a loose slovenliness in the wearing of it that struck Margaret; it was not the threadbare effort at smartness she had seen in London, but something careless, as if clothes were only another tool to be flung on and off.

“New Street,” said Mr. Hale, leaning forward to read a corner sign as they turned. “This, I believe, is the principal street in Milton. Bell has often spoken to me about it. It was the opening of this street—once only a lane—into a great thoroughfare, thirty years ago, that has caused his property to rise so much in value. Mr. Thornton’s mill must be somewhere not far off, for he is Mr. Bell’s tenant. But I fancy he dates from his warehouse.”

“Where is our hotel, papa?”

“Close to the end of this street, I believe.” He paused, considering their hours, their list, the train they must take back. “Shall we have lunch before or after we have looked at the houses we marked in the Milton Times?”

“Oh, let us get our work done first,” said Margaret; her impatience was less of zeal than dread—if she delayed, she might lose her courage.

“Very well. Then I will only see if there is any note or letter for me from Mr. Thornton—he said he would let me know anything he might hear about these houses—and then we will set off. We will keep the cab; it will be safer than losing ourselves, and being too late for the train this afternoon.”

There were no letters waiting. So they began their house-hunting.

Thirty pounds a year was all they could afford. In Hampshire, for that sum, they might have found a roomy house with a pleasant garden—walls warm with fruit, perhaps, and a kitchen where one could smell the year turning through stored apples, pickled walnuts, hanging herbs. Here, even the necessary accommodation of two sitting-rooms and four bedrooms seemed unattainable. The houses were cramped and over-ornamented, or damp and narrow, or else beyond their reach. They went through their list, rejecting each as they visited it, and at last found themselves looking at each other in dismay, as if the very streets had shut like a mouth against them.

“We must go back to the second, I think,” said Margaret at length, taking the reins of the problem because someone must. “That one—in Crampton, don’t they call the suburb? There were three sitting-rooms—do you remember how we laughed at the number compared with the three bedrooms? But I have planned it all.”

Her mind, once engaged, moved quickly, arranging rooms as she might have arranged the courses of a meal, making each serve a purpose and conceal a lack. “The front room downstairs is to be your study and our dining-room—poor papa!—for you know we settled mamma is to have as cheerful a sitting-room as we can get. And that front room upstairs, with the atrocious blue and pink paper and the heavy cornice—oh, papa, what taste!—had really a pretty view over the plain, with a great bend of river, or canal, or whatever it is, down below. Then I could have the little bedroom behind, in that projection at the head of the first flight of stairs over the kitchen—you know—and you and mamma the room behind the drawing-room; and that closet in the roof will make you a splendid dressing-room.”

Mr. Hale listened with the half-smile of a man grateful to be saved from details. “But Dixon, and the girl we are to have to help?”

“Oh, wait a minute,” said Margaret, a flash of humour cutting through her weariness. “I am overpowered by the discovery of my own genius for management. Dixon is to have—let me see—I had it once—the back sitting-room. I think she will like that. She grumbles so much about the stairs at Heston; and the girl is to have that sloping attic over your room and mamma’s. Won’t that do?”

“I dare say it will,” said he. Then his brow knit, as his eye returned to what offended him most: “But the papers. What taste! And the over-loading such a house with colour and such heavy cornices!”

“Never mind, papa!” Margaret answered, forcing cheerfulness as one forces a sauce to thicken when it threatens to break. “Surely you can charm the landlord into re-papering one or two of the rooms—the drawing-room and your bedroom—for mamma will come most in contact with them; and your bookshelves will hide a great deal of that gaudy pattern in the dining-room.”

“Then you think it the best? If so, I had better go at once and call on this Mr. Donkin, to whom the advertisement refers me. I will take you back to the hotel, where you can order lunch, and rest; and by the time it is ready, I shall be with you. I hope I shall be able to get new papers.”

Margaret hoped so too, though she said nothing. She had never come fairly into contact with the taste that loves ornament—however bad—more than plainness and simplicity, those quiet frameworks within which elegance can breathe. It felt to her not merely ugly, but as if some loud, dominant vocabulary had been pasted over the walls, drowning out a more delicate speech.

Her father brought her through the entrance of the hotel and left her at the foot of the staircase, then went out to find Mr. Donkin, the landlord of the house they had fixed upon. Just as Margaret put her hand on the door of their sitting-room, a quick-stepping waiter followed her.

“I beg your pardon, ma’am. The gentleman was gone so quickly, I had no time to tell him. Mr. Thornton called almost directly after you left; and as I understood, from what the gentleman said, you would be back in an hour, I told him so; and he came again about five minutes ago, and said he would wait for Mr. Hale. He is in your room now, ma’am.”

“Thank you,” said Margaret. “My father will return soon, and then you can tell him.”

She opened the door and went in with that straight, fearless, dignified presence that belonged to her as naturally as breathing. She felt no awkwardness; her habits of society served her as armour. Here was someone come on business to her father—someone who had been obliging—and she was disposed to treat him with full civility.

Mr. Thornton, however, was more surprised—and, in his way, discomfited—than she. Instead of the quiet, middle-aged clergyman he expected, a young lady came forward with frank dignity—a kind of woman different from most he was in the habit of seeing. Her dress was very plain: a close straw bonnet of the best material and shape, trimmed with white ribbon; a large Indian shawl hanging in long, heavy folds about her, worn with the unconscious majesty of drapery. He had heard Mr. Hale had a daughter, but had imagined a little girl. He did not understand who she was at once, and his words, for an instant, would not come.

“Mr. Thornton, I believe!” said Margaret, after a half-moment’s pause that seemed to settle the air. “Will you sit down. My father brought me to the door not a minute ago; but unfortunately he was not told that you were here, and he has gone away on some business. He will come back almost directly. I am sorry you have had the trouble of calling twice.”

He was a man used to authority, used to giving directions that were obeyed; yet she seemed to assume some quiet rule over him at once. A moment before, he had been getting impatient at the waste of his time on a market-day; now, he found himself taking the offered seat as if it were the only natural thing.

“Do you know where it is that Mr. Hale has gone to?” he asked. “Perhaps I might be able to find him.”

“He has gone to a Mr. Donkin in Canute Street. He is the landlord of the house my father wishes to take in Crampton.”

Mr. Thornton knew the house. He had seen the advertisement, and, at Mr. Bell’s request, had gone to look at it, meaning to assist Mr. Hale to the best of his power; and, if truth were told, he was stirred also by his own interest in the case of a clergyman who had given up his living under such circumstances. He had thought the Crampton house really just the thing—until he saw Margaret. Now, with her before him, he began to feel ashamed of having imagined it would do very well, in spite of the vulgarity that had struck him even then. The rooms, the cornices, the gaudy papers: they seemed suddenly more offensive, as if he had offered coarse bread to someone accustomed to finer baking.

Margaret could not help her looks; but the short curled upper lip, the round, massive up-turned chin, the manner of carrying her head, her movements full of a soft feminine defiance, always gave strangers the impression of haughtiness. She was tired now, and would much rather have remained silent and taken the rest her father had planned; but she owed it to herself, she thought, to behave like a gentlewoman—to speak courteously from time to time to this stranger, though her courtesy was not over-brushed, and not over-polished, after her rough encounter with Milton’s streets and crowds.

She wished he would go, as he had once spoken of doing, instead of sitting there and answering with curt sentences whatever small remarks she made. She took off her shawl and hung it over the back of her chair, and sat facing him and the light. Her full beauty met his eye: the round white, flexible throat rising out of her full yet lithe figure; the lips moving so slightly as she spoke, hardly breaking the cold serene look of her face; the eyes, with their soft gloom, meeting his with quiet maiden freedom.

He almost said to himself that he did not like her before their brief, stunted conversation ended. He tried, in irritation, to compensate for the mortification he felt—that while he looked at her with an admiration he could not repress, she looked at him, he thought, with proud indifference, taking him for what he told himself in a kind of angry bitterness he was: a great rough fellow, without grace or refinement. Her quiet coldness he interpreted as contempt, and resented it until he was near to rising and leaving, determined to have no more to do with these Hales and their superciliousness.

Just as Margaret had exhausted her last subject—and “conversation” was hardly the word for that thin exchange of short speeches—Mr. Hale came in. With his pleasant, gentlemanly courtesy and apology, he somehow reinstated his name and family in Mr. Thornton’s good opinion, as if warmth had been put back into a room that had grown chill.

Mr. Hale and his visitor spoke at length of their mutual friend, Mr. Bell. Margaret, glad her duty of entertaining was over, went to the window and tried to make herself more familiar with the strange aspect of the street below. She became so absorbed in watching that she scarcely heard her father speak, and he had to repeat himself.

“Margaret! the landlord will persist in admiring that hideous paper, and I am afraid we must let it remain.”

“Oh dear! I am sorry!” she replied, and turned over in her mind the possibility of hiding part of it with some of her sketches—brightening a wall by laying art over ugliness, as one might mask a harsh taste in broth with herbs. But she gave it up as likely only to make bad worse: a poor remedy makes a worse illness.

Meanwhile her father, with a kindly country hospitality that had carried him through many a parish call, pressed Mr. Thornton to stay to luncheon with them. It would have been very inconvenient for Mr. Thornton to do so; yet he felt he might have yielded if Margaret, by word or look, had seconded her father’s invitation. He was glad she did not. And yet he was irritated at her for not doing so—an irritation that surprised even himself, as if he had expected her, without any right, to speak his name into welcome.

She gave him a low, grave bow when he left. He went out feeling more awkward and self-conscious in every limb than he had ever done in his life before, as though that quiet bow had struck some hidden string.

“Well, Margaret,” said Mr. Hale, turning back as soon as the door closed, “now to luncheon as fast as we can. Have you ordered it?”

“No, papa. That man was here when I came home, and I have never had an opportunity.”

“Then we must take anything we can get. He must have been waiting a long time, I’m afraid.”

“It seemed exceedingly long to me,” Margaret answered, letting out a breath as if she had held it too long. “I was just at the last gasp when you came in. He never went on with any subject, but gave little, short, abrupt answers.”

“Very much to the point though, I should think,” said Mr. Hale, who liked clearness as he liked honesty. “He is a clear-headed fellow. He said—did you hear?—that Crampton is on gravelly soil, and by far the most healthy suburb in the neighbourhood of Milton.”

When they returned to Heston, there was the day’s account to be given to Mrs. Hale, who lay with her tea-tray near her, and asked questions in the pauses between sips. The tea had a sea-air tang to it, as if the moisture of the place insisted upon flavouring even their domestic comfort.

“And what is your correspondent, Mr. Thornton, like?” asked Mrs. Hale at last.

“Ask Margaret,” said her husband. “She and he had a long attempt at conversation while I was away speaking to the landlord.”

“Oh! I hardly know what he is like,” said Margaret lazily, too tired to tax her powers of description. Then, rousing herself as if accuracy were a duty, she added, “He is a tall, broad-shouldered man, about—how old, papa?”

“I should guess about thirty.”

“About thirty—with a face that is neither exactly plain nor yet handsome—nothing remarkable—not quite a gentleman; but that was hardly to be expected.”

“Not vulgar or common though,” put in Mr. Hale, rather jealous of any disparagement of the sole friend he had in Milton.

“Oh, no!” said Margaret. “With such an expression of resolution and power, no face, however plain in feature, could be either vulgar or common. I should not like to have to bargain with him; he looks very inflexible. Altogether a man who seems made for his niche, mamma—sagacious, and strong, as becomes a great tradesman.”

“Don’t call the Milton manufacturers tradesmen, Margaret,” said her father. “They are very different.”

“Are they?” Margaret replied, the faintest touch of resistance in her tone. “I apply the word to all who have something tangible to sell; but if you think the term is not correct, papa, I won’t use it. But, oh mamma! speaking of vulgarity and commonness, you must prepare yourself for our drawing-room paper. Pink and blue roses, with yellow leaves! And such a heavy cornice round the room!”

Yet when at last they removed to their new house in Milton, the obnoxious papers were gone. The landlord received their thanks very composedly, letting them believe—if they liked—that he had relented from his expressed determination not to re-paper. There was no particular need to tell them that what he would not do for a Reverend Mr. Hale, unknown in Milton, he was only too glad to do at the one short, sharp remonstrance of Mr. Thornton, the wealthy manufacturer.

It took the rooms’ new paper—its small sprigs and pale prettiness, the sort of pattern meant to coax cheerfulness out of plain plaster—to make the house in Milton seem even tolerable. And yet it needed more—more than paper and polish could supply; more than could be bought, or carried in a removal-van, or unpacked from straw.

The thick yellow fogs of November had come on before Mrs. Hale crossed the threshold. The bend of the river that was said to open the valley into something like a view lay utterly blotted out; the world beyond the panes had been rubbed away to a smear of choking white. Even indoors the mist seemed to creep, insinuating itself under door and sash, leaving a faint wet on the knuckles when you touched the latch, and a taste like soot on the tongue.

Margaret and Dixon had worked for two days without pause—lifting, setting, scolding, dusting, and making a kind of order out of other people’s disorderly packing. There were still boxes with their cords uncut, chair-legs wrapped in paper, and a litter of straw that clung in corners as if it had rooted there. But all their strength had gone, not to Margaret’s own room, nor to any showy part of the house, but into one purpose: to make Mrs. Hale’s chamber ready—warm, quiet, and as like Helstone as a smoky northern lodging could be made.

Mrs. Hale came in, stood for a moment as if the very air had struck her back, and then, with a blankness that frightened Margaret more than any tears, said—

“Oh, Margaret! are we to live here?”

Margaret’s heart answered before her lips could. She forced herself to speak evenly, as if this were only a trifling change of weather.

“Oh—the fogs in London are sometimes far worse.”

“But then you knew that London itself, and friends lay behind it. Here—well! we are desolate. Oh Dixon, what a place this is!”

Dixon’s face tightened as if she had been slapped.

“Indeed, ma’am, I’m sure it will be your death before long, and then I know who’ll—stay! Miss Hale, that’s far too heavy for you to lift.”

Margaret had her hands already under the edge of a chest. The wood was damp-cold, the iron nails gritty with dust.

“Not at all, thank you, Dixon,” she answered, with a coldness that was less anger than the sort of self-command that comes of having no time to break down. “The best thing we can do for mamma is to get her room quite ready for her to go to bed, while I go and bring her a cup of coffee.”

Coffee was one of the few immediate comforts she could promise—heat, bitterness, the clean, sharp smell of it rising in a room that otherwise smelt of damp paper, coal smoke, and the sourness of unpacked things. She went to the kitchen and made it herself; she measured the grounds with care—what little there was had to last—poured the water when it had just ceased its furious boiling, and let the dark infusion stand to gather strength. The small domestic ritual steadied her. The kettle sang, then subsided; the spoon tapped the cup; the thick liquid poured with a sound almost cheerful, and the smell—warm and honest—seemed for a moment to stand between her mother and that raw fog outside.

But the whole house was steeped in disheartenment. Mr. Hale, too, moved like a man who had lost his road in a familiar field and could not admit he was afraid.

“Margaret,” he said, going to the window as if the sight of the town might supply him with courage, “I do believe this is an unhealthy place. Only suppose that your mother’s health or yours should suffer. I wish I had gone into some country place in Wales; this is really terrible.”

There was no comfort to be given—not the kind he asked for. They were there. The smoke and fog were not a bad dream, to be shaken off by morning; they were circumstance, and circumstance had shut as thickly round them as the mist that pressed its pallid face to the glass.

Only the day before, when the last bills were gathered, and the little store of ready money told out and found nearly spent, Margaret had seen her father’s dismay—quiet, ashamed, and helpless in its gentleness. The move, the fortnight at Heston, the thousand small necessities that seem to spring up like nettles when you change your home—almost all had gone. There was no turning back, no choosing Wales after all.

That night, when the first exhaustion came and left her awake in its place, Margaret sat in her own room and understood it: Milton was not merely where they lodged; it was the wall against which their hopes must now learn to live.

Her bedroom was in the long narrow projection at the back. The window set sideways in the oblong looked upon another blank projection opposite, not ten feet away—brick, damp, and darkened by fog, looming through the vapour like a barrier built on purpose to forbid the idea of distance. The air in the room was heavy with smoke, though no fire burned there; it had travelled in from elsewhere, clung to the curtains, and settled on her skin as if it meant to stain her thoughts.

Inside, everything was confusion. She had spent the day arranging her mother’s comforts; her own trunk stood half-open, and a box served for a chair. On it lay a direction-card, and at the sight of it her mind sprang backward with the suddenness of pain: it might have been written at Helstone. Helstone—green, beloved, with its soft syllables that belonged to her tongue and memory alike. The name was like the taste of a fruit out of season—sweet, and almost unbearable.

She might have sunk into mere wretchedness; but some part of her, practical and proud, resisted the indulgence of despair. She remembered Edith’s letter—the one she had only half read amid the noise of arrival—and snatched at it as at any hand held out in the dark.

It was full of Corfu: their voyage along the Mediterranean; music and dancing on board; the new life opening as easily as a flower. Edith wrote fluently, with a certain graceful abundance—enough particulars to let Margaret build the scene for herself. A villa high upon rocks; a trellised balcony; white cliffs and deep blue sea; days passed in boating or picnics; everything out-of-doors and pleasure-seeking, as if the very air were a kind of freedom.

Captain Lennox attended drill. Edith, the most musical officer’s wife there, copied the new popular tunes from the latest English music for the bandmaster, as if that were labour. These were their hardships. And then, as if it were the simplest thing, she hoped that if the regiment stayed another year Margaret might come and make a long visit—an invitation tossed like a ribbon across leagues of sea and difference.

She reminded Margaret, affectionately, of a day twelve-month ago in Harley Street: rain all day long; her refusal to wear a new gown to a stupid dinner, lest it be splashed in going to the carriage; and how at that very dinner they had first met Captain Lennox.

Yes. Margaret remembered. She remembered the abundant dinners and smooth arrangements; the stately handsomeness; the noiseless service; the settled assumption that life was meant to be easy if only one kept within the right circle. That memory came back to her now with a sharpness that was almost physical: she could have named the scent of the drawing-room—flowers, wax, and warmed upholstery—and heard the soft rustle of dresses like the murmur of a sheltered sea.

That world rolled on without them. The habitual dinners, the calls, the dancing evenings would be going on as if forever; Aunt Shaw might be gone, Edith transported to a Mediterranean balcony, yet the set would close up like water after a ship passes—no mark left to show where any of them had been. And she—Margaret Hale, who had once moved within it—was surely less missed than any.

Perhaps only Henry Lennox would think of her; and he would strive not to, because of the pain she had caused him. He had often boasted of his power to put disagreeable thoughts away, as one shuts a drawer and forgets what lies in it.

Her mind went a little farther still, into that region where “what might have been” lives like a ghost. If she had cared for him as a lover, if she had accepted him, and then this change in her father’s opinions—and with it the loss of position—had come, she could not doubt how impatiently Mr. Lennox would have received it. The world’s rough wholesale judgment was ready to label her father degraded; and such judgment would have galled a man of Henry’s temper.

It mortified her; and yet she could bear it, because she knew her father’s purity of purpose. That knowledge—so plain, so solemn—was like bread in a time of scarcity: not delicacy, but sustenance. It strengthened her to endure his errors, grave though they seemed to her.

By the time she folded Edith’s letter, she had reached a weary kind of gratitude. They were at the lowest now; it could scarcely be worse. When Edith’s astonishment and Aunt Shaw’s dismay arrived in letters, they would meet them bravely.
