She undressed slowly, feeling the strange luxury of leisure after all the day’s hurry, though it was late. She fell asleep hoping for brightness—either in the world or in herself. Had she known how long it would be before any real brightness came, her heart might have failed.

The season was unpropitious to health as well as spirits. The fogs seemed to sit on the lungs. Mrs. Hale caught a severe cold almost at once; her voice grew thin and her breathing troubled, as if the air itself demanded payment. Dixon, too, was evidently not well; but Margaret could not insult her more than by proposing to spare her. Dixon would rather die than be “saved” by Miss Hale.

They could hear of no girl to assist. Such as might have come were at the factories. Those who applied were dismissed with sharp scolding by Dixon for imagining that girls of their kind could ever be trusted in a gentleman’s house. So a charwoman was kept in almost constant employ, coming and going with her buckets and her blunt, patient way of scrubbing away at Milton grime that seemed to breed afresh the moment your back was turned.

Margaret longed to send for Charlotte; but Charlotte was too good a servant for what they could now afford, and the distance was too great. Their new economy had edges that cut.

Meanwhile Mr. Hale found pupils—recommended by Mr. Bell, or by the more immediate influence of Mr. Thornton. Most were boys of an age when in other places they might still be at school; but Milton had its own stern education. Here, it was believed that to make a lad into a good tradesman he must be caught young and acclimated to the mill, the office, the warehouse. If he were sent to even the Scotch universities, he came back unsettled for commerce; how much more if he went to Oxford or Cambridge, where he could not enter till he was eighteen? So manufacturers set their sons to work at fourteen or fifteen, pruning away all off-shoots in the direction of literature in hopes the whole vigour of the plant might be forced into trade.

And yet there were wiser parents—men who knew their own deficiencies, and had sense enough to strive against them; and some, no longer youths but grown men, who had the stern humility to learn late what they should have learnt early.

Mr. Thornton was perhaps the oldest of Mr. Hale’s pupils. He was certainly his favourite.

So much did Mr. Hale quote his opinions, and with such regard, that in time it became a domestic joke to wonder what learning could be accomplished in an hour when so much of it appeared to have been spent in conversation. Margaret even encouraged the lightness with which her father spoke of Mr. Thornton, because she felt that her mother watched this new friendship with a kind of jealousy. In Helstone, where Mr. Hale’s days had been occupied with books and parishioners, Mrs. Hale had seemed to care little whether she saw much of him or not; but now, when he looked eagerly forward to each renewal of intercourse with Mr. Thornton, she was hurt, as if for the first time he preferred another companionship to her own.

Mr. Hale’s praise had the usual effect of praise too often repeated: it made others inclined to rebel against hearing Aristides called the Just. After more than twenty years of quiet life in a country parsonage, there was something dazzling to him in the energy that conquered difficulties, in the power of Milton—its machinery, its men. He yielded to the grandeur of it without caring to inquire much into the details of its exercise.

Margaret went less abroad among machinery and men; saw less of power in its public effect; and, as it happened, she was thrown into contact with those who suffered acutely in all measures meant for masses of people—exceptions trampled in the procession. The question that began to form in her mind, as steady as it was quiet, was whether everything had been done to make the sufferings of those exceptions as small as possible; whether the helpless had been gently lifted out of the conqueror’s road—or ground under his wheels.

It fell to her share, too, to look out for a servant to assist Dixon; Dixon had at first undertaken to find just the right person to do the rough work. But Dixon’s idea of a helpful girl was shaped by Helstone—by tidy elder scholars at the village school who had been proud to come to the parsonage on a busy day, and who treated Mrs. Dixon with the respect—and more than respect, with a kind of frightened homage—that they paid to Mr. and Mrs. Hale.

Dixon was not unconscious of that old reverence; she had enjoyed it. In Milton, where no one knew the past and no one cared for it, she was like a dethroned queen who still expected courtiers to shade their eyes from her splendour. Nothing but her faithful love for Mrs. Hale made her endure the rough independent way in which the Milton girls who came to ask for the place answered her questions. They even questioned her in return, doubtful of the solvency of a family that lived in a house of thirty pounds a year and yet kept two servants, one of them so high and mighty.

Mr. Hale was no longer “the Vicar”; he was a man who spent at a certain rate, and might not always be able to.

Margaret grew weary of the accounts Dixon brought to her mother—endless tales of insolence, of manners that seemed to Dixon almost criminal. Not that Margaret was insensible to it: she, too, was repelled by the rough uncourtesy; she, too, shrank with fastidious pride from hail-fellow familiarity, and resented the open curiosity of people who asked, without disguise, what business her family had in Milton if they were not “in trade.”

But the more she felt an impertinence, the more silent she became about it; and if she took the search upon herself, she could at least spare her mother the recital of every disappointment. So she went up and down, in and out of butchers’ shops and grocers’, asking after a nonpareil of a girl; lowering her expectations each week as she learnt how difficult it was, in a manufacturing town, to tempt any one from the better wages and greater independence of the mill.

It was a trial to go out alone in this busy bustling place. Mrs. Shaw’s notions of propriety, and her own reliance on attendants in London, had made it an established thing that a footman must accompany Edith and Margaret if they went beyond Harley Street or the immediate neighbourhood. Margaret had silently rebelled against those limits at the time; and later, in Helstone, she had doubly enjoyed her freedom, walking as fancy led her—sometimes bounding into a run, sometimes standing still as stone to listen.

There, the soundscape had been her companion: the soft scold of a thrush in the holly; the drip of water in ditches; the hush that is not emptiness but living quiet. Even the church-bell, when it spoke, seemed to be speaking the dialect of home, with a tone that belonged to the place and to her childhood.

Here, in Milton, the streets imposed an even decorous pace, and worse than that—an unceasing clatter and roar that seemed to grind the nerves. The town did not so much speak as shout. Carts rattled over stones; iron rang on iron; voices rose and collided; and far off, through everything, there was that continual undertone—like a giant breathing through a sooty cloth—the mills’ labouring sound. It was as if the air itself had become a machine.

The side of the town on which Crampton lay was especially a thoroughfare for the factory people. In the back streets there were many mills out of which poured streams of men and women two or three times a day. Until Margaret learned their hours of ingress and egress, she constantly fell among them.

They came rushing along, bold-faced, fearless, loud with laughs and jests—often aimed at those who appeared above them. The unrestrained voices, the careless breaking of common street politeness, frightened Margaret at first. The girls, with rough but not unfriendly freedom, commented on her dress; even touched her shawl or gown to discover the exact material, as if cloth were a language they all understood. Once or twice she was asked, directly and without embarrassment, where such an article had been bought.

There was such simple reliance on her womanly sympathy in their love of dress, and on her kindliness, that, once she understood, she answered readily enough, even smiling.

She did not mind meeting any number of girls, boisterous as they were. But she alternately dreaded and fired up against the workmen, who commented not on her dress but on her looks, with the same open fearlessness. She, who had always felt that even a refined remark on her appearance was an impertinence, had now to endure undisguised admiration shouted across a street.

And yet the outspokenness had in it a sort of blunt innocence. They meant no harm to her delicacy; but she was too startled by the disorderly tumult at first to perceive it. Out of fear came indignation. Her cheeks would burn, her dark eyes flash, at some speech that struck her like a thrown stone.

Later, safe at home, she would find herself half amused even while she resented it. Once, after she had passed a group of men, several wishing openly that she were their sweetheart, one lingerer called after her, “Your bonny face, my lass, makes the day look brighter.”

Another day, as she walked with an unconscious smile at some passing thought, a poorly dressed middle-aged workman said to her, “You may well smile, my lass; many a one would smile to have such a bonny face.”

He looked so careworn that Margaret’s immediate impulse was not anger but pity. She gave him an answering smile—glad, in spite of herself, to think that her looks, such as they were, might have called up a pleasant thought in a man whose life seemed all labour and want.

He appeared to understand her glance. From that time a silent recognition was established between them whenever chance threw them across each other’s paths. They never exchanged another word; nothing passed but that first compliment, and yet Margaret found herself thinking of him with more interest than of anyone else in Milton.

Once or twice on Sundays she saw him walking with a girl—evidently his daughter—who looked, if possible, more unhealthy than he was.

One day, early spring, Margaret and her father had walked as far as the fields that lay round the town. The air there, away from the close streets, was thinner and seemed for a moment to wash the soot from the lungs; yet even there the distant sounds of Milton followed like a great pulse—now louder, now fainter, never wholly absent. Margaret gathered such hedge and ditch flowers as she could find—dog-violets, lesser celandines—each little blossom a quiet miracle in that soiled neighbourhood. She gathered them with an unspoken lament for Helstone’s profusion, where spring came like a festival and not like a grudged charity.

Her father left her to go into Milton upon some business; and on the road home she met the man and his daughter. The girl’s pale eyes fixed wistfully on the flowers in Margaret’s hand.

Acting on sudden impulse, Margaret held them out.

“Will you take them?”

The girl’s pale blue eyes lightened as she received the small bunch, as if she had been given something far beyond its worth. Her father spoke for her, his voice roughened by feeling he did not know how to show.

“Thank yo, Miss. Bessy’ll think a deal o’ them flowers; that hoo will; and I shall think a deal o’ yor kindness. Yo’re not of this country, I reckon?”

“No,” said Margaret, and the word came out with a half-sigh. “I come from the South—from Hampshire.” She chose the safer description, fearing to wound him by a name he might not know.

“That’s beyond London, I reckon? And I come fro’ Burnleyways, and forty miles to th’ North. And yet, yo see, North and South has both met and made kind o’ friends in this big smoky place.”

Margaret slackened her pace to walk beside them. The girl’s steps were slow, governed by weakness. Margaret turned to her, and spoke gently; the pity in her tone went straight, like warm broth to an empty stomach, to the father’s heart.

“I’m afraid you are not very strong.”

“No,” said the girl quietly, “nor never will be.”

“Spring is coming,” Margaret said, trying to suggest hope, as she might have offered a sweetmeat to a sick child.

“Spring nor summer will do me good,” the girl answered. It was not dramatic; it was simply said, as if she had long ago tasted that truth and found it bitter but certain.

Margaret looked up at the father, almost expecting him to contradict, or soften it. Instead he added, with a grim straightforwardness—

“I’m afeared hoo speaks the truth. I’m afeared hoo’s too far gone in a waste.”

“I shall have a spring where I am boun’ to,” Bessy said, her voice taking on a strange brightness, “and flowers, and amaranths, and shining robes besides.”

“Poor lass, poor lass!” her father murmured. “I’m none so sure o’ that; but it’s a comfort to thee, poor lass, poor lass. Poor father! it’ll be soon.”

Margaret was shocked—shocked to hear death spoken of so plainly, as if it were a neighbour expected at any hour. Yet she was not repelled. On the contrary, something in the blunt naming of things drew her nearer; it was another language, another dialect of feeling, and she could not yet translate it, but she could not doubt its sincerity.

“Where do you live?” she asked. “I think we must be neighbours; we meet so often on this road.”

“We put up at nine Frances Street—second turn to th’ left at after yo’ve past th’ Goulden Dragon.”

“And your name? I must not forget that.”

“I’m none ashamed o’ my name,” he answered, almost as if she had accused him. “It’s Nicholas Higgins. Hoo’s called Bessy Higgins. Whatten yo’ asking for?”

The last question startled Margaret. In Helstone it would have been understood that such enquiries meant a visit—a gentle, unquestioned sequence: name, place, call. Here, her intention seemed suddenly to wear the shape of intrusion. She felt shy; her face grew hot.

“I thought—I meant to come and see you.”

He looked at her as if measuring her right to do so; and she read, in his eye, a suspicion she had not expected.

“I’m none so fond of having strange folk in my house.”

Then, relenting as he saw the heightened colour on her cheeks, he added, with a grudging kindness that was still kindness—

“Yo’re a foreigner, as one may say, and maybe don’t know many folk here, and yo’ve given my wench here flowers out of yo’r own hand;—yo may come if yo like.”

Margaret was half amused, half nettled. Permission offered as if it were a favour conferred did not soothe her pride. For an instant she doubted whether she would ever cross their threshold.

But at the turn into Frances Street the girl stopped, held her flowers closer as if they were a treasure, and said with a quiet insistence—

“Yo’ll not forget yo’re to come and see us.”

“Aye, aye,” said her father impatiently, as if tenderness must be hurried lest it shame him. “Hoo’ll come. Hoo’s a bit set up now, because hoo thinks I might ha’ spoken more civilly; but hoo’ll think better on it, and come. I can read her proud bonny face like a book. Come along, Bess; there’s the mill bell ringing.”

And indeed the bell was ringing—metallic, urgent, not like the clear church-bell of Helstone marking holy time, but like a command that cut the air and drove bodies forward. Its sound folded itself into the town’s larger roar as naturally as smoke into fog.

Margaret went home, still hearing the bell in her head, wondering at her new acquaintances, and smiling in spite of herself at the man’s insight into what had passed in her mind.

From that day Milton grew brighter to her—not because spring made the streets beautiful (it did not), nor because time had reconciled her to smoke and fog (it had not), but because among the harsh voices and grimy stones she had found something living: a human interest, like a small fire kindled in an unkind climate, by which one might warm one’s hands and, perhaps, one’s heart.

The morning after Mr. Hale had come home from that strange, grave talk with Higgins and the pale, watchful girl who clung to her father’s sleeve, he mounted the narrow stairs to the little drawing-room at an hour when he was not commonly seen there. Milton’s day had begun with its usual accompaniments: a low, ceaseless grind as of hidden wheels; a pulse of distant stamping that shook the cups on the shelf; the thin, spiteful whistle of a wind that found every crack in the window-frame and made it sing. Even indoors, the town’s noise had a way of lodging under the skin.

Mr. Hale moved from one object to another, pausing as though to examine a vase, the stitch of the antimacassar, the very pattern of the carpet. Margaret, sewing near the fire, watched the restless pilgrimage. It was not curiosity that drove him; it was delay—a man touching harmless things to keep his fingers from trembling over the thing he feared to say.

At last he stopped short, as if he had come to a wall.

“My dear,” he began, and the words fell quickly, as though he must get them said before his courage cooled, “I’ve asked Mr. Thornton to come to tea to-night.”

Mrs. Hale lay back in her easy-chair, eyes closed, the habitual shadow of pain about her mouth. She started as if the name had been a draught through her thin frame.

“Mr. Thornton!—and to-night!” she cried, querulous in the way illness makes even gentle women sharp. “What in the world does the man want to come here for? And Dixon is washing my muslins and laces, and there is no soft water with these horrid east winds—which I suppose we shall have all the year round in Milton.”

“The wind is veering round, my dear,” said Mr. Hale, turning to look out as if the sky might justify him. The smoke from the chimneys drifted in a determined sheet, and the air outside had that iron taste of coal and wet brick. He spoke of compass-points with the uncertain confidence of one still new to the town, arranging east and west by the mere behaviour of the smoke.

“Don’t tell me!” Mrs. Hale shuddered up and pulled her shawl closer, as though she could shut out a whole climate with a fold of wool. “East or west wind, I suppose this man comes.”

Margaret’s lips curved with a flash of spirit, half amusement, half defiance—more colour than the room had held all morning.

“Oh, mamma, that shows you never saw Mr. Thornton. He looks like a person who would enjoy battling with every adverse thing he could meet with—enemies, winds, or circumstances. The more it rains and blows, the more certain we are to have him. But I’ll go and help Dixon. I’m getting to be a famous clear-starcher. And he won’t want any amusement beyond talking to papa.” She turned her bright, vexed gaze upon her father. “Papa, I am really longing to see the Pythias to your Damon. You know I never saw him but once, and then we were so puzzled to know what to say to each other that we did not get on particularly well.”

Mr. Hale’s face softened; yet there was a little anxious crease between his brows.

“I don’t know that you would ever like him, or think him agreeable, Margaret. He is not a lady’s man.”

Margaret drew her throat back, almost scornfully, as though the phrase itself were something sticky on the tongue.

“I don’t particularly admire ladies’ men, papa. But Mr. Thornton comes here as your friend—as one who has appreciated you—”

“The only person in Milton,” put in Mrs. Hale, with the languid bitterness of one who felt herself exiled among strangers.

“So we will give him a welcome,” Margaret answered, refusing to let the sentence end there, “and some cocoa-nut cakes. Dixon will be flattered if we ask her to make some; and I will undertake to iron your caps, mamma.”

It sounded easy when she said it—like the smoothing of a table-cloth with the palm. Yet, as the morning wore on, she found herself wishing, again and again, that Mr. Thornton were far enough away to make tea a matter of mere family bread and talk. She had meant to write to Edith; she had planned a good stretch of Dante, with its stern, orderly music that could drown Milton’s irregular clamour; she had meant to go down to the Higginses, to carry what little comfort words could carry where there was hunger. All those intentions were put aside and folded away, as neatly as Dixon demanded a cap should be folded, for the sake of an evening’s civility.

In the poky kitchen the air was thick with steam, soap, and that peculiar smell linen has when it is half clean and half still holding the memory of bodies and perfume. Dixon’s great copper bubbled like a temper; every time the wind shoved at the back door the flame under the boiler answered with a sudden roar, and the roof-beams gave a small complaint. Above it all came the town: the far-off, rhythmic thud that seemed to set its own measure to the beating of sheets; the sharp, intermittent shrieks—whether of engine or human throat, Margaret could not always tell—cutting the domestic sounds like a knife.

Dixon complained as she worked, as if complaint were the proper starch to stiffen her resolve against Milton. She lamented the hard water that would not rinse white, the east winds that made the muslin dry rough, the soot that settled like a curse no brushing could wholly remove. Margaret stood for hours, sleeves rolled, fingers reddened, coaxing cloth into obedience with iron and wrist, her mind doing the same thing—pressing down its own impatience for her father’s sake.

She listened, too, with a kind of strained sympathy, hoping that by giving Dixon the full satisfaction of her audience she might prevent the woman from carrying the tale of grievances upstairs to Mrs. Hale, whose nerves were like exposed threads. Margaret spoke little; the constant lift and set of the iron made its own mute conversation. Sometimes the smell of heated starch rose sweetly, like browned flour, and the thought of cocoa-nut cakes—Dixon’s careful beating of eggs, the rasp of the nut, the warm, buttery scent as they baked—seemed the only tender thing the day promised.

But weariness stole over her at last, with a slow, creeping certainty. It began behind her eyes, like a tightening band, and passed down into her throat until even her words felt heavy. More than once she had to remind herself—Mr. Hale’s gentle delight in his new friend, his gratitude at being treated as something other than a dissenting curiosity in Milton—to keep from letting irritation speak.

When at last she sat beside her mother again, she could hardly force her voice into playfulness.

“I am no longer Peggy the laundry-maid, mamma,” she said faintly, trying for a joke, “but Margaret Hale the lady.”

It was meant as a light thing tossed into the air to break the heaviness. But her mother, with pain sharpening every thought, took it as a confession of humiliation, and her colour rose with offended memory.

“Yes!” cried Mrs. Hale, and her voice had in it the old accent of the county drawing-rooms, proud and wounded. “If any one had told me, when I was Miss Beresford, and one of the belles of the country, that a child of mine would have to stand half a day in a little poky kitchen, working away like any servant, that we might prepare properly for the reception of a tradesman—and that this tradesman should be the only—”

“Oh, mamma!” Margaret sat upright, suddenly stung, as if the iron had touched her skin. “Don’t punish me for so careless a speech. I don’t mind ironing, or any kind of work for you and papa. I am myself a born and bred lady through it all—even though it comes to scouring a floor, or washing dishes. I am tired now, just for a little while; but in half an hour I shall be ready to do the same over again.” She drew a breath, and the effort of it showed. “And as to Mr. Thornton’s being in trade—why he can’t help that now, poor fellow. I don’t suppose his education would fit him for much else.”

Even as she defended him, something in her recoiled from the whole necessity—this shaping of their domestic peace to the presence of a man she did not know how to meet without constraint. The headache pressed harder; every sound from the street came in sharper, more jangling lines. She rose slowly and went to her own room, because just then she could not bear much more—neither her mother’s sharp, sick pride nor her own divided feelings.

At that very hour, in another house of Milton, there was a different kind of preparation going forward—one as exact, as severe, as a well-kept account-book.

Mrs. Thornton sat in her dining-room, large-boned and upright, a woman long past middle age whose strength had never been allowed to soften into ease. The room was handsomely furnished in a grim fashion: solid, heavy pieces that looked as though they had been chosen to withstand not fashion but time. She wore stout black silk, spotless as a creed. In her hands she held a great, long table-cloth of the finest texture, lifting it now and then against the light to search out thin places with the keen, practical care that wasted nothing. Her face moved slowly from one decided expression to another—no fluttering shades, no easy smiles; yet one looked twice at her, as passers-by in the street did, half turning their heads to gaze longer at the firm, severe dignity that went straight on without yielding.

There were no scattered books, no idle papers. Only Matthew Henry’s Bible commentaries lay in a neat, unquestioned pile on the massive side-board—six volumes, sombre as authority—flanked by a tea-urn on one side and a lamp on the other, as if devotion and domestic order had their appointed places.

From some remote apartment came the sound of a piano: a morceau de salon practised with great speed and little accuracy. Notes were missed; chords struck false; yet the performer, satisfied with mere loudness at the ends, drove on. In that house the music did not soothe; it jabbed at the air, careless of ear or nerve, an ornament that took no account of silence. Mrs. Thornton worked through it without flinching, as she worked through most things.

She heard a step—decisive, like her own—pass the dining-room door.

“John! Is that you?” she called.

Her son opened the door and showed himself.

“What has brought you home so early?” she asked, without softening her tone. “I thought you were going to tea with that friend of Mr. Bell’s—Mr. Hale?”

“So I am, mother. I am come home to dress!”

“Dress! humph!” Mrs. Thornton’s mouth tightened. “When I was a girl, young men were satisfied with dressing once in a day. Why should you dress to go and take a cup of tea with an old parson?”

“Mr. Hale is a gentleman,” said Mr. Thornton steadily, “and his wife and daughter are ladies.”

“Wife and daughter!” Mrs. Thornton repeated, as if the words were strange coin she must test between finger and thumb. “Do they teach too? What do they do? You have never mentioned them.”

“No! mother,” he answered, with a restrained impatience, “because I have never seen Mrs. Hale; I have only seen Miss Hale for half an hour.”

Mrs. Thornton’s needle paused. Her eyes, strong and unblinking, went over him as if she could read the future in the set of his shoulders.

“Take care you don’t get caught by a penniless girl, John.”

“I am not easily caught, mother, as I think you know.” His voice grew harder, and there was a quick flush, not of shame but of offence. “But I must not have Miss Hale spoken of in that way, which, you know, is offensive to me. I never was aware of any young lady trying to catch me yet, nor do I believe that any one has ever given themselves that useless trouble.”

Mrs. Thornton would not yield, whether from pride or from the habit of standing firm in her own house as she stood firm in the street.

“Well! I only say, take care. Perhaps our Milton girls have too much spirit and good feeling to go angling after husbands; but this Miss Hale comes out of the aristocratic counties, where, if all tales be true, rich husbands are reckoned prizes.”

Mr. Thornton’s brow contracted. He stepped farther into the room, as if he must come nearer to meet this suspicion head-on.

“Mother,” he said, and with the word there was a short, scornful laugh that seemed to crack like a whip in the air, “you will make me confess. The only time I saw Miss Hale, she treated me with a haughty civility which had a strong flavour of contempt in it. She held herself aloof from me as if she had been a queen, and I her humble, unwashed vassal. Be easy, mother.”

“No! I am not easy nor content either,” returned Mrs. Thornton, the very set of her jaw proclaiming her refusal. “What business had she—a renegade clergyman’s daughter—to turn up her nose at you! I would dress for none of them—a saucy set!—if I were you.”

He turned to leave; at the door he spoke back with the controlled courtesy that was, with him, a kind of iron.

“Mr. Hale is good, and gentle, and learned. He is not saucy. As for Mrs. Hale—I will tell you what she is like to-night, if you care to hear.”

He shut the door and was gone, his decisive step swallowed by the house’s other sounds: the piano’s reckless tinkling, the distant clink of work in some unseen room.

Mrs. Thornton sat rigid a moment, needle poised above the fine damask, as though the cloth itself might bear witness to insult.

“Despise my son!” she muttered at last, in a low voice thick with wrath. “Treat him as her vassal, indeed! Humph! I should like to know where she could find such another! Boy and man, he’s the noblest, stoutest heart I ever knew. I don’t care if I am his mother; I can see what’s what, and not be blind. I know what Fanny is; and I know what John is. Despise him!” Her lips pressed into a hard line. “I hate her!”

Mr. Thornton left his own house without returning to the dining-room, and set off at once for Crampton, walking as men do who are accustomed to measure minutes by the striking of a mill-clock and the turning of a shaft. He had no mind to seem careless of punctuality to Mr. Hale, whom he had begun to honour as friend and teacher; so, when the church-clock sent out its half-past seven—clear, metallic, and a little lonely through the evening air—he was already at the Hales’ door, waiting while Dixon’s steps advanced with the particular slowness of one who resents the very act of opening.

He was shown into the little drawing-room. Mr. Hale met him with that gentle, cordial manner which made welcome seem less like ceremony than like habit. Mrs. Hale sat wrapped in a shawl, the pallor of her face and the droop of her figure apologising for the faint languor of her greeting more plainly than any words could have done.

Margaret, who had been lighting the lamp because the dusk pressed early upon Milton, turned as he entered. The flame gathered itself into steadiness, and the lamplight made an island in the room’s deepening shadow; beyond it the windows were not smothered up and blinded as they were in many town houses, but left to admit the night—its dimness, and its quiet, and what scanty starlight Milton’s air would allow. The room itself seemed to Mr. Thornton to be the opposite of the great, handsome, weighty place he had lately quitted, where everything—chair, table, very wall—appeared built for eating and drinking, and where the single sign of womanhood was the one fixed seat his mother took, because her will ruled the house like law.

Here there was nothing glittering to throw back the light; no mirror, no scrap of bright glass to make an answering gleam. Yet the room held warmth—sober colour, breadth, and a kind of tender persistence of home, as if comfort were not an effect to be produced, but a memory kept alive. The old Helstone chintz—dear, familiar, almost rustic in its faded roses—hung in curtains and covered chairs, like a dialect spoken softly among strangers. An open davenport stood in the window opposite the door; in the other, a tall white china vase lifted wreaths of ivy and pale birch, with beech-leaves that had that coppery tint of late autumn, as if some southern hedge-row had sent its own token north. Work-baskets waited where hands might fall to them without thinking; books lay on a table as if lately set down, not displayed for binding. And behind the door another table stood ready for tea, covered with a white cloth on which cocoa-nut cakes were set, and oranges and ruddy American apples heaped on leaves—fruit that looked, even in their stillness, like stored sunlight.

To Mr. Thornton it had the air of being no special preparation, but the family’s ordinary decency and grace—their daily bread made visible. It seemed of a piece with Margaret.

She stood by the tea-table in a light muslin gown touched with pink, as if she had brought a little of Helstone’s bloom into Milton’s smoke. Her hands—round, ivory, quiet in their movement—went among the cups with a noiseless quickness that belonged to careful practice. A bracelet on her taper arm slid down over her wrist, troublesome with its own prettiness. He found his eyes straying to it again and again, following its fall and her impatient little push to send it back, until it tightened the soft flesh, and then loosening again—dropping as inevitably as a leaf that will not stay.

So little remained to be done when he came in, that he almost regretted how soon the necessity of eating and drinking must interrupt his watching of these small domestic motions. When Margaret handed him his cup she did it with the air of a proud person compelled into service; yet she noticed with exactness the instant he was ready for more. He saw her father take her finger and thumb—using them as if they were sugar-tongs—while he laughed softly at his own device; and he saw, too, the quick upward look she gave him, eyes full of light, half laughter and half love, in that mute household play.

Her head ached still; her paleness and her silence might have confessed it. Yet she held herself as if she would not let any pause, any awkwardness, any sense of neglect fall on her father’s guest through her failing. But there was no need; Mr. Hale and Mr. Thornton were already deep in their subject. When the tea-things were taken away, Margaret drew into a corner near her mother with her work, and let her thoughts go, as people do when they feel they will not be suddenly called upon to mend a gap.

She was brought back by a low remark from Mrs. Hale, and, looking up, was struck afresh by the visible difference between her father and Mr. Thornton—difference that spoke of opposite natures meeting, and, by their very opposition, attracting. Mr. Hale’s figure was slight; there were soft, wavering lines in his face, and a perpetual tremor of expression passing over it as every change of feeling showed itself. His eyelids were large and arched, giving his eyes a languid beauty almost feminine; his brows were finely curved and lifted high by that dreamy breadth of lid.

Mr. Thornton’s brows fell straighter and lower over deep-set eyes that were intent—keen enough to seem as if they would pierce to the core of what they looked upon, yet not sharp in a petty way. The lines of his face were few and firm, as though carved rather than grown; chiefly about the lips, which were slightly compressed. When he smiled—and it was rare—the effect was like sudden sunlight breaking through cloud: it altered the whole countenance from resolved severity to an honest, childlike relish of the moment. Margaret, against her will, liked that smile. It was the first thing she had admired in him; and now, as she saw him and her father leaning towards each other in talk, she thought she understood how two men so unlike could feel so strongly drawn.

She set her mother’s worsted-work in order and went back to her own, almost forgotten by Mr. Thornton, so wholly was he absorbed in describing the steam-hammer—its tremendous power, and the delicate obedience with which that might could be measured, controlled, and made to do small, exact work. The very sound of it seemed to enter the room through his words: the imagined thunder of iron on iron, the shudder through the earth, the quick pause, the repeated stroke, ordered by human thought. Mr. Hale listened with the delight of a man to whom power becomes wonderful precisely when it is governed; and it called up for him the old tales where genii fill the sky one instant and the next compress themselves into a vessel a child can carry.

“And this imagination of power,” said Mr. Thornton, “this practical realisation of a gigantic thought, came out of one man’s brain in our good town. That very man has it in him to mount, step by step, from wonder to wonder; and if he were gone, I’ll be bound there are those among us who could spring into the breach and carry on the war that compels—all material power shall be compelled—to yield to science.”

“Your boast reminds me,” said Mr. Hale, smiling, “of the old lines—‘I’ve a hundred captains in England,’ he said, ‘As good as ever was he.’”

At the sudden leap from cog-wheels to Chevy Chace, Margaret looked up with a puzzled wonder, as if she had heard two dialects collide in one sentence.

“It is no boast of mine,” Mr. Thornton replied. “It is plain matter-of-fact. I won’t deny I am proud of belonging to a town—or district, rather—whose necessities give birth to such grandeur of conception. I would rather be a man toiling, suffering—nay, failing and successless—here, than lead a dull prosperous life in the old worn grooves of what you call more aristocratic society in the South, with their slow days of careless ease. One may be clogged with honey and unable to rise and fly.”

It was the word “honey,” perhaps—the easy contempt in it, as if sweetness were only a weight—that pricked Margaret into speech. She had sat quiet, working, keeping down her headache; but now her cheeks flushed, and angry tears came, because he had touched the place where her love of Helstone lived like an old song that will not be translated.

“You are mistaken,” she said, with fond vehemence. “You do not know anything about the South. If there is less adventure, or less progress—I suppose I must not say less excitement—from the gambling spirit of trade that seems requisite to force out these inventions, there is less suffering also. I see men here in the streets who look ground down by some pinching sorrow or care—who are not only sufferers but haters. In the South we have our poor, but there is not that terrible expression in their faces of a sullen sense of injustice which I see here. You do not know the South, Mr. Thornton.”

And with that she shut her lips, angry with herself for speaking so much, and yearning, in the silence she forced upon herself, after the green lanes and homely fields of Hampshire—after the very sounds of Helstone, where the loudest thing was wind in the leaves or the distant ring of a church-bell that seemed made to bless, not to command. Here, even in a quiet room, Milton’s far-off roar was always somewhere—like a continual threat under speech, as if the town’s iron lungs could never truly rest.

“And may I say you do not know the North?” he asked. There was an inexpressible gentleness in his tone, because he saw he had hurt her.

She would not answer; she could not trust her voice.

“At any rate,” said Mrs. Hale, who had been listening with the fretfulness of a sufferer, “you will allow, Mr. Thornton, that Milton is a much more smoky, dirty town than you will ever meet with in the South.”

“I’m afraid I must give up its cleanliness,” he said, and that quick gleam of a smile came and went. “But we are bidden by parliament to burn our own smoke; so I suppose, like good little children, we shall do as we are bid—some time.”

“But I think you told me you had altered your chimneys so as to consume the smoke,” said Mr. Hale.

“Mine were altered by my own will, before parliament meddled. It was an immediate outlay; it repays me in the saving of coal. I’m not sure I should have done it if I had waited for the act. At any rate, I should have waited to be informed against and fined, and given all the trouble in yielding that I legally could. But laws that depend upon informers and fines become inert by the odiousness of their own machinery. I doubt if there’s been a chimney in Milton informed against for five years past, though some are constantly sending out one-third of their coal in what is called here unparliamentary smoke.”

“I only know,” Mrs. Hale persisted, “that it is impossible to keep muslin blinds clean here above a week together; and at Helstone we have had them up for a month and more, and not had them look dirty then. And as for hands—Margaret, how many times did you say you had washed your hands this morning before twelve o’clock? Three times, was it not?”

“Yes, mamma.”

The small domestic fact—hands made grimy by air itself—fell among the larger talk like flour on a dark board: it showed at once what could not be argued away. Margaret, looking down at her work, felt again that Milton did not merely look different; it sounded different, and smelt different, and laid its claim on skin and cloth and breath, as if it meant to write itself on every living thing.

“You seem to have a strong objection to acts of parliament and all legislation affecting your mode of management down here,” said Mr. Hale.

“Yes, I have. Many others have as well, and with justice, I think. The whole machinery—I don’t mean the wood and iron now—of the cotton trade is so new, there’s no wonder it does not work well in every part all at once. Seventy years ago what was it? And now what is it not? Raw, crude materials came together. Men of the same level, as regarded education and station, took suddenly the different positions of masters and men, owing to the mother-wit that made some far-seeing as to what future lay concealed in that rude model of Sir Richard Arkwright’s. The rapid development of a new trade gave those early masters enormous power—wealth and command. Not merely over the workmen; over purchasers—over the whole world’s market. Why, I can give you an instance: an advertisement, not fifty years ago, in a Milton paper, that so-and-so—one of the half-dozen calico-printers—would close his warehouse at noon each day; therefore all purchasers must come before that hour. Fancy a man dictating the time when he would sell and when he would not sell. Now, I believe, if a good customer chose to come at midnight, I should get up, and stand hat in hand to receive his orders.”

Margaret’s lip curled; yet she listened in spite of herself. She could not drift away now; his words had the hard savour of fact, like strong tea without sugar—bitter perhaps, but warming.

“I name such things to show what almost unlimited power the manufacturers had at the beginning of this century. The men were rendered dizzy by it. Because a man was successful in his ventures, there was no reason his mind should be well-balanced in other things. On the contrary, his sense of justice—his simplicity—were often smothered under the glut of wealth. They tell strange tales of the wild extravagance of living indulged in on gala-days by those early cotton-lords. There can be no doubt, too, of the tyranny they exercised over their work-people. You know the proverb, Mr. Hale—‘Set a beggar on horseback, and he’ll ride to the devil.’ Well—some of these early manufacturers did ride to the devil in magnificent style—crushing human bone and flesh under their horses’ hoofs without remorse. But by-and-by came a reaction: more factories, more masters; more men were wanted. The power of masters and men became more evenly balanced; and now the battle is pretty fairly waged between us. We will hardly submit to the decision of an umpire, much less to the interference of a meddler with only a smattering of the facts of the case, even though that meddler be called the High Court of Parliament.”

“Is there necessity for calling it a battle between the two classes?” asked Mr. Hale. “I know, from your using the term, it is one which gives a true idea of the real state of things to your mind.”

“It is true,” Mr. Thornton answered. “And I believe it to be as much a necessity as that prudent wisdom and good conduct are always opposed to—and doing battle with—ignorance and improvidence. It is one of the great beauties of our system, that a working-man may raise himself into the power and position of a master by his own exertions and behaviour; that every one who rules himself to decency and sobriety of conduct, and attention to duty, comes over to our ranks. It may not always be as a master; but as an overlooker, a cashier, a book-keeper, a clerk—one on the side of authority and order.”

“You consider all who are unsuccessful in raising themselves in the world, from whatever cause, as your enemies, then—if I understand you rightly,” said Margaret. Her voice was clear and cold; the words were like the click of a shut knife.

“As their own enemies, certainly,” he returned quickly, piqued by the haughty disapproval in her tone and in the very shape of her sentence. But almost at once his honesty checked him. The answer had been too nimble, too much of a dodge; and, proud as she was, scornful as she might choose to be, he owed it to himself to speak the truth of what he meant.

He could best explain by telling something of his own life. The thought made him flush—only for a moment, a dark colour rising in his cheek as if he disliked the exposure. Yet he went straight on.

“I am not speaking without book. Sixteen years ago my father died under very miserable circumstances. I was taken from school, and had to become a man—as well as I could—in a few days. I had such a mother as few are blest with—a woman of strong power and firm resolve. We went into a small country town, where living was cheaper than in Milton, and where I got employment in a draper’s shop—a capital place, by the way, for obtaining a knowledge of goods. Week by week our income came to fifteen shillings, out of which three people had to be kept. My mother managed so that I put by three out of those fifteen shillings regularly. That made the beginning. That taught me self-denial. Now that I am able to afford my mother such comforts as her age, rather than her own wish, requires, I thank her silently on each occasion for the early training she gave me. And when I feel that in my own case it is no good luck, nor merit, nor talent—but simply the habits of life which taught me to despise indulgences not thoroughly earned—indeed, never to think twice about them—I believe that the suffering Miss Hale speaks of, stamped on the faces of the people of Milton, is but the natural punishment of dishonestly-enjoyed pleasure at some former period of their lives. I do not look on self-indulgent, sensual people as worthy of my hatred. I look upon them with contempt for their poorness of character.”

“But you have the rudiments of a good education,” said Mr. Hale. “The quick zest with which you are now reading Homer shows me you do not come to it as an unknown book. You have read it before, and are only recalling old knowledge.”

“That is true. I had blundered along it at school; I dare say I was even considered a pretty fair classic in those days, though my Latin and Greek have slipt away since. But I ask you—what preparation were they for such a life as I had to lead? None at all. Utterly none at all. On the point of education, any man who can read and write starts fair with me in the amount of really useful knowledge that I had at that time.”

“Well! I don’t agree with you,” said Mr. Hale. “But there I am perhaps somewhat of a pedant. Did not the recollection of the heroic simplicity of the Homeric life nerve you up?”

“Not one bit!” cried Mr. Thornton, and laughed outright. “I was too busy to think about any dead people, with the living pressing alongside me—neck to neck—in the struggle for bread. Now that I have my mother safe in the quiet peace that becomes her age, and duly rewards her former exertions, I can turn to all that old narration and thoroughly enjoy it.”

“I dare say my remark came from the professional feeling of there being nothing like leather,” Mr. Hale replied, with a smile.

When at last Mr. Thornton rose to go, he shook hands with Mr. and Mrs. Hale. Then, as a frank familiar custom of the place, he advanced to Margaret, putting out his hand to her also.

Margaret was not prepared. She bowed—only bowed—her farewell. In the instant she saw his hand half offered and then quickly drawn back, she was sorry—sorry with a sudden, involuntary shame, as if she had refused not a courtesy but a common human warmth because she did not understand the local language of manners. But he did not know her sorrow. He drew himself up to his full height, and went away with a stiffness that was anger made into posture.

Outside, the town’s distant din seemed to meet him—the far rumble and faint metallic cries that Milton never altogether hushed. He walked off, muttering, the words bitter in his mouth, as if he wanted them to be as hard as wrought iron.

“A more proud, disagreeable girl I never saw. Even her great beauty is blotted out of one’s memory by her scornful ways.”

“Margaret!” Mr. Hale said, coming back upstairs after seeing his pupil to the door. The last echo of boots on the stair had died into the close, woollen hush of the Milton house, where even silence felt dusted-over. “I watched your face with some anxiety when Mr. Thornton spoke of having been a shop-boy. I knew it from Mr. Bell, and yet I half expected you—impulsive creature—to rise and leave the room.”

Margaret had been gathering her mother’s work into its basket with a care that was almost tenderness made visible—folding the silk, smoothing the little strip of linen as if it could be comforted into lying flat. She looked up, and her colour came and went, not from shame, but from the remembered force of the man’s plain statement.

“Oh, papa! you cannot truly have thought me so foolish. That was the best thing he said—the only thing that did not set my teeth on edge. Everything else—his hardness—revolted me. But when he spoke of himself, there was no brag in it; no greasy pretence of gentility such as makes the vulgarity of shop-people. And his manner of speaking of his mother—so tender, so respectful—it was then I was least likely to leave the room. I could have risen when he boasted of Milton, as if there were no other place under heaven; or when he coolly despised people for being careless and improvident, as if it were not his duty—since he has had such training—to try and make them different, to give them some share of what his mother gave him. No! his being a shop-boy—that was what I liked best.”

Mrs. Hale’s hands had paused over her work. The lamplight showed the faint shadow under her eyes, and the way fatigue had begun to sit, like an unwelcome lodger, on her delicate features. Still, her voice held its old gentility of protest.

“I am surprised at you, Margaret. You, who were always calling people ‘shoppy’ at Helstone! And I do think, Mr. Hale, you have not quite done right to introduce such a person without telling us what he had been. I was afraid of showing him how much I was shocked at some parts. His father dying in miserable circumstances—why, it might have been in the workhouse.”

“I am not sure it was not worse,” Mr. Hale answered gravely. He drew a chair nearer the fire as if warmth could make the telling kinder. “Mr. Bell told me much of his early life before we came here. Since Mr. Thornton has told you part, I may fill what he left unsaid. His father speculated wildly, failed, and then—killed himself because he could not bear the disgrace. Friends fell away when the dishonest gambling was discovered; the struggles made with other people’s money to regain his own small portion. No one came forward to help the mother and the boy. There was another child too—a girl—too young to earn, but needing bread all the same. And Mrs. Thornton is not a woman to sit waiting until tardy kindness remembers her.”

Margaret’s fingers tightened on the work-basket handle as if she felt, in her own palm, the weight of years carried without complaint.

“So they left Milton. I knew he went into a shop, and that his earnings, with some fragment of property secured to his mother, kept them for a long while. Mr. Bell says they lived on water-porridge for years—how, he could not say. And then, long after the creditors had given up hope of payment—if indeed they ever hoped, after the suicide—the young man came back to Milton, went quietly to each creditor, and paid the first instalment. No noise. No summoning of men, no flourish. Very silently—and all was paid at last; helped, in good measure, by one creditor, a crabbed old fellow, who took him in as a kind of partner.”

“That really is fine,” Margaret said, and in the word there was genuine admiration—warm as bread drawn from an oven—before the familiar chill of Milton’s iron came over it. “What a pity such a nature should be tainted by his position as a manufacturer!”

“How tainted?” her father asked.

“Oh, papa—by testing everything by the standard of wealth. When he spoke of mechanical power, he seemed to see it only as a new way of extending trade and making money. And the poor men around him—they were poor because they were—because they had not his iron nature, because they could not be rich. They were out of the pale of his sympathies.”

“Not vicious,” Mr. Hale corrected gently. “He did not say that. Improvident and self-indulgent—those were his words.”

Margaret, now ready to leave, hesitated on the threshold—drawn by the wish to be honest with her father, and yet reluctant to speak what would trouble him. At last she gave it, like a small confession offered with both hands.

“Papa, I do think Mr. Thornton a very remarkable man; but personally I do not like him at all.”

“And I do!” Mr. Hale said, laughing in his quiet way. “Personally, and all. I don’t make him a hero. Good-night, child. Your mother looks sadly tired to-night, Margaret.”

The remark went with Margaret upstairs like a hand laid upon her heart. For some time now she had watched her mother’s strength ebb—first in little things: how she sat as if the very air pressed on her shoulders; how the close, soot-laden atmosphere of Milton seemed to thicken around her, robbing her breath of ease. At Helstone Mrs. Hale’s life had been in and out perpetually, the house opening on green and sun, the world full of bird-calls and leaves whispering. Here, even the street noises—cart-wheels on stone, distant factory pulses, the iron cough of the town—came to the ear like a perpetual wrong note, and the windows admitted not freshness but a dimmed light, as if daylight itself had been handled by grimy fingers.

There were other signs too. She and Dixon held mysterious consultations in her bedroom; Dixon would come out crying and cross, as she always did when her grief had no other language. Once Margaret, passing soon after Dixon’s heavy step withdrew, had looked in and found her mother on her knees; and, stealing away, caught a few words—broken prayer for strength and patience to endure severe bodily suffering.

Margaret longed to re-knit the old intimacy that had loosened during her years at her aunt Shaw’s. She pressed nearer with softened words, with gentle touches—bringing her mother a shawl before she asked for it, arranging the pillows as if comfort could be contrived by hands alone. Mrs. Hale met her with caresses and endearments enough—more, perhaps, than in former days—yet Margaret felt the withheld secret, like a closed drawer whose very lock proclaimed something precious and perilous within. She believed, with a dread that would not speak its name, that it concerned her mother’s health.

That night she lay awake long, listening—half unwillingly—to Milton’s soundscape through the thin walls: a late shout, a cart, the faint throb that never seemed wholly to cease, as if the town had a giant heart beating without repose. She made plans in the dark with the desperate industry of love. Dixon must have permanent assistance. A servant must be found if Margaret gave herself wholly to it. Then, at least, her mother might have the personal attention she had had all her life, and not be left to struggle against soot and worry with only faithful Dixon’s overburdened hands.

For days Margaret’s thoughts were taken up with what seemed, in Milton, as difficult as any moral problem—finding a servant. She went to register offices; she spoke to women who promised much and meant nothing; she saw faces that were sullen with suspicion or sharpened by hunger. She came home with her mind tired, and her senses full of the mingled odours of the streets: coal smoke that coated the tongue, stale beer from open doors, damp woollen clothing steaming on bodies that had no leisure to be clean.

One afternoon, as she returned, she met Bessy Higgins in the street—a pale, delicate creature, moving slowly as if each step were paid for with breath.

“Well, Bessy,” Margaret said, stopping at once, “how are you? Better, I hope, now the wind has changed.”

“Better and not better, if yo’ know what that means.”

“Not exactly,” Margaret replied, smiling a little.

“I’m better in not being torn to pieces by coughing o’ nights; but I’m weary and tired o’ Milton, and longing to get away to th’ land o’ Beulah; and when I think I’m farther and farther off, my heart sinks, and I’m no better—I’m worse.”

Margaret turned and walked beside her. For a minute or two she could find no words that were not too small. At last she spoke low, as if afraid the air might carry it to some listening ear.

“Bessy—do you wish to die?”

Bessy was silent, then answered in a voice that had the thin steadiness of someone who has lived too long with pain to be startled by its name.

“If yo’d led the life I have, and getten as weary on it as I have, and thought at times ‘maybe it’ll last for fifty or sixty years—it does wi’ some,’—and got dizzy and dazed, and sick, as each o’ them years seemed to spin about me and mock me wi’ its length o’ hours and minutes, and endless bits o’ time—oh, wench! I tell thee thou’d been glad enough when th’ doctor said he feared thou’d never see another winter.”

“Why, Bessy—what kind of life has yours been?”

“Nought worse than many others’, I reckon. Only I fretted again it, and they didn’t.”

“But what was it? You know—I’m a stranger here. Perhaps I don’t catch your meaning quick, as I might if I’d lived all my life in Milton.”

“If yo’d come to our house when yo’ said yo’ would, I could maybe ha’ told you. But father says yo’re just like th’ rest on ’em—out o’ sight out o’ mind wi’ you.”

“I don’t know who ‘the rest’ are,” Margaret said quietly. “And I’ve been very busy; and—to tell the truth—I had forgotten my promise.”

“Yo’ offered it; we asked none on it.”

“I had forgotten what I said for the time,” Margaret went on, without sharpness. “I should have thought of it again when I was less busy. May I go with you now?”

Bessy threw her a quick look, searching for pity that was not patronage. The keen glance softened into something wistful when it met Margaret’s steady kindness.

“I ha’ none so many to care for me; if yo’ care, yo’ may come.”

So they walked on together. Margaret heard, with a new attention, the sounds of the streets as if the town’s harsh music were part of Bessy’s illness: the slam of doors, the quarrelling voices, the clatter that never seemed to rest. When they turned into a small court off a squalid street, the noise altered—narrowed and echoed, as if every shout and every step struck back from the walls twice over.

“Yo’ll not be daunted if father’s at home,” Bessy said, breath failing a little. “He speaks a bit gruffish at first. He took a mind to ye, yo’ see, and he thought a deal o’ your coming; and just because he liked yo’ he were vexed and put about.”

“Don’t fear, Bessy.”

But Nicholas Higgins was not at home when they entered. A great slatternly girl—not so old as Bessy, but taller, stronger—was at a wash-tub, knocking about the furniture with rough capability, making so much noise that Margaret shrank, not from the girl, but from the assault on Bessy’s weary senses. The room smelt of soap-suds and damp clothes, of stale smoke embedded in walls that had never known clean air.

Margaret asked for a cup of water. While the sister went, tumbling over a chair and sending the fire-irons clattering, Margaret loosened Bessy’s bonnet-strings to ease her panting breath.

“Do you think such life as this is worth caring for?” Bessy gasped at last.

Margaret did not answer. She held the water to Bessy’s lips. Bessy drank long and feverishly, then fell back and shut her eyes. In the hush between one crash and the next, Margaret heard her murmur, as if repeating a taste she longed for but had never known in her mouth:

“They shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more; neither shall the sun light on them, nor any heat.”

Margaret bent over her. “Bessy, don’t be impatient with your life—whatever it is, or has been. Remember who gave it you, and made it what it is.”

She started; Nicholas Higgins’s voice came from behind. He had entered so quietly, in spite of his size, that she had not heard him—an odd mercy in such a noisy place, as if he carried his own silence.

“Now, I’ll not have my wench preached to,” he said. “She’s bad enough as it is, wi’ her dreams and her methodee fancies, and visions o’ cities wi’ goulden gates and precious stones. If it amuses her, I let it abe; but I’m none going to have more stuff poured into her.”

“But surely,” Margaret said, turning and meeting his rough gaze steadily, “you believe in what I said—that God gave her life, and ordered what kind of life it was to be?”

“I believe what I see, and no more,” he answered, blunt as a hammer. “That’s what I believe, young woman. I don’t believe all I hear—no! not by a big deal. I did hear a young lass make an ado about knowing where we lived, and coming to see us. And my wench here thought a deal about it—flushed up many a time, when hoo little knew I were looking at her, at sound o’ a strange step. But hoo’s come at last, and hoo’s welcome—so long as hoo’ll keep from preaching on what hoo knows nought about.”

Bessy had been watching Margaret’s face with anxious eyes; now she half raised herself and laid a thin hand on Margaret’s arm, pleading.

“Don’t be vexed wi’ him—there’s many a one thinks like him: many and many a one here. If yo’ could hear them speak, yo’d not be shocked at him. He’s a rare good man, is father—but oh!” She fell back with a despairing little motion. “What he says at times makes me long to die more than ever, for I want to know so many things, and am so tossed about wi’ wonder.”

“Poor wench—poor old wench,” Nicholas said, his harshness breaking into a rough sorrow. “I’m loth to vex thee, I am; but a man mun speak out for th’ truth. When I see th’ world going all wrong at this time o’ day—bothering itself wi’ things it knows nought about, and leaving undone all th’ things that lie in disorder close at its hand—why, I say, leave a’ this talk about religion alone, and set to work on what yo’ see and know. That’s my creed. It’s simple, and not far to fetch, nor hard to work.”

But Bessy only clung the more to Margaret’s sleeve, as if she feared the door would close and shut hope out with it.

“Don’t think hardly on him—he’s a good man, he is. I sometimes think I shall be moped wi’ sorrow even in th’ City o’ God, if father is not there.”

The feverish colour flamed into her cheek, into her eye. “But you will be there, father! you shall! Oh! my heart!”

She put her hand to her breast and turned ghastly pale. Margaret gathered her at once, strong young arms making a shelter where the world had made none. She laid the weary head on her bosom, lifted the thin soft hair from the temples, and bathed them with water. Nicholas, helpless in speech, understood every look and gesture with the quickness of love; even the round-eyed sister moved with clumsy gentleness at Margaret’s urgent “Hush!”

Presently the spasm that seemed to foreshadow death passed, leaving Bessy exhausted, like a flame that has dropped low for want of air. She roused herself and whispered:

“I’ll go to bed—it’s best place; but”—and she caught at Margaret’s gown with a child’s desperate insistence—“yo’ll come again. I know yo’ will—but just say it.”

“I will come again to-morrow,” Margaret said.

Bessy leaned back against her father, who prepared to carry her upstairs as if she were light as a bundle of clothes. As Margaret rose to go, Nicholas struggled with words that did not belong to his usual creed, but forced themselves up through the cracks of his grief.

“I could wish there were a God,” he said hoarsely, “if it were only to ask Him to bless thee.”

Margaret went away sad and thoughtful, and the street’s harsh din seemed to strike her more sharply after the close misery of that room. She was late for tea at home. In Helstone unpunctuality at meals had been a fault that roused her mother’s quick irritability; now, as with so many little things, the power of complaint appeared to have died away. Margaret almost longed for the old reproof, as one longs for a familiar bird-song in a place where the only music is machinery.

“Have you met with a servant, dear?” Mrs. Hale asked, her voice mild from weariness.

“No, mamma. That Anne Buckley would never have done.”

“Suppose I try,” Mr. Hale said. “Everybody else has had their turn at this great difficulty. Now let me try. I may be the Cinderella to put on the slipper after all.”

Margaret could scarcely smile; the image of Bessy’s pinched face, of that court’s echoing clamour, lay upon her too heavily.

“What would you do, papa? How would you set about it?”

“Why, I should apply to some good house-mother to recommend me one known to herself or her servants.”

“Very good. But we must first catch our house-mother.”

“You have caught her,” Mr. Hale answered, with a quiet twinkle. “Or rather she is coming into the snare, and you will catch her to-morrow, if you’re skilful.”

“What do you mean, Mr. Hale?” Mrs. Hale asked, roused by curiosity as if it were a draught of wine.

“Why—my paragon pupil (as Margaret calls him) has told me that his mother intends to call on Mrs. and Miss Hale to-morrow.”

“Mrs. Thornton!” Mrs. Hale exclaimed.

“The mother of whom he spoke to us?” Margaret said.

“Mrs. Thornton; the only mother he has, I believe,” Mr. Hale replied quietly.

“I shall like to see her,” Mrs. Hale said. “She must be an uncommon person. Perhaps she may have a relation who might suit us, and be glad of our place. She sounded such a careful economical person that I should like any one out of the same family.”

“My dear,” Mr. Hale said, with sudden alarm, “pray do not go off upon that idea. I fancy Mrs. Thornton is as haughty and proud in her way as our little Margaret here is in hers, and that she completely ignores that old time of trial and poverty and economy of which he speaks so openly. I am sure, at any rate, she would not like strangers to know anything about it.”

“Take notice that is not my kind of haughtiness, papa, if I have any at all—which I do not agree to, though you are always accusing me.”

“I don’t know positively that it is hers either,” he answered, “but from little things I have gathered, I fancy so.”

They cared too little to ask in what manner the son had spoken of the mother. Margaret’s mind was on the morrow for another reason: if Mrs. Thornton called, she must stay to receive her, and that would keep her from Bessy until late; yet her mother must not be left to bear alone the weight of entertaining a stranger. Outside, Milton went on sounding—wheel, step, distant throb—while within, in the quiet room, Margaret measured her duties as one measures ingredients, knowing that the smallest imbalance might ruin what little strength remained at the table.

Mr. Thornton had found it easier to set iron in motion than to persuade his mother to be gracious.

Mrs. Thornton did not squander herself in society. When she paid calls, she did it as she did everything else—solidly, with a sense of obligation and a certain ceremonial weight, as if civility were a fabric to be cut straight, pinned firmly, and worn without frill. Her son had given her a carriage; she would not keep horses for it. Horses were hired like extra hands at harvest-time—only for needful occasions, when custom demanded she should go forth and be seen.

Not a fortnight before, she had hired them for three days and had, as she said with a dry satisfaction, “killed off” her acquaintances—visited all who could claim her attention, so that now they might take their turn and spend their own money and time in returning it. Yet Crampton lay too far for her to compass on foot; and more than once she had looked up from her stitching to ask, in the tone of one reckoning flour by the ounce, whether his wish that she should call upon the Hales was truly strong enough to bear the cost of a cab.

She would have been quietly relieved if it had not been. “I see no use,” she said, “in making up friendships and intimacies with all the teachers and masters in Milton. Why, you’ll be wanting me to call on Fanny’s dancing-master’s wife next.”

“And so I would, mother,” he answered, quick as a knife laid down on a board, “if Mr. Mason and his wife were friendless in a strange place—like the Hales.”

“Oh! you need not speak so hastily. I’m going to-morrow. I only wanted you exactly to understand about it.”

“If you are going to-morrow, I shall order horses.”

“Nonsense, John. One would think you were made of money.”

“Not quite, yet. But about the horses I’m determined. The last time you were out in a cab, you came home with a headache from the jolting.”

“I never complained of it, I’m sure.”

“No. My mother is not given to complaints,” he said, and there was pride in it, as if endurance were a family possession. “But so much the more I have to watch over you. Now, as for Fanny—there—a little hardship would do her good.”

“She is not made of the same stuff as you are, John. She could not bear it.”

At that Mrs. Thornton grew still. The words touched a sore place she kept covered, even from herself. She had an instinctive contempt for weakness—an unreasoning, almost bodily dislike of it—yet her daughter was weak exactly where she and her son were hard and strong. Mrs. Thornton did not argue herself into opinions; she struck them out, as a flint gives sparks. She knew—without ever admitting it aloud—that nothing could steel Fanny into patience, nor teach her to meet trouble squarely. The knowledge mortified her; and the mortification turned oddly to a pitying tenderness, like that with which some mothers handle a sickly child: careful, shielding, indulgent.

A stranger might have thought she loved Fanny best, because to her she said “dear” and “love,” while to her son she said only “John.” But her gratitude went after him like an unspoken prayer; and for his sake she walked proud among women.

“Fanny dear,” she said presently, as if arranging a household matter, “I shall have horses to the carriage to-day, to go and call on these Hales. Should not you go and see nurse? It’s in the same direction, and she’s always so glad to see you. You could go on there while I am at Mrs. Hale’s.”

“Oh, mamma, it’s such a long way—and I am so tired.”

“With what?” Mrs. Thornton asked; and her brow drew together just a little, like linen pulled tight.

“I don’t know—the weather, I think. It is so relaxing. Couldn’t you bring nurse here, mamma? The carriage could fetch her, and she could spend the rest of the day here, which I know she would like.”

Mrs. Thornton laid her work down upon the table. The needle stopped; the thread slackened. She considered, weighing comfort against propriety, expense against feeling, as women do who have been poor and remember it in the muscles of their hands.

“It will be a long way for her to walk back at night,” she said at last.

“Oh, but I will send her home in a cab. I never thought of her walking.”

At that moment Mr. Thornton came in, hat in hand, on his way to the mill, bringing with him—almost as a draught brings in smoke—a sense of the outer world: of wheels, of engines, of those unceasing Milton sounds that seemed to live in the very boards and brick. He looked from one to the other with the impatience of a man who cannot bear delays in things he thinks plain.

“Mother! I need hardly say, that if there is any little thing that could serve Mrs. Hale as an invalid, you will offer it, I’m sure.”

“If I can find it out, I will,” she replied. “But I have never been ill myself, so I am not much up to invalids’ fancies.”

“Well! here is Fanny then, who is seldom without an ailment. She will be able to suggest something, perhaps—won’t you, Fan?”

“I have not always an ailment,” Fanny said sharply; the peevishness rose in her like heat in milk when it is watched too late. “And I am not going with mamma. I have a headache to-day, and I shan’t go out.”

Mr. Thornton’s face darkened; annoyance came over it as over a clear broth when something bitter is dropped in. His mother bent over her work again and began to stitch with a brisk, business-like speed.

“Fanny! I wish you to go,” he said, with the authority he used in his counting-house. “It will do you good, instead of harm. You will oblige me by going, without my saying anything more about it.”

He went out abruptly, as if any further speech would only loosen his temper. Had he stayed another minute Fanny would have cried—his tone commanded tears from her as surely as some people’s tenderness commanded them. As it was, she grumbled the moment the door had shut.

“John always speaks as if I fancied I was ill, and I am sure I never do fancy any such thing. Who are these Hales that he makes such a fuss about?”

“Fanny, don’t speak so of your brother,” Mrs. Thornton answered, though the question struck in her own mind like a refrain. “He has good reasons of some kind or other, or he would not wish us to go. Make haste and put your things on.”

Yet the little clash between son and daughter did not soften her towards “these Hales.” Jealousy—quiet, respectable jealousy, that hid itself behind duty—kept asking, “Who are they, that he is so anxious we should pay them all this attention?” It went on repeating itself long after Fanny had forgotten everything in the pleasant flutter of trying her new bonnet before the glass, turning her head this way and that, as if a different angle might make her brother’s command sit easier.

Mrs. Thornton was shy; her sternness covered it. It was only in late years she had had leisure to go among people, and she did not relish it. She could take satisfaction in dinners—in giving them, in judging them, in the quiet triumph of serving something well and seeing it appreciated or, better still, envied. That was a kind of mastery she understood: the ordering of plates and joints, the proper hotness of a dish when it came to table, the exact moment a pudding should be cut so it stood and did not sink. But to go and make acquaintance with strangers, without the defence of her own board between them, left her ill at ease. She looked more than usually forbidding as she entered the Hales’ little drawing-room, as if she feared she might be cheated of her dignity if she let it drop for an instant.

Margaret Hale sat with her embroidery—cambric stretched fine beneath her fingers—for some small article of dress for Edith’s expected baby. Mrs. Thornton’s glance fell on it at once. Flimsy work, she thought; useless, too—pretty enough, perhaps, but no more nourishing to life than froth. Her eye travelled next to Mrs. Hale’s double knitting, and there she felt a grudging approval. That was sensible in its way; it made warmth; it had a purpose.

The room itself seemed full of knick-knacks—little ornaments and trifles that would take time to dust. And time, to people of limited means, was money. These reflections came and went through her mind while her mouth delivered the correct phrases of a morning call—those easy commonplaces people can utter as mechanically as stirring tea. Mrs. Hale answered with a little more effort than her health might have spared; yet a certain interest had been kindled in her by the lace Mrs. Thornton wore—real old lace, not new-fangled mimicry.

Afterwards, Mrs. Hale told Dixon, with the air of one tasting something rare and recognising it at once, that it was old English point, such as had not been made for seventy years and could not be bought. It must be an heirloom, she said; it showed the woman had ancestors. So the ancestral lace, like a spice that gives value to an otherwise plain dish, made its wearer worth more attention than mere politeness would have required.

Meanwhile Margaret, racking her wits to talk to Miss Thornton, heard the older women sink—as if by a natural gravitation—into the subject of servants, that inexhaustible domestic history-book in which ladies read each other’s fortunes and failings.

“I suppose you are not musical,” Fanny said, looking round with a faint disdain, “as I see no piano.”

“I am fond of hearing good music,” Margaret replied; “I cannot play well myself; and papa and mamma don’t care much about it; so we sold our old piano when we came here.”

“I wonder how you can exist without one. It almost seems to me a necessary of life.”

Margaret felt the words as she might feel a draught of cold air across warm skin. Fifteen shillings a week, and three saved out of them! The thought came sharp and vivid—like the exact measure of flour in a poor household where every loaf must be counted. She looked at Fanny’s face and tried to be just: the girl must have been very young; perhaps she had forgotten. Yet surely she must have known, by some memory, that people did without such “necessaries.”

When Margaret spoke again there was a new chill in her courtesy, a clear edge to it. “You have good concerts here, I believe.”

“Oh, yes! Delicious! Too crowded—that is the worst. The directors admit so indiscriminately. But one is sure to hear the newest music there. I always have a large order to give to Johnson’s the day after a concert.”

“Do you like new music simply for its newness, then?”

“Oh! one knows it is the fashion in London, or else the singers would not bring it down here. You have been in London, of course.”

“Yes,” said Margaret. “I have lived there for several years.”

“Oh! London and the Alhambra are the two places I long to see!”

“London and the Alhambra!”

“Yes! ever since I read the Tales of the Alhambra. Don’t you know them?”

“I don’t think I do. But surely it is a very easy journey to London.”

“Yes; but somehow,” Fanny said, lowering her voice and leaning a little nearer, as if the secret were a sweetmeat to be shared, “mamma has never been to London herself, and can’t understand my longing. She is very proud of Milton—dirty, smoky place as I feel it to be. I believe she admires it the more for those very qualities.”

“If it has been Mrs. Thornton’s home for some years, I can well understand her loving it,” Margaret answered; and her voice, clear as a bell, carried further than Fanny intended.

Mrs. Thornton turned her head. “What are you saying about me, Miss Hale? May I inquire?”

Margaret, taken by surprise, found her mind blank for an instant—as if a word she knew in one dialect would not come when demanded in another. Fanny stepped in quickly.

“Oh, mamma! we are only trying to account for your being so fond of Milton.”

“Thank you,” said Mrs. Thornton, and the words fell like a shut lid. “I do not feel that my very natural liking for the place where I was born and brought up—and which has since been my residence for some years—requires any accounting for.”
