Margaret coloured, vexed with herself and with the other. Fanny had indeed sounded impertinent; and yet Mrs. Thornton’s offence, so stiffly shown, seemed itself a kind of dominion—an insistence that even talk about her must be measured in her terms.

After a moment Mrs. Thornton went on, her manner controlled but sharpened. “Do you know anything of Milton, Miss Hale? Have you seen any of our factories? our magnificent warehouses?”

“No,” Margaret said. “I have not seen anything of that description as yet.” And then, unwilling to let even politeness make her speak falsely, she added, “I dare say papa would have taken me before now if I had cared. But I really do not find much pleasure in going over manufactories.”

“They are very curious places,” Mrs. Hale put in gently, as if trying to soften the angle between them; “but there is so much noise and dirt always. I remember once going in a lilac silk to see candles made, and my gown was utterly ruined.”

“Very probably,” Mrs. Thornton returned shortly, displeased—whether at the lilac silk or at the tone of complaint, it was hard to say. “I merely thought, that as strangers newly come to reside in a town which has risen to eminence in the country from the character and progress of its peculiar business, you might have cared to visit some of the places where it is carried on—places unique in the kingdom, I am informed. If Miss Hale changes her mind and condescends to be curious as to the manufactures of Milton, I can only say I shall be glad to procure her admission to print-works, or reed-making, or the more simple operations of spinning carried on in my son’s mill. Every improvement of machinery is, I believe, to be seen there, in its highest perfection.”

Margaret bowed slightly. The offer was made like a favour, yet it carried with it an assertion of power; the very words “condescends” and “procure her admission” seemed to set the terms of who granted and who received. Outside, beyond the curtained windows, the town’s sound lay like an invisible weather: the far throb and hammer of industry—so constant that Milton folk ceased to hear it, as they ceased to taste the hardness of their water—yet to strangers it was an oppression that could not be translated into ordinary talk.

“I am so glad you don’t like mills and manufactories, and all those kind of things,” Fanny whispered, as she rose when her mother began to take leave with rustling dignity.

“I think I should like to know all about them, if I were you,” Margaret replied quietly; and if there was a rebuke in it, it was delivered without heat.

Mrs. Thornton’s farewell to Mrs. Hale was correct, neither warm nor cold; and then the two Thorntons withdrew, leaving behind them the faint scent of well-kept clothes and old lace, and the impression—like the lingering taste of something strong—that their visit had been less an interchange than a trial of strength.

As the carriage rolled away, Mrs. Thornton spoke at once, as she often did when the door had closed upon other people and she could set her judgments down plain.

“Fanny! we will be civil to these Hales; but don’t form one of your hasty friendships with the daughter. She will do you no good, I see. The mother looks very ill, and seems a nice, quiet kind of person.”

“I don’t want to form any friendship with Miss Hale, mamma,” Fanny said, pouting. “I thought I was doing my duty by talking to her, and trying to amuse her.”

“Well! at any rate John must be satisfied now,” Mrs. Thornton answered; and as the wheels carried them back through Milton’s ceaseless din, she let the matter drop—as if shutting away a spice she did not care to use, but had agreed to keep in the house for her son’s sake.

As soon as the last of their visitors had gone down the stair and the street-door shut with its thin, sharp clap, Margaret was already flying up again, snatching bonnet and shawl with the haste of one who runs not toward a diversion but toward a duty that has begun to taste like love. She meant to see how Bessy Higgins bore the day, and to sit with her as long as the household clock would allow before dinner called her back.

Milton’s streets received her with their usual press—close-built brick, jostling shoulders, children’s cries, the perpetual shuffle of feet on stone. Yet the very narrowness had altered since she had learned to care for one life that was lived here. The place no longer seemed merely a passage of grim commerce; it had become a map in which one door mattered more than a hundred shop-fronts, and one upstairs window could hold a whole human world. Above all, there was the sound: the town’s ceaseless undertone, as if the air itself were always being worked—wheels, carts, voices bouncing off walls, and, far behind it, the mill’s dry, persistent thunder. She felt that noise in the bones, and understood, with a new unwilling reverence, what it must be to have it for one’s lullaby and one’s waking bell.

Mary Higgins had made what preparation she could. She had scraped and rough-stoned a wide patch in the middle of the flagged floor until it looked paler, raw, and newly worried, while under the chairs and along the walls the stones lay dark with old unwashed grease and soot, as if the dirt had chosen those safe borders to brood in. Though the day was hot—hot enough that the very window-light seemed thick—there was a great fire burning in the grate, so that the room breathed like an oven. Margaret, pausing a moment in the doorway, thought first with a kind of dismay of Mrs. Hale upstairs and the cool cloths she needed; then she guessed, imperfectly, what Mary meant by it—coal flung on lavishly as a sign of welcome, warmth offered as if warmth could stand in for all the gentler comforts a poor house cannot afford.

Bessy lay on her short sofa under the window, the thin daylight falling on her face and making it seem more transparent than yesterday. She had grown weaker in the space of one night; even her waiting had tired her. Mary said, in her slatternly, half-defensive tone, that Bessy had kept lifting herself up, again and again, to see if it were Miss Hale coming along the street.

Now that Margaret was there, seated close, Bessy sank back with a child’s content, speaking little at first—only looking, looking, as if Margaret’s face were a picture she could rest on. Her hand wandered to Margaret’s sleeve, her bonnet-ribbon, the edge of her shawl, stroking the textures with a wonder that was not envy so much as hungry curiosity, like a palate tasting something it has heard of but never known.

“I never knew why folk i’ th’ Bible cared for soft raiment afore,” Bessy said at last. Her voice was thin, but the words came with a homely certainty. “But it must be nice, to go dressed as yo’ do. It’s different fro’ common. Most fine folk tire my eyes out wi’ their colours; but some how yours rest me. Where did ye get this frock?”

“In London,” Margaret answered, smiling in spite of herself.

“London!” Bessy’s eyes opened wider. “Have yo’ been in London?”

“Yes. I lived there for some years. But my home was in a forest—in the country.”

“Tell me about it,” Bessy whispered, and the longing in her made the small room feel smaller. “I like to hear speak o’ th’ country, and trees, and such like things.”

She lay quite still now, as if arranging her body to receive a draught of coolness by the ear. Her hands folded over her breast. She shut her eyes, not to refuse the world but to make room for another one.

Margaret had not spoken of Helstone—of that name that, in her own thoughts, had become as tender and unhandled as a pressed flower—except in passing. It came to her most vividly at night, when the town’s noises went on without her having to answer them, and memory could steal back to green shade and birds. Yet here, with Bessy’s starving attention, her heart opened as if it had been waiting for precisely such a listener—one to whom “forest” was not a pretty word but a promise.

“Oh, Bessy,” she said, and her voice softened, thickened with pictures, “I loved the home we have left so dearly. I wish you could see it. I cannot tell you half its beauty. There are great trees standing all about it, with their branches stretching long and level, making a deep shade of rest even at noonday. And yet—though every leaf may seem still—there is a continual rushing sound of movement all around, not close at hand. It is as if the forest were breathing in some language too large for one ear to catch at once.

“Then sometimes the turf is as soft and fine as velvet; and sometimes quite lush with the perpetual moisture of a little hidden brook near by, always tinkling—never loud enough to trouble you, only enough to make silence feel alive. And then, in other parts, there are billowy ferns—whole stretches of fern; some in the green shadow; some with long streaks of golden sunlight lying on them—just like the sea.”

“I have never seen th’ sea,” Bessy murmured, as if that was an omission the world ought to be ashamed of. “But go on.”

“Then here and there,” Margaret continued, carried forward by Bessy’s eagerness, “there are wide commons, high up, as if above the very tops of the trees—”

“I am glad o’ that,” Bessy broke in quickly. “I felt smothered like down below. When I have gone for an out, I’ve always wanted to get high up and see far away, and take a deep breath o’ fulness in that air. I get smothered enough in Milton; and I think the sound yo’ speak of among th’ trees, going on for ever and ever, would send me dazed; it’s that made my head ache so i’ th’ mill. Now on these commons, I reckon, there is but little noise?”

“No,” said Margaret. “Nothing but, here and there, a lark high in the air. Sometimes I used to hear a farmer speaking sharp and loud to his servants; but it was so far away that it only reminded me pleasantly that other people were hard at work somewhere in the distance, while I sat on the heather and did nothing.”

Bessy’s lips quivered with something between a smile and a pain.

“I used to think once,” she said slowly, “that if I could have a day o’ doing nothing, to rest me—a day in some quiet place like that yo’ speak on—it would maybe set me up. But now I’ve had many days o’ idleness, and I’m just as weary ’o them as I was o’ my work. Sometimes I’m so tired out I think I cannot enjoy heaven without a piece o’ rest first. I’m rather afeard o’ going straight there without getting a good sleep i’ th’ grave to set me up.”

“Don’t be afraid, Bessy,” Margaret said, and laid her hand over the girl’s hand—so slight beneath it, so hot and dry, as if fever had drunk away all the natural moisture. “God can give you more perfect rest than even idleness on earth, or the dead sleep of the grave.”

Bessy moved uneasily, turning her head as if the very words had stirred a draught through some sore place.

“I wish father would not speak to me as he does,” she said at length, voice sharpening with a sudden edge. “He means well, as I telled yo’ yesterday, and tell yo’ again and again. But yo’ see—though I don’t believe him a bit by day, yet by night—when I’m in a fever, half asleep and half awake—it comes back upon me—oh! so bad!”

She drew breath, and it rasped, thin and catching.

“And I think, if this should be th’ end o’ all, and if all I’ve been born for is just to work my heart and my life away, and to sicken i’ this dree place, wi’ them mill-noises in my ears for ever—until I could scream out for them to stop, and let me have a little piece o’ quiet—and wi’ th’ fluff filling my lungs, until I thirst to death for one long deep breath o’ the clear air yo’ speak on—and my mother gone, and I never able to tell her again how I loved her, and o’ all my troubles—”

Her voice rose, and with it her whole frail body, as if something fierce had leapt up inside her like flame finding draught.

“I think if this life is th’ end, and there’s no God to wipe away all tears from all eyes—yo’ wench, yo’!” She sat upright, and clutched Margaret’s hand with a violence out of all proportion to her weakness, almost as if she meant to hold on by force to anything solid. “I could go mad, and kill yo, I could.”

It was not a threat so much as a cry of terror given teeth. Immediately after, the strength broke. She fell back, spent, panting, her eyes half shut, her face damp with the effort.

Margaret slid down from her chair and knelt by the sofa, close enough that Bessy might feel her steadiness.

“Bessy,” she said, very low, “we have a Father in Heaven.”

“I know it! I know it,” Bessy moaned, turning her head uneasily from side to side as if she wanted to hide from her own words. “I’m very wicked. I’ve spoken very wickedly. Oh! don’t be frightened by me and never come again. I would not harm a hair o’ your head.”

Then she opened her eyes and looked at Margaret with a kind of earnest pride, as if she would set right, at once, what her fever had disordered.

“And,” she added, “I believe, perhaps, more than yo’ do o’ what’s to come. I read th’ book o’ Revelations until I know it off by heart, and I never doubt when I’m waking, and in my senses, of all th’ glory I’m to come to.”

“Don’t let us talk of what fancies come into your head when you are feverish,” Margaret answered, smoothing the coverlet where it was rucked, as one does to quiet both cloth and mind. “I would rather hear something about what you used to do when you were well.”

Bessy’s gaze drifted toward the grate, where the fire made the air tremble.

“I think I was well when mother died,” she said, after a pause. “But I have never been rightly strong sin’ somewhere about that time. I began to work in a carding-room soon after, and th’ fluff got into my lungs, and poisoned me.”

“Fluff?” Margaret asked; the word was so small for so great a ruin.

“Fluff,” repeated Bessy, as if naming an enemy by its proper name gave a kind of mastery. “Little bits, as fly off fro’ th’ cotton when they’re carding it, and fill th’ air till it looks all fine white dust. They say it winds rounds th’ lungs, and tightens ’em up. Anyhow, there’s many a one as works in a carding-room, that falls into a waste, coughing and spitting blood, because they’re just poisoned by th’ fluff.”

Margaret could not help but imagine it—those pale fibres, light as thistledown, drifting into mouths, into throats, into the warm dark of the chest, where they did not dissolve like flour in broth but clung and gathered. She thought of a kitchen sieve shaken too hard, of meal making its own little fog—only this was a fog a body could never sweep away. And outside, the town’s noises went on, each clatter and whirr a proof of work, of profit, of the world’s indifference.

“But can’t it be helped?” Margaret asked.

“I dunno,” Bessy said, with the weary practicality of the poor. “Some folk have a great wheel at one end o’ their carding-rooms to make a draught, and carry off th’ dust; but that wheel costs a deal o’ money—five or six hundred pounds, maybe—and brings in no profit; so it’s but a few o’ th’ masters as will put ’em up. And I’ve heard tell o’ men who didn’t like working in places where there was a wheel, because they said as how it made ’em hungry, at after they’d been long used to swallowing fluff, to go without it, and that their wages ought to be raised if they were to work in such places. So between masters and men th’ wheels fall through. I know I wish there’d been a wheel in our place, though.”

The thought struck Margaret with a bitter irony: that human lungs should be the cheapest filters, that habit should turn even poison into something a man might claim as part of his due. The very language of it—profit, wages, cost—seemed to swallow up the simple fact of breath.

“Did not your father know about it?” Margaret asked.

“Yes,” said Bessy, and there was tenderness in the word, folded in with her complaint. “And he was sorry. But our factory were a good one on the whole; and a steady likely set o’ people; and father was afeard o’ letting me go to a strange place. For though yo’ would na think it now, many a one then used to call me a gradely lass enough.”

A faint, brief colour came into her cheeks at the remembered praise, as if a ghost of her old self had walked through.

“And I did na like to be reckoned nesh and soft. And Mary’s schooling were to be kept up, mother said, and father he were always liking to buy books, and go to lectures o’ one kind and another—all which took money—so I just worked on till I shall ne’er get th’ whirr out o’ my ears, or th’ fluff out o’ my throat i’ this world. That’s all.”

“The whirr out of your ears”—Margaret heard, behind the phrase, the tyranny of sound: noise that does not merely fill the day but lodges in the mind, like a tune you never chose and cannot stop humming. It seemed to her a cruelty almost worse than hunger, to be pursued by a din even in illness, even in memory.

“How old are you?” she asked softly.

“Nineteen, come July.”

“And I too am nineteen,” Margaret said.

For a moment she could not speak after that; the contrast between them lay across her mind like a shadow that would not be shifted. She thought of her own girlhood—rooms that could be kept clean, gardens, books, the gentle silence of trees—and of Bessy’s—fluff and whirr, flags that could never be fully washed, and air that came to her already used. The thought rose in her throat and made it hard to swallow.

“About Mary,” Bessy said suddenly, rousing herself with a purpose that gave her voice new steadiness. “I wanted to ask yo’ to be a friend to her. She’s seventeen, but she’s th’ last on us. And I don’t want her to go to th’ mill, and yet I dunno what she’s fit for.”

Margaret’s glance, unwilling but honest, swept the room: the gritty middle patch Mary had scoured; the untouched corners; the sooty walls; the very way disorder had settled as if it belonged. She felt the weight of what Bessy asked—love trying to purchase a future with no coin but hope.

“She could not do—” Margaret began, and stopped. Then she said, carefully, not wishing to wound. “She could hardly undertake a servant’s place, could she? We have an old faithful servant, almost a friend, who wants help, but who is very particular; and it would not be right to plague her with giving her any assistance that would really be an annoyance and an irritation.”

“No, I see,” Bessy answered, without resentment. She had asked, and the truth had come; she accepted it as she accepted the heat of the fire, the narrowness of the room. “I reckon yo’re right. Our Mary’s a good wench; but who has she had to teach her what to do about a house? No mother, and me at th’ mill till I was good for nothing but scolding her for doing badly what I didn’t know how to do a bit. But I wish she could ha’ lived wi’ yo’, for all that.”

“But even though she may not be exactly fitted to come and live with us as a servant—and I don’t know about that—I will always try to be a friend to her for your sake, Bessy,” Margaret said quickly, leaning closer as if to make the promise warmer than the room’s fierce heat. “And now I must go. I will come again as soon as I can; but if it should not be to-morrow, or the next day, or even a week or a fortnight hence, don’t think I’ve forgotten you. I may be busy.”

“I’ll know yo’ won’t forget me again,” Bessy said, and for a moment she sounded almost like a child being soothed. “I’ll not mistrust yo’ no more. But remember—in a week or a fortnight I may be dead and buried!”

“I’ll come again as soon as I can, Bessy,” Margaret replied, and squeezed her hand hard, as if by pressure she could force life back into it. “But you’ll let me know if you get worse.”

“Ay, that will I,” Bessy said, returning the pressure as much as her strength allowed.

From that day forward Mrs. Hale became more and more a suffering invalid. The year was turning round toward the anniversary of Edith’s marriage, and when Margaret looked back upon that circle of months, the heap of troubles seemed so high she wondered—quietly, without vanity—how they had been borne at all. If she could have foreseen them, she thought, she would have shrunk away as from a bitter draught. Yet each day, taken alone, had been endurable, and sometimes, like a bright herb unexpectedly bruised between the fingers, some small, keen enjoyment had risen fragrant in the very midst of sorrow.

A year ago—when she had first returned to Helstone and first become silently conscious of the querulousness in her mother’s temper—she would have groaned at the thought of a long illness borne in a strange place: a desolate, noisy town where even silence seemed manufactured, where the air was thick, the streets restless, and comforts diminished on every side. But now, with the increase of serious and just ground for complaint, a new kind of patience had sprung up in Mrs. Hale. She grew gentle and quiet in intense bodily suffering, almost in proportion as she had been restless and depressed when there had been no real cause for grief; as if pain, once undeniable, steadied what mere discontent had fretted.

Mr. Hale, meanwhile, was in that stage of apprehension which, in men of his kind, takes the shape of wilful blindness. Margaret’s expressed anxiety irritated him more than she had ever known.

“Indeed, Margaret, you are growing fanciful!” he said, with a forced brightness that did not ring true. “God knows I should be the first to take the alarm if your mother were really ill. We always saw when she had her headaches at Helstone, even without her telling us. She looks quite pale and white when she is ill; and now she has a bright healthy colour in her cheeks, just as she used to have when I first knew her.”

“But papa,” Margaret said, hesitating—because to contradict him was like stepping on a weak plank above deep water—“do you know I think that is the flush of pain.”

“Nonsense, Margaret. I tell you, you are too fanciful. You are the person not well, I think. Send for the doctor to-morrow for yourself; and then, if it will make your mind easier, he can see your mother.”

“Thank you, dear papa. It will make me happier, indeed,” Margaret answered; and she went up to kiss him.

But he put her away—gently, yet unmistakably—like one pushing aside a thought that threatens to become a fear. The motion hurt her more than harshness would have done, because it came from love struggling against truth.

He began to walk uneasily up and down the room. Margaret heard the boards answer his steps with their dry creak; even this small domestic sound seemed part of the town’s larger unrest, as if in Milton nothing could be entirely still.

“Poor Maria!” he said half to himself. “I wish one could do right without sacrificing others. I shall hate this town, and myself too, if she—” He broke off, then turned with sudden questioning. “Pray, Margaret, does your mother often talk to you of the old places: of Helstone, I mean.”

“No, papa,” Margaret said sadly.

“Then, you see, she can’t be fretting after them, eh? It has always been a comfort to me to think that your mother was so simple and open that I knew every little grievance she had. She never would conceal anything seriously affecting her health from me: would she, eh, Margaret? I am quite sure she would not. So don’t let me hear of these foolish morbid ideas. Come, give me a kiss, and run off to bed.”

Margaret obeyed. Yet long after her slow, languid undressing was finished—long after she lay down and tried to command her thoughts into order—she heard him still pacing, up and down, up and down, as Edith and she had once laughingly called it, “racooning.” The sound went on in the darkness, a troubled footfall marking time, as if he could walk away from dread by wearing a path into the floor.

It soothed Margaret, in those days, to find her mother drawing her nearer with a tenderness she had not known since childhood. Mrs. Hale began to lean on her as on a companion—almost a friend admitted behind the curtain of small daily feelings; and Margaret, who had so often watched Dixon occupy that place, answered every summons to sympathy, even when the matter was some delicate discomfort of the room, a draught that set a candle wavering, a teacup that tasted faintly of soap. She listened, and made much of what her mother made much of, the way one might stoop to lift a pin that another cannot bear to see trodden underfoot.

So it happened that, without knowing she had earned it, she found herself paid in the very coin her heart had long desired.

One evening, when Mr. Hale was out, the house settling into its hush between tea-things cleared away and the lamps properly turned, Mrs. Hale began to speak of Frederick.

The name, which Margaret had carried like a covered dish—fragrant, forbidden, too precious to unveil at the wrong moment—was brought out of its hiding-place with a suddenness that made her breath catch. All the while she had hungered for knowledge, she had never dared ask; the more she wanted it, the more her voice failed her.

“Oh, Margaret,” Mrs. Hale said, shifting as if the sheets themselves remembered a storm, “it was so windy last night! It came howling down the chimney in our room. I could not sleep. I never can when it is like that. I got into a wakeful habit when poor Frederick was at sea; and now, even if I don’t waken all at once, I dream of him in some storm, with great, clear, glass-green walls of waves on either side his ship—higher than her very masts—curling over with that cruel white foam, like a gigantic crested serpent. It is an old dream, but it always comes back on windy nights, till I am thankful to waken, sitting straight up in bed with my terror.”

Outside, Milton’s night had its own soundscape: the far-off, steady thunder of industry, a pulse under the nearer noises of the street. The wind worrying at the chimney-pot did not sound like Helstone’s wind through leaves; it had a harsher edge, as if it scraped soot and grit along the brick. Mrs. Hale’s nerves—trained long ago to the sea’s imagined roar—took the town’s clang and hiss as if they were warnings.

“Poor Frederick! He is on land now, so wind can do him no harm. Though I did think it might shake down some of those tall chimneys.”

Margaret, leaning close, caught the faint scent of her mother’s lavender-water and the warm linen; and with it, suddenly, the remembered smell of letters that had travelled—paper that had slept in salt air and been handled by hands that had held ropes.

“Where is Frederick now, mamma? Our letters are directed to the care of Messrs. Barbour, at Cadiz. I know that; but where is he himself?”

Mrs. Hale knit her brows, as if trying to steady a name that slid away. “I can’t remember the place. But he is not called Hale; you must remember that, Margaret. Notice the F. D. in every corner of the letters. He has taken the name of Dickenson. I wanted him to have been called Beresford—to which he had a kind of right—but your father thought he had better not. He might be recognised, you know, if he were called by my name.”

Margaret’s timidity gave way before this opening. “Mamma,” she said softly, “I was at Aunt Shaw’s when it all happened; and I suppose I was not old enough to be told plainly. But I should like to know now—if I may—if it does not give you too much pain to speak of it.”

“Pain! No.” Mrs. Hale’s cheek flushed with a quick proud heat. “Yet it is pain to think I may never see my darling boy again. Or else he did right, Margaret. They may say what they like, but I have his own letters to show, and I’ll believe him—though he is my son—sooner than any court-martial on earth. Go to my little japan cabinet, dear; in the second left-hand drawer you will find a packet of letters.”

Margaret rose at once. The cabinet—black and shining, with its small painted birds and flowers—had always seemed to her as much a shrine as a piece of furniture. When she drew out the drawer, it came with a soft rasp of wood on wood; within lay the packet, tied with a silken string, and the paper edges yellowed as if by sun and salt. The smell rose at once: a faint briny odour, like dried seaweed on stone, mingled with the dust of years—an intimate scent, as if one could taste distance.

She carried them back as carefully as if bearing something that might spill.

Mrs. Hale’s hands trembled as she untied the string. The silk slid through her fingers with a little whisper. She peered at dates, lips moving, and then, in a hurry of anxious love, began to speak over the very words Margaret was trying to take in.

“You see,” she said, pressing the first sheet into Margaret’s hand, “how from the first he disliked Captain Reid. He was second lieutenant then—on the Orion—when Frederick went out the first time. Poor little fellow—how well he looked in his midshipman’s dress, with his dirk in his hand, cutting open all the newspapers with it, as if it were a paper-knife! But Mr. Reid—as he was then—took a dislike to Frederick from the beginning.”

She shifted to another letter. “And then—stay!—these are the letters from the Russell, when Frederick was appointed to her and found his old enemy Captain Reid in command. He did mean to bear it patiently. Look—this is the letter. Just read it, Margaret. Where is it he says—Stop—‘my father may rely upon me, that I will bear with all proper patience everything that one officer and gentleman can take from another. But from my former knowledge of my present captain, I confess I look forward with apprehension to a long course of tyranny on board the Russell.’ You see, he promises—he promises!”

Margaret read slowly. The ink had paled; parts were blurred, as if some spray had once kissed the page and left its mark. Even in that faintness the voice came through—a young man trying to set down restraint like a rule of seamanship, trying to measure his own temper as carefully as a course.

Mrs. Hale hurried on, unable to stop the tide of memory. “Is that the letter where he speaks of the captain’s impatience with the men, for not going through the manœuvres as quickly as the Avenger? You see, he says the Russell had many new hands; while the Avenger had been nearly three years on the station, with nothing to do but keep slavers off and work her men, till they ran up and down the rigging like rats or monkeys.”

As Margaret made out the lines, she could feel the ship in them: the cramped deck, the tarred ropes, the hot iron smell of fittings warmed by sun, the rank breath of many bodies in close quarters. It might be, she thought, that the letter exaggerated—written too close to the sting of anger, with the heat of the scene still in his blood. Yet the picture it painted was sharp as a knife.

Some sailors, Frederick wrote, had been aloft in the main-topsail rigging. Captain Reid ordered them to race down, threatening the hindmost with the cat. The man farthest on the spar, seeing he could not pass, and dreading the flogging like a shame worse than pain, threw himself desperately down to catch a rope lower. He missed. He struck the deck senseless, and lived only a few hours after. The crew’s indignation boiled; and Margaret could almost hear it—the sudden hush after the thud, then the muttered surge, the dangerous animal sound of men restrained.

Mrs. Hale pressed her lips together, as if tasting bitterness. “But we did not receive this letter till long, long after we heard of the mutiny. Poor Fred! I dare say it was a comfort to him to write it, even though he could not have known how to send it.”

She sat up a little straighter, as if bracing herself against what came next. In the pause the house made its own noises: a distant door shut; somewhere a kettle-lid clicked as if a servant were settling the last things for the night; and beyond all, the town’s ceaseless industrial breath—a reminder that there are powers that never sleep, that grind on regardless of one family’s grief.

“And then,” Mrs. Hale went on, “we saw a report in the papers—long before Fred’s letter reached us—of an atrocious mutiny on board the Russell, and that the mutineers had remained in possession of the ship, which had gone off, it was supposed, to be a pirate; and that Captain Reid was sent adrift in a boat with some men—officers, or something—whose names were all given, for they were picked up by a West Indian steamer.”

Her voice trembled as she came to the list, that brutal catalogue of the saved. “Oh, Margaret! how your father and I turned sick over that list when there was no name of Frederick Hale. We thought it must be a mistake. Poor Fred was such a fine fellow—only perhaps too passionate; and we hoped the name of Carr, which was in the list, was a misprint for Hale. Newspapers are so careless.”

Margaret imagined the newspaper itself: the cheap ink, the coarse paper, the words set in hard black—dominant, public, and careless. How quickly a name—misspelt, omitted, replaced—could become a verdict. How easily a living person could be translated into a label and then lost in it.

“And towards post-time the next day,” Mrs. Hale continued, “papa set off to walk to Southampton for the papers; and I could not stop at home, so I went to meet him. He was very late—much later than I thought—and I sat down under the hedge to wait. He came at last, his arms hanging loose, his head sunk, walking heavily, as if every step was a labour. Margaret, I see him now.”

“Don’t go on, mamma,” Margaret said, her heart tightening. She slid closer, and kissed her mother’s hand, which felt thin and hot. “I can understand.”

“No, you can’t. No one can who did not see him then.” Mrs. Hale’s eyes shone, fixed on something far away. “I could hardly lift myself to go and meet him—everything reeled around me. And when I got to him, he did not speak, or seem surprised to see me there—more than three miles from home, beside the Oldham beech-tree. But he put my arm in his, and kept stroking my hand, as if he wanted to soothe me to be very quiet under some great heavy blow.”

Her hand, remembering, twitched faintly in Margaret’s grasp.

“And when I trembled so all over I could not speak, he took me in his arms, and stooped his head on mine, and began to shake and cry in a strange muffled groaning voice, till I—out of fright—stood quite still, only begging him to tell me what he had heard. And then, with his hand jerking, as if someone else moved it against his will, he gave me a wicked newspaper to read—calling our Frederick a ‘traitor of the blackest dye,’ ‘a base, ungrateful disgrace to his profession.’ Oh! I cannot tell what bad words they did not use.”

The words themselves seemed to scrape the air, like grit on teeth.

“I took the paper,” Mrs. Hale said, her breath quickening, “and as soon as I had read—I tore it up to little bits. I tore it—I believe, Margaret, I tore it with my teeth. I did not cry. I could not. My cheeks were as hot as fire, and my very eyes burnt. Your father looked grave at me. I said it was a lie, and so it was.”

She drew one of Frederick’s letters close, as if it were a warm loaf taken from the oven—proof of honest labour against the coldness of print. “Months after, this letter came, and you see what provocation Frederick had. It was not for himself, or his own injuries, he rebelled; but he would speak his mind to Captain Reid, and so it went on from bad to worse; and you see, most of the sailors stuck by Frederick.”

Margaret held the paper and felt, with a kind of helpless clarity, how power moved: how one man’s voice, because it had a captain’s title, could become law; how another’s, because it was the voice of a younger officer, might be called insolence; and how the newspaper—using its own proud dialect—could coin a story that would stick to a family name like soot.

After a pause Mrs. Hale spoke again, her strength spent, her tone low and shaking. “I think, Margaret… I am glad of it. I am prouder of Frederick standing up against injustice than if he had been simply a good officer.”

“I am sure I am,” Margaret answered, with a steadiness that surprised herself. “Loyalty and obedience to wisdom and justice are fine; but it is finer to defy arbitrary power—unjustly and cruelly used—not on behalf of ourselves, but on behalf of others more helpless.”

Mrs. Hale’s proud look faltered into yearning. “For all that, I wish I could see Frederick once more—just once. He was my first baby, Margaret.”

She spoke as if apologising for the hunger of it, as if a mother’s longing might wrong the child beside her. But Margaret felt no such jealousy; she was already turning the desire over in her mind, as one turns a problem of household management—how to make a little go far, how to contrive warmth where there is none.

“It is six or seven years ago,” she said. “Would they still prosecute him, mother? If he came and stood his trial—what would be the punishment? Surely he might bring evidence of his provocation.”

“It would do no good,” Mrs. Hale replied, and the plainness of the words fell like a heavy lid. “Some of the sailors who accompanied Frederick were taken, and there was a court-martial held on them on board the Amicia. I believed all they said in their defence—poor fellows—because it just agreed with Frederick’s story. But it was of no use—”

For the first time that evening she cried. The tears came slowly, as if drawn from deep reserves; they shone on her lashes and slid down without sound.

And yet something in Margaret—some stern necessity of knowing the whole—drove her to ask what she dreaded.

“What happened to them, mamma?”

“They were hung at the yard-arm,” said Mrs. Hale, solemnly; and the sentence seemed to ring in the room like a struck bell, harsh and final. “And the worst was that the court, in condemning them to death, said they had suffered themselves to be led astray from their duty by their superior officers.”

Silence followed—thick, airless. The house noises continued their small indifferent music; far off, Milton’s engines kept up their iron chant. Margaret listened to that industrial roar and thought how it drowned out so much—how a town could make one kind of sound constant and call it prosperity, while other sounds—water, wind in trees, a dialect spoken softly at a hearth—grew faint, as if the world had decided they were unnecessary.

“And Frederick was in South America for several years, was he not?” she asked at length, to steady the talk into facts.

“Yes. And now he is in Spain. At Cadiz, or somewhere near it.” Mrs. Hale’s voice dropped. “If he comes to England he will be hung. I shall never see his face again—for if he comes to England he will be hung.”

There was nothing to be done with such a truth—not folded up neatly like linen, not sweetened like bitter tea. Mrs. Hale turned her face to the wall and lay still in a despair that seemed older than the day’s sorrow, as if it had been simmering all these years and now, uncovered, filled the room with its heavy, inescapable smell. She drew her hand out of Margaret’s with a small impatient movement, not unkind, only craving solitude with the image of her son.

When Mr. Hale came in, his step and voice stirring the air, Margaret slipped away. She went out as one leaves a room where something has burned too long and too darkly, oppressed with gloom, and seeing no promise of brightness on any side of the horizon.

“Margaret,” her father said the next day, drawing the words out as if he feared to give them shape, “we must return Mrs. Thornton’s call. Your mother is not very well, and thinks she cannot walk so far; but you and I will go this afternoon.”

They set out while the day still held a thin, pale light, and the town’s breath met them at the first turning—coal-smoke and damp stone, with the faint sourness that always seemed to cling to Milton, as if the very air had been boiled too long in iron pots. Mr. Hale, who had walked as one might in a country lane, began now to speak with a guarded earnestness, as though the clatter of the streets had driven his thoughts inward.

“Did you consult the doctor, Margaret? Did you send for him?”

“No, papa. You spoke of his coming to see me, and I was well. But if I only knew of some good doctor, I would go this afternoon and ask him to come—for I am sure mamma is seriously indisposed.”

She said it with the plainness she had used once before and had been met with a gentle rebuke for “fancies.” She could not bear that softness now; her mother’s very voice seemed to have thinned of late, like broth that has been watered and warmed again and again until it holds no strength.

He answered, and the note in his tone was new to her—despondent, as if he had been holding a door shut against fear and at last felt the latch give.

“Do you think she has any hidden complaint? Do you think she is really very ill? Has Dixon said anything? Oh, Margaret! I am haunted by the fear that our coming to Milton has killed her. My poor Maria!”

“Oh, papa! don’t imagine such things,” Margaret cried, shocked into tenderness. “She is not well, that is all. Many a one is not well for a time; and with good advice gets better and stronger than ever.”

“But has Dixon said anything about her?”

“No. You know Dixon enjoys making a mystery out of trifles; and she has been a little mysterious about mamma’s health, which has alarmed me rather, that is all. Without any reason, I dare say. You know, papa, you said the other day I was getting fanciful.”

“I hope and trust you are. But don’t think of what I said then. I like you to be fanciful about your mother’s health! Don’t be afraid of telling me your fancies.” His voice shook into a quicker warmth. “We will ask Mrs. Thornton if she can tell us of a good doctor. We won’t throw away our money on any but some one first-rate. Stay—we turn up this street.”

The street they turned into seemed too mean to contain the commanding figure Margaret had pictured. Marlborough Street ran in long ranks of small houses and blank walls, the bricks darkened as if rubbed daily with soot. No porch announced importance; no trees softened the line. Only the town’s constant sound went on—wheels scouring the stones, a far-off hammering, and underneath it that ceaseless industrial note, like a giant breathing through metal.

“He told me he lived in Marlborough Street, I’m sure,” Mr. Hale said, perplexed.

“Perhaps it is one of the economies he still practises,” Margaret answered. “But here are people about; let me ask.”

She questioned a passer-by and was told, not of a house-front, but of gates: Mr. Thornton lived close to the mill. They were directed to a lodge-door at the end of the long dead wall.

It was no grand entrance—only a door like one to a garden, with great closed gates beside it for wagons and lorries. The lodge-keeper admitted them, and they passed into a large oblong yard. On one side, offices sat primly for the transaction of business; opposite rose the mill itself, immense, many-windowed, and alive with sound. The continual clank of machinery struck the ear like blows. The steam-engine’s groan rolled out and back again, so that the air seemed thick with it; it was a noise that had weight, that pressed on the skull. Margaret found herself listening as one listens to a storm—not for beauty, but for endurance—and she thought how a place’s sounds might wear a person down more surely than hunger.

On one of the narrow sides of the yard stood the house, handsome in its proportions, stone-coped and older in fashion—built, perhaps, fifty or sixty years ago—blackened by smoke, yet with paint and windows and steps kept scrupulously clean. Flights of steps rose to the front door from either side, guarded by railings that spoke of an age that still liked symmetry. Margaret wondered, with a sudden pang, why those who could afford such order did not choose a smaller dwelling somewhere with hedgerows and quiet; why anyone would choose to sleep and eat and speak under the perpetual mill-roar.

Her ears, unused to such a din, could scarcely catch her father’s voice as they stood on the steps. The yard’s dead wall made the view from the windows a prison-yard prospect; and when they entered and were shown upstairs into the drawing-room, the place struck her as a sort of sealed chamber set down in the midst of labour—kept as if to deny that labour.

There was no one there. It seemed as though no one had lived in it since the furniture had been bagged up with care enough for a house to be buried by lava and unearthed centuries later. Pink and gold walls gleamed. A carpet patterned with flower-bunches lay hidden beneath a linen drugget, glazed and colourless from long protection. Lace curtains, netted veils over each chair and sofa, alabaster groups under glass shades—everything guarded from dust as if dust were a moral failing. In the centre, beneath the bagged chandelier, a circular table shone with smartly-bound books arranged at set intervals like coloured spokes. Everything reflected light; nothing absorbed it. The room had an icy purity that made Margaret’s skin draw tight. It was clean in the way a pantry may be clean that never sees bread kneaded on its boards, never feels the warm steam of broth, never hears the domestic stir that belongs to nourishment and rest. There was evidence of labour everywhere, but of labour that served ornament alone—made and preserved against the town’s soot—rather than labour that made a home easeful.

They spoke in low voices while they waited, as if the unused echoes might be startled awake. Then Mrs. Thornton came in, rustling in her usual handsome black silk. Her muslins and laces rivalled the room’s severe whiteness without ever softening it.

Margaret explained why her mother had not come; but in her anxiety not to revive her father’s fears, she spoke awkwardly, and left Mrs. Thornton with the impression of a temporary, fine-ladyish indisposition—something that might have been put aside for a stronger motive, or, if it were real, might have warranted deferring the call. Mrs. Thornton, remembering her own carriage and horses hired for her visit to the Hales, and how Fanny had been ordered by Mr. Thornton to go pay them every respect, drew up slightly offended and gave Margaret no sympathy—hardly any credit.

“How is Mr. Thornton?” Mr. Hale asked. “I was afraid he was not well, from his hurried note yesterday.”

“My son is rarely ill; and when he is, he never speaks about it, or makes it an excuse for not doing anything,” she replied. “He told me he could not get leisure to read with you last night, sir. He regretted it, I am sure; he values the hours spent with you.”

“I am sure they are equally agreeable to me,” Mr. Hale said. “It makes me feel young again to see his enjoyment and appreciation of all that is fine in classical literature.”

“I have no doubt classics are very desirable for people who have leisure.” Mrs. Thornton’s voice took on that tone which made opinion sound like law. “But I confess, it was against my judgment that my son renewed his study of them. The time and place in which he lives require all his energy and attention. Classics may do very well for men who loiter away their lives in the country or in colleges; but Milton men ought to have their thoughts and powers absorbed in the work of to-day. At least, that is my opinion.”

“But surely,” Margaret said, “if the mind is too long directed to one object only, it will get stiff and rigid, and unable to take in many interests.”

“I do not quite understand what you mean by a mind getting stiff and rigid. Nor do I admire those whirligig characters that are full of this thing to-day, to be utterly forgetful of it in their new interest to-morrow. Having many interests does not suit the life of a Milton manufacturer. It is—or ought to be—enough for him to have one great desire, and to bring all the purposes of his life to bear on the fulfilment of that.”

“And that is—?” Mr. Hale asked.

Mrs. Thornton’s sallow cheek flushed; her eye lightened, as if she were putting her hand on a cherished loaf and feeling its warmth through the cloth.

“To hold and maintain a high, honourable place among the merchants of his country—the men of his town. Such a place my son has earned for himself. Go where you will—I don’t say in England only, but in Europe—the name of John Thornton of Milton is known and respected amongst all men of business. Of course, it is unknown in the fashionable circles,” she added scornfully. “Idle gentlemen and ladies are not likely to know much of a Milton manufacturer, unless he gets into parliament, or marries a lord’s daughter.”

Mr. Hale and Margaret were both conscious—half uneasy, half absurdly amused—that they had never heard this great name until Mr. Bell had written to them that Mr. Thornton would be a good friend to have in Milton. Mrs. Thornton’s world of ledgers and markets was not the world of Harley Street or of country parsonages. Margaret tried to keep her face neutral, but the proud mother caught the shade of feeling.

“You think you never heard of this wonderful son of mine, Miss Hale. You think I’m an old woman whose ideas are bounded by Milton, and whose own crow is the whitest ever seen.”

“No,” Margaret answered, with spirit. “It may be true that I was thinking I had hardly heard Mr. Thornton’s name before I came to Milton. But since I have come here, I have heard enough to make me respect and admire him, and to feel how much justice and truth there is in what you have said of him.”

“Who spoke to you of him?” Mrs. Thornton asked—mollified a little, yet jealous, as if praise were a spice she wished to measure herself.

Margaret hesitated; she disliked this authoritative questioning. Mr. Hale, thinking to save her, said—

“It was what Mr. Thornton said himself that made us know the kind of man he was. Was it not, Margaret?”

Mrs. Thornton drew herself up.

“My son is not the one to tell of his own doings. May I again ask you, Miss Hale, from whose account you formed your favourable opinion of him? A mother is curious and greedy of commendation of her children, you know.”

“It was as much from what Mr. Thornton withheld,” Margaret replied, “of that which we had been told of his previous life by Mr. Bell—it was more that, than what he said, that made us all feel what reason you have to be proud of him.”

“Mr. Bell! What can he know of John? He, living a lazy life in a drowsy college. But I’m obliged to you, Miss Hale. Many a missy young lady would have shrunk from giving an old woman the pleasure of hearing that her son was well spoken of.”

“Why?” Margaret asked, looking at her in bewilderment.

“Why! because I suppose they might have consciences that told them how surely they were making the old mother into an advocate for them, in case they had any plans on the son’s heart.”

She smiled grimly. Margaret, startled by the picture, laughed outright—so frankly that it grated upon Mrs. Thornton’s ear, as if the notion must be entirely ridiculous.

Margaret stopped as soon as she saw the offended look.

“I beg your pardon, madam. But I really am very much obliged to you for exonerating me from making any plans on Mr. Thornton’s heart.”

“Young ladies have, before now,” Mrs. Thornton returned stiffly.

“I hope Miss Thornton is well,” Mr. Hale put in, eager to change the stream.

“She is as well as she ever is. She is not strong,” replied Mrs. Thornton shortly.

“And Mr. Thornton? I suppose I may hope to see him on Thursday?”

“I cannot answer for my son’s engagements. There is some uncomfortable work going on in the town; a threatening of a strike. If so, his experience and judgment will make him much consulted by his friends. But I should think he could come on Thursday. At any rate, I am sure he will let you know if he cannot.”

“A strike!” Margaret said. “What for? What are they going to strike for?”

“For the mastership and ownership of other people’s property,” Mrs. Thornton answered, with a fierce snort. “That is what they always strike for. If my son’s work-people strike, I will only say they are a pack of ungrateful hounds. But I have no doubt they will.”

“They are wanting higher wages, I suppose?” Mr. Hale asked.

“That is the face of the thing. But the truth is, they want to be masters, and make the masters into slaves on their own ground. They are always trying at it; they always have it in their minds; and every five or six years, there comes a struggle between masters and men. They’ll find themselves mistaken this time, I fancy—a little out of their reckoning. If they turn out, they mayn’t find it so easy to go in again. I believe the masters have a thing or two in their heads which will teach the men not to strike again in a hurry, if they try it this time.”

“Does it make the town very rough?” Margaret asked.

“Of course it does. But surely you are not a coward, are you? Milton is not the place for cowards. I have known the time when I have had to thread my way through a crowd of white, angry men, all swearing they would have Makinson’s blood as soon as he ventured to show his nose out of his factory; and he, knowing nothing of it, some one had to go and tell him, or he was a dead man; and it needed to be a woman—so I went. And when I got in, I could not get out. It was as much as my life was worth. So I went up to the roof, where there were stones piled ready to drop on the heads of the crowd, if they tried to force the factory doors. And I would have lifted those heavy stones, and dropped them with as good an aim as the best man there, but that I fainted with the heat I had gone through. If you live in Milton, you must learn to have a brave heart, Miss Hale.”

“I would do my best,” Margaret said, rather pale. “I do not know whether I am brave or not till I am tried; but I am afraid I should be a coward.”

“South country people are often frightened by what our Darkshire men and women only call living and struggling. But when you’ve been ten years among a people who are always owing their betters a grudge, and only waiting for an opportunity to pay it off, you’ll know whether you are a coward or not, take my word for it.”

The visit ended under that harsh prophecy. As Margaret and her father went back through the yard, the mill’s voice followed them like a held note. It was not merely loud; it was unceasing. In the pauses between one clang and the next, she could hear—strangely—her own heart, as if her body were trying to make a softer music for itself.

That evening Mr. Thornton came to Mr. Hale’s. He was shown into the drawing-room, where Mr. Hale was reading aloud to his wife and daughter; the lamplight made a small, warm circle, and the quiet cadence of Mr. Hale’s voice was like water poured steadily into a cup—so different from the mill’s roar that Margaret felt, for an instant, as if this domestic sound were itself a kind of sustenance.

“I am come partly to bring you a note from my mother,” Mr. Thornton said, “and partly to apologise for not keeping to my time yesterday. The note contains the address you asked for—Dr. Donaldson.”

“Thank you,” Margaret said hastily, holding out her hand for the note; she did not wish her mother to hear that they had been inquiring about a doctor. Mr. Thornton seemed at once to understand the wish. He put the paper into her hand without explanation, and the small discretion touched her more than many loud sympathies could have done.

Mr. Hale soon began to speak of the strike. At once Mr. Thornton’s face took on that hard expression Margaret had noticed in his mother—the look of one who stands, not in debate, but in defence.

“Yes,” he said. “The fools will have a strike. Let them. It suits us well enough. But we gave them a chance. They think trade is flourishing as it was last year. We see the storm on the horizon and draw in our sails. But because we don’t explain our reasons, they won’t believe we’re acting reasonably. We must give them line and letter for the way we choose to spend or save our money. Henderson tried a dodge with his men out at Ashley, and failed. He rather wanted a strike; it would have suited his book well enough. So, when the men came to ask for the five per cent. they are claiming, he told ’em he’d think about it, and give them his answer on the pay day; knowing all the while what his answer would be, of course, but thinking he’d strengthen their conceit of their own way. However, they were too deep for him, and heard something about the bad prospects of trade. So in they came on the Friday and drew back their claim, and now he’s obliged to go on working. But we Milton masters have to-day sent in our decision. We won’t advance a penny. We tell them we may have to lower wages; but can’t afford to raise. So here we stand, waiting for their next attack.”

“And what will that be?” Mr. Hale asked.

“I conjecture a simultaneous strike. You will see Milton without smoke in a few days, I imagine, Miss Hale.”

“But why,” Margaret said, “could you not explain what good reason you had for expecting a bad trade? I don’t know whether I use the right words, but you will understand what I mean.”

“Do you give your servants reasons for your expenditure, or your economy in the use of your own money? We, the owners of capital, have a right to choose what we will do with it.”

“A human right,” Margaret murmured, very low—so low it seemed meant to be swallowed by the room.

“I beg your pardon, I did not hear what you said.”

“I would rather not repeat it,” she replied; “it related to a feeling which I do not think you would share.”

“Won’t you try me?” he pleaded, and his eagerness was so sudden it altered the air between them, as a hand might change a conversation’s temperature by moving nearer to a fire.

She was displeased by his pertinacity, yet would not make her words into a greater matter than they were.

“I said you had a human right. I meant that there seemed no reason but religious ones why you should not do what you like with your own.”

“I know we differ in our religious opinions,” he said, lowering his voice as if speaking to her alone, “but don’t you give me credit for having some, though not the same as yours?”

Margaret did not wish to be singled out thus. She answered in her usual tone, letting it be heard as part of the room’s general talk.

“I do not think that I have any occasion to consider your special religious opinions in the affair. All I meant to say is, that there is no human law to prevent employers from utterly wasting or throwing away all their money, if they choose; but that there are passages in the Bible which would rather imply—to me at least—that they neglected their duties as stewards if they did so. However, I know so little about strikes and rate of wages, and capital, and labour, that I had better not talk to a political economist like you.”

“Nay, the more reason,” he said eagerly. “I shall only be too glad to explain to you all that may seem anomalous or mysterious to a stranger; especially at a time like this, when our doings are sure to be canvassed by every scribbler who can hold a pen.”

“Thank you,” she answered coldly. “Of course I shall apply to my father in the first instance for any information he can give me, if I get puzzled with living here amongst this strange society.”

“You think it strange. Why?”

“I don’t know—because, on the very face of it, I see two classes dependent on each other in every possible way, yet each evidently regarding the interests of the other as opposed to their own. I never lived in a place before where there were two sets of people always running each other down.”

“Who have you heard running the masters down?” he asked quickly. “I don’t ask who you have heard abusing the men; for I see you persist in misunderstanding what I said the other day. But who have you heard abusing the masters?”

Margaret reddened, then smiled—more out of refusal than mirth.

“I am not fond of being catechised. I refuse to answer your question. Besides, it has nothing to do with the fact. You must take my word for it, that I have heard some people—or it may be only some one of the workpeople—speak as though it were the interest of the employers to keep them from acquiring money—that it would make them too independent if they had a sum in the savings’ bank.”

“I dare say it was that man Higgins who told you all this,” Mrs. Hale said from her chair. Mr. Thornton kept his face as if he had not heard; but Margaret could tell he had caught the name and stored it, like a ledger-entry made without looking down.

“I heard, moreover,” Margaret continued, “that it was considered to the advantage of the masters to have ignorant workmen—not hedge-lawyers, as Captain Lennox used to call those men in his company who questioned and would know the reason for every order.”

She had meant the last words rather for her father; but she saw Mr. Thornton’s expression alter at the name, as if it had struck him like an unwelcome sound—a note from some other world that did not belong in his.

Who is Captain Lennox? he asked himself, with a sharp displeasure that held him silent for a moment.

Mr. Hale took up the thread. “You never were fond of schools, Margaret, or you would have seen and known before this how much is being done for education in Milton.”

“No,” she said, suddenly meek. “I know I do not care enough about schools. But the knowledge and the ignorance I was speaking of did not relate to reading and writing—the teaching or information one can give to a child. I am sure what was meant was ignorance of the wisdom that shall guide men and women. I hardly know what that is. But he—that is, my informant—spoke as if the masters would like their people to be merely tall, large children—living in the present moment—with a blind unreasoning kind of obedience.”

“In short, Miss Hale,” Mr. Thornton said, and the offended edge returned to his voice, “it is very evident that your informant found a pretty ready listener to all the slander he chose to utter against the masters.”

Margaret did not reply. The personal thrust stung her; she felt as if he had taken her very words and stamped them with a meaning she had not intended. A silence fell that made the room’s gentler sounds—Mrs. Hale’s faint breathing, the small settling of the fire—more distinct, as if quiet itself were trying to patch what harshness had torn.

Mr. Hale spoke next.

“I must confess that, although I have not become so intimately acquainted with any workmen as Margaret has, I am very much struck by the antagonism between the employer and the employed, on the very surface of things. I even gather this impression from what you yourself have from time to time said.”

Mr. Thornton paused before answering. Margaret had left the room, and he was vexed—vexed at the misunderstanding and at the sense that he had lost ground with her. Yet the annoyance cooled him into thoughtfulness, and when he spoke again his manner had more dignity than heat.

“My theory is that my interests are identical with those of my workpeople, and vice-versa. Miss Hale, I know, does not like to hear men called ‘hands,’ so I won’t use that word—though it comes most readily to my lips as the technical term, whose origin, whatever it was, dates before my time. On some future day—in some millennium—in Utopia, this unity may be brought into practice—just as I can fancy a republic the most perfect form of government.”

“We will read Plato’s Republic as soon as we have finished Homer,” Mr. Hale said, and his voice, falling again into its accustomed scholar’s cadence, tried to bring the room back under the older, quieter dominion of books—those preserved words that outlast storms, and yet cannot always translate what a living voice means when it speaks in anger or in fear.

The next afternoon brought Dr. Donaldson to Marlborough Street, and with him the old, sharp-edged privacy that had lately seemed to soften within the Hale rooms. The drawing-room door closed; Margaret was left outside it as if she were again a child, while Dixon—keys, apron, and authority—passed in without so much as a glance.

Margaret would not sit. She went into her mother’s bedchamber—the little room that backed the drawing-room like a pantry behind a kitchen—and walked its narrow length, heel to toe, heel to toe, counting the boards without meaning to. The house had its usual London undertone: a far cart-rumble, a hawker’s call blurred by distance, the faint, ceaseless hiss of the city that never truly paused. Over it, she strained for the smallest domestic sound—her mother’s breath, the drag of a slipper, the sigh that might become a groan.

Once—surely—there was a moan. It threaded through the wall like steam through a cracked lid. Margaret stopped so abruptly that the blood seemed to stop with her; she held her breath and pressed her clenched hands against her own ribs, as if she could keep her heart quiet by force. Silence followed—too complete, too careful. Then the scrape of a chair-leg, voices raised into the courteous pitch of departure, the polite little disturbances that always came when someone had been told more than they wished to hear.

The drawing-room door opened. Margaret was out of her mother’s room before the latch had finished clicking.

“My father is from home, Dr. Donaldson,” she said. “He is with a pupil at this hour. Will you be so good as to come into his room—downstairs?”

Dixon made a sound like a disapproving cough, and half turned as if to interpose herself—housekeeper against daughter; keeper of the sick-room against an intruder. But Margaret, all at once, took up her place as if she had been born into it and had merely forgotten to claim it. There was something in her carriage—head lifted, voice steady, step decisive—that checked Dixon more effectually than argument. For an instant the very oddity of it—Margaret feeling herself look grand, Dixon looking scandalised—sent a flash of amusement through Margaret’s terror, like tasting sharp lemon in the middle of bitterness. It held her for the length of the staircase.

Then she was in her father’s study, and the business of breath and blood returned. The familiar smell of books—leather and dust and the faintest tang of ink—seemed suddenly too dry, too lifeless. It was a moment before she could make her tongue obey her.

“What is the matter with mamma?” she said at last. “You will oblige me by telling me the simple truth.”

Dr. Donaldson had taken his place with the ease of a man accustomed to sorrowful parlours, accustomed to being made both confessor and enemy. He looked at her, measured her, and Margaret felt the measurement as a kind of pressure.

“My dear young lady,” he began, in the tone that was meant to soothe, “your mother seems to have a most attentive and efficient servant—more like her friend—”

“I am her daughter, sir.”

A pause—his eyes narrowing a fraction, as if he had expected this.

“But when I tell you she expressly desired you might not be told—”

“I am not good or patient enough to submit to the prohibition,” Margaret answered; and though her voice shook, it did not waver. “Besides, I am sure you are too wise—too experienced—to have promised to keep the secret.”

His mouth twitched, half smile and half sorrow. “There you are right. I did not promise. In fact, I fear the secret will be known soon enough without my revealing it.”

Margaret’s hands—so still—tightened upon each other. She did not sit down. She did not plead. She waited with the stillness of someone who will be told whether she begs or not.

He spoke at last—two short sentences, lowered as if the words themselves were indecently loud. He watched her while he spoke. The pupils of her eyes widened until they seemed to swallow all colour; the pale skin of her cheeks turned livid, as if the life had been drained in one sudden draught. When he stopped, he did not at once speak again. He waited for her breath to return.

She drew it in with effort, as if her lungs had become too small for London air. “I thank you most truly, sir,” she said. “That dread has haunted me for many weeks. It is a true, real agony. My poor, poor mother!”

Her lips began to tremble; tears came, not in a storm but in a brief, hot relief, and Dr. Donaldson—who had seen women collapse and scream and rage—let them come, certain she would arrest them when she must. She wiped them away with the back of her hand, almost impatient with herself, and her need for particulars broke through.

“Will there be much suffering?”

He shook his head. “That we cannot tell. It depends on constitution—on a thousand things. But the late discoveries of medical science have given us large power of alleviation.”

“My father,” Margaret said, and the words made her tremble all over. “Oh—my father!”

“I do not know Mr. Hale well,” he replied slowly. “It is difficult to advise. But I should say—bear on for a little while with the knowledge you have forced me to give you so abruptly, until the fact has become in some degree familiar to you. Then you will be able, without too great an effort, to give what comfort you can to your father. Before then—my visits, which I shall repeat from time to time, though I fear I can do nothing but alleviate—a thousand little circumstances will occur to awaken his alarm, to deepen it. He will be the better prepared.”

He softened then, as if finding his way past professional caution. “Nay—my dear young lady—nay. I saw Mr. Thornton, and I honour your father for the sacrifice he has made, however mistaken I may believe him to be. Well—this once, if it will please you—my dear. Only remember: when I come again, I come as a friend. You must learn to look upon me as such; for seeing each other—getting to know each other—at such times as these is worth years of morning calls.”

Margaret could not answer; her throat closed on every word. But at parting she took his hand and wrung it with a strength that surprised him.

“That’s what I call a fine girl,” Dr. Donaldson thought, once he was seated in his carriage and had leisure to look down at his ringed fingers, slightly sore from her grip. “Who would have thought that little hand could give such a squeeze? But the bones are well put together; that gives immense power. What a queen she is—head thrown back at first to force me into the truth; then bent forward, eager as a hawk, to catch it. Poor thing. I must see she does not overstrain herself. Though it’s astonishing what these thorough-bred creatures can do and suffer. That girl’s game to the backbone. Another, gone that deadly colour, would have fainted or fallen into hysterics. But she wouldn’t—not she. The very force of her will brought her round. Such a girl would win my heart, if I were thirty years younger. Too late now. Ah—here we are at the Archers’.”

And he was out, ready to be called upon as if no other household in all London had pain but this.

Margaret went back into her father’s study for one instant, as if she must gather herself like a cook gathering her wits before a spoiled dish—no time to lament, only time to begin again. The air in the room seemed suddenly stale; she could almost taste the soot in it, the city’s fine ash settling on every surface, even on the tongue. Noise outside thickened and thinned as a cart passed, iron-hooped wheels singing harshly over stone. She pressed her hands to her face.

“Oh, my God—my God—this is terrible,” she whispered. “How shall I bear it? Such a deadly disease—no hope! Oh, mamma, mamma! I wish I had never gone to Aunt Shaw’s, and been all those precious years away from you. Poor mamma—how much you must have borne—alone. Oh—pray, my God, that her sufferings may not be too acute, too dreadful. How shall I bear to see them? How can I bear papa’s agony? He must not be told yet—not all at once. It would kill him. But I won’t lose another moment of my own dear, precious mother.”

She ran upstairs.

Dixon was not in the room. Mrs. Hale lay back in an easy-chair, wrapped in a soft white shawl that had been folded about her with practised hands, and in a becoming cap set on with that particular care women used to take when illness had begun to steal their dignity. The exertion of the examination had left her with a faint flush; exhaustion gave her, for the moment, a kind of peace that was like the quiet after bread has been kneaded and set to rise—stillness that is not rest, but waiting.

Margaret was struck by the calm.

“Why, Margaret—how strange you look! What is the matter?” Mrs. Hale said; and then suspicion slid into her voice, as if it pained her to suspect. “You have not been seeing Dr. Donaldson and asking him questions—have you, child?”

Margaret did not answer; she could only look, her whole face confessing what her lips would not.

Mrs. Hale’s quiet turned to displeasure. “He would not surely break his word to me—and—”

“Oh yes, mamma, he did,” Margaret said quickly. “I made him. It was I—blame me.”

She knelt by the chair, caught her mother’s hand, and held it as if she could anchor her there. Mrs. Hale tried to draw it back; Margaret would not let go. She kissed the thin fingers again and again, and tears—hot, salt, shamefully abundant—fell on the skin and made it shine.

“Margaret, it was very wrong of you. You knew I did not wish you to know.”

But the struggle tired her; her hand remained in Margaret’s grasp, and after a moment her fingers pressed faintly back, as if, against her will, comfort had begun to creep in.

That small return of pressure gave Margaret courage. “Oh, mamma—let me be your nurse. I will learn anything Dixon can teach me. But you know I am your child, and I do think I have a right to do everything for you.”

“You don’t know what you are asking,” Mrs. Hale said, with a shudder, as if the word nurse carried with it images of pain that could not be spoken.

“Yes, I do,” Margaret answered—too urgently, too earnestly. “I know a great deal more than you are aware of. Let me be your nurse. Let me try, at any rate. No one has ever—shall ever—try so hard as I will do. It will be such a comfort, mamma.”

“My poor child! Well—you shall try. Do you know, Margaret—Dixon and I thought you would quite shrink from me if you knew—”

“Dixon thought!” Margaret’s lip curled before she could stop it; the bitter taste of Dixon’s judgement rose in her mouth like burnt sugar. “Dixon could not give me credit for enough true love—for as much as herself. She thought, I suppose, that I was one of those poor sickly women who like to lie on rose leaves and be fanned all day. Don’t let Dixon’s fancies come any more between you and me, mamma. Don’t—please!” The last word broke into entreaty.

“Don’t be angry with Dixon,” Mrs. Hale said anxiously, as if even now she must keep the household peace.

Margaret caught herself, ashamed. “No. I won’t. I will try and be humble—and learn her ways—if you will only let me do all I can for you. Let me be in the first place, mother—I am greedy of that. I used to fancy you would forget me while I was away at Aunt Shaw’s, and cry myself to sleep at nights with that notion in my head.”

“And I used to think,” Mrs. Hale answered, her voice softening into something like confession, “how will Margaret bear our make-shift poverty after the thorough comfort and luxury in Harley Street; till I have many a time been more ashamed of your seeing our contrivances at Helstone than of any stranger finding them out.”

“Oh, mamma—and I did so enjoy them!” Margaret said, and for a moment her smile came as naturally as if sorrow had not moved in at all. “They were so much more amusing than all the jog-trot Harley Street ways. The wardrobe shelf with handles that served as a supper-tray on grand occasions! And the old tea-chests stuffed and covered for ottomans! I think what you call make-shift contrivances at dear Helstone were a charming part of the life there.”

“I shall never see Helstone again, Margaret,” Mrs. Hale said; tears brimmed slowly, as if they had a long way to travel.

Margaret could not reply. The word Helstone rose in her mind with its remembered sounds—the clean hush of fields after rain, the birds’ calls that seemed to set one’s own breathing right, the church-bells that rang over green, not over stone. London, by contrast, was always grinding—always rattling, clanging, pushing its harsh music into every corner. She thought, with a pang that was almost anger, how the city’s ceaseless noise left no space for the gentle acoustics of a life remembered; as if grief itself required quiet to speak properly, and here one must shout it down.

Mrs. Hale went on, in the tone of one pronouncing sentence on herself. “While I was there, I was for ever wanting to leave it. Every place seemed pleasanter. And now I shall die far away from it. I am rightly punished.”

“You must not talk so,” Margaret said impatiently, more afraid of her mother’s resignation than of her mother’s pain. “He said you might live for years. Oh, mother! we will have you back at Helstone yet.”

“No—never! That I must take as a just penance.” She drew a quick breath, as if bracing herself, and then the word that had been kept, like a spice too strong to be brought out, leapt from her. “But, Margaret—Frederick!”

At the sound of that name her composure broke as if a cord had snapped. She cried out—not softly, not as a woman meant to cry in a sick-room, but loud, sharp, as if the cry itself were a pain.

“Frederick! Frederick!” It came again and again, each time more wild, more urgent. “Come to me. I am dying. Little first-born child—come to me once again!”

The room filled with her voice, and Margaret’s terror rose until it seemed to stop her hands from working. Mrs. Hale’s body shook with violent hysterics; her fine fingers clawed at the shawl as if it were choking her.

Margaret ran for Dixon.

Dixon came in on the high wind of resentment, as if called from a kitchen where something had boiled over. One look at Mrs. Hale’s agitation, and her eyes flashed at Margaret.

“There now!” she cried. “I told you! You’ve over-excited her—just because you would be meddling and prying—”

Margaret took the blame without a word, as if punishment could purchase calm. “Only help her,” she begged in her look and in the quick obedience of her hands. She fetched what Dixon demanded, held what Dixon bade her hold, moved when Dixon ordered her to move. She did not once defend herself. She only listened for the sound of her father’s step in the passage—dreading it as one dreads the sudden slam of a door in a quiet sick-room.

Between them they got Mrs. Hale into bed at last; the violent storm wore itself out into sobs, and the sobs into heavy sleep. Margaret sat by the bedside while the breathing deepened and steadied, watching each rise and fall of her mother’s chest as if counting it could keep it going. The city noise outside went on—wheels, voices, a distant hammering—but within the room there was, for a little while, the frail sanctuary of sleep.

At length Dixon beckoned her out, shutting the door with careful hands, and took her into the drawing-room. Her face was sour, as if she were about to do something distasteful, though her very distaste carried kindness. On the table stood a cup of coffee—fresh made, strong, the bitter scent rising at once, comforting and reproachful; Dixon had roasted it too far, perhaps, as anxious people do, so that it smelled of scorched beans and necessity. She stood over Margaret like a commander while Margaret drank.

“You shouldn’t have been so curious, Miss, and then you wouldn’t have needed to fret before your time,” Dixon said. “It would have come soon enough. And now, I suppose, you’ll tell master, and a pretty household I shall have of you!”

“No, Dixon,” Margaret answered, sorrowfully. “I will not tell papa. He could not bear it as I can.”

And as if to prove she bore it well, she burst into tears, sudden and helpless.
