“Ay! I knew how it would be,” Dixon said, but her own voice broke into something thinner. “Now you’ll waken your mamma, just after she’s gone to sleep so quietly. Miss Margaret, my dear—I’ve had to keep it down this many a week; and though I don’t pretend I can love her as you do, yet I loved her better than any other man, woman, or child—no one but Master Frederick ever came near her in my mind.”

She wiped at her eyes with her apron, fierce with shame at her own softness, and went on as if speech were a dam holding back a flood.

“Ever since Lady Beresford’s maid first took me in to see her dressed out in white crape, and corn-ears, and scarlet poppies, and I ran a needle down into my finger and broke it in—such a fright I had!—and she tore up her worked pocket-handkerchief, after they’d cut it out, and came in to wet the bandages again with lotion when she returned from the ball—where she’d been the prettiest young lady of all—I’ve never loved any one like her. I little thought then I should live to see her brought so low. I don’t mean no reproach to nobody. Many a one calls you pretty and handsome, and what not. Even in this smoky place, enough to blind one’s eyes, the owls can see that. But you’ll never be like your mother for beauty—never; not if you live to be a hundred.”

“Mamma is very pretty still,” Margaret whispered. “Poor mamma!”

“Now don’t you set off again,” Dixon said hastily, and a whimper slipped through in spite of her. “Or I shall give way at last. You’ll never stand master’s coming home and questioning, at this rate. Go out and take a walk, and come in something like. Many’s the time I’ve longed to walk it off—the thought of what was the matter with her, and how it must all end.”

“Oh, Dixon!” Margaret cried, with the sudden generosity that sorrow brings. “How often I’ve been cross with you, not knowing what a terrible secret you had to bear!”

“Bless you, child!” Dixon said, rallying, glad to clutch at familiar pride. “I like to see you showing a bit of spirit. It’s the good old Beresford blood. Why, the last Sir John but two shot his steward down, there where he stood, for just telling him that he racked the tenants—and he’d racked the tenants till he could get no more money off ’em than he could get skin off a flint.”

“Well, Dixon,” Margaret said, through her tears, “I won’t shoot you. And I’ll try not to be cross again.”

“You never have,” Dixon replied quickly, as if to wipe out her own harshness. “If I’ve said it at times, it has always been to myself—just in private—by way of making a little agreeable conversation, for there’s no one here fit to talk to. And when you fire up you’re the very image of Master Frederick. I could find it in my heart to put you in a passion any day, just to see his stormy look coming like a great cloud over your face.”

Then, brisk again, she pointed Margaret to the door. “But now you go out, Miss. I’ll watch over Missus. And as for master—his books are company enough for him, if he should come in.”

“I will go,” Margaret said.

She lingered for a minute, hovering near Dixon as if she were afraid to step beyond the circle of lamplight and familiar walls. Then, suddenly, she bent and kissed Dixon—quick, grateful, unexpected—and went out at once, as if speed could outrun the thought of what waited upstairs.

“Bless her!” Dixon said, standing alone in the drawing-room. “She’s as sweet as a nut. There are three people I love: it’s Missus, Master Frederick, and her. Just them three. That’s all. The rest be hanged, for I don’t know what they’re in the world for. Master was born, I suppose, for to marry Missus. If I thought he loved her properly, I might get to love him in time. But he should ha’ made a deal more on her, and not been always reading, reading, thinking, thinking. See what it has brought him to. Many a one as never reads or thinks neither gets to be Rector, and Dean, and what not; and I daresay master might, if he’d just minded Missus and let the weary reading and thinking alone.”

She went to the window as the front door shut, the sound of it carrying up the stairwell like the closing of a lid.

“There she goes,” Dixon muttered, watching Margaret’s figure fall into the stream of London. “Poor young lady! her clothes look shabby to what they did when she came to Helstone a year ago. Then she hadn’t so much as a darned stocking or a cleaned pair of gloves in all her wardrobe. And now—and now—!”

Margaret set out as if she were going to some appointed punishment, her cloak drawn close, her thoughts heavy as damp wool. Yet Milton had a way of taking hold of the senses in spite of oneself. Before she had gone the length of a long street—the particular, unmistakable air of a Milton street—her blood answered the raw morning. The wind tasted of soot and wet stone; the iron tang of it sat on the tongue. Somewhere a mill-bell had done tolling, and the sound still seemed to vibrate in the very paving-stones, like a great struck vessel that would not be quiet.

And then she began to see rather than brood.

There were men loitering where men, on working-days, should have moved with that set, purposeful haste of hands going to their frames: idle figures with their hands buried in pockets, shoulders slack, walking as if time were suddenly too large for them. There were knots of girls, loud with a kind of forced gaiety, their laughter pitched high, their speech roughened by excitement and the show of independence. The worst-looking of the men—few, but ugly enough to stain the whole prospect—hung on beer-house steps and at gin-shop doors, smoking and calling out free comments on those who passed, as if the street were their stage and every face their lawful amusement.

Margaret had meant to press on beyond the town, to where the fields began and the air uncoiled itself from smoke; but the thought of a long walk through such streets, with the coarse staring and the thickened noise, turned her aside. She would go instead to see Bessy Higgins. It would not be the same kind of refreshment as a country walk, but perhaps it would be kinder; and kindness, she told herself, was a steadier thing than seeking comfort.

In the Higgins’ room the fire had been built low; it did not roar, but breathed—a dull red bed with an occasional flicker that laid a warm colour on the blackened kettle. Nicholas Higgins sat close enough to it that the smoke from his pipe mingled with the smell of peat-like coal and damp clothes. Bessy was on the other side, rocking herself with that weary motion that seemed less a choice than a habit the body clung to when it could do nothing else.

Nicholas drew the pipe from his mouth, stood, and with a rough civility pushed his chair toward Margaret. Then, as if he could not endure the stiffness of standing in a manner too respectful, he leaned against the chimney-piece in a lounging posture, watching while Margaret bent to Bessy.

“How are you to-day?”

Nicholas answered for her in his broad fashion. “Hoo’s rather down i’ th’ mouth in regard to spirits, but hoo’s better in health. Hoo doesn’t like this strike. Hoo’s a deal too much set on peace and quietness at any price.”

Bessy sighed, the sound thin as a thread pulled through cloth. “This is th’ third strike I’ve seen,” she said, and spoke as if that numbered fact were explanation enough of all the tiredness in her face.

“Well, third time pays for all,” Nicholas burst out, as if a groan were an insult to be slapped away. “See if we don’t dang th’ masters this time. See if they don’t come and beg us to come back at our own price. That’s all. We’ve missed it afore time, I grant yo’; but this time we’n laid our plans desperate deep.”

Margaret looked from father to daughter. The word had been thrown about in her hearing since coming to Milton, like a stone skipped across conversation: strike. It had never belonged to her old life; down in Helstone, time was counted by seed and harvest, by the sound of scythes, by rain on leaf and the slow hush of summer evenings.

“Why do you strike?” she asked, simply. “Striking is leaving off work till you get your own rate of wages, is it not? You must not wonder at my ignorance; where I come from I never heard of a strike.”

“I wish I were there,” Bessy said, with a longing that made it more than a complaint. Then, as if she had no strength for arguing with the present, she added wearily, “But it’s not for me to get sick and tired o’ strikes. This is the last I’ll see. Before it’s ended I shall be in the Great City—the Holy Jerusalem.”

Nicholas gave a short sound, half affection, half impatience. “Hoo’s so full of th’ life to come, hoo cannot think of th’ present. Now I, yo see, am bound to do the best I can here. I think a bird i’ th’ hand is worth two i’ th’ bush. So them’s the different views we take on th’ strike question.”

Margaret, trying to lay hold of the thing by comparing it with what she knew, said, “But if the people struck, as you call it, where I come from, as they are mostly all field labourers, the seed would not be sown, the hay got in, the corn reaped.”

“Well?” Nicholas put it, pipe between his fingers again, the word made into a challenge.

“Why,” she went on, “what would become of the farmers?”

He puffed steadily, as if smoke were thought made visible. “I reckon, they’d have either to give up their farms, or to give fair rate of wage.”

“But suppose they could not, or would not do the last; they could not give up their farms all in a minute, however much they might wish to do so; but they would have no hay, nor corn to sell that year; and where would the money come from to pay the labourers’ wages the next?”

Still he puffed, his face set. At last he spoke, the words coming with a heat that had been banked, not cooled. “I know nought of your ways down South. I have heerd they’re a pack of spiritless, down-trodden men; welly clemmed to death; too dazed wi’ clemming to know when they’re put upon. Now, it’s not so here. We known when we’re put upon; and we’en too much blood in us to stand it. We just take our hands fro’ our looms, and say, ‘Yo’ may clem us, but yo’ll not put upon us, my masters!’ And be danged to ’em, they shan’t this time!”

“I wished I lived down South,” Bessy murmured again, as if the words were a charm.

“There’s a deal to bear there,” Margaret said, unable to let the picture be painted wholly in soft colours.

“There are sorrows to bear everywhere,” Bessy answered, but her own sorrow had one note that would not be stilled. “It’s out of doors,” she added quickly, as if clinging to that one difference. “And away from the endless, endless noise, and sickening heat.”

Margaret heard, behind that phrase, the remembered clatter of power-looms—iron insisting upon iron, the air shaken till thought itself seemed shaken. She said, gently but truthfully, “It’s sometimes in heavy rain, and sometimes in bitter cold. A young person can stand it; but an old man gets racked with rheumatism, and bent and withered before his time; yet he must just work on the same, or else go to the workhouse.”

“I thought yo were so taken wi’ the ways of the South country.”

“So I am,” Margaret said, and smiled a little at being caught. “I only mean, Bessy, there’s good and bad in everything in this world; and as you felt the bad up here, I thought it was but fair you should know the bad down there.”

“And yo say they never strike down there?” Nicholas asked, abruptly.

“No,” Margaret replied. “I think they have too much sense.”

“And I think,” he returned, and with an angry dash knocked the ashes from his pipe so violently that the bowl cracked, “it’s not that they’ve too much sense, but that they’ve too little spirit.”

“Oh, father!” Bessy cried, a sudden sharpness in her tired voice. “What have ye gained by striking? Just think o’ that first strike when mother died—how we all had to clem—you the worst of all; and yet many a one went in every week at the same wage, till all were gone in that there was work for; and some went beggars all their lives at after.”

“Ay,” Nicholas said, and for a moment his face altered, as if that memory had bitten him. Then he hardened again. “That there strike was badly managed. Folk got into th’ management of it, as were either fools or not true men. Yo’ll see, it’ll be different this time.”

“But all this time you’ve not told me what you’re striking for,” Margaret persisted, refusing to be put off by vehemence or contempt. “What is it, plainly?”

“Why, yo see,” he said, seizing the chance to marshal his anger into reason, “there’s five or six masters who have set themselves again paying the wages they’ve been paying these two years past, and flourishing upon, and getting richer upon. And now they come to us, and say we’re to take less. And we won’t. We’ll just clem them to death first; and see who’ll work for ’em then. They’ll have killed the goose that laid ’em the golden eggs, I reckon.”

“And so you plan dying, in order to be revenged upon them!” Margaret’s voice rose in spite of herself. She saw Bessy’s hollow cheek, the lungs that laboured for each breath, and Nicholas speaking of starvation as if it were merely a weapon.

“No,” he answered, stubbornly. “I dunnot. I just look forward to the chance of dying at my post sooner than yield. That’s what folk call fine and honourable in a soldier, and why not in a poor weaver-chap?”

“But a soldier dies in the cause of the Nation—in the cause of others.”

He laughed grimly, the sound like something scraped. “My lass, yo’re but a young wench, but don’t yo think I can keep three people—that’s Bessy, and Mary, and me—on sixteen shillings a week? Dun yo think it’s for mysel’ I’m striking work at this time? It is just as much in the cause of others as yon soldier—only m’appen, the cause he dies for is just that of somebody he never clapt eyes on, nor heerd on all his born days, while I take up John Boucher’s cause, as lives next door but one, wi’ a sickly wife, and eight childer, none on ’em factory age; and I don’t take up his cause only, though he’s a poor good-for-nought, as can only manage two looms at a time, but I take up th’ cause o’ justice. Why are we to have less wage now, I ask, than two year ago?”

“Don’t ask me,” Margaret said. “I am very ignorant. Ask some of your masters. Surely they will give you a reason for it. It is not merely an arbitrary decision of theirs, come to without reason.”

“Yo’re just a foreigner, and nothing more,” he said, with rough contempt, as if her accent itself were a kind of offence. “Much yo know about it. Ask th’ masters! They’d tell us to mind our own business, and they’d mind theirs. Our business being, yo understand, to take the bated wage, and be thankful; and their business to bate us down to clemming point, to swell their profits. That’s what it is.”

“But,” Margaret said, holding her ground though she saw his eyes darken, “the state of trade may be such as not to enable them to give you the same remuneration.”

“State o’ trade! That’s just a piece o’ masters’ humbug. It’s rate o’ wages I was talking of. Th’ masters keep th’ state o’ trade in their own hands; and just walk it forward like a black bug-a-boo, to frighten naughty children with into being good. I’ll tell you it’s their part,—their cue, as some folks call it,—to beat us down, to swell their fortunes; and it’s ours to stand up and fight hard,—not for ourselves alone, but for them round about us—for justice and fair play. We help to make their profits, and we ought to help spend ’em. It’s not that we want their brass so much this time, as we’ve done many a time afore. We’n getten money laid by; and we’re resolved to stand and fall together; not a man on us will go in for less wage than th’ Union says is our due. So I say, ‘hooray for the strike,’ and let Thornton, and Slickson, and Hamper, and their set look to it!”

“Thornton!” Margaret repeated, startled as if a bell had been struck close by her ear. “Mr. Thornton of Marlborough Street?”

“Aye! Thornton o’ Marlborough Mill, as we call him.”

“He is one of the masters you are striving with, is he not? What sort of a master is he?”

Nicholas’s mouth twitched into something like relish. “Did yo’ ever see a bulldog? Set a bulldog on hind legs, and dress him up in coat and breeches, and yo’n just getten John Thornton.”

“Nay,” Margaret said, and could not help laughing, the image so grotesque, and yet the naming of Mr. Thornton so quickening to her thoughts. “I deny that. Mr. Thornton is plain enough, but he’s not like a bulldog, with its short broad nose, and snarling upper lip.”

“No! not in look, I grant yo. But let John Thornton get hold on a notion, and he’ll stick to it like a bulldog; yo might pull him away wi’ a pitchfork ere he’d leave go. He’s worth fighting wi’, is John Thornton. As for Slickson, I take it, some o’ these days he’ll wheedle his men back wi’ fair promises; that they’ll just get cheated out of as soon as they’re in his power again. He’ll work his fines well out on ’em, I’ll warrant. He’s as slippery as an eel, he is. He’s like a cat,—as sleek, and cunning, and fierce. It’ll never be an honest up and down fight wi’ him, as it will be wi’ Thornton. Thornton’s as dour as a door-nail; an obstinate chap, every inch on him,—th’ oud bulldog!”

Margaret turned to Bessy, who had listened as if every word were another hammer-stroke in the din that had wearied her all her life. “Poor Bessy,” Margaret said softly. “You sigh over it all. You don’t like struggling and fighting as your father does, do you?”

“No!” Bessy answered, heavily. “I’m sick on it. I could have wished to have had other talk about me in my latter days, than just the clashing and clanging and clattering that has ever wearied a’ my life long, about work and wages, and masters, and hands, and knobsticks.”

Nicholas’s roughness melted at once, as if tenderness were the true master in him, waiting only for her weakness to command it. “Poor wench! latter days be farred! Thou’rt looking a sight better already for a little stir and change. Beside, I shall be a deal here to make it more lively for thee.”

“Tobacco-smoke chokes me!” she said, querulous in her feebleness, the complaint slipping out like a child’s.

“Then I’ll never smoke no more i’ the house!” he replied, quick as a vow. “But why didst thou not tell me afore, thou foolish wench?”

Bessy did not answer at once. When she spoke again it was so low that only Margaret heard, the words like a confession whispered over cooling embers. “I reckon, he’ll want a’ the comfort he can get out o’ either pipe or drink afore he’s done.”

Her father, as if he had understood the drift of her complaint without hearing her murmur, took his broken pipe and went out of doors to finish what tobacco he could, leaving the room suddenly thinner of air. Yet even with him gone, the place did not grow quiet; the strike itself seemed to sit there—a third presence, restless and watchful.

Bessy’s self-reproach broke out as soon as the door had closed. “Now am not I a fool,—am I not, Miss?—there, I knew I ought for to keep father at home, and away fro’ the folk that are always ready for to tempt a man, in time o’ strike, to go drink,—and there my tongue must needs quarrel with this pipe o’ his’n—and he’ll go off, I know he will,—as often as he wants to smoke—and nobody knows where it’ll end. I wish I’d letten myself be choked first.”

“But does your father drink?” Margaret asked.

“No—not to say drink,” Bessy answered, still excited, her words crowding one another. “But what win ye have? There are days wi’ you as wi’ other folk, I suppose, when yo’ get up and go through th’ hours, just longing for a bit of a change—a bit of a fillip, as it were. I know I ha’ gone and bought a four-pounder out o’ another baker’s shop to common on such days, just because I sickened at the thought of going on for ever wi’ the same sight in my eyes, and the same sound in my ears, and the same taste i’ my mouth, and the same thought (or no thought, for that matter) in my head, day after day, for ever.”

As she spoke, the little room filled in Margaret’s imagination with those “same sounds”—the factory’s unending assault, the air made harsh with vibration, so that even silence afterwards rang like a bruised ear. Bessy went on, her thin hands tightening on her apron as if she were kneading some stubborn dough of days into shape.

“I’ve longed for to be a man to go spreeing, even if it were only a tramp to some new place in search o’ work. And father—all men—have it stronger in ’em than me to get tired o’ sameness and work for ever. And what is ’em to do? It’s little blame to them if they do go into th’ gin-shop for to make their blood flow quicker, and more lively, and see things they never see at no other time—pictures, and looking-glass, and such like. But father never was a drunkard, though maybe, he’s got worse for drink, now and then.”

Then her voice dropped, the excitement collapsing into a mournful pleading. “Only yo’ see, at times o’ strike there’s much to knock a man down, for all they start so hopefully; and where’s the comfort to come fro’? He’ll get angry and mad—they all do—and then they get tired out wi’ being angry and mad, and maybe ha’ done things in their passion they’d be glad to forget. Bless yo’r sweet pitiful face! but yo’ dunnot know what a strike is yet.”

“Come, Bessy,” Margaret said, trying to steady her as one might steady a pot beginning to boil over. “I won’t say you’re exaggerating, because I don’t know enough about it: but, perhaps, as you’re not well, you’re only looking on one side, and there is another and a brighter to be looked to.”

“It’s all well enough for yo’ to say so,” Bessy returned bitterly, “who have lived in pleasant green places all your life long, and never known want or care, or wickedness either, for that matter.”

Margaret’s cheek flushed; the rebuke, so unjustly given, struck into the tender places of her heart. She lifted her head, and her eyes shone, not with vanity wounded but with sorrow made sudden and sharp.

“Take care,” she said, her voice trembling with the effort to keep it clear, “how you judge, Bessy. I shall go home to my mother, who is so ill—so ill, Bessy, that there’s no outlet but death for her out of prison of her great suffering; and yet I must speak cheerfully to my father, who has no notion of her real state, and to whom the knowledge must come gradually. The only person—the only one who could sympathise with me and help me—whose presence could comfort my mother more than any other earthly thing—is falsely accused—would run the risk of death if he came to see his dying mother. This I tell you—only you, Bessy. You must not mention it. No other person in Milton—hardly any other person in England knows. Have I not care? Do I not know anxiety, though I go about well-dressed, and have food enough? Oh, Bessy, God is just, and our lots are well portioned out by Him, although none but He knows the bitterness of our souls.”

Bessy’s face changed as if a hand had passed over it, smoothing away the hard look. “I ask your pardon,” she said humbly.

After a pause she spoke again, but now in a tone that had in it the old longing for a language beyond her own worn words. “Sometimes, when I’ve thought o’ my life, and the little pleasure I’ve had in it, I’ve believed that, maybe, I was one of those doomed to die by the falling of a star from heaven; ‘And the name of the star is called Wormwood; and the third part of the waters became wormwood; and men died of the waters, because they were made bitter.’ One can bear pain and sorrow better if one thinks it has been prophesied long before for one: somehow, then it seems as if my pain was needed for the fulfilment; otherways it seems all sent for nothing.”

“Nay, Bessy—think!” Margaret pleaded. “God does not willingly inflict. Don’t dwell so much on the prophecies, but read the clearer parts of the Bible.”

“I dare say it would be wiser,” Bessy answered, and yet her hunger clung to the strange, solemn cadences. “But where would I hear such grand words of promise—hear tell o’ anything so far different fro’ this dreary world, and this town above a’ as in Revelations? Many’s the time I’ve repeated the verses in the seventh chapter to myself, just for the sound. It’s as good as an organ, and as different from every day, too. No, I cannot give up Revelations. It gives me more comfort than any other book i’ the Bible.”

“Let me come and read you some of my favourite chapters,” Margaret said, eager to give her what comfort she could, in words that were not all thunder and wormwood.

“Ay,” Bessy said greedily, “come. Father will maybe hear yo’. He’s deaved wi’ my talking; he says it’s all nought to do with the things o’ to-day, and that’s his business.”

“Where is your sister?”

“Gone fustian cutting. I were loth to let her go; but somehow we must live; and th’ Union can’t afford us much.”

Margaret rose. The room seemed closer than when she had come in; the smoke, the heat, the human breath, the whole town’s pressure were gathered in those four walls. And yet, oddly, she felt steadier.

“Now I must go,” she said. “You have done me good, Bessy.”

“I done you good!” Bessy echoed, astonished, as if kindness could only travel one way—from those who had plenty to those who lacked.

“Yes. I came here very sad, and rather too apt to think my own cause for grief was the only one in the world. And now I hear how you have had to bear for years, and that makes me stronger.”

“Bless yo’!” Bessy said, a faint brightness for a moment in her eyes. “I thought a’ the good-doing was on the side of gentlefolk. I shall get proud if I think I can do good to yo’.”

“You won’t do it if you think about it,” Margaret answered, smiling in spite of herself. “But you’ll only puzzle yourself if you do, that’s one comfort.”

“You’re not like no one I ever seed,” Bessy said slowly, with that grave wonder people have when they meet a dialect not their own, and yet recognise a human truth inside it. “I dunno what to make of yo’.”

“Nor I of myself,” Margaret said simply. “Good-bye!”

Bessy stilled her rocking to gaze after her when she had gone, as if the doorway had kept a trace of her—like a breath of country air straying in and refusing, for a moment, to be choked by smoke.

“I wonder if there are many folk like her down South,” she said to the empty room. “She’s like a breath of country air, somehow. She freshens me up above a bit. Who’d a thought that face—as bright and as strong as the angel I dream of—could have known the sorrow she speaks on? I wonder how she’ll sin. All on us must sin. I think a deal on her, for sure. But father does the like, I see. And Mary even. It’s not often hoo’s stirred up to notice much.”

When Margaret came back into the little parlour, the table wore its accustomed look of scanty order—work-basket shut, the tea-things pushed aside from the morning—yet two letters lay there with a foreign air, as if they had strayed in from another climate. One was for her mother, plain and English; the other, by the thinness of its paper and its silvery rustle, announced Aunt Shaw before ever the foreign post-marks had done their part. The envelope crackled like dried bay-leaves.

She had taken up her mother’s note, weighing it a moment between finger and thumb, when her father entered quickly, with that light haste he used when he would fain persuade himself that nothing was amiss.

“So your mother is tired, and gone to bed early! I’m afraid such a thundery day was not the best in the world for the doctor to see her. What did he say? Dixon tells me he spoke to you about her.”

Margaret’s eyes dropped. The room seemed full of the day’s heaviness still: the close air after storm, the faint, gritty smell that Milton’s smoke left on curtains and paper, and, beneath all, the restless undertone of the town—wheels in the street, distant hammers, a far-off, never-ending pulse as of machinery breathing. Even here, in a house that tried to keep its peace like a covered dish keeps warmth, sound crept in and altered the temper of one’s thoughts.

Her hesitation drew him on.

“He does not think her seriously ill?”

“Not at present; she needs care, he says. He was very kind, and he said he would call again, and see how his medicines worked.”

“Only care?—he did not recommend change of air?—he did not say this smoky town was doing her any harm, did he, Margaret?”

“No! not a word,” she replied, gravely. “He was anxious, I think.”

“Doctors have that anxious manner; it’s professional,” said he; but his voice betrayed him. The first touch of fear, once admitted, made everything else in him attentive. He could not set it down again, as one lays aside a book. He began to move about on tiptoe, as if quietness itself could keep illness from being named.

Margaret turned, to give him other matter, as one sets a cup of broth before a sick person who refuses the thought of stronger food.

“This letter is from Aunt Shaw, papa. She has got to Naples, and finds it too hot, so she has taken apartments at Sorrento. But I don’t think she likes Italy.”

“He did not say anything about diet, did he?” he broke in, with that eager change of subject which always returned to the same point.

“It was to be nourishing, and digestible. Mamma’s appetite is pretty good, I think.”

“Yes! and that makes it all the more strange he should have thought of speaking about diet.”

“I asked him, papa.”

He stood still, as if that confession had pulled a thread he would rather not have felt in his hands.

Margaret went on, forcing a small smile into her tone because it was easier for him to take comfort from her voice than from any argument.

“Aunt Shaw says she has sent me some coral ornaments, papa: but she’s afraid the Milton dissenters won’t appreciate them. She has got all her ideas of Dissenters from the Quakers, has she not?”

He scarcely heard. The house held him, divided between the desire to go and look at his wife and the shame of seeming to watch her sleep.

“If ever you hear or notice that your mother wishes for anything, be sure you let me know. I am so afraid she does not tell me always what she would like. Pray, see after that girl Mrs. Thornton named. If we had a good, efficient house-servant, Dixon could be constantly with her, and I’d answer for it we’d soon set her up amongst us, if care will do it. She’s been very much tired of late, with the hot weather, and the difficulty of getting a servant. A little rest will put her quite to rights—eh, Margaret?”

“I hope so,” said Margaret; but the sadness that clung to her words was like a taste that will come through spice.

He noticed it. He pinched her cheek with a poor attempt at playfulness, as if colour could be summoned like blush on a painted face.

“Come; if you look so pale as this, I must rouge you up a little. Take care of yourself, child, or you’ll be wanting the doctor next.”

Yet he could not settle. Through the evening he went backwards and forwards, returning again and again to the landing as if drawn by a cord, pausing to listen for the breath above—listening not only for his wife’s, but for the whole sound of the house. Margaret felt, with a kind of bodily ache, his effort to stifle the terror that was rising in him like smoke in a closed room.

At last he came back with a look of relief, as if he had found a door unbarred.

“She’s awake now, Margaret. She quite smiled as she saw me standing by her. Just her old smile. And she says she feels refreshed, and ready for tea. Where’s the note for her? She wants to see it. I’ll read it to her while you make tea.”

Margaret went to the table and began the familiar offices. The kettle was filled; the fire coaxed; the tea caddy opened. In that homely action there was comfort—a small ritual against the vast, unmanageable thing upstairs. The tea-leaves, dry and dark, gave out their faint, sharp scent when she measured them; the cups, warmed, seemed to promise that some part of life could still be kept in order. Even the clink of spoon against china had its own softness, a domestic music that for a moment muffled Milton’s harsher chorus.

The note for Mrs. Hale proved, when it was opened, to be a formal invitation from Mrs. Thornton, to Mr., Mrs., and Miss Hale to dine on the twenty-first instant. Margaret, holding the tray ready, was surprised to hear her father reading it aloud in that clear, careful voice of his, as if the very act of reading were an assertion that their days went on as usual.

She went upstairs with the tea, and found her mother propped among pillows, the shadow on her face softened by the little flush of having something to anticipate. The invitation had already kindled a kind of wilful brightness in her, like a candle lit in a draught.

“It will do me good,” Mrs. Hale said, almost pleading, before Margaret had time to object. “It is so long since I have been anywhere. It will be a change.”

Margaret would have urged her to husband her strength, to spare herself; but her father’s eyes entreated her help in keeping up this new hope, as if the dinner were a medicine.

“Nay, Margaret: if she wishes it, I’m sure we’ll both go willingly. She never would wish it unless she felt herself really stronger—really better than we thought she was, eh, Margaret?” he said, anxious, while Mrs. Hale’s hand lay like a light weight on the paper.

“Eh! Margaret?” he repeated, with a nervous motion of his fingers.

It seemed cruel to deny him the comfort. Besides, his passionate refusal to admit fear almost infected Margaret with a momentary belief.

“I do think she is better since last night,” she said, letting her eyes rest on her mother’s face as if she could will the truth into it. “Her eyes look brighter, and her complexion clearer.”

“God bless you,” said her father, with earnestness that made the words almost a prayer of hunger. “But is it true? Yesterday was so sultry every one felt ill. It was a most unlucky day for Mr. Donaldson to see her on.”

So, the next day, the note of acceptance was prepared, and Mr. Hale went out to his duties, now increased by the labour of lectures he had promised to deliver to the working people at a neighbouring Lyceum. He had chosen Ecclesiastical Architecture—more to his own taste and stored knowledge than to any direct hunger for it among those who came for instruction. Yet the institution, being in debt, caught at the credit of his name and the cheapness of his gift, as one catches at any wholesome food in lean times and does not ask too curiously if it be the dish one would have chosen.

That night, in a very different house, where order was kept like a strict account-book and economies were remembered as if they had a conscience, Mrs. Thornton sat with her son and daughter, and the subject of the dinner was gone over as punctiliously as a bill of fare.

“Well, mother,” asked Mr. Thornton, “who have accepted your invitations for the twenty-first?”

“Fanny, where are the notes? The Slicksons accept, Collingbrooks accept, Stephenses accept, Browns decline. Hales—father and daughter come—mother too great an invalid—Macphersons come, and Mr. Horsfall, and Mr. Young. I was thinking of asking the Porters, as the Browns can’t come.”

“Very good.” His tone was composed, yet something in him tightened. “Do you know, I’m really afraid Mrs. Hale is very far from well, from what Dr. Donaldson says.”

“It’s strange of them to accept a dinner-invitation if she’s very ill,” said Fanny, quick, with that small, nervous laugh she used like a fan to stir her own feelings away.

“I didn’t say very ill,” said her brother, rather sharply. “I only said far from well. They may not know it either.”

And then, as if a thought struck him like the sound of a dropped coin, he remembered that, by Donaldson’s account, Margaret must at least know something nearer to the truth than her father chose to hear.

“Very probably they are quite aware of what you said yesterday, John—of the great advantage it would be to them—to Mr. Hale, I mean, to be introduced to such people as the Stephenses and the Collingbrooks.”

“I’m sure that motive would not influence them. No! I think I understand how it is.”

“John!” said Fanny, laughing again, but this time with the faint malice of one who enjoys setting a pin where it will prick. “How you profess to understand these Hales, and how you never will allow that we can know anything about them. Are they really so very different to most people one meets with?”

She had not meant, perhaps, to vex him; but the words did their work. He walked to and fro, the boards answering his steps with a steady, domestic sound—quiet enough, yet not soothing, for his mind kept its own harsher rhythm.

“They do not seem to me out of the common way,” said Mrs. Thornton. “He appears a worthy kind of man enough; rather too simple for trade—so it’s perhaps as well he should have been a clergyman first, and now a teacher. She’s a bit of a fine lady, with her invalidism; and as for the girl—she’s the only one who puzzles me when I think about her,—which I don’t often do. She seems to have a great notion of giving herself airs; and I can’t make out why. I could almost fancy she thinks herself too good for her company at times. And yet they’re not rich; from all I can hear they never have been.”

“And she’s not accomplished, mamma,” Fanny put in, with childish spitefulness, yet as if she spoke of a fault in a pudding that refused to rise. “She can’t play.”

“Go on, Fanny. What else does she want to bring her up to your standard?” said Mrs. Thornton, dryly.

“Nay! John,” continued Mrs. Thornton, turning to her son, “that speech of Fanny’s did no harm. I myself heard Miss Hale say she could not play. If you would let us alone, we could perhaps like her, and see her merits.”

“I’m sure I never could!” murmured Fanny, sheltering under her mother’s toleration.

Mr. Thornton heard, but did not choose to answer. He kept walking, wishing for candles, wishing for the interruption of work—anything to stop this talk that beat upon a tender place in him like a dull hammer.

But Mrs. Thornton observed her household ways as if they were laws, and he did not meddle in them. The old economies lived in her as naturally as breath.

“Mother,” he said at last, stopping short, and speaking with a candour that startled even himself, “I wish you would like Miss Hale.”

“Why,” asked she, sharp and startled, “you’re never thinking of marrying her?—a girl without a penny.”

“She would never have me,” said he, with a short laugh that cut like a knife through pride.

“No, I don’t think she would,” answered his mother, with blunt certainty. “She laughed in my face, when I praised her for speaking out something Mr. Bell had said in your favour. I liked the girl for doing so frankly, for it made me sure she had no thought of you; and the next minute she vexed me so by seeming to think—well, never mind! Only you’re right in saying she’s too good an opinion of herself to think of you! The saucy jade! I should like to know where she’d find a better!”

“Well, as I’m just as much convinced of the truth of what you have been saying as you can be; and as I have no thought or expectation of ever asking her to be my wife, you’ll believe me for the future that I’m quite disinterested in speaking about her.” He paused, as if weighing the words, then went on more steadily. “I foresee trouble for that girl—perhaps, want of motherly care—and I only wish you to be ready to be a friend to her, in case she needs one. Now, Fanny,” he added, turning with sudden severity, “I trust you have delicacy enough to understand, that it is as great an injury to Miss Hale as to me—in fact, she would think it a greater—to suppose that I have any reason, more than I now give, for begging you and my mother to show her every kindly attention.”

“I cannot forgive her her pride,” said Mrs. Thornton. “I will befriend her, if there is need, for your asking, John. I would befriend Jezebel herself if you asked me. But this girl, who turns up her nose at us all—who turns up her nose at you—”

“Nay, mother; I have never yet put myself, and I mean never to put myself, within reach of her contempt.”

“Contempt, indeed!”—and one of Mrs. Thornton’s expressive snorts did duty for a whole sentence. “Don’t go on speaking of Miss Hale, John, if I’ve to be kind to her. When I’m with her, I don’t know if I like or dislike her most; but when I think of her, and hear you talk of her, I hate her. I can see she’s given herself airs to you as well as if you’d told me out.”

“And if she has,” said he; then he stopped, and when he spoke again his voice had the hardness of a man striking flint. “I’m not a lad, to be cowed by a proud look from a woman, or to care for her misunderstanding me and my position. I can laugh at it!”

“To be sure! and at her too, with her fine notions, and haughty tosses!”

“I only wonder why you talk so much about her, then,” said Fanny. “I’m sure, I’m tired enough of the subject.”

“Well!” said her brother, with a shade of bitterness, as if he tasted something sour and would wash it down with a harsher draught. “Suppose we find some more agreeable subject. What do you say to a strike, by way of something pleasant to talk about?”

“Have the hands actually turned out?” asked Mrs. Thornton, kindling at once; this was a subject she could handle, as she would a joint on the table—firmly, with no shrinking.

“Hamper’s men are actually out. Mine are working out their week, through fear of being prosecuted for breach of contract. I’d have had every one of them up and punished for it, that left his work before his time was out.”

“The law expenses would have been more than the hands themselves were worth—a set of ungrateful naughts!” said his mother.

“To be sure. But I’d have shown them how to keep my word, and how I mean them to keep their’s. They know me by this time. Slickson’s men are off—pretty certain he won’t spend money in getting them punished. We’re in for a turn-out, mother.”

“I hope there are not many orders in hand?”

“Of course there are. They know that well enough. But they don’t quite understand all, though they think they do.”

“What do you mean, John?”

Candles had been brought in at last. Their flames steadied the room’s shadows, and Fanny, relieved to have something to do with her hands, took up her interminable worsted-work. The soft rasp of wool drawn through canvas made a small sound of its own, like quiet rain; yet it did not drown the bigger sound that seemed always near in Milton—industry, anger, wealth, want: a town’s continual grinding.

“Why,” said he, “the Americans are getting their yarns so into the general market, that our only chance is producing them at a lower rate. If we can’t, we may shut up shop at once, and hands and masters alike go on tramp. Yet these fools go back to the prices paid three years ago—nay, some of their leaders quote Dickinson’s price now—though they know as well as we do that, what with fines pressed out of their wages, as no honourable man would extort them, the real rate of wage paid at Dickinson’s is less than at ours.”

His voice rose with the injustice of being thwarted by men he called ignorant; and the very words he used—fools, hands—had in them the old power of a dominant lexicon, sorting human lives into categories fit for ledgers. It made the room feel harder.

“Upon my word, mother, I wish the old combination laws were in force. It is too bad to find out that fools—ignorant, wayward men like these—just by uniting their silly heads, are to rule over the fortunes of those who bring all the wisdom that knowledge and experience, and often painful thought and anxiety, can give. The next thing will be—indeed, we’ve all but come to it now—that we shall have to go and ask—stand hat in hand—and humbly ask the secretary of the Spinner’s Union to be so kind as to furnish us with labour at their own price. That’s what they want—they, who haven’t the sense to see that, if we don’t get a fair share of the profits to compensate us for our wear and tear here in England, we can move off to some other country; and that, what with home and foreign competition, we are none of us likely to make above a fair share, and may be thankful enough if we can get that, in an average number of years.”

“Can’t you get hands from Ireland?” asked Mrs. Thornton, prompt and practical. “I wouldn’t keep these fellows a day. I’d teach them that I was master, and could employ what servants I liked.”

“Yes! to be sure, I can; and will, too, if they go on long. It will be trouble and expense, and I fear there will be some danger; but I will do it, rather than give in.”

“If there is to be all this extra expense, I’m sorry we’re giving a dinner just now,” said his mother; her frugality saw the strike first as waste.

“So am I,—not because of the expense, but because I shall have much to think about, and many unexpected calls on my time. But we must have had Mr. Horsfall, and he does not stay in Milton long. And as for the others, we owe them dinners, and it’s all one trouble.”

He went back to walking, drawing a deep breath now and then as if to throw off some thought that clung like smoke in his lungs. Fanny asked small questions—about ribbons, about morning calls, about nothing at all—each one a little tap at her mother’s attention; and received short answers, for Mrs. Thornton’s mind was set on the coming contest, the way a cook’s mind sets on bread that must be watched through the proving.

At ten, the servants came in, filing quietly for prayers. Mrs. Thornton always read them; first a chapter. They were working steadily through the Old Testament, as steadily as her son worked through figures, and with the same sense that endurance was a virtue in itself. When the prayers were ended, she wished her son good-night with that long, steady look which held no outward softness, but had the force of a benediction.

Mr. Thornton, left alone, did not go to bed. He continued his walk. The check upon his business plans was like a sudden pull on a tightly drawn thread. The forethought of many anxious hours—his careful reckonings, his arrangements—seemed flung aside by what he called their insane folly, which would hurt them even more than him, though he spared no pity for that part of it. The town outside, quieter now, still spoke in undertones: a late cart, a watchman’s step, far away the continuous murmur of great buildings where men and engines had laboured all day.

Hamper had said, only that day, that if he were ruined by the strike, he would begin again, comforted by the conviction that those who had brought it on would be worse off; for he had head as well as hands, while they had only hands, and if they drove away the market they could not follow it, nor turn to anything else.

But such thoughts gave Mr. Thornton no comfort. Whether revenge pleased him little, or whether he valued the hard-earned place he had won too keenly to think of any consequence beyond its peril, he paced up and down with his teeth set, feeling the ground of his authority threatened by men whose speech—Union, prices, rights—had begun to carry weight like a newly-coined currency.

At last the clock struck two. The candles guttered, their grease running, their flames leaning as if tired. He took up one to light his own, and muttered, as if fixing an oath into a plan made it firmer:

“Once for all they shall know whom they have got to deal with. I can give them a fortnight,—no more. If they don’t see their madness before the end of that time, I must have hands from Ireland. I believe it’s Slickson’s doing,—confound him and his dodges! He thought he was overstocked; so he seemed to yield at first, when the deputation came to him,—and of course, he only confirmed them in their folly, as he meant to do. That’s where it spread from.”

Mrs. Hale took the notion of Mrs. Thornton’s dinner-party into her sick-room as if it were a warm coal cupped in both hands—turning it, admiring it, asking over and over about its glow. Illness had narrowed her days to the width of a bed and a window; within those bounds, any coming event swelled until it filled the whole horizon. The soft vanities that had once quickened her as a girl—long smothered under parsonage economies—stirred again, not loud but persistent, and most of all in one bright desire: to see Margaret dressed, to know what silk would whisper as she moved, what colour would set off her dark, steady face.

“So you think you shall wear your white silk,” she said, with that fretful eagerness which made her seem, at times, younger than her daughter. “Are you sure it will fit? It is nearly a year since Edith was married.”

“Oh, yes, mamma. Mrs. Murray made it; it is sure to be right. It may be a straw’s breadth shorter, or longer-waisted, according to whether I’ve grown fat or thin. But I don’t think I’ve altered in the least.”

“Hadn’t you better let Dixon see it? It may have gone yellow with lying by.”

“If you like. But if the worst comes to the worst, I’ve a very nice pink gauze Aunt Shaw gave me only two or three months before Edith was married. That can’t have gone yellow.”

“No: but it may have faded.”

“Well! then I’ve a green silk. I feel more as if it were the embarrassment of riches.”

“I wish I knew what you ought to wear,” Mrs. Hale said, and the very tremble in her voice made it sound like an anxious prayer.

Margaret’s look softened instantly. “Shall I go and put them on one after another, mamma, and then you can see which you like best?”

“But—yes. Perhaps that will be best.”

So Margaret went, with the air of one called to a serious office, though the unusual hour and the rustle of kept-away finery half-tempted her into mischief. She longed, for a moment, to make the white silk puff and balloon absurdly, to sweep backward like a queen in a masque, and to let her mother laugh; but Mrs. Hale, intent on the matter as if a kingdom depended on the choice, was jarred by any play. Margaret, checked by that fragile earnestness, grew grave.

And yet the same flutter of dress and consequence had found her, absurdly, out-of-doors. Only that afternoon she had mentioned her engagement—lightly, as something incidental—to Bessy Higgins, while speaking of the servant Mrs. Thornton had promised to inquire about. Bessy, who could lie listless for hours and then blaze up at a word, started as if some bell had sounded in her.

“Dear! and are you going to dine at Thornton’s at Marlborough Mills?”

“Yes, Bessy. Why are you so surprised?”

“Oh, I dunno. But they visit wi’ a’ th’ first folk in Milton.”

“And you don’t think we’re quite the first folk in Milton, eh, Bessy?”

Colour came into Bessy’s thin cheeks; her eyes shifted, then fixed on Margaret’s face with their eager, pained sincerity.

“Well,” she said, “yo’ see, they thinken a deal o’ money here; and I reckon yo’ve not getten much.”

“No,” said Margaret, quietly. “That is very true. But we are educated people, and have lived among educated people. Is there anything so wonderful in our being asked to dinner by a man who owns himself inferior to my father by coming to him to be instructed? I don’t mean to blame Mr. Thornton. Few drapers’ assistants, as he was once, could have made themselves what he is.”

“But can yo’ give dinners back, in yo’re small house? Thornton’s house is three times as big.”

“Well, I think we could manage to give Mr. Thornton a dinner back, as you call it. Perhaps not in such a large room, nor with so many people. But I don’t think we’ve thought about it at all in that way.”

“I never thought yo’d be dining with Thorntons,” Bessy repeated, as if turning the words in her mouth to test their taste. “Why, the mayor hissel’ dines there; and the members of Parliament and all.”

“I think I could support the honour of meeting the mayor of Milton.”

“But them ladies dress so grand!” Bessy said, and her anxious glance dropped to Margaret’s plain print gown, priced by Milton eyes as exactly as flour and coal were priced.

Margaret laughed, and the laugh had a little ring in it like a spoon tapping china. “Thank you, Bessy, for thinking so kindly about my looking nice among all the smart people. But I’ve plenty of grand gowns,—a week ago I should have said they were far too grand for anything I should ever want here. But as I’m to dine at Mr. Thornton’s, and perhaps meet the mayor, I shall put on my very best gown, you may be sure.”

“What win yo’ wear?” Bessy asked, eased a little.

“White silk,” said Margaret. “A gown I had for a cousin’s wedding a year ago.”

“That’ll do!” Bessy sank back as if the choice itself had soothed her. “I should be loth to have yo’ looked down upon.”

“Oh! I’ll be fine enough, if that will save me from being looked down upon in Milton.”

“I wish I could see you dressed up,” said Bessy, and her voice altered, slipping into that strange earnestness that often came to her like a change of weather. “I reckon, yo’re not what folk would ca’ pretty; yo’ve not red and white enough for that. But dun yo’ know, I ha’ dreamt of yo’, long afore ever I seed yo’.”

“Nonsense, Bessy!”

“Ay, but I did. Yo’r very face,—looking wi’ yo’r clear steadfast eyes out o’ th’ darkness,—wi’ yo’r hair blown off from yo’r brow, and going out like rays round yo’r forehead, which was just as smooth and straight as it is now,—and yo’ always came to give me strength, which I seemed to gather out o’ yo’r deep comforting eyes,—and yo’ was drest in shining raiment—just as yo’r going to be drest. So, yo’ see, it was yo’!”

“Nay, Bessy,” Margaret answered gently; she could feel in her own bones the way Bessy’s room held sound—the small clink of a kettle-lid, the creak of a chair, the far-off thud of a cart, and under all the steady, maddening undertone of the town’s machinery like surf that never ceased. “It was but a dream.”

“And why might na I dream a dream in my affliction as well as others? Did not many a one i’ the Bible? Ay, and see visions too! Why, even my father thinks a deal o’ dreams! I tell yo’ again, I saw yo’ as plainly, coming swiftly towards me, wi’ yo’r hair blown back wi’ the very swiftness o’ the motion,—and the white shining dress on yo’ve getten to wear. Let me come and see yo’ in it. I want to see yo’ and touch yo’ as in very deed yo’ were in my dream.”

“My dear Bessy, it is quite a fancy of yours.”

“Fancy or no fancy,—yo’ve come, as I knew yo’ would, when I saw yo’r movement in my dream,—and when yo’re here about me, I reckon I feel easier in my mind, and comforted, just as a fire comforts one on a dree day. Yo’ said it were on th’ twenty-first; please God, I’ll come and see yo’.”

“Oh, Bessy! you may come, and welcome; but don’t talk so—it really makes me sorry. It does indeed.”

“Then I’ll keep it to mysel’, if I bite my tongue out. Not but what it’s true for all that.”

Margaret let the talk fall, because it seemed safer to touch nothing further that had the heat and danger of prophecy in it. After a little she asked, softly, “Has your father turned out?”

“Ay!” Bessy’s voice dropped as if a shutter had been pulled down inside her. “He and many another,—all Hamper’s men,—and many a one besides. Th’ women are as bad as th’ men, in their savageness, this time. Food is high,—and they mun have food for their childer. Suppose Thorntons sent ’em their dinner out,—th’ same money, spent on potatoes and meal, would keep many a crying baby quiet, and hush up its mother’s heart for a bit!”

“Don’t speak so!” Margaret cried; the image struck like the sharp smell of scorching—fine dishes on one side, and on the other the plain, desperate cookery of hunger: meal stirred into water, potatoes boiled until they fell into a grey mash, nothing to sweeten, nothing to spare. “You’ll make me feel wicked and guilty in going to this dinner.”

“No!” Bessy said, with a bitter steadiness. “Some’s pre-elected to sumptuous feasts, and purple and fine linen,—may be yo’re one on ’em. Others toil and moil all their lives long—and the very dogs are not pitiful in our days, as they were in the days of Lazarus. But if yo’ ask me to cool yo’re tongue wi’ th’ tip of my finger, I’ll come across the great gulf to yo’ just for th’ thought o’ what yo’ve been to me here.”

“Bessy; you’re very feverish,” Margaret said, feeling the heat and then the sudden chill in the girl’s hand. “I can tell it in the touch of your hand as well as in what you’re saying. It won’t be division enough, in that awful day, that some of us have been beggars here and some of us rich,—we shall not be judged by that poor accident, but by our faithful following of Christ.”

She rose, found water, and, as if she were in her own house again, did what could be done with the simplest things—soaked her handkerchief, laid it cool upon Bessy’s forehead, and rubbed the stone-cold feet until life seemed to creep back by degrees. Bessy’s eyelids sank; the rocking stopped. Outside, Milton’s ceaseless din pressed against the walls; within, the small sounds of tending—water wrung from linen, the whisper of cloth on skin—made a gentler world.

At last Bessy spoke, weakly. “Yo’d ha’ been deaved out o’ yo’r five wits, as well as me, if yo’d had one body after another coming in to ask for father, and staying to tell me each one their tale. Some spoke o’ deadly hatred, and made my blood run cold wi’ the terrible things they said o’ th’ masters,—but more, being women, kept plaining, plaining (wi’ the tears running down their cheeks, and never wiped away, nor heeded), of the price o’ meat, and how their childer could na sleep at nights for th’ hunger.”

“And do they think the strike will mend this?” Margaret asked. Her mind caught at the question as one catches at a handhold in a river.

“They say so. They do say trade has been good for long, and the masters has made no end o’ money; how much father doesn’t know, but, in course, th’ Union does; and, as it is natural, they wanted their share o’ th’ profits, now that food is getting dear; and th’ Union says they’ll not be doing their duty if they don’t make th’ masters give ’em their share. But masters has getten th’ upper hand somehow; and I’m feared they’ll keep it now and evermore. It’s like th’ great battle o’ Armageddon, the way they keep on, grinning and fighting at each other, till even while they fight, they are picked off into the pit.”

At that instant Nicholas Higgins came in, catching the last words as if they were thrown to him.

“Ay! and I’ll fight on too; and I’ll got it this time. It’ll not take long for to make ’em give in, for they’ve getten a pretty lot of orders, all under contract; and they’ll soon find out they’d better give us our five per cent. than lose the profit they’ll gain; let alone the fine for not fulfilling the contract. Aha, my masters! I know who’ll win.”

There was something excited in him—too rapid, too loud—as if he needed the sound of his own voice to keep up his courage. Margaret, listening, thought she caught the blurred edge of speech that meant drink; Bessy, with a glance of distress, hurried her to go.

“The twenty-first—that’s Thursday week,” Bessy said quickly, clinging back to the bright thread of the dinner as if it were a charm against the dark. “I may come and see yo’ dressed for Thornton’s, I reckon. What time is yo’r dinner?”

Before Margaret could answer, Higgins broke out with a coarse, reckless sort of triumph.

“Thornton’s! Ar’ t’ going to dine at Thornton’s? Ask him to give yo’ a bumper to the success of his orders. By th’ twenty-first, I reckon, he’ll be pottered in his brains how to get ’em done in time. Tell him, there’s seven hundred ’ll come marching into Marlborough Mills, the morning after he gives the five per cent., and will help him through his contract in no time. You’ll have ’em all there. My master, Hamper. He’s one o’ th’ oud-fashioned sort. Ne’er meets a man bout an oath or a curse; I should think he were going to die if he spoke me civil; but arter all, his bark’s waur than his bite, and yo’ may tell him one o’ his turn-outs said so, if yo’ like. Eh! but yo’ll have a lot of prize mill-owners at Thornton’s! I should like to get speech o’ them, when they’re a bit inclined to sit still after dinner, and could na run for the life on ’em. I’d tell ’em my mind. I’d speak up again th’ hard way they’re driving on us!”

“Good-bye!” Margaret said hastily, her cheeks burning with a confusion she would not name. “Good-bye, Bessy! I shall look to see you on the twenty-first, if you’re well enough.”

In the Hales’ house the medicines and treatment Dr. Donaldson had ordered did, at first, so much good that even Margaret—who had held hope like a candle in a draught, shielding it with both hands—let herself believe that he might have been mistaken, that her mother’s breath might lengthen into months and years. Mrs. Hale smiled more; the cough loosened; her eyes had moments of brightness as if a little window had been opened. Mr. Hale, who had never understood how near the fear had come, triumphed with an almost boyish relief, proving by that very triumph how much his half-glimpsed dread had weighed upon him. Only Dixon croaked on, a household raven, croaking in kitchen and passage and sick-room alike, until Margaret—by sheer will—defied the sound and chose to hope.

They needed that small patch of light indoors; for outside, even to their uninstructed eyes, Milton’s air seemed thick with a brooding discontent. Mr. Hale, with his gentle habit of listening, had drawn around him acquaintances among the working men; their quietly told tales of suffering, of long endurance, depressed him more than any open clamour could. They would have scorned to complain to one who, by his station, ought to have known without being told; but he was a stranger from a distant county, perplexed by the machinery of a system into which he had been dropped, and each man was eager to make him judge—to lay before him, as evidence, his own irritations and wrongs.

And then Mr. Hale, unable to keep these stories to himself, would take his budget of grievances to Mr. Thornton and beg him to arrange them, to explain their origin. Mr. Thornton always did—calmly, clearly, on what he called sound economical principles. Trade, he said, must wax and wane; and in the waning a certain number of masters as well as men must go down into ruin, slipping out of the ranks of the prosperous as inevitably as weak swimmers slip under a current. He spoke of the consequence as if it were not merely probable but logical—so logical that neither employer nor employed had a right to complain when it became their fate: the employer to turn aside from a race he could no longer run, bitten by failure, trampled by his fellows in their haste to be rich, slighted where he had once been honoured, forced to ask for employment instead of dispensing it with a lordly hand.

And because he could picture so sternly the possible doom of masters, he had the less sympathy to spare for the workmen who were cast out by swift alteration—men who would willingly lie down and quietly die out of a world that did not need them, if only they could die without hearing in their last moment the clinging cries of the helpless they would leave behind; men who envied even a wild bird that can feed her young with her heart’s blood.

Margaret’s whole soul rose against him when he reasoned so—as if commerce were everything and humanity nothing. It made her teeth set, it made her throat ache, when that very evening he came to offer help with a delicacy that kept it private—every convenience for illness that his wealth, or his mother’s foresight, had gathered: things Dr. Donaldson had hinted Mrs. Hale might need. His presence, his grave voice, the pity in his eyes, brought close the doom Margaret was trying—by day and by night—to push back into darkness. What right had he, of all people, to share the awful secret she kept in the most sacred recess of her heart—barely daring to look at it unless she called for strength from God—that some day soon she would cry aloud for her mother and no answer would come, only blank, dumb darkness?

Yet he knew. She saw it in the softened look he tried not to let rest on her. She heard it in the tremor that would not quite leave his careful speech. And how could she reconcile those eyes and that voice with the hard, dry, merciless axiom-making by which he had spoken of men’s misery as if it were a necessary subtraction in a sum? The discord jarred upon her beyond bearing—especially with Bessy’s tales in her mind, full of hunger’s plain cookery and the wailing it brewed: children waking at night because their bellies were empty, mothers counting pennies as they would count grains.

To be sure, Nicholas Higgins spoke differently. He had been made a committee-man, and now carried himself as one who held secrets from those outside. He said so openly on the day before Mrs. Thornton’s dinner-party, when Margaret went in to see Bessy and found him in argument with John Boucher—a neighbour often named in the Higgins household, sometimes with compassion as a weak workman overburdened with a great family, and sometimes with anger for his lack of what Higgins called spirit.

Higgins was in a passion when Margaret entered. Boucher stood with both hands braced on the mantelpiece, swaying a little as if his arms were the only things keeping him upright. He stared into the fire with a wild despair that pricked Higgins like an insult even while it tore at his heart. Bessy rocked herself violently, as she did when agitation seized her; her sister Mary, tying on her bonnet with clumsy bows that her clumsy fingers made, blubbered aloud and longed to escape the room.

Margaret paused at the door. Then, with her finger to her lips, she stole to the squab near Bessy and sat down. Nicholas, catching her movement, gave her a gruff nod that was not unfriendly. Mary, snatching at the open door like a sudden mercy, hurried away and cried aloud once she was out of her father’s presence. Only Boucher seemed to notice nothing—neither comings nor goings—only the fire and what it could not warm.

“It’s no use, Higgins,” he said hoarsely. “Hoo cannot live long a’ this’n. Hoo’s just sinking away—not for want o’ meat hersel’—but because hoo cannot stand th’ sight o’ the little ones clemming. Ay, clemming! Five shilling a week may do well enough for thee, wi’ but two mouths to fill, and one on ’em a wench who can well earn her own meat. But it’s clemming to us.” His voice rose, then broke, as if words were torn out of him. “An’ I tell thee plain—if hoo dies, as I’m ’feard hoo will afore we’ve getten th’ five per cent., I’ll fling the money back i’ th’ master’s face, and say, ‘Be domned to yo’; be domned to th’ whole cruel world o’ yo’; that could na leave me th’ best wife that ever bore childer to a man.’ An’ look thee, lad, I’ll hate thee, and th’ whole pack o’ th’ Union. Ay, an’ chase yo’ through heaven wi’ my hatred,—I will, lad! I will,—if yo’re leading me astray i’ this matter.”

He swallowed, then forced on, as if each detail were a nail he must hammer in. “Thou saidst, Nicholas, on Wednesday sennight—and it’s now Tuesday i’ th’ second week—that afore a fortnight we’d ha’ the masters coming a-begging to us to take back our work, at our own wage—and time’s nearly up,—and there’s our lile Jack lying a-bed, too weak to cry, but just every now and then sobbing up his heart for want o’ food,—our lile Jack, I tell thee, lad! Hoo’s never looked up sin’ he were born, and hoo loves him as if he were her very life,—as he is,—for I reckon he’ll ha’ cost me that precious price,—our lile Jack, who wakened me each morn wi’ putting his sweet little lips to my great rough fou’ face, a-seeking a smooth place to kiss,—an’ he lies clemming.”

The sobs rose and choked him. Higgins looked up then—eyes brimming—towards Margaret, as if some witness were needed to bear what he had heard.

“Hou’d up, man,” Higgins said at last, with effort, fumbling in a teapot where he kept his money. “Thy lile Jack shall na’ clem. I ha’ gotten brass, and we’ll go buy the chap a sup o’ milk an’ a good four-pounder this very minute. What’s mine’s thine, sure enough, i’ thou’st i’ want. Only, dunnot lose heart, man!” He thrust the coins into his palm as if their cold weight could be turned into life by speed. “I lay yo my heart and soul we’ll win for a’ this: it’s but bearing on one more week, and yo’ just see th’ way th’ masters ’ll come round, praying on us to come back to our mills. An’ the Union—that’s to say, I—will take care yo’ve enough for th’ childer and th’ missus. So dunnot turn faint-heart, and go to th’ tyrants a-seeking work.”

Boucher turned then—slowly—showing a face so white and gaunt and tear-furrowed and hopeless that its very stillness undid Margaret. The sound of Milton, outside, seemed to press in at the cracks—far-off iron, far-off wheels—yet the most terrible noise was the quiet certainty in his voice.

“Yo’ know well, that a worser tyrant than e’er th’ masters were says, ‘Clem to death, and see ’em a’ clem to death, ere yo’ dare go again th’ Union.’ Yo’ know it well, Nicholas, for a’ yo’re one on e’m. Yo’ may be kind hearts, each separate; but once banded together, yo’ve no more pity for a man than a wild hunger-maddened wolf.”

Nicholas had his hand on the door-lock. He stopped, and turned back, Boucher close behind as if the words had pulled him after.

“So help me God!” Higgins cried, with sudden fierceness that sounded like a vow against the roaring town itself. “Man alive—if I think not I’m doing best for thee, and for all on us. If I’m going wrong when I think I’m going right, it’s their sin, who ha’ left me where I am, in my ignorance. I ha’ thought till my brains ached,—beli’ me, John, I have. An’ I say again, there’s no help for us but having faith i’ th’ Union. They’ll win the day, see if they dunnot!”

Not a word had Margaret or Bessy spoken. Their eyes met, and each seemed to beg the other not to break into the men’s terrible tide. At last Bessy whispered, more to herself than to Margaret, “I never thought to hear father call on God again. But yo’ heard him say, ‘So help me God!’”

“Yes,” Margaret said. The words tasted like iron. “Let me bring you what money I can spare—let me bring you a little food for that poor man’s children. Don’t let them know it comes from anyone but your father. It will be but little.”

Bessy lay back as if the strength to answer had ebbed out of her. She did not cry; she only shivered in her breath.

“My heart’s drained dry o’ tears,” she said at length. “Boucher’s been in these days past, a telling me of his fears and his troubles. He’s but a weak kind of chap, I know, but he’s a man for a’ that; and tho’ I’ve been angry, many a time afore now, wi’ him an’ his wife, as knew no more nor him how to manage, yet yo’ see, all folks isn’t wise, yet God lets ’em live—ay, an’ gives ’em some one to love, and be loved by, just as good as Solomon. An’ if sorrow comes to them they love, it hurts ’em as sore as e’er it did Solomon. I can’t make it out. Perhaps it’s as well such a one as Boucher has th’ Union to see after him. But I’d just like for to see th’ men as make th’ Union, and put ’em one by one face to face wi’ Boucher. I reckon, if they heard him, the’d tell him (if I cotched ’em one by one), he might go back and get what he could for his work, even if it weren’t so much as they ordered.”

Margaret sat silent, feeling the pull of two worlds at once—the coming dinner with its silver, its hot savoury dishes carried in and set down, its polite talk that would float above want like music above a street; and here, this room with its thin bodies and the very word clemming like a dry crust in the throat. How was she to go into comfort and forget that voice, the tone of unutterable agony that said more than the words?

She drew out her purse. There was not much she could call her own, but what she had she put into Bessy’s hand without speaking.

“Thank yo’,” Bessy said, rousing a little, as if the warmth of kindness had reached her even through weakness. “There’s many on ’em gets no more, and is not so bad off,—leastways does not show it as he does. But father won’t let ’em want, now he knows. Yo’ see, Boucher’s been pulled down wi’ his childer,—and her being so cranky, and a’ they could pawn has gone this last twelvemonth. Yo’re not to think we’d ha’ letten ’em clem, for all we’re a bit pressed oursel’; if neighbours doesn’t see after neighbours, I dunno who will.” She spoke quickly now, almost anxiously, as if to guard the pride of their poor household. “Besides, father is sure and positive the masters must give in within these next few days,—that they canna hould on much longer. But I thank yo’ all the same,—I thank yo’ for mysel’, as much as for Boucher, for it jus makes my heart warm to yo’ more and more.”

She looked quieter to-day, but there was a dreadful languor upon her, as if the smallest effort cost her dear. When she finished, her eyelids drooped; her face, sharpened by illness, seemed suddenly too large for its bones. Margaret, struck with alarm at that faint weariness, leaned nearer, listening not only to Bessy’s breathing but to the sounds beyond the wall—the town’s harsh, ceaseless undertone—and wondered how any sick body could heal while Milton’s iron voice never slept.

Margaret went home as one carries a dish too full through a crowded room: every step a peril, every jostle a spill. What she had seen and heard clung to her, not as an idea but as a taste—metallic and bitter at the back of the tongue—so that when she crossed the threshold and met her mother’s expectant look, she had to gather herself, as if to set a table for cheerfulness while her hands still smelt of another house’s grief.

Mrs. Hale, immured now, made of Margaret’s smallest errand a messenger of the world.

“And can your factory friend come on Thursday to see you dressed?” she asked, with that half-pleading eagerness of an invalid who lives by reports and descriptions, as by spoonfuls.

“She was so ill I never thought of asking her,” said Margaret; and her voice had the flatness of sorrow that has been held too long.

“Dear! Everybody is ill now, I think,” returned Mrs. Hale, with the quick, sharp jealousy sick people sometimes turn upon other sufferers, before their natural kindness resumes its place. “But it must be very sad to be ill in one of those little back streets.” The Helstone habit of imagining cottages with honeysuckle and a clean doorstep came back upon her. “It’s bad enough here. What could you do for her, Margaret? Mr. Thornton has sent me some of his old port wine since you went out. Would a bottle of that do her good, think you?”

“No, mamma! I don’t believe they are very poor,—at least, they don’t speak as if they were; and, at any rate, Bessy’s illness is consumption—she won’t want wine. Perhaps I might take her a little preserve, made of our dear Helstone fruit.”

As she spoke, she saw in fancy the glass jar, the clear amber set thick with soft pieces of plum and apricot, as if sunshine had been sealed for winter. The very thought brought the orchard-scent—warm skins, crushed leaves, the green sharpness of stalks—up against the city’s soot and steam. But even that comfort turned, for another family rose before her; and then the day’s sights broke their bounds.

“No! there’s another family to whom I should like to give—Oh mamma, mamma! how am I to dress up in my finery, and go off and away to smart parties, after the sorrow I’ve seen to-day?” she cried, and told her mother all—Higgins’s close room, the sick girl’s breath, the talk of hunger and pride, and the story of the man who had been driven to desperation.

It distressed Mrs. Hale as if Margaret had brought the back street into the drawing-room. She could not sit still with knowledge that demanded action; she must do something, at once, to turn pain into a visible, handleable remedy.

“Pack up a basket,” she said, and would not hear of delay. The drawing-room became a kind of improvised pantry and store. Margaret brought out what could be spared—the loaf with its firm crust, slices of cold meat, a little tea, sugar wrapped carefully against damp; the jar of preserve she had named, its lid tied down, as if the very sweetness might escape. The linen smelt faintly of lavender, that domestic scent of old order. Mrs. Hale watched and directed, restless, her cheeks a little flushed with the agitation of charity.

“It will do if it goes in the morning,” Margaret ventured, because she had left money with Bessy and knew Higgins had not let them go wholly unfed for the moment.

Mrs. Hale’s eyes flashed. “Unfeeling!” she said, and would not breathe freely until Dixon had been summoned and the basket sent out that instant, as if the speed itself were a salve.

Only when the door had closed upon it, and the house had resumed its quiet, did doubt creep in like a draught.

“After all,” Mrs. Hale said, “we may have been doing wrong. It was only the last time Mr. Thornton was here that he said, those were no true friends who helped to prolong the struggle by assisting the turn-outs. And this Boucher-man was a turn-out, was he not?”

Mr. Hale came up then, as he often did, after a lesson with Mr. Thornton that had slipped into their accustomed talk. The question was put to him, and he, trying to hold the scales evenly, repeated what had sounded so clear half an hour before, when it had been spoken in Mr. Thornton’s steady voice. Yet when he looked at his wife and daughter, and at Margaret’s set, pale face, logic softened into human compromise.

“You have done right—quite right—in this instance,” he said. “I do not see how you could have done otherwise.” Then, as if he must save the principle though he spared the particular case, he added, “Still, as a general rule, what Mr. Thornton says has truth. If a strike is prolonged, it ends—often as it has ended before—in masters bringing hands from a distance; or else in the invention of some machine that lessens the need of hands altogether. Then refusing help is, in a certain view, the kindest thing; it will not bolster men up in folly.”

But he would go himself in the morning to see Boucher, to learn the man’s condition, and to judge what might be done without feeding the quarrel. Margaret hardly heard the policy; her mind stayed with the children’s faces, the thinness of the wife’s arms, the way a teacup had seemed in that house as precious as a jewel.

Mr. Hale went as he had said, early. Boucher was out; but the wife, worn into a kind of quiet endurance, talked with him. He promised to ask for an Infirmary order for her; and seeing what Mrs. Hale had sent—good things laid out, already attacked with the eager fingers of children who had learned by want to snatch at plenty while it lasted—he came back with a more consoling account than Margaret had dared to hope for. Indeed, she had prepared him the night before for a misery so complete, that, by the rebound of imagination, he described all as brighter than the truth.

“But I will go again, and see the man himself,” he said. “I hardly know, as yet, how to compare one of these houses with our Helstone cottages. I see furniture here which our labourers would never have thought of buying, and food commonly used which they would consider luxuries; yet for these very families there seems no other resource now that their weekly wages are stopped, but the pawn-shop. One had need to learn a different standard, up here in Milton.”

Bessy, too, was rather better that day; so weak, however, that she seemed to have forgotten the feverish longing to see Margaret dressed, if ever it had been more than a wandering fancy. And now Thursday came, with its strange demand that Margaret should put on splendour while her heart felt hung with lead.
