The toilette, once a girlish pleasure shared with Edith—laughing over ribbons and the fall of a sleeve—was now a duty, performed like laying out best linen for a guest one does not wish to entertain. Still, there was one sweetness in it: her mother’s delight. Mrs. Hale watched every touch, as if the sight fed her.

Dixon, flinging the drawing-room door open with ceremony, cried out to her mistress, “Miss Hale looks well, ma’am,—doesn’t she? Mrs. Shaw’s coral couldn’t have come in better. It just gives the right touch of colour, ma’am. Otherwise, Miss Margaret, you would have been too pale.”

Margaret’s black hair, too thick for plaiting, had been twisted and compressed into heavy coils that circled her head like a crown, then gathered into a great spiral knot behind, the glossy strands catching light as oil catches flame. Two long coral pins—small arrows—held the weight in place. Her white silk sleeves were looped with white strings, and at her throat lay a heavy necklace of coral beads, the colour of crushed berries, or the inner flesh of a shell—warm against her skin’s milk-white coolness.

“Oh, Margaret!” Mrs. Hale said, and the old life in her broke out in a little burst of maternal vanity. “How I should like to be going with you to one of the old Barrington assemblies,—taking you as Lady Beresford used to take me.”

Margaret kissed her, and tried to answer with a smile, but it was faint. “I would rather stay at home with you,—much rather, mamma.”

“Nonsense, darling! Be sure you notice the dinner well. I shall like to hear how they manage these things in Milton. Particularly the second course, dear. Look what they have instead of game.”

Margaret promised, as one promises a child, though she thought it bitter that, in the midst of talk of courses and second courses, men and women were measuring out hunger by the day. Yet she carried her mother’s wish with her like a small task, and perhaps it gave her a way of turning away from the heavier thoughts.

At the Thorntons’ the dinner-table, when she saw it, was less a meal than a display of conquest. The linen lay white and hard as if ironed into pride; silver flashed; cut glass cut the candlelight into sharp stars. Dishes came up in a succession that seemed meant to prove there was no limit: soups rich with long-boiled bones and herbs, fish dressed to whiteness, joints that had been basted till the outer fat turned to a crisp brown shell. Sauces—thick, glossy, carefully strained—clung to spoon and tongue. There were small dainties too—jellies quivering like captured light, creams whipped to air, fruits out of their season, as if the very climate had been purchased. Margaret, with her cultivated taste, felt the abundance oppressive. Half would have been enough; less would have been more elegant. Yet it was one of Mrs. Thornton’s rigorous laws that of each separate dainty there should be enough for every guest to choose, as if hospitality meant not offering, but supplying.

Mrs. Thornton herself, careless to abstemiousness in daily life, set feasts as a point of honour; and her son shared the same feeling, though he was denying himself, privately, the expenditure of an unnecessary sixpence. He had more than once regretted sending out the invitations at such a time; and yet, since the thing was done, he was glad of the old magnificence, as if it proved that nothing—not even this strike—could disorder his household.

Margaret and her father were the first to arrive, Mr. Hale anxiously punctual. Upstairs, in the drawing-room, only Mrs. Thornton and Fanny waited. Every cover had been taken off; the room blazed with yellow silk damask and a carpet thick with brilliant flowers. Ornaments filled every corner until the eye grew weary of being asked to admire. And through the windows the great mill-yard stared back—wide folding gates open for carriages, and the factory itself looming on the left, high and many-storied, throwing a shadow that darkened the summer evening before its time.

“My son was engaged up to the last moment on business. He will be here directly, Mr. Hale. May I beg you to take a seat?” said Mrs. Thornton.

Mr. Hale had been looking out. He turned, and spoke with the delicate discomfort of a man new to Milton. “Don’t you find such close neighbourhood to the mill rather unpleasant at times?”

Mrs. Thornton drew herself up, as if he had spoken ill of a member of the family. “Never. I am not become so fine as to desire to forget the source of my son’s wealth and power. Besides, there is not such another factory in Milton. One room alone is two hundred and twenty square yards.”

“I meant that the smoke and the noise—the constant going out and coming in of the workpeople—might be annoying!”

“I agree with you, Mr. Hale!” cried Fanny. “There is a continual smell of steam and oily machinery—and the noise is perfectly deafening.”

Mrs. Thornton’s sternness hardened into scorn. “I have heard noise that was called music far more deafening. The engine-room is at the street-end of the factory; we hardly hear it, except in summer weather, when all the windows are open; and as for the continual murmur of the workpeople, it disturbs me no more than the humming of a hive of bees. If I think of it at all, I connect it with my son, and feel how all belongs to him, and that his is the head that directs it. Just now, there are no sounds to come from the mill; the hands have been ungrateful enough to turn out, as perhaps you have heard. But the very business”—and she bit the words as if they had grit in them—“had reference to the steps he is going to take to make them learn their place.”

The room, with its heavy fabrics and crowded ornaments, seemed to hold in sound. Outside, Milton’s accustomed iron breathing was muted by the strike: no clatter of clogs, no ceaseless mechanical throb. That absence had a quality of its own, like a pause in a harsh song. Margaret, later, would feel it as keenly as any noise—silence, not peace.

Mrs. Thornton’s dark anger did not clear away when Mr. Thornton entered. She saw, at once, the weight of care he could not shake off, though he greeted his guests with a cheerfulness that looked cordial.

He shook hands with Margaret. He knew—though she did not—that it was the first time their hands had met; the touch was brief, as if manners were a glove. He inquired after Mrs. Hale, and listened to Mr. Hale’s sanguine account; then glanced at Margaret to see if she contradicted it by expression. Her face gave no dissent.

And in that glance he was struck anew by her beauty. He had not seen her thus dressed. Now it seemed to him that such elegance belonged to her, as if she ought always to move in white silk and coral, her head crowned with that massive, glossy hair. She was talking to Fanny; he could not hear the words. He watched his sister’s fidgeting—hands tugging at a ribbon, eyes wandering without aim—and compared it, uneasily, to Margaret’s steady composure. Her large soft eyes rested on one object at a time, as if their look could quiet whatever they touched. Her red lips curved and parted in listening; her head bent a little forward, making a long sweeping line from the light on her raven hair down to the smooth ivory shoulder. Her round white arms and taper hands lay lightly across each other, perfectly still.

He sighed at the sight, then, with an effort, turned away and threw himself into conversation with Mr. Hale, as if business of the mind were safer ground than the sight of a woman who could stir him into unrest.

More people arrived. Fanny went to help her mother receive them. In the influx, Mr. Thornton became conscious—almost irritably—of one thing: no one was speaking to Margaret. It was like a discord in the room’s hum. Yet he did not go to her; he did not look at her. Still he knew, with an odd exactness, what she did and did not do, more certainly than he knew any other movement in the crowded room.

Margaret, for her part, was unconscious of herself. She watched, quietly amused, the stir and show, as if observing a play whose rules she did not quite believe in. Somebody took her down to dinner—she did not catch the name—and he did not trouble himself to talk much.

At table, the gentlemen’s talk rose and fell with animation; the ladies, for the most part, were silent, busy noting dishes, criticising dress, measuring one another by lace and the fall of a sleeve. Margaret’s mind, starved for earnest speech, caught the gentlemen’s discussion like a hand closing over warmth. Mr. Horsfall, a stranger—the visit that had been the germ of the party—asked questions about the trade and manufactures; the Milton men answered, eager, technical, proud. A dispute sprang up, contested warmly; it was referred to Mr. Thornton, who had scarcely spoken. Now he gave his opinion, the grounds laid out as plainly as if he were setting down accounts. Even opponents yielded.

Margaret’s attention fixed on him. Here, as master of his house and among his equals, his manner was straightforward, simple, modest—thoroughly dignified. She thought she had never seen him to such advantage. When he had come to their home, there had always been something of over-eagerness, or of vexed annoyance, as if he pre-supposed himself unjustly judged and yet was too proud to explain. But here there was no uncertainty of place. These men regarded him as force, as power. He did not struggle for their respect; he had it, and he knew it. Security gave him a grand quietness of voice and gesture that she had missed before.

He spoke little to ladies; what he did say was formal. To Margaret he hardly spoke at all.

To her surprise she enjoyed the dinner. She understood now many local interests; she even caught technical words. She took, silently, a decided part in the question, aligning herself with arguments, rejecting others. At least these men talked as if what they said mattered; there was none of the used-up wit and languid phrases that had wearied her in London drawing-rooms. And she wondered, with a sort of puzzled relief, that no one alluded to the strike. She did not yet know how coolly such things were taken by masters, as having only one possible end. The men, they thought, were hurting themselves as they had done before. If they chose to be fools and put their fate into the hands of paid delegates, they must take consequences. Thornton would lose, of course; it was an accident that might visit any of them. But Thornton was iron; he would manage a strike as well as any. The hands had mistaken their man.

After dinner, when the ladies were left together, the talk shrank to smallness again. Margaret grew sleepy with it, and glad when the gentlemen returned—not only for the comfort of catching her father’s eye, which always seemed to steady her, but because she could listen once more to something larger than petty rivalries.

She liked, too, the exultation in power these Milton men displayed. It could be rampant; it could savour of boasting. Yet there was something admirable in their intoxication, not with wine but with achievement—with the memory of what had been wrested from matter, and the anticipation of what would yet be done. Their imagination leaped forward beyond their own lifetimes. They spoke of changes none of them would live to see, and forgot themselves in that far triumph. In her cooler moments she might not approve the spirit in all things; but she could not deny the vigour.

She started a little when Mr. Thornton spoke suddenly close at her elbow.

“I could see you were on our side in our discussion at dinner,—were you not, Miss Hale?”

“Certainly. But then I know so little about it. I was surprised, however, to find from what Mr. Horsfall said, that there were others who thought in so diametrically opposite a manner, as the Mr. Morison he spoke about. He cannot be a gentleman—is he?”

He looked at her, and there was a brief hardness in his mouth, as if the word pricked him.

“I am not quite the person to decide on another’s gentlemanliness, Miss Hale. I mean, I don’t quite understand your application of the word. But I should say that this Morison is no true man. I don’t know who he is; I merely judge him from Mr. Horsfall’s account.”

“I suspect my ‘gentleman’ includes your ‘true man.’”

“And a great deal more, you would imply. I differ from you. A man is to me a higher and a completer being than a gentleman.”

“What do you mean?” asked Margaret. “We must understand the words differently.”

“I take it that ‘gentleman’ is a term that only describes a person in his relation to others; but when we speak of him as ‘a man,’ we consider him not merely with regard to his fellow-men, but in relation to himself,—to life—to time—to eternity. A cast-away lonely as Robinson Crusoe—a prisoner immured in a dungeon for life—nay, even a saint in Patmos, has his endurance, his strength, his faith, best described by being spoken of as ‘a man.’ I am rather weary of this word ‘gentlemanly,’ which seems to me to be often inappropriately used, and often, too, with such exaggerated distortion of meaning, while the full simplicity of the noun ‘man,’ and the adjective ‘manly’ are acknowledged—that I am induced to class it with the cant of the day.”

Margaret paused, feeling a slow conviction shaping itself, as if she were trying to translate one dialect into another and finding no exact equivalence. Before she could answer, he was called away by the eager manufacturers.

She could not hear their speeches, but the meaning came through in scraps, as sound carries through walls: anxiety, counsel, risk. Mr. Thornton’s replies came back short, clear, steady—like the boom of a distant minute-gun marking time with inevitability.

“That has been done,” she heard him say.

A hurried murmur, more than one voice.

“All those arrangements have been made.”

Mr. Slickson, anxious and insinuating, took hold of Mr. Thornton’s arm as if to anchor him. Doubts were urged, difficulties named. Mr. Thornton moved slightly away—only slightly—and lifted his eyebrows a fraction.

“I take the risk,” he said. “You need not join in it unless you choose.”

Still more fears: hints of what men might do in anger when they are hungry, and when the mills stand silent but for resentment.

“I’m not afraid of anything so dastardly as incendiarism,” Mr. Thornton answered, with a contempt that rang through his composure. “We are open enemies; and I can protect myself from any violence that I apprehend. And I will assuredly protect all others who come to me for work. They know my determination by this time, as well and as fully as you do.”

Mr. Horsfall drew him a little aside; Margaret supposed it was to ask more about the strike. In truth, it was to inquire who she was—so quiet, so stately, so beautiful.

“A Milton lady?” asked he.

“No! from the south of England—Hampshire, I believe,” said Mr. Thornton, and the cold indifference of his tone was like a shutter closing.

Elsewhere in the room, Mrs. Slickson, with the cheerful curiosity of those who love to place people upon a social shelf, was catechising Fanny.

“Who is that fine distinguished-looking girl? a sister of Mr. Horsfall’s?”

“Oh dear, no! That is Mr. Hale, her father, talking now to Mr. Stephens. He gives lessons; that is to say, he reads with young men. My brother John goes to him twice a week, and so he begged mamma to ask them here, in hopes of getting him known. I believe we have some of their prospectuses, if you would like to have one.”

“Mr. Thornton! Does he really find time to read with a tutor, in the midst of all his business,—and this abominable strike in hand as well?”

Fanny coloured, uncertain whether pride or shame was expected of her, as if her feelings must take their rule from another’s “ought.” But the company began to break up; shawls were drawn on, farewells said, the flow of voices thinned. The night air outside received them, and with it the faint, far-off stir of Milton—its mixed breath of smoke and summer, the hush where the mill’s usual roar should have been, and beneath that hush the uneasy sense of men waiting, as if the whole town were listening for the next sound it would be forced to learn.

Margaret and her father went home through a night washed clean, the flagstones still holding the day’s warmth, but the air turned lively and sharp, as if the town had loosened its collar after the heat. She had lifted her white silk a little from the dust and damp, the hem gathered in her hand in the old, half-childish way, and walked with a step that might have been a dance if dread had not kept time with it.

“I rather think Mr. Thornton is not quite easy in his mind about this strike,” she said. “He seemed very anxious to-night.”

“I should wonder if he were not,” Mr. Hale answered. “Yet he spoke with his usual coolness when they were proposing different plans, just before we came away.”

“So he did after dinner. It would take a good deal to stir him from that manner of speaking; but his face strikes me as anxious.”

“I should be, if I were he. He must know of the growing anger—of the hatred that is only half smothered—among his people. They look upon him as what Scripture calls a hard man; not unjust, perhaps, but unfeeling; standing upon his rights as if any rights of ours were much, in the sight of God. I am glad you think he looks anxious. When I remember Boucher’s half-mad words and ways, I cannot bear to think how coolly Mr. Thornton spoke.”

“In the first place, I am not so convinced as you are of Boucher’s utter distress. Badly off for the moment, no doubt. But there is always that mysterious supply of money from the Unions; and, from what you told me, he is of a passionate nature—demonstrative; he gives voice to everything he feels.”

“Oh, papa!”

“Well! I only want you to do justice to Mr. Thornton. He is, I suspect, a man of the opposite kind—too proud to show his feelings. Just the character I should have fancied beforehand you would admire, Margaret.”

“So I do—so I should,” she replied quickly, and then, because her conscience was exacting, she added, more slowly, “but I don’t feel quite so sure as you do of the existence of those feelings. He has great strength of character—unusual intellect, considering the few advantages he has had.”

“Not so few. He has lived a practical life from early youth; he has been obliged to use judgment and self-control. That develops one part of the mind. He needs, to be sure, more knowledge of what has gone before—the past gives the truest ground for guessing the future; but he knows the want—he perceives it. And that is something. You are prejudiced against him, Margaret.”

“He is the first manufacturer I ever had the opportunity of studying, papa. He is my first olive: let me make a face while I swallow it. I know he is good of his kind, and by and by I shall like the kind. I rather think I am already beginning to do so.” She tried to smile, with that brave habit she had of snatching at whatever looked like common daylight. “I was very much interested by what the gentlemen were talking about, though I did not understand half of it. I was quite sorry when Miss Thornton came to take me to the other end of the room, saying she was sure I should be uncomfortable as the only lady among so many gentlemen. I had never thought of it, I was so busy listening; and the ladies were so dull, papa—oh, so dull! Yet it was clever, too. It reminded me of our old game of having each so many nouns to put into a sentence.”

“What do you mean, child?” he asked.

“Why, they took nouns that were signs of things that give evidence of wealth—housekeepers, under-gardeners, extent of glass, valuable lace, diamonds—and each one made her speech so as to bring them all in, as if by accident, and prettily.”

“You will be as proud of your one servant when you get her, if all Mrs. Thornton says is true.”

“To be sure I shall. I felt like a hypocrite to-night, sitting there in my white silk, with my idle hands before me, when I remembered all the good thorough house-work they had done to-day. They took me for a fine lady, I’m sure.”

“Even I was mistaken enough to think you looked like a lady, my dear,” said Mr. Hale, with that quiet smile which softened his face more than any laughter could have done.

But the smile died and left them blanched when Dixon opened the door.

“Oh, master!—oh, Miss Margaret! Thank God you are come! Dr. Donaldson is here. The servant next door went for him, for the charwoman is gone home. She’s better now; but—oh, sir!—I thought she’d have died an hour ago.”

Mr. Hale caught at Margaret’s arm as if the floor had tilted under him. His look went to her face for guidance; and what he saw there was surprise and extremest sorrow—an awe that had no sharp terror in it, as if she had been living for weeks in the shadow of this very moment.

“Oh! I should not have left her—wicked daughter that I am!” Margaret murmured; and though she supported her father, she felt as if she were the one who needed holding up, so heavy was the thought of what waited above.

Dr. Donaldson met them on the landing, speaking low, as if any loudness would jar some fragile thread.

“She is better now. The opiate has taken effect. The spasms were very bad; no wonder they frightened your maid; but she’ll rally this time.”

“This time!” Mr. Hale’s voice broke upon the words. “Let me go to her!”

Half an hour ago he had been a man in his strength; now he moved with dim sight and wavering sense, old in an instant. Dr. Donaldson took his arm, and led him into the bedroom. Margaret followed close.

There lay Mrs. Hale—sleeping, quiet enough to deceive any heart that did not know the handwriting of that stillness. She might be better: she was not recovered. Death had set his seal upon her face, faint but unmistakeable, like wax taking a signet. She breathed; yet the room already felt as if something had been taken away from it, as if the familiar household air had lost a note.

Mr. Hale stood looking long, without speech. Then his whole frame began to shake. He turned away from the bed and groped, blindly, as if he could not remember where the door stood, though several candles—brought up in sudden fright—burned and flared with shaken flames. He staggered into the drawing-room and felt for a chair. Dr. Donaldson wheeled one to him and placed him in it, then took his pulse with firm fingers.

“Speak to him, Miss Hale. We must rouse him.”

“Papa!” Margaret cried. The word came out wild with pain. “Papa! Speak to me!”

The old speculative look—the one that belonged to him when he was far off in thought—came back into his eyes, and he made a great effort.

“Margaret, did you know of this? Oh, it was cruel of you!”

“No, sir, it was not cruel,” said Dr. Donaldson quickly, as if he would not let injustice settle anywhere in that room. “Miss Hale acted under my directions. There may have been a mistake, but it was not cruelty. Your wife will be a different creature to-morrow, I trust. She has had spasms, as I anticipated—though I did not tell Miss Hale of my apprehensions. She has taken the opiate I brought; she will have a good long sleep; and to-morrow that look which has alarmed you will have passed away.”

“But not the disease?” Mr. Hale asked, with a dreadful quietness.

Dr. Donaldson glanced at Margaret. Her head was bent; her face, when it lifted, made no entreaty for a reprieve bought by any kindly lie. The doctor, who understood quick, did not pretend.

“Not the disease. We cannot touch it, with all our vaunted skill. We can only delay its progress—alleviate the pain. Be a man, sir—a Christian. Have faith in the immortality of the soul, which no pain, no mortal disease, can assail or touch!”

But the answer came, choked and human: “You have never been married, Dr. Donaldson; you don’t know what it is.” And then the sobs—deep, manly, helpless—went through the stillness of the house, pulse after pulse, like heavy blows in the dark.

Margaret knelt beside him and put her arms about him, kissing his cold hand, smoothing it, holding him as if by touch she could keep him from falling into some abyss where she could not follow. No one—not even Dr. Donaldson—noticed how time went by, for time is a thing one only hears when the heart is not in torment.

At last Mr. Hale, by some effort that was almost duty rather than strength, spoke of what must be done.

“What must we do?” he asked. “Tell us both. Margaret is my staff—my right hand.”

Dr. Donaldson gave clear directions: there was no fear for the night—nay, even peace for to-morrow, and for many days yet, perhaps—but no enduring hope. He advised Mr. Hale to go to bed and leave only one watcher, that the sleep might not be disturbed by restless moving and anxious whispering. He promised to come early in the morning; then he took their hands with a warmth that was more comfort than any words, and went away into the outer darkness.

They said little after that. Terror leaves one exhausted, like hard labour. Mr. Hale was resolved to sit up all night; Margaret could only prevail upon him to lie down on the drawing-room sofa. Dixon, stout and blunt, refused to go to bed at all; and as for Margaret, she could no more leave her mother than she could leave her own breath, let doctors speak as they pleased of “husbanding resources,” and “one watcher only.”

So the watch began: a domestic vigil, plain and terrible, made up of small familiar things—candles guttering, a jug of water, folded cloths warmed and re-warmed, the faint medicinal sweetness of laudanum hanging in the air and clinging to the back of the throat; and under it all the sound of the house itself, which she had never listened to so intently before. A house has its own acoustic life: boards that creak with temperature, a distant drip, a coal settling in the grate. In Milton, beyond their walls, there was always the town’s heavy breathing; even when machinery was stilled, the habit of it seemed to remain, like a pulse you miss only when you put your ear to the pillow and cannot find it.

Dixon sat and stared and winked and drooped, then jerked herself upright with offended pride, as if sleep were a betrayal; but at last her head fell forward and she gave up the struggle and snored, the sound rough and homely, almost comforting in its vulgar certainty.

Margaret had taken off her gown and tossed it aside with impatient disgust, as if the white silk had been a costume borrowed for an hour from some other life. She put on her dressing-gown, and sat where she could see her mother’s face by the shaded candlelight. She felt she could never sleep again. Her senses seemed sharpened for watching: every change of breath, every twitch of eyelid, every pause in the wind outside pressed on her like a finger. Even thoughts were not silent; they came with edges.

For more than two hours she heard her father moving restlessly in the next room. Again and again he came to the door of the sick chamber and paused there to listen, afraid to enter and afraid to go away. Margaret, not hearing his unseen presence at first, would rise and open the door and tell him, softly, how all went on, answering questions his dry lips could hardly shape.

At last he too fell asleep, and the house grew still.

Margaret sat behind the curtain and thought. Far away in time, far away in space, seemed all that had filled yesterday. Not more than six-and-thirty hours ago she had cared for Bessy Higgins and her father; her heart had been wrung for Boucher; she had gone out into the streets with purpose and returned with plans. Now all that was like a dream remembered from some former life—unreal because it was not her mother. Everything that happened beyond these walls seemed separated, and therefore untrue.

Harley Street appeared more distinct than Milton: she remembered, as if it were yesterday, tracing her mother’s features in Aunt Shaw’s face; letters arriving, making her ache for home. Helstone itself lay in a dim past, a green silence she had once thought secure. The dull grey days of winter and spring, so monotonous, so uneventful, now seemed richer than any festival, because her mother had been there through them, alive, complaining, loving, disappointed—alive.

She would have caught at the skirts of that departing time and begged it to return, to give her back what she had not valued enough while she possessed it.

Life looked to her like a vain show—unsubstantial, flickering, flitting. The thought came with a sound, not an idea: as if from some airy belfry, high above the jar of earth, a bell were always tolling, and the words it tolled were untranslatable into comfort—only into knowledge: All are shadows. All are passing. All is past. No dialect she knew could soften it; it was a dominant lexicon, pitiless in its plainest terms, making everything else—love, duty, pride—seem like smaller words.

When morning came, cool and grey, like many a happier morning before, she looked one by one at the sleepers—Dixon heavy in her chair, her father on the sofa with his hand fallen open—and it seemed, for an instant, as if the terrible night had been unreal; as if it too were a shadow, and now it was past.

Mrs. Hale herself, when she awoke, did not know how ill she had been. She was surprised at Dr. Donaldson’s early visit, perplexed by the anxious faces bending over her, and consented to remain in bed that day because she admitted she was tired. The next day she insisted on getting up; and Dr. Donaldson consented to her returning to the drawing-room.

But comfort would not stay in any posture. She shifted and sighed, the restlessness not of impatience but of a body that could not find ease within its own boundaries; and before night she grew feverish. Mr. Hale, after that first shock, seemed emptied of decision, listless as if all his will had run out in tears.

“What can we do to spare mamma such another night?” Margaret asked on the third day, when the very thought of darkness made her hands cold.

“It is, to a certain degree, the reaction after the powerful opiates I have been obliged to use,” Dr. Donaldson answered. “It is more painful for you to see than for her to bear, I believe. But I think, if we could get a water-bed, it might be a good thing. Not but what she will be better to-morrow—pretty much like herself as she was before this attack. Still, I should like her to have a water-bed. Mrs. Thornton has one, I know. I’ll try and call there this afternoon. Stay—” His eye caught Margaret’s face, blanched with watching, her mouth set as if she had forgotten the taste of food. “I’m not sure I can go; I have a long round to take. It would do you no harm to have a brisk walk to Marlborough Street and ask Mrs. Thornton if she can spare it.”

“Certainly,” said Margaret. “I could go while mamma is asleep this afternoon. I’m sure Mrs. Thornton would lend it to us.”

The doctor’s experience proved right in this: Mrs. Hale brightened that afternoon more than Margaret had dared hope. After dinner she sat in her easy-chair, her hand lying in her husband’s; and though Mr. Hale looked more worn and suffering than she, he could smile now—slowly and faintly, it is true; but two days ago Margaret had never thought to see him smile again.

It was about two miles from Crampton Crescent to Marlborough Street. At three o’clock an August sun beat straight down into the street, turning the air thick, as if it had been stirred with a spoon and left to stand. Margaret went along without noticing much for the first mile and a half; her mind, trained by these days of nursing, moved as if it were carrying a covered dish that must not be jarred. She threaded her way through the irregular stream of Milton people with an instinct she had learnt here—step, pause, sidestep—like passing through a kitchen at full work without upsetting pans or scalding oneself.

But by and by she became aware of an unusual heaving among the crowd. It was not a crowd that went anywhere; it was a crowd that gathered, talked, listened—buzzing with excitement while scarcely shifting its feet, as if the street itself held them. They made way for her; and because she was bent upon her errand and upon the necessity that suggested it, she observed less quickly than she might have done if her mind had been at ease.

Only when she had almost reached Marlborough Street did the full conviction force itself upon her: there was an oppressive irritation abroad, a thunderous atmosphere—moral as well as physical—pressing down upon the town. From every narrow lane opening into Marlborough Street came up a low, distant roar, like myriads of voices kneaded into one sound. It was not speech so much as a soundscape of anger, the kind that enters the body through the ear and sets the heart beating out of time.

The inhabitants of each poor, squalid dwelling were gathered at doors and windows, or standing in the middle of the narrow ways, all looking towards one point. And Marlborough Street itself was the focus of those eyes—some fierce with wrath, some lowering with threats, some widened with fear or beseeching entreaty.

Margaret, reaching the small side-entrance by the folding doors in the great dead wall of Marlborough mill-yard, waited for the porter to answer the bell. She looked round, and heard—far off—the first long roll of the coming tempest; saw the first slow-surging wave of the dark crowd rise at the far end of the street, lift its threatening crest, tumble forward, and then retreat. A moment ago the street had seemed full of repressed noise; now it was ominously still, as if the town held its breath.

All these circumstances forced themselves on her notice, but did not sink down into her preoccupied heart. She did not know what they meant; she could not read their deep significance. She only knew the keen, sharp pressure of the knife that was soon to stab her through by leaving her motherless, and she was trying to make herself ready—ready to bear it, ready to comfort her father when it fell.

The porter opened the door cautiously, not nearly wide enough to admit her.

“It’s you, is it, ma’am?” he said, drawing a long breath, and widening the entrance—still not flinging it wide, as if even a doorway might be a weakness.

Margaret went in. He hastily bolted it behind her.

“Th’ folk are all coming up here, I reckon?” he asked.

“I don’t know. Something unusual seemed going on; but this street is quite empty, I think.”

She crossed the yard and went up the steps to the house door. There was no near sound—no steam-engine at work with beat and pant, no click of machinery, no mingling and clashing of many sharp voices; the mill’s usual din, that industrial chorus which made Milton’s days, had fallen away. Yet far off the ominous gathering roar deepened—clamouring, approaching—like thunder heard through walls.

Margaret was admitted without delay; yet when the door shut behind her, the house seemed to hold its breath, as if it too listened for danger.

The drawing-room had been made ready again for company—chairs sheathed, tables swaddled in holland, a thin propriety pulled back over the disorder of daily life. Heat pressed in from the street. The windows stood half open, and the Venetian blinds cut the daylight into sickly strips: a hard grey glare thrown upward from the flags below, and, above it, a faint greenish wash as the slats tinted the sun. The light turned every reflection treacherous. When Margaret caught her own face in a mirror, it looked as if it had been steeped in ash—wan, hollow-eyed, and stranger-like.

She waited. No one came.

Now and then the air—though it did not stir a curtain—carried to her the far-off massed sound of people: a murmuring, a trampling, as if an enormous beast moved somewhere out of sight. Then, between one pulse and the next, the noise fell away into a stillness so deep it made the house feel deserted.

At last Fanny Thornton hurried in, flushed and fretful, with the sharp impatience of one who resented being made to fear.

“Mamma will come directly, Miss Hale. She begged me to apologise. Perhaps you know my brother has imported hands from Ireland, and it has irritated the Milton people beyond all bearing—as if he hadn’t a right to get labour where he could. And the stupid wretches here wouldn’t work for him; and now they’ve frightened these poor Irish starvelings so with their threats, that we daren’t let them out. You may see them huddled in the top room in the mill, and they’re to sleep there, to keep them safe from those brutes, who will neither work nor let them work. And mamma is seeing about their food, and John is speaking to them—for some of the women are crying to go back. Ah! here’s mamma!”

Mrs. Thornton entered with a stern darkness on her face, a look that made the room itself feel colder. Margaret, who had come only because Mrs. Thornton had once said, with brisk command, that she was to ask for whatever might be needed during Mrs. Hale’s illness, felt suddenly as if she brought a selfish request into a house on fire.

Yet she spoke quietly, her voice careful and low. She told of her mother’s restless suffering; of Dr. Donaldson’s recommendation; of the strange mercy of a water-bed, which could take the body’s weight as dough takes a hand—yielding without bruising, easing the perpetual ache. She made it sound practical, not plaintive. Still Mrs. Thornton’s mouth tightened while she listened, as if every word cost her patience.

Margaret ceased.

Mrs. Thornton did not answer. Her attention had slid elsewhere, to something beyond the walls. She started upright, face changing in an instant from suppressed irritation to alarm.

“They’re at the gates! Call John, Fanny—call him in from the mill! They’re at the gates! They’ll batter them in. Call John, I say!”

As she spoke, the sound Margaret had been hearing at intervals rushed near as if it had been waiting for permission. Tramp—tramp—tramp, a thickening of footsteps. Then the sharp rage of voices rose up from behind the wooden barrier outside. The great gates shook. The crowd, unseen, hit them as bodies become battering-rams: a surge, a recoil, then a more united drive. The very hinges groaned under it, and the wood quivered like a reed in a storm.

The women were drawn to the windows as if fear had its own fascination. Mrs. Thornton, the servants, Margaret—all stood peering down through slats and half-opened panes. Fanny returned from the stairhead with screams as if she were being chased, and flung herself, sobbing hysterically, upon a sofa.

Mrs. Thornton waited for her son. He was still in the mill.

At last he came out into the yard, visible through the distorted angles the blinds allowed. He looked up at the pale cluster of faces and smiled—briefly, as if courage were a thing you could pass from hand to hand. Then he locked the factory door and called for one of the women to come down and undo the house-door, which Fanny had fastened in her panic. Mrs. Thornton went herself.

His voice—well-known, controlled, used to command—seemed to taste in the air like blood to the angry multitude. Until that moment they had strained and struck the gates almost in silence, as if their breath was wanted for brute effort. Now, hearing him speak within, they gave a fierce groan that did not sound human: it rose from them as hunger rises from beasts denied their food.

Mrs. Thornton went white as she preceded him into the room. He entered a little flushed; his eyes shone, answering danger as if it were a trumpet-call. His face had a proud defiance that made him noble even where it did not make him handsome.

Margaret had always dreaded an emergency that would expose her as cowardly. Yet now, in real peril, with fear reasonable and close, she forgot herself; she felt only an intense sympathy, sharp as pain, for the struggle about to be fought.

Mr. Thornton came forward frankly.

“I am sorry, Miss Hale, you should have visited us at this unfortunate moment; I fear you may be involved in whatever risk we have to bear. Mother—hadn’t you better go into the back rooms? I’m not sure they may not have made their way from Pinner’s Lane into the stable-yard; but if not, you will be safer there than here. Go, Jane,” he added to the upper-servant.

Jane went, followed by the other women-servants, their skirts snatched up as if they ran through fire.

“I stop here,” said his mother. “Where you are, there I stay.”

And in truth, retreat seemed useless; the roar came now from behind as well as before. The crowd had swung around to the rear outbuildings and sent its threats into the house like a foul wind. The servants fled upward into garrets, crying and shrieking. Mr. Thornton smiled scornfully at the sound.

Then he looked at Margaret. She stood alone by the window nearest the mill; her eyes bright, her colour heightened, as if terror had poured a fierce life into her veins. Feeling his glance, she turned and asked what had been pressing in her mind from Fanny’s first words.

“Where are the poor imported workpeople? In the factory there?”

“Yes. I left them cowed up in a small room at the head of a back flight of stairs, bidding them run all risks and escape down there if they heard any attack made on the mill-doors. But it is not them—it is me they want.”

“When can the soldiers be here?” asked Mrs. Thornton, low-voiced but steady.

He took out his watch with the same composure he seemed to keep for everything. His thumb moved; his eyes calculated.

“Supposing Williams got straight off when I told him, and hadn’t to dodge about amongst them—it must be twenty minutes yet.”

“Twenty minutes!” Mrs. Thornton’s voice betrayed her for the first time.

“Shut down the windows instantly, mother,” he exclaimed. “The gates won’t bear such another shock. Shut down that window, Miss Hale.”

Margaret obeyed, then crossed to help Mrs. Thornton’s trembling hands. The blinds rattled faintly in their frames; the house seemed to vibrate with the waiting weight outside.

For a few minutes there was an odd pause, a listening lull. Mrs. Thornton stared at her son’s face as if she could read in it what the silence meant. But his features were set into rigid contempt. No hope and no fear showed—only resolve.

Fanny lifted her tear-streaked face.

“Are they gone?” she whispered.

“Gone!” he answered. “Listen.”

They listened. All of them heard it: the one great straining breath of the multitude; the slow creak of wood yielding; the wrench of iron; then, with a sound like something living being brought to its knees, the mighty fall of the ponderous gates.

Fanny staggered up, made two steps toward her mother, and dropped forward in a faint. Mrs. Thornton, by sheer will as much as by bodily strength, lifted her and carried her out.

“Thank God!” said Mr. Thornton, watching them go. “Had you not better go upstairs, Miss Hale?”

Margaret formed a “No” with her lips, but her voice was lost. The mob’s innumerable feet thudded under the very wall. The growl of their voices rose—low, deep, satisfied. Satisfaction, in such a sound, was more dreadful than baffled rage.

“Never mind,” he said, thinking to encourage her. “I am very sorry you should have been entrapped into all this alarm; but it cannot last long. A few minutes more, and the soldiers will be here.”

“Oh, God!” cried Margaret suddenly. “There is Boucher. I know his face, though he is livid with rage—he is fighting to get to the front—look! look!”

“Who is Boucher?” asked Mr. Thornton coolly, moving to the window to find the man she meant.

As soon as the crowd saw Mr. Thornton near the glass, they set up a yell—so fierce it sounded like an animal’s demoniac hunger for withheld prey. Even he drew back, one instant dismayed by the concentrated hatred.

“Let them yell,” he said. “In five minutes more—. I only hope my poor Irishmen are not terrified out of their wits by such a fiendlike noise. Keep up your courage for five minutes, Miss Hale.”

“Don’t be afraid for me,” she said quickly. “But what in five minutes? Can you do nothing to soothe these poor creatures? It is awful to see them.”

“The soldiers will be here directly, and that will bring them to reason.”

“To reason!” Margaret’s reply was swift, almost bitter. “What kind of reason?”

“The only reason that does with men that make themselves into wild beasts. By heaven! they’ve turned to the mill-door!”

“Mr. Thornton,” she said, shaking with passion, “go down this instant, if you are not a coward. Go down and face them like a man. Save these poor strangers, whom you have decoyed here. Speak to your workmen as if they were human beings. Speak to them kindly. Don’t let the soldiers come in and cut down poor creatures who are driven mad. I see one there who is. If you have any courage or noble quality in you, go out and speak to them—man to man!”

He turned and looked at her while she spoke. A dark cloud passed over his face. His jaw tightened.

“I will go,” he said at last. “Perhaps I may ask you to accompany me downstairs, and bar the door behind me; my mother and sister will need that protection.”

“Oh! Mr. Thornton! I do not know—I may be wrong—only—”

But he was gone.

Margaret followed, sick at heart and dizzy-headed, unbarred and then rebarred as he went out. She clambered up the stairs again and took her place at the farthest window. Through the shifting bodies and the blind’s slats she saw a thousand eyes converge. He stood below on the steps—she knew it by that collective direction, that sudden tightening of attention which made the crowd feel like one creature.

She flung the window wide. Many in the throng were mere boys, with the cruel thoughtlessness of youth. Some were men gaunt as wolves, made wild by hunger. She understood it—understood Boucher’s livid despair: starving children at home, the hope of higher wages, and then the rage of finding Irishmen brought to take the little bread their own children might have had.

If Mr. Thornton would only speak—if they could only hear a human voice from him instead of stony silence—it seemed it must help. For a moment there was a hush, inarticulate, animal-like, as if instinct told them to listen. Margaret tore off her bonnet and bent forward.

Whether he spoke or not, the instinct passed. The noise surged again—worse, wilder. Mr. Thornton stood with arms folded, statue-still; his face was pale with repressed excitement. They were trying to make him flinch, each urging the other toward some act of personal violence.

Margaret saw it like a flash: one touch, one blow, and everything would burst beyond control. In the back she saw boys stoop and pull off their heavy wooden clogs—the nearest weapons. She saw the gesture, the preparation, the spark poised over powder.

A cry tore from her throat, unheard. She ran.

Down the stairs, through the hall, her hands lifting the great iron bar with a force she did not know she possessed—she flung the door wide and stood before them, facing that angry sea. Her eyes struck them like reproach made visible.

The clogs halted mid-air. Faces, a moment ago so fell, turned uncertain, as if asking what this interruption meant. She was between them and their enemy.

She could not speak at first. She held out her arms, palms forward, until breath came.

“Oh, do not use violence! He is one man, and you are many—” Her words died into a hoarse whisper.

Mr. Thornton stood a little aside, as if jealous of anything that should come between him and danger.

“Go!” she tried again, and now her voice rose to a cry. “The soldiers are sent for—are coming. Go peaceably. Go away. You shall have relief from your complaints, whatever they are.”

“Shall them Irish blackguards be packed back again?” shouted a man with fierce menace.

“Never, for your bidding!” Mr. Thornton flung back.

In that instant the storm broke. Hooting filled the air; it seemed to shake the very bricks. Margaret did not hear it clearly. Her eyes were fixed on the boys whose hands had already armed themselves. She saw their aim settle. She knew where those clogs would fly.

Another second, and he might be struck down—he whom she had urged into danger. She thought of nothing but stopping it. She flung herself against him, put her arms around him, made her body a shield.

Still with his arms folded, he shook her off.

“Go away,” he said in his deep voice. “This is no place for you.”

“It is,” she answered. “You did not see what I saw.”

If she had hoped her sex might soften them—if she had imagined they would shrink from hurting a woman—she was wrong. Reckless passion had carried some too far; and it is often the savage boys, hungry for excitement, who lead a riot to blood.

A clog whizzed through the air. Margaret’s fascinated eyes tracked it; it missed. Nausea turned her cold, but she did not move. She hid her face against Mr. Thornton’s arm and spoke again, forcing her words out.

“For God’s sake! do not damage your cause by this violence. You do not know what you are doing.”

A sharp pebble flew—grazed her forehead and cheek. A blinding sheet of light seemed to burst before her eyes. She dropped, as if dead, against Mr. Thornton’s shoulder.

His arms unfolded at last; he held her for an instant—encircling her as if he could keep harm from her by the mere fact of contact.

“You do well!” he cried, his voice ringing out. “You come to oust the innocent stranger. You fall—you hundreds—on one man; and when a woman comes before you to ask you, for your own sakes, to be reasonable creatures, your cowardly wrath falls upon her! You do well!”

They fell silent while he spoke. What stilled them was not his scorn alone, but the thin dark-red blood that began to show, trickling down her temple and cheek. It was as though the sight woke them from trance. Those nearest the door edged away, ashamed. A movement ran through the crowd—backward, loosening.

Only one voice called out, trying to kindle their brutality again:

“Th’ stone was meant for thee; but thou wert sheltered behind a woman!”

Mr. Thornton quivered with rage.

Margaret’s consciousness returned dimly, as if she rose through deep water. He placed her gently on the door-step, her head against the frame.

“Can you rest there?” he asked.

Without waiting, he stepped down, slowly, into the midst of them.

“Now kill me, if it is your brutal will. There is no woman to shield me here. You may beat me to death—you will never move me from what I have determined upon—not you!”

He stood among them with arms folded, the same immovable posture as before.

But their retreat had begun, as blind and simultaneous as their rage had been. Perhaps the thought of soldiers coming helped; perhaps the pallor of her upturned face, her closed eyes so still, the tears caught in her lashes and spilling slowly; and beneath them, heavier than tears, the steady drip of blood. Even the most desperate—Boucher himself—drew back, scowled, faltered, and went off muttering curses.

Retreat shifted into flight, as such mobs do once they turn. The instant the tide broke, Mr. Thornton sprang back up to Margaret.

She tried to rise without his help.

“It is nothing,” she said, a sick little smile trembling on her lips. “The skin is grazed, and I was stunned at the moment. Oh, I am so thankful they are gone!” And then she cried, helplessly, as if tears were the only safe release left.

He could not share her relief. His anger had not cooled; if anything, it rose as danger passed. In the distance came the metallic clank and measured tread of soldiers—authority arriving five minutes too late to do more than remind the vanished crowd of how near they had been to consequence.

Margaret clung to the doorpost, unsteady. A film slid over her eyes. Mr. Thornton caught her as she swayed.

“Mother—mother!” he called. “Come down. They are gone, and Miss Hale is hurt!”

He carried Margaret into the dining-room and laid her on the sofa, carefully, as if she were a precious burden. When he looked upon her face—white now to the lips, purity made stark by blood—the knowledge of what she was to him struck so sharply that speech broke from him like a sob.

“Oh, my Margaret—my Margaret! no one can tell what you are to me! Dead—cold as you lie there, you are the only woman I ever loved! Oh, Margaret—Margaret!”

He started up, ashamed, as his mother entered. Mrs. Thornton saw nothing but her son, a little paler, a little sterner than usual.

“Miss Hale is hurt, mother. A stone has grazed her temple. She has lost a good deal of blood, I’m afraid.”

“She looks very seriously hurt—I could almost fancy her dead,” said Mrs. Thornton, genuinely alarmed.

“It is only a fainting-fit. She has spoken to me since.” Yet his body betrayed him; the blood seemed to rush inward to his heart. He trembled.

“Go and call Jane,” said Mrs. Thornton sharply. “She can find me the things I want. And you—go to your Irish people. I can hear them crying and shouting as if they were mad with fright.”

He went, but it was as if weights hung from every limb that carried him away from Margaret. He called Jane; he called for his sister. There would be womanly care, gentle attendance. Yet every pulse in him repeated the image of Margaret stepping out—placing herself in the very mouth of danger. Had she done it to save him? At the time he had pushed her away, gruff and blind, seeing only the risk she took. Now the thought burned.

He went to the Irish hands—crowded, frightened, some weeping, all clamouring that they would not stay, that they must be sent back. He tried to soothe them; tried to understand their broken phrases. But his mind skittered, returning again and again to her face.

Mrs. Thornton bathed Margaret’s temples with eau de Cologne. The sharp spirit touched the wound—one they had not at first perceived beneath the blood and hair—and Margaret’s eyes opened. Yet they were the eyes of one who wakes in a strange room from a fever: seeing, not knowing. Dark circles deepened beneath them; her lips quivered; then she slipped again into insensibility.

“She has had a terrible blow,” said Mrs. Thornton. “Is there anyone who will go for a doctor?”

“Not me, ma’am, if you please,” said Jane, shrinking back. “Them rabble may be all about; and I don’t think the cut is so deep, ma’am, as it looks.”

“I will not run the chance,” replied Mrs. Thornton. “She was hurt in our house. If you are a coward, Jane, I am not. I will go.”

“Pray, ma’am, let me send one of the police. There’s ever so many come up, and soldiers too.”

“And yet you’re afraid to go! I will not have their time taken up with our errands. They’ll have enough to do to catch some of the mob. You will not be afraid to stop in this house,” she added contemptuously, “and go on bathing Miss Hale’s forehead, shall you? I shall not be ten minutes away.”

“Couldn’t Hannah go, ma’am?”

“Why Hannah? Why any but you? No, Jane—if you don’t go, I do.”

Mrs. Thornton went first to the room where she had left Fanny, stretched upon the bed. Fanny started up at her entrance, wild-eyed with fear.

“Oh, mamma, how you terrified me! I thought you were a man that had got into the house.”

“Nonsense. The men are all gone away. There are soldiers all round the place, seeking for their work now it is too late. Miss Hale is lying on the dining-room sofa badly hurt. I am going for the doctor.”

“Oh! don’t, mamma—they’ll murder you.” Fanny clung to her mother’s gown. Mrs. Thornton wrenched it free with no gentle hand.

“Find me someone else to go; but that girl must not bleed to death.”

“Bleed! Oh, how horrid! How has she got hurt?”

“I don’t know. I have no time to ask. Go down to her, Fanny, and try to make yourself of use. Jane is with her; and I trust it looks worse than it is. Jane has refused to leave the house—cowardly woman! And I won’t put myself in the way of any more refusals from my servants, so I am going myself.”

“Oh, dear—dear,” cried Fanny, weeping; yet she prepared to go down rather than be left alone with thoughts of blood and violence in the very house.

She crept into the dining-room.

“Oh, Jane! what is the matter? How white she looks! How did she get hurt? Did they throw stones into the drawing-room?”

Margaret looked indeed white and wan, though her senses hovered near returning. The sick daze of the swoon made her miserably faint. She was aware of hands moving, of the keen reviving scent of eau de Cologne—a craving for it to go on without pause. But when it stopped for speech, she could no more open her eyes or ask for the soothing touch than those in death-like trance who hear the preparations for their burial and cannot stir to prevent them.

Jane paused in her bathing to answer.

“She’d have been safe enough, miss, if she’d stayed in the drawing-room, or come up to us. We were in the front garret and could see it all, out of harm’s way.”

“Where was she then?” Fanny asked, edging nearer by slow degrees, as she grew used to the pallor of Margaret’s face.

“Just before the front door—with master!” Jane replied, with meaning.

“With John! with my brother! How did she get there?”

“Nay, miss, that’s not for me to say,” said Jane, with a slight toss. “Sarah did—”

“Sarah what?” demanded Fanny, curiosity pricked sharp.

Jane resumed the bathing as if she would rather not speak what she knew.

“Sarah what?” Fanny insisted, impatient.

“Well, miss, since you will have it—Sarah was in the best place for seeing, being at the right-hand window; and she says, and said at the very time too, that she saw Miss Hale with her arms about master’s neck—hugging him—before all the people.”

Margaret had scarcely been gone five minutes when Mr. Thornton came in, his whole face lit as if he had been running against a wind that stung and brightened the blood. The dining-room smelt faintly of bruised lavender and the sharp, clean ghost of eau de Cologne, as if the air itself had been wiped and polished after violence.

“I could not come sooner: the superintendent would—” His words broke off. He looked round, first at the place where she had sat, then—almost with a kind of fierceness—at his mother, who was setting chairs straight again, turning a displaced table-napkin as if the room were a dish to be re-laid after an accident. “Where is she?”

Mrs. Thornton did not answer at once. She folded the napkin with measured exactness, as one might fold a cloth over cooling bread to keep it from taint.

“Where is Miss Hale?” he asked again.

“Gone home,” said she, curtly.

“Gone home!”

“Yes. She was a great deal better. Indeed, I don’t believe it was so very much of a hurt; only some people faint at the least thing.”

“I am sorry she has gone home,” he said, and began to pace—an uneasy, caged movement, as if the walls kept time with his strides. “She could not have been fit for it.”

“She said she was; and Mr. Lowe said she was. I went for him myself.”

“Thank you, mother.” He stopped and half held out his hand, the impulse frank and grateful; but she did not see it—or would not.

“What have you done with your Irish people?” he asked, taking refuge in what could be spoken without that name making his throat close.

“Sent to the Dragon, for a good meal for them, poor wretches. And then, luckily, I caught Father Grady, and I’ve asked him in to speak to them, and dissuade them from going off in a body.”

Even in that brief statement there was the whole sound of a town: the clatter of plates at an inn, the murmur of a priest’s brogue, the damp shuffle of hungry feet made suddenly docile by broth and bread. Beyond it, like a constant mill-wheel in the mind, the day’s din returned—iron gates groaning, stones striking, a thousand throats made hoarse by anger. He forced his attention back.

“How did Miss Hale go home? I’m sure she could not walk.”

“She had a cab. Everything was done properly, even to the paying. Let us talk of something else. She has caused disturbance enough.”

“I don’t know where I should have been but for her.”

“Are you become so helpless as to have to be defended by a girl?” Mrs. Thornton’s contempt fell clipped and cold.

He reddened, not from shame but from a sudden heat of remembered touch, the shock of her arms round his neck—soft, clinging, and yet strong with purpose. “Not many girls would have taken the blows on herself which were meant for me;—meant with right down goodwill, too.”

“A girl in love will do a good deal,” replied Mrs. Thornton, briefly, as if she had tasted something too sweet and would not own it pleased her.

“Mother!” He stepped forward, then held himself still. The effort to master what rose in him made his breath thicken. His eyes shone; his whole frame seemed enlarged by conflicting forces—pride, anger, glad astonishment, a trembling doubt he hated. She could not read it; she only felt the danger of strong feeling unshared.

She went to the side-board, pulled out a drawer, and took up a duster kept there for chance blemishes. A drop of cologne had freckled the polished arm of the sofa; she rubbed at it as if she could wipe away the day’s disorder with the same small, brisk motions. She kept her back to him longer than needful; and when she spoke, her voice had a constraint that did not belong to her.

“You have taken some steps about the rioters, I suppose? You don’t apprehend any more violence, do you? Where were the police? Never at hand when they’re wanted!”

“On the contrary,” he answered, forcing his mind into the hard grooves of business, “I saw three or four of them, when the gates gave way, struggling and beating about in fine fashion; and more came running up just when the yard was clearing. I might have given some of the fellows in charge then, if I had had my wits about me. But there will be no difficulty; plenty of people can identify them.”

“But won’t they come back to-night?”

“I’m going to see about a sufficient guard for the premises. I have appointed to meet Captain Hanbury in half an hour at the station.”

“You must have some tea first.”

“Tea! Yes, I suppose I must.” He glanced at the clock as if time were a debtor. “It’s half-past six, and I may be out for some time. Don’t sit up for me, mother.”

“You expect me to go to bed before I have seen you safe, do you?”

“Well, perhaps not.” He hesitated; and then, as if the word had been waiting behind his teeth, it came. “But if I’ve time, I shall go round by Crampton, after I’ve arranged with the police and seen Hamper and Clarkson.”

Their eyes met—held. In that pause the room seemed to sharpen: the tick of the clock, the faint crackle of the coal, the far-off roar of Milton’s looms like a sea that never ceased. It was the town’s ceaseless sound that had driven men to fury in the streets; it was the same sound that now pressed on a private room, insisting that no heart should be left quiet.

“Why are you going round by Crampton?” Mrs. Thornton asked at last.

“I want to ask after Miss Hale.”

“I will send. Williams must take the water-bed she came to ask for. He shall inquire how she is.”

“I must go myself.”

“Not merely to ask how Miss Hale is?”

“No, not merely for that. I want to thank her for the way in which she stood between me and the mob.”

“What made you go down at all? It was putting your head into the lion’s mouth!”

He looked keenly at her, and saw she did not know what had passed between him and Margaret earlier—whatever might have been spoken upstairs, here it had not been told. He answered her question with another, not cowardly, but urgent with the press of duty.

“Shall you be afraid to be left without me, until I can get some of the police; or had we better send Williams for them now, and they could be here by the time we have done tea? There’s no time to be lost. I must be off in a quarter of an hour.”

Mrs. Thornton left the room. The servants, accustomed to her decisions falling as clean and sure as a knife through pastry, were surprised by the indistinctness of her orders now—directing, retracting, directing again.

Mr. Thornton stayed in the dining-room, trying to think of his business at the police-office—and thinking, instead, of Margaret. The world beyond her seemed blurred: gates, mob, superintendent, Captain Hanbury, all dim; and only one thing cruelly clear—the feel of her arms, the sudden shelter and surrender of that clasp. The colour rose and fell in his cheek as if it obeyed her touch still.

Tea came. It should have been a comfort—hot liquid, bread, the small domestic rites that promise stability—but it tasted of interruption. The cups clinked too loudly in the hush between them, and the coal’s whisper seemed an echo of the mill’s breath. Fanny filled the silence with her own recital, repeated and ornamented, like a cook who cannot stop describing the heat of a kitchen fire she has escaped: how she had been alarmed—and then thought they were gone—and then felt sick and faint and trembling in every limb.

“There, that’s enough,” said her brother at last, rising. “The reality was enough for me.”

He moved to leave, but his mother laid her hand upon his arm—light, yet arresting him as surely as a bar across a door.

“You will come back here before you go to the Hales’,” she said in a low, anxious voice.

“I know what I know,” thought Fanny to herself, with a mean triumph.

“Why? Will it be too late to disturb them?”

“John, come back to me for this one evening. It will be late for Mrs. Hale. But that is not it. To-morrow, you will—” Her voice faltered on what she could not bear to name. “Come back to-night, John!”

She seldom pleaded; pride had made supplication an unfamiliar language on her lips. But she had never pleaded in vain.

“I will return straight here after I have done my business.” He paused, as if the words pulled at him like a cord. “You will be sure to enquire after them?—after her?”

Mrs. Thornton did not answer directly; but her eyes hardened into the look that meant she would do what she chose, and that would be enough.

While he was away, she was neither talkative to Fanny nor a good listener; the girl’s chatter fell like crumbs on a table no one intends to clear. Yet when John returned, her attention fastened—eager, exact—on every detail of locks, guards, and men to be set in place, as if the night were a joint to be trussed and tied so that no knife could slip.

He spoke plainly. Punishment and suffering, to him, were the natural consequence of riot. Property must be protected; order must cut clean, like a sharpened blade. In the way he described it there was the cold certainty of the master of a house who will not let thieves or vermin into his pantry.

Then, in a pause—when she had, at least, forgotten Margaret for a moment—he turned suddenly, driven back to what he had been holding in all day.

“Mother! You know what I have got to say to Miss Hale, to-morrow?”

The question struck her like a bell in the stillness. She looked up.

“Yes! I do. You can hardly do otherwise.”

“Do otherwise! I don’t understand you.”

“I mean that, after allowing her feelings so to overcome her, I consider you bound in honour—”

“Bound in honour!” His scorn was sharp. “I’m afraid honour has nothing to do with it. ‘Her feelings overcome her!’ What feelings do you mean?”

“Nay, John, there is no need to be angry. Did she not rush down and cling to you to save you from danger?”

“She did!” he said; and then he stopped short in front of her, as if the ground under him had changed. His voice altered—lower, shaken. “But, mother—” He could scarcely bring it out. “I dare not hope. I never was faint-hearted before; but I cannot believe such a creature cares for me.”

“Don’t be foolish, John. Such a creature! Why, she might be a duke’s daughter, to hear you speak. And what proof more would you have, I wonder, of her caring for you? I can believe she has had a struggle with her aristocratic way of viewing things; but I like her the better for seeing clearly at last.” She smiled slowly; tears stood in her eyes, the unaccustomed moisture of a pride that had been long dry. “It is a good deal for me to say,” she went on, the truth breaking through her stiffness, “for after to-night, I stand second. It was to have you to myself, all to myself, a few hours longer, that I begged you not to go till to-morrow.”

“Dearest mother!” he cried; and kissed her with real feeling. Yet love, even when true, can be selfish; almost at once he was pulled back to his own fear and desire, and the small, cold shadow of that neglect crept over her heart.

“But I know she does not care for me,” he said, with the obstinacy of a man who cannot bear hope because it makes him helpless. “I shall put myself at her feet—I must. If it were but one chance in a thousand—or a million—I should do it.”

“Don’t fear!” Mrs. Thornton said, crushing down the pang of jealousy that had revealed how fierce her maternal love had been, and how little it was noticed. Her voice grew colder as she mastered herself. “Don’t be afraid. As far as love may go she may be worthy of you. It must have taken a good deal to overcome her pride. Don’t be afraid, John.” She kissed him as she wished him good-night.

She went out slowly and with her usual majesty; but when she reached her own room she locked the door and sat down to cry tears she had not wept for years—quiet, unwitnessed, bitter as strong spirits taken alone.

* * * * *

Margaret entered the sitting-room where her father and mother still sat, speaking low together in the manner illness teaches—half whisper, half sigh. The room was dim with lamplight; it smelt of tea-leaves and the faint medicinal sweetness that clings to invalid rooms like a second curtain. Margaret looked very pale; she came close before she could trust her voice.

“Mrs. Thornton will send the water-bed, mamma.”

“My dear, how tired you look! Is it very hot, Margaret?”

“Very hot,” said Margaret, and the remembered heat of bodies pressed together in the street seemed to rise at the words, “and the streets are rather rough with the strike.”

A vivid colour sprang up in her cheeks as if the blood itself protested at the memory; then it ebbed away, leaving her face whiter than before.

“Here has been a message from Bessy Higgins, asking you to go to her,” said Mrs. Hale. “But I’m sure you look too tired.”

“Yes,” said Margaret. “I am tired, I cannot go.”

She made the tea with hands that trembled despite her will—measuring, pouring, setting down cups with a care that felt like acting. The familiar domestic sounds—the spoon against china, the soft rush of water—should have steadied her; instead, they seemed too thin to cover the day’s harsher music. She was thankful her father was so taken up with her mother—adjusting her shawl, speaking to her, watching her breath—as not to notice Margaret’s looks.

Even after Mrs. Hale went to bed, Mr. Hale was not content to leave her; he undertook to read her to sleep, his gentle voice and slow cadence like a lullaby meant to keep pain at bay. When at last he went, Margaret found herself alone.

“Now I will think of it—now I will remember it all,” she said aloud, as if speech could force order on what had happened. “I could not before—I dared not.”

She sat quite still, hands clasped on her knees, lips pressed, eyes fixed with the gaze of one who sees a thing that is not in the room. The air seemed to thicken with remembered sounds: the mill’s hoarse roar, the sudden shout when the gates gave way, the stones skittering, the fierce chorus of men’s voices swelling and breaking like waves. Underneath it all was the sharper noise inside her head—her own heart, beating too loudly.

She drew a deep breath.

“I, who hate scenes—I, who have despised people for showing emotion—who have thought them wanting in self-control—I went down and must needs throw myself into the mêlée, like a romantic fool! Did I do any good? They would have gone away without me, I dare say.”

Even as she said it, her steadier judgment rose and checked her. “No—perhaps they would not. I did some good. But what possessed me to defend that man as if he were a helpless child! Ah!” She clenched her hands. “It is no wonder those people thought I was in love with him, after disgracing myself in that way. I in love—and with him too!”

Her cheeks flamed; she covered her face. When she drew her hands away, her palms were wet with tears that felt scalding, as if shame itself had a heat.

“Oh, how low I am fallen that they should say that of me!” she whispered. “I could not have been so brave for any one else, just because he was so utterly indifferent to me—if, indeed, I do not positively dislike him.”

She forced herself on. If she let the thought drift, it would return to the wrong place—to his neck beneath her hands, to his astonished eyes, to the sensation that she had claimed him for an instant in front of all those watching faces.

“It made me the more anxious that there should be fair play on each side,” she said, more firmly, as if argument were a shield. “And I could see what fair play was. It was not fair,” she continued, vehement now, “that he should stand there—sheltered, awaiting the soldiers, who might catch those poor maddened creatures as in a trap—without an effort on his part, to bring them to reason. And it was worse than unfair for them to set on him as they threatened. I would do it again, let who will say what they like of me. If I saved one blow, one cruel, angry action that might otherwise have been committed, I did a woman’s work. Let them insult my maiden pride as they will—I walk pure before God!”

She looked up. The tightness in her face loosened; something like a noble calm descended, and for a moment she was very still—stiller than carved stone.

Dixon came in.

“If you please, Miss Margaret, here’s the water-bed from Mrs. Thornton’s. It’s too late for to-night, I’m afraid, for missus is nearly asleep; but it will do nicely for to-morrow.”

“Very,” said Margaret. “You must send our best thanks.”

Dixon went out and returned almost at once, her curiosity and duty both pulling her back.

“If you please, Miss Margaret, he says he’s to ask particular how you are. I think he must mean missus; but he says his last words were, to ask how Miss Hale was.”

“Me!” Margaret drew herself up, as if the very idea were an impertinence that demanded posture. “I am quite well. Tell him I am perfectly well.”

But as she spoke, her face went as white as the handkerchief in her hand, and a heavy pain began to pulse behind her eyes.

Mr. Hale came in then, leaving his sleeping wife because his own gentle restlessness needed companionship. Margaret saw at once that he wanted to be amused, to be drawn away from the sick-room’s hush. With patient sweetness—without one complaint—she bore the ache in her head and rummaged up small subjects for talk: bits of London memory, a book she had seen, a trivial incident in the street. She never once named the riot. The thought of it made her feel physically sick, as if the smoke and sweat and clamour had lodged in her throat.

At last he kissed her good-night.

“Good-night, Margaret. I have every chance of a good night myself, and you are looking very pale with your watching. I shall call Dixon if your mother needs anything. Do you go to bed and sleep like a top; for I’m sure you need it, poor child!”

“Good-night, papa!”

When he was gone, the false smile slipped away. Her eyes dulled with pain; the muscles of her face relaxed as if she had been holding up a weight. She gave up the hard work of seeming well.

She lay down and scarcely moved. To lift a hand, to turn a finger, seemed beyond either will or strength. She was so tired—so stunned—that she thought she never slept at all. Her feverish thoughts slid back and forth across the boundary between waking and sleeping, keeping their miserable sameness. She could not be alone. A cloud of faces looked up at her—faces without distinct anger or personal menace now, but full of attention; and in that attention she felt again the day’s worst wound.

Not fear—shame.

An unwinking glare of many eyes seemed to hold her pinned, as if she were displayed, named, judged in a language she could not answer. The sound of their shouting haunted her—words turned into noise, meaning swallowed by the town’s roar—until she longed, with an aching intensity, to burrow into the earth and hide; and yet she could not escape the gaze that followed her even into the dark.

The morning came on with a dull, white heat, as if the night had merely cooled itself to begin again. Margaret lifted herself from sleep with a kind of gratitude that it was ended, though her limbs felt as if the hours had been spent in watching rather than resting. In the next room her mother had stirred only once; the house had gone on in that careful hush which makes every small sound—cloth laid down, a door eased to its latch—seem louder for being meant to be quiet.

A little breeze, rare in Milton’s sultry streets, crept through the half-open sash. There were no boughs at their window to show it, no leaves to clap and answer, no orchard branches to make that soft, green applause she had grown up with. Yet she knew—she could not help knowing—that somewhere beyond the brick and cinder, by a hedge or in a copse, there would be the old country music: a rustle like skirts over grass, a murmuring as of bees in clover, a light rushing and falling—sounds that had once been part of the day’s bread, baked into it like the taste of wheat. The thought of that lost sound came back with an almost bodily comfort, an echo of gladness in a heart that had been strained too hard.

She sat in her mother’s room by the shaded window, her needle moving through linen with the patient precision of habit. The work had the plain, domestic steadiness of it: draw the thread, set the seam, smooth it with the thumb; and with each small action she laid a kind of order upon herself. When her mother’s forenoon slumber should be over, she would help her to dress; after dinner she would go to see Bessy Higgins and take what she could—words, company, perhaps some little food that Bessy might fancy. She told herself, sharply, that she would banish all recollection of the Thorntons. There was no need to think of them until they stood before her in flesh and blood.

But the mind, like a kitchen fire that has been damped, smoulders on under the ash; the very effort not to feed it gives it air. From time to time the hot flush swept over her pallor, sudden as a sunbeam breaking through watered cloud and running across the sea. She bent closer to her stitching, as if fine thread could bind in unruly thought.

Dixon opened the door with a softness that was almost a rebuke to sound. She came in on tiptoe, as though the house were a sick-room from threshold to hearth.

“Mr. Thornton, Miss Margaret. He is in the drawing-room.”

Margaret’s hand stopped; the needle paused bright above the linen.

“Did he ask for me? Isn’t papa come in?”

“He asked for you, miss; and master is out.”

“Very well. I will come,” said Margaret, and made her voice quiet as she could.

Yet she lingered—strangely, involuntarily—as if her feet had forgotten their obedience. She drew one breath, then another, and with the second she went.

In the drawing-room Mr. Thornton stood by one of the windows, his back to the door, looking down into the street as though he watched some common passage of carts and men. In truth he was afraid of himself. The very stillness of the room, with its faint smell of the night’s closed air and yesterday’s extinguished fire, seemed to hold his heart-beat and throw it back at him. He could not forget the touch of her arms about his neck—the quick, impatient clasp that had been so unconsidered at the time and was now unbearable in remembrance. It had changed its nature in his mind, as wine turns in the cask; what was merely an act became a sign.
