Her clinging defence of him thrilled through him, melting every resolution, every proud self-command, as if his will were wax held to a flame.

He dreaded—yes, dreaded—that when she entered he should go forward without thought, arms opened in mute entreaty, asking her again to come and rest where she had rested yesterday, unheeded then, never unheeded again. His heart throbbed thick; his breath came short with the strain of what he had to say and of how it might be received. In one moment he saw her droop and flush and flutter into his arms as if to her natural home; in the next, he saw the passionate rejection that would wither up all future, and he refused to look fully at that image, as a man will not look over a cliff.

He was startled by the sense that he was no longer alone. He turned.

She had entered so gently that he had not heard her at all; the street noises—far wheels, a distant cry, the faint clang from some yard—had been more distinct to his inattentive ear than her slow movement in her soft muslin gown. She stood by the table and did not sit. Her eyelids were dropped half over her eyes; her lips were parted a little, showing the white line of her teeth. She breathed slowly and deeply; it was the only motion on her face. The fine-grained skin and oval cheek were wan to-day, the want of colour made more evident by the heavy shadow of her dark hair drawn down over her temples to conceal the mark of yesterday’s blow. Her head, for all its drooping eyes, was thrown a little back in the old proud attitude; her long arms hung motionless at her sides.

She looked like a prisoner falsely accused of a crime she loathed, too indignant to justify herself.

Mr. Thornton made two hasty steps forward, checked himself, and went instead to the door she had left open. He shut it with quiet firmness—as if sound itself must be kept from waking Mrs. Hale. Then he came back and stood opposite her, taking in, in one long moment, the impression of her beautiful presence before he dared to disturb it, perhaps to repel it, by what he had to say.

“Miss Hale,” he began, “I was very ungrateful yesterday—”

“You had nothing to be grateful for,” she answered, raising her eyes and looking full and straight at him. “You mean, I suppose, that you believe you ought to thank me for what I did.”

In spite of herself, in defiance of anger, thick blushes came over her face, burning up into her very eyes; yet her look did not fall.

“It was only a natural instinct. Any woman would have done just the same. We all feel the sanctity of our sex as a high privilege when we see danger. I ought rather”—she spoke hastily, as if to get the words out and have done—“to apologise to you, for having said thoughtless words which sent you down into the danger.”

“It was not your words; it was the truth they conveyed, pungently as it was expressed. But you shall not drive me off upon that, and so escape the expression of my deep gratitude, my—”

He checked himself as if he had been running downhill too fast. He would not speak in the rush of hot passion; he would weigh each word. He would—and his will, for an instant, was triumphant.

“I do not try to escape from anything,” she said. “I simply say that you owe me no gratitude; and I may add that any expression of it will be painful to me, because I do not feel that I deserve it. Still, if it will relieve you from even a fancied obligation, speak on.”

“I do not want to be relieved from any obligation,” he replied, goaded by her calmness. “Fancied or not fancied—I question not myself to know which—I choose to believe I owe my very life to you. Ay—smile, and think it an exaggeration if you will. I believe it, because it adds a value to that life to think—oh, Miss Hale!”

His voice sank, and with it came that tender intensity which is more commanding than loudness. She shivered before it, as if the air had changed.

“To think circumstances so wrought that whenever I exult in existence henceforward, I may say to myself, ‘All this gladness in life, all honest pride in doing my work in the world, all this keen sense of being, I owe to her!’ And it doubles the gladness, it makes the pride glow, it sharpens the sense of existence till I hardly know if it is pain or pleasure to think that I owe it to one—nay, you must, you shall hear—” He stepped forward with stern determination. “To one whom I love, as I do not believe man ever loved woman before.”

He had taken her hand; his grasp closed on it hard, as if he held not merely fingers but fate. He panted, listening for what should come.

When her answer came, his indignation flung her hand away as if it burned him. Her tone was icy—icy, though the words faltered, as if she scarcely knew where to find them.

“Your way of speaking shocks me. It is blasphemous. I cannot help it if that is my first feeling. It might not be so, I dare say, if I understood the kind of feeling you describe. I do not want to vex you; and besides, we must speak gently, for mamma is asleep; but your whole manner offends me—”

“How!” he cried. “Offends you! I am indeed most unfortunate.”

“Yes!” She drew herself up; dignity came back like a clasp fastened. “I do feel offended; and I think justly. You seem to fancy that my conduct of yesterday”—again the deep carnation rushed up, but now with eyes kindling more with indignation than with shame—“was a personal act between you and me; and that you may come and thank me for it, instead of perceiving, as a gentleman would—yes! a gentleman,” she repeated, with a keen remembrance of former talk on that very word, “that any woman, worthy of the name of woman, would come forward to shield, with her reverenced helplessness, a man in danger from the violence of numbers.”

“And the gentleman thus rescued is forbidden the relief of thanks!” he broke in, contempt sharp on his tongue. “I am a man. I claim the right of expressing my feelings.”

“And I yielded to the right,” she replied, proudly. “Simply saying that you gave me pain by insisting upon it.”

“But you seem to have imagined,” she went on, and here the long-held tears surged up in spite of struggle, choking her voice, “that I was not merely guided by womanly instinct, but—that I was prompted by some particular feeling for you—you! Why, there was not a man—not a poor desperate man in all that crowd—for whom I had not more sympathy—for whom I should not have done what little I could more heartily.”

“You may speak on, Miss Hale. I am aware of these misplaced sympathies of yours. I now believe it was only your innate sense of oppression—(yes; I, though a master, may be oppressed)—that made you act so nobly as you did. I know you despise me; allow me to say it is because you do not understand me.”

“I do not care to understand,” she said, and caught the edge of the table, for she thought him cruel—and she was weak with indignation.

“No, I see you do not. You are unfair and unjust.”

Margaret compressed her lips. She would not give him the satisfaction of an answer to such accusation. She stood very still, and in that stillness her wounded pride broke its bounds; tears fell, hot and fast, like scalding drops that one cannot help but feel.

For all his savage words, for all the bitterness he had flung out like iron filings, he could have cast himself at her feet and kissed the hem of her gown. He waited, craving her speech—any speech, even a taunt he might answer. But she was silent.

At last he took up his hat. He held it a moment, smoothing the nap with his coat-sleeve as if to occupy his hands, to keep them from betraying him.

“One word more. You look as if you thought it tainted you to be loved by me. You cannot avoid it. Nay, I, if I would, cannot cleanse you from it. But I would not if I could. I have never loved any woman before. My life has been too busy; my thoughts too much absorbed with other things. Now I love, and will love. But do not be afraid of too much expression on my part.”

“I am not afraid,” she answered, lifting herself straight up, as if to show she would not be bent by fear. “No one yet has ever dared to be impertinent to me, and no one ever shall. But, Mr. Thornton”—and here she changed her whole tone and bearing to a womanly softness, thinking of her father, of kindness received and owed—“you have been very kind to my father. Don’t let us go on making each other angry. Pray don’t!”

He took no notice. He looked down, busy with the hat as though it were of vast importance; and when she held out her hand, grave with regret, he rejected it as if he did not see. He turned abruptly and left the room.

She caught one glance of his face as he went. She thought—only for an instant, as a swallow flashes by—that she saw the gleam of washed tears in his eyes. And that sight changed her proud dislike into something different and kinder, though it was nearly as painful: self-reproach, sharp as salt on a cut, for having caused such mortification to any one.

“But how could I help it?” she asked herself, alone with the hush again, the house’s careful silence settling down as if nothing had happened. “I never liked him. I was civil; but I took no trouble to conceal my indifference. Indeed, I never thought about myself or him, so my manners must have shown the truth. All that yesterday, he might mistake. But that is his fault, not mine. I would do it again, if need were, though it does lead me into all this shame and trouble.”

Margaret began to suspect that offers, in whatever house they were made, had a cruel likeness: they came unbidden, struck like a sudden draught through a door flung wide, and left the air altered long after the speaker had gone. She tried, as women do when the mind is bruised, to arrange her feelings as one might set in order a cupboard after some careless hand has overturned it—putting back what belonged together, wiping away what had spilled, finding solace in the familiar labour of naming and placing. Yet the comparison she made—between Henry Lennox and John Thornton—refused to lie neatly.

With Mr. Lennox, it had been as if a friend had stepped, by accident and for a moment, across a chalk-line neither of them had meant to cross; regret had come quickly on the trespass, and she could pity him even while she shrank. With Mr. Thornton there had been no such gentle prelude. Their acquaintance had been all collision—argument upon argument, her words flung back from him as from a rock face; and what troubled her now was not merely that he had spoken of love, but that he had done so as if love were another form of mastery. He had not seemed to care for her opinions because they were hers; only because they resisted him. And then, in that strange, wild way—passion bare as a blade—he had told her that he loved her, had loved her, would love her still.

It had crossed her mind at first—like the first sourness that rises when milk is near turning—that his offer might have been goaded out of him by what she had done the day before; that he, like others, might misread a woman’s act of mercy and courage into some foolish confession. But even before he left the room, and certainly within five minutes of his leaving, conviction rose clear and hard: he did love her. Not a fancy, not a whim, not any gentle-growing attachment that might be turned aside by prudence; it was fixed, deliberate, enduring. And Margaret shrank as if a great hand had come down upon her life—strong, alien, and repugnant to all she had been taught to call peace.

She tried to hide from the thought of him, but it followed, importunate as a scent that clings to clothes after fire: you may step out into fresh air, yet the smoke is in your hair, in the folds at the throat, in the cuffs. His voice seemed still to hang in the chamber, and, worse, the remembrance of his eyes—deep, intent, passionate—made hers fall again within her mind, as they had fallen before him.

How dared he say he would love her still, even if she shook him off with contempt? How dared he threaten her with constancy—as if her refusal were a small thing, a surface thing, that could not alter the rock beneath? Sharp speeches came to her now—keen, decisive, such as would have struck and ended the matter—only they came too late, when there was no ear to receive them. The impression of the interview lay upon her like a horror in a dream that remains after waking: you rub your eyes, you force a stiff smile, you busy your hands—yet in some corner of the room the thing crouches, listening, and you dare not name it aloud.

She rose at last from where she had stood as if rooted. She went to the window and flung it open. The air outside was hot, thick with the town’s summer heaviness; yet it relieved her like water dashed upon a burning skin. The house was hushed in the noonday stillness kept for an invalid’s stolen sleep—no cheerful clatter, no bright domestic sounds, only that strained quiet which makes a footstep seem an intrusion. Margaret opened the door with an impulse as sudden as her need: she would not be alone.

Then came, like the click of a latch within her mind, the remembrance of the message sent the night before. Bessy Higgins. Of course. The thought gave her something plain to do, and she took her bonnet and went quickly.

Bessy lay on the settle drawn close to the fire, though the day outside was sultry and the air in the room already close. The hearth had that faint, stale smell of yesterday’s coal—dusty, iron-edged—mixed with the more human odours of sickness: camphor, damp linen, and the sour-sweet taint of breath that has laboured too long. The poor girl was stretched flat, as if the least lift of her chest were an effort, her face turned a little away, her eyelids heavy.

Margaret, taking in at once how the posture cramped her breathing, did not waste words. She slid her arm behind Bessy’s shoulders and raised her gently, arranging the pillows with the quiet practised care of a woman who has nursed: one pillow under the shoulder-blades so the lungs might open; another to keep the head from falling back; the thin quilt drawn so it warmed without pressing. It was homely work—like trussing a fowl so it roasts evenly, or setting a dough to rise where the air is kindest—small adjustments that decide whether there will be ease or pain.

“I thought I should na’ ha’ seen yo’ again,” Bessy said at last, turning her large wistful gaze on Margaret’s face.

“I’m afraid you’re much worse,” Margaret answered softly. “But I could not come yesterday—my mother was so ill—for many reasons.” She coloured as she spoke, the blood rising with the memory she would not taste again.

Bessy watched her, and the corner of her mouth twitched, not unkindly. “Yo’d m’appen think I went beyond my place in sending Mary for yo’. But th’ wraglin’ and th’ loud voices had just torn me to pieces, and I thought when father left—oh! if I could just hear her voice, reading me some words o’ peace and promise, I could die away into th’ silence and rest o’ God, just as a baby’s hushed up to sleep by its mother’s lullaby.”

The room, for all its poverty, held its own acoustics—thin walls, a boarded floor that answered every shift of weight, the small tick of a clock that seemed loud in the pauses. Outside, far off, lay Milton’s ceaseless roar—mills, carts, iron on stone—like the sea heard from a sick-bed. Here, within, every sound was intimate: Margaret’s breath, the faint crackle of the fire, the rasp of Bessy’s lungs. Margaret felt, with a sudden tenderness, how much this girl craved not only words, but the very hush and cadence of a human voice laid upon the din.

“Shall I read you a chapter now?” she asked.

“Ay, do,” said Bessy. “M’appen I shan’t listen to th’ sense at first; it’ll seem far away. But when yo’ come to words I like—to th’ comforting texts—it’ll seem close in my ear, and go through me, as it were.”

Margaret opened the Bible, and began. Her voice was low and even, like water poured from a steady hand. Yet Bessy tossed to and fro. Each moment of attention seemed to wrench her into double restlessness after; her fingers plucked at the edge of the quilt as if it were a thread she could pull to unpick her pain.

At last she broke out, the words coming harsh and breathy. “Don’t go on reading. It’s no use. I’m blaspheming all th’ time in my mind, wi’ thinking angrily on what canna be helped.—Yo’d hear of th’ riot, m’appen, yesterday at Marlborough Mills? Thornton’s factory, yo’ know.”

Margaret’s heart gave a hard beat. “Your father was not there, was he?” she asked, and felt the heat leap into her cheeks.

“Not he. He’d ha’ given his right hand if it had never come to pass. It’s that that’s fretting me. He’s fairly knocked down in his mind by it. It’s no use telling him, fools will always break out o’ bounds. Yo’ never saw a man so downhearted as he is.”

“But why?” Margaret said. “I don’t understand.”

Bessy spoke with pauses, as if each sentence cost breath. “Why, yo’ see, he’s a committee-man on this special strike. Th’ Union appointed him because—though I say it as shouldn’t say it—he’s reckoned a deep chap, and true to th’ back-bone. And he and t’other committee-men laid their plans. They were to hou’d together through thick and thin; what th’ major part thought, t’others were to think, whether they would or no. And above all there was to be no going again th’ law of th’ land.

“Folk would go with ’em if they saw ’em striving and starving wi’ dumb patience; but if there was once any noise o’ fighting and struggling—even wi’ knobsticks—all was up, as they know by th’ experience of many and many a time before. They would try and get speech o’ th’ knobsticks, and coax ’em, and reason wi’ ’em, and m’appen warn ’em off; but whatever came, th’ Committee charged all members o’ th’ Union to lie down and die, if need were, without striking a blow; and then they reckoned they were sure o’ carrying th’ public with ’em.

“And besides all that, Committee knew they were right in their demand, and they didn’t want to have right all mixed up wi’ wrong, till folk can’t separate it—no more nor I can th’ physic-powder from th’ jelly yo’ gave me to mix it in; jelly’s much th’ biggest, but powder tastes it all through.”

Even in her weakness, Bessy’s mind flew to the mouth—to taste as truth. Margaret remembered the jelly—sweet, trembling, made to carry bitterness without protest—and felt how apt the image was. Wrong, once stirred in, flavoured the whole.

Bessy’s voice thinned. “Well, I’ve told yo’ at length about this’n, but I am tired out. Yo’ just think for yoursel’ what it mun be for father to have a’ his work undone, and by such a fool as Boucher, who must needs go right again th’ orders o’ Committee, and ruin th’ strike, just as bad as if he meant to be a Judas. Eh! but father giv’d it him last night! He went so far as to say he’d go and tell police where they might find th’ ringleader o’ th’ riot; he’d give him up to th’ mill-owners to do what they would wi’ him. He’d show th’ world that th’ real leaders o’ th’ strike were not such as Boucher, but steady thoughtful men; good hands, and good citizens, friendly to law and judgment, who’d uphold order; who only wanted their right wage, and wouldn’t work, even though they starved, till they got ’em; but who would ne’er injure property or life. For—” she dropped her voice, as if the very walls might carry scandal—“they do say, that Boucher threw a stone at Thornton’s sister, that welly killed her.”

“That’s not true,” Margaret said quickly. The words were out before she could school them, as if her tongue had leapt to defend what she had seen. “It was not Boucher that threw the stone.” Her face went first red, then white.

“Yo’d be there then, were yo’?” Bessy asked languidly, too worn for surprise.

“Yes. Never mind.” Margaret forced herself quieter. “Go on. Only—it was not Boucher.”

Bessy’s eyes closed again. “He did na’ speak words. He were all in such a tremble wi’ spent passion, I could na’ bear to look at him. I heard his breath coming quick, and at one time I thought he were sobbing. But when father said he’d give him up to police, he gave a great cry, and struck father on th’ face wi’ his closed fist, and he off like lightning.

“Father were stunned wi’ th’ blow at first—for all Boucher were weak wi’ passion and wi’ clemming. He sat down a bit, and put his hand afore his eyes; and then made for th’ door. I dunno where I got strength, but I threw mysel’ o’er th’ settle and clung to him. ‘Father, father!’ said I. ‘Thou’ll never go peach on that poor clemmed man. I’ll never leave go on thee, till thou sayst thou wunnot.’

“‘Dunnot be a fool,’ says he. ‘Words come readier than deeds to most men. I never thought o’ telling th’ police on him; though by G—he deserves it, and I should na’ ha’ minded if some one else had done th’ dirty work, and got him clapped up. But now he has strucken me, I could do it less nor ever, for it would be getting other men to take up my quarrel. But if ever he gets well o’er this clemming, and is in good condition, he and I’ll have an up and down fight, purring an’ a’, and I’ll see what I can do for him.’”

Bessy’s breath came short with the telling; the words were like hard crusts she had to chew and swallow. “And so father shook me off—for indeed I was low and faint enough—and his face were all clay-white where it weren’t bloody, and turned me sick to look at. And I know not if I slept or waked, or were in a dead swoon, till Mary come in; and I telled her to fetch yo’ to me.

“And now dunnot talk to me, but just read out th’ chapter. I’m easier in my mind for having spit it out; but I want some thoughts o’ th’ world that’s far away to take th’ weary taste of it out o’ my mouth. Read me not a sermon chapter, but a story chapter; they’ve pictures in ’em, which I see when my eyes are shut. Read about th’ New Heavens, and th’ New Earth; and m’appen I’ll forget this.”

Margaret read again, softly. The familiar cadences fell into the small room like a hand laid upon a fevered brow. Though Bessy’s eyes stayed shut, she listened for a while; tears gathered on her lashes and stood there, heavy as dew. At last sleep took her—broken, startled, with muttered pleadings that rose and fell like a frightened child’s talk in dreams. Margaret drew the covering up, tucking it round the thin shoulders, and sat a moment longer, her own mind too full for prayer.

When she rose to go, she felt the pull of two duties—the dying girl and the sick mother at home—like a cord tightened at both ends. The streets outside brought their own assault: the clank and rumble, the shrill cries, the harsh beat of labour. The very air seemed to ring. She hurried back, craving the comparative quiet of her own rooms.

Mrs. Hale was in the drawing-room when Margaret returned. It was one of her better days, and her voice had that weak brightness which illness sometimes borrows from temporary ease. She praised the water-bed warmly; it had been more like the beds at Sir John Beresford’s than anything she had slept on since they left the south. There was, she declared, a lost art in bed-making. Feathers might still be had, certainly; yet somehow beds were not what they had been in her youth.

Mr. Hale suggested gently that something of the merit of former beds might be due to the activity of youth, which gives a relish to rest. Mrs. Hale received this with the affronted air of a woman whose suffering is being explained away.

“No indeed, Mr. Hale, it was those beds at Sir John’s. Now, Margaret, you’re young enough, and go about i’ th’ day; are the beds comfortable? I appeal to you. Do they give you a feeling of perfect repose when you lie down upon them; or rather, don’t you toss about, and try in vain to find an easy position, and wake in the morning as tired as when you went to bed?”

Margaret laughed in spite of herself. “To tell the truth, mamma, I’ve never thought about my bed at all, what kind it is. I’m so sleepy at night that if I only lie down anywhere, I fall off directly. So I don’t think I’m a competent witness. Besides—you know I never had the opportunity of trying Sir John Beresford’s beds. I never was at Oxenham.”

“Were you not? Oh, no—to be sure.” Mrs. Hale’s face softened, and her voice took on the colour of remembrance. “It was poor darling Fred I took with me, I remember. I only went to Oxenham once after I was married—to your Aunt Shaw’s wedding; and poor little Fred was the baby then. And I know Dixon did not like changing from lady’s maid to nurse, and I was afraid that if I took her near her old home, and amongst her own people, she might want to leave me. But poor baby was taken ill at Oxenham, with his teething; and, what with my being a great deal with Anna just before her marriage, and not being very strong myself, Dixon had more of the charge of him than she ever had before; and it made her so fond of him—and she was so proud when he would turn away from every one and cling to her—that I don’t believe she ever thought of leaving me again; though it was very different from what she’d been accustomed to.

“Poor Fred! Everybody loved him. He was born with the gift of winning hearts. It makes me think very badly of Captain Reid when I know that he disliked my own dear boy. I think it a certain proof he had a bad heart. Ah! Your poor father, Margaret. He has left the room. He can’t bear to hear Fred spoken of.”

“I love to hear about him, mamma,” Margaret said, and the words were true; they were like bread in a house grown hungry. “Tell me all you like; you never can tell me too much. Tell me what he was like as a baby.”

Mrs. Hale smiled through the beginning of tears. “Why, Margaret, you must not be hurt, but he was much prettier than you were. I remember, when I first saw you in Dixon’s arms, I said, ‘Dear, what an ugly little thing!’ And she said, ‘It’s not every child that’s like Master Fred, bless him!’ Dear! how well I remember it. Then I could have had Fred in my arms every minute of the day, and his cot was close by my bed; and now—now, Margaret—I don’t know where my boy is, and sometimes I think I shall never see him again.”

Margaret sat on a low stool by the sofa, took her mother’s hand, and kissed it, stroking it as one might soothe a child. Mrs. Hale wept openly, without shame. The room held the sound of it—soft, persistent—until at last she drew herself upright, stiff with effort, and turned on Margaret with tearful solemnity.

“Margaret, if I can get better—if God lets me have a chance of recovery—it must be through seeing my son Frederick once more. It will waken up all the poor springs of health left in me.”

She paused, gathering breath, as if what remained were a step into a place she feared.

“And, Margaret, if I am to die—if I am one of those appointed to die before many weeks are over—I must see my child first. I cannot think how it must be managed; but I charge you, Margaret, as you yourself hope for comfort in your last illness, bring him to me that I may bless him. Only for five minutes, Margaret. There could be no danger in five minutes. Oh, Margaret, let me see him before I die!”

Margaret did not weigh the reasonableness; reason has no dominion over the pleadings of the dying. Memory stung her with all the neglected chances of kindness that can never be redeemed. And here the wish was so natural—so just—that it seemed to her almost a sin to hesitate. Frederick’s face, as she remembered it in childhood—sun-browned, laughing—rose like a picture in a long-closed book; it hurt to think of him wandering far away, cut off by law and shame and fear, while his mother’s life ebbed daily in this smoke-dark town.

She rose and stood opposite her mother, striving to let steadiness show in her face, so that the sick woman might drink confidence from it.

“Mamma, I will write to-night, and tell Frederick what you say. I am as sure that he will come directly to us as I am sure of my life. Be easy, mamma; you shall see him—as far as anything earthly can be promised.”

“You will write to-night?” Mrs. Hale’s eagerness quickened, fever-bright. “Oh, Margaret! the post goes out at five—you will write by it, won’t you? I have so few hours left—I feel, dear, as if I should not recover, though sometimes your father over-persuades me into hoping; you will write directly, won’t you? Don’t lose a single post; for just by that very post I may miss him.”

“But, mamma—papa is out.”

“Papa is out! and what then?” Mrs. Hale cried, and the injustice born of suffering flashed out. “Do you mean that he would deny me this last wish, Margaret? Why, I should not be ill—be dying—if he had not taken me away from Helstone, to this unhealthy, smoky, sunless place.”

“Oh, mamma!” Margaret said, wounded, yet patient.

“Yes; it is so indeed. He knows it himself; he has said so many a time. He would do anything for me; you don’t mean he would refuse me this last wish—prayer, if you will. And indeed, Margaret, the longing to see Frederick stands between me and God. I cannot pray till I have this one thing; indeed I cannot. Don’t lose time, dear, dear Margaret. Write by this very next post. Then he may be here—here in twenty-two days! For he is sure to come. No cords or chains can keep him. In twenty-two days I shall see my boy.”

She fell back, exhausted, and for a little while took no heed of Margaret sitting motionless, her hand shading her eyes.

“You are not writing!” Mrs. Hale said at last, the impatience of fear rising again. “Bring me some pens and paper; I will try and write myself.” She struggled upright, trembling with the effort.

Margaret took her hand down and looked at her mother, sad with the knowledge of how little time there might be for consent or planning. “Only wait till papa comes in. Let us ask him how best to do it.”

“You promised, Margaret—not a quarter of an hour ago—you said he should come.”

“And so he shall, mamma,” Margaret answered, voice breaking. “Don’t cry, my own dear mother. I’ll write here—now—you shall see me write—and it shall go by this very post; and if papa thinks fit he can write again when he comes in. It is only a day’s delay. Oh, mamma, don’t cry so pitifully—it cuts me to the heart.”

But Mrs. Hale did not check herself. Her tears came hysterically, and she made no effort to restrain them; rather she fed them with pictures—the happy past, and a future where she lay dead and Frederick bent over her too late, she unconscious of the sight for which she had starved her prayers. The sobbing wore her down into a spent calm at last. Then, with greedy eyes, she watched Margaret set paper on a small table, dip the pen, and begin.

Margaret wrote swiftly, the sentences urgent with entreaty. She told Frederick of their mother’s state, of her passionate longing, of the one hope she clung to. She sealed the letter quickly, for fear her mother should ask to see it and find, in Margaret’s words, either too much alarm or too much command. And then, to make the security sure, she took it herself to the post-office, as Mrs. Hale bade her—walking fast, as if speed could shorten distance and bring a ship across the ocean.

She was on her way home when her father overtook her in the street.

“And where have you been, my pretty maid?” he asked, trying for lightness.

“To the post-office—with a letter. A letter to Frederick.” The confession came out with the suddenness of truth that has been held back too long. “Oh, papa, perhaps I have done wrong; but mamma was seized with such a passionate yearning to see him—she said it would make her well again—and then she said she must see him before she died—I cannot tell you how urgent she was. Did I do wrong?”

Mr. Hale did not answer at once. The noise of Milton—its grinding wheels and iron cries—seemed to press upon the silence between them, as if the town itself listened. At length he said, quietly, “You should have waited till I came in, Margaret.”

“I tried to persuade her—” Margaret began, and then stopped; the rest was in her face.

“I don’t know,” Mr. Hale said after a pause. “She ought to see him, if she wishes it so much; for I believe it would do her much more good than all the doctor’s medicine—and perhaps set her up altogether. But the danger to him, I’m afraid, is very great.”

“All these years since the mutiny, papa?”

“Yes.” Mr. Hale’s voice had a grave steadiness, the tone of one reciting what he hates to remember. “It is necessary, of course, for government to take very stringent measures for the repression of offences against authority—more particularly in the navy, where a commanding officer needs to be surrounded, in his men’s eyes, with a vivid consciousness of all the power there is at home to back him, and take up his cause, and avenge any injuries offered to him, if need be. Ah! it’s no matter to them how far their authorities have tyrannised—galled hasty tempers to madness—or if that can be any excuse afterwards; it is never allowed for in the first instance. They spare no expense; they send out ships; they scour the seas to lay hold of the offenders. The lapse of years does not wash out the memory of the offence; it is a fresh and vivid crime on the Admiralty books till it is blotted out by blood.”

Margaret shivered as if the words had opened a cold door. Blotted out by blood. She saw—too vividly—her brother drawn home by their mother’s cry, only to be seized, to be made an example. The thought turned her sick with remorse, as if she had seasoned a family meal with poison by mistake.

“Oh, papa,” she whispered. “What have I done! And yet—it seemed so right at the time. I’m sure Frederick himself would run the risk.”

“So he would; so he should!” Mr. Hale’s voice softened, and his eyes filled with that mingling of fear and tenderness which belongs to fathers. “Nay, Margaret—I’m glad it is done, though I durst not have done it myself. I’m thankful it is as it is; I should have hesitated till, perhaps, it might have been too late to do any good. Dear Margaret, you have done what is right about it; and the end is beyond our control.”

It was comfort, and yet it was not. She heard, beneath his encouragement, the deeper current of his anxiety. She slipped her hand through his arm, and they walked home together—slowly now, as if each step carried a weight—through the harsh Milton soundscape that never rested, the town’s loud life beating on while, within their narrow circle, love and law drew tight like cords about a single desired five minutes.

When Mr. Thornton left the Hales’ house that morning, the street met him like the clang of a dropped iron bar. The light was too white, the sky too near; every wheel that passed worried his skull as if the very cobbles had grown teeth. He walked as a man does after a blow, stunned into moving, half-blind with passion he could not place, and yet felt as bodily pain—headache beating in time with his pulse, a throbbing that rose and fell like a cruel accompaniment to the town’s ceaseless din.

Milton made its own music whether a man wished to hear it or no: the rattle of carts, the thin cries of hawkers, the long, low rumble that never quite died—noise lying over everything like soot. It was not only in his ears; it seemed to press on his eyes, to scrape the inside of his mouth. He wanted quiet as a thirsty man wants water. He told himself he was a fool—told himself so often the words grew tasteless—and yet, in the first sharp minutes, he could hardly recollect what had cut him, whether the wound deserved such smarting. It would have been a relief to sit down on any door-step and weep outright, as a child does, raging even through tears at the injustice of a hurt; but he would not grant himself that softness. He shaped the thought, I hate her, and, at the same instant, love cleft through him—quick and keen as lightning through thunder.

His one comfort lay in hugging the torment close, as if pain were proof. She might despise him; she might treat him with that proud, sovereign indifference; she could not make him change. He loved her; he would love her; and he would defy her and defy this misery that had taken possession of his body.

He stopped, on the pavement, to set the resolve firm—stood very still, as though holding himself upright against the press of sound. An omnibus happened to be passing, bound out of town; the conductor, mistaking his pause for a signal, drew up with a jerk and a shout. It was too much trouble to explain. Mr. Thornton mounted, and let himself be carried away as if he were only another parcel in motion.

Milton slid backwards: long ranks of houses first, then detached villas with their trim little gardens, then hedgerows beginning to look like the real country, and after that a small town with a market-place. People climbed down and dispersed, their voices thinning in the clearer air. He got down too, because they did; and because the quiet beyond the last shop-front tugged at him like a hand.

He went into the fields and walked fast, letting the sharp movement spend what his heart could not. Here the world had another soundscape: wind combing the hedge, a bird’s note that struck cleanly and was gone, the hush that seemed to widen round him with every step. It should have soothed him. It did not. Now that the din had fallen away, memory began its own pounding.

He could see the pitiful figure he must have cut, hear his own voice as it had sounded—pleading without meaning to plead; could taste again the bitterness of having done the very thing he had always agreed with himself was the most foolish in the world. And he had met, precisely, the end he had foretold for such folly.

Was he bewitched by those beautiful eyes? By that soft, half-open, sighing mouth that had lain so close upon his shoulder only yesterday? He could not shake off the recollection that she had been there; that her arms had been round him once—if never again. He had only caught glimpses of her. He did not understand her altogether. One hour she seemed brave, another timid; now tender, then haughty and regally proud; and each change made her only more herself, more impossible to forget.

As if determination could be built by repetition, he tried to think over every time he had ever seen her, once again, to wear her image out. He saw her in every dress, in every mood, and did not know which became her best. Even this morning—how magnificent she had looked, eyes flashing at the mere idea that because she had shared his danger yesterday she must therefore care for him the least! Her scorn had struck like a smart spice upon the tongue: not agreeable, yet awakening every sense.

If he was a fool in the morning—as he had assured himself at least twenty times—he did not grow much wiser in the afternoon. The only gain of the sixpenny ride and the long walk was a more vivid conviction: there never was, never could be, any one like Margaret; she did not love him and never would; but she—no, nor the whole world—should ever hinder him from loving her.

And so he turned back, crossed into the market-place, and remounted the omnibus that would take him into the town’s grinding roar again.

It was late in the afternoon when he was set down near his warehouse. The accustomed sights drew back the accustomed habits as surely as the smell of oil and damp wool draws a man’s thoughts into business. He knew how much there was to do—more than usual, because of the commotion of the day before. He must see his brother magistrates. He must complete the arrangements, only half made in the morning, for the comfort and safety of the newly imported Irish hands; he must secure them from all chance of communication with the discontented workpeople of Milton. And last of all, hardest though it had nothing to do with looms or law, he must go home and encounter his mother.

Mrs. Thornton had sat in the dining-room all day, each minute drawn tight with expectation. She had been waiting for news—waiting for the step that would tell her her son had been accepted by Miss Hale. Again and again some sudden noise in the house had made her start; again and again she had caught up her dropped work and driven her needle hard, though her spectacles dimmed and her hand shook in spite of her. Many times the door had opened only to admit some indifferent person upon some insignificant errand. Then the rigid look—like gray frost bound upon her face—had melted into a despondency so strange upon her sternness that it seemed almost indecent, as though she had been caught without armour.

To wrench her mind from the dread of change—of being displaced—she forced it into household channels. If there was to be a new mistress in the house, there must be fresh household stores. Clothes-basket after clothes-basket was brought in, filled with table-cloths and napkins; and she began to reckon the stock as if numbers could keep grief at bay.

There was confusion between what was hers—marked G. H. T. for George and Hannah Thornton—and what belonged to her son, bought with his money and marked with his initials. Some of those bearing G. H. T. were old Dutch damask, exquisitely fine—linen that had a dense, cool smoothness under the fingers, woven so evenly it seemed almost to hold light. Nothing made now was like it. She stood looking at them long. They had been her pride when she was first married; in their whiteness lived a whole history of careful keeping, of boiling and blueing, of sunshine and ironing, of a young woman’s pleasure in making a home well-appointed.

Then her brows knit. Her lips pinched themselves into a line. With small, precise stitches she began to unpick the G. H. from the corner, as if by undoing thread she could undo what it signified—her old claim, her old place. She searched for the Turkey-red marking-thread to put in new initials, to alter possession by dye as clearly as by law; but it was all used, and she had no heart to send for more—not yet. So she sat fixedly looking at vacancy, while a series of visions passed before her in which her son was the principal, the sole object—her son, her pride, her property.

Still he did not come. Doubtless he was with Miss Hale. The thought struck her like sudden physical pain: jealousy, sharp and vain, darting through her so that she hardly knew whether it was mind or body that suffered. For a moment it forced her to sit down. In the next she was up again, straight as ever, with a grim smile—ready for the door to open and the triumphant one to enter, the man who should never know the sore regret his mother felt at his marriage.

In all this there was little thought of the future daughter-in-law as an individual. She was to be John’s wife. To take Mrs. Thornton’s place as mistress of the house was only one consequence among many that glittered round the supreme glory. Household plenty and comfort, honour and obedience, troops of friends, would come as naturally, in Mrs. Thornton’s imagination, as jewels on a king’s robe—things assumed, not considered for their separate worth. To be chosen by John would raise a kitchen-wench above the rest of the world.

And Miss Hale—she was not so bad. If she had been a Milton lass, Mrs. Thornton would have liked her. There was pungency in her, taste, spirit, flavour. True, she was sadly prejudiced and very ignorant; but that might be expected from southern breeding. A mortified comparison with Fanny went on in Mrs. Thornton’s mind; and for once she spoke harshly to her daughter, abused her roundly, and then, as penance, took up Henry’s Commentaries and tried to fix her attention upon the print instead of continuing her inspection of the linen.

His step at last.

She heard it while her eyes passed over a sentence she could afterwards repeat word for word without having taken its meaning in. The house itself seemed to tell her he was coming: the hall-door, the sound at the hat-stand, the pause before the room-door. Why did he pause? Let her know the worst. Yet her head remained bent over the book; she did not look up.

He came close to the table and stood there, waiting till she should have finished the paragraph that appeared to absorb her. At length, by a visible effort, she raised her eyes.

“Well, John?”

He knew what the little speech meant. He had steeled himself, and yet the answering words would not come readily. A jest rose—bitter, ready-shaped; but his mother deserved better. He moved behind her chair so that she could not see his face, bent down, and kissed her gray, stony cheek.

“No one loves me,—no one cares for me, but you, mother,” he murmured.

Then he turned away and stood with his head leaning against the mantelpiece. Tears forced themselves into his manly eyes, as if the restraint of the day had at last found a crack.

Mrs. Thornton stood up—she tottered. For the first time in her life the strong woman tottered. She laid her hands on his shoulders; she was tall and had always looked as if she could bear weight without bending. She made him turn; she looked into his face and compelled him to meet her gaze.

“Mother’s love is given by God, John. It holds fast for ever and ever. A girl’s love is like a puff of smoke,—it changes with every wind. And she would not have you, my own lad, would not she?”

Her teeth set; she showed them like a dog for the whole length of her mouth. He shook his head.

“I am not fit for her, mother; I knew I was not.”

She ground out words between closed teeth. He could not catch them, but the look in her eyes translated them well enough—a curse, if not coarse in sound, as fell in intent as any ever spoken. And yet her heart leapt light to know he was hers again.

“Mother!” he said, hurriedly, as if to shut the door on what he had seen in her face. “I cannot hear a word against her. Spare me,—spare me! I am very weak in my sore heart;—I love her yet; I love her more than ever.”

“And I hate her,” said Mrs. Thornton, low and fierce. “I tried not to hate her, when she stood between you and me, because,—I said to myself,—she will make him happy; and I would give my heart’s blood to do that. But now, I hate her for your misery’s sake. Yes, John, it’s no use hiding up your aching heart from me. I am the mother that bore you, and your sorrow is my agony; and if you don’t hate her, I do.”

“Then, mother, you make me love her more. She is unjustly treated by you, and I must make the balance even. But why do we talk of love or hatred? She does not care for me, and that is enough, too much. Let us never name the subject again. It is the only thing you can do for me in the matter. Let us never name her.”

“With all my heart. I only wish that she, and all belonging to her, were swept back to the place they came from.”

He stood still a minute or two longer, gazing into the fire as if heat could cauterize thought. Mrs. Thornton’s dry, dim eyes filled with tears she would not acknowledge; but when he spoke again her face was as grim and quiet as ever, the voice back in its accustomed groove.

“Warrants are out against three men for conspiracy, mother. The riot yesterday helped to knock up the strike.”

And Margaret’s name was mentioned no more between mother and son. They returned to their old manner—talk of facts, not opinions, far less feelings. Their voices sank into calm, cold tones; and a stranger, hearing them, might have gone away thinking there had never been nearer kinship clad in such frigid indifference. Outside, Milton kept up its harsh chorus without pause, as if the town itself had no other language left for sorrow or love than noise.

Mr. Thornton moved through the next day as if some hand had scoured his mind clean in the night, rubbing away yesterday’s humiliation until only a hard, bright edge of purpose remained. Trade, law, and town-business—he went into them with that direct, unflinching force that made older men, richer men—men whose money had long since been settled into acres and stone—turn, without knowing they turned, to the manufacturer whose wealth still ran like quicksilver through looms and ledgers.

There was a slight demand for finished goods, and he took it as a man takes a favourable wind: he leaned into it, drove bargains close and sharp, and came away with terms that showed no softness for any one’s convenience. At the meeting of magistrates he was punctual to the minute, his judgment fast, his sense of consequences quicker still; and when talk threatened to wander, he brought it back to the bone and sinew of action. He was deputed, almost as a matter of course, to see the police, to settle the requisite steps, to lead the necessary measures; and he accepted their unspoken deference as he accepted the weather—an element to move through, not a thing to be proud of. If he had once grown aware of it, it would have hampered him like praise does a runner: something catching at the sleeve.

It was his mother who drank in, with an eager pride that had something of hunger in it, what the women of those magistrates said in parlour and carriage. Mr. This had declared no one else would have managed it so. Mr. That had said matters would have gone very badly indeed if Mr. Thornton had not been there. She stored these sentences as if they were coin.

He swept his business aside right and left. The mortification of yesterday—so hot, so sharp—had left behind it a kind of fierce clearness. He felt his own power and, for a few hours, revelled in it; it was as if he could set his heart, too, under lock and key, and throw away the key by sheer will.

Evidence against Boucher and other ring-leaders of the riot was taken before him; that against three others, charged with conspiracy, failed. He dismissed the failing charge without hesitation, but he gave the police a stern, exact order to watch: the law’s right arm was to be ready—ready to strike the instant fault could be proved. Then, leaving the close, overheated borough court—where sweat and ink and the sour breath of a crowd lay thick—he went out into the street.

The air outside was fresher, but still heavy with heat. It held Milton’s constant flavour: coal-smoke hanging like a bitter seasoning over everything, and the metallic tang of industry that made even summer seem dark. From the distant mills came the never-resting grind and thud—the rasp of belts, the hammering pulse of engines—noise that had become to the town what sea-sound is to a coast: so constant it can soothe or maddens, depending on the heart that listens. To Thornton, it had long been mere accompaniment; yet today it struck him oddly, as if the town’s great din were trying to drown a different sound in him.

All at once he gave way. His limbs felt languid, his thoughts slipping their reins. They would not stay where he drove them—on law, on trade, on the coming week. They strayed, and always returned to her. Not to the sharp scene of yesterday’s refusal—he thrust that away—but to the looks and actions of the day before that: the sudden clinging, the quick beating of a heart against his, the brief human warmth in the midst of a roaring crowd. Memory, like a taste that comes back unbidden—salt on the lips after one has left the sea—returned and returned.

He threaded the crowded streets mechanically, avoiding people without seeing them, when a voice cut across his abstraction.

“Why, Mr. Thornton! you’re cutting me very coolly, I must say. And how is Mrs. Thornton? Brave weather this! We doctors don’t like it, I can tell you!”

He stopped as if checked by a hand. Dr. Donaldson stood before him, his professional cheerfulness riding on a tired knowledge.

“I beg your pardon, Dr. Donaldson. I really didn’t see you. My mother’s quite well, thank you. It is a fine day, and good for the harvest, I hope. If the wheat is well got in, we shall have a brisk trade next year, whatever you doctors have.”

“Ay, ay. Each man for himself. Your bad weather, and your bad times, are my good ones. When trade is bad, there’s more undermining of health, and preparation for death, going on among you Milton men than you’re aware of.”

“Not with me, Doctor. I’m made of iron. The news of the very worst bad debt I ever had, never made my pulse vary. This strike, which affects me more than any one else in Milton,—more than Hamper,—never comes near my appetite. You must go elsewhere for a patient, Doctor.”

The doctor’s look sharpened; he did not smile this time.

“By the way, you’ve recommended me a good patient, poor lady! Not to go on talking in this heartless way, I seriously believe that Mrs. Hale—that lady in Crampton, you know—hasn’t many weeks to live. I never had any hope of cure, as I think I told you; but I’ve been seeing her to-day, and I think very badly of her.”

Mr. Thornton’s vaunted steadiness failed him—only for an instant, but enough to make him feel it. The roar of Milton seemed to drop back a pace, as if giving room to that single sentence.

“Can I do anything, Doctor?” he asked; and the change in his voice betrayed him more than any words could.

“You know—you would see, that money is not very plentiful, are there any comforts or dainties she ought to have?”

“No,” said Dr. Donaldson, shaking his head. “She craves for fruit,—she has a constant fever on her; but jargonelle pears will do as well as anything, and there are quantities of them in the market.”

“You will tell me if there is anything I can do, I’m sure,” said Mr. Thornton. “I rely upon you.”

“Oh! never fear! I’ll not spare your purse,—I know it’s deep enough. I wish you’d give me a carte-blanche for all my patients, and all their wants.”

But Thornton’s feeling did not spread wide like a public subscription; it ran in a straight channel. He went, at once, without any more talk, to the first fruit-shop he met.

The shop was cool in comparison to the street, smelling of damp straw and green leaves, with a sweetness rising like a soft breath from bruised skins and cut stems. Baskets stood in ranks: pears with their pale speckled sides, peaches blushing under down, clusters of grapes with their translucent globes and powdery bloom. The shopman’s knife flashed as he trimmed a stem; somewhere a fly droned, trapped between window and fruit-scented air.

Mr. Thornton chose as if he were choosing for a palate that mattered. He took a bunch of purple grapes, heavy and tight, with the bloom unbroken; peaches the colour of late sunset, firm enough to yield slowly under the thumb; and fresh vine-leaves, still cool as if they remembered shade. He had them packed with care into a basket, the fruit cushioned so it would not bruise, straw tucked in, leaves laid over like a green cloth.

The shopman, respectful, waited. “Where shall we send them to, sir?”

Thornton did not answer at once. Something like a struggle passed over his face—quick, silent, fierce.

“To Marlborough Mills, I suppose, sir?”

“No!” Thornton said, sharply, as if the very thought offended him. “Give the basket to me,—I’ll take it.”

It took both his hands. He went out into the busiest part of town, where women were shopping and the pavements were thick with skirts and parcels. Many a young lady of his acquaintance turned to look at him—Mr. Thornton, who walked like a man with a purpose even when he had none, now carrying a basket like an errand-boy. He heard a faint ripple of voices, but Milton’s larger noise swallowed it up: cart-wheels on stone, a hawker’s cry, a distant hammering that never ceased, like some monstrous heart beating in iron.

Inside himself he argued, as if argument could fence off pain.

I will not be daunted from doing as I choose by the thought of her. I like to take this fruit to the poor mother, and it is simply right that I should. She shall never scorn me out of doing what I please. A pretty joke, indeed, if, for fear of a haughty girl, I failed in doing a kindness to a man I liked! I do it for Mr. Hale; I do it in defiance of her.

He went at an unusual pace, as if speed could keep his mind from slipping back. Soon Crampton was behind him; the air altered, losing some of its coal-bitter edge. Even so, the town’s sound followed, like a distant surf of industry.

He went up the stairs two steps at a time, entered the drawing-room before Dixon could announce him. His face was flushed from haste; his eyes shone with that earnest kindness which looks almost startling on a strong man used to command and hard dealing.

Mrs. Hale lay on the sofa, fever-bright, her breath quick and shallow. Mr. Hale was reading aloud in a gentle voice that tried to smooth the world. Margaret sat low by her mother, working—needle flashing, thread drawn through cloth with that quiet perseverance that held household life together when everything else threatened to break.

If Margaret’s heart fluttered, his did not show it. He made no sign that he saw her. He scarcely seemed to see even Mr. Hale. He went straight to Mrs. Hale, basket in hand, and spoke in a subdued tone, made tender by the effort of gentleness.

“I met Dr. Donaldson, ma’am, and as he said fruit would be good for you, I have taken the liberty—the great liberty—of bringing you some that seemed to me fine.”

Mrs. Hale’s eyes brightened with eager pleasure; her thin hand trembled as if already reaching in imagination for the cool burst of a grape, the fragrant softness of peach. In sickness, the body clings to such small comforts with the greed of a child.

Mr. Hale, with fewer words, expressed deeper gratitude—gratitude that came not only from the gift but from the thought behind it.

“Fetch a plate, Margaret—a basket—anything.”

Margaret rose and went to the table, moving as if noise might shatter something. She was half afraid of stirring Thornton into the full consciousness of her presence; she dreaded, in a way she could not have explained, the moment when their eyes might meet, and all the past two days flash between them like lightning. She fancied—because she wished it—that he had overlooked her in his haste; she had been low at first, and now she stood behind her father.

As if he did not feel her presence all over the room, like a pressure of air before thunder, though his eyes never rested on her.

“I must go,” he said. “I cannot stay. If you will forgive this liberty,—my rough ways,—too abrupt, I fear—but I will be more gentle next time. You will allow me the pleasure of bringing you some fruit again, if I should see any that is tempting. Good afternoon, Mr. Hale. Good-bye, ma’am.”

And he was gone.

Not one word. Not one look to Margaret.

She truly believed he had not seen her. She went for a plate in silence and lifted the fruit out tenderly, her taper fingers careful not to crush the bloom or bruise the velvet of the peaches. The vine-leaves gave a faint green scent as she moved them. It was good of him to bring it; and after yesterday too. The gift had the quiet, unmistakable weight of intention.

“Oh! it is so delicious!” Mrs. Hale said, in her feeble voice, after she had tasted. The grape’s cool juice seemed to ease her burning mouth for a moment. “How kind of him to think of me! Margaret love, only taste these grapes! Was it not good of him?”

“Yes!” said Margaret, quietly; and her quietness was not indifference so much as restraint.

“Margaret!” Mrs. Hale’s tone grew querulous, sharpened by pain and weakness. “You won’t like anything Mr. Thornton does. I never saw anybody so prejudiced.”

Mr. Hale had taken a peach and, with the careful domestic skill of one who has learned to make small luxuries for an invalid, began to peel it. The skin came away in a thin curl, releasing that rich scent—honeyed, warm, almost like summer made edible. He cut a slice for his wife, then, smiling faintly, a little piece for himself.

“If I had any prejudices,” he said, “the gift of such delicious fruit as this would melt them away. I have not tasted such fruit—no! not even in Hampshire—since I was a boy; and, to boys, I fancy, all fruit is good. I remember eating sloes and crabs with a relish. Do you remember the matted-up currant bushes, Margaret, at the corner of the west-wall at the garden at home?”

Did she not?

The words, so simple, touched the tenderest nerve. She remembered not only currant bushes but the very air: the soft hush of Hampshire evenings, the birds’ small calls, the particular quiet that lies between hedges, where even silence seems alive and kindly. She remembered the old stone wall—every weather-stain; the gray and yellow lichens mapping it like continents; the little crane’s-bill in crevices. The memory rose with scents—leaf-mould and sun-warmed earth—and with sounds, too: not Milton’s iron pulse, but the home-language of fields, the dialect of wind in apple-boughs.

She had been shaken by the last two days; her life was a strain upon her fortitude; and those careless words, reaching back to the sunny old time, loosened her. She started up, dropped her sewing on the floor, and went hastily out of the room into her little chamber.

She had scarcely given way to the first choking sob when she became aware of Dixon standing at her drawers, rummaging as if in search of some particular thing. The movement of linen brought out a familiar scent of lavender, stored there long ago to keep away moth and damp—a scent that carried its own small history of women’s hands, of careful household ways, of customs that persisted even when all else changed.

“Bless me, miss! How you startled me! Missus is not worse, is she? Is anything the matter?”

“No, nothing. Only I’m silly, Dixon, and want a glass of water. What are you looking for? I keep my muslins in that drawer.”

Dixon did not answer at once. She went on searching, lips tight, as if reluctant to speak. At last she found what she wanted—something Margaret could not see clearly in Dixon’s grasp.

Dixon turned round, faced her, and said, with the air of one who dislikes carrying bad news.

“Now I don’t like telling what I wanted, because you’ve fretting enough to go through, and I know you’ll fret about this. I meant to have kept it from you till night, may be, or such times as that.”

“What is the matter? Pray, tell me, Dixon, at once.”

“That young woman you go to see—Higgins I mean.”

“Well?”

“Well! she died this morning, and her sister is here—come to beg a strange thing. It seems, the young woman who died had a fancy for being buried in something of yours, and so the sister’s come to ask for it,—and I was looking for a night-cap that wasn’t too good to give away.”

“Oh! let me find one,” said Margaret, tears still on her face. “Poor Bessy! I never thought I should not see her again.”

“Why, that’s another thing. This girl downstairs wanted me to ask you, if you would like to see her.”

“But she’s dead!” Margaret said, turning a little pale. “I never saw a dead person. No! I would rather not.”

“I should never have asked you, if you hadn’t come in. I told her you wouldn’t.”

Margaret’s breath caught. Her first recoil was fear—fear of the stillness of death, of the sight that would not be softened by speech. But a different fear followed: that Dixon’s bluntness would strike the grieving sister like a blow, that the poor girl would go away feeling refused, refused even that small tribute of respect which, among their people, meant something deep and wordless.

“I will go down and speak to her,” Margaret said. She took the cap in her hand and went down to the kitchen.

Mary Higgins stood there, her face swollen with crying, red-eyed and spent. At the sight of Margaret she broke afresh into sobs.

“Oh, ma’am, she loved yo’, she loved yo’, she did indeed!”

For a long while that was all she could say, as if the phrase were the only plank left in her. Margaret, moved with pity, waited; Dixon’s sharp scolding—meant, perhaps, to force speech—at last helped to press a few facts out through the grief.

Nicholas Higgins had gone out in the morning, leaving Bessy as well as she had been the day before. But within an hour she had grown worse; some neighbour had run to the room where Mary was working. They did not know where to find her father. Mary had only reached home a few minutes before Bessy died.

“It were a day or two ago she axed to be buried in somewhat o’ yourn,” Mary said, wiping her face with her apron. “She were never tired o’ talking o’ yo’. She used to say yo’ were the prettiest thing she ever clapped eyes on. She loved yo’ dearly. Her last words were ‘Give her my affectionate respects; and keep father fro’ drink.’ Yo’ll come and see her ma’am. She would ha’ thought it a great compliment, I know.”

Margaret shrank, again, from the thought of going, from the strangeness of the sight, from the hush of a poor room where the usual noises—coughing, scolding, the clink of a cup—would be replaced by that other silence. Yet the sound of Mary’s dialect, the very shape of her words—so different from drawing-room speech, carrying a whole world of belonging and class and power in its syllables—made Margaret feel, sharply, the weight of what was being asked. In Mary’s tongue, “respect” was not a pretty word; it was a duty, a recognition. To refuse might be read as contempt, and contempt is an easy language for the comfortable to speak without meaning to.

“Yes, perhaps I may. Yes, I will. I’ll come before tea. But where’s your father, Mary?”

Mary shook her head and began to move as if to go.

“Miss Hale,” Dixon said low, drawing near, “where’s the use o’ your going to see the poor thing laid out? I’d never say a word against it, if it could do the girl any good; and I wouldn’t mind a bit going myself, if that would satisfy her. They’ve just a notion, these common folks, of its being a respect to the departed.”

Then, turning sharply to Mary, Dixon added in a louder voice, as if cutting the matter short would make it clean, “Here. I’ll come and see your sister. Miss Hale is busy, and she can’t come, or else she would.”

Mary’s eyes lifted, wistful and doubtful, to Margaret. Dixon’s coming might be something—better than nothing—but it was not what Bessy had meant. Margaret could see it in the girl’s face: the old little jealousy, perhaps, that had once pricked between sisters, now turned into a grief that wanted one particular comfort.

“No, Dixon!” Margaret said, with sudden decision. “I will go. Mary, you shall see me this afternoon.”

And, fearing her own cowardice—fearing that if she stayed in the kitchen another minute she might begin to argue herself out of it—she went away at once, holding to her resolve as if it were something she must clutch tightly lest it slip from her in the next breath.

That afternoon Margaret went quickly through the smoky streets, as if speed could outstrip sorrow. The air itself seemed altered—thicker with the mill-breath that hung over Milton, and threaded with the hard, metallic beat of distant machinery. Even in the narrow courts the sound traveled: a ceaseless churning like an ill-tuned organ grinding out one note until the mind grew raw. Yet between one clatter and the next there were small human noises—children’s bare feet on stone, a kettle beginning to sing somewhere unseen—that made the grief she was going to meet feel at once homely and immense.

Mary Higgins was watching for her, half distrust in her face, as if kindness were another thing that could fail. Margaret gave her a steady smile, and Mary, reassured without words, drew her in. They passed through the house-place—dark with years of coal smoke and close living—and climbed the crooked stair. Above, the room had the hush that comes when the ordinary sounds of a dwelling have been stopped, not by command, but by awe.

Bessy lay there.

Margaret had seen pain carve its sharp lines into that young face often enough; she had heard the short breath, the fretful startings, the bitter, weary talk that had come and gone like wind across a field. Now the muscles were unknit. The lips had settled into a faint softness, as if the last thing she had tasted was not bitterness but sleep. Margaret’s eyes filled slowly; she did not sob. A deep stillness entered her—so calm it frightened her a little, because it seemed too like consent.

So this was death. Peaceful—more peaceful than life had ever been to Bessy. Scripture rose unbidden, in phrases that came with their own quiet music: They rest from their labours. The weary are at rest. He giveth his beloved sleep.

She turned away at last, slowly, as if turning a page that could not be read again. In the background Mary sobbed, low and humble, as if she begged pardon even for grief. Without speaking, they went down.

In the room below, Nicholas Higgins stood with one hand on the table, planted in the middle of the floor as if bracing himself against a blow. His great eyes were open wide—startled, fierce, dry. The news had met him in the court, flung from mouth to mouth; it had run ahead of him with a cruel speed, and now he was trying to force his mind to accept what his heart still refused. Bessy had been sick so long that he had let himself believe she would never quite die; that she would “pull through,” as if the body could be reasoned with and the grave delayed by sheer obstinacy.

Margaret felt suddenly like an intruder. This was his sorrow’s house, his child, his loss; and she had already stood in the “quiet presence” that he, the father, had not yet faced. On the stair, when she first caught sight of him, she had paused. Now she tried to slip past him, to leave him within the solemn circle of his own misery.

Mary sank into the first chair she found and pulled her apron over her head, and her crying grew louder for the cloth that muffled it.

The sound roused him as if it were an insult. He caught Margaret’s arm in a grip that hurt, not from malice but from a man’s bewildered strength.

“Were yo’ with her? Did yo’ see her die?”

“No,” Margaret answered, perfectly still. She did not flinch. He held her as though by holding her he could hold the fact at bay.

There was a long pause. His throat worked; when his words came they were thick and hoarse.

“All men must die,” he said at last, with a strange gravity that made Margaret think—only for an instant—that he had been drinking: not enough to topple his steps, but enough to turn thought murky and uneven. “But she were younger than me.”

He stared past Margaret, studying the event as if it were something laid on the table to be judged true or false. Then he snapped his eyes upon her with wild inquiry.

“Yo’re sure and certain she’s dead—not in a dwam, a faint? she’s been so before, often.”

“She is dead,” Margaret said.

He searched her face, and the fierce light in his eyes seemed to gutter as if a lamp had been starved of oil. Then, all at once, he let go of her arm, flung himself half across the table, and sobbed with a violence that shook not only his body but the furniture around him, as if wood and iron ought to answer for what had been done.

Mary rose, trembling, and went to him.

“Get thee gone!—get thee gone!” he cried, striking at her blindly. “What do I care for thee?”

Margaret caught Mary’s hand and held it—soft, steady, as one might hold a frightened creature that does not know where to put itself. Nicholas tore at his hair, beat his head against the hard wood, then sagged into a stunned, stupid exhaustion.

They did not move. Mary trembled from head to foot.

After what might have been minutes or an hour—grief mangles time—he lifted himself up. His eyes were swollen and bloodshot. For a moment he looked as if he had forgotten there was anyone in the room at all; then he saw them and scowled, resentful of witnesses. He shook himself heavily, cast them one sullen glance, said nothing, and made for the door.

“Oh, father, father!” Mary clung to his arm. “Not to-night! Any night but to-night. Oh, help me! he’s going out to drink again! Father, I’ll not leave yo’. Yo’ may strike, but I’ll not leave yo’. She told me last of all to keep yo’ fro’ drink!”

Margaret stepped into the doorway. She did not speak. She only stood—silent, unmoving, with her serious eyes fixed upon him. Nicholas shook Mary off so violently she fell against a chair and her face struck it; blood showed at her lip. He turned on Margaret as if he would strike her too.

“It’s my own house. Stand out o’ the way, wench, or I’ll make yo’!”

Yet he did not move her. Something in her stillness held him, as if he had run against an invisible wall. He stared, gloomy and defiant; but the longer he stared the more his defiance slipped, replaced by a reluctant awe.

“What are yo’ looking at me in that way for?” he demanded at last, half cowed and angry at being cowed. “If yo’ think for to keep me from going what gait I choose, because she loved yo’—and in my own house, too, where I never asked yo’ to come, yo’re mista’en. It’s very hard upon a man that he can’t go to the only comfort left.”

Margaret knew, by the very bitterness of his complaint, that he had already granted her power. She felt the weight of it. He sat down in a chair near the door, half conquered, half resentful—ready to go out the moment she yielded place, yet unwilling to use the violence he had threatened.

She laid her hand on his arm.

“Come with me,” she said. “Come and see her.”

Her voice was low and solemn. It held neither fear of him nor doubt of his obedience, only a quiet insistence, as if she spoke to the best part in him and expected it to answer.

He rose sullenly. He stood with dogged irresolution on his face, lingering as if delay could make the next moment less true. Margaret waited—patiently, without pressing. He took a grim satisfaction in making her wait. At last he moved toward the stairs.

They stood by the bed.

“Her last words to Mary were, ‘Keep my father fro’ drink.’”

“It canna hurt her now,” he muttered. “Nought can hurt her now.” Then his voice broke into a wailing cry that came out of him like a torn thing. “We may quarrel and fall out—we may make peace and be friends—we may clem to skin and bone—and nought o’ all our griefs will ever touch her more. Hoo’s had her portion on ’em. What wi’ hard work first, and sickness at last, hoo’ led the life of a dog. And to die without knowing one good piece o’ rejoicing in all her days! Nay, wench, whatever hoo said, hoo can know nought about it now, and I mun ha’ a sup o’ drink just to steady me again sorrow.”

“No,” said Margaret, and because his voice had softened, hers softened too. “You shall not. If her life has been what you say, at any rate she did not fear death as some do. You should have heard her speak of the life to come—the life hidden with God, that she is now gone to.”

He shook his head, glancing sideways at her—wary, as if he expected a trap even in comfort. His pale, haggard face struck her painfully; it had the drained look of a man who has lived too long in noise—noise of looms, noise of argument, noise of hunger—and cannot find the quiet place inside his own skull.

“You are sorely tried,” she said. “Where have you been all day—not at work?”

“Not at work, sure enough,” he answered with a short grim laugh. “Not at what you call work. I were at the Committee, till I were sickened out wi’ trying to make fools hear reason. I were fetched to Boucher’s wife afore seven this morning. She’s bed-fast, but she were raving and raging to know where her dunner-headed brute of a chap was, as if I’d to keep him—as if he were fit to be ruled by me. The d—d fool, who has put his foot in all our plans! And I’ve walked my feet sore wi’ going about for to see men who wouldn’t be seen, now the law is raised against us.” He swallowed, as if something in his throat resisted. “And I were sore-hearted, too, which is worse than sore-footed; and if I did see a friend who ossed to treat me, I never knew hoo lay a-dying here. Bess, lass, thou’d believe me, thou wouldst—wouldstn’t thou?” He turned the wild appeal upon the poor still form, as if she might contradict the world’s accusation.

“I am sure,” Margaret said, “I am sure you did not know; it was quite sudden. But now you do know; you do see her lying there; you hear what she said with her last breath. You will not go?”

He did not answer. Where was he to turn for comfort, now the ordinary place of it was a covered face?

At last Margaret, daring more than she had meant to dare, said, “Come home with me. At least you shall have some comfortable food, which I’m sure you need.”

It was the plainness of the offer—the domestic, bodily mercy of it—that gave it force. A man might argue against doctrine; it was harder to argue against a warm drink, a slice of bread, the human decency of being fed when grief had emptied him.

He looked at her sharply, his thoughts turning aside with the suddenness of a wind-shift.

“Yo’r father’s a parson?” he asked.

“He was,” Margaret replied, briefly.

“I’ll go and take a dish o’ tea with him, since yo’ve asked me,” Nicholas said. “I’ve many a thing I often wished to say to a parson, and I’m not particular as to whether he’s preaching now, or not.”

Margaret’s heart gave a quick, uneasy leap. Tea with her father—who would be wholly unprepared; and her mother so ill—seemed impossible. Yet if she drew back now, she could see the gin-shop’s door opening in her mind as plainly as if it stood before her. If she could only get him into her own house, it would be a great step gained; after that, she must trust to whatever providence governed small events.

Nicholas bent over Bessy one last time.

“Good-bye, ou’d wench! We’ve parted company at last, we have! But thou’st been a blessin’ to thy father ever sin’ thou wert born. Bless thy white lips, lass,—they’ve a smile on ’em now! and I’m glad to see it once again, though I’m lone and forlorn for evermore.”

He kissed her fondly, covered her face, and turned to follow Margaret.

Margaret hurried downstairs to tell Mary what she meant to do—to say it was the only place she could think of to keep him from the gin-palace; to urge her to come too, for her conscience smote her at the thought of leaving the poor affectionate girl alone. But Mary said the neighbours would come in and sit with her; it was all right; only father—

Nicholas was already there, and whatever more Mary might have pleaded was cut off. He had snapped his emotion shut again, ashamed of it, and leapt past himself into a bitter mirth that sounded like dry sticks crackling in a fire.

“I’m going to take my tea wi’ her father, I am.”

He slouched his cap low over his brow as he went out, looking neither right nor left. He feared the sympathy in neighbours’ faces more than their words; pity might tip him over again. The street was full of Milton’s clamor—carts, shouts, the far iron cadence of the mills—and through it he and Margaret walked in silence, two figures moving against a tide of sound.

As they neared the street where he knew she lived, he glanced down at his clothes, his hands, his shoes, as if he suddenly felt the whole weight of being seen.

“I should m’appen ha’ cleaned mysel’, first.”

“It will be easy,” Margaret said quickly. “You shall go into the yard, and have soap and towel. Come.”

She would not let him slip from her hands.

While the servant led him along the passage and through the kitchen, he stepped cautiously on every dark mark in the oil-cloth’s pattern, trying to place his clogs so as to hide the trace of dirt—an awkward, touching care, as if cleanliness might buy him some right to sit in peace. Margaret ran upstairs. Dixon met her on the landing.

“How is mamma?—where is papa?”

Mrs. Hale was tired and had gone into her own room. She had wanted to go to bed, but Dixon had persuaded her to lie on the sofa and have tea there; it was better than lying wakeful and restless.

So far, so good. Mr. Hale was in the drawing-room.

Margaret went in almost breathless and told him what had happened—imperfectly, hurriedly, because it was a story that seemed to breed new trouble the more clearly it was spoken.
