Her father looked taken aback at the notion of Nicholas Higgins waiting in his quiet study, expected to drink tea, brought in as a last barrier between a grieving man and the gin-shop. Mr. Hale was kind and gentle; he would have gone readily to comfort any sufferer. But Margaret, in her anxiety, pressed most on Higgins having been drinking, and on her having fetched him home as the only expedient left. One small event had led to another so naturally she had hardly known what she was doing until she saw the slight recoil—no more than a shadow—on her father’s face.

“Oh, papa! he really is a man you will not dislike—if you won’t be shocked to begin with.”

“But, Margaret, to bring a drunken man home—and your mother so ill!”

Margaret’s face fell. “I am sorry, papa. He is very quiet—he is not tipsy at all. He was only rather strange at first, but that might be the shock of poor Bessy’s death.”

Her eyes filled. Mr. Hale took her pleading face between his hands and kissed her forehead.

“It is all right, dear. I’ll go and make him as comfortable as I can. You attend to your mother. Only, if you can come in and make a third in the study, I shall be glad.”

“Oh, yes—thank you.”

As he was leaving she ran after him, a new fear catching her.

“Papa—you must not wonder at what he says: he’s an— I mean he does not believe much in what we do.”

“Oh dear! a drunken infidel weaver!” Mr. Hale thought, dismayed; but aloud he only said, “If your mother goes to sleep, be sure you come directly.”

Margaret went into her mother’s room. Mrs. Hale lifted herself from a doze, her face worn with illness and that particular fretfulness that comes when the body is weak and the mind has too much time to brood.

“When did you write to Frederick, Margaret? Yesterday, or the day before?”

“Yesterday, mamma.”

“And the letter went?”

“Yes. I took it myself.”

Mrs. Hale’s eyes widened with fear that was almost childish in its helplessness. “Oh, Margaret, I’m so afraid of his coming! If he should be recognized! If he should be taken! If he should be executed, after all these years that he has kept away and lived in safety! I keep falling asleep and dreaming that he is caught and being tried.”

“Oh, mamma, don’t be afraid. There will be some risk, no doubt; but we will lessen it as much as we can. And it is so little! If we were at Helstone, there would be twenty—a hundred times as much. There everybody would remember him; and if there was a stranger known to be in the house, they would be sure to guess it was Frederick. Here nobody knows or cares for us enough to notice what we do. Dixon will keep the door like a dragon—won’t you, Dixon—while he is here?”

“They’ll be clever if they come in past me!” Dixon said, showing her teeth at the idea, fierce as any watchdog.

“And he need not go out, except in the dusk,” Margaret added.

“Poor fellow!” Mrs. Hale echoed. Then, wavering, “But I almost wish you had not written. Would it be too late to stop him if you wrote again, Margaret?”

“I’m afraid it would, mamma,” Margaret said, remembering her own urgent words—come directly, if you wish to see your mother alive.

“I always dislike that doing things in such a hurry,” Mrs. Hale complained, as if the world could be regulated by preference.

Margaret said nothing.

“Come now, ma’am,” Dixon put in, with that brisk cheerfulness she used like a medicine, “you know seeing Master Frederick is just the very thing of all others you’re longing for. And I’m glad Miss Margaret wrote off straight, without shilly-shallying. I’ve had a great mind to do it myself. And we’ll keep him snug, depend upon it. There’s only Martha in the house that would not do a good deal to save him on a pinch; and I’ve been thinking she might go and see her mother just at that very time. She’s been saying once or twice she should like to go, for her mother has had a stroke since she came here; only she didn’t like to ask. But I’ll see about her being safe off, as soon as we know when he comes, God bless him! So take your tea, ma’am, in comfort, and trust to me.”

Mrs. Hale trusted Dixon more than she trusted Margaret. Dixon’s certainty quieted her, as a steady hand quiets a trembling cup. Margaret poured out the tea in silence. The tray made small, comforting sounds—spoon against china, the soft pour and pause—and the smell of the tea rose warm and tannic, threading through the sickroom air. Yet Margaret’s mind would not follow it into comfort. The more she tried to think of anything else, the more the image of Frederick—recognized, seized, tried—returned, sticking like burrs to cloth. Her mother prattled with Dixon and seemed to have forgotten the dangers she had thrown out a moment before; she was one of those who could spark terror like a rocket, then let it fall away, while the person it landed upon smouldered.

Margaret was glad when she could go down into the study. She wondered how her father and Higgins had fared.

She found, to her relief, that the decorous, kind-hearted, simple old-fashioned gentleman had, without knowing it, called up the best in the other. Mr. Hale treated all fellow-creatures alike; rank did not come into his mind as a reason for manners. He had placed a chair for Nicholas, stood until at his request the weaver sat, and had called him “Mr. Higgins” with steady courtesy—never “Nicholas,” never “Higgins” in the curt way to which the man was used.

And Nicholas was not an habitual drunkard, nor a thorough infidel. He drank to drown care, as he would have said; and if he had no faith it was because he had not yet found any form of it he could clasp with his whole heart.

Margaret was surprised—and pleased—at the sight before her. Higgins, clean and tidied at least by water and effort, sat composedly, speaking with earnestness. His hair was slicked down damp; his neck-handkerchief sat more evenly; he had borrowed an odd candle-end and polished his clogs till they shone in patches. Even his voice was lowered, as if the quiet of the room demanded a quieter human sound. Mr. Hale listened attentively, interested in spite of disagreement.

Mr. Hale looked up as Margaret entered, smiled, and offered her his chair; then, with a small bow to his guest as apology for the interruption, sat down again quickly. Higgins nodded to her. She arranged her work at the table with a soft rustle and prepared to listen.

“As I was a-saying, sir,” Nicholas went on, “I reckon yo’d not ha’ much belief in yo’ if yo’ lived here,—if yo’d been bred here. I ax your pardon if I use wrong words; but what I mean by belief just now, is a-thinking on sayings and maxims and promises made by folk yo’ never saw, about the things and the life yo’ never saw, nor no one else. Now, yo’ say these are true things, and true sayings, and a true life. I just say, where’s the proof?

“There’s many and many a one wiser, and scores better learned than I am around me,—folk who’ve had time to think on these things,—while my time has had to be gi’en up to getting my bread. Well, I sees these people. Their lives is pretty much open to me. They’re real folk. They don’t believe i’ the Bible,—not they. They may say they do, for form’s sake; but Lord, sir, d’ye think their first cry i’ th’ morning is, ‘What shall I do to get hold on eternal life?’ or ‘What shall I do to fill my purse this blessed day? Where shall I go? What bargains shall I strike?’ The purse and the gold and the notes is real things; things as can be felt and touched; them’s realities; and eternal life is all a talk, very fit for— I ax your pardon, sir; yo’r a parson out o’ work, I believe. Well! I’ll never speak disrespectful of a man in the same fix as I’m in mysel.

“But I’ll just ax yo’ another question, sir, and I dunnot want yo’ to answer it, only to put in yo’r pipe, and smoke it, afore yo’ go for to set down us, who only believe in what we see, as fools and noddies. If salvation, and life to come, and what not, was true—not in men’s words, but in men’s hearts’ core—dun yo’ not think they’d din us wi’ it as they do wi’ political ’conomy? They’re mighty anxious to come round us wi’ that piece o’ wisdom; but t’other would be a greater convarsion, if it were true.”

“But the masters have nothing to do with your religion,” Mr. Hale said gently. “All that they are connected with you in is trade,—so they think,—and all that it concerns them, therefore, to rectify your opinions in is the science of trade.”

“I’m glad, sir,” Higgins returned, a curious gleam in his eye, “that yo’ put in, ‘so they think.’ I’d ha’ thought yo’ a hyprocrite, I’m afeard, if yo’ hadn’t, for all yo’r a parson, or rayther because yo’r a parson. Yo’ see, if yo’d spoken o’ religion as a thing that, if it was true, it didn’t concern all men to press on all men’s attention, above everything else in this ’varsal earth, I should ha’ thought yo’ a knave for to be a parson; and I’d rather think yo’ a fool than a knave. No offence, I hope, sir.”

“None at all,” Mr. Hale said. “You consider me mistaken, and I consider you far more fatally mistaken. I don’t expect to convince you in a day,—not in one conversation; but let us know each other, and speak freely to each other about these things, and the truth will prevail. I should not believe in God if I did not believe that.” His voice dropped, reverent without being theatrical. “Mr. Higgins, I trust, whatever else you have given up, you believe—you believe in Him.”

Nicholas sprang to his feet so suddenly that Margaret started up too, thinking for an instant some fit had seized him; his face worked as if struck from within. Mr. Hale looked at Margaret, dismayed.

At last Higgins found words, broken and fierce with feeling.

“Man! I could fell yo’ to the ground for tempting me. Whatten business have yo’ to try me wi’ your doubts? Think o’ her lying theere, after the life hoo’s led; and think then how yo’d deny me the one sole comfort left—that there is a God, and that He set her her life.”

He sat down heavily, and stared drearily toward the fire, as if it were the only steady thing in the room.

“I dunnot believe she’ll ever live again,” he went on. “I dunnot believe in any other life than this, in which she dreed such trouble, and had such never-ending care; and I cannot bear to think it were all a set o’ chances, that might ha’ been altered wi’ a breath o’ wind. There’s many a time when I’ve thought I didna believe in God, but I’ve never put it fair out before me in words, as many men do. I may ha’ laughed at those who did, to brave it out like—but I have looked round at after, to see if He heard me, if so be there was a He; but to-day, when I’m left desolate, I wunnot listen to yo’ wi’ yo’r questions, and yo’r doubts. There’s but one thing steady and quiet i’ all this reeling world, and, reason or no reason, I’ll cling to that. It’s a’ very well for happy folk—”

Margaret touched his arm, very softly, as if to lower the volume of the room’s pain—like laying a hand on a vibrating string to stop its harshness. She had not spoken before.

“Nicholas,” she said, “we do not want to reason; you misunderstand my father. We do not reason—we believe; and so do you. It is the one sole comfort in such times.”

He turned and caught her hand, clinging as if her words were something he could hold.

“Ay! it is, it is,” he said, brushing the tears away with the back of his hand. “But yo’ know, she’s lying dead at home; and I’m welly dazed wi’ sorrow, and at times I hardly know what I’m saying. It’s as if speeches folk ha’ made—clever and smart things as I’ve thought at the time—come up now my heart’s welly brossen.” His voice sank. “Th’ strike’s failed as well; dun yo’ know that, miss? I were coming whoam to ask her, like a beggar as I am, for a bit o’ comfort i’ that trouble; and I were knocked down by one who telled me she were dead—just dead. That were all; but that were enough for me.”

The next morning’s post brought Margaret a letter with the faint, far-off scent of sea-air clinging to it, as if the paper had lain for a moment on some sun-warmed table near an open window, where salt and orange-blossom drifted in and out with the tide-breath. Edith’s hand—always hurrying, always turning corners too quickly—had dashed across the page with affectionate extravagance, as inconsequent as birdsong.

It began with rapture, and ran on without pausing to take breath.

“Oh, Margaret, it is worth a journey from England to see my boy! He is a superb little fellow, especially in his caps, and most especially in the one you sent him, you good, dainty-fingered, persevering little lady! Having made all the mothers here envious, I want to show him to somebody new, and hear a fresh set of admiring expressions; perhaps, that’s all the reason; perhaps it is not—nay, possibly, there is just a little cousinly love mixed with it; but I do want you so much to come here, Margaret! I’m sure it would be the very best thing for Aunt Hale’s health; everybody here is young and well, and our skies are always blue, and our sun always shines, and the band plays deliciously from morning till night; and, to come back to the burden of my ditty, my baby always smiles. I am constantly wanting you to draw him from me, Margaret. It does not signify what he is doing; that very thing is prettiest, gracefullest, best. I think I love him a great deal better than my husband, who is getting stout, and grumpy—what he calls ‘busy.’ No! he is not. He has just come in with news of such a charming picnic, given by the officers of the Hazard, at anchor in the bay below. Because he has brought in such a pleasant piece of news, I retract all I said just now. Did not somebody burn his hand for having said or done something he was sorry for? Well, I can’t burn mine, because it would hurt me, and the scar would be ugly; but I’ll retract all I said as fast as I can. Cosmo is quite as great a darling as baby, and not a bit stout, and as ungrumpy as ever husband was; only, sometimes he is very, very busy. I may say that without love—wifely duty— where was I?—I had something very particular to say, I know, once. Oh, it is this—Dearest Margaret!—you must come and see me; it would do Aunt Hale good, as I said before. Get the doctor to order it for her. Tell him that it’s the smoke of Milton that does her harm. I have no doubt it is that, really. Three months (you must not come for less) of this delicious climate—all sunshine, and grapes as common as blackberries, would quite cure her. I don’t ask my uncle—”

Here the lines tightened, as if Edith had felt her pen checked by a presence in the room; the handwriting grew more careful, the froth subsiding into decorum. Margaret could see it without being told—her father somewhere near, a quiet gravity pulling Edith’s words into better order.

“—because, I dare say, he disapproves of war, soldiers, and bands of music; at least, I know that many Dissenters are members of the Peace Society, and I am afraid he would not like to come; but, if he would, dear, pray say that Cosmo and I will do our best to make him happy; and I’ll hide up Cosmo’s red coat and sword, and make the band play all sorts of grave, solemn things; or, if they do play pomps and vanities, it shall be in double slow time. Dear Margaret, if he would like to accompany you and Aunt Hale, we will try and make it pleasant, though I’m rather afraid of any one who has done anything for conscience’ sake. You never did, I hope. Tell Aunt Hale not to bring any warm clothes, though I’m afraid it will be late in the year before you can come. But you have no idea of the heat here! I tried to wear my great beauty Indian shawl at a picnic. I kept myself up with proverbs as long as I could; ‘Pride must abide,’—and such wholesome pieces of pith; but it was no use. I was like mamma’s little dog Tiny with an elephant’s trappings on; smothered, hidden, killed with my finery; so I made it into a capital carpet for us all to sit down upon. Here’s this boy of mine, Margaret—if you don’t pack up your things as soon as you get this letter, and come straight off to see him, I shall think you’re descended from King Herod!”

Margaret let the sheet fall softly into her lap and sat quite still. The house around her seemed to contract into its familiar, muffled Milton quiet: a thin clink somewhere below of a fire-irons’ adjustment; Dixon’s tread on the stair—careful, yet too heavy ever to be thought light; and under everything, at a distance, the town’s incessant iron breath, a far grinding and throb that no closed curtain could quite deny. Edith’s world had sounded, in contrast, like brightness made audible—the “delicious” band-music, the laughter on a picnic cloth, the sea’s larger hush behind it all. Margaret longed, for one day only, to exchange her mother’s sick-room air for that easy sunshine, to feel youth return as simply as appetite returns when one steps from smoke into a clean wind.

Not yet twenty—and yet, in these last weeks, care had pressed on her so heavily that she felt old.

Then she read the letter again, and Edith’s very self rose before her—fluttering, affectionate, absurd, endearing—and Margaret laughed out, merrily and helplessly, as if the sound might shake off, for an instant, the weight upon her chest.

Mrs. Hale came in at that moment, leaning on Dixon’s arm. Margaret sprang up, her hands practised now in all the small ministries of illness—straightening a pillow, arranging the shawl so it would not slip, easing her mother down upon the sofa as if laying a tired child into bed. Mrs. Hale’s face had the worn translucence of long suffering; even her breath seemed a labour.

“What were you laughing at, Margaret?” she asked, when she had recovered from the exertion of settling herself.

“A letter I have had this morning from Edith. Shall I read it to you, mamma?”

Mrs. Hale’s eyes brightened a little—news from the child who had escaped all this—and Margaret read aloud. For a while the letter’s airy inconsequence did its work. Mrs. Hale smiled faintly, and kept stopping Margaret with questions—wondering what name Edith had given the boy, suggesting one after another, and reasons for each: a father’s name, a grandfather’s name, a saint’s, a fashionable one, a romantic one—each possibility turning her mind, for a moment, from her own weakness.

In the midst of these musings Mr. Thornton was announced.

He came in with fruit—peaches, their skins like soft bloom, as if they held the memory of summer and southern walls. He offered them with that grave gentleness Margaret had seen him use with her mother, the same steady kindness that seemed to him almost a point of honour. He could not—perhaps he would not—deny himself the chance of being in the same room as Margaret. Yet, as he entered, and his eyes took in everything at a glance—Mrs. Hale propped among cushions, Dixon hovering, Margaret near—he bowed to Margaret with a cold, distant formality, and afterwards behaved as though she had ceased to exist.

He spoke to Mrs. Hale, and to Mr. Hale when he came in, in tones softened from his usual strong decisiveness; he placed the fruit as if he were setting something precious within reach; he stayed a little, only long enough to offer this small attention and to say a few kindly words. Then, as he left, his grave offended eyes met Margaret’s for an instant in a farewell that had no warmth in it.

Margaret sat down again, silent, her colour gone. The room felt altered by his presence and his withdrawal—like a hearth when a log has been shifted, leaving the warmth uneven and the air suddenly full of draughts.

“Do you know, Margaret,” said Mrs. Hale, after a moment, “I really begin to like Mr. Thornton.”

Margaret did not answer at first.

“Well?” her mother persisted, with the fragile obstinacy of the sick.

Margaret forced out an icy little “Do you?”

“Yes! I think he is really getting quite polished in his manners.”

The word polished struck Margaret oddly—like the shine on something hard that has been rubbed to a brilliance. Her voice steadied.

“He is very kind and attentive—there is no doubt of that.”

“I wonder Mrs. Thornton never calls. She must know I am ill, because of the water-bed.”

“I dare say she hears how you are from her son.”

“Still, I should like to see her. You have so few friends here, Margaret.”

Margaret felt, with a sudden painful clearness, what lay beneath that simple sentence. It was not vanity in Mrs. Hale, nor mere loneliness; it was the instinct of a mother, already half withdrawing from the world, trying—tenderly, anxiously—to secure some other woman’s kindness around her daughter, as one might tuck extra blankets over a child before leaving the room for the last time.

But Margaret could not speak.

“Do you think,” Mrs. Hale went on, after a pause, “that you could go and ask Mrs. Thornton to come and see me? Only once—I don’t want to be troublesome.”

“I will do anything, if you wish it, mamma—but if—but when Frederick comes—”

The name fell into the room like a stone into still water.

“Ah, to be sure!” said Mrs. Hale; her hand tightened a little on the shawl at her throat. “We must keep our doors shut—we must let no one in. I hardly know whether I dare wish him to come or not. Sometimes I think I would rather not. Sometimes I have such frightful dreams about him.”

“Oh, mamma! we’ll take good care. I will put my arm in the bolt sooner than he should come to the slightest harm. Trust the care of him to me, mamma. I will watch over him like a lioness over her young.”

Mrs. Hale’s eyes filled, not with tears, but with that look of clinging dependence which pain and fear make in the helpless.

“When can we hear from him?”

“Not for a week yet, certainly—perhaps more.”

“We must send Martha away in good time. It would never do to have her here when he comes, and then send her off in a hurry.”

“Dixon is sure to remind us of that,” Margaret said. “I was thinking that, if we wanted any help in the house while he is here, we could perhaps get Mary Higgins. She is very slack of work, and is a good girl, and would take pains to do her best, I am sure, and would sleep at home, and need never come upstairs, so as to know who is in the house.”

“As you please. As Dixon pleases.” Then Mrs. Hale’s faint animation returned in a different direction, seizing on a small grievance as if it were safer than fear. “But, Margaret, don’t get to use these horrid Milton words. ‘Slack of work:’ it is a provincialism. What will your aunt Shaw say, if she hears you use it on her return?”

“Oh, mamma! don’t try and make a bugbear of aunt Shaw,” Margaret answered, and her laugh, though light, had an edge, like a spoon tapping thin china. “Edith picked up all sorts of military slang from Captain Lennox, and aunt Shaw never took any notice of it.”

“But yours is factory slang.”

“And if I live in a factory town, I must speak factory language when I want it. Why, mamma, I could astonish you with a great many words you never heard in your life. I don’t believe you know what a knobstick is.”

“Not I, child. I only know it has a very vulgar sound; and I don’t want to hear you using it.”

“Very well, dearest mother, I won’t. Only I shall have to use a whole explanatory sentence instead.”

“I don’t like this Milton,” Mrs. Hale said, sinking back. The familiar undertone of the town seemed to swell in Margaret’s ears at the words, as if the very walls were listening. “Edith is right enough in saying it’s the smoke that has made me so ill.”

Margaret started up. At that instant Mr. Hale entered. She had seen, of late, an uncertain impression forming in his mind—that perhaps the air of Milton had injured his wife’s health—and Margaret, with a quick fear, was desperate that nothing should deepen it into certainty. She could not tell whether he had heard Mrs. Hale’s last sentence. To forestall it, to cover it, she began speaking hurriedly, almost at random, catching at the nearest harmless thread.

“Mamma is accusing me of having picked up a great deal of vulgarity since we came to Milton.”

The word vulgarity, in Margaret’s meaning, had been no more than local phrases, the homely dialect of a place that had its own life and names. But behind Mr. Hale, just then entering, came Mr. Thornton.

Margaret felt, rather than saw, the change in him. His brow darkened, and something in his set face hardened at the very sound. She realised, with a hot rush of shame, how her careless sentence might strike him—how it could be heard as condemnation of the people and work that made Milton what it was, and of him as their representative. The sweetness in her—the instinct that hated to give pain where none was meant—urged her forward. She forced herself into a little greeting, and went on speaking, turning deliberately towards him, trying to make her meaning clear.

“Now, Mr. Thornton, though ‘knobstick’ has not a very pretty sound, is it not expressive? Could I do without it, in speaking of the thing it represents? If using local words is vulgar, I was very vulgar in the Forest,—was I not, mamma?”

It was unlike Margaret to thrust her conversation upon another; it came from anxiety, not vanity. And the moment she had finished speaking she blushed all over, conscious of herself, conscious of the effort, conscious—too—that he did not in the least take up her appeal. He seemed hardly to understand why she had said it at all. With a cold reserve of ceremonious movement, he passed her by and went straight to Mrs. Hale, as though Margaret’s voice were merely part of the room’s general sound, like the ticking of a clock.

The sight of him brought back to Margaret, with sudden sharpness, her mother’s wish: to see Mrs. Thornton—to draw, if possible, some thread of feminine kindness from that stern woman towards their house. Margaret sat in burning silence, vexed with herself, ashamed of her own awkwardness and of the strange difficulty she always had in keeping a steady, natural place when Mr. Thornton was present.

She heard her mother, slowly and timidly, ask him if Mrs. Thornton would come and see her—only once—soon; to-morrow, if it were possible. Mrs. Hale’s voice had that frail pleading note that illness brings, a note which, even to unwilling ears, is hard to resist.

Mr. Thornton promised that she should. He spoke a little longer—quietly, properly—and then he took his leave.

And when the door closed behind him, Margaret felt as if invisible chains had fallen away. She drew breath more freely; her voice, when she spoke to her parents, came back to its natural tone; even her hands seemed less clumsy.

He had never looked at her; and yet, in the very care with which he kept his eyes away, she read a knowledge of her—of where she sat, of where she moved—as exact as if he had been watching her all the while. If she spoke, he gave no sign of hearing; yet his next words to some one else would be shaped by what she had said, as if her speech had entered him in spite of himself. Sometimes he even answered her remark—but turned it, perversely, into an answer addressed to another person, as though her voice had not been the source.

It was not ignorance; it was wilfulness—wilful bad manners born of a deep offence.

And Margaret—who had believed herself merely indifferent—found her mind returning to him again and again. Not with what people called love; rather with regret that she had wounded him so deeply, and with a patient desire to come back to their former footing of antagonistic friendship. She understood now that, before all this, he had held a friend’s place in her regard, as he had in her father’s and mother’s.

There was, in her manner towards him in these days, a pretty humility, as if she were mutely apologising for the over-strong words that had sprung, in reaction, from the terrible scene of the riot. But he resented those words bitterly; they rang in his ears like a harsh phrase shouted over and over amid the din of looms. Proud of his own sense of justice, he compelled himself to every kindness he could offer to her parents; he even exulted in the power he showed in facing Margaret whenever he could think of any act that might give Mr. or Mrs. Hale pleasure. He told himself he disliked seeing her—told himself it was a duty, and nothing more.

He was mistaken.

To be in the room with her, and feel her presence—silent, vivid, inescapable—was a stinging pleasure. Yet he did not analyse himself; he mistook the very pulse of his own heart, and called it merely pride and offence.

Mrs. Thornton came the next morning with the rigid punctuality of a woman who believed time itself should obey her. She had come because her son had asked it as a personal favour, and because she had yielded—tight-lipped, as if yielding were a kind of hunger she would not admit to feeling.

All the way, her mind had been marching through its old grievances. She told herself—again—that the Hales brought only disorder into a house that had stood straight without them; that Mr. Hale’s learning was a useless weight, and the dead languages dead for good reason. She had said as much to her son the night before, with that harsh relish she had when she thought she was telling a truth no one else dared to speak. He had listened as he always did when his mother flung her judgments like stones: silently, letting them fall where they might. But when she had finished, and imagined she had moved him, he had only repeated, in his curt way, the time he wished her to go.

So she went—proud, offended, and secretly a little pleased with him for insisting. She exaggerated, as she walked, his perseverance into some extraordinary goodness, and her compliance into a sacrifice.

And then she entered the sick-room.

Whatever pride she had carried in like armour seemed suddenly absurd before that bed. Mrs. Hale lay there as if the night had drained her. In one short space of hours suffering had taken a great visible stride; the face—once soft with timid graces—had become gray and hollow, and the skin, drawn tight, seemed too thin for the bones beneath. Even the air of the room had changed: not merely warm and close, but steeped in that faint, sick sweetness of exhausted breath and cooling tea, of linen that has been turned often and hands that have been washed often. There were the small sounds—so few and so sharp they seemed to cut the silence: the faint click of a cup set down, the brush of a dress, the delicate hush with which Dixon moved like a creature trained to respect pain.

Mrs. Thornton, strong with health, with her firm step and full pulse, felt the room take the strength out of her as a wind takes heat from a coal. Mrs. Hale did not open her eyes at once. Yet her face, so still, showed consciousness; and when she at last looked up, heavy tears lay on her eyelashes like dew.

Her hand groped weakly over the bedclothes, searching—blindly—for something steady. Mrs. Thornton, almost against her will, put her own large, warm fingers where they were sought. Mrs. Hale’s touch was light, like a bird resting.

“Margaret—you have a daughter—my sister is in Italy,” she whispered, words broken and thin as threads. “My child will be without a mother;—in a strange place,—if I die—will you—”

She could not finish. But her eyes fixed themselves on Mrs. Thornton’s face with such desperate entreaty that even that stern countenance could not evade it.

For a minute Mrs. Thornton’s features remained hard. A cloud crossed them—swift, dark. Not for her son, not for her living daughter, did her heart loosen; but for a ghost. Something in the room—the careful ordering, the mother’s helplessness—brought back, as sudden as a smell carried on heat, the memory of her own child long dead in infancy, that had once lain so small in her arms. The recollection melted the ice in her, though no softness appeared in her voice.

“You wish me to be a friend to Miss Hale,” she said, measured and distinct.

Mrs. Hale pressed her hand, unable to speak.

“I will be a true friend, if circumstances require it,” Mrs. Thornton continued, as if weighing each word on a scale. “Not a tender friend. That I cannot be. It is not my nature to show affection even where I feel it; nor do I volunteer advice in general. Still—at your request—if it will be any comfort to you, I will promise you.”

It was as if she were signing a bond.

“I promise,” she said again, with grave severity, “that in any difficulty in which Miss Hale—”

“Call her Margaret!” gasped Mrs. Hale, a small passionate insistence, like the last assertion of a mother’s right.

“In which she comes to me for help,” Mrs. Thornton amended, “I will help her with every power I have, as if she were my own daughter. I also promise that if ever I see her doing what I think is wrong—”

“But Margaret never does wrong—not wilfully wrong,” pleaded Mrs. Hale, her breath fluttering with the effort.

Mrs. Thornton went on as if she had not heard; there was something merciless in her honesty, something that made it feel more secure than kindness.

“If ever I see her doing what I believe to be wrong—such wrong not touching me or mine, in which case I might be supposed to have an interested motive—I will tell her of it faithfully and plainly, as I should wish my own daughter to be told.”

The pause that followed was long and full. Mrs. Hale’s mind, weakened, caught at the promise and yet felt the spaces within it—the reservations she could not name. Still it steadied her, as a hard chair steadies a fainting person better than a soft pillow.

“I thank you,” she murmured at last. “I pray God to bless you. I shall never see you again in this world. But my last words are, I thank you for your promise of kindness to my child.”

“Not kindness,” Mrs. Thornton replied—truthful even there, even then.

Perhaps the words were not heard; perhaps mercy lay in the dying woman’s failure to take them in. Mrs. Thornton pressed the languid hand once more and left without seeing anyone, as if she feared that one other human face might demand some softness she had not the habit of paying out.

While this took place upstairs, Margaret and Dixon were below, heads bent together like conspirators over a kitchen table that smelled faintly of yesterday’s bread and the clean sharpness of soap.

Frederick might come any day. A letter might arrive—might already be on its way—but he would follow quickly, letter or no letter; Margaret’s heart had known that with the surety of hunger. Yet his coming must be hidden as if it were a crime.

Martha must be sent away at once on her holiday; Dixon must keep stern guard at the front door, and admit only the few visitors who ever came—and those to Mr. Hale’s room downstairs, for Mrs. Hale’s worsening gave excuse enough. If Mary Higgins was called in to help in the kitchen, she must hear and see as little as possible; Frederick, if named at all, should be “Mr. Dickinson.” But Mary’s own slow incuriosity was their best lock and key.

They resolved Martha should go that afternoon. Margaret wished, with a pang, that it had been done the day before; it might seem strange to grant a holiday when her mistress lay so ill. Yet necessity presses its own logic upon the scruples of the tender-hearted.

All that afternoon Margaret had to be strong on borrowed strength. Mr. Hale, broken by fear, swung between hope and despair as a pendulum swings between two truths. In the spaces between pain, he would persuade himself the worst was over—that the respite meant recovery. Then, when the paroxysms returned, each more cruel than the last, they were fresh agonies, sharpened by disappointment.

He could not bear his study; he sat in the drawing-room, head buried in his folded arms on the table, as if he could hide from grief by not looking at it. Margaret sat by the window watching the lamps bloom one by one in the street, though she saw nothing but darkness thickened by her own thoughts. The house seemed to have drawn in its breath and held it. Dixon was with Mrs. Hale. Martha had gone. No one moved to fetch candles; dusk gathered like soot.

Margaret did not like to leave her father even to light the house, fearing that if her presence were withdrawn he might break into some violence of sorrow with no one to steady him. Yet she was thinking she must at least see to the kitchen fire—there was no one else—when the bell rang.

It was not loud, but it was pulled hard; the wires jingled through the house with a shaken, nervous music. That sound—so small, and yet so startling in the hush—seemed to strike into her bones. She rose, passed her father—who did not stir—and came back to kiss him, tenderly, on the temple. He neither moved nor seemed aware. Then she went down through the dark, her hand on the banister, feeling her way like a blind person.

At the door, the street’s light made a pale rectangle on the floor. A tall figure stood between her and that light. Dixon would have put the chain on before opening; but Margaret’s mind, crowded with grief and plans, had no room left for fear.

The man turned at the sound of the latch.

“Is this Mr. Hale’s?” he asked. The voice was clear and full and delicate, and something in it—some remembered cadence—made Margaret’s body shake.

She could not answer at once. Her breath caught; then the name broke out of her as if it had been waiting behind her teeth all these years.

“Frederick!”

She stretched out both hands to seize his; to draw him in; to make him real.

“Oh, Margaret!” he said, and after they kissed, he held her by the shoulders, keeping her a little away as if even in that dim hall he could read the truth in her face faster than she could speak it.

“My mother! Is she alive?”

“Yes,” Margaret whispered, and the word seemed to taste like prayer. “She is alive, dear, dear brother! She—as ill as she can be she is; but alive! She is alive!”

“Thank God,” he said, with a breath that trembled.

“Papa is utterly prostrate with this great grief.”

“You expect me, don’t you?”

“No. We have had no letter.”

“Then I have come before it. But my mother knows I am coming.”

“Oh! we all knew you would come.” She took his hand again, as if she must keep hold of him. “But wait a little. Step in here. Give me your hand. What is this?—your carpet-bag. Dixon has shut the shutters; but this is papa’s study. I can take you to a chair to rest for a few minutes while I go and tell him.”

She groped for the taper and the lucifer matches. When the small flame sprang up, the first thin light made them suddenly visible to each other; and she felt shy, foolishly, as if they were strangers. She saw his face was darker than she remembered, the complexion swarthy as if the sun of other seas had baked it into him; and his eyes—long-cut, blue, and oddly bright—lifted to meet hers with a quick, amused consciousness that they were both, in that instant, taking stock. Their glance held a moment of kinship that needed no words.

Margaret’s heart felt lighter even as she ran upstairs; the sorrow remained, but it was no longer solitary. She could face her father now with a new tool in her hands—the spell of good news.

He was still as she had left him, bowed over the table like a broken man.

“Papa,” she said, and put her arms round his neck, lifting his weary head with a gentle insistence until it rested against her, and she could make him look into her eyes. “Papa! Guess who is here!”

He stared at her. The idea flickered across his face—hope and disbelief in the same breath—and then was rejected as a madness.

He threw himself forward again, hiding his face. Margaret bent close and heard the whisper, raw with fear.

“I don’t know. Don’t tell me it is Frederick—not Frederick. I cannot bear it—I am too weak. And his mother is dying!”

And he began to cry aloud, like a child—wailing, helpless. It was so unlike what Margaret had imagined—so far from the joy she had wanted to give him—that a sickness of disappointment rose in her throat. For a moment she could not speak. Then she changed her tone, made it careful, as if handling glass.

“Papa, it is Frederick. Think of mamma—how glad she will be! And for her sake, how glad we ought to be. For his sake, too—our poor, poor boy!”

Her father did not lift his head, but she felt him trying to understand the fact, as one feels someone in the dark reaching for a wall.

“Where is he?” he asked at last, face still hidden.

“In your study. Quite alone. I lighted the taper and ran up to tell you. He is quite alone, and will be wondering why—”

“I will go to him,” Mr. Hale broke in, and rose with a sudden desperate purpose. He leaned on Margaret’s arm, not as on a daughter’s, but as on a guide’s.

She led him to the study door; but her own spirits, so strained, so shaken by relief, could not bear the sight of the meeting. She turned away and ran upstairs, and cried, sobbing as if her very body had been waiting for permission to break. For days she had not dared to yield; now the tears were like water let out of a sluice. Frederick was here—her one precious brother—safe among them again. She stopped suddenly, almost frightened by the ease of believing it. Had she dreamt?

She opened her door and listened. No voices reached her. She went down, softly, and stood by the study door. Then she heard the low buzz of two voices together, and that was enough. She fled to the kitchen with the same restless need to do something with her hands.

She stirred up the fire; she set coals; she coaxed a flame as carefully as if it were life itself. She lit the house, room by room, candle by candle, and the smell of warm tallow and fresh struck match-heads threaded through the earlier scent of grief. She began preparing something for Frederick: not merely sustenance, but welcome—bread and butter cut thick, tea strong enough to taste through travel-weariness, whatever the cupboard could offer. Even in that mourning house, she could not help noticing how hunger made its own clean demand, how the body insists. The very act of spreading butter—firm, pale, and cool—over bread that yielded softly under the knife gave her a steadiness no reasoning could.

How fortunate her mother slept. Margaret knew it from the thin line of candlelight thrust under Mrs. Hale’s door, and from Dixon’s hushed movements beyond. Let Frederick be warmed and fed; let the first sharpness of meeting his father pass; let their hearts settle before the greater tremor of a dying mother’s joy.

When all was ready, Margaret opened the study door and entered like a serving-maid, arms extended with a heavy tray. She was proud—fiercely, tenderly proud—of serving him.

But Frederick sprang up at once and took the tray from her hands, as if the gesture were a promise: you shall not carry this alone now.

They arranged the little meal together. They spoke little; their fingers brushed; their eyes did the talking in that swift, intimate language of blood that needs no translation. The fire in the study had gone out, leaving a cold, dead smell of ash. Margaret knelt to lay kindling, trying to do it quietly, because every noise seemed a potential cruelty to the sick room above.

“Dixon says it is a gift to light a fire,” she said softly, “not an art to be acquired.”

“Poeta nascitur, non fit,” murmured Mr. Hale; languid, yes, but the old habit of quotation was a sound from former life, and Margaret felt a strange comfort in it—the house remembering its own voice for an instant.

“Dear old Dixon!” Frederick said, with a sudden brightness. “How we shall kiss each other! She used to kiss me, and then look in my face to be sure I was the right person, and then set to again. But, Margaret—what a bungler you are! I never saw such a little awkward good-for-nothing pair of hands. Run away and wash them, ready to cut bread-and-butter for me, and leave the fire. I’ll manage it. Lighting fires is one of my natural accomplishments.”

So Margaret went, and washed her hands, and came back; and passed in and out of the room in a glad restlessness that could not be satisfied with sitting still. The more he wanted—tea, bread, more coal—the more pleased she was. He understood without asking. The joy was stolen in the house of mourning, and therefore tasted sharper, like a mouthful of something sweet when one has been living on bitterness. Beneath it lay the knowledge of what was coming, like a heavy pan set on the back of the stove, warming slowly.

In the middle of this, they heard Dixon’s foot on the stairs.

Mr. Hale started from his dreamy watching, and a strange anxiety seized him—an instinctive need to conceal Frederick from any entering eyes, even Dixon’s faithful ones. He stood and faced the door as if someone hostile might burst in. Margaret’s heart shivered. A new fear had entered their lives, and it had a sound: it made every tread on the stairs ring like threat.

She caught Frederick’s arm and held it tight, her jaw set with a sternness that surprised even herself. Yet they knew the step: measured, heavy, familiar. They heard Dixon walk the length of the passage—then into the kitchen.

Margaret rose.

“I will go to her, and tell her,” she said. “And I shall hear how mamma is.”

Mrs. Hale was awake. She rambled at first, the mind wandering like a hand searching in darkness. They gave her tea—carefully, with the spoon against the cup kept from clinking, as if even that tiny metallic note might hurt. The warmth revived her a little, though she did not care to speak. It seemed best that the night should pass before she was told Frederick had come. Dr. Donaldson’s visit later would bring excitement enough; perhaps he would advise how to prepare her for seeing her son. Frederick was in the house; that knowledge was a kind of medicine, ready to be administered at the right moment.

Margaret could not be still. It relieved her to help Dixon with every preparation for “Master Frederick.” In the kitchen the fire made its own living noise: coal shifting, a soft roar when the draught caught, the kettle beginning its low prelude. Against the remembered clatter of Milton streets and mill-bells, these domestic sounds were a refuge—an older music, one that held the mind together instead of tearing it into nervous fragments. Margaret thought, with sudden bitterness, how the town’s industrial din had trained them all to start at every sharp sound, as if danger came always with noise; and how in this sick-house they were fighting for quiet as for breath.

Each glimpse she caught into the room where Frederick sat with her father—talking, she knew not what, nor cared—gave her strength. Her time for listening and speaking would come; she was certain of that. Meanwhile she took in her brother’s appearance and liked it. The delicacy of his features was redeemed from any softness by the swarthiness of his skin, by the quick intensity that crossed his mouth and eyes. Most often he looked merry; but at moments, in a flash, his expression hardened into something fierce—latent passion surfacing like flame when the lid is lifted from a pot. It was not dogged, not vindictive; rather that instantaneous wildness one sees in children of southern climates, a heat that vanishes as quickly as it appears. It made her a little afraid of the violence of his impulses, but it did not make her recoil. She trusted him at once; and their intercourse, from the beginning, was charming.

He understood their father and mother with an ease Margaret had forgotten was possible—he knew their weaknesses and their habits of pain, and yet moved among them with a careless freedom that never bruised. He seemed to know, without being told, when his natural brilliancy might jar, and when it might soothe. When gaiety would be cruelty, he became patient and watchful, an admirable nurse. He knew how to hold a cup, how to move a chair without scraping it, how to quiet his very breath. That kind of care is its own skill, learned not from books but from love.

And he spoke often of their childish days in the New Forest—of Helstone as if he had carried its green hush in his pocket all these years, taking it out at need, like a charm. He had not forgotten her; he had not forgotten the place. Margaret could talk to him of it without fear of wearying him, and the old names tasted in her mouth like something homely and good—words from a dialect of the heart that no one else in Milton spoke.

She had been afraid of him before he came. Seven or eight years had changed her so much; she had imagined his wandering life must have substituted another Frederick for the tall stripling in his middy’s uniform. But absence had oddly made them nearer. They met now not as child and grown brother, but almost as equals—two people bearing the same sorrow, the same secret, the same longing.

So the weight lifted a little from her. Other light she had none.

For a few hours after Mrs. Hale was told, she rallied on seeing her son. She sat with his hand in hers and would not let it go even when sleep came. When he tried to move, she tightened her faint fingers with surprising strength. Margaret had to feed him like a baby—lifting bread to his mouth—rather than he should disturb their mother by withdrawing even a finger. Mrs. Hale woke while they were thus engaged; she slowly turned her head on the pillow and smiled, understanding at once, as mothers do.

“I am very selfish,” she said. “But it will not be for long.”

Frederick bent and kissed the feeble hand that held him prisoner, as if he were grateful for the bondage.

This tranquillity could not last. Dr. Donaldson told Margaret so plainly. Not many days—perhaps not many hours. His voice, kind as it was, carried the hard discipline of truth.

After he had gone, Margaret stole down to Frederick. During the visit he had been commanded to remain concealed in the back parlour—Dixon’s room usually, now given up to him like a hiding-place in a house that had become a fortress.

Margaret repeated what the doctor had said.

“I don’t believe it,” Frederick cried. “She is very ill; she may be dangerously ill, in immediate danger too; but I can’t imagine she could be as she is if she were on the point of death. Margaret! She should have other advice—some London doctor. Have you never thought of that?”

“Yes,” Margaret answered. “More than once. But I don’t believe it would do any good. And we have not the money to bring any great London surgeon down. Besides, I am sure Dr. Donaldson is only second in skill to the very best—if, indeed, he is second to them.”

Frederick began to pace, impatience in every step, like a man walking the quarter-deck while storms gather.

“I have credit in Cadiz,” he said, “but none here, owing to this wretched change of name. Why did my father leave Helstone? That was the blunder.”

“It was no blunder,” Margaret said gloomily. “And above all possible chances, avoid letting papa hear anything like what you have just been saying. I can see he is tormenting himself already with the idea that mamma would never have been ill if we had stayed at Helstone—and you don’t know papa’s agonising power of self-reproach.”

Frederick walked away, then stopped sharply and faced her. He looked at her drooping posture, the wetness on her cheeks she had not known she was showing.

“My little Margaret,” he said, and drew her to him with a tenderness that made her feel, for the first time in days, not solely responsible. “Let us hope as long as we can. Poor little woman! What—is this face all wet with tears? I will hope. I will, in spite of a thousand doctors. Bear up, Margaret, and be brave enough to hope!”

She tried to answer, but her voice choked. When words came they were low.

“I must try to be meek enough to trust. Oh, Frederick! mamma was getting to love me so. And I was getting to understand her. And now comes death to snap us asunder!”

“Come, come, come!” Frederick said, as if briskness could beat back fate for an hour. “Let us go upstairs and do something, rather than waste time that may be so precious. Thinking has, many a time, made me sad, darling; but doing never did in all my life. My theory is a sort of parody on the maxim of ‘Get money, my son, honestly if you can; but get money.’ My precept is: ‘Do something, my sister; do good if you can; but, at any rate, do something.’”

“Not excluding mischief,” Margaret said, and a faint smile—thin as a slice of bread in famine, yet real—trembled through her tears.

The October morning came in upon Milton like an unbidden guest who had forgotten to wipe his boots. It was not the country’s October, with its tender pearl-grey veils that lift as the sun warms the hedgerows into colour; it was the town’s—heavy with fog that seemed to have learned its weight from the factory chimneys, a damp pressing on brick and skin alike, and turning every sound duller. Even the street-cries came as if muffled under wet cloth; the distant clank of iron and the faint, ceaseless breath of machinery threaded through the mist, a harsh counterpoint to the hush within the Hales’ little house.

Margaret moved from room to room with a languor that was not idleness, but the fatigue of a mind that must do duty for three. Dixon had the shutters half-opened, letting in a weak, colourless light; and Margaret helped as she could—straightening chair-backs, smoothing a coverlet, placing things with a kind of desperate exactness, as if the proper order of a breakfast-table might keep the world from further disorder. Her eyes smarted and blurred, not from smoke, but from tears that would come and go without asking leave. She had not the leisure for any full abandonment to grief. While her father and brother were lost in it, she must be the hand that measured and the voice that decided.

Dixon had been making the room as homely as she could: the fire bright and crackling, its resinous scent sharp against the damp; the kettle singing with that thin, domestic insistence which, on other mornings, had been comfort enough to summon everyone to life. The teacups stood ready. Toast was laid by the fender to keep warm, and its smell—brown crust and butter beginning to melt—rose up like an appeal to ordinary appetite; but nothing about this day had any right to be ordinary.

Margaret took one last look round, longing that cheerfulness might be possible, and hating it when it appeared. The contrast between the bright hearth and the dull weight within her made her throat ache. She dropped to her knees by the sofa and hid her face in the cushions so no one might hear the sound she could not keep back.

A hand, not gentle by nature yet softened now, touched her shoulder.

“Come, Miss Hale—come, my dear,” said Dixon. There was an unusual tremor under the primness. “You must not give way, or where shall we all be? There is not another person in the house fit to give a direction of any kind, and there is so much to be done. There’s who’s to manage the funeral; and who’s to come to it; and where it’s to be; and all to be settled. Master Frederick’s like one crazed with crying, and master never was a good one for settling; and, poor gentleman, he goes about now as if he was lost. It’s bad enough, my dear, I know; but death comes to us all; and you’re well off never to have lost any friend till now.”

Perhaps she was. Yet this loss seemed solitary, unmatched—an eclipse that blotted out other measures of sorrow. Dixon’s commonplaces gave no comfort; but the tenderness in her voice—so rare from her—went straight to Margaret’s heart. For that tenderness’ sake, as much as for any resolution of her own, she forced herself upright, managed a wan smile in answer to Dixon’s anxious gaze, and went to summon her father and Frederick.

Mr. Hale came as if called from a distance only he could see—moving with the unconscious obedience of a sleep-walker, whose eyes are open on another world. Frederick entered more briskly, with a cheerfulness strained into place; he grasped Margaret’s hand, looked once into her face, and the strain broke. Tears came as if they had been waiting behind his eyes for permission.

Through breakfast she talked of little nothings—of the fire, of the fog, of some trifling need in the house—because she could not bear that their thoughts should settle too heavily on the last meal taken with that perpetual listening for a sound from the sick-room. The kettle’s song seemed almost indecent now, too lively for so solemn a table; and outside, as if in rebuke, the town’s muffled roar went on—wheels, distant shouts, a faint metallic beat—Milton insisting on its own business while their private world fell in.

Afterwards, she tried to speak to her father of the funeral. He assented to all she suggested, and in his listlessness contradicted himself without knowing it; his “yes” had no more weight than a leaf. Margaret obtained no real decision; and she was turning away to consult Dixon when Mr. Hale motioned her back with a feeble urgency.

“Ask Mr. Bell,” he said, hollow-voiced.

“Mr. Bell?” She was startled. “Mr. Bell of Oxford?”

“Mr. Bell,” he repeated. “Yes. He was my groom’s-man.”

She understood in a moment how memory had leaped back to the old phrase and the old friend. “I will write to-day,” she answered; and he sank again into that stunned passivity, like a man who has used his last strength on a single word.

The hours went on in a whirl of mournful errands—messages, arrangements, the necessary commerce with strangers which death demands. It seemed to Margaret that the house had become a place where the living were only the hands of duty. Toward evening Dixon came to her with the air of one who has acted on her own authority.

“I’ve done it, miss,” she began, speaking quickly, as if she feared to lose her courage. “I was really afraid for master, that he’d have a stroke with grief. He’s been all this day with poor missus; and when I’ve listened at the door, I’ve heard him talking to her, and talking to her, as if she was alive. When I went in he would be quite quiet, but all in a maze like. So I thought to myself, he ought to be roused; and if it gives him a shock at first, it will, maybe, be the better for him afterwards. So I’ve been and told him, that I don’t think it’s safe for Master Frederick to be here. And I don’t.”

Margaret’s heart tightened. “Why? What has happened?”

“It was only on Tuesday, when I was out, that I met a Southampton man—the first I’ve seen since I came to Milton; they don’t make their way much up here, I think. Well, it was young Leonards, old Leonards the draper’s son, as great a scamp as ever lived—who plagued his father almost to death, and then ran off to sea. I never could abide him. He was in the Orion at the same time as Frederick, I know; though I don’t recollect if he was there at the mutiny.”

“Did he know you?” Margaret asked, suddenly eager, the question tasting bitter in her mouth.

“Why, that’s the worst of it. I don’t believe he would have known me but for my being such a fool as to call out his name. He were a Southampton man, in a strange place, or else I should never have been so ready to call cousins with him, a nasty, good-for-nothing-fellow. Says he, ‘Miss Dixon! who would ha’ thought of seeing you here? But perhaps I mistake, and you’re Miss Dixon no longer?’ So I told him he might still address me as an unmarried lady, though if I hadn’t been so particular, I’d had good chances of matrimony. He was polite enough: ‘He couldn’t look at me and doubt me.’ But I were not to be caught with such chaff from such a fellow as him, and so I told him; and, by way of being even, I asked him after his father (who I knew had turned him out of doors), as if they were the best friends as ever was.”

Dixon’s indignation made her voice ring sharper than she perhaps intended; then she lowered it, as if the very walls might carry sound out into the street.

“So then, to spite me—for you see we were getting savage, for all we were so civil to each other—he began to inquire after Master Frederick, and said, what a scrape he’d got into, and how he’d be hung for mutiny if ever he were caught, and how a hundred pound reward had been offered for catching him, and what a disgrace he had been to his family—all to spite me, you see, my dear, because before now I’ve helped old Mr. Leonards to give George a good rating, down in Southampton.”

Margaret felt as if the thick town fog had crept into the room and laid itself upon her chest. “What did you say? Did you—”

“So I said, there were other families as I knew, who had far more cause to blush for their sons, and to be thankful if they could think they were earning an honest living far away from home. To which he made answer, like the impudent chap he is, that he were in a confidential situation, and if I knew of any young man who had been so unfortunate as to lead vicious courses, and wanted to turn steady, he’d have no objection to lend him his patronage. He, indeed! Why, he’d corrupt a saint. I’ve not felt so bad myself for years as when I were standing talking to him the other day. I could have cried to think I couldn’t spite him better, for he kept smiling in my face, as if he took all my compliments for earnest; and I couldn’t see that he minded what I said in the least, while I was mad with all his speeches.”

“Did you tell him anything about us—about Frederick?” Margaret pressed, her voice low.

“Not I,” said Dixon, with fierce pride. “He had never the grace to ask where I was staying; and I shouldn’t have told him if he had asked. Nor did I ask him what his precious situation was. He was waiting for a bus, and just then it drove up, and he hailed it. But, to plague me to the last, he turned back before he got in, and said, ‘If you can help me to trap Lieutenant Hale, Miss Dixon, we’ll go partners in the reward. I know you’d like to be my partner, now wouldn’t you? Don’t be shy, but say yes.’ And he jumped on the bus, and I saw his ugly face leering at me with a wicked smile to think how he’d had the last word of plaguing.”

The words left a taste like iron on Margaret’s tongue. In the street beyond, a cart rattled over stones; a distant shout rose and fell; somewhere, a door banged—each sound now seemed an enemy, a signal that Milton was wide awake and watchful.

“Have you told Frederick?” she asked.

“No,” Dixon answered. “There was so much else to think about that I did not dwell on it all. But when I saw master sitting so stiff, and with his eyes so glazed and sad, I thought it might rouse him to have to think of Master Frederick in hiding, he would have to go, poor fellow, before Mr. Bell came.”

“Oh, I’m not afraid of Mr. Bell,” said Margaret quickly; “but I am afraid of this Leonards. I must tell Frederick. What did he look like?”

“A bad-looking fellow, I can assure you, miss. Whiskers such as I should be ashamed to wear—they are so red. And for all he said he’d got a confidential situation, he was dressed in fustian just like a working-man.”

It was enough. The necessity sprang up like a knife: Frederick must go.

Go—now, when he had vaulted back into his place among them as if he had never been absent; when his very care for the dying and his sorrow for the dead had bound him by a peculiar tie—those fierce, sacred attachments formed around loss. Go—when their grief had made them a small island in a loud, indifferent town, and he had been the strongest rock of it.

Margaret sat by the drawing-room fire, staring into the coals that crumbled and renewed, as if they could teach her how to endure. Her father moved restlessly, shifting as though the chair pricked him; this new fear was pressing on him too, though he had not yet spoken it aloud. The house held itself in that strained quiet where every footfall is heard, every small sound takes on meaning: the soft scrape of Dixon’s shoes in the passage; the faint clink of a spoon set down too carefully; the sullen far-off pulse of industry that never stopped.

Frederick came in at last, his brightness dimmed, though the wildest violence of grief had passed. He went straight to Margaret and kissed her forehead, as if the gesture were both blessing and apology.

“How wan you look, Margaret!” he said under his breath. “You have been thinking of everybody, and no one has thought of you. Lie on this sofa—there is nothing for you to do.”

“That is the worst,” she answered, in a sad whisper.

Still, she obeyed, letting her tired limbs sink into the cushions. He drew a shawl over her feet with an odd tenderness, then sat down on the floor beside her, close as when they were children. Their voices, when they spoke, were kept low, as if loud speech might break what little composure remained in the house.

Margaret told him Dixon’s story. As she described the red whiskers and the leering promise of partnership in betrayal, she watched her brother’s face harden. He gave a long, low whew—half dismay, half anger.

“I should just like to have it out with that young fellow. A worse sailor was never on board ship—nor a much worse man either,” Frederick said, his voice sharpened by old contempt. “I declare, Margaret—you know the circumstances of the whole affair?”

“Yes. Mamma told me.”

“Well, when all the sailors who were good for anything were indignant with our captain, this fellow to curry favour—pah! And to think of his being here! Oh, if he’d a notion I was within twenty miles of him, he’d ferret me out to pay all old grudges. I’d rather anybody had the hundred pounds they think I am worth than that rascal. What a pity poor old Dixon could not be persuaded to give me up, and make a provision for her old age!”

“Oh, Frederick, hush! Don’t talk so.”

Mr. Hale had come towards them; his face was eager and trembling. He had overheard enough. Taking Frederick’s hand in both of his, he spoke as a man who forces himself to pronounce sentence.

“My boy, you must go. It is very bad—but I see you must. You have done all you could—you have been a comfort to her.”

“Oh, papa, must he go?” Margaret pleaded, though the pleading fought against her own clear knowledge.

Frederick’s mouth twisted in a bitter smile. “I declare, I’ve a good mind to face it out, and stand my trial. If I could only pick up my evidence! I cannot endure the thought of being in the power of such a blackguard as Leonards. I could almost have enjoyed—in other circumstances—this stolen visit: it has had all the charm which the Frenchwoman attributed to forbidden pleasures.”

“One of the earliest things I can remember,” Margaret said, the memory rising strangely like a hearth-smell from far back, “was your being in some great disgrace, Fred, for stealing apples. We had plenty of our own—trees loaded with them; but some one had told you that stolen fruit tasted sweetest, which you took au pied de la lettre, and off you went a-robbing. You have not changed your feelings much since then.”

Frederick gave a short breath that might have been a laugh on any other day; but it died almost at once.

“Yes—you must go,” Mr. Hale repeated, answering the question Margaret had asked some time before, as if he had only just heard it. His mind clung to the one necessity; the turns of their talk seemed to cost him effort he could not afford.

Brother and sister looked at each other, and in that swift moment a whole understanding passed—quick as taste, like the first sharpness of grief on the tongue. Their sympathy could not be put into phrases; it lived only in a glance, and it would be theirs no longer when he went. The thought went round and round in both, like a refrain in a familiar old song, until it lost itself in sadness.

Frederick shook it off first, forcing the talk into safer channels.

“Do you know, Margaret, I was very nearly giving both Dixon and myself a good fright this afternoon. I was in my bedroom; I had heard a ring at the front door, but I thought the ringer must have done his business and gone away long ago; so I was on the point of making my appearance in the passage, when, as I opened my room door, I saw Dixon coming downstairs; and she frowned and kicked me into hiding again. I kept the door open, and heard a message given to some man that was in my father’s study, and that then went away. What could it have been? Some of the shopmen?”

“Very likely,” Margaret replied, indifferently; her mind was full of other footsteps, other rings, other men at doors.

“There was a little quiet man who came up for orders about two o’clock.”

“But this was not a little man—a great powerful fellow; and it was past four when he was here.”

“It was Mr. Thornton,” said Mr. Hale.

“Mr. Thornton!” Margaret repeated, surprised in spite of herself. “I thought—”

“Well, little one, what did you think?” Frederick asked, because she stopped.

“Oh—only,” she said, colouring and looking straight at him, “I fancied you meant some one of a different class, not a gentleman; somebody come on an errand.”

“He looked like someone of that kind,” Frederick answered carelessly. “I took him for a shopman, and he turns out a manufacturer.”

Margaret was silent. The remembrance of her own first mistake—how she had spoken and judged before she knew—came back with a sting. It was natural, she told herself; and yet she felt an unreasonable annoyance, an unwillingness to let Frederick keep that superficial picture.

Mr. Hale went on, glad perhaps to speak of any kindness that touched their grief. “He came to offer any assistance in his power, I believe. But I could not see him. I told Dixon to ask him if he would like to see you—I think I asked her to find you, and you would go to him. I don’t know what I said.”

“He has been a very agreeable acquaintance, has he not?” Frederick asked, tossing the question as if anyone might catch it.

“A very kind friend,” Margaret answered, when her father did not.

Frederick was quiet a moment, then spoke with a sudden gravity. “Margaret, it is painful to think I can never thank those who have shown you kindness. Your acquaintances and mine must be separate. Unless, indeed, I run the chances of a court-martial, or unless you and my father would come to Spain.”

The suggestion was thrown lightly; then, as if he could no longer keep the secret in, he plunged forward, colouring like a girl.

“You don’t know how I wish you would. I have a good position—the chance of a better. That Dolores Barbour that I was telling you of, Margaret—I only wish you knew her; I am sure you would like—no, love is the right word, like is so poor—you would love her, father, if you knew her. She is not eighteen; but if she is in the same mind another year, she is to be my wife. Mr. Barbour won’t let us call it an engagement. But if you would come you would find friends everywhere, besides Dolores. Think of it, father. Margaret be on my side.”

“No—no more removals for me,” Mr. Hale said, and his voice, though low, had an iron fixity. “One has cost me my wife. No more removals in this life. She will be here; and here will I stay out my appointed time.”

“Oh, Frederick,” Margaret said, turning eagerly to what could still be hopeful, “tell us more about her. I never thought of this; but I am so glad. You will have some one to love and care for you out there. Tell us all about it.”

“In the first place, she is a Roman Catholic,” Frederick replied. “That’s the only objection I anticipated. But my father’s change of opinion—nay, Margaret, don’t sigh.”

She could not help it. Before the talk ended she had reason to sigh more deeply. Frederick, in fact if not yet in open profession, was Roman Catholic too. It cast a backward light on his letters—on the faintness of his expressed sympathy when his father had left the Church of England. She had once attributed it to a sailor’s careless temper; now she saw it was the pull of his own tending away from the form into which he had been baptized, though toward a direction opposite to their father’s. How much love had shaped that change Frederick himself could not have said; but Margaret heard in his voice that mingling of conviction and passion which makes creed part of a man’s flesh and blood.

She let that branch of the subject drop at last; there were enough divisions already. Returning to the engagement, she looked at it with a different steadiness.

“But for her sake, Fred, you surely will try and clear yourself of the exaggerated charges brought against you, even if the charge of mutiny itself be true. If there were to be a court-martial, and you could find your witnesses, you might, at any rate, show your disobedience to authority was because that authority was unworthily exercised.”

Mr. Hale roused himself to listen, his eyes fixed on Frederick with anxious hunger for the answer.

“In the first place, Margaret,” Frederick said, “who is to hunt up my witnesses? All of them are sailors, drafted off to other ships, except those whose evidence would go for very little, as they took part or sympathised in the affair. In the next place allow me to tell you, you don’t know what a court-martial is, and consider it as an assembly where justice is administered, instead of what it really is—a court where authority weighs nine-tenths in the balance, and evidence forms only the other tenth. In such cases, evidence itself can hardly escape being influenced by the prestige of authority.”

“But is it not worth trying,” Margaret persisted, “to see how much evidence might be discovered and arrayed on your behalf? At present, all those who knew you formerly, believe you guilty without any shadow of excuse. You have never tried to justify yourself, and we have never known where to seek for proofs of your justification. Now, for Miss Barbour’s sake, make your conduct as clear as you can in the eye of the world. She may not care for it; she has, I am sure, that trust in you that we all have; but you ought not to let her ally herself to one under such a serious charge, without showing the world exactly how it is you stand. You disobeyed authority—that was bad; but to have stood by, without word or act, while the authority was brutally used, would have been infinitely worse. People know what you did; but not the motives that elevate it out of a crime into an heroic protection of the weak. For Dolores’ sake, they ought to know.”

“But how must I make them know?” Frederick demanded, almost impatient at the helplessness of it. “I am not sufficiently sure of the purity and justice of those who would be my judges, to give myself up to a court-martial, even if I could bring a whole array of truth-speaking witnesses. I can’t send a bell-man about, to cry aloud and proclaim in the streets what you are pleased to call my heroism. No one would read a pamphlet of self-justification so long after the deed, even if I put one out.”

“Will you consult a lawyer as to your chances of exculpation?” Margaret asked; and as she spoke she felt herself redden—how odd that this name should still have the power to colour her cheek.

“I must first catch my lawyer, and have a look at him, and see how I like him, before I make him into my confidant. Many a briefless barrister might twist his conscience into thinking, that he could earn a hundred pounds very easily by doing a good action—in giving me, a criminal, up to justice.”

“Nonsense, Frederick!” Margaret answered, forcing steadiness. “Because I know a lawyer on whose honour I can rely; of whose cleverness in his profession people speak very highly; and who would, I think, take a good deal of trouble for any of—Aunt Shaw’s relations. Mr. Henry Lennox, papa.”

“I think it is a good idea,” Mr. Hale said, slowly. “But don’t propose anything which will detain Frederick in England. Don’t, for your mother’s sake.”

“You could go to London by a night-train,” Margaret went on, warming to the plan as if it were a task like laying the breakfast-table—something that could be arranged into order. “He must go to-morrow, I’m afraid, papa,” she added, tenderly, “we fixed that, because of Mr. Bell, and Dixon’s disagreeable acquaintance.”

“Yes; I must go to-morrow,” Frederick said, decisively.

Mr. Hale gave a sound that was almost a groan. “I can’t bear to part with you, and yet I am miserable with anxiety as long as you stop here.”

“Well then,” Margaret said, “listen to my plan. He gets to London on Friday morning. I will—you might—no! it would be better to give him a note to Mr. Lennox. You will find him at his chambers in the Temple.”

“I will write down a list of all the names I can remember on board the Orion,” Frederick said, catching at the practical part. “I could leave it with him to ferret them out. He is Edith’s husband’s brother, isn’t he? I remember your naming him in your letters. I have money in Barbour’s hands. I can pay a pretty long bill, if there’s any chance of success. Money, dear father, that I had meant for a different purpose; so I shall only consider it as borrowed from you and Margaret.”

“Don’t do that,” Margaret said quickly. “You won’t risk it if you do. And it will be as risk; only it is worth trying. You can sail from London as well as from Liverpool?”

“To be sure, little goose,” Frederick replied, and for a moment his old playfulness came back, like the brief warmth of the fire when a new log catches. “Wherever I feel water heaving under a plank, there I feel at home. I’ll pick up some craft or other to take me off, never fear. I won’t stay twenty-four hours in London, away from you on the one hand, and from somebody else on the other.”

It was a strange relief to Margaret that Frederick chose to look over her shoulder while she wrote to Mr. Lennox. The steady movement of pen on paper—ink pooling and thinning, the scratch of the nib, the disciplined forming of words—kept her from hesitating, from being caught in the awkwardness of beginning again an intercourse that had last ended so uncomfortably. She wrote concisely, plainly; and before she could even read it over, Frederick took the note from her hand and put it away with care in his pocket-book.

As he did so, something slipped out—a long lock of black hair. The sight of it made his eyes glow, as if in an instant all the grey of Milton’s fog and sorrow were exchanged for sun.

“Now you would like to see that, wouldn’t you?” he said, holding it lightly.

“No! you must wait till you see her herself,” he went on, with a boy’s pride transfigured into a man’s devotion. “She is too perfect to be known by fragments. No mean brick shall be a specimen of the building of my palace.”

All the next day they sat together—three figures gathered as if the room itself had learned to hold its breath. The house was hushed in the strange way a home becomes after death has passed through it: not only emptied of a voice, but altered in its very sounds. The clock seemed louder, the coal settling in the grate sharper, the street beyond a nearer, harsher murmur; every wheel on the stones came with an edge, every distant shout from Milton’s throats struck the ear like a blow. Even the kettle—set on out of habit, left to cool without purpose—gave no kindly promise; it only clicked and fell silent, like something that had forgotten its own language.

Mr. Hale hardly spoke, except when his children questioned him and forced him, by sheer tenderness, to step into the present. He looked as if his thoughts had narrowed to one long corridor where fear walked up and down: fear of recognition, fear of a knock at the door, fear of a name spoken too loud. Since Mrs. Hale’s death that fear had grown more tyrannical; it filled the spaces she had once softened. He started at any unusual sound, and was never at ease unless Frederick sat where no one entering could see him at once.

Frederick’s grief was no longer audible. The first violent storm had spent itself, leaving a stillness that was almost more dreadful. He was ashamed of having been mastered so openly, as men are taught to be ashamed of tears; and though sorrow sat deep in him, it was a sorrow that would be carried like a sealed thing.
