He would not speak of his mother again. Margaret, who had been steadier at first, suffered more now. Her eyes would overflow without warning, and even when she spoke of something indifferent there was a mournful softness in her voice, as if every word touched the bruise underneath. Whenever she looked at Frederick, she saw, not only her mother’s absence, but his swiftly approaching departure; it made even the daylight feel temporary.

She was glad he was going, for her father’s sake, however much she grieved for her own. The anxious terror in which Mr. Hale lived lest his son should be detected and captured outweighed all the comfort of having him near. Presence had become another kind of danger.

Towards evening Mr. Hale said, with the constrained decision of a man taking refuge in arrangements because feeling is unmanageable, “You will go with Frederick to the station, Margaret? I shall want to know he is safely off. You will bring me word that he is clear of Milton, at any rate?”

“Certainly,” said Margaret. “I shall like it, if you won’t be lonely without me, papa.”

“No, no! I should always be fancying some one had known him, and that he had been stopped, unless you could tell me you had seen him off. And go to the Outwood station. It is quite as near, and not so many people about. Take a cab there. There is less risk of his being seen. What time is your train, Fred?”

“Ten minutes past six; very nearly dark. So what will you do, Margaret?”

“Oh, I can manage. I am getting very brave and very hard. It is a well-lighted road all the way home, if it should be dark. But I was out last week much later.”

She was thankful, when the time came, that she could hurry him away. There are partings that multiply if you let them—at the chamber door, at the stair, at the threshold; she would have none of that. The last look at his mother’s body was bitter enough for her father without prolonging the scene. She got Frederick into the cab quickly, and made her father remain behind, with the gentlest firmness she could command, as if her briskness were only care for his comfort and not the desperate need to keep fear from growing larger.

The cab’s wheels struck the roadway with a hollow clatter that seemed to echo in Mr. Hale’s nerves. Margaret, sitting close to her brother, listened to every sound outside as if the town itself were an eavesdropper—Milton with its quick feet, its constant grind, its rough-voiced life. Even here, on the way out, the air had the city’s familiar taste: smoke laid on the tongue like stale bitterness, and somewhere, faint and far, the sour-sweet breath of fermenting grain or spirit. Sounds and scents—both were warnings; both could carry a name.

Partly because she had hurried, and partly because one of those common errors in the Railway Guide had shifted the times at the smaller stations, they found, on reaching Outwood, that they had nearly twenty minutes to spare. The booking-office was not open; they could not even take the ticket. The platform lights flared with a raw, impatient glare, throwing hard shadows and making the darker spaces beyond seem fuller of watchers than of mere night.

So they went down the flight of steps to the level ground below the railway. A broad cinder-path crossed a field diagonally beside the road, and they walked there, back and forth, as if movement could keep mischance from finding them. The cinders, black and crisp, gave under their feet with a dry, gritty sound—so different from the soft, honest hush of country earth that Margaret had known as a girl. Even Outwood bore the railway’s voice: a place taught to listen for the long metallic sigh of an approaching train.

Margaret’s hand lay on Frederick’s arm. He took it, holding it with a warmth that made her think, suddenly and painfully, of the way her mother’s hands had always moved about the teacups and bread, the small daily ministries by which a household remembers itself. Now all those acts were stopped; the memory of them felt like a dialect no one spoke aloud for fear it might die altogether.

“Margaret!” Frederick said. His voice had steadied; he spoke now with that controlled earnestness which comes after we have been ashamed of weakness. “I am going to consult Mr. Lennox as to the chance of exculpating myself so that I may return to England whenever I choose, more for your sake than for the sake of anyone else. I can’t bear to think of your lonely position if any thing should happen to my father. He looks sadly changed—terribly shaken. I wish you could get him to think of the Cadiz plan, for many reasons. What could you do if he were taken away? You have no friend near. We are curiously bare of relations.”

She could hardly keep from crying at the anxious tenderness with which he spoke of a future she dared not examine too closely. The last months had hollowed her father; she knew it. She tried to rally herself, because Frederick needed courage from her.

“There have been such strange unexpected changes in my life during these last two years,” she said, “that I feel more than ever that it is not worth while to calculate too closely what I should do if any future event took place. I try to think only upon the present.”

She paused. They had stopped for a moment near the stile that led into the road. The low sun, slipping towards its end, fell on their faces in a colour like diluted wine. Frederick held her hand and searched her expression as if he could read, in the set of her mouth and the shadow about her eyes, what she would not give him in words. She went on, with effort:

“We shall write often to one another, and I will promise—for I see it will set your mind at ease—to tell you every worry I have. Papa is—”

She started—a small, involuntary start—but Frederick felt it, and turned his head sharply. Along the road, passing the very stile where they stood, a horseman rode slowly by. Hoofbeats—measured, controlled—came and went with a distinctness that made Margaret’s heart stumble, for in that moment sound was fate.

Margaret bowed. Her bow was stiffly returned.

“Who is that?” Frederick asked, almost before the rider was out of hearing.

Margaret’s colour rose and fell; she looked drooping and flushed as she answered, “Mr. Thornton; you saw him before, you know.”

“Only his back. He is an unprepossessing-looking fellow. What a scowl he has!”

“Something has happened to vex him,” said Margaret, apologetic in spite of herself. “You would not have thought him unprepossessing if you had seen him with mamma.”

Frederick glanced towards the station as if time, too, had begun to watch them. “I fancy it must be time to go and take my ticket. If I had known how dark it would be, we wouldn’t have sent back the cab, Margaret.”

“Oh, don’t fidget about that. I can take a cab here, if I like; or go back by the rail-road, when I should have shops and people and lamps all the way from the Milton station-house. Don’t think of me; take care of yourself. I am sick with the thought that Leonards may be in the same train with you. Look well into the carriage before you get in.”

They went back up to the station. Margaret insisted on going into the full light of the flaring gas to take the ticket, as if brightness could protect them. The air in the office had the smell of oil and smoke and damp woollen coats; the very place seemed made of irritation and impatience. Some idle-looking young men lounged about with the station-master. Margaret thought she had seen the face of one of them before. He stared at her with an impertinent, undisguised admiration—the bold look of a man who believes every woman in a public place has been put there for his entertainment. She met it with a proud, offended dignity that made his mouth twitch, and went hastily out to Frederick, taking his arm as though the touch anchored her.

“Have you got your bag? Let us walk about here on the platform,” she said. She tried to keep her voice steady, but her courage was already leaking away, drop by drop, at the thought of being left alone, and at the thought of what the next few minutes might hold.

She heard a step behind them along the flagged stones: it stopped when they stopped. The sound was too deliberate, too attentive; it pricked her like a thorn. They stood near the edge and looked out along the line. Far off there was the first thin whizz—like a knife drawn quickly—of the coming train. They did not speak. Their hearts were too full; and besides, speech felt dangerous, as if words might carry further than they intended.

Another moment and the train would be here; a minute more and Frederick would be gone. Margaret almost repented the urgency with which she had pressed him to go to London; it flung him into more chances of being seen. If he had sailed for Spain from Liverpool, he might have been out of reach in hours, with only water between him and his pursuers. Here, on land, everything could stop him: a look, a name, a hand on his sleeve.

Frederick turned round, facing the lamp. The gas shot up in vivid, expectant flames, making his features sharp and pale. At that instant a man in the dress of a railway porter started forward—a bad-looking man with the heavy, brutal face of one who has drunk until coarseness has settled into him like a habit. Yet his senses were not dulled; there was a grim precision in his movement that was more alarming than mere drunken clumsiness.

“By your leave, miss!” he said, pushing Margaret rudely aside. He seized Frederick by the collar with a grip meant to hold, not to jostle. “Your name is Hale, I believe?”

Time broke. In an instant—how, Margaret could not afterwards tell, for everything leapt and reeled before her eyes—Frederick wrenched and wrestled. There was a quick, practised movement; the porter was tripped, thrown off balance, and fell from the platform’s height—three or four feet—down onto the soft ground beside the line. He lay there.

“Run, run!” Margaret gasped, her voice tearing out of her throat. “The train is here. It was Leonards, was it? oh, run! I will carry your bag.”

She snatched at the bag, seized Frederick’s arm, and pushed him along with all the force her fear could lend her. The iron scream of brakes, the rush of air, the shuddering approach of the train came together like one monstrous breath. A door opened; Frederick sprang in. He leaned out for the briefest second—just long enough for a face and a voice to be made memory.

“God bless you, Margaret!”

Then the train rushed past her; the wind of it struck her skirt and hair, and she was left standing alone with the platform lights glaring and the dark beyond swallowing the last sound of the wheels.

Sickness rose in her like a tide. She felt herself turn cold and empty, as if the fear had scooped out her insides. She was thankful to reach the ladies’ waiting-room and sit down for an instant. At first she could do nothing but gasp. It had been such a hurry, such a sickening alarm, such a near chance—so near that the taste of it remained in her mouth, bitter as soot.

If the train had not been there at that very moment, the man might have scrambled up and called assistance to arrest Frederick. She tried to remember whether she had seen him stir. Had he been badly hurt? The thought of leaving a man broken by her brother’s struggle—even a brutal, drunken informer—clung to her, and yet the greater dread was still Frederick’s safety.

She forced herself up and ventured out. The platform was all alight, but it was deserted now; the soundscape had thinned to distant, indifferent noises. She walked to the end and looked over with a fear she hated in herself. No one was there. The ground below was empty. Relief loosened her tight breathing; at least, she told herself, she would not be haunted by the image of a body lying unseen in the dark.

Even so she trembled, and the road home, which she could see from the blaze of the station, looked lonely and dark. The quiet out there was not the gentle quiet of fields; it was a silence made ominous by the memory of sudden voices. She knew she could not walk it. She would wait for the down train and take her seat in it.

But what if Leonards—if it was Leonards—recognized her as Frederick’s companion? Her heart began to hammer again, listening for heavy footsteps, for a thick laugh, for that particular swaggering cadence drunken men have when they believe they are still masters of themselves. She peered about before she dared go into the booking-office for her ticket. Only railway officials were there, standing in a knot and talking loud to one another, their voices bouncing off the bare walls.

“So Leonards has been drinking again!” said one, in the tone of an authority disgusted by a habitual offender. “He’ll need all his boasted influence to keep his place this time.”

“Where is he?” asked another.

Margaret stood with her back towards them, counting her change with trembling fingers. She did not dare turn her head until she heard the answer, as if her very glance might summon him.

“I don’t know. He came in not five minutes ago, with some long story or other about a fall he’d had, swearing awfully: and wanted to borrow some money from me to go to London by the next up-train. He made all sorts of tipsy promises, but I’d something else to do than listen to him; I told him to go about his business; and he went off at the front door.”

“He’s at the nearest vaults, I’ll be bound,” said the first speaker. “Your money would have gone there too, if you’d been such a fool as to lend it.”

“Catch me! I knew better what his London meant. Why, he has never paid me off that five shillings—”

Their talk slid on into common complaint. Margaret’s hands still shook, but the knowledge that Leonards had gone—gone away from the station, away from her—was like finding a door unbarred. Now all her anxiety fixed itself on the coming train. She hid again in the ladies’ waiting-room, where the air smelled faintly of damp shawls and extinguished fires, and where every creak of wood, every passing voice, made her start. In such a state, sound did not merely enter the ear; it ruled the mind. She found herself longing, absurdly, for some remembered domestic noise—her mother’s gentle stir in the kitchen, the soft scrape of a knife spreading butter, the quiet clink of a cup set down with care—anything that spoke of a world in which danger did not announce itself with a boot-step and a shout.

No one came near her until the down train drew up. A porter helped her civilly into a carriage. She did not dare look full into his face until they were in motion; then, as the wheels took their rhythm and the station’s glare slid away behind her, she saw it was not Leonards’. She let her breath out, and sat rigidly still, listening to the train’s long, steady sound as it carried her back towards Milton, where even the lights and crowds and noise could feel, for that night at least, like safety.

Home had the hush of a kitchen after the fire has been damped down—no clatter of pans, no kettle’s homely singing to stitch the hours together—only the thick, stunned silence that follows a day of shouting and running and dread. Even the house’s ordinary breath seemed afraid to make a sound, as if the very boards underfoot knew there lay, behind the closed door upstairs, a stillness beyond all scolding, beyond all calling.

Mr. Hale, who had made sure, with the anxious care of one who can do nothing else, that there should be some little refreshment ready for Margaret’s return, dropped at last into his accustomed chair. His hand rested upon the worn arm as it always had; yet he sat as if the chair belonged to another man—sunk in one of those waking dreams that were not rest, only a slow drowning.

Dixon had taken refuge in action. She had fetched Mary Higgins to the kitchen, and between them they made a kind of stern domestic order out of disorder—bread cut, broth warmed, linen laid straight. Mary’s tongue was in full employ; but she drove it in an angry whisper, as though the very idea of speaking above breath might be a desecration while death was in the house. Her murmured scoldings went on like a suppressed simmer, the sort of sound that ordinarily would have comforted Margaret with its familiarity—yet now only sharpened the sense of what was missing: the old, gentle household noises, the easy talk, the freedom to call up the stairs.

Margaret, for her part, had resolved on one silence within another. She would not tell her father of the last crowning terror—how close peril had come, and with what sickening suddenness. It had ended well. There was no use in laying that weight on him when it could not now alter anything. The only fear worth fearing was that Leonards might scrape together money enough to follow Frederick to London and hunt him there. Yet the chances were many against such a pursuit. Frederick would be on his guard. In a day or two, at most, he would be safely out of England. Margaret forced herself to accept this as one accepts the day’s bread: not because it is delicious, but because one must live.

“I suppose we shall hear from Mr. Bell to-morrow,” she said at length, grasping for any thread of ordinary expectation.

“Yes,” her father answered, without moving his eyes. “I suppose so.”

“If he can come, he will be here to-morrow evening, I should think.”

“If he cannot come,” Mr. Hale went on, the words heavy as if lifted one by one, “I shall ask Mr. Thornton to go with me to the funeral. I cannot go alone. I should break down utterly.”

“Don’t ask Mr. Thornton, papa. Let me go with you,” Margaret cried, too quickly—her feeling outrunning her caution.

“You!” he said, startled. “My dear, women do not generally go.”

“No; because they can’t control themselves. Women of our class don’t go because they have no power over their emotions, and yet are ashamed of showing them. Poor women go, and don’t care if they are seen overwhelmed with grief.” Her voice shook once, but steadied. “But I promise you, papa, if you will let me go, I will be no trouble. Don’t have a stranger, and leave me out. Dear papa—if Mr. Bell cannot come, I shall go. I won’t urge my wish against your will, if he does.”

Mr. Bell could not come. The letter arrived with its kind, affectionate pain in every line—gout had laid him holdfast. He was truly grieved; he hoped, if they would have him, to come soon, for his Milton property needed his personal looking after. His agent had written that his presence was absolutely necessary. He confessed, too, with that honest self-knowledge which is almost tenderness, that he had avoided Milton as long as he could; and that now the only thought that reconciled him to the journey was the hope of seeing and perhaps comforting his old friend.

When Mr. Hale spoke of inviting Mr. Thornton nevertheless, Margaret felt something in her draw back as if from a cold iron. She could not give it a tidy name. It was not mere dislike; it was a bodily repugnance, as if some flavour had been suddenly tainted and would spoil all the dish. She pleaded, coaxed, reasoned—anything rather than have that request go from their door.

On the night before the funeral there came a stately note from Mrs. Thornton to Miss Hale, saying that, at her son’s desire, their carriage should attend the funeral, if it would not be disagreeable to the family.

Margaret read it, and in a motion half impatience, half helplessness, tossed it to her father.

“Oh, don’t let us have these forms,” she said. “Let us go alone—you and me, papa. They don’t care for us; or else he would have offered to go himself, and not have proposed this sending an empty carriage.”

“I thought you were so extremely averse to his going, Margaret,” Mr. Hale said, looking up with mild surprise.

“And so I am. I don’t want him to come at all; and I should especially dislike the idea of our asking him. But this—this seems such a mockery of mourning that I did not expect it from him.”

Her own words broke something in her. Tears came, hot and sudden, as if the day’s iron restraint had at last found its weakest seam. She startled her father by the burst; for she had been so quiet in her grief, so thoughtful for others, so patient and gentle in all things, that he could not understand this restlessness now. He tried to soothe her with a tenderness that had been almost absent from him in the first stunned hours—not from want of love, but from being overborne; yet the more he sought to comfort, the more she wept. The night would not settle. It passed in broken dozes and listening, as if she waited for some familiar sound that would never come again: the soft step on the stair, the faint clink of china, the little domestic music by which a household knows itself alive.

In the morning, when she was already ill prepared for any new shaking of the nerves, a letter came from Frederick.

Mr. Lennox was out of town. His clerk had said he would return by the following Tuesday at latest, perhaps on Monday. After consideration, Frederick had determined upon remaining in London a day or two longer. The temptation to come down to Milton again had been very strong; but the thought of Mr. Bell domesticated in his father’s house, and the alarm at the last moment at the railway station, had decided him. Margaret might be assured he would take every precaution against being tracked by Leonards.

She was thankful—thankful with a kind of shame at being thankful—that she received this letter while her father was absent in her mother’s room. Had he been there, he would have expected her to read it aloud; and the allusions, slight as Frederick made them, to recognition and pursuit would have raised such a nervous alarm in him as she could not have soothed away. Even she felt her blood run cold as her eyes went over the lines again: London; delay; Leonards. How could she have urged the plan of consulting Mr. Lennox? At the time it had appeared prudent—so small a delay, so slight an added risk. Yet since then everything had conspired to make it seem folly. She fought against the regret because it could do nothing but sting; yet it stung all the same. She knew, too, how differently such remorse would prey upon her father. His mind, in its weakened state, would not cast off morbid self-accusation as one shakes off dust; it would cling like soot.

So she gathered herself, summoning every force. Her father, when he came down, seemed to have forgotten that they expected a letter at all. He was absorbed in a single idea—that the last visible token of his wife’s presence, the poor familiar shape of her body in the house, was to be taken away and hidden from his sight for ever.

When the undertaker’s man began to arrange the crape draperies about him, Mr. Hale trembled pitifully, as if the stiff black folds were not cloth but some living thing binding him. His eyes went to Margaret with the beseeching look of one who cannot bear his own weakness.

When the man at last released him, he tottered towards her, murmuring brokenly, “Pray for me, Margaret. I have no strength left in me. I cannot pray. I give her up because I must. I try to bear it; indeed I do. I know it is God’s will. But I cannot see why she died. Pray for me, Margaret, that I may have faith to pray. It is a great strait, my child.”

In the coach Margaret sat close, almost supporting him with her arm as if he were a sick man on a jolting road. She spoke to him in the low steady voice one uses to keep a kettle from boiling over—no flourish, no dramatics, only what must be done to prevent a breaking. She repeated the noble verses of comfort she could remember, and the texts that speak of resignation and rest. Her voice did not falter; and in the act of ministering she seemed to draw strength as a hearth draws heat when a log is set rightly. Her father’s lips moved after her. He repeated the familiar words when her voice prompted them, in that terrible patient struggle of one who knows what he ought to feel and yet cannot force the feeling to grow in him.

At the graveside her fortitude nearly gave way. Dixon, with the smallest motion of her hand—more a twitch than a gesture—directed Margaret’s notice to Nicholas Higgins and his daughter, standing a little aloof, yet deeply attentive to the ceremonial. Nicholas wore his usual fustian; but there was a bit of black stuff sewn round his hat—an awkward, homely mark of mourning, all the more touching because he had never shown such outward sign for his own Bessy. It was as if this death, in the master’s house, had reached into the worker’s life too, stitching a black band round a rough hat in silent acknowledgment of a shared human loss.

But Mr. Hale saw nothing. He went on repeating, mechanically, the funeral service as the clergyman read. When all was ended, he sighed twice or thrice, like a man surfacing only to sink again. Then he laid his hand upon Margaret’s arm and, without words, entreated to be led away, as if he were blind and she his guide.

Dixon sobbed aloud, her handkerchief over her face. She was so wrapped in her own grief that she did not perceive the crowd dispersing—those inevitable lookers-on who gather wherever death makes a public pause—until someone spoke close to her.

It was Mr. Thornton.

He had been there all the time, standing with bent head behind a group of people, so that no one had recognised him. His voice, when he spoke, was low and constrained, as if grief had turned it to stone.

“I beg your pardon—but can you tell me how Mr. Hale is? And Miss Hale, too? I should like to know how they both are.”

“Of course, sir,” Dixon answered, wiping her eyes with an angry jerk, as if tears insulted as well as hurt. “They are much as is to be expected. Master is terribly broke down. Miss Hale bears up better than likely.”

Mr. Thornton would rather, in his selfish heart, have heard that she had been overcome. There was enough of passionate egotism in him to take fierce pleasure in imagining her leaning on him for comfort, as a drooping child nestles into its mother, dependent upon her warmth for life. A few days ago he would have indulged that delicious vision even after all Margaret’s repulse.

Now it was miserably disturbed—no, haunted, torn through—by what he had seen near the Outwood station. The remembrance of the handsome young man beside her, and the attitude of familiar confidence in which she had stood, shot through him like agony until he clenched his hands hard to master the pain.

At that late hour—so far from home! To galvanise his old trust in Margaret’s pure maidenliness into life cost him a great moral effort; and when the effort relaxed, the trust fell dead again, and wild fancies chased each other through his mind like fever-dreams. Dixon’s words gave him a little miserable gnawing confirmation.

“She bore up better than likely.” Then she had hope to look to, some bright prospect that could lighten even the newly-made motherless daughter’s hours. He knew how she would love. He had not loved her without gaining the instinct that her heart, once given, would fill the world with sunlight for the one who deserved it. Even in mourning she would rest with a peaceful faith upon sympathy.

His sympathy? Whose? That other man’s.

The thought made his pale, grave face grow doubly wan and stern.

“I suppose I may call,” he said, coldly. “On Mr. Hale, I mean. He will perhaps admit me after to-morrow or so.”

He spoke as if the answer were indifferent. It was not. For all his pain he longed to see the very author of it. Though he could hate Margaret at moments, when that gentle, familiar attitude rose before him, he yet had a restless desire to renew her image, a craving for the very air she breathed, as if the soundscape of his life had been altered and he must seek the lost note again though it cut him. He circled and circled nearer to the fatal centre of his own passion.

“I dare say, sir, master will see you,” Dixon said. “He was very sorry to have to deny you the other day; but circumstances was not agreeable just then.”

For some reason—chance, or stubborn pride, or the curious power that grief has of rearranging what one tells and what one holds back—Dixon never named to Margaret this little meeting by the grave. So it came about that Margaret never knew Mr. Thornton had stood unseen among the mourners at her mother’s funeral.

The effort of seeming to bear it—of carrying her days as if they were not weighted with a new and hollow absence—strained Margaret until she felt the fibres of her will sing like overstretched wire. At odd instants, in the midst of the quietest talk with her father, the thought would dart through her with a knife’s sharpness—there is no longer a mother in the house—and she must press her lips together, and keep her breath even, and go on as if the words she was answering were the only reality.

And Frederick—Frederick was a worse uncertainty, because it could not even be mourned openly. The Sunday post had broken the accustomed course of their London letters, and when Tuesday came and still there was nothing, the silence grew loud in the rooms, louder than the faint crackle of the coals, louder than the respectful tread of Dixon outside the door. Margaret had no chart of his intentions; her father had no anchorage for his fears.

Mr. Hale’s late habit of sitting half a day in one easy chair, hands folded, eyes dulled by grief, was shattered by this want of tidings. He rose and paced, and went out and in again, and Margaret heard him on the landing opening and shutting bedroom doors as if each sound, each little click of latch and hinge, might call a letter into being. The house itself seemed to listen—stairs holding their breath, curtains still, the very clock’s tick sounding like a question unanswered.

She tried to steady him by reading aloud, choosing passages with a cadence she thought might soothe, as one might set a simmer to a sauce that threatens to boil over; but his attention broke, wandered, came back for a phrase, was lost again. He could not be held long by any thread of narrative while his mind fretted at that other thread—Frederick, out there somewhere, beyond their reach.

How thankful she was then—thankful with a guilty, bitter gratitude—that she had kept to herself the fresh cause for anxiety, the chance encounter with Leonards. If her father’s grief had been a broth already too salted, this would have been the handful that made it uneatable. She had tasted fear lately as distinctly as if it had been on her tongue—metallic, sour, lingering—and she would not pour it into his cup.

When Mr. Thornton was announced, the relief was almost physical; his presence promised a diversion, a different current. He came in with no wasted motion, as if he brought with him the steadiness of mills and ledgers and fixed hours. He went straight to Mr. Hale, took both his hands, and wrung them hard without speaking, holding them so for a minute or two, his face and eyes saying what his voice did not attempt. Sympathy in him was not a florid thing; it was like a warm loaf set down in a hungry kitchen—plain, sustaining, wordless.

Then he turned to Margaret.

Not “better than likely” did she look. Her stately beauty was dimmed by watching and weeping; the skin about her eyes had a fine drawn look, as if sorrow had handled it too often. There was no theatrical despair upon her—only that patient, gentle sadness which, because it is quiet, is the more unmistakably suffering. He had meant to greet her with the studied coldness he had practised of late; he had resolved to keep distance, as if distance were a kind of remedy. But the sight of her, standing a little aside with the cautious timidity her uncertainty of his altered manner had bred, undid his resolution in an instant. He went to her and said the few necessary commonplace words—nothing remarkable in themselves—only his tone was so tender, so involuntarily softened, that her eyes filled and she turned away quickly, as if to hide a weakness that burned her cheeks.

She took up her work and sat down, very quiet, very silent, hands moving with a docility that was almost mechanical. Mr. Thornton’s heart beat hard; for that moment he forgot Outwood Lane altogether, forgot even the habits of self-command that usually held him like armour. He tried instead to talk to Mr. Hale, and—as always—his decisiveness, his practical thought, his very power of choosing an opinion and adhering to it, was a kind of safe harbour to a mind like Mr. Hale’s, easily blown from one gentle supposition to another. Margaret saw her father’s face take on a little steadiness as their conversation went on.

The room had settled into that uneasy calm—tea-things still unbrought in, the air faint with the old scent of mourning crape and extinguished candles—when Dixon appeared at the door.

“Miss Hale, you are wanted.”

Dixon’s tone, her flurried, breath-catching manner, struck Margaret like a hand upon the heart. In a moment she was cold, and then hot. Something had happened to Fred. She did not doubt it; she only wondered how the blow had chosen its shape. It was well, she thought with a swift flash of gratitude, that her father and Mr. Thornton were deep in talk.

“What is it, Dixon?” she asked the instant the drawing-room door was shut behind her.

“Come this way, miss,” Dixon said, and opened the door of what had been Mrs. Hale’s bed-chamber—now Margaret’s, because her father could not bear to sleep there again. The room still held the ghost of her mother in a hundred small domestic memories: the place where a lavender sachet used to lie, the faint lingering perfume as if linen had once been aired there, the hush that belonged to illness and last goodbyes.

“It’s nothing, miss,” Dixon said, choking a little. “Only a police-inspector. He wants to see you, miss. But I dare say it’s about nothing at all.”

“Did he name—” Margaret began; her voice would scarcely form the sound.

“No, miss; he named nothing. He only asked if you lived here, and if he could speak to you. Martha went to the door, and let him in; she has shown him into master’s study. I went to him myself, to try if that would do; but no—it’s you, miss, he wants.”

Margaret said no more until her hand rested on the study lock. She turned then, her face suddenly set, and spoke low and quickly.

“Take care papa does not come down. Mr. Thornton is with him now.”

She opened the door.

The inspector rose as she entered. He was a man practised in measuring other people’s faces and voices, used to flurry and evasion, to tears that were meant to soften, to anger meant to frighten. Yet the sight of Margaret Hale, with her controlled indignation and the haughty quiet of her carriage, checked him for an instant. She did not come in with curiosity, nor with the fidgeting eagerness of the innocent. She came as if she were a judge summoned to hear a charge, and would permit no liberties of manner.

She stood, waiting. She asked no question.

“I beg your pardon, ma’am,” he began, “but my duty obliges me to ask you a few plain questions. A man has died at the Infirmary, in consequence of a fall, received at Outwood station, between the hours of five and six on Thursday evening, the twenty-sixth instant. At the time, this fall did not seem of much consequence; but it was rendered fatal, the doctors say, by the presence of some internal complaint, and the man’s own habit of drinking.”

Her large dark eyes, fixed straight upon him, widened a little; it was no more than the opening of a shutter. Otherwise she did not stir. Her mouth held itself rigidly; the very curve of her lips seemed fuller with the strain of restraint, as if she were holding back words that would scorch her tongue. She neither blenched nor trembled. She simply looked at him, and made him go on.

“Well—go on!” she said at last, almost as if she would compel the story to reach its end.

“It is supposed that an inquest will have to be held,” he continued. “There is some slight evidence to prove that the blow, or push, or scuffle that caused the fall, was provoked by this poor fellow’s half-tipsy impertinence to a young lady, walking with the man who pushed the deceased over the edge of the platform. This much was observed by some one on the platform, who, however, thought no more about the matter, as the blow seemed of slight consequence. There is also some reason to identify the lady with yourself; in which case—”

“I was not there,” said Margaret.

Her voice sounded to her own ears heavy and remote, as if spoken through water. She did not flinch, did not try to explain, did not attempt to plead. The inspector bowed; he did not answer. The stillness of her denial, the steadiness of her gaze, gave him no easy handhold.

In truth his information was vague enough. A porter, rushing out to be ready for a train, had seen a scuffle at the far end of the platform between Leonards and a gentleman with a lady; he had heard no clear words, only seen the blur of movement. Then, before the train had reached full speed, the same porter had nearly been knocked down by Leonards himself running headlong, swearing and cursing in a frenzy that smelled of drink even at a distance. The porter had thought no more of it until the inspector, hunting up scraps, had found him and prised his recollection loose.

Further inquiry at the station had brought other fragments: the station-master remembered that a young lady and a gentleman had been there at about that hour; the lady remarkably handsome. A grocer’s assistant—one of those sharp-eyed lads who carry the names of neighbours and their purchases in their heads like a ledger—had said it was a Miss Hale living at Crampton, whose family dealt at his shop. None of it was certainty; it was merely a chain of may-bes that looked uncomfortably like a rope.

As for Leonards: he had gone half-mad with rage and pain to the nearest gin-palace, as if spirits could cauterise humiliation. His thick, tipsy words had not mattered to the busy waiters; yet they remembered him starting up suddenly, cursing himself for not having sooner thought of the electric telegraph—for some purpose they could not guess—and then leaving with that idea burning in him. On his way, overcome by pain or drink, he had lain down in the road. The police found him there and carried him to the Infirmary.

At the Infirmary he had never fully recovered consciousness. Once or twice he surfaced enough in his delirium that the authorities sent for the nearest magistrate, hoping to take down a dying deposition. But when the magistrate came, Leonards rambled of being at sea, mixing up names of captains and lieutenants with those of railway porters, as if his mind had dragged old, salt-stained memories into the same net as new grievances. His last words were a curse on a “Cornish trick” which, he said, had made him a hundred pounds poorer than he ought to have been.

All this the inspector carried in his thoughts while he watched Margaret’s face for the quick betrayals he was trained to expect. Yet her composure did not crack. If anything, it was too composed, too fixed—like a person who has forced herself to swallow something nauseating and is determined that not one muscle shall confess it.

“Then, madam,” he said at length, “I have your denial that you were the lady accompanying the gentleman who struck the blow, or gave the push, which caused the death of this poor man?”

A sharp pain shot through Margaret’s head, so swift it might have been light itself. Oh God! that I knew Frederick were safe! The thought tore at her with such violence that, for one instant, agony sprang in her eyes like a creature at bay. A deeper reader of faces might have seen it and understood. But the inspector’s keenness lay more in gathering facts than in sounding depths; he only noted, dimly, that her answer did not alter shape to meet his altered question.

“I was not there,” she said again, slowly, heavily.

The dull repetition stirred suspicion in him. It sounded like a lesson learned and repeated word for word, as if any variation might undo the speaker. He drew out his notebook and put it away with deliberate care, as if the very slowness of his motions might tempt her into a stumble.

“I hope you will not think me impertinent,” he said, looking up, “when I say, that I may have to call on you again. I may have to summon you to appear on the inquest, and prove an alibi, if my witnesses”—it was but one witness, but he spoke as if there were several—“persist in deposing to your presence at the unfortunate event.”

He watched for a wince. There was none. No rush of colour, no fluttering denial, no outraged exclamation. Her proud face held its quiet as a locked door holds the silence of a room.

He found himself a little abashed by what he took for innocence hardened into dignity. It must have been a mistake of identity; handsome young ladies were not so few as gossip imagined.

“It is very unlikely, ma’am, that I shall have to do anything of the kind,” he added, his voice falling into a more conciliatory tone. “I hope you will excuse me for doing what is only my duty, although it may appear impertinent.”

Margaret bowed her head slightly. Her lips were stiff and dry; she could not command even the common words of farewell. But suddenly she stepped forward, opened the study door, and went before him down the passage. At the front door she flung it wide for his exit, standing with the same fixed, dulled gaze upon him until he was fairly beyond the threshold and the street air had swallowed him up.

Then she shut the door.

She went halfway back into the study, as if she meant to return to whatever life had been a moment before. Then, as if a passionate instinct seized her, she turned sharply, pushed the key into the lock, and locked the door on the inside.

The click sounded loud—an iron note in the hush—like the last crack of a crust under a knife.

She moved into the study. She paused. The room swam; the edges of furniture seemed to waver, as if heat rose from the carpet. She tottered forward, paused again, swayed where she stood—upright for an instant by sheer habit of pride—and then fell prone upon the floor in a dead swoon.

Mr. Thornton remained, minute after minute, in Mr. Hale’s dim study, as if the very air within its walls had thickened into a kind of solemn bond. The house held its breath. Beyond the curtained windows Marlborough Street sent up its usual night-murmur—wheels scudding over the stones, a distant call, the faint clank and jangle that came with every passing vehicle—yet inside, those sounds seemed softened, as though muffled by the books, the heavy curtains, the close smell of ink and paper and extinguished fire.

Mr. Hale was glad of him—glad with that childlike, half-ashamed need which suffering gives to men who have been proud of standing alone. Again and again, with a weary hand lifted from the chair-arm as if to detain him, he said, softly, “Don’t go yet.” Mr. Thornton, who had come meaning only to fulfil a duty, found himself lingering, not for any hope of seeing Margaret, but because the presence of a mind so near the edge of life drew something earnest out of his own.

It was strange how Mr. Hale, who could speak to Margaret with tenderness and restraint, spoke to Thornton with a kind of unlocked candour. Thoughts long frost-bound broke and ran. Doubts, fears, those dark questionings that visit even good men when the lamp burns low and the body fails—he gave them voice here, because he dared not pain Margaret with them, or because he could not bear to see her quick sympathy recoil from the very idea of him entertaining such shadows. He could set them down, as one sets down a heavy tray at last, before Thornton.

Thornton answered little; but when he did, the words were like the sure placing of a hand on a trembling shoulder. He did not start away from uncertainty as if it were impiety; he spoke as one who had lived through that bleak country himself and knew where a line of light might be found. For all his daily hardness, all the worldly battle he waged with clenched teeth and stubborn will, there was a deeper, inarticulate religion in him than Mr. Hale had ever suspected—an inward allegiance not loudly professed, but tenacious as bone. They did not, as it chanced, speak so together again; yet this one hour, with its shared silence and its few grave sentences, made them peculiar to one another—more truly knit than any easy, public talk of sacred things could have done. When the inner chamber is flung open to all, where then is the Holy of Holies?

And while they spoke thus, Margaret lay on the floor of that very study, white and still as if she had already crossed beyond hearing.

She had sunk at last beneath the burden she had carried so long without complaint. It had been a weight of watchfulness, of secrecy, of fear—borne with patience until, all at once, the frail thread of her strength snapped, and she had groped for help and found none. The pain had drawn a pitiful contraction across her brows; the mouth which, a little while ago, had thrust itself forward in stubborn defiance was now relaxed and livid.

The first sign of returning life was a quiver at her lips, a mute effort at speech. The movement died; then came another, and she gathered her arms under her, pushing herself upright with a feebleness that was prideful in its very attempt. Her comb had fallen. The instinct that makes us, even in ruin, snatch at some poor semblance of order, drove her to look for it. She searched with hands that could scarcely obey her, and when the room swam she sat down, waited, and tried again. Her head drooped; her hands lay meekly one upon another for a moment, as if she were a penitent child.

She tried to recall the sharp details—the face, the questions, the tone—that had flung her into that deadly fright; but her mind, exhausted, could not reassemble them. Only two facts stood out like stones in a flood: Frederick had been in peril of pursuit and discovery, and she had lied to save him.

There was one comfort that came like a grudging crust to a starving creature—her falsehood had gained him time. If the inspector returned tomorrow, after she had the letter she longed for—after she knew Frederick was safe—she would bear the shame and stand in her bitter penance, she, Margaret Hale, acknowledging, if need be before a crowded room, that she had abased herself. But if he came again before any news arrived—if he returned, as he had half threatened, within a few hours—then she would tell the lie again. She did not know how she should shape the words now, after this awful pause wherein conscience had had leisure to speak; she did not know how she should keep her face from betraying her. Yet she would do it, for Frederick; she would do it to buy him time.

Dixon’s entrance roused her. She had only just let Mr. Thornton out, and the sound of the shutting door made Margaret’s heart jerk with a strange, sick longing to stop it—too late, too late.

Thornton had not gone ten steps into the street when an omnibus drew up near him, and a man got down, touched his hat, and came forward. It was the police-inspector. Thornton, who had once helped him into his first post, did not at first remember the face.

“My name is Watson—George Watson, sir—as you got—”

“Ah, yes. You are getting on famously, I hear.”

“Yes, sir. I ought to thank you. But it’s on a bit of business I’ve made so bold as to speak now. I believe you were the magistrate as took down the deposition of a poor man as died in the Infirmary last night.”

“Yes,” said Thornton. “A rambling statement—of little use, the clerk thought. He seemed a drunken fellow. There’s no doubt he came to his death by violence. One of my mother’s servants was engaged to him and is in great distress today. What of it?”

“Why, sir—his death is mixed up, oddly, with some one in the house you’ve just come out of. Mr. Hale’s, I believe.”

Thornton turned sharply; the inspector’s face swam into sudden importance.

“Yes. What about it?”

“Seems to me I’ve got a pretty distinct chain of evidence, inculpating a gentleman as was walking with Miss Hale that night at Outwood station—the man as struck, or pushed, Leonards off the platform. But the young lady denies she was there.”

“Miss Hale denies she was there!” Thornton repeated, and his voice changed on the words, as if some inward cord had been plucked too hard. “What evening? What time?”

“About six o’clock on Thursday the twenty-sixth.”

They walked for a little in silence, side by side. London’s sound-stream flowed around them—hoofs, wheels, a drunken shout, a vendor’s cry—but Thornton heard chiefly that one sentence: She denies she was there.

Watson spoke first again. “There’s like to be a coroner’s inquest, sir. I’ve a young man as was pretty positive—leastways at first. Since he’s heard of the young lady’s denial, he says he shouldn’t like to swear; but he’s pretty positive he saw Miss Hale at the station, walking about with a gentleman, not five minutes before the time. One of the porters saw a scuffle—took it for Leonards’ impudence, being the worse for drink—but it led to the fall as caused his death. And seeing you come out of the very house, sir, I thought I might ask if—well, disputed identity is awkward, and one don’t like to doubt the word of a respectable young woman unless one has proof.”

“And she denied having been at the station!” Thornton said again, low, as if he were repeating it to make it credible.

“Twice over, as clear as could be. I told her I should call again; but meeting you—coming back from questioning the young man—I thought I’d ask your advice, both as the magistrate as saw Leonards on his death-bed, and as the gentleman as got me my berth.”

“You were right,” said Thornton. “Don’t take any steps till you have seen me again.”

“The young lady will expect me, from what I said.”

“I only want to delay you an hour. It is three now. Come to my warehouse at four.”

“Very well, sir.”

They parted. Thornton went with rapid, stern strides, as if speed could outrun thought; yet the thoughts were already upon him, clinging, tearing. He reached his warehouse, forbade his clerks with a coldness that startled them to admit any interruption, and shut himself into his private room, turning the key as though he must lock out the whole world to wrestle with what was within.

Then he let the torture have its way.

How had he, even for an hour, lulled himself into that unsuspicious calm wherein Margaret’s image had come before him tearful and proud, and he had—weakly, he called it—pitied her and yearned toward her? How had he forgotten the savage jealousy with which the sight of her—at such an hour, in such a place, with some unknown man—had once struck him? How could one so pure have stooped? And even as he put the question, there came, like a flash of shame, an unworthy thought, an instant’s foul suggestion—gone as soon as born—yet it made him hate himself, because, while it lived, it carried with it that old, fierce attraction she had always held for him.

And then the lie. Not merely a denial, but an asserted falsehood, twice repeated—Margaret, whom he had believed incapable of bending! What fear of shame must bow her down so? For after all, in a case like this, Leonards’ drunken provocation might have been enough to justify an open statement; a scuffle at a station, a fall—there was nothing necessarily disgraceful. Yet she had chosen darkness. How creeping, how deadly must be the dread that could drive her to it!

He could almost pity her; and then contempt rose too, bitter and hot, and fought with pity until he could scarcely breathe.

What would be the end? If there was an inquest, if that wavering witness were pushed into an oath—what then? Her denial would be dragged into the light; she might be forced into perjury, or forced into confession. And suddenly, through all his tumult, one hard clear resolve lifted itself: there should be no inquest.

He would save her.

The decision, once made, steadied him like iron. The question of an inquest had hung, only the night before, trembling in the balance. The surgeon had spoken of internal disease—far advanced, sure to be fatal; death might have been hastened by the fall, or by the subsequent drinking and exposure. The medical evidence was uncertain—uncertain enough for a magistrate’s influence to turn the scale. If Thornton had known how Margaret would become entangled—if he had foreseen that she would stain herself by a lie—he might have saved her by a word.

Miss Hale might love another. She might be indifferent, even contemptuous, to him. He might despise her—he told himself he did. Yet the woman he had once loved should be kept from public shame. Shame it would be, to stand in a justice-room and pledge herself to a lie, or else to acknowledge, before strangers’ eyes, the reasons that made her choose concealment.

Very grey and stern he looked as he passed through the warehouse. The clerks, watching him, saw only that he went out and returned in about half an hour; but he brought back with him the look of a man who has laid his hand on a dangerous lever and pulled.

He wrote two lines on a slip of paper, sealed it, and gave it to one of the clerks.

“I appointed Watson—who was once a packer here, and went into the police—to call at four. A gentleman from Liverpool wishes to see me before he leaves town. Give this note to Watson when he calls.”

The note said:

“There will be no inquest. Medical evidence not sufficient to justify it. Take no further steps. I have not seen the coroner; but I will take the responsibility.”

Watson, when he received it, read it with relief.

“Well,” he thought, “it saves me an awkward job. None of the witnesses was certain of aught but the young woman. She was clear enough. The porter at the railroad had seen a scuffle—till it looked like he’d be wanted to swear, and then it might not have been a scuffle, only a bit of larking, and Leonards might have jumped off himself. He wouldn’t stick to anything. And Jennings, the grocer’s shopman—he wasn’t so bad; but I doubt I could have brought him to an oath after Miss Hale’s flat denial. It would have been trouble and no satisfaction. Now I must go tell them they won’t be wanted.”

So he went again to Mr. Hale’s that evening.

Within, the house held that close, domestic stillness which comes after fright—a stillness full of restrained movement, like a kitchen after a pan has boiled over and been hastily wiped, leaving only the smell of scalded milk and the memory of haste. Mr. Hale and Dixon would fain have persuaded Margaret to bed. They did not know why she refused so quietly, with so settled a look. Dixon knew part—but only part. Margaret had told her something of Frederick, enough to frighten and anger her into loyalty; yet she would not tell any human creature what she herself had said, nor did she reveal the fatal ending of Leonards’ fall.

Margaret lay on the sofa, white and worn. She spoke only when spoken to. When her father looked at her with anxious tenderness, she tried to smile back; but the wan lips sank into a sigh. Mr. Hale, miserable with uneasiness, at last persuaded her to go up to her room and prepare for sleep. It was past nine; Margaret began to think, dully, that the inspector would not come again that night.

She stood beside her father and held the back of his chair, clinging to it as if it were the one steady thing in a world that swayed.

“You will go to bed soon, papa, won’t you? Don’t sit up alone.”

What he answered she did not hear. Another sound—far smaller—filled her brain. The door-bell rang, low and thin; but to her fear it swelled until it drowned everything else.

She kissed her father and glided downstairs with a swiftness no one would have believed possible from the creature they had watched upon the sofa. Dixon was in the passage; Margaret put her aside.

“Don’t come. I will open the door. I know it is him—I can—I must manage it all myself.”

“As you please, miss!” Dixon replied, testily; then, softened by the sight of her, added, “But you’re not fit for it. You’re more dead than alive.”

“Am I?” said Margaret, turning, and Dixon saw the strange fire in her eyes, the flush in her cheeks, while her lips remained baked and livid.

Margaret opened the door. The inspector stood there. She preceded him to the study, set the candle on the table, and—because she must do something precise, something orderly, to keep herself from shaking apart—she snuffed it carefully before turning to face him.

“You are late,” she said. “Well?” She held her breath.

“I am sorry to have given any unnecessary trouble, ma’am,” Watson answered. “For, after all, they’ve given up all thoughts of holding an inquest. I’ve had other work, or I should have been here sooner.”

“Then it is ended,” said Margaret. “There is to be no further enquiry.”

“I believe I’ve got Mr. Thornton’s note about me,” said Watson, fumbling in his pocket-book.

“Mr. Thornton’s!” The name came from her lips like a startled cry.

“Yes, ma’am. He’s a magistrate. Ah—here it is.”

She took the paper. The candle’s flame seemed to flare and dazzle; the lines swam. Though she held it close, she could not read; yet she stared as if she were studying every stroke.

“I’m sure, ma’am,” Watson went on, “it’s a great weight off my mind; for the evidence was so uncertain, whether the man had received any blow at all. And if any question of identity came in, it complicated it, as I told Mr. Thornton—”

“Mr. Thornton!” she repeated again, faintly, as if the word itself hurt.

“I met him this morning, just as he was coming out of this house. He’s an old friend of mine, besides being the magistrate as saw Leonards last night. I made so bold as to tell him my difficulty.”

Margaret sighed—deep, involuntary. She wished the man would go; she was afraid of what she had heard and of what she might yet hear. But she forced herself to speak, stiffly, with manners like armour.

“Thank you for calling. It is very late—I dare say past ten. Oh! here is the note!” she added suddenly, understanding at last his outstretched hand. He was putting it away when she said, “It is cramped—dazzling writing. I cannot read it. Will you read it to me?”

He read Thornton’s words aloud.

When he had finished, she said, “Thank you. You told Mr. Thornton that I was not there?”

“Oh, of course, ma’am. I’m sorry now I acted upon information as seems to have been erroneous. At first the young man was so positive. Now he says he doubted all along, and hopes his mistake won’t have annoyed you so as to lose their shop your custom. Good night, ma’am.”

“Good night.”

She rang for Dixon to show him out. As Dixon returned along the passage, Margaret passed her swiftly, like a shadow slipping past a wall.

“It is all right,” she said, without looking at Dixon; and before any question could be flung after her, she was upstairs, inside her room, and had bolted the door.

She threw herself, dressed as she was, upon the bed. She was too exhausted to think. Time slid by—half an hour, more—until the cramped posture and the chill that follows great fatigue roused her numb body into a vague discomfort. Then thought began again, slow, reluctant, as a fire begins under damp wood.

First came the sense that Frederick’s immediate danger of pursuit was over; the strain had loosened. Next came a frantic desire to remember every syllable that concerned Mr. Thornton. When had Watson met him? What exactly had he said? What exactly had Thornton written? Margaret’s mind refused to move on until it had recited the note word for word, as if each article, each omitted “the,” were a crumb of proof that might change its meaning. But one conviction was clear, and it struck like a blow: Thornton had seen her near Outwood station that Thursday night; he had been told of her denial. She stood a liar in his eyes.

She was a liar.

No penitence rose in her mind then—no ordered prayer, no humble turning toward God. Only chaos and night, and in the midst one lurid fact burning her: in Mr. Thornton’s judgment she was degraded. She did not pause to argue excuse. To her it seemed beside the point; it could not alter what he knew. He had a right to judge her.

“Oh, Frederick! Frederick!” she cried into the pillow. “What have I not sacrificed for you!” Even sleep, when it came, forced her thoughts to travel the same circle, only with monstrous, exaggerated shapes of pain.

In the morning she woke with an idea that flashed bright as the day itself. Thornton had learned her falsehood before he went to the coroner; perhaps that knowledge had influenced him—perhaps he had interfered to spare her from being questioned again, to save her from repeating the denial. For an instant the thought held a strange sweetness; then she thrust it away with a sick, wilful recoil, like a child pushing back a hand that would comfort.

If it were so, she felt no gratitude. It would only prove how clearly he saw she was already disgraced, how contemptuously he must think of her, if he took such pains to spare her any further trial of truthfulness—which had failed so signally. She would have borne the whole. She would have perjured herself to save Frederick—far rather—than Mr. Thornton should have known enough to pity and intervene. What ill-fate had brought Thornton across Watson’s path? What made him the very magistrate called to receive Leonards’ dying deposition? What had Leonards said? How much had been intelligible? And might Thornton already know of the old accusation against Frederick, through their common friend Mr. Bell? If so, Thornton had striven to save the son who came, in defiance of the law, to a mother’s death-bed. Under that notion—under that alone—Margaret found she could be grateful, though even then not freely; for if his interference had been prompted by contempt, she could not bear it.

Had any one just cause to feel contempt for her?

Mr. Thornton—of all people—on whom she had looked down from imaginary heights until now.

She found herself suddenly, as in a dream, at his feet, and the fall distressed her strangely. She shrank from following the thought to its conclusion—from admitting, even to herself, how much she valued his respect. Whenever that confession rose at the end of her long avenues of reasoning, she turned aside and would not go down that path. She would not believe it.

It was later than she fancied. In last night’s agitation she had forgotten to wind her watch, and Mr. Hale had given special orders that she should not be disturbed by the usual morning call. At length the door opened cautiously, and Dixon put her head in. Seeing Margaret awake, she came forward with a letter.

“Here’s something to do you good, miss. A letter from Master Frederick.”

“Thank you, Dixon. How late it is!”

The words were languid. Dixon laid the letter on the counterpane. Margaret did not yet put out her hand.

“You want your breakfast, I’m sure,” Dixon went on. “I’ll bring it in a minute. Master’s got the tray all ready, I know.”

Margaret did not answer. Dixon left. Only then did Margaret take the letter, feeling she must be alone to break the seal—alone to let herself taste, without witness, whatever relief or sorrow lay within.

The first thing her eye caught was the date: two days earlier than its arrival. Frederick had written when he promised; their terror might have been spared. Her throat tightened as if she had swallowed something too dry; she read.

It was hasty, but it brought safety in every line. He had seen Mr. Henry Lennox, who at first shook his head, called it daring, warned him how dangerous it was to return to England with such an accusation hanging over him, backed by powerful influence. Yet, talking it through, Mr. Lennox acknowledged there might be a chance of acquittal—if credible witnesses could be found to prove Frederick’s statements. If so, it might be worth standing trial; if not, the risk was great. Mr. Lennox would examine the matter, would take pains.

“It struck me,” Frederick wrote, “that your introduction, little sister of mine, went a long way. Is it so? He made so many inquiries, I can assure you. He seemed a sharp, intelligent fellow, and in good practice too, to judge from the signs of business and the number of clerks about him. But these may be only lawyer’s dodges.

“I have just caught a packet on the point of sailing—I am off in five minutes. I may have to come back to England again on this business, so keep my visit secret. I shall send my father some rare old sherry, such as you cannot buy in England (such stuff as I’ve got in the bottle before me)! He needs something of the kind—my dear love to him—God bless him. I’m sure—here’s my cab.

“P.S.—What an escape that was! Take care you don’t breathe of my having been—not even to the Shaws.”

At the mention of the sherry—of Frederick with a bottle before him, tasting, judging, choosing some strong old comfort for the father he loved—Margaret’s mind gave a little helpless lurch toward ordinary life: a decanter catching lamplight; a cork drawn with that soft, satisfying pop; the deep, raisined scent of wine that has slept long in darkness; the warm burn in the throat that can, for a moment, make sorrow seem less sharp. Such homely images moved through her like ghosts of peace.

But peace did not come. Relief for Frederick’s immediate safety lay on one side of her heart; on the other lay the knowledge that Mr. Thornton had read her, judged her, acted for her—had taken responsibility—while she lay in the ashes of her own pride, scorched by the untranslatable misery of being one thing to herself and another in the eyes of the man whose opinion she would not yet confess she prized.

At the hour fixed the day before, they went out together to find Nicholas Higgins and his daughter. The very act of stepping side by side into the street—newly clothed, newly altered by sorrow—made them shy of one another, as if grief had changed the fit of their bodies and the manner of their walking. It was the first time, after many weeks, that they had chosen to go forth together; and without speaking of what was gone, they drew nearer in unuttered accord, keeping pace as though their feet had learned the measure of the same lament.

Milton met them with its usual harsh chorus: the metallic clink from some distant yard; the faint roar that never quite ceased, like a sea made of coal and wheels; and beneath it, nearer at hand, the domestic noises that struggled to survive—doors opening, a baby’s thin cry, a woman calling from an upper window, the soft scuff of clogs on flagstones. Mr. Hale, who had once lived among church-bells and the hush of country lanes, seemed to listen as one listens for a language half-forgotten; Margaret, whose senses had grown acute in this place, felt the sound press upon her mind as much as the soot pressed upon the sills. Even grief had its acoustics here: it did not fall like snow, it beat like rain on tin.

Higgins sat where they always found him, in his corner by the hearth; but his pipe lay untouched. The fire had sunk; the room smelt of cold ash and damp wool, as if warmth had been withdrawn not by weather but by will. He leaned his head on his hand, elbow on knee, and did not rise when they came in. Yet Margaret saw the welcome in his eye, as clear as a lamp in a dark place.

“Sit ye down, sit ye down,” he said, and jabbed the poker into the grate with a rough vigour, as though the iron could stir up more than embers. “Fire’s welly out.”

He looked more unkempt than she had ever seen him: a black stubble of beard shaded his hollowed cheeks; his jacket wanted mending; the paleness of his face showed harsher for the darkness about it. Hunger, she thought, had a look as unmistakable as smoke; and want of work left its own soot on a man.

“We thought we should have a good chance of finding you, just after dinner-time,” said Margaret, striving for a simple commonplace.

“We have had our sorrows too, since we saw you,” Mr. Hale added softly.

“Ay, ay,” said Higgins, and his voice had in it that grim jesting which is half-defiance, half-confession. “Sorrows is more plentiful than dinners just now; I reckon, my dinner hour stretches all o’er the day; yo’re pretty sure of finding me.”

“Are you out of work?” asked Margaret.

“Ay.” He gave it as one gives a blow—short, flat. Then, after a pause, he lifted his eyes. “I’m not wanting brass. Dunno yo’ think it. Bess, poor lass, had a little stock under her pillow, ready to slip into my hand, last moment, and Mary is fustian-cutting. But I’m out o’ work a’ the same.”

“We owe Mary some money,” said Mr. Hale, before Margaret’s quick pressure on his arm could stop the words.

Higgins’s head came up; his whole aspect hardened, like clay set in fire. “If hoo takes it, I’ll turn her out o’ doors. I’ll bide inside these four walls, and she’ll bide out. That’s a’.”

“But we owe her many thanks for her kind service—” Mr. Hale began again, his courtesy moving forward like a habit of old days.

“I ne’er thanken your daughter theer for her deeds o’ love to my poor wench,” said Higgins, and for a moment his roughness broke to show a sore, shy tenderness. “I ne’er could find th’ words. I’se have to begin to try now, if yo’ start making an ado about what little Mary could sarve yo’.”

Margaret would have turned him from this raw, defensive pride by gentler inquiry.

“Is it because of the strike you’re out of work?” she asked.

“Strike’s ended. It’s o’er for this time.” He stared into the dead fire as if reading there the bitter print of recent days. “I’m out o’ work because I ne’er asked for it. And I ne’er asked for it, because good words is scarce, and bad words is plentiful.”

He said it with a kind of stubborn relish, as though he had found some crooked satisfaction in putting their questions aside. Yet Margaret felt—felt as one feels the readiness of dough beneath the heel of the hand—that he wanted to be pressed, wanted to be made to yield and explain.

“And good words are—?” she prompted.

“Asking for work.” He spoke more fully now, the thought warming like broth on a rekindled flame. “I reckon them’s almost the best words that men can say. ‘Gi’ me work’ means ‘and I’ll do it like a man.’ Them’s good words.”

“And bad words are refusing you work when you ask for it?”

“Ay. Bad words is saying, ‘Aha, my fine chap! Yo’ve been true to yo’r order, and I’ll be true to mine. Yo’ did the best yo’ could for them as wanted help; that’s yo’re way of being true to yo’re kind: and I’ll be true to mine. Yo’ve been a poor fool, as knowed no better nor be a true faithful fool. So go and be d—d to yo’. There’s no work for yo’ here.’ Them’s bad words.” He drew breath as if the remembered insult had struck him anew. “I’m not a fool; and if I was, folk ought to ha’ taught me how to be wise after their fashion. I could m’appen ha’ learnt, if any one had tried to teach me.”

“Would it not be worth while,” said Mr. Hale, “to ask your old master if he would take you back again? It might be a poor chance, but it would be a chance.”

Higgins looked up sharply, his glance like a knife testing a seam. Then a low, bitter titter escaped him—no laughter, but something cracked.

“Measter! if it’s no offence, I’ll ask yo’ a question or two in my turn.”

“You’re quite welcome,” Mr. Hale replied, still with that gentle smile which tried to keep the world civil.

“I reckon yo’n some way of earning your bread. Folk seldom lives i’ Milton just for pleasure, if they can live anywhere else.”

“You are quite right. I have some independent property, but my intention in settling in Milton was to become a private tutor.”

“To teach folk.” Higgins nodded once, slow. “Well! I reckon they pay yo’ for teaching them, dunnot they?”

“Yes,” said Mr. Hale, and smiled a little more. “I teach in order to get paid.”

“And them that pays yo’, dun they tell yo’ whatten to do, or whatten not to do wi’ the money they gives you in just payment for your pains—in fair exchange like?”

“No; to be sure not!”

“They dunnot say, ‘Yo’ may have a brother, or a friend as dear as a brother, who wants this here brass for a purpose both yo’ and he think right; but yo’ mun promise not give it to him. Yo’ may see a good use, as yo’ think, to put yo’r money to; but we don’t think it good, and so if yo’ spend it a-thatens we’ll just leave off dealing with yo’.’ They dunnot say that, dun they?”

“No: to be sure not!”

“Would yo’ stand it if they did?”

“It would be some very hard pressure that would make me even think of submitting to such dictation.”

“There’s not the pressure on all the broad earth that would make me,” said Higgins, and now the reason stood up between them, plain as a bare table. “Now yo’ve got it. Yo’ve hit the bull’s eye. Hampers—that’s where I worked—makes their men pledge ’emselves they’ll not give a penny to help th’ Union or keep turn-outs fro’ clemming. They may pledge and make pledge,” he went on, contempt curling his lip; “they nobbut make liars and hypocrites. And that’s a less sin, to my mind, to make men’s hearts so hard that they’ll not do a kindness to them as needs it, or help on the right and just cause, though it goes again the strong hand.

“But I’ll ne’er forswear mysel’ for a’ the work the king could gi’e me. I’m a member o’ the Union; and I think it’s the only thing to do the workmen any good. And I’ve been a turn-out, and known what it was to clem; so if I get a shilling, sixpence shall go to them if they axe it from me. Consequence is, I dunnot see where I’m to get a shilling.”

“Is that rule about not contributing to the Union in force at all the mills?” Margaret asked.

“I cannot say. It’s a new regulation at ours; and I reckon they’ll find that they cannot stick to it. But it’s in force now. By-and-by they’ll find out, tyrants makes liars.”

Silence settled for a moment. The room held its small domestic details—Mary’s things, the worn chair, the cold hearth—like a poor pantry holding only the memory of meals. Margaret weighed her words. She knew how easily any hint of blame could turn Higgins’s mood sour as spoiled milk; yet the thought within her would not keep, and at last it broke out, softened by reluctance.

“Do you remember poor Boucher saying that the Union was a tyrant? I think he said it was the worse tyrant of all. And I remember, at the time I agreed with him.”

Higgins did not answer at once. He bent forward, head in his hands, staring down as if the black grate were a well. When he spoke, his voice was lower, and with it came something like a dark honesty.

“I’ll not deny but what th’ Union finds it necessary to force a man into his own good. I’ll speak truth. A man leads a dree life who’s not i’ th’ Union. But once i’ th’ Union, his interests are taken care on better nor he could do it for himsel’, or by himsel’, for that matter. It’s the only way working men can get their rights, by all joining together. More the members, more chance for each one separate man having justice done him.

“Government takes care o’ fools and madmen; and if any man is inclined to do himsel’ or his neighbour a hurt, it puts a bit of a check on him, whether he likes it or no. That’s all we do i’ th’ Union. We can’t clap folk into prison; but we can make a man’s life so heavy to be borne, that he’s obliged to come in, and be wise and helpful in spite of himsel’. Boucher were a fool all along, and ne’er a worse fool than at th’ last.”

“He did you harm?” Margaret asked.

“Aye, that did he. We had public opinion on our side, till he and his sort began rioting and breaking laws. It were all o’er wi’ the strike then.”

“Then would it not have been far better to have left him alone, and not forced him to join the Union? He did you no good; and you drove him mad.”

“Hale,” Mr. Hale murmured, warning in his tone, for he saw the storm in Higgins’s face.

But Higgins surprised them; he flung the gathering anger aside and spoke out with a strange abrupt admiration. “I like her. Hoo speaks plain out what’s in her mind. Hoo doesn’t comprehend th’ Union for all that. It’s a great power: it’s our only power.

“I ha’ read a bit o’ poetry about a plough going o’er a daisy, as made tears come into my eyes, afore I’d other cause for crying. But the chap ne’er stopped driving the plough, I’se warrant, for all he was pitiful about the daisy. He’d too much mother-wit for that. Th’ Union’s the plough, making ready the land for harvest-time. Such as Boucher—’twould be settin’ him up too much to liken him to a daisy; he’s liker a weed lounging over the ground—mun just made up their mind to be put out o’ the way. I’m sore vexed wi’ him just now. So m’appen, I dunnot speak him fair. I could go o’er him wi’ a plough mysel’, wi’ a’ the pleasure in life.”

“Why? What has he been doing? Anything fresh?” Margaret asked, startled.

“Ay, to be sure. He’s ne’er out o’ mischief, that man. First of a’ he must go raging like a mad fool, and kick up yon riot. Then he’d to go into hiding, where he’d a been yet, if Thornton had followed him out as I’d hoped he would ha’ done. But Thornton, having got his own purpose, didn’t care to go on wi’ the prosecution for the riot. So Boucher slunk back again to his house. He ne’er showed himsel’ abroad for a day or two. He had that grace.

“And then, where think ye that he went? Why, to Hampers’. Damn him! He went wi’ his mealy-mouthed face, that turns me sick to look at, a-asking for work, though he knowed well enough the new rule, o’ pledging themselves to give nought to th’ Unions; nought to help the starving turn-out! Why he’d a clemmed to death, if th’ Union had na helped him in his pinch.

“There he went, ossing to promise aught, and pledge himsel’ to aught—to tell a’ he know’d on our proceedings, the good-for-nothing Judas! But I’ll say this for Hamper, and thank him for it at my dying day, he drove Boucher away, and would na listen to him—ne’er a word—though folk standing by, says the traitor cried like a babby!”

“Oh! how shocking! how pitiful!” cried Margaret; and then, carried beyond prudence by the rawness of pity, she spoke as if she must save some remnant of humanity from being crushed under that plough. “Higgins, I don’t know you to-day. Don’t you see how you’ve made Boucher what he is, by driving him into the Union against his will—without his heart going with it. You have made him what he is!”

Made him what he is.

The words were scarcely gone when another sound came creeping, gathering, thickening along the narrow street, as if the air itself were being trodden into shape. It was not the mill-roar, not the ordinary clatter of Milton’s day. This had a solemn deliberateness—a slow, heavy rhythm that drew all other noises down into hush. Voices outside fell low. Feet shifted, but not onwards, not with purpose of labour; rather as if they circled about one dreadful centre.

Then it came clearly, that one distinct measured tramp: the laboured pace of men carrying a weight that was not merely heavy, but sacred in its horror.

Without speaking, they were all drawn to the door—impelled not by idle curiosity, but by some blast of fate that made the skin prickle and the heart contract. Out in the road six men advanced, three of them policemen. Across their shoulders lay a door wrenched from its hinges; upon it lay a human body. From either side of the door, drops fell steadily, ticking on the stones like a cruel clock.

Neighbours poured from their houses, and as they came, they followed, asking questions in quick whispers. The bearers answered at last, grudgingly, weary of repeating sorrow.

“We found him i’ th’ brook in the field beyond there.”

“Th’ brook!—why there’s not water enough to drown him!”
