“He was a determined chap. He lay wi’ his face downwards. He was sick enough o’ living, choose what cause he had for it.”

Higgins edged close to Margaret, so near she could feel his sleeve brush hers, and he spoke in a thin, piping voice she hardly knew as his. “It’s not John Boucher? He had na spunk enough. Sure! It’s not John Boucher! Why, they are a’ looking this way! Listen! I’ve a singing in my head, and I cannot hear.”

They set the door down gently on the stones. All could see. The dead man’s eyes were glassy; one lid hung half-open, staring upward to a pale strip of sky between roofs and chimneys. His face was swollen and darkened, and stained besides by the foul water of that brook—water long used for dyeing, turned to a sickly hue by the trades that fed Milton and poisoned it. The front of his head was bald; behind, thin hair lay in lank, dripping strands, each lock a channel for water that kept running, running, as if even death could not stop the seep of misery.

Through all the disfigurement Margaret knew him. John Boucher.

A kind of instinct—piety, reverence, a fierce refusal to let that poor distorted face be made a public thing—shot through her. She stepped forward and covered his countenance with her handkerchief, softly, as one covers bread from flies. It seemed sacrilege to stare; and in that moment of small, tender defiance, she did the only service left.

Eyes followed her, and then, guided by that movement, fixed upon Higgins, who stood rooted, like a man planted in frozen ground.

The bearers conferred. One came to Higgins; Higgins shrank backward as though his own threshold were now a punishment.

“Higgins, thou knowed him! Thou mun go tell the wife. Do it gently, man, but do it quick, for we canna leave him here long.”

“I canna go,” Higgins said. “Dunnot ask me. I canna face her.”

“Thou knows her best,” the man insisted. “We’n done a deal in bringing him here—thou take thy share.”

“I canna do it,” Higgins repeated, and now his voice held no stubbornness, only a kind of struck-down weakness. “I’m welly felled wi’ seeing him. We wasn’t friends; and now he’s dead.”

“Well, if thou wunnot thou wunnot. Some one mun though. It’s a dree task; but it’s a chance, every minute, as she doesn’t hear on it in some rougher way nor a person going to make her let on by degrees, as it were.”

“Papa, do you go,” Margaret whispered.

“If I could—if I had time to think of what I had better say; but all at once—” Mr. Hale was trembling, every nerve of him shaken by the suddenness and the public brutality of it.

“I will go,” said Margaret.

“Bless yo’, miss,” said the man, and his rough face softened. “It will be a kind act; for she’s been but a sickly sort o’ body, I hear, and few hereabouts know much on her.”

Margaret crossed to the Bouchers’ door and knocked; but within was such a tumult of small, ill-governed children that no answer could be heard. She doubted even her knocking had reached any adult ear. Each second of delay made her heart recoil. She opened the door and went in, shutting it behind her, and, unseen by the woman within, she slipped the bolt, as if to keep the crowd of the street from pouring in after her.

Mrs. Boucher sat in a rocking-chair across from the hearth. The fireplace was ill kept; the whole room looked as if no hand had tidied it for days. There was a sour smell of unwashed clothes and stale food—or rather the absence of food, that lingering odour of empty pans and cold grates. The children’s cries and quarrels ricocheted off the walls, shrill and incessant, so that Margaret’s first words vanished like breath into a storm.

She tried again, leaning forward as if her voice might be carried on kindness. “How are you, Mrs. Boucher? But very poorly, I’m afraid.”

“I’ve chance o’ being well,” the woman answered, querulous and worn to a thin edge. “I’m left alone to manage these childer, and nought for to give ’em for to keep ’em quiet. John should na ha’ left me, and me so poorly.”

“How long is it since he went away?”

“Four days sin’. No one would give him work here, and he’d to go on tramp toward Greenfield. But he might ha’ been back afore this, or sent me some word if he’d getten work. He might—”

“Oh, don’t blame him,” Margaret said quickly, as if she could hold back the coming truth by tenderness. “He felt it deeply, I’m sure—”

“Willto’ hold thy din, and let me hear the lady speak!” Mrs. Boucher snapped at a little child of about a year, who was tugging and clamouring. Then she turned back with a poor apology. “He’s always mithering me for ‘daddy’ and ‘butty’; and I ha’ no butties to give him, and daddy’s away, and forgotten us a’, I think.”

But even as she said it, her mood shifted like a gust through a weak flame. “He’s his father’s darling, he is,” she added, and dragged the child onto her knee, kissing him with sudden fierce love.

Margaret laid her hand on the woman’s arm, not to restrain her affection, but to claim her attention. Their eyes met. In Margaret’s face the woman read what no words had yet spoken.

“Poor little fellow!” Margaret said slowly, and the tense pause before the verb held a world. “He _was_ his father’s darling.”

“He _is_ his father’s darling,” Mrs. Boucher cried, starting up as if to fight the sentence itself. She stood face to face with Margaret. For a moment neither spoke. Then the widow’s voice dropped into a low growl that gathered wildness as it went on. “He _is_ his father’s darling, I say. Poor folk can love their childer as well as rich. Why dunno yo’ speak? Why dun yo’ stare at me wi’ your great pitiful eyes? Where’s John?”

Weak as she was, she seized Margaret and shook her, as though truth could be shaken out by force.

“Oh, my God!” she whispered, and the meaning struck her. She fell back into the chair.

Margaret lifted the child and placed him in the woman’s arms, as if giving her something living to cling to. “He loved him,” Margaret said, each word like a crumb offered to a starving heart.

“Ay,” Mrs. Boucher answered, shaking her head, and now the hardness fell away. “He loved us a’. We had some one to love us once. It’s a long time ago; but when he were in life and with us he did love us, he did. He loved this babby m’appen the best on us; but he loved me and I loved him, though I was calling him five minutes agone.”

Then, in a sudden rush of desperate bargaining with fate, she tried to rise. “Are yo’ sure he’s dead? If it’s only that he’s ill and like to die, they may bring him round yet. I’m but an ailing creature mysel’—I’ve been ailing this long time.”

“But he is dead—he is drowned!”

“Folk are brought round after they’re dead-drowned.” Mrs. Boucher’s mind clutched at scraps of hope the way a hungry child clutches at crusts. “Whatten was I thinking of, to sit still when I should be stirring mysel’? Here, whisth thee, child—whisth thee! tak’ this, tak’ aught to play wi’, but dunnot cry while my heart’s breaking! Oh, where is my strength gone to? Oh John—husband!”

She swayed; Margaret caught her before she could fall. Margaret sat down in the rocking-chair and held her, the woman’s head on Margaret’s shoulder as if Margaret were suddenly made into mother and pillar both. The other children, huddled in frightened clusters, began slowly to understand. Their dull young minds received the knowledge like cold water, late but irresistible. They lifted a cry so raw that it seemed to tear the air, a grief noisier than any machine—an acoustic wound. The baby, Johnnie, cried loudest of all, not knowing why, only knowing the room had changed its sound.

Mrs. Boucher trembled in Margaret’s arms.

A noise came at the door—voices, movement, the street pushing its way indoors.

“Open it. Open it quick,” Margaret said to the eldest child. “It’s bolted; make no noise—be very still. Oh, papa—let them go upstairs very softly and carefully, and perhaps she will not hear them. She has fainted—that’s all.”

“It’s as well for her, poor creature,” said a woman who came in with the bearers’ following. “But yo’re not fit to hold her. Stay, I’ll run fetch a pillow, and we’ll let her down easy on the floor.”

This neighbour, evidently new to the place, moved with a practised kindness that made room in the stifled air. Her hands were quick, and her voice had that firm domestic authority which can turn chaos into an ordered sickroom. Margaret felt, with relief that was almost guilt, that she was no longer the only one bearing the weight.

She looked round for Higgins. He was not there.

So she spoke to the woman who had taken command of placing Mrs. Boucher gently down. “Can you give all these people a hint that they had better leave in quietness? So that when she comes round, she could only find one or two that she knows about her. Papa, will you speak to the men, and get them to go away. She cannot breathe, poor thing, with this crowd about her.”

Margaret knelt and bathed Mrs. Boucher’s face with vinegar. The sharp scent rose, cutting through the close odours of poverty and sweat. In a few minutes, she felt a sudden coolness—fresh air, as if a window had opened in the world. She looked up, and saw a smile pass between her father and the neighbour woman.

“What is it?” Margaret asked.

“Only our good friend here,” Mr. Hale answered, “hit on a capital expedient for clearing the place.”

“I bid ’em begone,” said the neighbour, plain and satisfied, “and each take a child with ’em, and to mind that they were orphans, and their mother a widow. It was who could do most, and the childer are sure of a bellyful to-day, and of kindness too.” She paused and looked at Margaret, practical even in sorrow. “Does hoo know how he died?”

“No,” Margaret said. “I could not tell her all at once.”

“Hoo mun be told because of th’ Inquest. See! Hoo’s coming round; shall you or I do it? or m’appen your father would be best?”

“No; you, you,” Margaret said, knowing her own voice would fail, and her father’s tenderness would make the truth impossible.

They waited in silence until Mrs. Boucher’s eyes opened with full knowledge. Then the neighbour sat down on the floor and lifted the widow’s head and shoulders onto her lap, as if grief were a fever and must be nursed like one.

“Neighbour,” she said, “your man is dead. Guess yo’ how he died?”

“He were drowned,” Mrs. Boucher answered faintly, and began to cry for the first time—not in wildness, but in a slow, leaking sorrow, like water through a crack. “He were found drowned.”

“He were found drowned,” the neighbour repeated, steady as a bell tolling. “He were coming home very hopeless o’ aught on earth. He thought God could na be harder than men; m’appen not so hard; m’appen as tender as a mother; m’appen tenderer. I’m not saying he did right, and I’m not saying he did wrong. All I say is, may neither me nor mine ever have his sore heart, or we may do like things.”

“He has left me alone wi’ a’ these children!” moaned the widow—less shaken by the manner of his death than Margaret had expected, but shaken to the core by the practical desolation of it, the empty pot, the empty bed, the empty hand to earn.

“Not alone,” Mr. Hale said solemnly, his voice like a quiet chord beneath the wailing. “Who is with you? Who will take up your cause?”

Mrs. Boucher’s eyes widened, startled by this strange gentleness in a strange man. “Who has promised to be a father to the fatherless?” he continued.

“But I’ve getten six children, sir,” she said, overwhelmed and helpless, “and the eldest not eight years of age. I’m not meaning for to doubt His power, sir,—only it needs a deal o’ trust”; and she fell again into weeping.

“Hoo’ll be better able to talk to-morrow, sir,” the neighbour murmured to Mr. Hale, not unkindly. “Best comfort now would be the feel of a child at her heart. I’m sorry they took the babby.”

“I’ll go for it,” said Margaret.

She went out and returned in a few minutes with little Johnnie in her arms. His face was smeared with eating—evidence of some neighbour’s hurried charity; his hands clutched treasures gathered as if to make a feast of play against famine: shells, bits of crystal, the broken head of a plaster figure. Margaret laid him into his mother’s arms. The child settled there, warm and living, and for an instant the room’s sound changed: grief still cried, but it had something to hold it.

“There!” said the neighbour woman. “Now you go. They’ll cry together, and comfort together, better nor any one but a child can do. I’ll stop with her as long as I’m needed, and if you come to-morrow, you’ can have a deal o’ wise talk with her, that she’s not up to to-day.”

When Margaret and her father went slowly up the street, the town seemed louder again, as if it resented the brief hush sorrow had imposed. Yet now every sound had altered meaning: the tramp of feet might turn to a funeral rhythm at any corner; the hiss of steam might be breath cut short. The day itself felt circular, as though what had been spoken in Higgins’s room—plough and daisy, force and mercy—had come round and made its harsh proof in the street.

Margaret paused at Higgins’s closed door.

“Shall we go in?” Mr. Hale asked. “I was thinking of him too.”

They knocked. No answer came. They tried the latch. It was bolted; but they heard movement within, a dull shifting, and then a sudden fall, as of a book dropped from a hand that could not hold it.

“Nicholas!” Margaret called.

No response.

“Nicholas!” she said again. “It is only us. Won’t you let us come in?”

“No,” Higgins answered from within, and his voice sounded thick, as if he spoke through wool. “I spoke as plain as I could, ’bout using words, when I bolted th’ door. Let me be, this day.”

Mr. Hale would have urged; but Margaret, understanding the need for silence as she understood the need for bread, touched her father’s lips.

“I don’t wonder at it,” she said quietly. “I myself long to be alone. It seems the only thing to do one good after a day like this.”

Higgins’s door was locked when they went the next day to pay their call on the widow Boucher. This time an officious neighbour—one of those who live half on other people’s news—leaned from her threshold to tell them he was truly out, though he had been in early to see Mrs. Boucher before going upon whatever work, or quest of work, now filled his hours.

The visit itself left a dull taste behind, like weak tea long stewed—warm, bitter, and offering no comfort. Mrs. Boucher sat sunk in her chair with the sullenness of an invalid who has turned grievance into a kind of nourishment. She held herself for an ill-used woman by her husband’s suicide; and there was just truth enough, just the ragged edge of reason, to make it hard to tear away without wounding her. Yet it was grievous to see how completely her thoughts circled back upon herself—her wrongs, her helplessness, her claim upon the world—and how that selfishness spread, like soot, even over her relations with her children. They were “incumbrances,” she said, even while her rough, animal affection clung to them as property clings.

Margaret tried to draw near to one or two of the little ones while her father strove—patiently, earnestly—to lift the widow’s mind into some channel higher than querulousness. It was the children who mourned truly, with a simplicity that could not counterfeit. Daddy had been kind. Each, in eager stammering fragments, brought up some tenderness—an apple shared, a penny saved, a piggyback ride, a sheltering arm when a scold or blow threatened.

One of them said, with eyes wide and haunted, “Is yon thing upstairs really him? it doesna look like him. I’m feared on it, and I never was feared o’ daddy.”

Margaret’s heart contracted. The mother, in her hungry requirement of sympathy, had dragged them upstairs to look upon their dead father—disfigured, made strange—mixing the coarseness of horror with the profoundness of natural grief, as if she had seasoned a child’s bread with ashes and wondered it would not be eaten.

She bent to them instead, speaking softly, not of the body upstairs but of what lay close to their hands: what they could do for mother, and—more potent still—what father would have wished them to do. Duties that could be touched and finished were like crumbs laid for frightened birds. They began, shyly, to stir into action: one fetched a cloth, another picked up a fallen garment, another carried a cup to the table. Under Margaret’s direction the slatternly room was “redded up,” little by little, their grief finding a safer outlet in small, steady motions.

Mr. Hale’s way was different. He set too high a standard, too abstract a view, before the indolent, self-absorbed invalid. She could not rouse her torpid mind into any vivid imagining of what her husband’s misery had been before that last terrible step; she could only see how it injured her. She could not enter into the enduring mercy of a God who had not, by miracle, held back the water from drowning her prostrate husband. Secretly she blamed him for despair; aloud she blamed everything and everyone who could be imagined as having driven him to it.

The masters—the Union—her own children for being numerous, hungry, noisy—made up one great army of personal enemies. Mr. Thornton in particular was named with peculiar bitterness: the very man whose mill Boucher had attacked, and who afterwards had caused the warrant for Boucher’s apprehension to be withdrawn. In her mouth even that mercy turned to accusation: had the law been allowed to take its course, she hinted darkly, things would have been different; yet she also demanded protection from the very world she cursed.

Margaret heard enough to dishearten her. When at last they came away into the damp Milton air, she could not cheer her father. The streets were wet; the stones shone; wheels hissed and clattered; iron-shod hoofs rang sharply, and every sound seemed doubled by the close brick walls. The town’s harsh music—hammer, cart, bell, shouting—pressed on the ear without pause, as if it would not allow a heart to gather itself into quiet.

“It is the town life,” Margaret said at length, almost as if she were trying to lay her hand on some tangible cause. “Their nerves are quickened by the haste and bustle and speed of everything around them; to say nothing of the confinement in these pent-up houses, which of itself is enough to induce depression and worry of spirits. Now in the country, people live so much more out of doors, even children, and even in the winter.”

“But people must live in towns,” Mr. Hale replied. “And in the country some get such stagnant habits of mind that they are almost fatalists.”

“Yes; I acknowledge that. I suppose each mode of life produces its own trials and its own temptations. The dweller in towns must find it as difficult to be patient as the country-bred man must find it to be active and equal to unwonted emergencies. Both must find it hard to realise a future of any kind—the one because the present is so living and hurrying and close around him; the other because his life tempts him to revel in the mere sense of animal existence, not knowing of, and consequently not caring for any pungency of pleasure, for the attainment of which he can plan, and deny himself, and look forward.”

“And thus both the necessity for engrossment, and the stupid content in the present, produce the same effects,” said Mr. Hale, following her thought with the gentleness of one who liked to see her mind at work. “But this poor Mrs. Boucher! how little we can do for her.”

“And yet we dare not leave her without our efforts, although they may seem so useless. Oh papa! it’s a hard world to live in!”

“So it is, my child. We feel it so just now, at any rate; but we have been very happy, even in the midst of our sorrow. What a pleasure Frederick’s visit was!”

“Yes, that it was,” said Margaret, brightening as warmth returns to chilled fingers. “It was such a charming, snatched, forbidden thing.”

But the brightness stopped short, as if a shutter had fallen. She had spoiled the memory by what had happened—by her own cowardice. Of all faults she most despised in others, it was want of bravery; the meanness of heart which leads to untruth. And she had been guilty of it.

Then came the thought of Mr. Thornton’s knowledge of her falsehood. She wondered whether she should have minded detection half so much from any one else. She tried, as if testing a wound, to imagine her aunt Shaw and Edith knowing, her father knowing, Captain Lennox, Frederick. Frederick’s disapproval—even if he understood it had been done for him—would have been pain enough; the brother and sister were in the first flush of recovered regard. Yet even that seemed small beside the shame, the shrinking shame, she felt at the thought of meeting Mr. Thornton again.

And yet she longed to see him, to have the meeting over, to know where she stood in his opinion.

Her cheeks burned as she recalled how proudly—how rashly—she had implied, early in their acquaintance, an objection to trade because it so often led to deceit: inferior goods passed for superior; credit assumed for wealth and resources not possessed. She remembered Mr. Thornton’s look of calm disdain as he answered that, in the great scheme of commerce, all dishonourable ways were sure to injure a man in the long run; and that, even tested by the poor standard of success, deceit was folly, not wisdom. She remembered her own then-untempted truth asking whether buying in the cheapest and selling in the dearest market did not show some want of that transparent justice connected with truth; she remembered her use of the word “chivalric,” and her father’s correction to the higher word, “Christian,” drawing the argument upon himself while she sat silent with a slight contempt.

No more contempt for her now. No more talk of “chivalric.” Henceforward she must feel humiliated—disgraced—in his sight.

But when should she see him?

All that day her heart sprang up, startled, at each ring of the door-bell; and then, when it sank again to calmness, it felt strangely sick and saddened at the disappointment. It was evident her father expected him too, and was surprised he did not come. There were points in their conversation the other night which time had not allowed them to enlarge; it had been understood that if possible on the succeeding evening—if not then, at least the first evening Mr. Thornton could command—they should meet again for discussion. Mr. Hale had looked forward to it. He had not yet resumed instruction to his pupils, having relinquished it at the beginning of his wife’s more serious illness; his occupations were few, and the recent tragedy of Boucher’s suicide had driven him back more eagerly than ever upon his speculations.

He was restless all evening, pacing, sitting down, rising again. “I quite expected to have seen Mr. Thornton,” he said more than once. “I think the messenger who brought the book last night must have had some note, and forgot to deliver it. Do you think there has been any message left to-day?”

“I will go and inquire, papa,” said Margaret, after the phrases had been rung in varied order once or twice. “Stay—there’s a ring!”

She sat down instantly and bent her head attentively over her work, as if she could stitch her agitation into the cloth. A step came on the stairs—only one; she knew Dixon’s tread. She lifted her head and sighed, and believed she felt glad.

“It’s that Higgins, sir,” said Dixon, coming in with compressed lips. “He wants to see you, or else Miss Hale. Or it might be Miss Hale first, and then you, sir; for he’s in a strange kind of way.”

“He had better come up here, Dixon; and then he can see us both, and choose which he likes for his listener.”

“Oh! very well, sir. I’ve no wish to hear what he’s got to say, I’m sure; only, if you could see his shoes, I’m sure you’d say the kitchen was the fitter place.”

“He can wipe them, I suppose,” said Mr. Hale.

Dixon flung off to send him up. She was a little mollified, however, when Higgins looked down at his feet with a hesitating air; then, sitting on the bottom stair, he took off the offending shoes and, without a word, walked up in his stockings.

“Sarvant, sir!” he said, slicking his hair down as he entered. Then, looking at Margaret, he added, with an awkward kind of apology, “If hoo’ll excuse me for being i’ my stockings; I’se been tramping a’ day, and streets is none o’ th’ cleanest.”

Fatigue might account for the change in his manner. He was unusually quiet and subdued, and he seemed to have difficulty pushing his words out as if they stuck. Mr. Hale, ever quick in sympathy with shyness or hesitation, came to his aid as naturally as one offers a chair.

“We shall have tea up directly, and then you’ll take a cup with us, Mr. Higgins. I am sure you are tired, if you’ve been out much this wet relaxing day. Margaret, my dear, can’t you hasten tea?”

Margaret could only “hasten” tea by taking preparation into her own hands, and so offending Dixon, who was emerging out of sorrow for her late mistress into a touchy, irritable state. But Martha, like all who came within Margaret’s influence—even Dixon herself in the end—found pleasure and honour in forwarding her wishes. Her ready hands, and Margaret’s sweet forbearance, soon made Dixon ashamed.

“Why master and you must always be asking the lower classes up-stairs, since we came to Milton, I cannot understand,” Dixon grumbled below. “Folk at Helstone were never brought higher than the kitchen; and I’ve let one or two of them know before now that they might think it an honour to be even there.”

Upstairs, Higgins found it easier to unburden himself to one than to two. When Margaret left the room, he went to the door and assured himself it was shut. Then he came and stood close to Mr. Hale, as if warmth or courage might be borrowed by proximity.

“Master,” he said, “yo’d not guess easy what I’ve been tramping after to-day. Special if yo’d remember my manner o’ talk yesterday. I’ve been a seeking work. I have.”

“I said to mysel’, I’d keep a civil tongue in my head, let who would say what ’em would. I’d set my teeth into my tongue sooner nor speak i’ haste. For that man’s sake—yo’ understand,” he added, jerking his thumb back towards some imagined point behind him.

“No, I don’t,” said Mr. Hale, bewildered.

“That chap as lies theer,” Higgins continued, with another jerk, “Him as went and drownded himself, poor chap! I did na think he’d got it in him to lie still and let the water creep o’er him till he died. Boucher, yo’ know.”

“Yes, I know now,” said Mr. Hale. “Go back to what you were saying: you’d not speak in haste—”

“For his sake. Yet not for his sake,” Higgins went on, stumbling into clearer speech as he warmed. “For where’er he is, and whate’er, he’ll ne’er know other clemming or cold again; but for the wife’s sake, and the bits o’ childer.”

“God bless you!” Mr. Hale cried, starting up with a sudden movement, then checked himself, breathless. “What do you mean? Tell me out.”

“I have telled yo’,” said Higgins, surprised at such agitation. “I would na ask for work for mysel’; but them’s left as a charge on me. I reckon, I would ha guided Boucher to a better end; but I set him off o’ th’ road, and so I mun answer for him.”

Mr. Hale seized Higgins’s hand and shook it heartily without speaking. Higgins looked awkward, almost ashamed of having drawn such warmth.

“Theer, theer, master! Theer’s ne’er a man, to call a man, amongst us, but what would do th’ same; ay, and better too; for, belie’ me, Is’e ne’er got a stroke o’ work, nor yet a sight of any. For all I telled Hamper that, let alone his pledge—which I would not sign—no, I could na, not e’en for this—he’d ne’er ha’ such a worker on his mill as I would be—he’d ha’ none o’ me—no more would none o’ th’ others. I’m a poor black feckless sheep—childer may clem for ought I can do, unless, parson, yo’d help me?”

“Help you! How? I would do anything—but what can I do?”

At that moment Margaret re-entered, and Higgins’s eyes went towards her as if she were some stronger light in the room.

“Miss there,” he said, “has often talked grand o’ the South, and the ways down there. Now I dunnot know how far off it is, but I been thinking if I could get ’em down theer, where food is cheap and wages good, and all the folk, rich and poor, master and man, friendly like; yo’ could, may be, help me to work. I’m not forty-five, and I’ve a deal o’ strength in me, measter.”

“But what kind of work could you do, my man?” Mr. Hale asked, gently practical.

“Well, I reckon I could spade a bit—”

“And for that,” Margaret said, stepping forwards, “for anything you could do, Higgins, with the best will in the world, you would, may be, get nine shillings a week; may be ten, at the outside. Food is much the same as here, except that you might have a little garden—”

“The childer could work at that,” said he quickly, catching at the notion as a hungry man catches at bread. “I’m sick o’ Milton anyways, and Milton is sick o’ me.”

“You must not go the South,” said Margaret, firmly, “for all that. You could not stand it. You would have to be out in all weathers. It would kill you with rheumatism. The mere bodily work at your time of life would break you down. The fare is far different to what you have been accustomed to.”

“I’se nought particular about my meat,” he said, offended, as if she had accused him of daintiness.

“But you’ve reckoned on having butcher’s meat once a day, if you’re in work,” Margaret answered, not yielding, her voice full of that earnestness which came from having watched want close at hand. “Pay for that out of your ten shillings, and keep those poor children if you can. I owe it to you—since it’s my way of talking that has set you off on this idea—to put it all clear before you. You would not bear the dulness of the life; you don’t know what it is; it would eat you away like rust. Those that have lived there all their lives are used to soaking in the stagnant waters. They labour on from day to day, in the great solitude of steaming fields—never speaking or lifting up their poor, bent, downcast heads. The hard spadework robs their brain of life; the sameness of their toil deadens their imagination. They don’t care to meet to talk over thoughts and speculations, even of the weakest, wildest kind, after their work is done; they go home brutishly tired, poor creatures! caring for nothing but food and rest. You could not stir them up into any companionship, which you get in a town as plentiful as the air you breathe—whether it be good or bad—and that I don’t know; but I do know that you of all men are not one to bear a life among such labourers. What would be peace to them would be eternal fretting to you. Think no more of it, Nicholas, I beg. Besides, you could never pay to get mother and children all there—that’s one good thing.”

“I’ve reckoned for that. One house mun do for us a’, and the furniture o’ t’other would go a good way. And men theer mun have their families to keep—m’appen six or seven childer. God help ’em!” he said; then, as if his own rapid setting out of obstacles convinced him more than any opposition could, the idea fell away from him, leaving him tired and bare.

“God help ’em! North an’ South have each getten their own troubles. If work’s sure and steady theer, labour’s paid at starvation wages; while here we’n rucks o’ money coming in one quarter, and ne’er a farthing th’ next. For sure, th’ world is in a confusion that passes me or any other man to understand; it needs fettling, and who’s to fettle it if it’s as yon folks say, and there’s nought but what we see?”

Mr. Hale was busy cutting bread and butter. Margaret was glad of it; she saw Higgins was better left to himself. If her father began to speak, even mildly, on the subject of Higgins’s thoughts, Higgins would feel himself challenged into argument and bound to maintain his ground. So they kept up indifferent talk while Higgins, scarcely aware whether he ate or not, made a substantial meal.

When he pushed his chair away, he tried to take interest again in their words; but his attention would not hold. He fell back into a kind of dreamy gloom, as if listening to some far-off inward noise louder than anything in the room.

Suddenly Margaret said—she had been shaping the question for some time, feeling the words stick in her throat—“Higgins, have you been to Marlborough Mills to seek for work?”

“Thornton’s?” he asked.

“Ay,” said Margaret. “I’ve been at Thornton’s.”

“And what did he say?” Mr. Hale asked, leaning forwards.

“Such a chap as me is not like to see the measter. Th’ o’erlooker bid me go and be d——d.”

“I wish you had seen Mr. Thornton,” said Mr. Hale. “He might not have given you work, but he would not have used such language.”

“As to th’ language, I’m welly used to it; it dunnot matter to me. I’m not nesh mysel’ when I’m put out. It were th’ fact that I were na wanted theer, no more nor ony other place, as I minded.”

“But I wish you had seen Mr. Thornton,” Margaret said again, and her voice had an entreaty that made it more than a repetition. “Would you go again—it’s a good deal to ask, I know—but would you go to-morrow and try him? I should be so glad if you would.”

“I’m afraid it would be of no use,” Mr. Hale murmured, low.

Margaret still looked at Higgins, waiting. Those grave, soft eyes of hers—eyes that saw suffering and would not turn away—were hard to resist. Higgins drew a long breath.

“It would tax my pride above a bit,” he said. “If it were for mysel’, I could stand a deal o’ clemming first; I’d sooner knock him down than ask a favour from him. I’d a deal sooner be flogged mysel’. But yo’re not a common wench, axing yo’r pardon, nor yet have yo’ common ways about yo’. I’ll e’en make a wry face, and go at it to-morrow. Dunna yo’ think that he’ll do it. That man has it in him to be burnt at the stake afore he’ll give in. I’ll do it for yo’r sake, Miss Hale, and it’s first time in my life as e’er I give way to a woman. Neither my wife nor Bess could e’er say that much again me.”

“All the more do I thank you,” said Margaret, smiling—relieved, and yet troubled for what she was asking. “Though I don’t believe you: I believe you have just given way to wife and daughter as much as most men.”

“And as to Mr. Thornton,” said Mr. Hale, “I’ll give you a note to him, which, I think I may venture say, will ensure you a hearing.”

“I thank yo’ kindly, sir,” Higgins answered, stiffening, “but I’d as lief stand on my own bottom. I dunnot stomach the notion of having favour curried for me, by one as doesn’t know the ins and outs of the quarrel. Meddling ’twixt master and man is liker meddling ’twixt husband and wife than aught else: it takes a deal of wisdom to do ony good. I’ll stand guard at the lodge door. I’ll stand there fro’ six in the morning till I get speech on him. But I’d liefer sweep th’ streets, if paupers had na’ got hold on that work. Dunna yo’ hope, miss. There’ll be more chance o’ getting milk out of a flint. I wish yo’ a very good night, and many thanks to yo’.”

“You’ll find your shoes by the kitchen fire; I took them there to dry,” said Margaret.

He turned and looked at her steadily. Then he brushed his lean hand across his eyes, as if angry to find them wet, and went his way.

When the door had closed behind him, Mr. Hale said, with a little vexation, “How proud that man is!”

“He is,” Margaret replied. “But what grand makings of a man there are in him, pride and all.”

“It’s amusing to see how he evidently respects the part in Mr. Thornton’s character which is like his own.”

“There’s granite in all these northern people, papa, is there not?” Margaret said, thinking of the set mouths and resolute brows she had learnt to read in Milton, and of the hard, incessant sound of the place—the mills’ ceaseless thunder that seemed to beat into men’s hearts until they answered it with a like unyieldingness.

“There was none in poor Boucher, I am afraid; none in his wife either.”

“I should guess by their tones that they had Irish blood in them,” said Margaret, half to herself; and then, as if already living a little forward into the morrow, “I wonder what success he’ll have to-morrow. If he and Mr. Thornton would speak out together as man to man—if Higgins would forget that Mr. Thornton was a master, and speak to him as he does to us—and if Mr. Thornton would be patient enough to listen to him with his human heart, not with his master’s ears—”

“You are getting to do Mr. Thornton justice at last, Margaret,” said her father, pinching her ear with a fondness that had no suspicion of the sharp inward pang his words caused.

Margaret’s throat tightened; she could not answer. A thought rose, bitter and helpless: If she had been a man, she could have gone and forced the matter to speech—forced him to express his disapprobation, and told him plainly she knew she had deserved it. It seemed hard to lose him as a friend just when she had begun to feel his value. How tender he had been with dear mamma! If only for her sake, she wished he would come—come soon—so that at least she might know how far she was abased in his eyes.

It was not only that Margaret Hale had been known to Mr. Thornton to have spoken falsely—though she told herself that this alone had turned his mind against her—but that the falsehood, in his thoughts, clung like a burr to one conclusion: another man.

He could not dislodge the image—fond, earnest, unmistakably intimate—of the look he had once seen pass between her and that other. The posture of trust, of familiar confidence (and, if he would be honest, something nearer to endearment). It rose before him in the clatter of the mill, in the hush of his own room, in the very rhythm of his tread across the hearthrug. And then—because misery never comes with one barb only—the setting returned with its cruel exactness: dusk thickening into twilight; a place far from home, and lonely enough to make even innocence appear like secrecy.

His better self had argued, at first, that circumstances might be accidental, innocent, justifiable. But once grant her the right to love and be beloved (and had he any ground to deny it, after the clear severity with which she had cast his own love from her?), it was easy—terribly easy—to imagine she had been drawn on to linger, to walk farther, to stay later than she had meant.

Yet always the same thought cut him deeper than the rest: that lie.

A lie implied consciousness; something wrong to be hidden; a shame crouched somewhere behind the bright candour in which he had believed she lived. And that was what made it agony rather than simple contempt. He did her the justice—though it would have relieved him to call her utterly unworthy—that falsehood was unlike her. Therefore, in his tortured reasoning, the stain became proof not of her baseness, but of the strength of her attachment: she had loved another so blindly as to violate her own truthful nature for him. The dark, slight, elegant, handsome man—while he himself was rough and stern, strongly made, a Milton manufacturer whose hands were more used to iron and cotton than to tenderness.

Jealousy lashed him as if it were a scourge. He went back, point by point, to her sharp words; to the sting of her saying she would have done as much for any man in the crowd—more readily than for him. He had tried to value the mechanical courage with which she had flung herself between him and the mob; now he mocked himself for it. That act, he told himself bitterly, had been for peace, for the crowd, for the common good. But with the other man there had been something withheld from the world: looks, words, hand-clasps, concealments—lies—all set apart and saved for him alone.

He was conscious he had never been so irritable in his life. Every question asked of him seemed to deserve a short, abrupt answer—more like a bark than speech. And the consciousness hurt his pride; he had always prided himself on self-control, and control himself he would. So he smoothed the manner into quiet deliberation; but the substance of what he said was harder, sterner than usual. At home he grew more silent still, passing his evenings in a continual pacing to and fro—an exercise that would have irritated his mother exceedingly had it been practised by anyone less dear than her son, and did little to soften her own tongue.

“Can you stop—can you sit down for a moment?” she cried at last. “I have something to say to you, if you would give up that everlasting walk, walk, walk.”

He sat down instantly, on a chair against the wall, as if obedience cost him less than motion.

“I want to speak to you about Betsy. She says she must leave us; that her lover’s death has so affected her spirits she can’t give her heart to her work.”

“Very well,” he said, his voice quiet with effort. “Other cooks are to be met with.”

“That’s so like a man. It’s not merely the cooking; it is that she knows all the ways of the house.” Mrs. Thornton’s mouth tightened. “Besides, she tells me something about your friend Miss Hale.”

“Miss Hale is no friend of mine. Mr. Hale is my friend.”

“I am glad to hear you say so,” returned his mother quickly, “for if she had been your friend, what Betsy says would have annoyed you.”

“Let me hear it,” he said, in that very composed tone he had been forcing on himself for days.

“Betsy says that the night on which her lover—I forget his name, for she always calls him ‘he’—”

“Leonards,” he answered, without looking at her.

“The night on which Leonards was last seen at the station—when he was last seen on duty, in fact—Miss Hale was there, walking about with a young man who, Betsy believes, killed Leonards by some blow or push.”

“Leonards was not killed by any blow or push.”

Mrs. Thornton’s head lifted. “How do you know?”

“Because I distinctly put the question to the surgeon of the Infirmary. He told me there was an internal disease of long standing, caused by Leonards’ habit of drinking to excess; that the fact of his becoming rapidly worse while in a state of intoxication, settled the question as to whether the last fatal attack was caused by excess of drinking, or the fall.”

“The fall!” she repeated sharply. “What fall?”

“Caused by the blow or push of which Betsy speaks.”

“Then there was a blow or push?”

“I believe so.”

“And who did it?”

“As there was no inquest,” he replied, the words clipped, “in consequence of the doctor’s opinion, I cannot tell you.”

“But Miss Hale was there?” His mother’s eyes bored into him.

He did not answer.

“And with a young man?” she persisted.

Still he said nothing. At last, as if to put up a barrier with a legal phrase, he observed: “I tell you, mother, that there was no inquest—no inquiry. No judicial inquiry, I mean.”

“Betsy says that Woolmer—some man she knows, who is in a grocer’s shop out at Crampton—can swear that Miss Hale was at the station at that hour, walking backwards and forwards with a young man.”

“I don’t see what we have to do with that,” he returned. “Miss Hale is at liberty to please herself.”

“I’m glad to hear you say so,” said Mrs. Thornton, with a kind of eager relish. “It certainly signifies very little to us—not at all to you, after what has passed! But I—I made a promise to Mrs. Hale, that I would not allow her daughter to go wrong without advising and remonstrating with her. I shall certainly let her know my opinion of such conduct.”

“I do not see any harm in what she did that evening,” he said, rising and coming nearer, as though the subject drove him from his seat. He stood by the chimney-piece with his face turned away, as if he could not endure to have his mother read his features.

“You would not have approved of Fanny’s being seen out, after dark, in rather a lonely place, walking about with a young man. I say nothing of the taste which could choose the time, when her mother lay unburied, for such a promenade. Should you have liked your sister to have been noticed by a grocer’s assistant for doing so?”

He answered without turning. “In the first place, as it is not many years since I myself was a draper’s assistant, the mere circumstance of a grocer’s assistant noticing any act does not alter the character of the act to me. And in the next place, I see a great deal of difference between Miss Hale and Fanny. I can imagine that the one may have weighty reasons, which may and ought to make her overlook any seeming impropriety in her conduct. I never knew Fanny have weighty reasons for anything. Other people must guard her. I believe Miss Hale is a guardian to herself.”

“A pretty character of your sister, indeed!” Mrs. Thornton snapped. “Really, John, one would have thought Miss Hale had done enough to make you clear-sighted. She drew you on to an offer, by a bold display of pretended regard for you,—to play you off against this very young man, I’ve no doubt. Her whole conduct is clear to me now. You believe he is her lover, I suppose—you agree to that.”

He turned. His face was grey, set like stone; and when he spoke, it was as if some part of him had been struck. “Yes, mother. I do believe he is her lover.” Then he wheeled away again, twisting as though in bodily pain. He leaned his forehead into his hand; and before she could seize on the confession, he swung back suddenly, quick as a man who cannot bear his own silence.

“Mother. He is her lover, whoever he is; but she may need help and womanly counsel;—there may be difficulties or temptations which I don’t know. I fear there are. I don’t want to know what they are; but as you have ever been a good—ay! and a tender mother to me, go to her, and gain her confidence, and tell her what is best to be done. I know that something is wrong; some dread, which must be a terrible torture to her.”

“For God’s sake, John!” His mother’s harshness gave way to a real shock. “What do you mean? What do you mean? What do you know?”

He did not reply.

“John! I don’t know what I shan’t think unless you speak. You have no right to say what you have done against her.”

“Not against her, mother! I could not speak against her.”

“Well! you have no right to say what you have done, unless you say more. These half-expressions are what ruin a woman’s character.”

“Her character! Mother, you do not dare—” He faced her, eyes lit, and for one instant all his controlled composure seemed likely to shatter. Then he drew himself up, forcing dignity over passion like a lid clamped down.

“I will not say any more than this, which is neither more nor less than the simple truth, and I am sure you believe me,—I have good reason to believe, that Miss Hale is in some strait and difficulty connected with an attachment which, of itself, from my knowledge of Miss Hale’s character, is perfectly innocent and right. What my reason is, I refuse to tell. But never let me hear any one say a word against her, implying any more serious imputation than that she now needs the counsel of some kind and gentle woman. You promised Mrs. Hale to be that woman!”

“No!” said Mrs. Thornton, drawing in a breath that seemed to sharpen her. “I am happy to say, I did not promise kindness and gentleness, for I felt at the time that it might be out of my power to render these to one of Miss Hale’s character and disposition. I promised counsel and advice, such as I would give to my own daughter; I shall speak to her as I would do to Fanny, if she had gone gallivanting with a young man in the dusk. I shall speak with relation to the circumstances I know, without being influenced either one way or another by the ‘strong reasons’ which you will not confide to me. Then I shall have fulfilled my promise, and done my duty.”

“She will never bear it,” he said, the words coming out like a groan.

“She will have to bear it, if I speak in her dead mother’s name.”

“Well!” he broke away, as if her voice had struck him. “Don’t tell me any more about it. I cannot endure to think of it. It will be better that you should speak to her any way, than that she should not be spoken to at all.” Then, as he bolted himself into his private room, the last words escaped him between his teeth, half curse, half prayer. “Oh! that look of love! And that cursed lie; which showed some terrible shame in the background, to be kept from the light in which I thought she lived perpetually! Oh, Margaret, Margaret! Mother, how you have tortured me! Oh! Margaret, could you not have loved me? I am but uncouth and hard, but I would never have led you into any falsehood for me.”

The more Mrs. Thornton brooded on what her son had pleaded—mercy for Margaret’s “indiscretion”—the more bitter her feeling grew. She took a savage satisfaction in the thought of “speaking her mind” under the clean apron of duty. She liked the fancy of showing herself untouched by the glamour she knew Margaret could cast over weaker people, as if beauty were some costly spice that made harsh meat palatable. She went to bed turning the girl’s black hair and clear skin and lucid eyes over in her thoughts with contempt, as a housekeeper might look at a showy dish—handsome to see, but badly seasoned, and unsafe to trust.

When morning came she did not wait to be softened by time. She went.

“Is Miss Hale within?” she asked, though she had already seen Margaret at the window. She had her feet in the little hall before Martha had half shaped the answer.

Margaret was alone, writing to Edith—pages filled with her mother’s last days, set down with the careful tenderness of one who tries to keep the dead near by naming every small particular. It was softening work; tears came unbidden, and she brushed them away just as Mrs. Thornton was announced.

Margaret rose to receive her with a gentle, ladylike composure that disconcerted attack. Her voice, low and rich, was softer than usual; her manner more gracious, because gratitude warmed her—gratitude for the courteous attention of this call, for remembered kindnesses that now seemed doubly precious in bereavement. She tried to find easy subjects: she praised Martha, the servant Mrs. Thornton had found for them; she spoke of Edith and asked after the little Greek air of which Miss Thornton had told her. The very domesticity of it—the familiar names, the soft rustle of ordinary talk—made Mrs. Thornton’s prepared severity feel oddly out of place, like a sharp knife laid among rose-leaves.

She sat, silent at first, because she was forcing herself back into the posture of duty. Then suspicion pricked her: what if this sweetness were a coating—sugar poured over something bitter—meant to propitiate Mr. Thornton? What if the other attachment had failed, and it now suited Miss Hale to draw back her rejected lover? Poor Margaret—there was only this truth in it, that Mrs. Thornton was mother to the one person whose esteem Margaret dreaded she had lost; and that fear, unconfessed, lent an added eagerness to her wish to please.

At last Mrs. Thornton stood, as if to go; yet the words she had come to say clung in her throat. She cleared it and began.

“Miss Hale, I have a duty to perform. I promised your poor mother that, as far as my poor judgment went, I would not allow you to act in any way wrongly, or”—here she softened, grudgingly—“inadvertently, without remonstrating; at least without offering advice, whether you took it or not.”

Margaret stood before her, blushing like a culprit. Her eyes widened, searching Mrs. Thornton’s face. She thought the reproach was to be for the lie she had told—perhaps Mr. Thornton had sent his mother to warn her how near she had come to exposure, to public contradiction. Her heart sank that he had not come himself, to hear her penitence, to restore her—if restoration were possible—to his good opinion; but humility had beaten pride too low for resistance. On that charge she would have borne blame meekly.

Mrs. Thornton continued.

“At first, when I heard from one of my servants, that you had been seen walking about with a gentleman, so far from home as the Outwood station, at such a time of the evening, I could hardly believe it. But my son, I am sorry to say, confirmed her story. It was indiscreet, to say the least; many a young woman has lost her character before now—”

The word struck Margaret like a slap. Fire leapt in her eyes. This was new; this was insult. If Mrs. Thornton had come about the falsehood—well. That would have been deserved; she would have owned it, humbled herself, taken the pain as she must. But to interfere with her conduct—to speak of her character—she, a stranger, presuming to suspect—

She would not answer. Not a word.

Mrs. Thornton saw the battle in her eyes, and it called up her own combative temper like a matched flint.

“For your mother’s sake,” she went on, “I have thought it right to warn you against such improprieties; they must degrade you in the long run in the estimation of the world, even if in fact they do not lead you to positive harm.”

“For my mother’s sake,” Margaret said, her voice shaken with tears, “I will bear much; but I cannot bear everything. She never meant me to be exposed to insult, I am sure.”

“Insult, Miss Hale!”

“Yes, madam,” Margaret answered more steadily, “it is insult. What do you know of me that should lead you to suspect—Oh!” Her strength broke; she covered her face with her hands. “I know now. Mr. Thornton has told you—”

“No, Miss Hale,” said Mrs. Thornton; and her own truthfulness, stiff and unbending, made her check the confession that trembled on Margaret’s lips, though curiosity itched to hear it. “Stop. Mr. Thornton has told me nothing. You do not know my son. You are not worthy to know him.”

She drew herself up, and her voice grew hard with pride in him.

“He said this. Listen, young lady, that you may understand, if you can, what sort of a man you rejected. This Milton manufacturer, his great tender heart scorned as it was scorned, said to me only last night, ‘Go to her. I have good reason to know that she is in some strait arising out of some attachment; and she needs womanly counsel.’ I believe those were his very words. Farther than that—beyond admitting the fact of your being at the Outwood station with a gentleman, on the evening of the twenty-sixth—he has said nothing—not one word against you. If he has knowledge of anything which should make you sob so, he keeps it to himself.”

Margaret’s face stayed hidden; the tears ran between her fingers. The mention of his “tender heart” cut her with a strange double edge—pain and gratitude together. Mrs. Thornton, seeing the tears, felt herself a little mollified in spite of herself.

“Come, Miss Hale. There may be circumstances, I’ll allow, that, if explained, may take off from the seeming impropriety.”

Margaret could not—must not—explain. If she spoke, she would betray what she had sworn to keep silent. Yet she longed, with an almost childish longing, to stand well with this stern woman, because behind her stood the man whose judgement had become so terribly important.

“I can give you no explanation,” she said at last, low. “I have done wrong, but not in the way you think or know about. I think Mr. Thornton judges me more mercifully than you;”—it took all her strength not to choke—“but, I believe, madam, you mean to do rightly.”

“Thank you,” said Mrs. Thornton, stiffening. “I was not aware that my meaning was doubted. It is the last time I shall interfere. I was unwilling to consent to do it, when your mother asked me. I had not approved of my son’s attachment to you, while I only suspected it. You did not appear to me worthy of him. But when you compromised yourself as you did at the time of the riot, and exposed yourself to the comments of servants and workpeople, I felt it was no longer right to set myself against my son’s wish of proposing to you—a wish, by the way, which he had always denied entertaining until the day of the riot.”

Margaret winced, drawing in her breath with a long, hissing sound; but Mrs. Thornton, intent on her own case, took no notice.

“He came; you had apparently changed your mind. I told my son yesterday, that I thought it possible, short as was the interval, you might have heard or learnt something of this other lover—”

That was too much. Margaret threw her head back with proud disdain, the line of her throat curving outward like a swan’s.

“What must you think of me, madam?” she asked, each word cold with scorn. “You can say nothing more, Mrs. Thornton. I decline every attempt to justify myself for anything. You must allow me to leave the room.”

And she swept out with the noiseless grace of an offended princess, leaving Mrs. Thornton standing amidst the quiet furniture and the faint lingering scent of ink and paper—witness to grief made visible in a half-written letter.

Mrs. Thornton had enough natural humour to feel, even as she gathered her shawl, the ludicrousness of being dismissed like a tiresome servant. She was not greatly angered. She cared too little for Margaret for that. Indeed, Margaret’s flash of passion had mollified her more than meekness would have done; it proved her words had struck home. As she went down the street she thought, with grim satisfaction, that the girl had pride enough to shrink from talk.

“My young lady,” she said to herself, “you’ve a pretty good temper of your own. If John and you had come together, he would have had to keep a tight hand over you, to make you know your place. But I don’t think you will go a-walking again with your beau, at such an hour of the day, in a hurry. You’ve too much pride and spirit in you for that. I like to see a girl fly out at the notion of being talked about. It shows they’re neither giddy, nor bold by nature. As for that girl, she might be bold, but she’d never be giddy. I’ll do her that justice. Now as to Fanny—she’d be giddy, and not bold. She’s no courage in her, poor thing!”

Mr. Thornton was spending his morning far less satisfactorily than his mother had spent hers. She had at least carried out her purpose; he was left with figures that would not be bent by will. He tried to understand precisely where he stood—what the strike had done him. Much of his capital was locked in new and expensive machinery; and he had bought cotton largely, counting on great orders in hand. The stoppage had thrown him behind; even with his own trained men he would have struggled to meet the engagements, and now the incompetence of the Irish hands—forced into work they had to be taught while speed was most needed—was a daily irritation, like grit in the teeth.

It was not a favourable hour for Nicholas Higgins to make a request. But he had promised Margaret to do it at any cost, and he was a man who, once pledged, held to it as if it were a knot in rope. So, though every moment of waiting added to his repugnance, his pride, and the sulky set of his mouth, he stood hour after hour leaning against the dead wall—first on one leg, then on the other—hearing the mill’s relentless music: the distant thud and whirr, the iron pulse of industry beating on the air until it seemed to press on a man’s skull. The town’s noise—wheels, voices, the harsh cries of boys—lay over him like a net.

At last the latch was sharply lifted; out came Mr. Thornton.

“I want for to speak to yo’, sir.”

“Can’t stay now, my man. I’m too late as it is.”

“Well, sir, I reckon I can wait till yo’ come back.”

Mr. Thornton was already half-way down the street. Higgins sighed; but there was no help for it. To catch “th’ measter” in the street was his only chance. If he rang the lodge bell or went to the house, he would be turned aside to the overlooker like any other hand.

So he stood again. At dinner-time the crowd poured out of the millyard; he gave a short nod here and there to the few who knew him, and scowled with all his might at the newly imported Irish “knobsticks.” The very sound of them—strange vowels, quick chatter—seemed to him part of the same force that had broken their strike: not men, but a noisy instrument brought in to grind them down.

At last Mr. Thornton returned.

“What! you there still!”

“Ay, sir. I mun speak to yo’.”

“Come in here, then. Stay—we’ll go across the yard; the men are not come back, and we shall have it to ourselves. These good people, I see, are at dinner,” he added, shutting the door of the porter’s lodge so that the street-noise dulled to a distant murmur.

He stopped to speak to the overlooker, who bent and said in a low tone, with the cautious relish of a man passing on dangerous knowledge:

“I suppose you know, sir, that that man is Higgins, one of the leaders of the Union; he that made that speech in Hurstfield.”

“No, I didn’t,” said Mr. Thornton, looking round sharply at his follower. Higgins was known to him by name—turbulent spirit, agitator, a face out of meetings.

“Come along,” he said, rougher than before; and as he led the way into the counting-house, his thoughts hardened. It was men such as this, he told himself, who interrupted commerce, injured the very town they lived in—demagogues, lovers of power at whatever cost to others.

“Well, sir! what do you want with me?” Mr. Thornton demanded, facing him as soon as they were inside.

“My name is Higgins—”

“I know that,” Mr. Thornton broke in. “What do you want, Mr. Higgins? That’s the question.”

“I want work.”

“Work! You’re a pretty chap to come asking me for work. You don’t want impudence, that’s very clear.”

“I’ve getten enemies and backbiters, like my betters; but I ne’er heerd o’ ony of them calling me o’er-modest,” Higgins answered. The words were steady, but the blood rose; not so much at the insult as at the tone that tried to stamp him down.

Mr. Thornton’s eye fell on a letter addressed to himself upon the table. He took it up, broke the seal, and read it through, his face unmoving. When he had finished, he looked up as though Higgins were an interruption he had indulged too long.

“What are you waiting for?”

“An answer to th’ question I axed.”

“I gave it you before. Don’t waste any more of your time.”

“Yo’ made a remark, sir, on my impudence,” Higgins said, the stubborn pride in him coming out like a square shoulder, “but I were taught that it was manners to say either ‘yes’ or ‘no,’ when I were axed a civil question. I should be thankfu’ to yo’ if yo’d give me work. Hamper will speak to my being a good hand.”

Mr. Thornton’s mouth tightened. “I’ve a notion you’d better not send me to Hamper to ask for a character, my man. I might hear more than you’d like.”

“I’d take th’ risk,” Higgins replied, meeting him without flinching. “Worst they could say of me is, that I did what I thought best, even to my own wrong.”

Margaret shut the door of her own room with a care that was almost tenderness. The house was slight-built; it had that thin, listening quality of many Milton dwellings, where the very boards seemed trained by habit to carry a footfall along the joists as a loom carries vibration along its frame. She began, in the first gust of hurt pride, to pace; then checked herself, remembering how her agitation would sound—step answering step—through plaster and lath, till it reached Mrs. Thornton’s chamber like an accusation. She forced herself down into the chair by the window and waited, motionless, until she heard the outer door and the faint jar of departure; only then did she draw breath, as if the air in the room had been kept back with her.

When she was alone with silence, she made herself go over every word that had passed, speech by speech, as one might turn over slices of bread to see where the heat had scorched them. At the end she rose and spoke aloud, her voice low and bitterly steady.

“Her words do not touch me. They fall off from me—because I am innocent of what she attributes to me. And yet it is hard—hard—that any one, any woman, should believe such things of another so quickly.” She pressed her fingers hard together. “Where I have done wrong, she does not accuse me—she does not know. He never told her. I might have known he would not.”

A strange, involuntary pride lifted her head for an instant—pride in his forbearance, in that reserve which kept her falsehood locked within himself. And then, like a knife turning in a wound, a new thought entered; she clasped her hands tighter.

“He too must take poor Frederick for some lover.” The word brought a hot colour up into her face, and she hated herself for it. “I see it now. It is not only that he knows of my untruth—he believes that some one else cares for me; and that I—Oh, what shall I do? what do I mean? Why do I care what he thinks, beyond the mere loss of his good opinion as regards my telling the truth?”

The room seemed close; she went to the glass, not to look at herself, but because the movement saved her from sobbing. “I cannot tell,” she whispered, and the confession sounded like a foreign phrase in her own mouth—untranslatable into the steady, dutiful language she had always used for her life. “But I am very miserable. Oh, how unhappy this last year has been! I have passed out of childhood into old age. I have had no youth—no womanhood. The hopes of womanhood have closed for me—for I shall never marry; and I anticipate cares and sorrows as if I were an old woman, with the same tearful spirit.”

Outside, some distant machinery gave a dull, intermittent beat, like a giant’s pulse; and nearer, a hawker’s cry rose and fell in the street—sound after sound that belonged to Milton, that harshly made itself master of the air. It seemed to her that even noise had power here, and that her own heart must beat to the town’s rough measure whether it would or no. She was weary of being braced and tightened like a string.

“I am weary of this continual call upon me for strength,” she said. “I could bear up for papa—that is a natural duty. I could bear up against—yes, I could resent—Mrs. Thornton’s unjust suspicions. But it is hard to feel how completely he must misunderstand me.” She stopped, bewildered by the intensity of her own pain. “What has happened to make me so morbid to-day? I do not know. I only know I cannot help it. I must give way sometimes.”

Then, with a sudden impatience at her own softness, she sprang up. “No, I will not.” She spoke as if rebuking a child. “I will not—I will not think of myself and my position. I won’t examine my feelings. It would be no use now. Some time—if I live to be an old woman—I may sit over the fire, and looking into the embers, see the life that might have been.”

All this time she had been putting on her things with hurried fingers, as if dressing herself could dress her mind into composure. Twice she stopped to wipe her eyes, angry at the tears that came back with the same persistence as the town’s unceasing clang.

“I dare say there are many women who make as sad a mistake as I have done, and only find it out too late,” she went on, as she fastened her bonnet-strings too tightly. “And how proudly I spoke to him that day! I did not know then. It has come upon me little by little, and I don’t know where it began. Now I won’t give way. I shall find it difficult to behave in the same way to him, with this miserable consciousness upon me; but I will be calm and quiet, and say very little. But perhaps I may not see him at all—he keeps out of our way. That would be worse than all. And yet no wonder he avoids me, believing what he must about me.”

She went out at once, turning her face towards the fields beyond the smoke, and walked rapidly, as if swiftness could outstrip thought. The country air met her with a colder, purer smell—damp earth, raw hedgerow, and the faint sweetness of something green bruised underfoot. It was not the rich, domestic fragrance of bread in an oven or herbs crushed on a board; it was the austerity of winter soil. Even so, it soothed her, because it was a different world from heated rooms and sharp words.

When she returned and stood on the doorstep, her father came up the path with that gentle, trusting look which always pierced her most.

“Good girl!” said he. “You’ve been to Mrs. Boucher’s. I was just meaning to go there, if I had time, before dinner.”

“No, papa; I have not,” she answered, and felt the red shame rise at once—shame not for having neglected the poor, but for the strange fact that she had not even remembered them in her first rush of misery. “I never thought about her. But I will go directly after dinner; I will go while you are taking your nap.”

Accordingly she went.

Mrs. Boucher was very ill—really ill, not merely complaining. The close room smelt of stale fire, of damp clothes hung too near the hearth, and of that sickly sweetness that comes when breath is laboured and the body is failing. A kind, sensible neighbour—the same woman Margaret had noticed the other day—seemed to have taken charge with the quiet authority of one who knows how to measure out spoonfuls and make order in disorder. Some of the children had been sent away to neighbours. Mary Higgins had come for the three youngest at dinner-time; and since then Nicholas had gone for the doctor. He had not returned. The neighbour spoke in a low voice and with a certain plain reverence, as if death were already in the room and must not be startled by loudness. There was nothing to do but wait.

Margaret thought she should like to hear the doctor’s opinion, and that she could not do better than go to the Higginses in the meantime. Perhaps she might learn whether Nicholas had been able to make his application to Mr. Thornton.

At the Higginses’ she found, to her surprise, a domestic scene almost cheerful. Nicholas stood by the dresser, busily engaged in making a penny spin, setting it off with a practised finger so that it whirled with a humming, silver sound upon the worn wood. Three little children clung to him without fear, their eyes fixed on the trembling circle of coin as if it were a conjurer’s trick. The penny’s small, bright music—its thin, eager ring against the dresser—was oddly pleasant after the heavy noises of Milton; it was a sound that belonged to home, not to the mill.

Nicholas smiled, and the children smiled with him, and Margaret—watching the absorption in his face—thought the look of interest was a good sign, as if his own heart had not grown altogether hard.

When the penny’s spin slackened and fell into stillness, “lile Johnnie” began to cry, wailing as if the world had ended with the motion.

“Come to me,” said Margaret, and lifted him down. She held him close and, to divert him, put her watch to his ear, letting him hear the small, steadfast tick that spoke a quieter language than either crying or scolding. The child hushed a little, listening, his moist mouth open with wonder at the imprisoned sound.

In that softened moment she asked, “Have you seen Mr. Thornton?”

The change on Nicholas’s face was instant; the smile went as if a door had shut.

“Ay,” said he. “I’ve seen and heerd too much on him.”

“He refused you, then?” Margaret’s voice fell.

“To be sure. I knew he’d do it all along. It’s no good expectin’ marcy at th’ hands o’ them measters. Yo’r a stranger and a foreigner, and aren’t likely to know their ways; but I knowed it.”

“I am sorry I asked you. Was he angry? He did not speak to you as Hamper did, did he?”

“He weren’t o’er-civil!” said Nicholas, and he spun the penny again—half to occupy his hands, half for the children, though his eyes now looked past them. “Never yo’ fret. I’m only where I was. I’ll go on tramp to-morrow. I gave him as good as I got. I telled him I’d not that good opinion on him that I’d ha’ come a second time o’ mysel’; but yo’d advised me for to come, and I were beholden to yo’.”

“You told him I sent you?” Margaret asked quickly, alarmed.

“I dunno as I ca’d yo’ by your name. I dunnot think I did. I said a woman as knew no better had advised me for to come and see if there was a soft place in his heart.”

“And he—?” Margaret could hardly force out the question.

“Said I were to tell yo’ to mind yo’r own business.—That’s th’ longest spin yet, my lads.—And them’s civil words to what he used to me. But ne’er mind. We’re but where we was; and I’ll break stones on th’ road afore I let these little uns clem.”

Margaret set the struggling Johnnie back on the dresser. The child’s sobbing had turned to a hiccuping watchfulness, his eyes following the penny as if it might give him comfort.

“I am sorry I asked you to go to Mr. Thornton’s,” she said, quietly. “I am disappointed in him.”

There was a slight noise behind her—no more than a shift of weight, a brush of cloth against the doorpost—yet it struck both her and Nicholas into stillness. They turned at the same instant.

Mr. Thornton stood in the doorway.

His face had that look of displeased surprise which seemed to harden every line. For one second Margaret felt as if she had been caught doing something petty and malicious, when she had only spoken out of hurt. Her impulse was swift as pain. Without a word, she passed out before him, bowing low—not in courtesy, but to hide the sudden paleness she felt must have rushed over her face.

He bent equally low in return, and then shut the door after her.

As she hurried away towards Mrs. Boucher’s, she heard the door-clang behind her, the sharp iron sound of it striking through the air; it seemed to fill up the measure of her mortification. He too was annoyed to find her there.

And indeed he was. He had tenderness in him—a “soft place,” as Nicholas had called it—but he had the pride of keeping it hidden, as if pity were a treasure to be locked away from common handling. He was jealous of every circumstance that tried to enter and name his kindness for him. Yet if he dreaded the exposure of his feeling, he was equally desirous that all men should recognise his justice; and all day the thought of Higgins’s five hours’ waiting had lain on him like a weight. He had not five hours to spare himself; but he spent an hour—two hours—of his hard, penetrating labour, not at the mill, but in going about Milton, collecting evidence as to the truth of Higgins’s story, the nature of his character, the tenor of his life.

He tried not to be convinced; and then he was convinced. And when conviction came, it went in like a charm and touched what was warmest under the sternness. Higgins’s patience, the simple generosity of his motive—made plainer by what Thornton learnt of the quarrel between Boucher and Higgins—broke down, for a moment, the mere reasoning of justice. Thornton’s mind overleaped it by an instinct that felt almost like grace. He came to tell Higgins he would give him work.

That was why Margaret’s presence nettled him more than her last sentence; for now he understood that she was the “woman” who had urged Higgins to come, and he hated—yes, hated—the idea that any thought of her might be supposed to have moved him, when he wished to do this solely because it was right.

“So that was the lady you spoke of as a woman?” he said sharply to Higgins. “You might have told me who she was.”

“And then, maybe, yo’d ha’ spoken of her more civil than yo’ did,” returned Higgins, with a grim satisfaction. “Yo’d getten a mother as might ha’ kept yo’r tongue in check when yo’ were talkin’ o’ women bein’ at th’ root o’ all th’ plagues.”

“Of course you told that to Miss Hale?”

“In coorse I did. Leastways, I reckon I did. I telled her she weren’t to meddle again in aught as concerned yo’.”

“Whose children are those—yours?” Thornton asked, though he had a pretty good notion from what he had heard. He felt awkward, and shifted ground.

“They’re not mine, and they are mine.”

“They are the children you spoke of to me this morning?”

“When yo’ said,” Higgins answered, turning with ill-smothered fierceness, “that my story might be true or might not, but it were a very unlikely one. Measter, I’ve not forgotten.”

Thornton was silent for a moment; then he spoke with effort, in a voice that had been made blunt by long habit of command.

“No more have I. I remember what I said. I spoke to you about those children in a way I had no business to. I did not believe you. I could not have taken care of another man’s children myself, if he had acted towards me as I hear Boucher did towards you. But I know now you spoke truth. I beg your pardon.”

Higgins did not turn round at once. The penny spun on, making its thin ring and whirr; the children watched it, ignorant of the meanings being exchanged above their heads. At last Higgins spoke, his tone softened though the words remained gruff.

“Yo’ve no business to go pryin’ into what happened between Boucher and me. He’s dead, and I’m sorry. That’s enough.”

“So it is,” said Thornton. “Will you take work with me? That’s what I came to ask.”

Higgins’s obstinacy wavered, gathered itself, and stood firm. He would not speak. Thornton would not ask again. There was a pause; the penny fell; one child breathed out a disappointed “Oh!” as if it mattered more than any quarrel.

Higgins’s eye dropped to the children. “Yo’ve called me impudent, an’ a liar, an’ a mischief-maker, and yo’ might ha’ said wi’ some truth as I were now and then given to drink. An’ I ha’ called you a tyrant, an’ an oud bull-dog, an’ a hard, cruel master. That’s where it stands. But for th’ childer, Measter—do yo’ think we can e’er get on together?”

“Well!” Thornton said, half laughing in spite of himself, “it was not my proposal that we should go together. But there’s one comfort on your own showing. We neither of us can think much worse of the other than we do now.”

“That’s true,” Higgins said reflectively. “I’ve been thinkin’ ever sin’ I saw you, what a marcy it were yo’ did na take me on, for that I ne’er saw a man whom I could less abide. But that’s maybe been a hasty judgment; an’ work’s work to such as me. So, Measter, I’ll come; an’ what’s more, I thank yo’; and that’s a deal fro’ me.”

As he spoke he turned fully round and faced Thornton for the first time. Thornton met him, and gave his hand a strong, honest grip.

“And this is a deal from me,” Thornton answered.

Then, as if ashamed of softness, he resumed the master.

“Now mind you come sharp to your time. I’ll have no laggards at my mill. What fines we have, we keep pretty sharply. And the first time I catch you making mischief, off you go. So now you know where you are.”

“Yo’ spoke o’ my wisdom this morning. I reckon I may bring it wi’ me; or would yo’ rayther have me ’bout my brains?”

“’Bout your brains if you use them for meddling with my business; with your brains if you can keep to your own.”

“I shall need a deal o’ brains to settle where my business ends and yo’rs begins.”

“Your business has not begun yet, and mine stands still for me. So—good afternoon.”

Not long after, as Thornton approached Mrs. Boucher’s door, Margaret came out. She did not see him. He followed her for several yards, watching—against his will—the light, easy manner of her walk, the tall grace of her figure moving through the mean street like something finer than the place. For a moment the pleasure in looking at her was simple, and it softened him; then, suddenly, jealousy—poisonous, unreasonable—tainted it. He wished to overtake her and speak, to see how she would receive him now that he believed her attached elsewhere. He wished, too—though he was ashamed of the wish—that she should know he had justified her advice, had taken Higgins on, had repented of the morning.

He came up to her. She started.

“Allow me to say, Miss Hale, that you were rather premature in expressing your disappointment. I have taken Higgins on.”

“I am glad of it,” she replied coldly.

“He tells me he repeated to you what I said this morning about—” Thornton hesitated.

“About women not meddling,” Margaret took it up, the words brisker than her heart. “You had a perfect right to express your opinion, which was a very correct one, I have no doubt.
