But”—and here she spoke more eagerly, as if snatching at a chance to set one thing straight—“Higgins did not quite tell you the exact truth.”

The word truth struck her like a blow. It carried her back to that other truth she could not speak, and to the untruth she had uttered to shelter Frederick. She stopped short, feeling the discomfort spread, as if the very air had become heavy.

Thornton at first looked puzzled at her sudden silence; then he remembered—remembered the lie, remembered what it meant, and remembered what it made him believe.

“The exact truth!” he said. “Very few people do speak the exact truth. I have given up hoping for it. Miss Hale—have you no explanation to give me? You must perceive what I cannot but think.”

Margaret said nothing. In her mind loyalty to Frederick rose like an old, stern law; she could not break it without doing him harm.

“Nay,” Thornton went on, his voice changing, “I will ask no farther. I may be putting temptation in your way. At present—believe me—your secret is safe with me. But you run great risks—allow me to say—in being so indiscreet. I am only speaking as a friend of your father’s. If I had any other thought or hope, of course that is at an end. I am quite disinterested.”

“I am aware of that,” Margaret answered, forcing herself into an indifferent, careless tone that tasted like ash. “I am aware of what I must appear to you. But the secret is another person’s, and I cannot explain it without doing him harm.”

“I have not the slightest wish to pry into the gentleman’s secrets,” he said, and anger rose as if it were a defence against pain. “My own interest in you is—simply that of a friend. You may not believe me, Miss Hale, but it is—in spite of the persecution I’m afraid I threatened you with at one time—but that is all given up; all passed away. You believe me, Miss Hale?”

“Yes,” said Margaret quietly, sadly.

“Then, really, I don’t see any reason for us to go on walking together,” he replied. “I thought perhaps you might have had something to say, but I see we are nothing to each other. If you’re quite convinced that any foolish passion on my part is entirely over, I wish you good afternoon.”

He walked off very hastily, his step striking the pavement with a sharp decisiveness that seemed to cut the air behind him.

“What can he mean?” Margaret thought, standing still for an instant, as if her mind had to catch up with her body. “What could he mean by speaking so, as if I were always thinking he cared for me, when I know he does not; he cannot. His mother will have said all those cruel things about me to him.” A fierce effort rose in her. “But I won’t care for him. Surely I am mistress enough of myself to control this wild, strange, miserable feeling, which tempted me even to betray my own dear Frederick, so that I might but regain his good opinion—the good opinion of a man who takes such pains to tell me that I am nothing to him.”

She set her lips into a sort of trembling smile, as if coaxing her own heart. “Come, poor little heart! be cheery and brave. We’ll be a great deal to one another, if we are thrown off and left desolate.”

That morning her father was almost startled by her merriment. She talked incessantly, forcing her natural humour up into an unusual pitch; and if there was a tinge of bitterness in much she said—if her accounts of the old Harley Street set came out a little too pointed, a little too sharp—Mr. Hale could not bear to check her, as he might have done at another time. He was only glad to see her shake off care, and her voice, even when it laughed, was a sound of life in the house.

In the middle of the evening she was called down to speak to Mary Higgins; and when she came back, her father fancied he saw traces of tears upon her cheeks. But that could not be, he thought; for she brought good news—Higgins had got work at Mr. Thornton’s mill.

Yet her spirits were damped notwithstanding, and she found it difficult to go on talking at all, much more in that wild, forced way. For some days her mood varied strangely; and her father began to feel anxious, when news arrived from one or two quarters that promised change and variety.

Mr. Hale received a letter from Mr. Bell, in which that gentleman volunteered a visit. Mr. Hale imagined the promised society of his old Oxford friend would give an agreeable turn to Margaret’s ideas as it did to his own. Margaret tried to take interest in what pleased her father; but she was too languid to care about any Mr. Bell, even though he were twenty times her godfather.

She was more roused by a letter from Edith—full of sympathy about their aunt’s death; full of details of herself, her husband, and the baby; and at the end saying that the climate did not suit the child, and that as Mrs. Shaw talked of returning to England, she thought it probable Captain Lennox might sell out, and they might all go and live again in the old Harley Street house—which, however, would seem very incomplete without Margaret.

At that, Margaret’s heart yearned after the old house and the placid tranquillity of that well-ordered, monotonous life. She had found it occasionally tiresome while it lasted; but since then she had been buffeted about, and now felt so exhausted—exhausted by this recent struggle with herself—that she thought even stagnation would be rest and refreshment. She began to look forward to a long visit to the Lennoxes on their return as to a point—not of hope, she told herself, but of leisure, where she might regain power and command.

For at present it seemed as if all subjects tended towards Mr. Thornton, and that she could not forget him with all her endeavours. If she went to see the Higginses, she heard of him there. Her father had resumed their readings together, and quoted Thornton’s opinions perpetually. Even Mr. Bell’s proposed visit brought the tenant’s name upon the tapis; for he wrote word that he believed he must be occupied for some part of his time with Mr. Thornton, as a new lease was in preparation, and the terms must be agreed upon. So his name kept sounding through her days, now harsh as the mill’s beat, now soft as a watch ticking in a child’s ear; and in neither language could she find a word that exactly told what she felt.

Margaret had braced herself for Mr. Bell’s coming as for a duty done for her father’s sake rather than for her own pleasure; yet when the familiar step sounded on the stair, and the door opened upon that keen, kindly face under its scholar’s gravity, she found herself slipping, as easily as into her old place by the hearth, into the simplest friendship in the world.

He chose the warmest corner by the fire, holding out his hands to the glow as if it were a good thing to be thanked for.

“You’ve no merit in pleasing me, child,” said he. “It’s hereditary. You come in and take possession of my regard as if it were your rightful room.”

“And you,” she answered, with a look that made his mock dignity crumble, “have no right to look so fresh and young under that Fellow’s cap and gown.”

“Fresh and young?” He lifted his brows. “You mean fresh and young in warmth and kindness, I suppose; for I’m afraid I must own I think your opinions are the oldest and mustiest I have met with this long time.”

“Hear this daughter of yours, Hale!” cried Mr. Bell, turning upon Mr. Hale with relish. “Her residence in Milton has quite corrupted her. She’s a democrat, a red republican, a member of the Peace Society, a socialist—”

“Papa, it’s all because I’m standing up for the progress of commerce,” said Margaret. “Mr. Bell would have had it keep still at exchanging wild-beast skins for acorns.”

“No, no. I’d dig the ground and grow potatoes. And I’d shave the wild-beast skin and make the wool into broadcloth. Don’t exaggerate, missy. But I’m tired of this bustle. Everybody rushing over everybody, in their hurry to get rich.”

“It is not everyone who can sit comfortably in a set of college rooms and let his riches grow without any exertion of his own,” Mr. Hale said quietly. “No doubt there is many a man here who would be thankful if his property would increase as yours has done, without his taking any trouble about it.”

“I don’t believe they would,” said Mr. Bell. “It’s the bustle and the struggle they like. As for sitting still, and learning from the past, or shaping out the future by faithful work done in a prophetic spirit—Why! Pooh! I don’t believe there’s a man in Milton who knows how to sit still; and it is a great art.”

“Milton people, I suspect, think Oxford men don’t know how to move,” said Margaret. “It would be a very good thing if they mixed a little more.”

“It might be good for the Miltoners. Many things might be good for them which would be very disagreeable for other people.”

“Are you not a Milton man yourself?” Margaret asked. “I should have thought you would have been proud of your town.”

“I confess, I don’t see what there is to be proud of. If you’ll only come to Oxford, Margaret, I will show you a place to glory in.”

“Well!” said Mr. Hale, with that gentle air of bringing contrary minds together as if they were both children to be made friends. “Mr. Thornton is coming to drink tea with us to-night, and he is as proud of Milton as you of Oxford. You two must try and make each other a little more liberal-minded.”

“I don’t want to be more liberal-minded, thank you,” said Mr. Bell.

“Is Mr. Thornton coming to tea, papa?” Margaret asked, lowering her voice.

“Either to tea or soon after. He could not tell. He told us not to wait.”

*

Mr. Thornton had said nothing at home—had not even asked his mother whether she had carried out her purpose of speaking to Miss Hale. He could imagine too plainly what he should hear: not Margaret’s words as they were, but as they would be strained and sharpened through another mind. And yet her name, her image, haunted him with a kind of tyranny. He blamed her—he was jealous of her—he had renounced her; and, in spite of all, he loved her sorely, with a savage, unwilling fidelity.

In his sleep she came towards him with outspread arms, light and gay, the very air about her seeming to dance; and the vision allured him while it filled him with loathing, because it was Margaret’s form with Margaret’s truth and gravity torn out of it, as if something false had taken her place. Waking, he could hardly separate the Una from the Duessa; and the dislike he felt for the latter clung like a foul mist round the former.

Still, pride kept him from avoiding the sight of her. He would neither seek her nor run from her. To prove his command over himself, he drew the afternoon out into a long chain of deliberate acts—this paper examined twice, that direction given with painful slowness, each movement forced into unnatural composure—until it was past eight when he reached Mr. Hale’s.

There were matters of business to talk over with Mr. Bell in the study. Mr. Bell, after the figures were put away, sat on by the fire, talking on—pleasantly enough at another time, but now to Thornton’s fretful impatience as wearisome as a sermon when a man’s heart is elsewhere. Thornton would not suggest going upstairs; he would not betray himself by eagerness. So he chafed in silence, and called Mr. Bell prosy in his thoughts, while Mr. Bell, in equal secrecy, judged Thornton brusque beyond endurance, and (what was worse) curter in manner and thinner in intelligence than he had once been.

At last a faint stir overhead—a chair moved, the soft fall of something in the sitting-room—made even Mr. Bell concede that they might as well join the others. They went up together.

Margaret sat with a letter open before her; her face was lit with that eager hopefulness which comes seldom and is therefore the more like a sudden flame. She was speaking quickly to her father. At the entrance of the gentlemen she put the letter aside at once; but Mr. Thornton’s quick ear caught Mr. Hale’s half sentence to Mr. Bell—

“A letter from Henry Lennox. It makes Margaret very hopeful.”

Mr. Bell nodded, as one who understood.

Margaret was red as a rose when she lifted her eyes; and in that instant Mr. Thornton felt the wild desire to rise and go out, and never cross the threshold again. He kept his place by sheer force, as if he had clenched his hands upon the arms of the chair.

“We were thinking,” said Mr. Hale, anxious to smooth the evening into cheerful commonplaces, “that you and Mr. Thornton had taken Margaret’s advice, and were each trying to convert the other, you were so long in the study.”

“And you thought there would be nothing left of us but an opinion, like the Kilkenny cat’s tail,” said Mr. Bell. “Pray whose opinion did you think would have the most obstinate vitality?”

Mr. Thornton, who had not the least notion what they were laughing at, disdained to ask. Mr. Hale, with his considerate politeness, explained.

“Mr. Thornton, we were accusing Mr. Bell this morning of a kind of Oxonian mediæval bigotry against his native town; and we—Margaret, I believe—suggested that it would do him good to associate a little with Milton manufacturers.”

“I beg your pardon,” said Mr. Bell. “Margaret thought it would do the Milton manufacturers good to associate a little more with Oxford men. Now wasn’t it so, Margaret?”

“I believe I thought it would do both good to see a little more of the other,” she replied, very low. “I did not know it was my idea any more than papa’s.”

“And so you see, Mr. Thornton, we ought to have been improving each other down-stairs, instead of talking over vanished families of Smith’s and Harrison’s. However, I am willing to do my part now. I wonder when you Milton men intend to live. All your lives seem to be spent in gathering together the materials for life.”

“By living, I suppose you mean enjoyment,” said Mr. Thornton, with a stiffness that made the word sound like a challenge.

“Yes, enjoyment,—I don’t specify of what, because I trust we should both consider mere pleasure as very poor enjoyment.”

“I would rather have the nature of the enjoyment defined.”

“Well! enjoyment or leisure—enjoyment of the power and influence which money gives. You are all striving for money. What do you want it for?”

Mr. Thornton was silent; his face grew darker, as if a deep thought had been touched and resented. At length he said—

“I really don’t know. But money is not what I strive for.”

“What then?”

“It is a home question. I shall have to lay myself open to such a catechist, and I am not sure that I am prepared to do it.”

“No!” said Mr. Hale. “Don’t let us be personal in our catechism. You are neither of you representative men; you are each of you too individual for that.”

“I am not sure whether to consider that as a compliment or not,” said Mr. Bell. “I should like to be the representative of Oxford, with its beauty and its learning, and its proud old history. What do you say, Margaret; ought I to be flattered?”

“I don’t know Oxford,” she answered, trying to smile. “But there is a difference between being the representative of a city and the representative man of its inhabitants.”

“Very true, Miss Margaret. Now I remember, you were against me this morning, and were quite Miltonian and manufacturing in your preferences.”

Mr. Thornton’s eyes went quickly to her face at those words. The look was so swift, so sharp with interpretation, that Margaret felt her cheeks burn again—less with colour than with anger at the meaning he might put upon what was mere talk. Mr. Bell, unconscious, went on—

“Ah! I wish I could show you our High Street—our Radcliffe Square. I am leaving out our colleges, just as I give Mr. Thornton leave to omit his factories in speaking of the charms of Milton. I have a right to abuse my birth-place. Remember I am a Milton man.”

Mr. Thornton, already strung too tight, was more galled than he ought to have been. He was not in a mood for banter. The old friend’s half-testy, half-playful disparagement would have amused him at another time; now it pricked like salt upon a raw place.

“I don’t set up Milton as a model of a town,” he said.

“Not in architecture?” asked Mr. Bell, slyly.

“No! We’ve been too busy to attend to mere outward appearances.”

“Don’t say mere outward appearances,” said Mr. Hale gently. “They impress us all, from childhood upward—every day of our life.”

“Wait a little while,” replied Mr. Thornton, with a kind of vehement restraint. “Remember we are of a different race from the Greeks, to whom beauty was everything, and to whom Mr. Bell might speak of a life of leisure and serene enjoyment, much of which entered in through their outward senses. I don’t mean to despise them, any more than I would ape them. But I belong to Teutonic blood; it is little mingled in this part of England to what it is in others; we retain much of their language; we retain more of their spirit; we do not look upon life as a time for enjoyment, but as a time for action and exertion. Our glory and our beauty arise out of our outward strength, which makes us victorious over material resistance, and over greater difficulties still. We are Teutonic up here in Darkshire in another way. We hate to have laws made for us at a distance. We wish people would allow us to right ourselves, instead of continually meddling, with their imperfect legislation. We stand up for self-government, and oppose centralisation.”

“In short, you would like the Heptarchy back again,” said Mr. Bell. “Well, at any rate, I revoke what I said this morning—that you Milton people did not reverence the past. You are regular worshippers of Thor.”

“If we do not reverence the past as you do in Oxford,” answered Mr. Thornton, pressing on as if he could not stop, “it is because we want something which can apply to the present more directly. It is fine when the study of the past leads to a prophecy of the future. But to men groping in new circumstances, it would be finer if the words of experience could direct us how to act in what concerns us most intimately and immediately; which is full of difficulties to be encountered; and upon the mode in which they are met and conquered—not merely pushed aside for the time—depends our future. But no! People can speak of Utopia much more easily than of the next day’s duty; and yet when that duty is all done by others, who so ready to cry, ‘Fie, for shame!’”

“And all this time I don’t see what you are talking about,” said Mr. Bell. “Would you Milton men condescend to send up your to-day’s difficulty to Oxford? You have not tried us yet.”

Mr. Thornton laughed outright—an unwilling burst, as if some tension snapped.

“I believe I was talking with reference to a good deal that has been troubling us of late,” he said. “I was thinking of the strikes we have gone through, which are troublesome and injurious things enough, as I am finding to my cost. And yet this last strike, under which I am smarting, has been respectable.”

“A respectable strike!” cried Mr. Bell. “That sounds as if you were far gone in the worship of Thor.”

Margaret felt, rather than saw, how the jest fretted Mr. Thornton. The talk had drifted to a matter about which one man’s mind could play, while the other’s was bound up in pain and loss. She tried to draw it away, tried—awkwardly enough—to bring them back to the safer shallows of ordinary news.

“Edith says she finds the printed calicoes in Corfu better and cheaper than in London.”

“Does she?” said Mr. Hale. “I think that must be one of Edith’s exaggerations. Are you sure of it, Margaret?”

“I am sure she says so, papa.”

“Then I am sure of the fact,” said Mr. Bell. “Margaret, I go so far in my idea of your truthfulness, that it shall cover your cousin’s character. I don’t believe a cousin of yours could exaggerate.”

“Is Miss Hale so remarkable for truth?” said Mr. Thornton—bitterly.

The words had hardly left his mouth before he would have given much to recall them. What was he doing—what right had he to fling, before her and her father and her friend, that sharp reminder of a shame he himself had chosen to keep alive? Ill-humour possessed him—ill-humour at being kept so long from her, at hearing another man’s name, at being unable to meet Mr. Bell’s easy cheerfulness, at the sense of his own helplessness in the very room where he had once been master of himself.

Margaret did not rise and leave the room, as she had done at other times when his temper had wounded her. She sat quite still. For a moment she looked at him with grieved surprise—so childlike in its pain that it was like seeing a child struck unexpectedly. Then her eyes slowly widened and darkened into mournful, reproachful sadness; then they fell. She bent her head over her work and spoke no more.

But he could not keep from looking at her. He saw a sigh pass over her whole frame, as if a chill had reached her. He felt, in a strange way, like a mother who has been scolding, and is called away before the child’s slow, trusting smile can come and make peace. He answered with short, sharp words; he mistook jests for taunts, earnestness for reproach. He wanted one glance, one syllable from her—something that would give him leave to throw himself down, in heart at least, and confess his remorse. Yet she neither looked nor spoke. Her round taper fingers went in and out of her sewing with steady, swift precision, as if that narrow strip of cloth and those even stitches were the one business left in life.

He told himself she could not care—else his passionate will would have forced her, if only for an instant, to lift her eyes and read his late repentance. The thought stung him into a fierce desire to do something—anything—that would make his penitence unavoidable; as if some overt rudeness could purchase him the right to explain. It was well that, soon after, he rose and went away. The long walk through the cold open air steadied him into a grave resolve: henceforth he would see as little of her as possible, since the very sight of her, the very sound of her voice—soft as pure melody—had such power to unbalance him. He had learned what love was: a sharp pang, a fierce experience. Through the furnace he would fight his way out into the serenity of middle age—richer, perhaps, and more human for having known this passion.

*

When the door had closed upon him, Margaret rose and began folding her work without a word. The long seams felt heavier than they had any right to feel; her arms ached as if she had been labouring all day. The soft roundness of her face seemed drawn into straighter lines; she looked like one who has been worn with fatigue rather than with any sudden grief.

As they prepared to go to rest, Mr. Bell muttered his condemnation.

“I never saw a fellow so spoiled by success. He can’t bear a word; a jest of any kind. Everything seems to touch on the soreness of his high dignity. Formerly, he was as simple and noble as the open day; you could not offend him, because he had no vanity.”

“He is not vain now,” said Margaret, turning from the table and speaking with quiet distinctness. “To-night he has not been like himself. Something must have annoyed him before he came here.”

Mr. Bell shot one of his sharp glances over his spectacles. Margaret met it steadily; there was nothing to flinch from. When she had left the room, he asked suddenly—

“Hale! did it ever strike you that Thornton and your daughter have what the French call a tendresse for each other?”

“Never!” cried Mr. Hale, startled, then flurried by the thought as if it were a sacrilege. “No, I am sure you are wrong, I am almost certain you are mistaken. If there is anything, it is all on Mr. Thornton’s side. Poor fellow! I hope and trust he is not thinking of her, for I am sure she would not have him.”

“Well! I’m a bachelor, and have steered clear of love affairs all my life; so perhaps my opinion is not worth having. Or else I should say there were very pretty symptoms about her!”

“Then I am sure you are wrong,” repeated Mr. Hale, as if repetition could lay the fancy. “He may care for her, though she really has been almost rude to him at times. But she!—why, Margaret would never think of him, I’m sure. Such a thing has never entered her head.”

“Entering her heart would do,” said Mr. Bell. “But I merely threw out a suggestion of what might be. I dare say I was wrong. And whether I was wrong or right, I’m very sleepy; so, having disturbed your night’s rest (as I can see) with my untimely fancies, I’ll betake myself with an easy mind to my own.”

Mr. Hale resolved he would not be disturbed by any such nonsense; and lay awake, determined not to think about it.

*

Mr. Bell left the next day. He took Margaret’s hand in both of his, holding it a moment longer than mere farewell required.

“Look to me,” he said, “as one who has a right to help and protect you in all your troubles, of whatever nature they might be.”

To Mr. Hale he spoke warmly, as if he must get the feeling out.

“That Margaret of yours has gone deep into my heart. Take care of her, for she is a very precious creature,—a great deal too good for Milton—only fit for Oxford, in fact. The town, I mean; not the men. I can’t match her yet. When I can, I shall bring my young man to stand side by side with your young woman, just as the genii in the Arabian Nights brought Prince Caralmazan to match with the fairy’s Princess Badoura.”

“I beg you’ll do no such thing,” said Mr. Hale, half amused, half anxious. “Remember the misfortunes that ensued; and besides, I can’t spare Margaret.”

“No; on second thoughts, we’ll have her to nurse us ten years hence, when we shall be two cross old invalids. Seriously, Hale! I wish you’d leave Milton; which is a most unsuitable place for you, though it was my recommendation in the first instance. If you would, I’d swallow my shadows of doubts, and take a college living; and you and Margaret should come and live at the parsonage—you to be a sort of lay curate, and take the unwashed off my hands; and she to be our housekeeper—the village Lady Bountiful—by day; and read us to sleep in the evenings. I could be very happy in such a life. What do you think of it?”

“Never,” said Mr. Hale decidedly. “My one great change has been made and my price of suffering paid. Here I stay out my life; and here will I be buried, and lost in the crowd.”

“I don’t give up my plan yet. Only I won’t bait you with it any more just now. Where’s the Pearl? Come, Margaret, give me a farewell kiss; and remember, my dear, where you may find a true friend, as far as his capability goes. You are my child, Margaret. Remember that, and God bless you!”

After he was gone, life fell back into its quiet monotony. There was no longer an invalid to watch, no daily rise and fall of hope and fear. Even the Higginses—so long their vivid, pressing interest—seemed to recede from the front of thought. But the Boucher children, left motherless, drew Margaret often into the poorer streets. She went to see Mary Higgins, who had charge of them. The two families were living in one house. The elder children were sent to humble schools; the younger ones were tended, while Mary was away at work, by the sensible neighbour who had impressed Margaret on the day of Boucher’s death. She was paid for her trouble; and, in all the plans made for the orphans, Nicholas Higgins showed a sober judgment, a regulated method, very unlike his former abrupt, eccentric jerks of action.

He was so steady at his work that Margaret did not often see him through the winter; but when she did, she noticed how he winced away from any mention of the dead father whose children he had so heartily taken for his own charge. And he did not speak easily of Mr. Thornton.

“To tell the truth,” he said once, with his head a little aside, as if the puzzle would not fit his mind, “he fairly bamboozles me. He’s two chaps. One chap I knowed of old as were measter all o’er. T’other chap hasn’t an ounce of measter’s flesh about him. How them two chaps is bound up in one body, is a craddy for me to find out. I’ll not be beat by it, though. Meanwhile he comes here pretty often; that’s how I know the chap that’s a man, not a measter. And I reckon he’s taken aback by me pretty much as I am by him; for he sits and listens and stares, as if I were some strange beast newly caught in some of the zones. But I’m none daunted. It would take a deal to daunt me in my own house, as he sees. And I tell him some of my mind that I reckon he’d ha’ been the better of hearing when he were a younger man.”

“And does he not answer you?” Mr. Hale asked.

“Well! I’ll not say th’ advantage is all on his side, for all I take credit for improving him above a bit. Sometimes he says a rough thing or two, which is not agreeable to look at at first, but has a queer smack o’ truth in it when yo’ come to chew it. He’ll be coming to-night, I reckon, about them childer’s schooling. He’s not satisfied wi’ the make of it, and wants for t’ examine ’em.”

“What are they”—began Mr. Hale; but Margaret touched his arm and showed him her watch.

“It is nearly seven,” she said. “The evenings are getting longer now. Come, papa.”

She did not breathe freely till they were some distance from the house. Then, as her heart grew calmer, she was vexed with herself for having hurried him away so abruptly; for, somehow, they saw Mr. Thornton very seldom now; and he might truly have come only to see Higgins, and for the old friendship’s sake she should have liked to have met him to-night.

Indeed, he came very seldom—even for the dull, cold purpose of lessons. Mr. Hale was disappointed in his pupil’s lukewarmness about Greek, which not long ago had been so eager and animated. Now it often happened that a hurried note arrived at the last moment—Mr. Thornton so much engaged he could not come that evening. Other pupils filled the hours; none filled the place in Mr. Hale’s heart. He grew depressed by the partial cessation of an intercourse that had become dear to him, and sat pondering what could have caused the change.

One evening, while Margaret sat at her work, he startled her by asking suddenly—

“Margaret! had you ever any reason for thinking that Mr. Thornton cared for you?”

He almost blushed as he spoke; Mr. Bell’s half-mocking suggestion had returned to him, and the words escaped before he was aware.

Margaret did not answer at once; but by the droop of her head he read what was coming.

“Yes; I believe—oh, papa, I should have told you.” She let her work fall, and hid her face in her hands.

“No, dear; don’t think that I am impertinently curious,” said Mr. Hale, deeply moved. “I am sure you would have told me if you had felt that you could return his regard. Did he speak to you about it?”

For a moment there was no sound but her quiet breathing; then, after a pause, came a little gentle, reluctant—

“Yes.”

“And you refused him?”

So winter drew on, and the days, though they lengthened by a few grudging minutes, brought no increase of warmth to the heart. February’s pale sun shone as it always had, but in the Hales’ little drawing-room it seemed to fall upon the same quiet furniture, the same neat hearth, without coaxing any spring of hope to rise.

Mrs. Thornton, as might have been looked for, came no more. Mr. Thornton came at times; yet even his footfall belonged now to the passage that led to the study, not to the room where Margaret sat. He spoke with Mr. Hale; his business, tangled and overgrown during the strike, demanded him more closely than it had last year. Mr. Hale, who prized rare things as some men prize costly ones, valued the visits the more for their scantness, and praised the steadiness of Mr. Thornton’s mind. From such fragments as reached her—words carried out by a half-open door, a sentence repeated by her father with a gentle pleasure—Margaret could not even accuse Mr. Thornton of resentment. He neither sought her name nor avoided it; and when it came, it was spoken as calmly as if no sharp thing had ever passed between them.

Margaret could not lift her father’s spirits by the mere buoyancy of her own, as she had done in other days. Long anxiety, broken by storms, had beaten down the natural spring of her temper; now there was a dreary peace, like the hush after a mill-wheel has been stopped, when the ear expects thunder and hears only the thin drip of water. She made herself tasks, as if work could be a fire kindled without fuel: she taught the two younger Boucher children, bringing them to her parlour with their washed faces and clumsy shoes; she bent herself to goodness, and found it hard—hard, because her heart seemed numb to the end of all effort. If she did anything well, it was what she did without measuring it—the quiet tending of her father’s comfort. His smallest wish, scarcely shaped into speech, she forestalled; his moods, like changes of weather in a delicate spring, she felt before they fully came, and met with the ready tenderness that asked no thanks.

March brought tidings from Spain: Frederick’s marriage. He and Dolores both wrote. Dolores’s English went with a pretty, timid stumbling—Spanish words and turns of phrase slipping in as naturally as the scent of orange-blossom might cling to a garment carried across seas. Frederick, too, wrote with little inversions, little alien idioms, as if his very tongue were learning her country’s shape. Their letters had, to Margaret and her father, the charm of something young and careful; Dolores was evidently anxious, in every erased line and altered spelling, to please the unseen English relations of her husband. With the announcement came a mantilla—black lace, splendid and soft as shadow, chosen by Dolores herself for the sister-in-law she had never seen. Frederick had painted Margaret in such colours—beauty, wisdom, virtue—that the gift seemed like an offering laid down before an image.

Frederick’s worldly position rose too. Barbour and Co., one of the largest Spanish houses, took him in as a junior partner. Margaret smiled once, then sighed, remembering the vehement speeches of her younger self against trade: her preux chevalier turned merchant, trader! Yet even as the thought rose, she rebuked it. A Spanish merchant was not to her mind the same thing as a Milton mill-owner; her old confusions were unjust. Trade or no trade, Frederick was happy—very happy. Dolores must be charming; the mantilla was exquisite. And then Margaret returned to the present, which waited like an unlit room.

Mr. Hale had had, this spring, at times a difficulty in breathing—an oppression that distressed him while it lasted, and then passed away so completely that Margaret would not allow herself to be frightened. Still she longed to see the liability shaken off altogether; and so she urged him—urgently, almost with that quiet obstinacy she could put on when love was anxious—to accept Mr. Bell’s invitation to Oxford in April. Mr. Bell included Margaret too; nay, he wrote a special letter commanding her presence. But Margaret shrank from it as from a duty that asked more than she could give. To remain at home, alone, without the perpetual sense of responsibility, seemed to her like lying down at last after two years of watching.

When her father drove away to the station, the closing of the gate behind the wheels made a sound that startled her—so much had depended upon that daily coming and going of his step. The house seemed suddenly hollowed out. She stood and felt, almost stunned, the vastness of her liberty: no one now leaned upon her for cheerful care, if not for happiness; no invalid required planning; she might be idle, silent, forgetful—and, what seemed worth more than all, she might be unhappy if she liked, without having to hide it as one hides a forbidden thing.

For months she had stuffed her own griefs into a dark cupboard of the mind, and locked them there. Now she had time to take them out and look at them steadily. She sat for hours in the drawing-room, hardly moving, turning each remembrance as one turns over bitter herbs to know their true scent. She made herself face them with an unwincing resolution. Only once did she cry out aloud, stung by the thought of the faithlessness that had bred that abasing falsehood.

Now she would not so much as grant the temptation the dignity of strength. Her plans for Frederick had failed; the temptation lay there like a dead mockery. Seen by the light of what had followed, the lie was not even tragic—it was despicably foolish; and faith in truth appeared, in comparison, infinite wisdom.

In the nervous agitation of the moment she took up a book of her father’s that lay upon the table, opened it at random, and the words that met her eye seemed written for her self-abasement:

“Je ne voudrois pas reprendre mon cœur en ceste sorte: meurs de honte, aveugle, impudent, traistre et desloyal à ton Dieu, et sembables choses; mais je voudrois le corriger par voye de compassion. Or sus, mon pauvre cœur, nous voilà tombe dans la fosse, laquelle nous avions tant resolu d’eschapper. Ah! revelons-nous, et quittons-la pour jamais, reclamons la misericorde de Dieu, et esperons en elle qu’elle nous assistera pour desormais estra plus fermes; et remettons-nous au chemin de l’humilitè. Courage, soyons meshuy sur nos gardes, Dieu nous aydera.”

“The way of humility,” thought Margaret. “Ah! that is what I have missed. But courage, little heart. We will turn back; and by God’s help we may find the lost path.”

She rose at once, with the sudden need to do some work that should take her out of herself. To begin with, she called Martha as the girl passed the drawing-room door on her way upstairs. Martha’s manner was always grave, respectful—obedience crusted over individuality, as if life had taught her to be wooden for safety. Margaret tried gently to find what lay beneath, and found it difficult. Martha answered with short propriety, as if each personal word were a breach of rule. But Margaret touched at last upon the right chord when she named Mrs. Thornton.

Martha’s whole face brightened, as if a shutter had been flung open. With a little encouragement the story came out: her father, in earlier life, had been connected with Mrs. Thornton’s husband—had even once been able to do him a kindness, though Martha scarcely knew what, for she had been a small child then. Later, circumstances had severed the families. Martha’s father sank lower and lower from his first occupation as a clerk in a warehouse. Her mother died. She and her sister, Martha said plainly, would have been “lost” but for Mrs. Thornton, who sought them out, planned for them, cared for them with a steady hand.

“I’d had th’ fever, and were but delicate,” said Martha, the words gaining warmth as she went on. “And Mrs. Thornton and Mr. Thornton too—they never rested till they’d nursed me up in their own house, and sent me to th’ sea and all. Doctor said fever were catching, but they cared none for that—only Miss Fanny, and she went a-visiting them folk she’s going to marry into. So though she were frightened at th’ time, it’s ended well.”

“Miss Fanny going to be married!” Margaret exclaimed.

“Yes; and to a rich gentleman too, only he’s a deal older nor her. His name is Watson; and his mills is somewhere out beyond Hayleigh. It’s a very good marriage, for all he’s got such grey hair.”

At this, Margaret was silent long enough for Martha’s brightness to fade back into the familiar servant’s mask. Martha recovered propriety as if it were an apron she must not crease: she swept up the hearth, asked what hour tea was to be prepared, and left the room with the same composed face with which she had entered.

Margaret checked herself from a bad habit that had lately grown upon her—of imagining, whenever she heard anything that touched Mr. Thornton’s circle, how it would affect him; whether he would like or dislike it; whether he would feel it as she felt it. She scolded herself for it, as one checks a finger going to a sore place.

The next day she had the little Boucher children to teach, and afterwards she took a long walk. The evening ended with a visit to Mary Higgins. To her surprise Nicholas was already home; the lengthening light had deceived her into thinking it earlier. He too seemed to have come, in his way, a little nearer to humility; he was quieter, less sharp-edged in assertion.

“So th’ oud gentleman’s away on his travels, is he?” said he. “Little ’uns telled me so. Eh! but the’re sharp ’uns they are; I a’most think they beat my own wenches for sharpness—though m’appen it’s wrong to say so, and one on ’em in her grave. There’s summut i’ th’ weather, I reckon, as sets folk a-wandering. My measter—him at th’ shop yonder—is spinning about th’ world somewhere.”

“Is that the reason you’re so soon at home to-night?” asked Margaret, innocently.

“Thou know’st nought about it, that’s all,” said he, with a contempt that seemed rather against her ignorance than against herself. “I’m not one wi’ two faces—one for my measter, and t’other for his back. I counted a’ th’ clocks in th’ town striking afore I’d leave my work. No! yon Thornton’s good enough for to fight wi’, but too good for to be cheated. It were you as getten me the place, and I thank yo’ for it. Thornton’s is not a bad mill, as times go. Stand down, lad, and say yo’r pretty hymn to Miss Marget. That’s right; steady on thy legs, and right arm out as straight as a skewer. One to stop, two to stay, three mak’ ready, and four away!”

The child—Nicholas’s little boy—stood forth and began a Methodist hymn. The words were far beyond his understanding, full of phrases that fell on his young mind like pebbles on a tin roof; but the swinging rhythm had taken his ear, and he repeated it with an orator’s cadence, as if he were in the House itself. Margaret applauded as gravely as if he had been a trained singer. Nicholas called for another, and yet another—an odd sight, and to Margaret an unexpected one, that the man who had once scoffed should now be led, half-unconsciously, by his child’s chant into a kind of interest in sacred things.

When she reached home it was past the usual tea-time; yet she had the comfort of knowing no one had been waiting for her. The house, for once, asked nothing. She rested and let her thoughts come and go without watching another face to learn whether she must be grave or gay.

After tea she resolved to examine a large packet of letters, and pick out those that were to be destroyed. Among them she found four or five from Mr. Henry Lennox, all relating to Frederick’s affairs. She read them again carefully, at first only to see on how fine a chance her brother’s justification hung. But when she had finished the last, and weighed the pros and cons, a small revelation forced itself upon her—personal, unwilling. The stiffness of the words showed that Mr. Lennox had never forgotten his relation to her in any interest he took in the subject. They were clever letters; she saw that in a twinkling. Yet she missed in them any hearty, genial atmosphere—anything that warmed as well as enlightened. Still, they were valuable; she laid them carefully aside to be preserved.

Then she fell into a reverie; and that night her absent father ran strangely through her mind. She almost blamed herself for having felt solitude—and consequently his absence—as a relief. Yet these two days of quiet had set her up afresh, as a plant is strengthened by a brief shelter from wind. Plans that had lately seemed like tasks now looked like pleasures. The morbid scales seemed fallen from her eyes; she saw her position and her work more truly.

If only Mr. Thornton would restore the lost friendship—nay, if he would but come sometimes to cheer her father as in former days—though she herself never saw him, she felt as if her future life, not brilliant, might yet lie clear and even before her. She sighed as she rose to go to bed. In spite of “One step’s enough for me,” in spite of the plain duty of devotion to her father, there lay at her heart an anxiety, and a pang.

That same April evening Mr. Hale thought of Margaret almost as persistently as she was thinking of him. He had been fatigued by moving among old friends and old places in Oxford. He had exaggerated, in his sensitive fear, the change his altered opinions might make in their reception of him. Yet though some were shocked, grieved, even indignant in the abstract, when they saw the face of the man they had once loved, they forgot the opinion in the person; or remembered it only enough to deepen their tenderness.

Mr. Hale had belonged to one of the smaller colleges; he had been shy, reserved. Those who had cared in youth to penetrate to the delicacy beneath his indecision took him back now with a kind of protecting kindness—almost the manner men use to a woman. After years and an interval of such change, the renewal of that kindliness overpowered him more than any roughness could have done.

“I’m afraid we’ve done too much,” said Mr. Bell. “You’re suffering now from having lived so long in that Milton air.”

“I am tired,” said Mr. Hale. “But it is not Milton air. I’m fifty-five years of age, and that little fact of itself accounts for any loss of strength.”

“Nonsense! I’m upwards of sixty, and feel no loss of strength, either bodily or mental. Don’t let me hear you talking so. Fifty-five! why, you’re quite a young man.”

Mr. Hale shook his head. “These last few years!” he said. Then, after a minute’s pause, he raised himself from his half-reclining position in one of Mr. Bell’s luxurious easy-chairs, and spoke with trembling earnestness.

“Bell! you’re not to think that if I could have foreseen all that would come of my change of opinion, and my resignation of my living—no! not even if I could have known how she would have suffered—that I would undo it—the act of open acknowledgment that I no longer held the same faith as the church in which I was a priest. As I think now, even if I could have foreseen that cruellest martyrdom of suffering, through the sufferings of one whom I loved, I would have done just the same, as far as that step of openly leaving the church went. I might have done differently, and acted more wisely, in all that I subsequently did for my family. But I don’t think God endued me with over-much wisdom or strength,” he added, falling back into his old position.

Mr. Bell blew his nose ostentatiously before answering; it was his way of hiding softness. Then he said—

“He gave you strength to do what your conscience told you was right; and I don’t see that we need any higher or holier strength than that; or wisdom either. I know I have not that much; and yet men set me down in their fool’s books as a wise man—an independent character—strong-minded, and all that cant. The veriest idiot who obeys his own simple law of right, if it be but in wiping his shoes on a door-mat, is wiser and stronger than I. But what gulls men are!”

There was a pause. Mr. Hale spoke first again, as if his thought had gone on walking while the words stopped.

“About Margaret.”

“Well! about Margaret. What then?”

“If I die—”

“Nonsense!”

“What will become of her—I often think? I suppose the Lennoxes will ask her to live with them. I try to think they will. Her Aunt Shaw loved her very well in her own quiet way; but she forgets to love the absent.”

“A very common fault. What sort of people are the Lennoxes?”

“He—handsome, fluent, and agreeable. Edith, a sweet spoiled beauty. Margaret loves her with all her heart, and Edith with as much of her heart as she can spare.”

“Now, Hale; you know that girl of yours has got pretty nearly all my heart. I told you that before. Of course, as your daughter, as my god-daughter, I took great interest in her before I saw her the last time. But this visit that I paid you at Milton made me her slave. I went a willing old victim, following the car of the conqueror. For, indeed, she looks as grand and serene as one who has struggled, and may be struggling, and yet has the victory secure in sight. Yes, in spite of all her present anxieties, that was the look on her face. And so, all I have is at her service, if she needs it; and will be hers, whether she will or no, when I die. Moreover, I myself will be her preux chevalier—sixty and gouty though I be. Seriously, old friend, your daughter shall be my principal charge in life; and all the help that either my wit or my wisdom or my willing heart can give shall be hers. I don’t choose her out as a subject for fretting. Something, I know of old, you must have to worry yourself about, or you wouldn’t be happy. But you’re going to outlive me by many a long year. You, spare, thin men are always tempting and always cheating Death! It’s the stout, florid fellows like me, that always go off first.”

If Mr. Bell had had a prophetic eye, he might have seen the torch already sinking, and the composed angel standing close, beckoning. That night Mr. Hale laid his head upon the pillow where it never more would stir with life. In the morning the servant who entered spoke, and received no answer; drew near and saw the calm, beautiful face lying white and cold under the ineffaceable seal of death. His attitude was exquisitely easy. There had been no struggle—no pain. The action of the heart had ceased as he lay down.

Mr. Bell was stunned; and only recovered his wits enough to be angry at every suggestion of his man.

“A coroner’s inquest? Pooh. You don’t think I poisoned him! Dr. Forbes says it is just the natural end of a heart complaint. Poor old Hale! You wore out that tender heart of yours before its time. Poor old friend! how he talked of his— Wallis, pack up a carpet-bag for me in five minutes. Here have I been talking. Pack it up, I say. I must go to Milton by the next train.”

The bag was packed, the cab ordered, the railway reached in twenty minutes from the moment of decision. The London train whizzed by; it drew back some yards; Mr. Bell was hurried in by an impatient guard. He threw himself into his seat and shut his eyes, trying to make his mind take in the brutal swiftness of it—one alive yesterday, dead to-day. Tears stole out between his grizzled lashes. Feeling them, he opened his keen eyes and arranged his face into severe cheerfulness. He would not blubber before strangers. Not he.

Yet there were scarcely any to see. Only one man sat far from him on the same side. By-and-by Mr. Bell peered, to discover what kind of fellow he might be; and behind the great spread of the Times he recognised Mr. Thornton.

“Why, Thornton! is that you?” cried Mr. Bell, shifting hastily nearer. He shook Mr. Thornton’s hand vehemently; the grip ended suddenly, for his hand was needed to wipe away the obstinate tears that would come at such times. He had last seen Mr. Thornton with Hale.

“I’m going to Milton, bound on a melancholy errand. Going to break to Hale’s daughter the news of his sudden death!”

“Death! Mr. Hale dead!”

“Ay. I keep saying it to myself, ‘Hale is dead!’ but it doesn’t make it any the more real. Hale is dead for all that. He went to bed well, to all appearance, last night, and was quite cold this morning when my servant went to call him.”

“Where? I don’t understand!”

“At Oxford. He came to stay with me; hadn’t been in Oxford this seventeen years—and this is the end of it.”

For more than a quarter of an hour not a word was spoken. The train’s motion made its own relentless speech: iron upon iron, the steady clatter that never grieved, never pitied, driving through the country with the same hard haste whether it carried joy or bereavement. Then Mr. Thornton said, brokenly—

“And she!”—and stopped.

“Margaret, you mean. Yes. I am going to tell her. Poor fellow! how full his thoughts were of her all last night! Good God—last night only. And how immeasurably distant he is now! But I take Margaret as my child for his sake. I said last night I would take her for her own sake. Well—I take her for both.”

Mr. Thornton made one or two fruitless attempts before he could command his voice.

“What will become of her?”

“I rather fancy there will be two people waiting for her—myself for one. I’d take a live dragon into my house to live, if by hiring such a chaperon, and setting up an establishment of my own, I could make my old age happy with having Margaret for a daughter. But there are those Lennoxes!”

“Who are they?” asked Mr. Thornton, with a trembling interest.

“Oh, smart London people, who very likely will think they’ve the best right to her. Captain Lennox married her cousin—the girl she was brought up with. Good enough people, I dare say. And there’s her Aunt—Mrs. Shaw. There might be a way open, perhaps, by my offering to marry that worthy lady!—but that would be quite a pis aller. And then there’s that brother!”

“What brother? A brother of her aunt’s?”

“No, no; a clever Lennox—the captain’s a fool, you must understand; a young barrister who will be setting his cap at Margaret. I know he has had her in his mind these five years or more; one of his chums told me as much; and he was only kept back by want of fortune. Now that will be done away with.”

“How?” asked Mr. Thornton, too eagerly curious to be aware of the impertinence.

The blow had fallen too heavily to spend itself in any violent show. Margaret lay as if the life in her had been stunned—eyes closed, breath coming so low that it seemed borrowed, answering only when she must, and then in a whisper that sounded like a voice remembered rather than a voice spoken. It was not that tears were denied her by pride; it was that grief had seized on her like a frost, and held her dumb.

Mr. Bell sat by the fire, his broad hands idle in his lap, his thoughts chafing against the walls of necessity. He dared not leave her, and yet there were messages to send, arrangements at Oxford that waited on him. The plan he had shaped on his way to Milton—carrying her back with him into quieter courts and older stones—was now as impossible as asking a fainting bird to fly against a gale. Even the mere imagining of what she must pass through made him wince.

Dixon hovered, sobbing hospitality made into duty, and insisted—first with her hands, then with her voice—that Mr. Bell must eat. She had prepared a dinner downstairs, and there was something in her notion that proper food, properly administered, was an act of allegiance to the living, even in a house newly claimed by death. But he would not go.

At last he allowed a plate to be brought up. In other times he had been a man who could tell, with irritating accuracy, what herb had been overused, what butter had been too much clarified, what sauce had lost its edge by waiting. Now he put the morsel into his mouth, and it might have been planed wood for all the pleasure it gave him. The devilled chicken—so carefully pricked with cayenne, so conscientiously browned—had no heat for him, no savour, no meaning.

He tried, because one tries, to make it serve Margaret. He minced the fowl smaller, as if tenderness could be manufactured by the knife; he shook over salt and pepper, as if the tongue could be coaxed back to the world by pungency. Dixon, receiving his directions with the humility of a servant who would gladly take orders from any one that might save her young mistress, attempted to feed Margaret. The girl’s head moved a little—no, only no; not with petulance, but with a quiet refusal that said food would do her harm by reminding her she still had a body to be cared for.

Mr. Bell sighed—a great, old, helpless sound; then, stiff from travel and from sitting too long, he rose and followed Dixon out.

“I cannot leave her,” he said, stopping in the passage as if the distance between himself and the drawing-room were already treachery. “I must write to Oxford, to have my preparations made without me. And she must have a woman with her. Someone to talk her into a good fit of crying. Can’t Mrs. Lennox come?”

Dixon wiped her eyes with her apron, steadied her voice with an effort that was almost soldierly, and told him Mrs. Lennox was too near her confinement to undertake a journey.

“Then we must have Mrs. Shaw,” cried Mr. Bell, impatience breaking through his kindness. “She’s in England again, is she not?”

“Yes, sir; she’s come back,” said Dixon, reluctant as a dog guarding its wounded. “But I don’t think she’ll like to leave Mrs. Lennox at such an interesting time.”

“Interesting time be—” Mr. Bell checked himself with a cough, but his indignation went on speaking in his eyes. “She could be content enough to be at Venice or Naples, or some of those Popish places, at the last ‘interesting time,’ which happened in Corfu, I believe. And what does that little prosperous woman’s interesting time signify compared with that poor creature in there—homeless, helpless, friendless Margaret—lying as still as if the sofa were an altar-tomb and she the stone image upon it? Mrs. Shaw shall come. See that a room is ready by to-morrow night. I’ll take care she comes.”

So he wrote—no petition, no coaxing, but a command, sharp enough to pierce Mrs. Shaw’s indolence and her habit of arranging her sympathies at a distance. She received it with tears, declaring, as she dabbed at the corners of her eyes, that it was so like one of the dear general’s letters when he expected a fit of gout, that she should preserve it as a relic. Indeed, if Mr. Bell had offered her any choice—if he had urged instead of ordered—she might have remained in Harley Street, feeling herself very kind, and sending messages of tender regret. But being told she must come, she found energy enough to allow herself to be packed by her maid, boxes shut and corded with brisk authority.

Edith, all cap-strings and shawl and tears, came to the head of the stairs as Captain Lennox led Mrs. Shaw down to the carriage.

“Don’t forget, mamma—Margaret must come and live with us. Sholto goes to Oxford on Wednesday; you must send word by Mr. Bell when we are to expect you. And if you want Sholto, he can go on to Milton from Oxford. Don’t forget, mamma—you are to bring back Margaret.”

She went back into the drawing-room, where Mr. Henry Lennox sat with a new Review, cutting open the pages with deliberate neatness. Without looking up, he said, in the tone of a man who offers assistance because it is his due to offer it—

“If you don’t like Sholto to be so long absent, Edith, I hope you will let me go down to Milton and give what aid I can.”

“Oh, thank you,” she answered readily. “I dare say old Mr. Bell will do everything, and perhaps more help won’t be needed. Only one doesn’t expect much savoir-faire from a resident Fellow. Dear, darling Margaret! Won’t it be nice to have her here again? You were both great allies years ago.”

“Were we?” he asked indifferently, as if the printed column had more claim on him than memory.

“Well, perhaps not—I forget. I was so full of Sholto. But doesn’t it fall out well that if my uncle was to die it should be just now, when we’re come home and settled in the old house, quite ready to receive Margaret? Poor thing! what a change it will be from Milton. I’ll have new chintz for her bedroom—make it bright and fresh and cheerful.”

In that same spirit of kindly planning—kindly, and yet touching grief as one touches a bruise—Mrs. Shaw travelled to Milton, sometimes dreading the first meeting, more often thinking how quickly she might remove Margaret from what she always termed, with a shudder, “that horrid place,” back to the smooth upholstery and well-muffled street-sounds of Harley Street.

“Oh dear!” she said to her maid, as the train drew nearer and the air thickened. “Look at those chimneys! My poor sister Hale! I don’t think I could have rested at Naples if I had known it was like this. I must have come and fetched her and Margaret away.”

And though she had always thought Mr. Hale a weak man, she never judged him so weak as when she saw, with her own eyes, what he had chosen in exchange for Helstone—green silence for this perpetual breath of smoke; the natural music of birds and wind for a place where the very air seemed to throb with iron.

Margaret remained as she had been: white, motionless, without tears. They had told her her aunt was coming; she had not shown surprise or pleasure, dislike or gratitude. Mr. Bell, whose appetite had returned with the irrepressible selfishness of the living body, tried again to tempt her with something delicate—sweetbreads stewed with oysters, rich with a sea-scent, the sauce thickened carefully, and the whole intended to insinuate comfort into a failing frame. But Margaret shook her head with the same quiet obstinacy, as if nourishment were a foreign language she could not bear to hear.

Mr. Bell ate them himself, partly to spare Dixon’s feelings, partly because one must go on chewing something when the mind can do nothing else but grind sorrow.

It was Margaret, however, who first heard the cab stop at the door that brought Mrs. Shaw from the station. The sound itself—wheels ceasing, a door shutting, the faint stir of voices—broke into her stillness like a stone dropped into deep water. Her eyelids quivered; a little colour came and went in her lips, as if life tried once more to claim her.

Mr. Bell went down to meet Mrs. Shaw. When they returned upstairs, Margaret was standing—trying to steady her dizziness by mere force of will. She saw her aunt; she went forward, and the arms held out to her were not the polished embrace of a fashionable woman so much as the sudden shelter of blood and likeness. And there, on her aunt’s shoulder, she found at last the passionate relief of tears.

It was not only sorrow for the dead that melted then. It was the remembered tenderness of years; it was the soft compulsion of relationship; it was that inexplicable family resemblance in look and gesture, in tone and even in the way a hand was laid upon a sleeve—so like her mother in that instant that Margaret’s numbed heart gave way as ice breaks under a spring sun.

Mr. Bell stole out, grateful as any man is to be spared the sight of a grief he cannot mend. He went down into the study, ordered a fire, and tried to occupy himself by taking books down from the shelves. But each volume was a trap for memory. A name written within, a dog-eared page, a quotation marked—everything was Hale speaking again, in that quiet voice of his that had so often softened argument into persuasion. It was a change of labour from watching Margaret; it was no change of thought.

He was glad—almost startled into pleasure—to catch the sound of Mr. Thornton’s voice at the door.

Dixon, however, was at her most ungracious. The arrival of Mrs. Shaw’s maid had summoned in her mind whole processions of former grandeur—Beresford blood, ancient coaches, “station” (as she called it with satisfaction) from which her young mistress had been thrust down. In the kitchen she had been skilfully drawing out from the maid every circumstance of consequence connected with Harley Street, for the edification of Martha and the strengthening of her own self-importance. Those visions made her inclined to be supercilious toward any Milton man. She stood in awe of Mr. Thornton, but she was as curt as she dared.

He could see none of the inmates of the house that night.

It was uncomfortable to have her statement contradicted by Mr. Bell opening the study-door and calling out—

“Thornton! Is that you? Come in for a minute. I want to speak to you.”

So Mr. Thornton entered the study; and Dixon withdrew, to reinstate herself among pots and plates by repeating, with prodigious embellishment, the tale of Sir John Beresford’s coach and six when he was High Sheriff.

Mr. Bell, once Mr. Thornton was inside, looked at him with the vagueness of a mind overfull.

“I don’t know what I wanted to say to you after all,” he confessed. “Only it’s dull enough to sit in a room where everything speaks of a dead friend. Yet Margaret and her aunt must have the drawing-room to themselves.”

“Is Mrs—Is her aunt come?” asked Mr. Thornton; and the break in his voice betrayed more than the question.

“Come? Yes. Maid and all. One would think she might have come alone at such a time. And now I must turn out and find my way to the Clarendon.”

“You must not go to the Clarendon,” said Mr. Thornton quickly. “We have five or six empty bedrooms at home.”

“Well aired?” asked Mr. Bell, old habits of comfort asserting themselves in the midst of trouble.

“I think you may trust my mother for that.”

“Then I’ll run upstairs, wish that wan girl good-night, make my bow to her aunt, and go off with you straight.”

He was longer upstairs than Mr. Thornton expected. Mr. Thornton had business—workmen’s accounts, plans to decide, the heavy daily management that waited for no man’s private anguish—and he had only snatched time to run up to Crampton and ask how Miss Hale did. He paced, listening to the fire, to the small creaks of the room, to the distant under-note of Milton itself: that continual, restless hum which never quite ceased, and which some men took as the pulse of prosperity, while others felt it as a kind of perpetual intrusion, a forcing of the world’s harsh lexicon into the ear until a man forgot what natural quiet could be.

At length Mr. Bell came down, and they set out together through the night.

“I was kept by those women,” said Mr. Bell, with an impatience half comic, half bitter. “Mrs. Shaw is anxious to get home—on account of her daughter, she says—and wants Margaret to go off at once. Now she is no more fit for travelling than I am for flying. Besides, Margaret says—very justly—that she has friends she must see, people to wish good-bye to; and then her aunt plagued her about old claims, and whether she was forgetful of old friends. And Margaret burst out crying, and said she should be glad enough to go from a place where she had suffered so much. Now I must return to Oxford to-morrow, and I don’t know which way to throw in my voice.”

He paused as if asking counsel. Mr. Thornton did not answer. A phrase had fastened on him and would not loosen.

Where she had suffered so much.

So that was how she would remember Milton: not as the place where she had been seen, where she had been loved in secret and in pain; not as the ground on which every mile walked toward her door had been a kind of feast to him, richer than any banquet because anticipation seasoned it, because each step both brought him nearer and carried him away, making his mind rehearse some grace in her, some keen, pungent quality in her speech that stung and delighted together. To him, even its bitterness had been precious—an austere spice that made the sweetness sharper when it came. And she called it suffering.

The thought made the streets seem emptier than they were. The factories’ night-sounds—distant clanks, a hiss, a monotonous beat like a great heart made of metal—pressed upon his nerves. There are silences that heal, and silences that wound; but there are also noises that deaden feeling until grief has no room to move. Milton’s sound never asked permission of the soul.

They reached Marlborough Mills. In the dining-room Mrs. Thornton and Fanny were sitting. Fanny was in a flutter of small exultation while the maid held up glossy materials—one silk after another—to judge their effect by candle-light. The room was bright; the fabrics caught the flame, and threw back sheen, shadow, and the whispering rustle of money spent for ornament.

Mrs. Thornton made an effort to sympathise, but neither taste nor dress was within her proper dominions. She heartily wished Fanny had accepted her brother’s offer of having the wedding-clothes provided by a first-rate London dressmaker, without endless troublesome discussions and waverings born of Fanny’s desire to choose and superintend everything herself. Mr. Thornton, for his part, was only too willing to show his grateful approval of any sensible man who could be captivated by Fanny’s second-rate airs and graces, by giving her ample means for providing herself with the finery which rivalled—if it did not exceed—the lover in her estimation.

When Mr. Thornton and Mr. Bell entered, Fanny blushed, simpered, and fluttered over the signs of her occupation. It might have drawn attention from most; it drew none from Mr. Bell. If he thought of her and her satins at all, it was by contrast with the pale sorrow he had left behind—Margaret sitting motionless with bent head and folded hands in a room so still you might almost have believed the rush in your own ears was made by the spirits of the dead lingering near the beloved. For when he had first gone upstairs, Mrs. Shaw had fallen asleep on the sofa, and no sound had broken that solemn hush.

Mrs. Thornton gave Mr. Bell her formal welcome. She was never so gracious as when receiving her son’s friends in her son’s house; the more unexpected they were, the more honour to her admirable housekeeping.

“How is Miss Hale?” she asked.

“About as broken down by this last stroke as she can be.”

“I am sure it is very well for her that she has such a friend as you.”

“I wish I were her only friend, madam,” said Mr. Bell, with blunt feeling. “It sounds brutal; but here have I been displaced and turned out of my post of comforter by a fine lady aunt; and there are cousins and what not claiming her in London as if she were a lap-dog belonging to them. And she is too weak and miserable to have a will of her own.”

“She must indeed be weak,” said Mrs. Thornton, with an implied meaning her son understood.

“But where,” she continued, “have these relations been all this time that Miss Hale has appeared almost friendless, and has certainly had a good deal of anxiety to bear?”

Yet she did not care enough for the answer to wait. She left to make household arrangements, her mind already travelling over linen, sheets, fires laid, a room made ready—comforts she could command, and therefore trusted.

“They have been living abroad,” said Mr. Bell to Mr. Thornton when they were alone. “They have some claim, in justice. The aunt brought her up; she and the cousin have been like sisters. What vexes me is—I wanted to take her for a child of my own, and I am jealous of those who don’t seem to value their right. Now it would be different if Frederick claimed her.”

“Frederick!” exclaimed Mr. Thornton; and the name fell upon him like a blow in the dark. “Who is he? What right—” He stopped short, as if he had almost spoken too much.

“Frederick,” repeated Mr. Bell, surprised. “Why, don’t you know? He’s her brother. Have you not heard—”

“I never heard his name before. Where is he? Who is he?”

“Surely I told you, when the family first came to Milton—the son concerned in that mutiny.”

“I never heard of him till this moment,” said Mr. Thornton, and his voice grew hard with the effort of restraint. “Where does he live?”

“In Spain. Liable to be arrested the instant he sets foot on English ground. Poor fellow—he will grieve at not being able to attend his father’s funeral. We must be content with Captain Lennox; I know no other relation.”

“I hope I may be allowed to go?” said Mr. Thornton.

“Certainly; thankfully. You’re a good fellow, after all, Thornton. Hale liked you. He spoke of you only the other day at Oxford. He regretted he had seen so little of you lately. I am obliged to you for wishing to show him respect.”

“But about Frederick,” pursued Mr. Thornton, the same idea gnawing in him. “Does he never come to England?”

“Never.”

“He was not over here about the time of Mrs. Hale’s death?”

“No. Why, I was here then. I hadn’t seen Hale for years and years; and, if you remember, I came—No, it was some time after that I came. But poor Frederick was not here. What made you think he was?”

“I saw a young man walking with Miss Hale one day,” replied Mr. Thornton, “and I think it was about that time.”

“Oh, that would be this young Lennox—the Captain’s brother. He’s a lawyer. They were in constant correspondence with him, and Mr. Hale thought he would come down.”

Mr. Bell wheeled round suddenly, shutting one eye, the other sharpening itself into keen scrutiny of Mr. Thornton’s face.

“Do you know,” he said, “that I once fancied you had a little tenderness for Margaret?”

There was no answer. No change of countenance.

“And so did poor Hale. Not at first—not till I put it into his head.”

“I admired Miss Hale,” said Mr. Thornton at length, as if choosing the safest word as one chooses the safest dish when one’s appetite is watched. “Every one must. She is a beautiful creature.”

“Is that all!” cried Mr. Bell, anger flaring. “You can speak of her in that measured way—simply as a ‘beautiful creature’—something to catch the eye. I did hope you had nobleness enough to pay her the homage of the heart. Though I believe—in fact I know—she would have rejected you, still to have loved her without return would have lifted you higher than all those, be they who they may, that have ever known her to love. ‘Beautiful creature’ indeed! Do you speak of her as you would of a horse or dog?”

Mr. Thornton’s eyes glowed like embers.

“Mr. Bell,” he said, very low, “before you speak so, you should remember that all men are not as free to express what they feel as you are. Let us talk of something else.”

For every word Mr. Bell had spoken had struck his heart like a trumpet-call; yet he would not be forced into any confession. He was not a mocking-bird of praise, to be tried, to be set to out-sing another man’s extolling. He turned abruptly to matters that could be held between them without laying bare the quick.

“What is that heap of brick and mortar we came upon in the yard?” asked Mr. Bell, catching at the change. “Any repairs wanted?”

“No; none, thank you.”

“Are you building on your own account? If you are, I’m obliged to you.”

“I’m building a dining-room—for the men, I mean—the hands.”

“I thought you were hard to please if this room wasn’t good enough for you, a bachelor.”

“I’ve got acquainted with a strange kind of chap,” said Mr. Thornton, speaking now as if it were easier to confess practical matters than feeling. “And I put one or two children in whom he is interested to school. So, as I happened to be passing near his house one day, I went in about some trifling payment; and I saw such a miserable black frizzle of a dinner—a greasy cinder of meat—as first set me thinking. But it was not till provisions grew so high this winter that I bethought me how, by buying wholesale and cooking a quantity together, money might be saved and comfort gained.

“So I spoke to my friend—or my enemy—the man I told you of; and he found fault with every detail of my plan; and in consequence I laid it aside, as impracticable, and also because if I forced it I should be interfering with the independence of my men. Then suddenly this Higgins came to me and graciously signified his approval of a scheme so nearly the same as mine that I might have claimed it; and more, the approval of several fellow-workmen to whom he had spoken.

“I was a little riled, I confess, and thought of throwing the whole thing overboard. But it seemed childish to relinquish what I had once thought wise merely because I did not get the honour due to the originator. So I coolly took the part assigned me—something like steward to a club. I buy the provisions wholesale, and provide a fitting matron or cook.”

Mr. Bell’s humour returned for a moment, as if the mention of meals—even these plain, workmen’s meals—gave his mind something homely to hold.

“I hope you give satisfaction in your new capacity. Are you a good judge of potatoes and onions? But I suppose Mrs. Thornton assists you in your marketing.”

“Not a bit,” replied Mr. Thornton. “She disapproves of the whole plan, and now we never mention it to each other. But I manage pretty well—get stocks from Liverpool; butcher’s meat from our own family butcher. And I can assure you, the hot dinners the matron turns out are not to be despised.”

“Do you taste each dish as it goes in, in virtue of your office? I hope you have a white wand.”

“At first I was scrupulous,” said Mr. Thornton, “confined myself to purchasing; and even then I rather obeyed the men’s orders conveyed through the housekeeper than my own judgment. One time the beef was too large, another the mutton not fat enough. I think they saw how careful I was to leave them free, not to intrude my ideas; so one day two or three—Higgins among them—asked me if I would not come in and take a snack. It was a busy day; but I saw they would be hurt if I didn’t meet them half-way. So I went in; and I never made a better dinner in my life.

“I told them—my next neighbours, I mean, for I’m no speech-maker—how much I enjoyed it; and for some time, whenever that especial dinner recurred in their dietary, I was sure to be met with, ‘Master, there’s hot-pot for dinner to-day; win yo’ come in?’ If they had not asked me, I would no more have intruded on them than I’d have gone to the mess at barracks without invitation.”

Mr. Bell laughed a little, though the sound had no mirth in it.

“I should think you were rather a restraint on your hosts’ conversation. They can’t abuse masters while you’re there. I expect they take it out on non-hot-pot days.”

“Hitherto we’ve steered clear of vexed questions,” said Mr. Thornton. “But if any of the old disputes come up again, I shall speak out next hot-pot day. You are hardly acquainted with our Darkshire fellows, for all you’re a Darkshire man yourself. They’ve such a sense of humour—such a racy mode of expression. I am getting really to know some of them now, and they talk pretty freely before me.”

“Nothing like eating for equalising men,” said Mr. Bell. “Dying is nothing to it. The philosopher dies sententiously—the pharisee ostentatiously—the simple-hearted humbly—the poor idiot blindly, as the sparrow falls to the ground; but philosopher and idiot, publican and pharisee, all eat after the same fashion—given an equally good digestion. There’s theory for theory for you!”

“Indeed I have no theory,” replied Mr. Thornton shortly. “I hate theories.”

“I beg your pardon,” said Mr. Bell, with a sudden impulse of generosity that sought an outlet. “To show my penitence, will you accept a ten-pound note toward your marketing and give the poor fellows a feast?”

“Thank you; but I’d rather not,” answered Mr. Thornton. “They pay me rent for the oven and cooking-places at the back of the mill, and will have to pay more for the new dining-room. I don’t want it to fall into a charity. I don’t want donations. Once let in the principle, and people will go talking, and spoil the simplicity of the whole thing.”

“People will talk about any new plan,” said Mr. Bell. “You can’t help that.”

“My enemies—if I have any—may make a philanthropic fuss about this dinner-scheme,” returned Mr. Thornton. “But you are a friend, and I expect you will pay my experiment the respect of silence. It is but a new broom as yet, and sweeps clean enough. But by-and-by we shall meet with stumbling-blocks, no doubt.”

Mrs. Shaw’s dislike of Milton rose in her like a rash the instant she had set foot again on its pavements. The place offended her on every sense at once. The air was a soot-laden broth that clung to the palate and to the curtains; the streets rang with iron-shod wheels and the ceaseless clatter of work—noise that did not merely fill the ear but pressed on the nerves like a hand. Even the richer women she passed seemed to her dressed too loud, too showy, as if finery could drown the roar of the mills; and the poor, moving in and out of the factory-gates, looked to her not so much unfortunate as unbecomingly stained by the very town.

Margaret, weakened to the point where the simplest choice felt like a labour, endured her aunt’s earnest tirade as one endures a draught one cannot swallow and cannot refuse.
