Mrs. Shaw feared her own “nerves;” she feared, too, that Margaret’s colour would never come back in an air that tasted of smoke. Margaret must return to London with her—quickly. At last, with her spirit bruised and her body worn thin, Margaret yielded. When Wednesday was over—when her father had been laid in the ground far away from the green fields of his youth and far away from the grave where his wife lay among strangers—then she would go. Dixon should be left to settle accounts, dismiss furniture, close the house.

It was the distance that wrung Margaret most: not merely the miles, but the way death had scattered the Hales like seed blown from a torn pod—one in Milton’s little rented rooms, one in Oxford’s quiet earth, one in Helstone’s memory. She tortured herself with the thought that, had she not fallen into that heavy stupor of the first days, she might have contrived some tenderness of arrangement—might have brought husband and wife nearer even in burial. Now there was only the irrevocable.

Before that mournful Wednesday came, a letter arrived from Mr. Bell.

It was all Mr. Bell—blunt, affectionate, bustling, with jests thrust in like cloves into an apple to keep the sweetness from cloying. He could not return when he had intended; there was some rare duty at Oxford calling the Fellows together. Captain Lennox and Mr. Thornton were there. The captain, smart and well-meaning, had offered to go to Milton and help in searching for the will—though Mr. Bell was certain there was none, or Margaret would have found it already if she had followed his directions. The captain had declared, too, that he must take Margaret and his mother-in-law home; in Edith’s condition he could not remain away beyond Friday. Mr. Bell, with his practical kindliness, proposed to put matters into the hands of his Milton attorney if no will appeared; he distrusted the captain’s business capacity even while admiring his moustachios.

There would have to be a sale. Margaret must choose what she wished reserved. And then came the part that made her cheeks burn and her throat tighten—not the talk of sale and lists and attorneys, but the paternal assumption wrapped around her like a cloak she had not asked for and could not put off.

Mr. Bell reminded her that she was to have his money and goods when he died—not that he meant to die yet—only that she might understand what followed. Since these Lennoxes were fond of her now and might or might not continue so, it would be best to begin with a formal agreement: she was to pay them two hundred and fifty pounds a year as long as they found it pleasant to live together. That would secure her from being thrown adrift if the captain ever wanted his household to himself; she could take herself and her two hundred and fifty pounds elsewhere—unless Mr. Bell claimed her first to keep house for him. As for dress, Dixon, and “confectionery” (which he insisted all young ladies ate until wisdom came by age), he would consult some lady acquaintance and settle an allowance after ascertaining what Margaret would have from her father.

Then, under all the brisk command, the old love showed itself plainly: he had loved her father five and thirty years; he had stood by him on his wedding-day; he had closed his eyes in death. He was her godfather; if he could do her little spiritual good, he would at least endow her materially. He had no known relation on earth—“who is there to mourn for Adam Bell?”—and his whole heart was bent upon this one thing. Margaret Hale was not the girl to say him nay. She must write by return—two lines, if only two lines—and “no thanks.”

Margaret took up a pen. Her hand trembled; the ink seemed too black, too heavy for her weakened fingers. She wrote, slowly, as if each stroke were a weight lifted and set down:—

“Margaret Hale is not the girl to say him nay.”

She vexed herself even as she wrote; the words were his, not hers. Yet she had no strength to do better, and when the paper was folded her pulse beat with fatigue as if she had run a mile. She lay down again and tried not to think.

Mrs. Shaw, fluttering about her, peered at her with anxious softness. “My dearest child! Has that letter vexed or troubled you?”

“No,” said Margaret, though her voice was scarcely more than breath. “I shall be better when to-morrow is over.”

“I feel sure you won’t be better till I get you out of this horrid air. How you can have borne it these two years I can’t imagine.”

“Where could I go to? I could not leave papa and mamma.”

Mrs. Shaw softened at once into the complacent consolation of those who believe their comforts are proof of Providence. “Well, don’t distress yourself. I dare say it was all for the best; only I had no conception of how you were living. Our butler’s wife lives in a better house than this.”

“It is sometimes very pretty—in summer; you can’t judge by what it is now. I have been very happy here,” said Margaret; and she closed her eyes to stop the talk, as one shuts a door upon wind.

Yet the house, under Mrs. Shaw’s directions, teemed with comfort compared with the bare economies of the past months. Fires were lit in every bedroom—little islands of warmth against Milton’s damp chill. Mrs. Shaw bought delicacies and soft luxuries as if feeding and pampering could mend what grief had torn. There were broths that smelled of slow-simmered bones and herbs, jellies trembling on china, oranges gleaming like captured sun. But all this seemed to Margaret no more than a kindly ritual performed around her; it reached her only as gratitude to her aunt, not as temptation to appetite. Her own senses had dulled to one persistent taste—iron, like tears.

Restlessness drove her, though she was weak. All day long she kept herself from thinking of Oxford and the grave being opened there by wandering from room to room and touching, lifting, setting aside the things she meant to keep. The task had the quiet insistence of domestic duty—fold this, tie that—yet every object she handled gave back a faint echo, as if the house were an instrument and her grief kept striking the same note. Dixon followed her at Mrs. Shaw’s desire, ostensibly to take instructions, but in truth with orders to coax her into rest.

“These books, Dixon, I will keep. All the rest will you send to Mr. Bell? He will value them for themselves, as well as for papa’s sake.” Margaret paused, her fingers resting on a volume as if feeling for the warmth it once held. “This—this I should like you to take to Mr. Thornton after I am gone. Stay; I will write a note with it.”

She sat down hastily, as though afraid that if she stood still she would remember too much. The pen moved again over paper.

“DEAR SIR,—The accompanying book I am sure will be valued by you for the sake of my father, to whom it belonged.

“Yours sincerely,
“MARGARET HALE.”

Then she rose and went on, turning over shabby, old-fashioned things known to her since childhood with a kind of reluctant caress. The very textures spoke: worn cloth smoothed by years of hands; the faint smell of cedar in a drawer; a crack in porcelain that had been there since she was a girl. Dixon talked on steadily—little homely speeches meant to divert the mind—but afterwards she told Mrs. Shaw she doubted whether Miss Hale heard a word.

The consequence of being on her feet so long was that in the evening her body gave up, utterly spent. The exhaustion was merciful; it carried her into the first decent night’s rest she had had since her father died.

At breakfast next morning she said she wished to go and bid one or two friends good-bye.

Mrs. Shaw objected, scandalised and nervous. “I am sure, my dear, you can have no friends here with whom you are sufficiently intimate to justify you in calling upon them so soon; before you have been at church.”

“But to-day is my only day; if Captain Lennox comes this afternoon, and if we must—if I must really go to-morrow—”

“Oh, yes, we shall go to-morrow. I am more and more convinced this air is bad for you; it makes you look so pale and ill. Besides, Edith expects us; and she may be waiting for me; and you cannot be left alone, my dear, at your age. No; if you must make these calls, I will go with you. Dixon can get us a coach, I suppose?”

So Mrs. Shaw went, wrapped in shawls as though Milton’s very sound could chill her bones, and her maid followed behind to manage cushions and coverings. Margaret’s face was too sad for smiling at such parade. She had often walked alone to these places at any hour, with only the steadying rhythm of her own step and the familiar voices of the streets. Now she sat while the coach rattled, the iron tyres striking sparks of sound from the stones, and she dreaded naming one of her destinations: Nicholas Higgins’ court, where washing-lines strung from house to house slapped and snapped in the wind, where wet clothes breathed out a sour steam, and where the noise of children and neighbours was never quite still. She hoped her aunt’s delicacy would refuse to alight.

There was a small battle in Mrs. Shaw between ease and propriety; ease triumphed. With many warnings to Margaret not to catch fever—always lurking, Mrs. Shaw said, in such places—she permitted her to go in alone.

Nicholas was out. Only Mary was there, and one or two of the Boucher children, their faces pinched and inquisitive. Margaret was vexed with herself for miscalculating the time. She had meant to say a hundred small things—tender, practical, encouraging—things to tie the past to the future like knots in a cord. But Mary, blunt in mind though warm in heart, understood at once why Margaret had come, and began to cry openly, with such violent sobbing that words became useless.

Margaret could only try to comfort her with the vague, thin hope that they might meet again—sometime, somewhere—and she begged her to tell her father that if he could manage it, she wished him to come in the evening when work was done.

As she was leaving, she stopped and looked round the room, fixing it in her mind—the poor hearth, the worn table, the corner where Bessy had lain. Then she hesitated before she spoke, and when she did her voice shook.

“I should like to have some little thing to remind me of Bessy.”

At once Mary’s generosity flared. What could they give? There was so little; poverty makes even kindness consider its stock. Margaret’s eyes fell on a common drinking-cup, plain and cheap, but haunted for her by remembrance: Bessy’s feverish lips, and that cup always standing ready with water.

Mary cried, “Oh, take summat better; that only cost fourpence!”

“That will do, thank you,” said Margaret quickly; and she went away before she could see Mary’s face change again. For a moment the pleasure of giving—of having still something to offer—lit Mary’s features like a candle.

Now to Marlborough Mills’ master’s house—now to Mrs. Thornton. It must be done.

Margaret sat rigid in the coach, her hands clasped in her lap as if keeping down a trembling. The streets changed as they went, yet the town’s voice did not: a persistent undertone of machinery, a hammered rhythm that made conversation feel thin. It was not merely loud; it was incessant, and in that incessancy there was a kind of tyranny, as if the place insisted on its own vocabulary—iron, steam, profit—and drowned out gentler dialects.

She had hard work finding the right words to explain to her aunt who Mrs. Thornton was, and why she must go. Mrs. Shaw would not content herself with remaining in the coach at this respectable door; she alighted.

They were shown into a drawing-room where a fire had only just been kindled. The room still held the chill of unused air; the flame, newly fed, smelt of singeing dust and resin before it settled into steadier warmth. Mrs. Shaw huddled in her shawl and shivered. “What an icy room!”

They waited. At length Mrs. Thornton entered.

There was some softening in her now that Margaret was going out of sight. She remembered Margaret’s spirit more than her own resentments; and grief had carved Margaret’s face into something that commanded even Mrs. Thornton’s austere attention. She greeted her with a blander countenance, and there was—rarety indeed—a shade of tenderness when she observed the tear-swollen whiteness and heard the quiver Margaret struggled to steady.

“Allow me to introduce my aunt, Mrs. Shaw,” said Margaret. “I am going away from Milton to-morrow; I do not know if you are aware of it, but I wanted to see you once again, Mrs. Thornton, to—to apologize for my manner the last time I saw you; and to say that I am sure you meant kindly—however much we may have misunderstood each other.”

Mrs. Shaw looked extremely perplexed. Apologies, thanks, misunderstandings—she did not know what sort of intimacy could make these necessary between ladies. But Mrs. Thornton answered with her accustomed sense of duty.

“Miss Hale, I am glad you do me justice. I did no more than I believed to be my duty in remonstrating with you as I did. I have always desired to act the part of a friend to you. I am glad you do me justice.”

“And,” Margaret went on, blushing painfully, “will you do me justice, and believe that though I cannot—I do not choose—to give explanations of my conduct, I have not acted in the unbecoming way you apprehended?”

Her voice was low; her eyes pleaded. The charm of manner—hitherto a thing to which Mrs. Thornton had seemed armoured—touched her at last. “Yes, I do believe you. Let us say no more about it. Where are you going to reside, Miss Hale? I understood from Mr. Bell that you were going to leave Milton. You never liked Milton, you know,” she added, with a grim half-smile; “but for all that you must not expect me to congratulate you on quitting it. Where shall you live?”

“With my aunt,” said Margaret, turning towards Mrs. Shaw.

“My niece will reside with me in Harley Street,” said Mrs. Shaw, smoothing the statement into a social fact. “She is almost like a daughter to me. And I am glad to acknowledge my own obligation for any kindness that has been shown to her. If you and your husband ever come to town, my son and daughter, Captain and Mrs. Lennox, will, I am sure, join with me in wishing to do anything in our power to show you attention.”

Mrs. Thornton thought—sharply—that Margaret had not troubled to enlighten her aunt as to the relationship between the Thorntons and these fine offers. She replied shortly, cutting through the soft patronage.

“My husband is dead. Mr. Thornton is my son. I never go to London; so I am not likely to be able to avail myself of your polite offers.”

At that instant Mr. Thornton entered.

He had only just returned from Oxford; the black of his mourning declared why he had been there. His face bore that set look of one who has done what had to be done and will not speak of it. His mother said, “John, this lady is Mrs. Shaw, Miss Hale’s aunt. I am sorry to say that Miss Hale’s call is to wish us good-bye.”

“You are going then!” he said, and his voice came out low, as if he had spoken into his own chest.

“Yes,” said Margaret. “We leave to-morrow.”

“My son-in-law comes this evening to escort us,” added Mrs. Shaw.

Mr. Thornton turned away. He did not sit. He stood by the table as if some object there demanded his whole attention, as if he had discovered an unopened letter and must consider it immediately. It was hard to tell whether he heard anything else. He did not even seem aware when they rose to go.

Yet when they moved towards the door he started forward and handed Mrs. Shaw down to the carriage with the mechanical civility of a man who has learned to keep his hands busy when his heart is not. Margaret and he stood close together on the step for a moment, and it was impossible for either not to remember another day—how the crowd had surged, how the air had been full of shouting and stones, how her body had been between him and violence. The sound of Milton was in their ears now, too: not the roar of a riot, but the constant grinding chorus of industry, as if the town itself refused quiet even for farewell.

Into his mind came, linked and burning, the speeches of the day after—the remembrance of her words, passionate and cruel, that there was not a man in all that desperate crowd for whom she did not care as much as for him. At the recollection his brow grew stern, though his heart beat thick with longing.

No. He had put it to the touch once, and lost. Let her go—with her stony heart and her beauty. How terrible her look was now, for all the loveliness of her features! She feared he would speak, and that speaking would demand some stern repression. Let her go. Beauty and heiress as she might be, she would find it hard to meet with a truer heart than his. Let her go.

He said good-bye with no tone of regret, no visible emotion. His offered hand was taken; he dropped it as carelessly as if it were a dead, withered flower.

No one in his household saw him again that day. He was busily engaged—or so he said.

Margaret’s strength, already scant, was utterly exhausted by these visits. She could not resist her aunt’s watchfulness, the petted arrangements, the sighing “I told you so’s.” Dixon said she was as bad as on the first day she heard of Mr. Hale’s death, and she and Mrs. Shaw consulted anxiously about delaying the journey. When Mrs. Shaw reluctantly proposed a few days’ delay, Margaret writhed as if in acute pain.

“Oh! let us go,” she said. “I cannot be patient here. I shall not get well here. I want to forget.”

So the preparations went on. Captain Lennox came, bringing news of Edith and the little boy, and the easy, indifferent talk of a man who was kind without being too deeply entangled in sorrow did Margaret good, as plain food sometimes steadies a sick stomach better than rich dainties. She roused herself a little. When she knew she might expect Higgins, she left the room quietly and waited in her own chamber for the summons.

He came in with the awkward tenderness of the strong for the wounded, and stood turning his cap in his hands.

“Eh!” said he. “To think o’ th’ oud gentleman dropping off as he did! Yo’ might ha’ knocked me down wi’ a straw when they telled me. ‘Mr. Hale?’ says I; ‘him as was th’ parson?’ ‘Ay,’ says they. ‘Then,’ says I, ‘there’s as good a man gone as ever lived on this earth, let who will be t’other!’”

He spoke on, breathy with indignation at the obstruction he had met: the women in the kitchen who would not tell Margaret he was there, saying she was ill. He stared at her, troubled.

“Butter me, but yo’ dunnot look like the same wench. And yo’re going to be a grand lady up i’ Lunnon, aren’t yo’?”

“Not a grand lady,” said Margaret, and for a moment the ghost of a smile touched her mouth.

“Well! Thornton said—says he, a day or two ago, ‘Higgins, have yo’ seen Miss Hale?’ ‘No,’ says I; ‘there’s a pack o’ women who won’t let me at her. But I can bide my time, if she’s ill. She and I knows each other pretty well; and hoo’ll not go doubting that I’m main sorry for th’ oud gentleman’s death, just because I can’t get at her and tell her so.’ And says he, ‘Yo’ll not have much time for to try and see her, my fine chap. She’s not for staying with us a day longer nor she can help. She’s got grand relations, and they’re carrying her off; and we shan’t see her no more.’”

Higgins lifted his head, his rough pride rising. “‘Measter,’ says I, ‘if I dunnot see her afore hoo goes, I’ll strive to get up to Lunnon next Whitsuntide, that I will. I’ll not be baulked o’ saying her good-bye by any relations whatsomdever.’ But bless yo’, I knowed yo’d come. It were only for to humour th’ measter, I let on as if I thought yo’d mebbe leave Milton without seeing me.”

“You’re quite right,” said Margaret. “You only do me justice. And you’ll not forget me, I’m sure. If no one else in Milton remembers me, I’m certain you will—and papa too. You know how good and tender he was.”

She went to a drawer and drew out the Bible, holding it as if it were warm, though it was only leather and paper. It seemed to carry her father’s very touch, his voice silently moving between its leaves.

“Look, Higgins. Here is his Bible. I have kept it for you. I can ill spare it; but I know he would have liked you to have it. I’m sure you’ll care for it, and study what is in it, for his sake.”

“Yo’ may say that,” Higgins answered hoarsely. “If it were th’ deuce’s own scribble, and yo’ axed me to read in it for yo’r sake and th’ oud gentleman’s, I’d do it.”

Margaret’s hand moved again, quick, almost furtive, as she pressed money towards him.

“Whatten’s this, wench!” he cried, starting back. “I’m not going for to take yo’r brass, so dunnot think it. We’ve been great friends, ’bout the sound o’ money passing between us.”

“For the children—for Boucher’s children,” Margaret said hurriedly, as if afraid of her own tears. “They may need it. You’ve no right to refuse it for them. I would not give you one penny,” she added, and the faintest humour steadied her voice; “don’t think there’s any of it for you.”

He stood a moment, conquered not by the coin but by the purpose—by the way she named the children as if they were a duty laid on all human hands alike. Then he took it, as one takes a trust.

“Well, wench! I can nobbut say—Bless yo’! and bless yo’!—and amen.”

The hush of Harley Street, while Edith lay confined and slowly gathered strength again, was a kind of narcotic mercy to Margaret. It let her sleep; it let her stop trembling at every remembered footstep in a Milton passage; it let her discover, in the calm light of days that asked nothing of her, how utterly her life had altered within eight short weeks.

She was lodged now among thick carpets that drank sound, among curtains that fell in disciplined folds and muffled even the passing wheels outside, among chairs that invited languor as if it were a duty. In this house the bare notion that care might exist elsewhere seemed never to have travelled. The daily order moved like a well-fed kitchen—machinery oiled, service timed, everything smoothed before one could feel the edge of want. Mrs. Shaw and Edith could scarcely do enough in their petting welcome; they persisted in calling it Margaret’s “home,” and said it with the soft tyranny of those who think affection may rename a place and make it true.

Yet the word “home,” like a flavour that will not take, refused to settle on Margaret’s tongue. Home, to her secret mind, was Helstone—nay, even the little house in Milton with its scant economies, the anxious father, the ailing mother, the small tiresome cares that had once filled the hours with a sort of honest purpose. It was almost ungrateful, she thought, to feel this; and still she did. Edith, impatient to be well, spoke eagerly of refitting Margaret’s bedchamber with every pliant comfort—sofas that yielded, footstools, screens, the pretty, useless ornaments that caught light and proclaimed leisure. Mrs. Shaw and the maid, as if nothing could be kinder than to bury a woman beneath satin, found perpetual employment in restoring Margaret’s wardrobe to “elegant variety,” as though the cut of a sleeve could mend a wound.

Captain Lennox moved through it all with that easy, gentlemanly kindness which requires no imagination. He sat beside Edith in her dressing-room a dutiful hour or two each day; he played with Sholto for another; he spent the rest where men like him spent it—in his club, or at dinner—gliding from one warm room to another, never compelled to hear the rawer noises of life. And just as Margaret’s need for quiet began to ebb—just as she might have started to feel the days too long, too smooth, too empty—Edith came downstairs again and resumed her part as queen of the household.

Then Margaret slid, by old habit, into watching, admiring, and ministering. She was grateful, almost, for occupation that was occupation only in name: she took charge of the semblances of duty, answered Edith’s notes, reminded her of engagements, sat by her when there was no gaiety in prospect and Edith, by a kind of luxurious caprice, fancied herself ill. Margaret would smooth the pillows, fetch the shawls, ring for the little restoratives that were brought up with grave faces as if they were remedies and not indulgences. Edith repaid her with caresses and praises—“your eloquence du billet, Maggie!”—as though a knack for phrases could stand in place of a life.

But the rest of the family lived in the full hurry of the Season. The house often emptied, leaving Margaret alone in rooms too finished, too silent. In those hours her thoughts ran backward to Milton with an ache sharpened by contrast: the sharp clang of the streets there, the breath of the mills that seemed to thicken the very air, the human voices strained high to cross the din. She found herself surfeited with ease that required no effort, no endurance, no striving. She began to fear that such softness would make her forget; that she might be lulled into a sleepy deadness, unable to feel beyond the circle of luxury that lapped her round.

There were toilers somewhere in London—she knew it as one knows a fact in a book—yet she never saw them. Even the servants belonged to an underground world: they rose soundlessly, performed, vanished; their lives, their hopes and fears, were as unknown to her as if they had no language Margaret could hear. The house above was a theatre kept sweet by invisible hands, and the sweetness itself—polished silver, warmed plates, the faint perfume of hot water and soap and flowers—began to oppress her like a scent too constant.

Once, when she hinted something of this to Edith, her cousin—wearied with dancing the night before—stroked Margaret’s cheek languidly as she sat on her old footstool by the sofa.

“Poor child!” said Edith, with a soft, complacent pity. “It is a little sad for you to be left night after night, just at this time when all the world is so gay. But we shall be having our dinner-parties soon—as soon as Henry comes back from circuit—and then there will be a little pleasant variety for you. No wonder it is moped, poor darling!”

Dinner-parties, Margaret thought, could not cure a hunger like hers; yet she did not say so. Edith prided herself on these entertainments—“so different,” she declared, from the old dowager dinners under mamma’s régime. Mrs. Shaw took as much pleasure in the new arrangements and newer circle as she had once taken in the heavier formality of her own, as if one might change a menu and imagine the appetite changed with it.

Captain Lennox, for his part, was always kindly brotherly to Margaret. She was truly fond of him—except in those moments when his attention fixed anxiously on Edith’s dress and appearance, as if her beauty were a dish to be served at precisely the right temperature to impress the world. Then something fierce and proud woke in Margaret. She could feel it like heat rising; she could hardly keep from speaking. It was not that she despised adornment; it was that she hated the way admiration was demanded and parceled out, as if a woman’s value depended on the proper arrangement of lace.

Her days settled into a dull rotation. There would be a quiet hour or two before a late breakfast; then a languid, unpunctual meal, eaten by half-awake people who drew it out as if time itself were their property. She must sit through it all, because afterwards came the discussion of plans—calls, drives, purchases, parties—plans that did not concern her and yet required her sympathy, her nods, her dutiful murmurs. Then an endless number of notes to write—Edith always leaving them with kisses and compliments; a little play with Sholto fresh from his morning walk; the care of the children during the servants’ dinner; a drive or callers; then some engagement for aunt and cousins that left Margaret “free,” though freedom like this was merely empty space, and the day’s inactivity pressed upon her, heavy as indigestible food.

She looked forward, with a longing she did not name aloud, to the homely event of Dixon’s return from Milton, where the old servant had been winding up all the Hales’ affairs. The cessation of news felt like famine. Dixon wrote business-like letters: Mr. Thornton’s opinion about what should be done with furniture; how to deal with the landlord at Crampton Terrace. Names came in sparsely, like crumbs when one has remembered bread. Mr. Thornton’s was there now and then; Milton names, seldom; and for Margaret, who had lived so intensely among those people, it was like being made suddenly deaf.

One evening she sat alone in the Lennox drawing-room. Dixon’s letters lay in her hand, but she was not reading—only thinking over them, tasting each phrase as if it might carry some hidden savour of the life she had been torn from. Her mind moved among memories: the hot, close streets, the unceasing mill-sound, the way voices in Milton had to fight to be heard; and she pictured that busy whirl going on as if she and her father had never existed there, as if their absence made no hollow at all. Did no one miss her in all that crowd? (Not Higgins; it was not of him she was thinking.) The thought stung her with a shame she could not account for.

The door opened. Mr. Bell was announced.

Margaret started as if caught in theft, and hurried the letters into her work-basket. She rose, colour rushing into her face, ashamed even of her own secrecy.

“Oh, Mr. Bell! I never thought of seeing you!”

“But you give me a welcome, I hope, as well as that very pretty start of surprise.”

“Have you dined? How did you come? Let me order you some dinner.”

“If you’re going to have any. Otherwise, you know, there is no one who cares less for eating than I do. But where are the others? Gone out to dinner? Left you alone?”

“Oh yes—and it is such a rest. I was just thinking—But will you run the risk of dinner? I don’t know if there is anything in the house.”

“Why, to tell you the truth, I dined at my club. Only they don’t cook as well as they did, so I thought, if you were going to dine, I might try and make out my dinner. But never mind, never mind! There aren’t ten cooks in England to be trusted at impromptu dinners. If their skill and their fires will stand it, their tempers won’t. You shall make me some tea, Margaret. And now—what were you thinking of? you were going to tell me. Whose letters were those, god-daughter, that you hid away so speedily?”

“Only Dixon’s,” Margaret answered; and felt, absurdly, her cheeks grow hotter.

“Whew! is that all? Who do you think came up in the train with me?”

“I don’t know,” said Margaret, and set her mouth as if she would not be coaxed into guessing.

“Your what d’ye call him? What’s the right name for a cousin-in-law’s brother?”

“Mr. Henry Lennox?” she asked.

“Yes,” replied Mr. Bell. “You knew him formerly, didn’t you? What sort of a person is he, Margaret?”

“I liked him long ago,” she said, her eyes dropping for the briefest moment. Then, as if she refused to let the past take advantage of her, she looked up and continued in her natural tone: “You know we have been corresponding about Frederick since; but I have not seen him for nearly three years, and he may be changed. What did you think of him?”

“I don’t know. He was so busy trying to find out who I was, in the first instance, and what I was in the second, that he never let out what he was; unless indeed that veiled curiosity of his as to what manner of man he had to talk to was not a good piece, and a fair indication of his character. Do you call him good-looking, Margaret?”

“No! certainly not. Do you?”

“Not I. But I thought perhaps you might. Is he a great deal here?”

“I fancy he is when he is in town. He has been on circuit now since I came. But—Mr. Bell—have you come from Oxford or from Milton?”

“From Milton. Don’t you see I’m smoke-dried?”

“Certainly. But I thought that it might be the effect of the antiquities of Oxford.”

“Come now, be a sensible woman! In Oxford, I could have managed all the landlords in the place, and had my own way, with half the trouble your Milton landlord has given me, and defeated me after all. He won’t take the house off our hands till next June twelve-month. Luckily, Mr. Thornton found a tenant for it. Why don’t you ask after Mr. Thornton, Margaret? He has proved himself a very active friend of yours, I can tell you. Taken more than half the trouble off my hands.”

“And how is he? How is Mrs. Thornton?” Margaret asked quickly, her voice dipping as if she feared the sound might carry.

“I suppose they’re well. I’ve been staying at their house till I was driven out of it by the perpetual clack about that Thornton girl’s marriage. It was too much for Thornton himself, though she was his sister. He used to go and sit in his own room perpetually. He’s getting past the age for caring for such things, either as principal or accessory. I was surprised to find the old lady falling into the current, and carried away by her daughter’s enthusiasm for orange-blossoms and lace. I thought Mrs. Thornton had been made of sterner stuff.”

“She would put on any assumption of feeling to veil her daughter’s weakness,” Margaret said, low.

“Perhaps so. You’ve studied her, have you? She doesn’t seem over fond of you, Margaret.”

“I know it.”

“Oh, here is tea, at last!” Margaret exclaimed, with a relief that was almost too evident.

And with tea came Mr. Henry Lennox.

He had walked up after a late dinner, expecting to find his brother and sister-in-law at home. Margaret, seeing him, felt the old Helstone terrace rise as plainly before her as if the gravel were underfoot and the evening air full of that south-country scent of leaf and earth. She suspected that he, too, was grateful for the presence of a third person; their first meeting since the day of his offer and her refusal would have been hard enough with Edith and the Captain in the room, and was doubly awkward now, when she was the only lady there and must, by mere force of custom, bear the weight of most of his speech.

At first she could scarcely find words. She was thankful for tea-table occupations—the little clink of china, the measured pour, the faint steam rising—because they gave her a decent reason for silence, and him time to gather his composure. For he had rather forced himself there that evening, with the stern prudence of a man determined to step over an awkwardness by standing on it; and now, finding her alone, he had no refuge but talk.

Margaret recovered first. She began with what lay uppermost in her mind, and perhaps in her heart’s need of duty.

“Mr. Lennox, I have been so much obliged to you for all you have done about Frederick.”

“I am only sorry it has been so unsuccessful,” he replied; and his quick glance slid towards Mr. Bell, as if to measure how far he might speak.

Margaret, reading that glance, turned to Mr. Bell, both drawing him into the conversation and implying, by the very act, that he was already fully trusted.

“That Horrocks—that very last witness of all—has proved as unavailing as the others. Mr. Lennox discovered that he sailed for Australia only last August; only two months before Frederick was in England, and gave us the names of—”

“Frederick in England! you never told me that!” Mr. Bell broke out, astonished.

“I thought you knew. I never doubted you had been told. Of course, it was a great secret, and perhaps I should not have named it now,” Margaret said, dismayed, and feeling again that hot shame as if she had betrayed something sacred.

“I have never named it to either my brother or your cousin,” said Mr. Lennox, with the dry restraint of a professional man who rebukes by precision.

“Never mind, Margaret. I am not living in a talking, babbling world, nor yet among people who are trying to worm facts out of me; you needn’t look so frightened because you have let the cat out of the bag to a faithful old hermit like me. I shall never name his having been in England; I shall be out of temptation, for no one will ask me. Stay!” He interrupted himself abruptly. “Was it at your mother’s funeral?”

“He was with mamma when she died,” Margaret answered softly; and the room seemed, for a moment, to hold its breath.

“To be sure! To be sure! Why, some one asked me if he had not been over then, and I denied it stoutly—not many weeks ago—who could it have been? Oh! I recollect!”

He did not speak the name. Margaret’s mind leapt—she would have given much to know if her suspicion was right, if it had been Mr. Thornton who had asked. But she could not ask. There are questions that, once spoken, change the air.

A pause followed—one of those little pauses in which the very soundscape of a room asserts itself: the faint crackle of coal, the distant roll of a carriage, the soft footfall of a servant beyond the door. Then Mr. Lennox said, addressing Margaret:

“I suppose, as Mr. Bell is now acquainted with all the circumstances attending your brother’s unfortunate dilemma, I cannot do better than inform him exactly how the research into the evidence we once hoped to produce in his favour stands at present. So, if he will do me the honour to breakfast with me to-morrow, we will go over the names of these missing gentry.”

“I should like to hear all the particulars, if I may. Cannot you come here? I dare not ask you both to breakfast, though I am sure you would be welcome. But let me know all you can about Frederick, even though there may be no hope at present.”

“I have an engagement at half-past eleven. But I will certainly come if you wish it,” Mr. Lennox replied; and the afterthought of eagerness in his tone made Margaret shrink inwardly, almost wishing she had not asked so naturally.

Mr. Bell rose and began to look about for his hat, which had been moved to make room at the tea-table.

“Well!” said he. “I don’t know what Mr. Lennox is inclined to do, but I’m disposed to be moving off homewards. I’ve been a journey to-day, and journeys begin to tell upon my sixty and odd years.”

“I believe I shall stay and see my brother and sister,” said Mr. Lennox, making no movement.

A shy dread seized Margaret—quick, unreasonable, irresistible. To be left alone with him! Helstone seemed to press upon her again: the terrace, the soft southern air, the words spoken there that could not be unsaid. She could hardly help believing the scene was as present to him as to her.

“Don’t go yet, please, Mr. Bell,” she said hastily. “I want you to see Edith; and I want Edith to know you. Please!” And she laid a light, determined hand upon his arm.

He looked at her and saw the confusion stirred in her face. He sat down again, as if the touch had authority no argument could resist.

“You see how she overpowers me, Mr. Lennox,” he said, forcing a jest to give her time. “And I hope you noticed the happy choice of her expressions; she wants me to ‘see’ this cousin Edith, who, I am told, is a great beauty; but she has the honesty to change her word when she comes to me—Mrs. Lennox is to ‘know’ me. I suppose I am not much to ‘see,’ eh, Margaret?”

Margaret caught at the tone and returned it, grateful for any bridge over the awkwardness.

Mr. Lennox, watching her in the quiet black dress that made her paleness more distinct, wondered how his brother could have reported her as having lost her good looks. She was a contrast to Edith, who entered not long after—dancing, as it were, into the room in her white crape mourning, golden hair floating, all softness and glitter, the sort of brightness that seems made for candlelight and admiration.

Edith dimpled and blushed becomingly when Mr. Bell was introduced, conscious of her reputation and unwilling that even an old Oxford Fellow, from a college “nobody had ever heard of,” should refuse the proper homage. Mrs. Shaw and Captain Lennox, each in their own manner, welcomed him kindly and sincerely, winning him to like them almost in spite of himself, especially when he saw how naturally Margaret slipped into her place as if she had always belonged to this bright, easy circle—sister, daughter, helper, yet not mistress of herself.

“What a shame that we were not at home to receive you,” said Edith. “You, too, Henry! though I don’t know that we should have stayed at home for you. And for Mr. Bell! for Margaret’s Mr. Bell—”

“There is no knowing what sacrifices you would not have made,” said her brother-in-law. “Even a dinner-party! and the delight of wearing this very becoming dress.”

Edith did not know whether to frown or smile. Mr. Lennox, seeing he had driven her too near to displeasure, went on smoothly.

“Will you show your readiness to make sacrifices to-morrow morning—first by asking me to breakfast, to meet Mr. Bell, and secondly by being so kind as to order it at half-past nine, instead of at ten o’clock? I have some letters and papers that I want to show to Miss Hale and Mr. Bell.”

“I hope Mr. Bell will make our house his own during his stay in London,” said Captain Lennox. “I am only so sorry we cannot offer him a bedroom.”

“Thank you. I am much obliged to you. You would only think me a churl if you had, for I should decline it, I believe, in spite of all the temptations of such agreeable company,” Mr. Bell replied, bowing all round, and secretly congratulating himself on the neat polish of his phrase. Plain truth, he knew, would have been: he could not bear the restraint of so proper a household. Good manners, he thought with amusement, were a kind of seasoning; and he had just begun to catch the trick of them.

His self-satisfaction lasted him until he was fairly out in the street, walking side by side with Henry Lennox. Here the open air, with its harder noises—the clatter of hooves, the grind of wheels, the cries that rose and fell like brief, ragged melodies—shook other thoughts loose. He remembered Margaret’s quick look of entreaty as she begged him to stay; remembered, too, hints given long ago by an acquaintance of Lennox’s about the man’s admiration of her. A new suspicion took shape, and with it a certain protectiveness that pricked him on.

“You have known Miss Hale for a long time, I believe. How do you think her looking? She strikes me as pale and ill.”

“I thought her looking remarkably well. Perhaps not when I first came—now I think of it. But certainly, when she grew animated, she looked as well as ever I saw her do.”

“She has had a great deal to go through,” said Mr. Bell.

“Yes! I have been sorry to hear of all she has had to bear; not merely the common and universal sorrow arising from death, but all the annoyance which her father’s conduct must have caused her, and then—”

“Her father’s conduct!” Mr. Bell exclaimed, startled into sharpness. “You must have heard some wrong statement. He behaved in the most conscientious manner. He showed more resolute strength than I should ever have given him credit for formerly.”

“Perhaps I have been wrongly informed. But I have been told—by his successor in the living, a clever sensible man, and a thoroughly active clergyman—that there was no call upon Mr. Hale to do what he did; relinquish the living, and throw himself and his family on the tender mercies of private teaching in a manufacturing town. The bishop had offered him another living, it is true, but if he had come to entertain certain doubts, he could have remained where he was, and so had no occasion to resign. The truth is, these country clergymen live such isolated lives—isolated, I mean, from all intercourse with men of equal cultivation with themselves, by whose minds they might regulate their own, and discover when they were going either too fast or too slow—that they are very apt to disturb themselves with imaginary doubts as to the articles of faith, and throw up certain opportunities of doing good for very uncertain fancies of their own.”

“I differ from you. I do not think they are very apt to do as my poor friend Hale did.”

Mr. Bell felt himself chafe inwardly. The words “imaginary doubts” grated like grit between teeth.

“Perhaps I used too general an expression in saying ‘very apt.’ But certainly their lives are such as very often to produce either inordinate self-sufficiency, or a morbid state of conscience,” Mr. Lennox returned, with perfect coolness.

“You don’t meet with any self-sufficiency among the lawyers, for instance?” Mr. Bell asked, his tone hardening. “And seldom, I imagine, any cases of morbid conscience.”

His vexation made him forget his newly-practised urbanity. Mr. Lennox saw that he had annoyed his companion; and since he had spoken chiefly to fill the time while their road lay together, he was indifferent as to the side he defended. He came round quietly.

“To be sure, there is something fine in a man of Mr. Hale’s age leaving his home of twenty years, and giving up all settled habits, for an idea which was probably erroneous—but that does not matter—an untangible thought. One cannot help admiring him, with a mixture of pity in one’s admiration, something like what one feels for Don Quixote. Such a gentleman as he was, too! I shall never forget the refined and simple hospitality he showed to me that last day at Helstone.”

Mr. Bell was only half mollified. Yet he felt, in order to lull certain uneasy qualms of his own, a temptation to accept even the faintest hint of Quixotism in Hale’s conduct—anything that would make it less a stern, accusing integrity. He growled out:

“Aye! And you don’t know Milton. Such a change from Helstone! It is years since I have been at Helstone—but I’ll answer for it, it is standing there yet—every stick and every stone as it has done for the last century; while Milton! I go there every four or five years—and I was born there—yet I do assure you, I often lose my way—aye, among the very piles of warehouses that are built upon my father’s orchard.”

The London street around them rang and rasped, a restless iron music, and Mr. Bell thought of Milton’s deeper roar—how a town’s sound could swallow up a man’s memories until he needed landmarks for his own childhood.

“Do we part here? Well, good-night, sir; I suppose we shall meet in Harley Street to-morrow morning.”

The talk of Helstone, lightly dropped by Mr. Lennox in the clear daylight of yesterday, worked its way into Mr. Bell’s waking thoughts and, once the candles were out, took full possession of his sleep. In his dream he was young again—not young in the vague way of wishes, but with the particular vigour of a man whose limbs remember how to spring and whose lungs drink air as if it were wine. He was tutor once more in the old college, and the long vacation had come round, and he was staying with his friend newly married—the proud husband, the happy Vicar of Helstone.

It was not the Helstone of maps, measured by miles, but the Helstone of sense, measured by what the heart can bear. They went out over the lanes where the hedge-rows still held last year’s sweetness; there were brooks that talked all at once—water chuckling over pebbles, reed-stems clicking together, a blackbird lifting the whole phrase of the morning into song. Those sounds swam along the buoyant air, and in the dream they were as necessary as breath. They leaped—impossibly—over the babbling water, and for whole, suspended days it seemed they hung in the air, as if gravity had been set aside for friendship and youth. Time and space had no authority; nothing existed except the feeling of being there.

Yet everything looked so exact. The trees were gorgeously heavy with autumn leaf, each bough offering its own tint of russet and gold. Warm odours came up, not as a general “country smell,” but in their separate, homely truths—the bruised mint under a boot-heel, the damp iron-sweetness of turned earth, the faint pepper of crushed fern, the honeyed breath of late flowers kept back by the churchyard wall. Indoors, too, the dream insisted on household particulars. The young wife moved through the rooms with that very mixture Mr. Bell remembered from life—a quick, half-irritated sense of her position as to wealth, and, beneath it, an honest pride in her handsome, devoted husband. She lifted lids, directed servants, smelt at a jug of milk as if her nose were judge and jury, and cut bread with a firmness that had more meaning than many speeches. A joint hissed faintly before the fire; some herb—sage, perhaps—gave out a green, clean bitterness when her fingers tore it. Even the small noises of the house were there: a spoon against a basin, the soft thud of a loaf set down, the stir of skirts in a passage. It was a world made credible by its sounds and scents.

So like life it was, that when he woke, his present life turned unreal, as if the true thing had been snatched away and this were only the thin, hard copy.

Where was he? In the close, handsomely furnished room of a London hotel, where carpets drank up footfalls and the air had that flat, over-warmed smell of city lodging—coal, beeswax, and yesterday’s extinguished lamp. The silence was not the country’s listening hush, full of distant water and birds, but the deadened quiet of thick walls meant to keep out other people’s lives. A carriage rolled somewhere far off with a rasping, iron-edged rumble, and then it was swallowed again. The noise did not belong to any season; it belonged only to commerce.

And those who had been near him an instant ago—those voices, those hands that had touched him with the ease of the familiar—where were they? Dead. Buried. Gone beyond any calling back, as far as earth’s “for evermore” could reach. He was an old man—so lately exultant in the full strength of manhood—and the utter loneliness of it came down on him like a weight on the chest. He got up hastily, as if movement could shake off grief, and dressed in a hurry, trying to forget what would not be forgotten, because it was not a thought but a loss.

By the time he reached Harley Street for breakfast, his face had settled into its ordinary lines; but the dream had left a soreness behind the eyes, and something in him kept listening for the country sounds that were not there. Even at table, the clink of china and the murmur of voices felt sharp and purposeless; there was no brook’s persuasion in them, no leaf’s soft answer.

Mr. Lennox had his papers ready, and his manner was what it always was—regulated, methodical, professional. He went through details with a clearness that would have been admirable if it had been about an estate, or a lease, or any matter in which words could repair what was wrong. But these words were only nets drawn tighter.

Mr. Bell sat and tried to attend. He could not. He saw, instead, Margaret’s eyes as she listened—how they widened at one statement, how her lips lost their colour at another. The lawyer’s facts fell one by one, like stones dropped into a well, and with each fall it seemed that some morsel of ground on which she had been standing gave way and disappeared. This, then that—each little hope extinguished with a relentless minuteness. Mr. Lennox’s voice, so trained to be even, softened almost in spite of itself as he drew nearer to the extinction of the last possibility.

It was not that Margaret had not foreseen the result. She had known what was likely—she had lived with knowledge as one lives with hunger, endured rather than cured. But to have every separate disappointment named, and proved, and placed in order—this was like being made to taste drop by drop the bitterness of something one had already swallowed. At last the composure that had held her gave way, and tears gathered and fell, quietly at first, then with that helplessness that comes when the heart has been pressed too long.

Mr. Lennox stopped reading. “I had better not go on,” he said, and the concern in his voice was real.

“It was a foolish proposal of mine.” He paused, then spoke again with an instinctive gentleness. “Lieutenant Hale—” and even that title, belonging to the service from which Frederick had been so harshly expelled, went through Margaret like a touch meant to soothe.

“Lieutenant Hale is happy now; more secure in fortune and future prospects than he could ever have been in the navy; and has, doubtless, adopted his wife’s country as his own.”

“That is it,” said Margaret. The words came out as if she had been holding them down. “It seems so selfish in me to regret it,” she added, trying to smile through tears that would not be reasoned with; “and yet he is lost to me, and I am so lonely.”

Mr. Lennox turned over his papers. A thought crossed him—quick, private, and unspoken—that he wished himself as rich and prosperous as he believed he would be some day; as if wealth could give him the right to comfort where now he could only offer legal statements and restrained pity. Mr. Bell blew his nose with unnecessary vigour, which was the only way he knew to make a noise in place of speech; otherwise he, too, kept silence.

In a minute or two Margaret had gathered herself again, as people do who have long practice in making their own hearts behave. She thanked Mr. Lennox very courteously for his trouble—more courteously, indeed, because she was aware that her tears might make him believe he had inflicted needless pain. Yet it was pain she would not have spared herself; it was the pain of certainty, and certainty, however cruel, had its own stern mercy.

Mr. Bell rose to go. He came up to her, fumbling with his gloves in that awkwardness which often attends real feeling in an old man who dislikes making a scene.

“Margaret!” said he. “I am going down to Helstone to-morrow, to look at the old place. Would you like to come with me? Or would it give you too much pain? Speak out—don’t be afraid.”

“Oh, Mr. Bell,” she said; and could say no more. But she took his old, gouty hand and kissed it, as if gratitude had no other language.

“Come, come; that’s enough,” he returned, reddening and half-angry at his own emotion. “I suppose your aunt Shaw will trust you with me. We’ll go to-morrow morning, and we shall get there about two o’clock, I fancy. We’ll take a snack, and order dinner at the little inn—the Lennard Arms, it used to be—and go and get an appetite in the forest. Can you stand it, Margaret? It will be a trial, I know, to both of us, but it will be a pleasure to me, at least. And there we’ll dine—it will be but doe-venison, if we can get it at all—and then I’ll take my nap, while you go out and see old friends. I’ll give you back safe and sound, barring railway accidents, and I’ll insure your life for a thousand pounds before starting, which may be some comfort to your relations; but otherwise, I’ll bring you back to Mrs. Shaw by lunch time on Friday. So, if you say yes, I’ll just go upstairs and propose it.”

His speech ran on with that bluff, half-jesting practicality behind which tenderness hid itself. Yet in the midst of it Margaret caught at the words as at a rope thrown to one who is drowning: Helstone. The very name seemed to carry with it not only sights and faces, but the remembered sound of her father’s voice in its own cadence, the dialect-tinge he had never quite lost, the country vowels that London did not speak. A place could hold a language in its hedges and lanes; it could keep safe, for a while, what the town wore away.

“It’s no use my trying to say how much I shall like it,” she said, tears still shining on her lashes.

“Well, then, prove your gratitude by keeping those fountains of yours dry for the next two days. If you don’t, I shall feel queer myself about the lachrymal ducts, and I don’t like that.”

“I won’t cry a drop,” said Margaret, winking hard to shake the tears away and forcing a smile into shape.

“There’s my good girl. Then we’ll go upstairs and settle it all.”

Margaret was in a state of almost trembling eagerness while Mr. Bell discussed his plan with Mrs. Shaw. Her aunt, startled at first, then doubtful and perplexed, shifted from objection to objection—not out of hardness, but from that anxious regard for propriety which, in her mind, stood guard like a butler at every door. Was it right? Was it proper? Would it look well? She could not settle it to her own satisfaction. Mr. Bell, rougher and more decisive, pressed his point with the kind of force that is less argument than momentum, as if to carry scruples along before they had time to fasten themselves.

In the end Mrs. Shaw yielded—more to Mr. Bell’s hearty insistence and Margaret’s quiet, hungry longing than to her own conviction. And even then she did not feel decision enough to approve until the thing was done and safely over in imagination: until she could picture Margaret returning unhurt and composed, and hear herself say, with the comfortable air of one who had foreseen it all, that she was sure it had been a very kind thought of Mr. Bell’s, and just what she herself had been wishing for Margaret—giving her the very change she required after all the anxious time she had had.

Margaret had been ready long before the hour, as if haste could keep sorrow from overtaking her. There was time enough, even with her cloak folded and her gloves drawn on, to let the tears come—small, quiet drops that she brushed away before any eye could witness them; and then, when footsteps sounded in the passage, to lift her face into brightness as one lifts a lamp against dark.

Her last fear was the old, nervous fear of being too late, of missing the train—as though the world might punish her by leaving her stranded between one life and another. But they were in time. When she found herself seated opposite Mr. Bell, the carriage already loosening its hold on the station, she breathed as if the tightest hand had been taken off her chest.

They flew southward past the stations she had once counted with impatience, and now watched as a kind of rosary. The country unrolled itself in warm light, the air clear as strained broth, and the villages lay as if steeped—tiled roofs ruddy as baked clay, not the northern slate that always seemed to drink up colour and give none back. Pigeons hovered above peaked gables and, settling, ruffled their neck-feathers until each glossy fibre caught the sun. Even the stations had a different temper: no sharp bustle, no clanging hurry, no pressed faces and elbows; only here and there a man lounging, hands in pockets, listening to the quiet with the patient absorption of someone for whom sound was an element, not an irritant. In the North, Margaret remembered, the very rails had seemed to speak—metal on metal, shriek and hammer and the hard staccato of industry; here the wheels ran as if on softer nerves, and the pauses between noises were long enough to be inhabited.

She let herself drift into that half-waking dream where the fields looked like old poems remembered—farms lying golden and still, heat trembling above them like a veil, each hedge-row a line of script. Then the voice in the carriage, the guard’s cry, the decisive slowing: it was the place where they must leave the train and take a fly to Helstone.

At once the sweetness sharpened. Every mile after that was laden, as a kitchen is laden when preserves are opened—scents that are pleasure and pain together, because they are the past made physical. She would not have spared herself one association; yet each one made her heart cry out for days that could not be called back. The last time she had gone along this road, the sky had been dim and she herself dimmer, but her father and mother had been beside her—human warmth in the cold season. Now the road was drenched in summer sunlight, and the familiar trees stood in their old glory, as if nature had never learned bereavement. It hurt her that the world could look so unchanged.

Mr. Bell, knowing enough not to thrust words where they would bruise, let the silence keep her company.

They drove up to the Lennard Arms, half farm-house, half inn, set a little apart from the road with the confident air of one who need not beg custom. The building faced the village green. Before it stood an immemorial lime-tree with a bench round its girth; somewhere within the thickness of its leaves hung the grim escutcheon of the Lennards, like an old family story that refused to be forgotten. The door stood open, but no one hurried to greet them. When the landlady appeared at last—so quietly that they might indeed have carried off half the house—she welcomed them as if they were expected guests, and made her apology at once.

“It’s hay-time,” she said, not at all ashamed, but full of that competent pride by which country women rule the seasons. “The men’s provisions had to be sent a-field. I’ve been packing the baskets and never heard your wheels, not on the turf road.”

Then a bar of sunshine slipped across Margaret’s face, and Mrs. Purkis’s eyes widened as if she had seen a familiar saint step down from a painted glass.

“Why, bless me! It’s Miss Hale, Jenny!” she cried, running to the door to call her daughter. “Come here, come directly—it’s Miss Hale!”

And she took Margaret’s hand with motherly fondness, as though three years were nothing beside village memory.

“And how are you all? How’s the Vicar and Miss Dixon? The Vicar above all! God bless him! We’ve never ceased to be sorry he left.”

Margaret’s throat closed. She touched the deep black of her mourning, and the one word she could get out was the word that held her whole childhood.

“Papa.”

Mrs. Purkis turned sharply to Mr. Bell, dread entering her face like a shadow crossing a threshold.

“Surely, sir—it’s never so? There was a gentleman here in the spring—maybe last winter—told us a deal of Mr. Hale and Miss Margaret; and he said Mrs. Hale was gone, poor lady. But never a word of the Vicar being ailing!”

“It is so,” Mr. Bell said gently. “He died quite suddenly, when on a visit to me at Oxford. He was a good man, Mrs. Purkis, and many of us might be thankful for as calm an end. Come, Margaret, my dear. He was my oldest friend, and she’s my god-daughter. We thought we’d come down and see the old place; and I know you can give us comfortable rooms and a capital dinner. You don’t remember me, I see, but my name is Bell. Once or twice, when the parsonage was full, I’ve slept here—and tasted your good ale.”

“To be sure!” Mrs. Purkis exclaimed, half laughing at herself through the shock. “I ask your pardon, sir, but you see I was taken up with Miss Hale. Let me show you to a room, Miss Margaret, where you can take off your bonnet and wash your face. It’s only this morning I plunged some fresh-gathered roses head downward in the water-jug—for thought I, perhaps someone will be coming, and there’s nothing so sweet as spring-water scented by a musk rose or two. To think of the Vicar being dead! Well—to be sure, we must all die; only that gentleman said he was quite picking up after his trouble about Mrs. Hale’s death.”

Mr. Bell nodded to her with the air of a man who had already begun to plan comfort as a kind of medicine.

“Come down to me, Mrs. Purkis, when you’ve seen to Miss Hale. I want a consultation about dinner.”

In the little bedchamber, the casement window was almost filled by rose and vine; the green pressed close as if eager to enter. Margaret pushed the branches aside, and leaning out could see, above the trees, the tops of the parsonage chimneys—faint lines she knew by heart, like a tune whose ending one can always anticipate.

“Aye,” Mrs. Purkis said, smoothing the bed and sending Jenny for towels that smelled of lavender and sun, “times is changed, miss. Our new Vicar has seven children, and he’s building a nursery ready for more, just where the arbour and tool-house used to be. He’s had new grates put in, and a plate-glass window in the drawing-room. He and his wife are stirring people, and have done a deal of good—at least they say it’s doing good; if it were not, I should call it turning things upside down for very little purpose.

“The new Vicar is a teetotaller, miss, and a magistrate; and his wife has a deal of receipts for economical cooking, and is for making bread without yeast; and they both talk so much, and both at a time, that they knock one down as it were. He’ll be after the men’s cans in the hay-field, and peeping in; and then there’ll be an ado because it’s not ginger-beer, but I can’t help it. My mother and my grandmother before me sent good malt liquor to hay-makers, and took salts and senna when anything ailed them; and I must e’en go on in their ways, though Mrs. Hepworth does want to give me comfits instead of medicine—which, as she says, is a deal pleasanter, only I’ve no faith in it. But I must go, miss—though I’m wanting to hear many a thing. I’ll come back to you before long.”

Downstairs, Mr. Bell had arranged a rustic luncheon with a scholar’s relish for honest provisions: strawberries—still warm at their hearts from the field—set beside a bowl of thick cream; a loaf of brown bread, its crust dark and faintly sweet; and a jug of milk. A Stilton stood by for his own private consolation, and a bottle of port that caught the light like old rubies. Margaret ate because she must, but the strawberries, bursting cool and fragrant, seemed to carry within them the very taste of Helstone summers; it was like swallowing a memory.

Afterwards they went out to walk, and for a moment stood uncertain, as people do when every path tempts with its own history.

“Shall we go past the vicarage?” Mr. Bell asked.

“No—not yet. We will go this way, and make a round so as to come back by it,” Margaret answered, as if delaying could soften the blow.

Here and there changes pricked her: old trees felled the previous autumn, a rough cottage disappeared, another built in its place, tidier and more respectable, but lacking that crooked, familiar look of endurance. She grieved over each absence like a friend not met at the usual door. They came to the spot where she and Mr. Lennox had once sketched. The white, lightning-scarred trunk of the venerable beech—where they had sat among its roots—was gone; the old man who had lived in the ruinous cottage was dead; the cottage itself had been pulled down. In its stead there was a small garden, primly fenced, on the very ground that had once been shaded.

“I did not think I had been so old,” Margaret said at last, and turned away with a sigh that seemed to come from deeper than her lungs.

“Yes,” Mr. Bell replied. “It’s the first changes among familiar things that make such a mystery of time to the young. Afterwards we lose the sense of the mysterious. I take changes as a matter of course. The instability of all human things is familiar to me; to you it is new and oppressive.”

“Let us go on to see little Susan,” Margaret said, drawing him up a grassy roadway that led under the shadow of a forest glade.

“With all my heart—though I’ve not an idea who little Susan may be. But I have a kindness for all Susans, for simple Susan’s sake.”

“My little Susan was disappointed when I left without wishing her good-bye,” Margaret said. “It has been on my conscience ever since. I gave her pain which a little more exertion might have prevented. But it is a long way. Are you sure you will not be tired?”

“Quite sure—that is, if you don’t walk so fast. Here there are no views that can give one an excuse for stopping to take breath. You would think it romantic to be walking with a person ‘fat and scant o’ breath’ if I were Hamlet, Prince of Denmark. Have compassion on my infirmities for his sake.”

“I will walk slower for your own sake. I like you twenty times better than Hamlet.”

“On the principle that a living ass is better than a dead lion?”

“Perhaps so. I don’t analyse my feelings.”

“I’m content to take your liking me without examining too curiously into the materials it’s made of. Only we need not walk at a snail’s pace.”

“Very well. Walk at your own pace, and I will follow. Or stop still and meditate, like the Hamlet you compare yourself to, if I go too fast.”

“Thank you. But as my mother has not murdered my father, and afterwards married my uncle, I shouldn’t know what to think about—unless it were balancing the chances of our having a well-cooked dinner or not. What do you think?”

“I am in good hopes. She used to be considered a famous cook, as far as Helstone opinion went.”

“But have you considered the distraction of mind produced by all this haymaking?”

Margaret felt the tenderness beneath his levity. He was trying to keep her from turning too fiercely back upon the past; yet she would have chosen silence, if she had not known it ungrateful to wish him away.

They reached the cottage where Susan’s widowed mother lived. Susan was not there; she had gone to the parochial school. Margaret’s face fell before she could prevent it, and the poor woman read it and began apologising, as if education were an offence.

“Oh, it is quite right,” Margaret said quickly. “I am very glad to hear it. I might have thought of it. Only she used to stop at home with you.”

“Yes, she did; and I miss her sadly,” the mother answered, hands busy with some small task as if motion could keep grief from settling. “I used to teach her what little I knew at nights. It were not much, to be sure. But she were getting such a handy girl, that I miss her sore. But she’s a deal above me in learning now.” And she sighed—part pride, part loneliness.

“I’m all wrong,” growled Mr. Bell. “Don’t mind what I say. I’m a hundred years behind the world. But I should say the child was getting a better and simpler and more natural education stopping at home, helping her mother, and learning to read a chapter in the New Testament every night by her side, than from all the schooling under the sun.”

Margaret did not wish the discussion to swell in front of the woman. She turned instead, seeking safer ground.

“How is old Betty Barnes?”

“I don’t know,” the woman replied shortly. “We’se not friends.”

“Why not?” Margaret asked, remembering how she had once been the village peacemaker.

“She stole my cat.”

“Did she know it was yours?”

“I don’t know. I reckon not.”

“Well—could not you get it back again when you told her it was yours?”

“No. For she’d burnt it.”

“Burnt it!” both Margaret and Mr. Bell cried.

“Roasted it,” the woman corrected, as if that made it less terrible.

It did not. By questioning—gentle at first, then urgent—Margaret drew out the story: Betty Barnes, led by a gipsy fortune-teller to lend her husband’s Sunday clothes on promise of their return before he should miss them, became frantic when they did not come. In her fear of her husband’s anger she resorted to an old savage charm—the belief that the cries of a cat, boiled or roasted alive, could compel the powers of darkness to bring about the executioner’s wishes. The woman telling it believed in it; her indignation lay not in the horror, but in the injustice that her own cat had been chosen.

Margaret tried to reason with her, tried to lead her through the chain of plain facts, so that the truth might emerge like a clear broth from muddied water; but though the woman would admit each separate circumstance, she could not—or would not—draw them together. In the end she only repeated, stubborn and bewildered, that it was cruel—very cruel indeed—but that there was nothing like it for getting what one wished; she had heard it all her life. Margaret left her, sick at heart, the sunlight in the trees suddenly seeming a mockery.

“You are a good girl not to triumph over me,” Mr. Bell said when they were out of earshot.

“How? What do you mean?”

“I own I am wrong about schooling. Anything rather than have that child brought up in such practical paganism.”

“Oh—I remember. Poor little Susan! I must go and see her. Would you mind calling at the school?”

“Not a bit. I am curious to see something of the teaching she is to receive.”

They went on with fewer words. The path led them through bosky dells where leaves stirred in soft harmonies, and birds called from depth to depth; the place had an old, balanced sound, as if it knew how to keep peace in its own acoustic boundaries. Yet even this could not charm away the shock. Margaret could not forget the flat manner in which cruelty had been recounted—the want of imagination that meant a want of sympathy; the deadening of feeling that came, not from loud factory din, but from a lexicon of superstition that made suffering into a tool.

As they emerged from the forest onto the village green where the school stood, the noise of children rose like a hive—warm, busy, human. The door stood wide open. They entered. A brisk lady in black seemed to be everywhere at once—here correcting, there arranging, there smiling—her steps and voice making quick, decisive punctuation in the murmur. She welcomed them with the air of a hostess, and Margaret remembered, with an inward pang, how her own mother had once received visitors at the school—more softly, more languidly, as if she too belonged to the quiet of the place.

Margaret knew at once this was the present Vicar’s wife. She would have drawn back had she been able, but she conquered the impulse and advanced. Bright glances of recognition met her; half-smothered whispers ran: “It’s Miss Hale.” The name reached Mrs. Hepworth, and her manner warmed—yet, to Margaret’s discomfort, warmed with something that felt like condescension.

The lady held out her hand to Mr. Bell.

“Your father, I presume, Miss Hale. I see it by the likeness. I am sure I am very glad to see you, sir, and so will the Vicar be.”

Margaret explained, stammering, and spoke of her father’s death. Even as she did so, she wondered how her father could ever have borne to revisit Helstone, had he come under such an assumption. She scarcely heard Mrs. Hepworth’s words in response; Mr. Bell answered for her, while Margaret’s eyes searched for old faces.

“Ah!” Mrs. Hepworth exclaimed suddenly, turning with energetic kindness. “I see you would like to take a class, Miss Hale. I know it by myself. First class—stand up for a parsing lesson with Miss Hale.”

Margaret, who had come with a sentimental hunger, not an inspecting mind, felt herself caught; but the sight of the eager faces—children her father had baptised—went through her like a touch. She sat down, took the book, and for a moment forgot herself in tracing the changed outlines of the girls’ faces. Susan’s hand found hers; Margaret held it for a minute or two, secretly, while the class searched for their places. Meanwhile Mrs. Hepworth, as near as a lady could, kept Mr. Bell by the button and poured out an explanation of the Phonetic system, including a conversation she had had with the Inspector, as though the Inspector’s words were a kind of scripture.

Margaret bent over the page. The hum of voices, the scrape of shoes, the little coughs and whispers, the rustle of paper—sounds that had once been the daily music of her life—brought old times up around her until her eyes filled and she could scarcely see the print.

Then there was a pause. A girl stumbled over the word “a,” uncertain what to call it.

“A—an indefinite article,” Margaret said gently, as one speaks from habit.

“I beg your pardon,” said Mrs. Hepworth, all attention at once. “But we are taught by Mr. Milsome to call ‘a’ an—who can remember?”

“An adjective absolute,” cried half-a-dozen voices together.

Margaret sat abashed, feeling suddenly ignorant in the very place that had once been her ground. The children knew more than she did. Mr. Bell turned away and smiled.

Margaret spoke no more through the lesson. When it ended, she went quietly among a few old favourites and talked to them. They were growing out of childhood into large, awkward girlhood; and just as their faces altered and their voices deepened, so she too was fading from their recollection with her three years’ absence. She was glad to have seen them; yet sadness threaded itself through the pleasure, as a darker spice sometimes runs through a sweet dish and changes its whole flavour.

School over, the summer afternoon was still young. Mrs. Hepworth proposed that Margaret and Mr. Bell should accompany her to the parsonage and see—she almost said “improvements,” but substituted “alterations,” with a momentary caution.

Margaret did not care to see alterations that jarred against her memory; yet she longed to stand once more in the old place, even though she trembled for the pain she knew would be there.

In truth the parsonage was so altered inside and out that the pain was less keen than she had feared. It was not the same place, and that very difference blunted the blow. The garden—once so trim that even a stray rose-leaf seemed a disorder—was strewn with children’s things: a bag of marbles, a hoop, a straw-hat jammed down upon a rose-tree as if the living branch were only a peg, crushing a long tender stem loaded with flowers that in former days would have been trained as carefully as one tends a prized herb. The little square matted hall was filled with the same signs—merry, healthy rough childhood, loud in presence even when silent.

“Ah!” Mrs. Hepworth said, smiling with brisk apology, “you must excuse this untidiness, Miss Hale. When the nursery is finished I shall insist upon a little order. We are building a nursery out of your room, I believe. How did you manage, Miss Hale, without a nursery?”

“We were but two,” Margaret answered. “You have many children, I presume?”

“Seven. Look here! we are throwing out a window to the road on this side. Mr. Hepworth is spending an immense deal of money on this house; but really it was scarcely habitable when we came—for so large a family as ours, I mean, of course.”

Every room had been changed. The greatest change of all was in what had once been Mr. Hale’s study, where green gloom and delicious quiet had helped his meditative habit—perhaps had made him, as Margaret sometimes thought, fitter for thought than action. Now a new window opened onto the road. Mrs. Hepworth pointed out its advantages with satisfaction: from it her husband could see the wandering sheep of his flock straggling toward the tempting beer-house, unobserved as they hoped, but not unobserved in reality. The active Vicar kept his eye on the road even while composing his most orthodox sermons; hat and stick hung ready to snatch up before he sallied forth after parishioners, who needed quick legs if they hoped to take refuge in the “Jolly Forester” before the teetotal magistrate caught them.

The household, Margaret saw, was brisk and loud-talking, kind-hearted, and not troubled with much delicacy of perception. Mr. Bell, piqued by Mrs. Hepworth’s exultation in the “superior sense” of each change, expressed admiration with such pointed politeness that Margaret feared the lady must perceive he was laughing at her. But no: she took it all in perfect good faith.

As they walked slowly back to the inn, Margaret could not help speaking.

“Don’t scold, Margaret,” Mr. Bell said at once, before she had done. “It was all because of you. If she had not shown you every change with such evident exultation, I could have behaved well. But if you must go on preaching, keep it till after dinner, when it will send me to sleep and help my digestion.”

They were both tired; Margaret more than she admitted even to herself. She had meant to ramble again among the woods and fields that lay so close to the home of her childhood, but her limbs were heavy and her spirit heavier. And somehow Helstone had not been all—had not been exactly—what she had expected. There was change everywhere: slight, but pervading, like a new seasoning that alters an old dish so that you can taste the difference even when you cannot name it.

Households had changed by absence, death, marriage, by the quiet, continual turning of days and months and years that carry us from childhood to youth, through manhood to age, until at last we drop like fruit—fully ripe—into the patient earth.
