Places had changed too: a tree gone here, a bough cut there, letting in a long ray of light where once there had been shade; a road trimmed and narrowed; the green straggling pathway beside it enclosed and cultivated. A great improvement, people said. Margaret only sighed for the old picturesqueness—the old gloom—the grassy wayside. She sat by the window on the little settle, watching the gathering shades of night soften the outlines of the green. The evening sounds came one by one—the far-off call across the fields, the nearer footfall, the hush that settled when work ceased—and the quiet seemed to belong to her childhood more faithfully than any wall did.

Mr. Bell slept soundly after his unusual exercise. At last he was roused by the tea-tray, brought in by a flushed country-girl who had plainly found variety from waiting by helping in the hay-field that day; and the scent of warm leaves and crushed grass clung to her as she moved, as if summer itself had entered with the crockery.

Dixon came back from Milton at the very hour when Margaret’s days were beginning to taste of sameness, and, with her return, the past returned too—wrapped in lint and lavender, tied up with pins, and thrust into the drawers of the present as if it belonged there.

She stepped into her old place as though she had never left it, bringing with her a whole market-basket of tidings, each laid in as carefully as eggs in straw. Milton, it appeared, had not stood still because Margaret had gone away. It had married and eaten and talked, and set a sharp edge on its tongues, and Dixon’s were the sharpest of all.

Martha, she said, had gone to live with Miss Thornton—now Mrs. Thornton by marriage—“and such a wedding breakfast, Miss! I could tell by the very descriptions what was on the table. They’d have had cold fowls in jelly, and hams glazed till you could see your face in them, and a great cake cut up as if it were a sacrament.” Dixon spoke as one who had never forgiven strangers for dining without her. “And the dresses! And the bridesmaids! Folks said it was over-grand, considering Mr. Thornton had lost money by the strike, and had to pay for contracts failing. But rich folks in Milton, Miss, they’ll spend on show as if the clatter of knives and forks could drown out bad luck.”

Then she launched into the sale of furniture—those old, beloved pieces she had once counted on as if they were an inheritance of her own. They had fetched little, which Dixon called a shame, “seeing how Milton people boast of their wealth—yet they’ll haggle like women at a butter-stall.” Mrs. Thornton had come and taken “two or three bargains,” and Mr. Thornton, coming the next day, had bid against himself—so eager, so unguarded, so unlike the cold master Dixon liked to criticise—that the bystanders had laughed outright at it.

“So as I observed, Miss, it made things even. If his mother paid too little, he paid too much.”

Margaret listened, and the very names—Milton, Thornton—were like a spice jar opened for a moment: a sudden sharpness in the air, a pricking in the memory. Dixon, full of small domestic economics and great social judgments, did not understand that Margaret took in these scraps as one takes in a scent that has been lost for months, and cannot help following it through corridors of thought.

Mr. Bell, Dixon went on, had sent endless directions about his books. There was no pleasing him. He wanted this packed so, that wrapped thus, that labelled with an exactitude Dixon thought folly.

“There’s no understanding gentlemen, Miss, when they begin to fret about their paper and print. If he’d been there himself it would have been plain enough; but letters always were and always will be more puzzling than they’re worth.”

Of the Higginses she had almost nothing; her mind slipped away from that neighbourhood of her life as if it were greasy ground she did not care to step on. Nicholas, she believed, was well. He had come more than once to ask after Miss Margaret—the only person, Dixon said, who ever did ask, “except once Mr. Thornton.”

“And Mary?” Margaret asked, though she knew Dixon’s tone before the answer came.

“Oh! Mary’s well enough. A great stout slatternly thing, Miss! And I did hear—unless it was a dream, though it would be strange if I dreamt of such people—that she’d gone to work at Mr. Thornton’s mill, because her father wished her to know how to cook. As if mill-work taught a girl the difference between a clear broth and dish-water!”

The tale had indeed the ill-jointed look of a dream, and Margaret said as much. Yet she caught at it, because it proved that in Milton even the roughest lives had begun to turn, however clumsily, towards knowledge and home; that hunger there had not been only for bread, but for the skill of making bread good.

And it was pleasant—however Dixon shrank from it—to have someone near who could speak of Milton at all. Margaret found herself drawing Dixon on, as if by making the place vivid in talk she could make it nearer to being reached again in fact. But Dixon, for all her gossip, would rather cast that part of her history into shadow; she was fonder of telling over Mr. Bell’s sayings, and of shaping them into her own firm notion that he intended to make Margaret his heiress.

She watched Margaret as she brushed out her hair, or folded her gowns, as if a fortune might drop from a curl or a hem.

But Margaret gave her no hold. She would not answer insinuating questions, however disguised as prophecy. It was not that she despised the idea of wealth; she had learned too well how money could mean warmth and medicine and peace. Yet to be spoken of as an heiress, to be weighed and measured by what might be left her, had a taste in it like tin—sharp, lingering, unwelcome.

All the while, beneath the smooth hours, Margaret had a longing that would not shape itself into a clear thought: she wanted to hear that Mr. Bell had gone to Milton.

It had been understood between them—at Helstone, under that sunny leisure which had made even grave matters seem light—that the explanation she desired should be given to Mr. Thornton only by word of mouth, and even then should not be pressed upon him. Mr. Bell had taken that task upon himself, half in kindness, half in his own careless justice; and Margaret, though she would not confess hope even to herself, found each letter of his an occasion of secret listening.

Mr. Bell was no great correspondent. He wrote when the humour took him, and whether he sent many pages or only a line, Margaret always unfolded his notes with the faint expectation that some mention of Milton would fall out like a pressed flower from between the leaves.

But he said nothing—nothing of going there, nothing of seeing Thornton, nothing of clearing away the strange fog that had settled on Margaret’s life. She would put away the letter with a small disappointment that had no right, and yet was there.

Well—she must be patient. Sooner or later the mists would lift.

Yet even his letters were altered. They were short and complaining. Sometimes there was a bitterness in them that jarred like a wrong note in familiar music. Mr. Bell did not look forward; he regretted backward. He seemed tired of the present, as if the very air of Oxford had grown close to him.

Margaret began to fear he was ill. Once she asked outright after his health; and he answered by return with a little snappish jest—that there was an old-fashioned complaint called the spleen, and that he was suffering from it, and it was for her to decide whether it lay in mind or body; but he wished, he said, to grumble without being compelled to send a bulletin each time.

After that she asked no more.

One day Edith, letting slip a fragment of talk from when Mr. Bell had last been in London, planted a new idea in Margaret’s mind so suddenly that it was like the striking of a match in a dim room: Mr. Bell had half thought of taking her to Cadiz in the autumn—to see Frederick and his new wife, and to hear from Frederick himself the truth about the mutiny.

Margaret questioned Edith until Edith, tired and half wounded, protested there was nothing more. Mr. Bell had said he always went somewhere in the long vacation; why not Spain as well as anywhere? He wanted, perhaps, to hear with his own ears what Frederick had to say, and it would be a good opportunity for Margaret to become acquainted with her sister-in-law. That was all.

But to Margaret it was not all. Spain stood in her imagination like a bright dish set at the far end of a long table—exotic, sun-warmed, full of unknown flavour; an outlet from the monotony that had begun to lie on her days like over-boiled starch. It was a mere castle in the air, a Château en Espagne indeed; yet the thought of it delighted her as if she could already hear foreign streets, and smell garlic and oranges, and taste salt air on a tongue that had known only London’s soot.

Edith did not share this quickening of spirits. Edith was in the mood that made any pleasure taken elsewhere feel like treachery.

She began to cry—because she had nothing else particular to do, and because her own feelings always seemed to her to deserve immediate ceremony—and said she knew she cared far more for Margaret than Margaret did for her.

Margaret soothed her as best she could. She did not say, “It is not you I would leave, but myself,” because Edith would have heard only the leaving. So Margaret kept her gladness shut up, as one keeps a fragrant spice from someone who would call it too strong.

Only when Dixon came to dress her for dinner did Margaret allow herself the harmless luxury of speaking it aloud.

“Dixon,” she said, “should you not like to see Master Frederick and his new wife—very much indeed?”

Dixon’s face stiffened with a pious apprehension that had always in it a relish of drama.

“She’s a Papist, Miss, isn’t she?”

Margaret hesitated the smallest moment—then, with a recollected dampness of feeling, answered, “I believe—oh yes, certainly.”

“And they live in a Popish country?”

“Yes.”

“Then I’m afraid I must say my soul is dearer to me than even Master Frederick—his own dear self. I should be in perpetual terror, Miss, lest I should be converted.”

Margaret could not help smiling a little.

“Oh. I do not know that I am going. And if I go, I am not such a fine lady as to be unable to travel without you. No, dear old Dixon—you shall have a long holiday if we go. But I’m afraid it is a long ‘if.’”

Dixon did not like the speech. Margaret’s way of saying “dear old” to those she loved was meant as warmth; but Dixon, not much past fifty and holding herself still in her prime, winced as if Margaret had dusted her with flour and called it snow. Besides, she did not enjoy being taken at her word. Under all her terror of priests and Popish mysteries there lurked a keen curiosity—about Spain, and the Inquisition, and the strange rites she had heard whispered of, as children whisper of ghosts.

Clearing her throat, as if negotiation were a kind of moral labour, she asked whether, if she took care never to see a priest, nor to enter one of their churches, there would really be so much danger of conversion. Master Frederick had “gone over” unaccountably, to be sure.

“I fancy it was love,” Margaret said, and sighed, “that first predisposed him to conversion.”

“Indeed, Miss!” Dixon replied, with a sudden solemnity, as if love were a contagion worse than Catholicism. “Well! I can preserve myself from priests and from churches; but love steals in unawares. I think it’s as well I should not go.”

Margaret laughed a little more openly then; and yet she was afraid of letting her thoughts dwell too long on Spain, for fear the bright picture should sharpen the greyness of the actual day. Still, even a fancied journey drew her mind away from that other restless desire—to have everything explained to Mr. Thornton.

Mr. Bell, for the present, seemed fixed at Oxford. He did not speak of Milton, nor appear to have any immediate purpose of going there. Something like a restraint lay upon Margaret too, preventing her from asking him directly, or even alluding again to any such visit. She did not feel free to mention what Edith had said about Spain; it might have been no more than five minutes’ fancy in Mr. Bell’s mind. He had not named it at Helstone during that long, sunlit day; perhaps it had arisen later and would disappear again.

Yet, if true—what a bright outlet it would be from the present life, which was beginning to fall upon her with a sameness almost audible.

For Margaret had come to notice the sounds of the house as one notices the ticking of a clock in sickness. In Edith’s drawing-room everything was soft-footed—carpets swallowing steps, servants trained to make themselves noiseless, curtains shutting out street-cries. The hush was meant for comfort, but it could be oppressive: a quiet so complete that every small discord—an impatient tapping, a child’s shriek—rang as if in a church.

One of the few keen pleasures she had was in Edith’s boy.

He was the pride and plaything of both father and mother so long as he was good; and when he was good, he was displayed like a new ornament—blue sash, smooth hair, a little polished creature to be admired. But he had a will of his own, and when that will burst out, it came with a stormy passion that made the room echo and the servants freeze in the doorway. Edith would sink back as if struck, exhausted before she began to strive, and sigh—

“Oh dear, what shall I do with him! Do, Margaret, please ring the bell for Hanley.”

Margaret almost liked him better then, in those red-faced declarations of self, than in his tame, ribboned moods. She would carry him away into a room apart, where the battle could be fought without an audience. There, in the thick quiet broken by sobs and stamping, she would meet his rage with a firm steadiness that did not fear noise, yet did not answer it with noise. She would hold him, speak to him, sometimes say nothing at all until the storm began to exhaust itself; and then, with sudden little charms—some swift story, some change of tone, some play that turned his attention without bribing him—she would coax him back to peace on the side of right.

At last he would rub his hot, tear-smeared face over hers, kissing and clinging as if love were a kind of surrender; and often he fell asleep in her arms or on her shoulder, his breath evening out, the small sounds of distress changing into the steady, animal assurance of rest.

Those were Margaret’s sweetest moments. In them there was a taste of something she believed would be denied her for ever—a fulness that was more than duty, a tenderness with roots.

Into this household life Mr. Henry Lennox came often, and his presence altered the air as a sharper seasoning alters a dish that has grown bland. Margaret found him colder than formerly, if more brilliant; yet there were strong intellectual tastes in him, and much knowledge, and that gave flavour to conversation that otherwise would have been thin enough.

He looked—Margaret could not help seeing it—with a slight contempt upon his brother and sister-in-law, upon their way of spending time as if it were something to be killed gently between visits and dinners. Once or twice he spoke to his brother, in Margaret’s hearing, in a tone edged like a carving-knife, asking whether Captain Lennox meant entirely to relinquish his profession.

And when the Captain answered, contentedly, that he had quite enough to live upon, Mr. Lennox’s lip curled.

“And is that all you live for?”

Yet the brothers were attached in their fashion: the cleverer always leading, the other patient enough to be led, as cattle follow a familiar hand. Mr. Lennox himself was pushing hard on in his own profession, cultivating connections with a profound calculation. He was keen-sighted, far-seeing, intelligent, sarcastic, and proud; he moved among people as if he were always measuring their value, and could not forgive those who did not measure up.

Since that one long conversation with him—about Frederick’s affairs, on the first evening when Mr. Bell had been present—Margaret had had little intercourse with Mr. Lennox beyond what their common nearness in Edith’s house brought about. Yet it was enough to wear off shyness on her side, and to smooth away, on his, any remaining look of wounded vanity.

They met continually; but Margaret thought he avoided being alone with her. Perhaps he too knew that they had drifted far from where they had once seemed moored, side by side—not only in opinions, but in taste itself, in the very instinct of what made life savoury.

And yet, when he had spoken unusually well, when some epigram of his struck the table with a clean ring like a well-placed knife, she would see his eye seek her face first—only for an instant, but unmistakably—as if he waited for her to translate his cleverness into approval. In the family talk that constantly threw them together, her opinion was the one he listened for with a deference the more complete because he concealed it, and paid it as if against his will.

So the days went on: domestic, orderly, outwardly quiet. But in Margaret’s mind the past and the possible future kept stirring like leaven—Milton with its harsh music of wheels and voices; Spain with its imagined sun and foreign speech; and, between them, the unspoken explanation meant for one man’s ear alone, held back by tenderness, restraint, and time.

The dinners in Harley Street had a settled order, as regular as the striking of a well-wound clock. Mrs. Lennox provided the handsome room and the glittering appointments; her friends brought their beauty and their airy assurance; Captain Lennox, with his practised, agreeable intelligence, carried the talk lightly over politics and campaigns as if they were maps unrolled upon the table; while Mr. Henry Lennox, and the younger men who came in his train, supplied the sparkle—wit cut fine as lemon-peel, cleverness shaved to a translucent thinness, and learning worn so deftly that it never seemed a burden, only a brilliant accessory.

Margaret sat amongst them as one sits at a feast where every dish is contrived for show rather than nourishment. She had known, in her childhood, what it was to watch an old servant lift a lid and let out a wholesome steam—her mother’s broth, plain but restorative; she had known the honest country silence between spoonfuls, broken only by the small domestic sounds that make a meal feel like shelter: the clink of china, the soft scrape of a chair, the steady tick that seemed to measure safety. Here, the very talents of the company were served up as confections for admiration. Every feeling, every acquisition—nay, even every tendency towards virtue—was turned into fireworks. The hidden sacred fire that should have warmed and steadied life spent itself in sparkle and crackle, leaving no embers for solitude.

They talked of art as if it were only colour laid thick, as if the value of a picture lay solely in the sheen of its surface and the immediate sweetness to the eye. They whipped themselves into enthusiasm before witnesses, and when the room emptied and the lamps were turned down, they had no hunger left for the subject. They had squandered their capability of appreciation into a mere flow of the right phrases—fine words, like elaborate garnishes that smell of nothing and feed no one.

One evening, after the gentlemen had come up into the drawing-room, Mr. Lennox drew near to Margaret and spoke to her with something like intention—almost the first voluntary words he had offered since her return to live in his mother’s house.

“You did not look pleased at what Shirley was saying at dinner.”

“Didn’t I?” said Margaret, startled into a smile that did not soften her. “My face must be very expressive.”

“It always was. It has not lost the trick of being eloquent.”

“I did not like,” she answered hastily, “his way of advocating what he knew to be wrong—so glaringly wrong—even in jest.”

“But it was very clever,” said he, leaning upon the word as if cleverness were absolution. “How every word told! Did you remember the happy epithets?”

“Yes.”

“And despise them, you would like to add. Pray don’t scruple, though he is my friend.”

“There!” Margaret broke off, the blood rising hotly into her cheeks. “That is the exact tone in you, that—” She could not complete the sentence. It was as if the very language she must use had been taken from her and turned into something too sharp to hold. She turned away, and yet, before she had wholly withdrawn herself, she heard him speak again—low, clear, and for once unadorned.

“If my tones, or modes of thought, are what you dislike, will you do me the justice to tell me so, and so give me the chance of learning to please you.”

The words, for all their humility, carried power in them—the power of one who believes himself entitled to request a verdict, and to offer amendment upon his own terms. Margaret’s heart contracted with a distaste she could not easily translate into the neat speech this house prized. She felt, too, that the very cadence of the room—the laughter that never quite sank into silence, the continuous rustle and ring—shaped thought itself. One could hardly hear one’s own conscience in such a climate of sound.

Weeks went by, and there was no intelligence of Mr. Bell’s going to Milton. At Helstone he had spoken of it as a journey he might have to take very soon; but now it seemed he must have transacted his business by writing. Margaret had long thought—had long known—that if he could avoid going to a place he disliked, he would. She, with her private need, her secret importance attached to an explanation that could only be given face to face, understood too well how little weight her urgency must have seemed beside his aversion. He would do what he believed necessary; but whether in summer, autumn, or winter could signify very little to him.

It was now August. No mention came of the Spanish journey he had once alluded to in Edith’s hearing; and Margaret tried to school herself into accepting the fading away of that hope, as one watches a fragrance slip from a room when the door has been left open too long.

Then, one morning, a letter arrived in Mr. Bell’s hand. Next week he meant to come up to town; he wanted to see her about a plan he had in his head; and, moreover, he intended to treat himself to a little doctoring, as he had begun to come round to her opinion—that it would be pleasanter to think that his health was more in fault than his temper, when he found himself irritable and cross.

There was a forced cheerfulness in the lines—Margaret noticed it afterwards, as one recalls an odd aftertaste only when the meal is over. At the moment Edith’s exclamations filled the room.

“Coming up to town! Oh dear! and I am so worn out by the heat that I don’t believe I have strength enough in me for another dinner. Besides, everybody has left but our dear stupid selves, who can’t settle where to go to. There would be nobody to meet him.”

“I’m sure he would much rather come and dine with us quite alone than with the most agreeable strangers you could pick up,” said Margaret. “Besides, if he is not well he won’t wish for invitations. I am glad he has owned it at last. I was sure he was ill from the whole tone of his letters, and yet he would not answer me when I asked him, and I had no third person to whom I could apply for news.”

“Oh! he is not very ill, or he would not think of Spain.”

“He never mentions Spain.”

“No! but his plan that is to be proposed evidently relates to that. But would you really go in such weather as this?”

“Oh, it will get cooler every day. Yes! Think of it.” Margaret’s voice shook with a kind of shame at its own eagerness. “I am only afraid I have thought and wished too much—in that absorbing wilful way which is sure to be disappointed—or else gratified, to the letter, while in the spirit it gives no pleasure.”

“But that’s superstitious, I’m sure, Margaret.”

“No, I don’t think it is. Only it ought to warn me, and check me from giving way to such passionate wishes. It is a sort of ‘Give me children, or else I die.’ I’m afraid my cry is, ‘Let me go to Cadiz, or else I die.’”

“My dear Margaret! You’ll be persuaded to stay there; and then what shall I do? Oh! I wish I could find somebody for you to marry here, that I could be sure of you!”

“I shall never marry.”

“Nonsense, and double nonsense! Why, as Sholto says, you’re such an attraction to the house, that he knows ever so many men who will be glad to visit here next year for your sake.”

The words were lightly spoken; yet Margaret felt them like a hand laid upon her, turning her from a person into a commodity, a pleasant inducement. She drew herself up.

“Do you know, Edith, I sometimes think your Corfu life has taught you—”

“Well!”

“Just a shade or two of coarseness.”

Edith’s face crumpled; she began to sob in a frightened, childish way, declaring vehemently that Margaret had lost all love for her, that she no longer looked upon her as a friend. The sound of Edith’s crying filled the room, displacing any rational order, as loud music drives out thought. Margaret, stung by her own wounded pride and then remorseful at having struck so sharply, ended by yielding—by being Edith’s slave for the rest of the day. Edith lay like a victim on the sofa, heaving a profound sigh from time to time, until at last she fell asleep, exhausted by her own emotion and the attention it drew.

Mr. Bell did not make his appearance even on the day to which he had, for a second time, deferred his visit.

The next morning, at breakfast, a letter came from Wallis, his servant. Margaret’s hand, reaching for it, was steady; her face, as she read, turned suddenly white, as if all warmth had been withdrawn at once.

Wallis wrote that his master had not been feeling well for some time, which had been the true reason of his putting off his journey; and that at the very time when he should have set out for London, he had been seized with an apoplectic fit. It was, Wallis added, the opinion of the medical men that he could not survive the night; and more than probable that by the time Miss Hale received the letter, his poor master would be no more.

Margaret read to the end without a word. Then she placed the paper silently into Edith’s hands and left the room.

Edith, reading, gave a little cry and began to weep—sobbing, frightened, bewildered by the near approach of death as by an unfamiliar taste too strong upon the tongue. Her husband was distressed, and tried to soothe her; Mrs. Shaw, breakfasting in her own room, had to be told. It seemed to Edith, above all, monstrous that a man who was to have dined with them that day should instead be lying dead or dying. It brought the idea of mortality into her pretty, carefully arranged life like an unexpected loud sound in a delicate piece of music.

Only after a while did she remember Margaret. Then she started up and ran upstairs.

In Margaret’s room Dixon was packing a few toilette articles with quick, practised motions; Margaret, shedding tears continually, was putting on her bonnet in such haste that her hands trembled and she could scarcely tie the strings.

“Oh, dear Margaret! how shocking! What are you doing? Are you going out? Sholto would telegraph, or do anything you like.”

“I am going to Oxford,” said Margaret. The words came with the simplicity of necessity. “There is a train in half-an-hour. Dixon has offered to go with me, but I could have gone by myself. I must see him again. Besides, he may be better, and want some care. He has been like a father to me. Don’t stop me, Edith.”

“But I must. Mamma won’t like it at all. Come and ask her about it, Margaret. You don’t know where you’re going. I should not mind if he had a house of his own; but in his Fellow’s rooms! Come to mamma, and do ask her before you go. It will not take a minute.”

Margaret yielded—her habitual deference catching her at the very edge of action—and so she lost her train.

In the suddenness of the event Mrs. Shaw became bewildered and hysterical, and precious time slipped away in exclamations, in questions of what “people” would say, in fluttered directions that led nowhere. At length it was found there was another train in a couple of hours; and after various discussions on propriety and impropriety, it was decided that Captain Lennox should accompany Margaret—the one point on which she remained constant being her resolution to go, alone or otherwise, by the next train.

Her father’s friend—her own friend—was lying at the point of death. The thought came upon her with such vividness that she was surprised herself at the firmness with which she asserted, quietly but immovably, something of her right to act. And five minutes before the time of starting she found herself seated in a railway carriage opposite Captain Lennox.

The railway had its own harsh breath and metallic clamour: the shriek of the whistle, the thud and rush, the vibration that got into one’s bones. Margaret, who had so often felt the moral injury of Milton’s perpetual din, listened now with a strange patience. In such moments, noise became merely a vehicle—an indifferent force carrying her towards what she must do. Captain Lennox spoke little; his composure was of a kind that could sleep when circumstances required it.

At Oxford, the end had come. Margaret had not reached him in time for any last words. Yet it was a comfort—grave, bitter, but real—to have gone, even if only to hear that he had died in the night.

She saw the rooms he had occupied—those scholar’s chambers where books and papers lay about with the quietness of a life lived in thought—and they became for ever after entwined in her memory with her father, and with the idea of the one cherished, faithful friend who had remained when so much had been taken away. She stood and looked around as if she could take the place into herself: the sober walls, the familiar chair, the table at which he must have sat; and all the while it seemed to her that the true language of grief could not be spoken aloud in any dialect she possessed. There are experiences that refuse translation—not into another tongue only, but into any public form at all.

They had promised Edith, before starting, that if all had ended as they feared they would return to dinner. So that long, lingering look had to be interrupted; a quiet farewell had to be taken of the kind old face that had so often lighted at the sight of her, full of pleasant words, merry quips and cranks, as if cheerfulness were a dish he could always set before those he loved. Margaret bent to the stillness, and in her heart thanked God that He had spared the old man a long or painful illness.

On the journey home Captain Lennox fell asleep. The carriage rocked; the wheels beat out their relentless measure. Margaret could cry at leisure, unseen and unobserved, and let memory return in waves—Helstone’s green hush, her father’s voice, the gentler music of a life before this fatal year. No sooner did she grow fully aware of one loss than another seemed to come—not to supersede her grief, but to re-open wounds scarcely healed.

Yet when they arrived, when she heard again the tender voices of her aunt and Edith, when merry little Sholto’s glee rang out at her coming, and she saw the well-lighted rooms—Edith pretty in her paleness, eager, sorrowful, full of a softened attention—Margaret roused herself from a heavy trance of almost superstitious hopelessness. Even here, amid all that was shallow and all that was kind, joy and gladness might still gather, as warmth gathers about a hearth.

She took Edith’s place upon the sofa. Sholto was taught to carry Aunt Margaret’s cup of tea very carefully to her, his small hands intent upon the duty. The familiar domestic sounds—the teaspoon’s faint tap, the soft murmur of women’s voices, the child’s delighted exclamation—fell around her like a protecting cloth laid over a bare table. By the time she went upstairs to dress, her tears had not ceased, but her gratitude had found a place amongst them.

“And is not Margaret—” Edith began, whispering as though the very curtains might take offence at money spoken aloud. She had drawn her husband’s head down to her, standing on tiptoe with a conspirator’s tremor, “—the heiress?”

It was late; the lamps in their Oxford lodging had been lowered, and the house—tired with the solemn journey and the day’s constrained sorrow—settled into that thin night-silence in which every sound is magnified: a coal shifting in the grate, a distant footstep on boards, the soft sigh of wind against the sash.

Captain Lennox, roused from his half-doze, looked blankly at her; his mind, trained to winds and charts, had never kept a ledger of College Fellows’ fortunes.

“If I ever heard it, I’ve forgotten it,” he said. “And what can a Fellow of a small College leave? Not much, I should think. Your cousin never cost him wine, did she? Two hundred and fifty a year is something ridiculous to make a romance out of.”

Edith dropped down from her tiptoes with the faintest air of a heroine whose chapter has been mislaid. A whole little castle of imagination—Margaret poor, Margaret noble in poverty, Margaret to be consoled by Edith’s lavish pity—collapsed into common brick.

But Edith’s nature could not keep long to disappointment; it sprang back like a child’s india-rubber ball. A week after, she came in upon her husband with a rustle and a low, theatrical curtsey, her eyes bright with the relish of being right.

“I am right, and you are wrong, most noble Captain. Margaret has had a lawyer’s letter. She is residuary legatee—the legacies are about two thousand pounds, and the remainder about forty thousand, at the present value of property in Milton.”

“Forty thousand!” He sat up now. “And how does she take it?”

“Oh! as if she’d known it all her life—only she had no idea it was so much. She looks very white, and says she’s afraid of it; but that’s nonsense, you know, and will soon go off. I left mamma pouring congratulations down her throat, and stole away to tell you.”

After that, by a sort of family instinct, it was taken for granted that Mr. Henry Lennox must become, as it were, the steward of this unexpected abundance. Margaret’s ignorance of business was complete; the names of deeds and settlements, the very sound of legal phrases, had to her the same meaning as a foreign tongue heard too quickly—heavy syllables, authority without comprehension. So Henry chose out her attorney; he brought her papers, smoothed them, pointed to where her hand must go, and was never so well pleased as when he could translate the mysteries of property into tidy clauses and orderly consequences.

Edith watched those long consultations with the mischievous satisfaction of one who believes life exists chiefly to arrange itself into pleasing pairs.

“Henry,” she said one day, archly, “do you know what I hope and expect all these conversations with Margaret will end in?”

“I don’t,” he answered, colouring in spite of himself; and then, with the stiffness of a man who feels himself observed, “and I desire you not to tell me.”

“Oh, very well! Then I need not tell Sholto not to ask Mr. Montagu so often to the house.”

“Just as you choose,” he said, forcing an indifferent tone. “What you are thinking of may or may not happen; but this time, before I commit myself, I will see my ground clear. Ask whom you please. And—” he added, with a sudden flash of irritation at her meddling—“it may not be very civil, Edith, but if you meddle in it you will mar it. She has been very farouche with me for a long time, and is only just beginning to thaw a little from her Zenobia ways. She has the making of a Cleopatra in her, if only she were a little more pagan.”

“For my part,” said Edith, with a small malicious pleasure, “I am very glad she is a Christian. I know so very few!”

There was no Spain for Margaret that autumn. She held to the hope till it frayed into threads—some lucky turn, some summons that should call Frederick to Paris, whither she might go with an excuse, and a convoy, and the whole terrible sweetness of seeing him safely. But the days moved on with their ordinary punctuality, and nothing came. Instead of Cadiz and orange-scented nights, she had to content herself with Cromer.

Aunt Shaw and the Lennoxes were bound thither; they had wished Margaret to accompany them from the first, and with their kind, languid temper they made no eager effort to forward her own separate wish. Perhaps Cromer was, in one sense, the best. Her body needed bracing, and her mind needed a place where it might fall silent without being chidden into cheerfulness.

The hope that had most persistently haunted her—quietly, like a sound below hearing—was that Mr. Bell would have told Mr. Thornton the simple facts which had gone before that miserable accident in the station-yard: what had driven her, what had tempted her, why she had done as she did. Whatever judgement Mr. Thornton now held—however altered from what he had once believed—she had longed that it should be founded on truth. It would have been a kind of rest, a small clean hearth in the middle of so much cold misunderstanding.

But Mr. Bell was dead; and with him went the one possible channel for that plain, honourable explanation. Time had slid too far; the story could not be spoken now without seeming to be an excuse, a bid for pity, a stirring of ashes that ought to lie. She must submit, like many another, to be misread. She could reason herself into accepting that this, too, was a common lot; yet her heart ached no less with the craving that some day—years hence, if need be, but before he died—he might know how near she had been to falling, and yet how she had stood.

She told herself she did not need to hear that he understood, if only she could be sure that he would. But that, too, was vain, like so many wishes that rise warmly within us and then are dashed down by the mere weight of circumstance. When she had schooled herself to the conviction that there was no help to be looked for here, she turned, with all her heart and strength, to the life immediately before her, and resolved to strive to make the best of it.

At Cromer she sat long upon the beach. The sea there was not a picture; it was an occupation, a continual labour. Wave after wave came in, combed itself into foam, and worried the pebbly shore with a patient, perpetual insistence, as if it would grind every stone into a smoother truth. If she looked farther out, there was the broad heave and glitter that met the sky, as if the world’s edge were always being renewed. And through it all ran sound—the long inhaling and exhaling of water, the sudden hard clatter of pebbles sucked back, the hush that followed, the returning rush. It was an “eternal psalm,” not in words that could be translated into any dominion of speech, but in that older language which enters the nerves and settles the heart without asking permission.

She heard it, and yet was hardly conscious of hearing; it came to her like breath comes—necessary, unnoticed till it fails. In Milton, sound had been a tyranny: iron ringing on iron, wheels screaming on stone, a ceaseless commercial clamour that pressed upon the mind as a hand upon the mouth. Here the sound did not command; it accompanied. It did not thrust itself into her thoughts; it washed round them, and in that washing soothed without arguing, eased without explaining. She began to feel—dimly at first—that the very kind of noise a place breeds enters into the kind of person one is allowed to become.

Often she sat on the ground, her hands clasped round her knees, while her aunt Shaw did her small shoppings in the little town, and Edith and Captain Lennox rode far and wide along the shore and inland lanes. Nurses sauntered past with their charges; the children’s voices came and went like little flutes, and the women glanced at Margaret, whispering their wonder at the young lady who could look so long at nothing but water.

When they gathered at dinner-time, Margaret’s silence was so deep and absently sustained that Edith declared her “moped,” and with great satisfaction hailed her husband’s proposal that Mr. Henry Lennox should be invited down for a week, on his return from Scotland in October.

Yet those hours were not lost. The sea’s uncommercial music—so unlike the jangling engines and shouted reckonings of Milton—made room in her for a new ordering of memory. Events took their right places, not as she had suffered them in the moment, but as they had grown from causes, and as they might bear upon her future. Anyone with the perception to read a face could have seen something altering in hers: a quietness, not of indifference, but of settled strength; light, not of gaiety, but of a mind that has found where to stand.

Henry Lennox was struck by it at once. The first evening after his arrival, she left the room; he watched her go with an attention too practised to be merely casual.

“The sea has done Miss Hale an immense deal of good, I should fancy,” he said.

“That’s the bonnet I got her!” cried Edith, triumphantly. “I knew it would suit her the moment I saw it.”

“I beg your pardon,” said Henry, in the half-contemptuous, half-indulgent tone he used to Edith’s pretty certainties. “But I believe I know the difference between the charms of a dress and the charms of a woman. No mere bonnet would have made Miss Hale’s eyes so lustrous and yet so soft, or her lips so ripe and red—and her face altogether so full of peace and light.” Then, lowering his voice, as if naming Helstone were a thing to be touched reverently: “She is like, and yet more—like the Margaret Hale of Helstone.”

From that time the clever, ambitious man bent all his powers to gaining her. He loved her beauty; but he loved, too, the latent sweep in her mind, which he believed could be turned—gently, skilfully—towards the objects he had set his heart on. Her fortune was part of the completeness of her position; he did not pretend to himself that it was nothing, and he saw clearly what rise it would immediately enable him, the poor barrister, to take. Later he would earn such success, such honours, as would enable him to repay—handsomely—the first advance which he should owe to her.

He had been to Milton on business connected with her property on his return from Scotland; and with the quick eye of a lawyer trained to weigh contingencies, he had seen additional value accruing year by year to the lands and tenements she owned in that thriving, increasing town. He was glad, too, to find that the present relation between them—client and adviser—was gradually superseding the recollection of that unlucky, mismanaged day at Helstone. In this guise he had unusual opportunities of intimate intercourse besides those which arose naturally from the family connection.

Margaret, for her part, was only too willing to listen while he spoke of Milton. He had seen none of the people she most cared for; yet the mere name of the place, the mere calling up of its streets and air, stirred her more than Edith’s lively chatter or her aunt’s languid comments could stir her. It had been the tone with Mrs. Shaw and Edith to speak of Milton with dislike and contempt—just such feelings as Margaret was ashamed to remember she herself had once expressed when she first went to live there, shrinking from its smoke as from a stain.

But Henry Lennox almost exceeded Margaret in his appreciation of Milton and its inhabitants. Their energy, their power, their indomitable courage in struggling and fighting—their lurid vividness of existence—captivated and arrested him. He could not tire of describing it: the town’s unceasing pulse, the hard-driven days, the sense of lives measured in hours and output, in contracts and markets. Yet he had not, until Margaret pointed it out with candid pain even amid her gratification, perceived how selfish and material were too many of the ends proposed as the reward of all that mighty endeavour—how the very words men used for success had been narrowed till they could name only gain. It was, she told him, the tainting sin in much that was noble.

Still, when other subjects fell flat upon her, and her answers grew brief, Henry discovered that any enquiry into some Darkshire peculiarity of character, any mention of Milton’s temper and speech, called back the light into her eyes and the glow into her cheek. It was as if that harsh, unmusical town had left in her an inner hearing—trained by suffering to catch meanings beneath rough sounds—and as if, for all her criticism of its noise and greed, she could not help honouring the force of its living.

When they returned to town, Margaret fulfilled one of her seaside resolves and took her life into her own hands.

Before Cromer she had been as docile to her aunt’s laws as if she were still the frightened child who cried herself to sleep that first night in the Harley Street nursery. But the solemn hours by the sea had taught her that she must one day answer for her own life and what she had done with it. She tried, steadily and humbly, to settle that most difficult problem for a woman—how much is to be merged in obedience to authority, and how much may be set apart for freedom in working.

Mrs. Shaw was good-tempered; Edith had inherited that charming domestic quality; Margaret herself had probably the worst temper of the three, for her quick perceptions and over-lively imagination made her hasty, and her early isolation from sympathy had made her proud. Yet there was in her an indescribable childlike sweetness of heart, which made her manners, even in her rare wilful moods, irresistible once. Now, chastened even by what the world called her good fortune, she charmed her reluctant aunt into acquiescence with her will. She gained, quietly and firmly, the acknowledgment of her right to follow her own ideas of duty.

“Only don’t be strong-minded,” pleaded Edith. “Mamma wants you to have a footman of your own; and I’m sure you’re very welcome, for they’re great plagues. Only to please me, darling, don’t go and have a strong mind; it’s the only thing I ask. Footman or no footman, don’t be strong-minded.”

“Don’t be afraid, Edith. I’ll faint on your hands at the servants’ dinner-time the very first opportunity; and then, what with Sholto playing with the fire and the baby crying, you’ll begin to wish for a strong-minded woman, equal to any emergency.”

“And you’ll not grow too good to joke and be merry?”

“Not I. I shall be merrier than I have ever been, now I have got my own way.”

“And you’ll not go a figure, but let me buy your dresses for you?”

“Indeed I mean to buy them for myself. You shall come with me if you like; but no one can please me but myself.”

“Oh! I was afraid you’d dress in brown and dust-colour, not to show the dirt you’ll pick up in all those places. I’m glad you’re going to keep one or two vanities, just by way of specimens of the old Adam.”

“I am going to be just the same, Edith, if you and my aunt could but fancy so. Only, as I have neither husband nor child to give me natural duties, I must make myself some—in addition to ordering my gowns.”

In the little family conclave—Edith, her mother, and Captain Lennox—it was decided that perhaps all these plans of Margaret’s would only secure her the more for Henry Lennox. They kept her out of the way of other friends who might have offered eligible sons or brothers; and it was agreed, too, that she never seemed to take much pleasure in any society but Henry’s, out of their own family circle. Other admirers, attracted by her appearance or by the rumour of her fortune, were swept aside by her unconscious, smiling disdain into the paths frequented by beauties less fastidious or heiresses with a heavier weight of gold.

So Henry and Margaret grew, slowly, into closer intimacy; but neither he nor she were people to brook the slightest notice of their proceedings. Outside, London made its usual noises—wheels, calls, the endless bargaining of lives—while within, something quieter and more fateful was being kneaded and shaped, as silently as bread rises in a covered bowl: fed by time, by habit, by what was spoken and what remained untranslatable, lying under the common words they used.

All the while, Milton went on as it had always gone on—up and down, up and down—only now the fall seemed longer, the lift harder bought.

The chimneys wrote their sooty scripture across a low, wintry sky. The mills’ breath came in harsh gusts; steam hissed, iron clashed, belts slapped and worried at their wheels. The town’s very air tasted of coal-dust and damp cotton-fibre; it furred the tongue, it dried the throat, it clung to hair and sleeve as if Milton would mark a man for its own. And under that roof of noise—loom-thunder, engine-beat, the shriek of some ungreased axle crying for mercy—men moved with faces tightened into one question.

In the streets there were no saunterers. Even the costermongers, usually ready with a jest and a bell-like cry, pitched their voices lower, as if the town itself required quiet to listen for news. In the Mart, in the Exchange, talk did not bloom and meander; it snapped and struck like flint. Credit was thin as skim-milk; one splash of bad tidings and it curdled. A failure in a great shipping-house far away could be heard here as plainly as a crack in ice heard across a pond: one fissure, and all the frozen surface began to web with danger.

“Hitherto none in Milton,” men said, as if naming a charm; and yet they spoke with that caution that makes a rumour the more terrifying—dwelling on who was safe, and leaving who was not to be understood in the pause between words. Idle breath could topple a house in such weather; one firm going down dragged others after it, as a sinking cart draws the traces and the load.

“Thornton is safe,” they repeated—some with conviction, some with envy. His business had been large, and he had grown it, season by season, with a boldness that looked like prudence because it had been fortunate.

But there was always someone to stoop closer, to turn his head so his words fell into an ear, not the room.

“Large, ay,” murmured Mr. Harrison, who had inherited his father’s trade-made money and lived as if change were a sin. “But he’s spent his profits in stretching it. He’s no capital laid by. His machinery’s new within two years, and cost him—well!—a word to the wise.”

And folk called Harrison a croaker and went their way, because a croaker is useful only when he is wrong.

Yet John Thornton was hard pressed.

What touched him most sharply was not the mere ache of figures—though they ached like toothache, always returning—but the bruise upon that pride which had been the spine of him. He had built himself, stone by stone, out of poverty and discipline, out of a mother’s stern affection and a boy’s early knowledge that the world does not nurse the weak. Commerce, to him, had once seemed a grand, clean engine: put in courage, honesty, endurance, and it yielded power; a man’s name, spoken in distant ports where his face would never be known, could pass like good coin. He had begun with the hunger to be such a name—printed, repeated, trusted—head of a firm that would run on into generations.

His mother had fed that hunger with Scripture spoken like a trumpet: “Her merchants be like princes.” It had sounded to her like a promise addressed to her boy.

For years he had been alive to the far-off and dead to the near. He had desired influence abroad, and had scarcely perceived, close at hand, the lives that moved beside his own—parallel, near enough to touch, yet never touching—until, by what looked like accident, Higgins had come into his path, not at first as workman and master, but as man and man. That was the fine point of a wedge driven into an old timber. Once you hear another human heart beating close to your own, you cannot go back to imagining the world is made of classes and contracts only.

Lately, and too late, Thornton had felt something new: not merely the pride of a manufacturer, but an interest in his very place in Milton because it brought him into contact—direct, daily—with people sharp, stubborn, ignorant sometimes, but vivid with character and feeling. He had begun to plan—small experiments, tender things to his mind, the kind of changes that do not show in a ledger at once, but might alter the air between men. And now the dread of losing that—of having those plans cut off like green shoots by a late frost—gave a keener edge to his fear.

For the frost had come.

The strike a year and a half ago—long enough ago that it ought to have been folded away as the past, and yet it lived still, like a debt of time—had stopped his work in the middle of large contracts. He had locked capital into new machinery, bright steel and cunning gearing that had eaten money as a hungry horse eats oats. He had bought cotton heavily to fulfil orders taken under bond. When labour failed him, he had brought in Irish hands; but their want of skill had spoiled much work, damaging goods that his house could not, for pride’s sake, send out as first-rate.

For months the strike had been a stone in his shoe. When his glance fell on Higgins he sometimes felt a quick flare of resentment rise, hot and useless, without any present cause, merely because Higgins’s face called up the remembered injury. Thornton, ashamed of that, had curbed himself. It was not enough to avoid the man; he must prove mastery over himself by admitting him—by letting Higgins come when rules allowed, as if to say, I will not be ruled by a grudge.

And gradually resentment fell away, replaced by a kind of astonishment: how could two men—both living by the same trade, both labouring toward the same object—see duty and right in such utterly different lights? Out of that wonder had grown a rough intercourse that did not promise the end of all conflict, but promised something better: charity in the midst of conflict, patience where there had been hard contempt.

They had learned facts from each other too—the sort of facts no one tells you until you care.

Then trade turned, as it turns, with a cruel quietness.

The market fell and the value of Thornton’s stocks fell with it to near half. Orders dried up. The new machinery stood, not earning interest but demanding it; money went out in wages and coal and oil while money did not come in. Payments for completed orders were slow, evasive; he had to press, and hated pressing. Bills fell due for the cotton he had bought when the world looked steadier. Money was scarce, and what could be borrowed came at an interest like a bite.

He could not realise property; he could not sell without losing; he could not hold without sinking. Yet he did not despair. He watched, calculated, foresaw, provided—day and night, as if he could outwork misfortune. At home he was as gentle as ever with the women—his mother, his sister—keeping his voice even, his manners unaltered, as if manners could keep a roof from leaking. In the mill he spoke few words; but the men knew him now. A curt command did not sting as it once would have stung; they heard behind it the press of care, and even sympathy began to grow where antagonism had smouldered.

One day Higgins heard a sharp inquiry—why had such an order not been obeyed?—and, passing near, caught the sound of a sigh, held down and yet unmistakable, as if the master’s breath had to push through iron.

“Th’ measter’s a deal to potter him,” Higgins muttered.

That night he and another man stayed beyond hours, unknown to anyone, to finish the neglected piece of work. Thornton never knew; he thought the overlooker had done it. The mill’s noise swallowed gratitude before it could be spoken; but there are kindnesses that do not need a name.

Another day Higgins, walking along Marlborough Street, saw Thornton coming in his quick, resolved stride, eyes set as if on figures no one else could see.

“Eh,” Higgins thought, “I reckon I know who’d ha’ been sorry for to see our measter sittin’ so like a piece o’ grey calico! Th’ oud parson would ha’ fretted his woman’s heart out, if he’d seen the woeful looks I’ve seen.”

He stopped Thornton with the blunt courage of one man to another.

“Measter.”

Thornton started, annoyed at being pulled from inward work, and looked up sharply.

“Have yo’ heerd aught of Miss Marget lately?”

“Miss—who?” Thornton asked; the question was almost harsh from habit.

“Miss Marget—Miss Hale—th’ oud parson’s daughter—yo’ known who I mean well enough—if yo’ll only think a bit—”

There was no insolence in the dialect; it was simply Higgins’s way of pushing through fog.

“Oh—yes!” Thornton’s face changed as if a door had opened and a warmer air had come in. The frost-bound look of care loosened; though his mouth stayed firm, his eyes softened and smiled out, unguarded, on the questioner.

“She’s my landlord now, you know, Higgins. I hear of her through her agent here, every now and then. She’s well—and among friends—thank you, Higgins.”

That “thank you” lingered with a heat that surprised even Higgins. It lit something in him—a will-o’-the-wisp of understanding, perhaps, but bright enough to follow.

“And she’s not getten married, measter?”

“Not yet.” The cloud returned as quickly as it had lifted. “There is some talk of it, as I understand, with a connection of the family.”

“Then she’ll not be for coming to Milton again, I reckon.”

“No,” said Thornton, and the single syllable had in it the sound of a door shutting.

“Stop a minute, measter.” Higgins stepped closer, dropping his voice into a confidential undertone. “Is th’ young gentleman cleared?” He added a knowing wink, which only made the matter more puzzling to Thornton.

“The young gentleman? What young gentleman?”

“Th’ young gentleman—I mean—Master Frederick, they ca’ed him—her brother as was over here, yo’ know.”

“Over here?” Thornton repeated, as if the phrase itself were foreign.

“Ay, to be sure—at th’ missus’s death. Yo’ need na be feared o’ my telling; for Mary and me, we knowed it all along, only we held our peace, for we got it through Mary workin’ i’ th’ house.”

Thornton’s heart gave a strange leap; his whole attention came, quick as a knife, to that one point.

“And he was over. It was her brother.”

“Sure enough. And I reckoned yo’ knowed it, or I’d never ha’ let on. Yo’ knowed she had a brother?”

“Yes,” Thornton said; his voice was controlled, but his face had a tense pallor under it. “I know all about him. And he was over at Mrs. Hale’s death?”

“Nay! I’m not goin’ for to tell more,” Higgins replied, suddenly cautious. “I’ve maybe getten them into mischief already, for they kept it very close. I nobbut wanted to know if they’d getten him cleared?”

“Not that I know of.” Thornton drew back into reserve, the old wall rising. “I know nothing. I only hear of Miss Hale now, as my landlord, and through her lawyer.”

With that he turned away—back to the business that had been driving him when Higgins first called—leaving Higgins baffled, the bright thread of his discovery snapping in his fingers.

But within Thornton the words kept sounding, steady as a footstep: It was her brother.

“I am glad,” he said to himself, alone in his own mind. “I may never see her again; but it is a comfort—a relief—to know that much. I knew she could not be unmaidenly; and yet I yearned for conviction. Now I am glad.”

It was a little golden thread laid across a dark cloth. He held it in thought as one might hold, in a hungry season, the memory of a dish that once warmed the house: not merely the taste, but the clatter of plates, the murmur of voices, the peace of familiar sounds. In Milton now there was little peace in any sound. The mills’ roar pressed into the brain; even when a man lay down, the engines seemed still to beat in his blood.

And the web darkened.

His agent had trusted largely a house engaged in American trade. That house went down, and others followed, tumbling like a pack of cards: the fall of one compelling the fall of the next. Each morning brought new names, new gaps, new tightening of lips. Thornton sat late—night after night—with books and papers spread before him in his private room, adding, subtracting, reckoning, as if the act of calculation might bend fate. He thought no one knew. He heard the household go to bed; he heard the house settle; he heard the wind probe at shutters and eaves; and still he sat, staring at figures until the figures blurred and seemed to swim like dark fish in a grey stream.

One morning, when daylight stole in thin and cold through the crevices of his shutters, he realised he had not been in bed at all. A hopeless indifference came over him: he could do without an hour’s rest. There would be no real rest anywhere.

Then the door opened.

His mother stood there, dressed as she had been the day before. She too had never lain down. Her face was cold, rigid, wan from watching—like a statue cut out of grief.

“Mother! why are you not in bed?”

“Son John,” she said, “do you think I can sleep with an easy mind while you keep awake full of care? You have not told me what your trouble is; but sore trouble you have had these many days past.”

“Trade is bad.”

“And you dread—” Her steady voice trembled in an unwonted way.

“I dread nothing,” he replied, drawing his head up erect, as if the very posture might ward off humiliation. “I know that no man will suffer by me. That was my anxiety.”

“But how do you stand? Shall you—will it be a failure?”

“Not a failure. I must give up business, but I pay all men. I might redeem myself—I am sorely tempted—”

“How?” she cried, advancing; her hand closed on his arm. Her eyes had an eager, almost fierce light. She held her breath to catch his answer. “How redeem it?”

“By a speculation offered to me—full of risk; but, if successful, placing me high above water-mark, so that no one need ever know the strait I am in. Still, if it fails—”

“And if it fails,” she said, leaning nearer, voice hushed with intensity.

“Honest men are ruined by a rogue,” he answered gloomily. “As I stand now, my creditors’ money is safe—every farthing of it; but I don’t know where to find my own—it may be all gone, and I penniless at this moment. Therefore it is my creditors’ money that I should risk.”

“But if it succeeded, they need never know,” she urged. “Is it so desperate a speculation? I am sure it is not, or you would never have thought of it. If it succeeded—”

“I should be a rich man,” he said, and there was iron in the words, “and my peace of conscience would be gone.”

“Why! You would have injured no one.”

“No; but I should have run the risk of ruining many for my own paltry aggrandisement.” He paused; then the decision, long shaped in him, came out with a strange gentleness. “Mother, I have decided. You won’t much grieve over our leaving this house, shall you, dear mother?”

“No!” she cried. “But to have you other than what you are will break my heart. What can you do?”

“Be always the same John Thornton in whatever circumstances,” he answered, and his voice for once let the tiredness show. “Endeavouring to do right, and making great blunders; and then trying to be brave in setting to afresh. But it is hard, mother. I have worked and planned. I have discovered new powers in my situation too late—and now all is over. I am too old to begin again with the same heart. It is hard, mother.”

He turned away and covered his face with his hands, as if to shut out dawn, shame, the whole world.

She stood, rigid with love and anger—anger not at him, but at the shape of things.

“I can’t think,” she said, the defiance in her tone like a clash of metal, “how it comes about. Here is my boy—good son, just man, tender heart—and he fails in all he sets his mind upon. He finds a woman to love, and she cares no more for his affection than if he had been a common man. He labours, and his labour comes to nought. Other people grow rich, and hold their paltry names high and dry above shame.”

“Shame never touched me,” he said low; but she went on as if she could not stop.

“I sometimes have wondered where justice was gone to, and now I don’t believe there is such a thing in the world—now you are come to this; you, my own John Thornton—though you and I may be beggars together—my own dear son!”

She fell upon his neck and kissed him through her tears. Her tears were hot and salt against his cheek; he held her gently, as if she were suddenly older than he had ever allowed himself to see.

“Mother,” he said, when she had wept herself into a quieter breath, “who has sent me my lot in life, both of good and evil?”

She shook her head. She would have nothing to do with religion just then; grief had made her proud again.

“Mother,” he persisted, and his voice had the strange simplicity of a boy asking for the old story he once loved, “I too have been rebellious; but I’m striving to be so no longer. Help me, as you helped me when I was a child. Then you said many good words—when my father died, and we were sometimes sorely short of comforts—which we shall never be now; you said brave, noble, trustful words then, mother, which I have never forgotten, though they may have lain dormant. Speak to me again in the old way, mother. Do not let us have to think that the world has too much hardened our hearts.”

“I have had a many,” she sobbed, “but none so sore as this. To see you cast down from your rightful place! I could say it for myself, John, but not for you. Not for you! God has seen fit to be very hard on you, very.”

Her old body shook with the convulsive sobs that come when age weeps—when tears are no longer a quick shower but a storm that threatens to break the heart’s roof. At last the stillness in the room struck her. She looked and saw her son collapsed by the table, his arms flung half across it, his head bent downwards.

“Oh, John!” she cried, and lifted his face.

The pallor on it was so strange, the gloom so set, that for an instant she thought death had come quietly to claim him. Then the rigidity melted; colour returned; his eyelids stirred; and he was himself again. In that moment, all mortification—houses, names, rank, money—fell away like husks. The great blessing was that he existed; that he was hers.

She thanked God for that, and for that alone, with a fervour that washed rebellion out of her like soot from a stone.

He did not speak much after. He went and opened the shutters, letting in the ruddy flood of dawn. It showed the room as it was—papers, ink, the hard corners of furniture; it showed, too, the thin grey outside and the east wind cutting like a knife. The cold had lasted for weeks. No one would buy light summer goods in such weather. Even hope of a quick revival of trade must be given up; the year itself seemed against them.

Yet there was comfort—stern comfort—in having spoken. They might keep silence henceforward about anxieties, but they understood each other now; if not in harmony, at least in one shared discord against misfortune.

Fanny’s husband was vexed at Thornton’s refusal to take a share in the speculative venture he had offered—vexed as men are who cannot forgive another for being honest in a way that reflects on themselves. He withdrew from any possibility of being supposed able to assist Thornton with ready money—money he indeed needed for his own venture.

And at last the thing Thornton had dreaded, and prepared for, came like the closing of a gate.

He must give up the business in which he had been so long engaged with honour and success. Marlborough Mills and the adjacent dwelling were held under a long lease; they must, if possible, be relet. He must look out for a subordinate situation—a word that tasted bitter, like burnt crust, in his mouth.

There were offers almost at once. Mr. Hamper would have been only too glad to secure Thornton as steady, experienced partner for his son, whom he was setting up with a large capital in a neighbouring town. But the young man was half-educated in information and wholly uneducated in any responsibility beyond getting money—brutal in pleasures and brutal in pains. Thornton saw at once that such a partnership would strangle what few plans survived the wreck—those plans not of profit but of governance, of better relation between master and man. He would sooner be only a manager, with a certain degree of power beyond mere money-getting, than share authority with a tyrannical moneyed partner whose humours would breed quarrel within months.

So he waited. He stood aside—profoundly humble now—as news swept through the Exchange of the enormous fortune his brother-in-law had made by his daring speculation. It ran through Milton for nine days like a tune everyone whistles, half admiring, half resentful. Success brought its worldly consequence: extreme admiration. Men who had sneered yesterday called the speculator wise and far-seeing today.

No one was considered so wise, so far-seeing, as Mr. Watson.

It was one of those London evenings when the heat lies over the squares like a lid, and even the plane-trees seem to hoard their breath. The house held its own small weather: a hush of shut blinds, the faint medicinal coolness of shaded passages, and—wherever Dixon had lately been—an undercurrent of lavender-water and starched linen, as if cleanliness were the only defence against summer.

Edith swept into Margaret’s bed-room in her first impatience of dressing, and then, for the second time, returned fully prepared for dinner, as though she could not bear to be alone with her own arrangements. At first the room was empty. When she came again, Dixon was there, laying Margaret’s gown across the bed with the careful, almost reverent smoothing of a woman who had handled fine fabric in many households and knew how much authority hid in a well-set fold. Margaret herself was nowhere.

Edith began to hover and pull at trifles the way some people worry a stitch.

“Oh, Dixon! not those horrid blue flowers with that dead gold-coloured gown. What taste! Wait—wait; I will bring you some pomegranate blossoms.”

“It’s not dead gold, ma’am,” returned Dixon, stiff with offence, without ceasing to pin and arrange. “It’s straw-colour. And blue always goes with straw-colour.”

But Edith had already gone, and was back before Dixon’s protest could gather itself into a sermon, carrying the scarlet cluster as if she had plucked it from a hotter country. The blossoms seemed to throw off a bitter, green-tinged perfume of broken stem, sharp as a knife on rind.

“There!” Edith cried, holding them up against the dress with the triumph of one who believes colour is argument. “Now—where is Miss Hale? I can’t think,” she went on, as she adjusted the garniture, “how my aunt allowed her to get into such rambling habits in Milton! I’m always expecting to hear of her having met with something horrible among those wretched places she pokes herself into. I should never dare go down some of those streets without a servant. They’re not fit for ladies.”

Dixon, still smarting under the slight to her “taste,” answered shortly, as if clipping her words to save them from further insult.

“It’s no wonder to my mind, when I hear ladies talk such a deal about ladies—and when they’re such fearful, delicate, dainty ladies too—I say it’s no wonder to me that there are no longer any saints on earth—”

“Oh, Margaret! here you are!” Edith broke in, for at that moment Margaret came in—her face warmed, as if she had been out under the brazen sky or had climbed too quickly. There was a little disarray about her, not of dress but of spirit, as though she had been called back from thought. “I have been so wanting you. How your cheeks are flushed with the heat, poor child! But only think what that tiresome Henry has done—really he exceeds brother-in-law’s limits. Just when my party was made up so beautifully—fitted in so precisely for Mr. Colthurst—there has Henry come, with an apology it is true, and making use of your name for an excuse, and asked me if he may bring that Mr. Thornton of Milton—your tenant, you know—who is in London about some law business. It will spoil my number, quite.”

The name, dropped so airily into the room, went through Margaret like a sudden bell heard close at hand. The very stillness behind Edith’s chattering seemed to fill with it. Dixon paused in her pinning as if listening, though her eyes stayed on the gown.

“I don’t mind dinner. I don’t want any,” said Margaret, and her voice came low, as if the heat had dried it. “Dixon can get me a cup of tea here, and I will be in the drawing-room by the time you come up. I shall really be glad to lie down.”

“No, no! that will never do. You do look wretchedly white, to be sure; but that is just the heat, and we can’t do without you possibly. Those flowers a little lower, Dixon. They look glorious flames, Margaret, in your black hair. You know we planned you to talk about Milton to Mr. Colthurst. Oh! to be sure! and this man comes from Milton. I believe it will be capital after all. Mr. Colthurst can pump him well on all the subjects he is interested in, and it will be great fun to trace out your experiences, and this Mr. Thornton’s wisdom, in Mr. Colthurst’s next speech in the House. Really, I think it is a happy hit of Henry’s. I asked him if he was a man one would be ashamed of; and he replied, ‘Not if you’ve any sense in you, my little sister.’ So I suppose he is able to sound his h’s, which is not a common Darkshire accomplishment—eh, Margaret?”

Margaret stood still while Dixon’s practised fingers settled the pomegranate blossoms into her hair. The scent rose up at each touch—red fruitiness without sweetness, a memory of bruised rind—and in that sharpness there was something that steadied her. She made herself ask, evenly:

“Mr. Lennox did not say why Mr. Thornton was come up to town? Was it law business connected with the property?”

“Oh! he’s failed, or something of the kind, that Henry told you of that day you had such a headache—what was it? There, that’s capital, Dixon. Miss Hale does us credit, does she not? I wish I was as tall as a queen, and as brown as a gipsy, Margaret.”

“But about Mr. Thornton?”

“Oh! I really have such a terrible head for law business. Henry will like nothing better than to tell you all about it. I know the impression he made upon me was, that Mr. Thornton is very badly off, and a very respectable man, and that I’m to be very civil to him; and as I did not know how, I came to you to ask you to help me. And now come down with me, and rest on the sofa for a quarter of an hour.”

Downstairs the house had begun to sound as if it were putting on its public voice: the soft thud of a door eased to, the discreet clink of glass, the murmur of servants in the corridor, and over it all the distant, steady rumble of London—wheels on paving-stones, the far cry of a street-seller, the faint metallic ring of a horse’s shoe striking curb. The city’s noise did not come to them as Milton’s did, close and insistent; here it was a backdrop, like sea heard from behind a wall, and it lent to every word spoken in drawing-room tones a kind of artificial importance.

Henry Lennox came early, as the privileged brother-in-law may. Margaret, with the pomegranate red burning at her temples, began at once, as soon as they were near enough to speak without Edith’s fluttering interruptions, to ask what she needed to know.

“He came up about this sub-letting the property—Marlborough Mills, and the house and premises adjoining, I mean,” said Mr. Lennox. “He is unable to keep it on; and there are deeds and leases to be looked over and agreements to be drawn up. I hope Edith will receive him properly; but she was rather put out, as I could see, by the liberty I had taken in begging for an invitation for him. But I thought you would like to have some attention shown him: and one would be particularly scrupulous in paying every respect to a man who is going down in the world.”

He had dropped his voice for Margaret’s ear, and the words “going down” were spoken with a delicacy that yet carried the faint triumph of the prosperous over the fallen. But before Margaret could answer, he sprang up, for their guest had entered.

Mr. Thornton came in with that self-command that seems at once a shield and a proclamation. It was more than a year since Margaret had seen him. He was still distinguished by his height and the easy power of his carriage; but his face had altered as stone alters under weather—sharper about the mouth, lined where there had been smoothness, with a look of being used to bracing the will against disappointment. Yet there was a composure upon him, something quiet and indestructible, that made the talk of his changed position seem to those who watched him like talk of an accident that could not touch the core of the man.

He looked round the room at once and saw Margaret. He had caught her intent listening posture while Mr. Lennox spoke; and he came up to her with the perfectly regulated manner of an old friend. At his first calm words a vivid colour flashed into Margaret’s cheeks, and did not leave them again all evening.

She did not say much. She asked him, quietly, almost coldly, questions about Milton and their old acquaintances—questions that seemed to him merely the necessary civilities. Others came in—people more intimate with the house than he—and he fell back, as if he had no claim to any nearer place. From time to time he and Mr. Lennox talked together with the constrained politeness of men who have measured each other.

“You think Miss Hale looking well,” said Mr. Lennox, watching him with the curiosity of one who likes to read effect. “Milton didn’t agree with her, I imagine; for when she first came to London, I thought I had never seen any one so much changed. To-night she is looking radiant. But she is much stronger. Last autumn she was fatigued with a walk of a couple of miles. On Friday evening we walked up to Hampstead and back. Yet on Saturday she looked as well as she does now.”

“We!” The syllable dropped into Mr. Thornton’s mind like a pebble into deep water, making circles he could not stop.

At dinner Mr. Colthurst—clever, quick-eyed, already gaining that authority in the House which comes not only from speaking but from being listened to—caught on to a remark Mr. Thornton made, and asked Edith who he was. Edith, rather to her surprise, found that Mr. Thornton’s name was not wholly unknown to him; the “Indeed!” with which he received it was charged with more meaning than she had expected.

Edith’s dinner went off well. Henry was in good humour, and his dry, caustic wit showed to advantage. Mr. Thornton and Mr. Colthurst found one or two mutual subjects, which they could only touch upon then, reserving them for the more confidential after-dinner talk that men take as naturally as wine. Margaret, with the pomegranate blossoms against her dark hair, looked beautiful; and if she leaned back in her chair and spoke little, Edith was not vexed, for the talk flowed without her, and she could enjoy her own success.

Margaret watched Mr. Thornton’s face. He never looked at her; so she could study him unobserved and mark what the short span of time and the heavy press of events had done. Only when Mr. Lennox threw out some unexpected mot, Mr. Thornton’s face flashed into the old look of intense enjoyment: the merry brightness returned to his eyes, the lips parted to suggest the brilliant smile of former days; and for an instant his glance, by instinct, sought Margaret’s, as though he wanted her sympathy as he used to.
